Kickstarter backer here. I've been playing this game since alpha.  It's a nice twist on the single screen arena genre.  Since both you and your opponents are invisible most of the time, it demands some effort to track your own position as you play, but the payoff when this becomes second nature is worth it. It's simple to grasp but has a high skill ceiling, and has become a lunchtime favourite on the office couch. The pixel graphics are a perfect homage to 16 bit 90s consoles with lush palettes, the maps are varied and full of detail and interesting features, and the sound design is deep and multilayered.

From does it again, with a terrible port.  Granted, not as terrible as the first game, but at least in the first game, controllers had a workable control setup from the START.  I started up this game, and it said Press A to continue.  I then discovered that on my Logitech xbox-type controller, it had decided that A was instead X, A was now B, and B was Y.  What the hell.  Then I sat through the intro cinematic to discover that right stick was not used to control the camera. It was used to control my items, weapons, and spells.  This confused me, because my left D-pad ALSO did that, and that left me with precisely zero ways to control the camera with my controller.  I then looked in the options, and found to no surprise, that controllers had no rebinding options.  Lovely.  So, I was forced to try mouse and keyboard.  What greeted me there was a quite bizzare control setup, and when I actually tried to rebind them, I found to my dismay that rather than having customizeable rebinds, they have a list of preset options, all of which are as awkward as each other.  If only my problems with the game ended when I cobbled together a somewhat workable control set.  No, now we move on to gameplay issues.
Every time you die, you lose a little bit of max health.  Talk about kicking the dog whilst it's down.  You end up with only half your health, unless you find a ring, so you can retain 75% of your health.  Now, combine that with the fact that you can be invaded whilst you are hollow.  Trying to get something done? Trying to figure out a difficult area on half maximum HP, making small progress?  Maybe you finally get past that difficult part you've been struggling with!  Too bad, because here comes xxGoatMasticatorxXx to come kill you, fully equipped, with perfect PVP gear and full health, and probably 99 full healing items because these games are notoriously easy to break in that way.  Enjoy Dark Souls 2 kicking you in the nuts over and over again while anyone who is DOING the kicking shouts at you "Get gooooood, ♥♥♥♥♥♥!" in lieu of an actual argument.
Absolutely not.

I first played Invisigun at PAX, and I loved it. I immediately went home and backed it on kickstarter so I could get it as soon as possible. I followed it intensely, and had a month where I was checking my email and the forums multiple times every day just so I could get even a scrap of news about it. As soon as I got it, I promptly annoyed my friends incessantly to play with me. Sadly, I ended up playing mostly with bots. :Neko: That was fine, though. Even with the three worlds that there were when I got it, there was still a ton to do. The game only went uphill from there. Much to my delight, the bots AI was improved immensely until they actually became as good as a real player. Two new planets were added, full of new mechanics. New heroes were added, and the gameplay was completely changed based on the discussions on the forums. This game kept getting better and better, and it won't stop now. The dev is one of the best I've seen, and sure knows how to make a great game. Honestly, this game coudld go down in history as one of the first and THE best to pull off "everyone is invisible." (A surprising amount of companies have started developing games shockingly similar to this. I think they can see how successful this game will be! :P) Without a doubt, I highly recommend this game.
I look forward to seeing you join us; we need some more people to play online with! :D
Note: on most of my games, I leave my computer running for weeks, so the hours are greatly exaggerated. This is not the case with Invisigun. Me and my friends have actually played almost 162 hours and I'm not tired of it yet! It looks like I never play this game, but don't be fooled. It's one of my all-time favorites.

I think of Victor Vran compared to Grim Dawn as "Bend the Bracket" to "The Red" (Chevelle for those unfamiliar).
For all the complexities, builds, and strategies that make Grim Dawn awesome, Victor Vran takes a very simplistic, yet satisfying approach to its leveling and loot.
There are no trees, many different pathways, all this complexity.  Every weapon has 3 attacks, that's it.  Those 3 attacks change depending on the weapon you use.
There is a bit of added complexity with transmuting, demon powers, and cards, but it is hardly the plethora of strategy that Grim Dawn offers.
But Victor Vran is still a great game and tons of fun.  But while Grim Dawn is best with a M+KB, Victor Vran is actually best played with a controller sitting back on the couch or a comfy computer chair.
One additional nice touch about it as well is the difficulty can be altered at any time by activating hexes, which affect your character or the enemies in different ways, and for each hex, you get 10% more experience.  So that adds a bit of unique flavor.
For $20, it's definitely worth the buy.
And buy Grim Dawn too if you haven't.

This game is definitely worth a look for anybody that likes competitive party-style games!
Take the 4-player single-screen chaos of Bomberman, add invisibility, stealth tactics, class-based abilities, tons of maps, lots of game modes, and now you're starting to get the picture.  Relatively easy to pick up, but has a high skill ceiling if you really get into it.
Unlike a lot of indie competitive games, it has support for bots AND multiplayer AND shared screen playing.  All in the same match, if you want!  And then there are single player challenges on top of that.  So no worries about buying a game that you can't play when nobody else is at your house!
There is also great music and awesome pixel art with tons of little details in the active environments that give other players away (footsteps, water splashes, moving cameras, opening doors, etc)...just tons of love and polish in every aspect!  And it all impacts the gameplay.
Disclaimer: I am a friend of the developer, and he is one of the nicest and most genuine guys you could ever meet, so my opinion may be biased.  I'm OK with that.  :)

"Sonic the HedgeGod"
- Jim Sterling
Or as I'd like to call it, mechanical satyr running simulator 2016. Personally, I like it just for the storyline and atmosphere it sets. It's a fascinating tale it spins of life, death, jealousy, human hubris, victory at all cost and love.  The music is top notch.
As for the mechanics? Not as satisfying as I had hoped. The game has a marvelous sense of movement. You really feel like you have mechanical legs, landing with a satisfying metal thud and leaping across hills, lakes and chasms is utterly exilerating, but there's very few situations where the game's marvelous sense of movement counts. 80% of the time in this already very short adventure, you're just trudging through bland rooms and while there are very memorable moments, god knows why the Dev didn't seek to repeat those more often. Furthermore, the shooting and enemy mechanics are non existant.
I'm absolutely torn between these two qualities and if I had the option, I'd leave this review without a negative or positive recommendation. As I'm forced to do so however, and the game stands at a 96% Steam approval rating at the time of this writing, which I think is too high for its flaws, I feel forced to give it a thumbs down.
What a tale though.

Valley is a fairly short (about 5 hours) first person... game... thing... It's kind of hard to pin it to an exact genre, but I suppose it's a mix between FPS and platformer.  It's probably not going to blow your mind, but I found it a lot of fun.  Basically, you're given a suit of power armor that has all kinds of weird abilities (like super fast running and jumping) and asked to traverse a bunch of levels with it.
If I had to pick one flaw, it would be the lack of difficulty.  This isn't really an issue for me, I don't mind "easy" games, but if you're looking for a challenge, this probably isn't going to provide it.  The shooting is pretty rudimentary and you get enough health upgrades to make most encounters fairly easy.  The platforming is also pretty easy, and though there are a few instant death pits that might get you, the penalty for dying is pretty light.
However, while it might not be super challenging, I thought it was pretty fun.  You're given enough abilities that make moving around the world feel exciting and interesting.  While the platforming didn't make me sweat, it did get me to say "wheeeee" a bunch of times.  It's hard to describe, but I defintitely found a lot to like in the movement mechanics in this game.
The story is decent, if a bit cliche.  The visuals can be surprisingly gorgeous at times, and the soundtrack is really nice as well.  The level design is kind of middling, sometimes being really exhilirating to move through but boring to look at, and sometimes being really pretty to look at but kind of tedious to actually traverse.  I did like the touch that allows you to choose if the main character is male or female; since the game is in first person, it doesn't change much aside from the  "oof" noises you make when you get hit, but it's a nice feature.
Overall, I really liked this one.  A surprisingly entertaining and polished title from a fairly small studio that had me grinning  every time I booted it up.

You are a street racer named Alex. You drive your brother to some guy, he is shot and killed, you get framed for the murder and are sent to jail.
5 years later, an FBI agent named Zoe gets you out and you have to take down the illegal street gang 'The 5-10s' while in the process proving dirty FBI agent Coburn guilty, and getting justice for your brother.

I am able to play on medium settings with no lag at 60-75 degrees celcius with my PC (specs below.)
Alright, this is the highlight of the game. The open world is huge, it's a scaled down version of the USA, but driving 250-300kmph it took me over an hour to get from Miami to Seattle. The world isn't the most detailed, but with the size of it, it doesn't matter. I will often just drive to waste time if I'm bored.
I play with an Xbox One remote, and the controls are, okay. It is an arcade game so it doesn't feel realistic in any way, the cars are a bit slippery, but once you get used to it or get upgrades it's fine.

This is part of the game I do not like. You'll be in a race and you'll be in first forever, and it will be kind of boring, then boom one mistake and then boom the AI's have caught up with you, I suspect there is some teleporting or speed boosts involved there.
There are also events where you must takedown an enemy vehicle, these are just trial and error, it's hard to predict where the enemy is going to go, and if you miss them you are taken off track and you've just lost your gold medal, speaking of medals, these are horrible. You do not get a gold medal for first place, no no no, you get it for getting a good time, this turns all the races into time trials with cars behind you.

It's really hard for me to give this a negative review, because I will continue to play it in the future, but the flaws outweigh the positives.
I dont like the music, the controls are sloppy, the race difficulty and rewards are frustrating but it's the world that keeps bringing me back.
Buy it if you want, I enjoy it although it has too many flaws to give a positive review.

Banished is a city builder that gives an impressive amount of control to the player.  As long as you don't mind an absence of any sort of mission structure or winning conditions to the game, you will enjoy Banished.  You start out with little to no resources and a handful of people thrusted into the wilderness. People need a food and shelter obviously; but where the game shines is how it surprises you with problems to fix.  Each year might have random issues to tackle or submit to.  Perhaps there wasn't a lot animal migration through your territory one year, and people got sick from a non-varied diet. Maybe a natural disaster crumbles your balanced flow of civilization at play. Maybe your woodcutter didn't have enough lumber to cut before winter and people start to get pneumonia.  You might find out you didn't give the young people houses of their own so they could keep the population alive.
The UI in the game is organized well but doesn't look aesthetically pleasing.  It's fun to improve the infrastructure of your town by building rodes and watch your people complete their jobs faster.  And it can be exciting to see the merchant coming downstream to your trading post; especially when you're wanting seeds for new crops or trying to fix a low yield of a certain resource.
Getting deep into the many systems working together in Banished is what makes it so fun to play.  Watching settlers clear out a designated area of wood and stone a little bit at a time is very satisfying. Seeing the growth and prosperity of your people and how they advance their hometown is something to enjoy. But if you prefer a game to hold your hand and present long term goals upfront, then perhaps give Banished a pass. Otherwise pick this game up and support the ONE GUY that made it!

Banished is, at it's very basic core, a city-builder. That being said, it would be better to call it a "Town-builder"; instead of games such as SimCity where citizens are given in the thousands, and their well-being can be negligable at some points, this game focuses on keeping them alive and thriving. Food, warmth, and resources are arguably the core concepts. There is no defined currency in the game; resources are used (wood, stone, food, iron, leather, tools, etc.) to construct buildings or to trade. When beginning, the game might seem overly-difficult and overwhelming, though after "mastering" the game it can become repetetive and lacking.
Pros:
Mostly original take on city-builders
Challenging, but not challenging enough to ruin it
very few bugs
future workshop support
Cons:
Beginning can be daunting and frequent restarts are required
limited end-game content, expanding can become a grind for resources
**Could be fixed when the workshop is introduced**

It may look sort of bland from the outside, but maintaining that delicate balance between survival and progress is so absorbing that you'll never be bothered by any visual "shortcomings". Although, once you get into a groove with the town mechanics the game's visuals are incredibly atmospheric and soothing - that is, until you realize your town is suddenly failing.
The most interesting aspect is having to manage the town population, which consists of families with specific names and professions. Children grow up to marry and have children of their own. People die of old age and someone has to replace them in the workforce. Meanwhile, every now and then refugees will ask to join your town. I'd never seen population management quite like this in any other game of this type.
If you're up for the excruciating satisfaction of micromanaging a town into glorious success, pick this up and have a go!

Invisigun Heroes adds depth to the classic 'Bomberman' shared screen party game formula with the addition of invisibility for all players and special character abilities.  The game achieves complexity and depth without sacrificing ‘pickup and play’ simplicity.
Players can select from several characters each with their own special ability, then vary their gameplay with diverse strategies from deviously sneaky to fiercely aggressive while keeping opponents guessing due to the invisibility mechanic.
The game is not a run of the mill low-resolution game, every map is overflowing with lovingly created pixel art, from rain drops splashing onto the ground to particle effects floating in the air.  It seems there is always something new to notice.
Invisigun Heroes is remarkably flexible, allowing players to mix and match local players with online players and enjoy many modes across a vast selection of unique and engaging maps.
While the game is best playing against friends, the single player Survival Challenge mode is a great way to try maps, characters and refine your skills while invisible.
It is truly a pleasure to play. Even on a losing streak, a tricky play that surprises your opponent and leads to a kill will leave a smile on your face.  Moments like these will keep you playing for hours.

Bite Size Review - Victor Vran
The Good:
- Voice acting is pretty damn good considering it's a budget title (Main character is voiced by the Witcher)
- The boss battles are a lot more interesting than Diablo 3s
- Graphics are decent and colourful
- There is no death penalty, so feel free to experiment and die a few times with a boss (any boss health will regenerate though)
- I was timid to try the WASD controls but an hour or two in it just felt great
- Full camera control, not a fixed perspective
- Challanges add a bit of replay ability for anyone interested
The Bad:
- There are no classes or skill trees (the weapons and limited armour options you equip define your character)
- Each weapon only gets two active abilities to play with, which can get a little boring
- About 3/4 into the game I found the difficulty to spike for some reason, forcing me to change my tactics and chug potions
- Some weapon sets are just better than others (near the end of the game, most bosses I found did a lot of melee damage and it forced me to switch to the spellbook weapon which turned out to be really over powered)
-Stupid character name ... and his hat is also stupid ;)
The Verdict:

​This game is AMAZING! A very interesting take on the 4 player top down party style game. A must have for anyone who likes games such as Towerfall or Samurai Gunn. But, this game blows those games out of the water with it's extra features (online multiplayer) and novel mechanics.
Basics: Everyone is invisible. You can move on a grid orthogonality (up, down, left, right). Each step makes a noise. When you fire or use an ability (8 different characters) it reveals you for a short time. If you bump into or walk over certain terrain it can give away your location subtly via sounds or animation cues.
Graphics: If you like the pixelated art style, they NAILED IT!
Music: The diverse scores capture the feel of the different planets (5). I could listen to most of them on repeat.
Sound Effects: Sound is SO IMPORTANT in this game and they did a fantastic job at conveying things like footsteps to the players. I highly recommend headphones. I feel that people with hearing impairments will struggle with this game but it's not unplayable.
Multiplayer: Multiplayer is the core of this game. Invisigun Heroes allows you to play cross platform (Linux, Mac, Windows) multiplayer with anyone in the world. You can also add more local players seemlessly. There is basic matchmaking and you can even host private ip games. There is no online communication (you will want to join the discord).
Controls: Keyboard can be remapped to be any controls. This game is meant for controller though. My Xbox360 controller and iBuffalo classic USB gamepad worked like a charm. This game can be a little tricky to get your berrings on where you're at. I can see new players being frustrated by that learning curve.
Gamemodes: There are 7 different gamemodes of everything you might want in a game like this, all of which are free for all (no teams (っ- ‸ – ς) ).
TLDR Pros/Cons:
Pros: Cross platform local/online multiplayer (up to 4 playes/bots), fantastic pixel art, great retro inspired music, 50 stages, 7 gamemodes, easy to understand, high skill cap.
Cons: Free for all only (no teams), no real singleplayer game (bots only), learning curve to move while invisible, no online chat.​

Call of Cthulhu: Dark Corners of the Earth has always been one of my favorite horror games. It's primarily based off of The Shadow over Innsmouth, but it also mixes in elements from other Lovecraft stories. The first three or four hours of it are where most of the game's best moments are, spending plenty of time building atmosphere and leaving you defenseless, and once you get guns the game somewhat loses its horror aspect (though it does maintain the atmosphere pretty well), but if you use DCoTE Patch and check the option to unlock all difficulties from the start, playing on the hardest difficulty can be a lot of fun in that it makes both you and the enemies fairly fragile and encourages you to rely on stealth and resource conservation.
Unfortunately, age hasn't done this game any favors, and in my latest playthrough it was even more broken than the last time I played it. You'll almost certainly need to use DCoTE Patch to skip the game-breaking bugs, and you may encounter a few more crashes here and there, particularly when you minimize the game. You can get DCoTE Patch here
, but you might want to read up on the guide in the Steam Community section for the game to get instructions on getting it all worked out since it doesn't work with the default Steam version of the game's exe. But if you can get it working, it's well worth the effort.

This is a game I only play occasionally when I want to relax and I'm not in the mood for playing anything else. That's not a bad thing, that's just the role it has for me and it serves it extremely well. It's a 2D side scrolling puzzle platformer. There's no direct combat (though you can be killed), the game is more about block puzzles, figuring out what you need to move, where and the correct timing. It's pretty simple at first but after a few sets of levels, things get a little more challening with puzzles really requiring players to know the ins and outs of mechanics, sometimes forcing the player to learn new things as they come up with a solution.
Each puzzle is satisfying and so far, not frustrating in the slightest. The visuals are really charming and the music is just nice and relaxing, it doesn't make you feel at all rushed.
I think my favourite thing about it is the game just doesn't get boring for me and it fits into my life perfectly, being there for whenever I need it without feeling like I'm forgetting anything. If I'm stuck for something to play or just not having a great week, I can put this on and even though it doesn't solve those problems, it's a nice way to spend some time.
I highly recommend picking this game up. It's not very expensive at full price and is worth every penny.

The plot is essentially the H.P. Lovecraft novel "Shadows over Innsmouth", which means that the story is genuinely very good. The graphics are fairly dated, as it is nearly 10 years old by now, but this doesn't stop the game from having its scary moments.
A lot of what this game does right is that it does not show you what the danger is, all it really tells you is that there is a danger. The way it achieves this is by having your character suffer from odd visions where you can see through the eyes of your enemies. This can vary from having a vision of guards walking in an area up ahead, to a vision of something quickly gaining on you. I found this mechanic worked extremely well and was probably my favourite part of this game. There are other horror mechanics in this game that work well too, such as the implementation of a sanity system. If you stare at a body or a horrific scene for too long your character starts to freak out a little, with your vision blurring or with your character rambling about something out to get him.
At the halfway mark the horror elements start to disappear, which is fine as you are armed to the teeth. The game switches from a survival-horror game to an action-horror game at this point, leaning more towards action than horror.
The enemies in this game vary from angry towns folk to crazed flying wind demons, so it has a decent enemy variety. It also has 4 or 5 boss fights, which can be quite challenging. There's also a large variety of weapons, about 10 I believe.
Unfortunately, there is one major issue with this game: Bugs.
So many bugs.
Most of them are not game breaking, and they can vary from peoples sentences cutting out half way through, to opening your inventory only to have your game crash. There are a few game breaking bugs I came across, fortunately there is a fan made patch to resolve a few. One bug I experienced I could not find a solution for, and whats even worse is that it happened at the final boss too. I tried to beat the boss about 8 times but kept experiencing the bug so I was forced to give up and watch the ending on youtube.
In conclusion, this is a great game that is unfortunately plagued by bugs. I'd give it a 9/10 but the bugs bring it down to about a 7/10.

I happened to play this game back in 2005 when it came out. It stood out with it's great horror element, tough puzzles and the outstanding incorporation of the Lovecraft universe. For a huge Lovecraft fan, like myself, the latter was the reason to pick up this title once more, after ten years.
Now, there are a some cons to point out:
- The game hasn't aged well when compared to other games of 2005 like Call Of Duty 2, Battlefield 2, Doom 3, GTA: San Andreas, Splinter Cell: Chaos Theory. On 1920x1200 display the graphics gets pixelated and the low-resolution textures start to hurt the eye.
- The AI is crazy stupid. If you're far enough, enemies won't react to you shooting at them. If you shoot enemies from close distance, they rather react to the sound of the gun than taking damage. At times enemies would fail to shoot at you because there's some obstacle in their way, blocking the gun.
- The depth of field is so low that enemies will see you before you see them
- Dark Corners Of The Earth was designed to be a stealth game. You've got the 'crouch' option, the 'sneak' option and the game also tells you to hide in the shadows, to avoid detection. The reality is much more simple: if the enemy is turned towards you, he will see you and if he's turned the other way, he won't. Being in sneak mode or in shadows won't affect detection at all. The only differece is between walking or crouching, as one makes more sound than the other and that's the only part of 'stealthiness' that they did get to work.
- Lengthy unskippable cutscenes right before some of the toughest places of the game, which you then have to endure over and over every time you die.
Having said that, the pros are still there as well:
+ The atmosphere is still damn gloomy with absolutely superb looking Innsmouth and it's degenrate citizens.
+ The way you go from being a sneaky mouse to having the upper hand with considerable firepower carries the idea of remarkable character evolvement.
+ The horrors are revealed to you piece by piece, delivering the expected theatrical effect.
+ The story is typical Lovecraft - you stumble upon something unpleasant and get pulled into unimaginable horrors. Then it's your duty to struggle to stay alive while not going completely mad from everything that's being exposed to you.
+ Voice acting was one thing that echoed in my mind through all these years. I don't think I'm overstating when I say that the voice acting was perfect. The way the 'affected ones' struggle to sound articulate and finally fail to do so as the game advances, is an experience of itself. 'Halt stranger!' will be something, that will ring in your ears for a long time, shouted in a robust, disturbing voice.
+ Dark Corners Of The Earth is not an easy game, you have to struggle even with the lowest difficulty, getting shot or falling from a height will hurt a lot and health packages/save points are scarce. Fortunately you're packed with considerable firepower, so you've got the teeth to bite back.
Verdict:
Throughout the years Dark Corners Of The Earth has stayed one of the most memorable and bright horror survival experiences. They've nailed it with atmosphere and it definitely deserves the attention.

In the first installation of the series, we were playing as the Little Defenders ( sons and daughters of the real heroes). These little heroes defended the Eternia Crystals and put an end to the Evil's plans but just when these littlelings lost all their power and hopes at the end of the first game, their beloved parents came to rescue at the right time and defeat the evil of the evillest.
With Dungeon Defenders II, the developers giving us the "Real" heroes and their real adventures. Oracular graphics, incredible character models and wondrously designed maps and gameplay mechanics that mostly operating like cogwheels; these are also what they are throwing at us. And as a Early Access it stand out like a sore thumb among others.
Lets start with seperating facts of DD1 and DD2:
-DD1 adopted the simplest co-op game formula; buy the game and its ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ of DLC's. DD 2 will be free when it is released ( People who bought the game before f2p release get cosmetic items, in-game crystals for costumes and some other premium gifts)
-DD1 has cell-shade and simple graphics. DD2's graphics are resembling a good animation movie, it has cartoon/animation like graphic concept.
-DD1 use mana as currency, DD 2 differentiate mana and currency. Now we have gold coins $$.
-DD1 just have 1-2 basic costume per character and you need to buy DLCs for them. In DD2 we have evolving and much more detailed costumes ( even at this stage, there are many compared to DD1), which you can buy with real money currency.
-DD1 has tons of DLCs, (it is not %100 clear but) developers thinking of earning money from cosmetic items like MOBA's and supporting the game with free expansions.
-DD1 has offline private option. İn DD2, you need to be online even though you are playing solo.
Yes DD2 has core mechanics from the first installation; but it looks better on the surface, it feels better when you play it and it is much more refined than most of the other Early Access' and DD1.
Let's get to pros and cons part:
+ Will be F2P!
+ Fantastic graphics and colour palette
+ Refined gameplay mechanics ( developers are trying to make it much more stable )
+ Developers that are listening to us.
+ Good animations and rigging

Victor Vran, a Witcher and Torchlight hybrid, is a top-down, monster-hunter hack’n slash. Blessed with fun combat, great ambiance and large level design, it is cursed with mediocre voice acting, been-there-done-that story and an overly generous loot system (hello, clogged inventory). Four-player coop and a detailed challenge system are welcome additions. Worth a purchase at 66% off or more.
Total size on my hard-drive: 4.3 GB
+ Large level design. While there are a few smaller levels that house challenge bosses, most are large and spacious, with secrets hidden everywhere. One of the best features of Victor Vran.
+ Good level of challenge. New areas are difficult, and after leveling and becoming OP, activate different hexes (Hex of Pain reduces Victor Vran’s health over time, Hex of Time speeds enemies, and so on) for additional challenge and greater rewards.
+ Nice graphics. Won’t knock your socks off, but the level of detail (especially in the city levels) is excellent.
+ Smooth and stable. Not a single crash or hang in 24 hours of gameplay.
+ Good choice of weapons. Shotguns, lightning guns, swords, rapiers, scythes, hammers, spell books. Each type of weapon can be found with a large number of different specializations – which bring their own buffs and debuffs.
+ The card-based skills system. Victor can equip of number of cards for passive combat bonuses. There are over a dozen varieties, and again each can be had in a number specializations. One of my favorites was “The Moon” card, which, when equipped, grants an ice-explosion when Victor lands a critical hit. Another good one is the “Blademaster” card, which adds over-drive at a faster rate and grants health-regen on crit with swords. Each card is available in a number of levels as well; Levels 1 through 4 were most common, but I did loot a Level 8 card (yes, the bonuses were massive!). There is limited number of points available to equip cards, though, and each level counts as a point; equipping four Level 4 cards isn’t possible when the point limit is less than 16 (the point limit increases as Victor levels up), forcing a continual mix-and-match of available cards in search of the best build.
+ Nicely ambient soundtrack.
+ Four-player coop. Drop-in / drop-out works well. The large levels work well with four players.
+ You can trade items with a demon named Geban. 10/10 would trade with Geban again.
+/- Demon powers. There are about a dozen to choose from, but their usefulness is limited because their use requires over-drive. It can take a while for the over-drive bar to fill in the early stages. Certain weapons and cards can boost the charge rate, making them more useful. Then there are other cards that provide bonuses only if the over-drive bar is full – rendering demon powers useless, because emptying the over-drive bar by using a demon power would deactivate the bonus.
+/- Bosses are nicely placed and paced, but don’t require any special tactics to defeat.
+/- Someone made a pact with a demon and now the kingdom has to pay when the demons come to collect on the debt. There. That’s the story.
+/-  Victor Vran is voiced by the same actor who provides the English-language voice of Geralt in the Witcher games (Doug Cockle). Victor is a near carbon-copy of Geralt. I’m not sure if Cockle was told to do this, or if this is the limit of his skills as a voice actor. Other voice actors are good, but not special.
+/- Too much loot. There are several different ways to sort it, but even for a loot-based game, there is a ton of loot. There is no limit on inventory space, though, so the primary issue is managing it.
+/- + Leveling gear. Most things can be leveled using Transmutation in the hub. Weapons, cards, powers. The outcome is completely RNG, though (unlike in Borderlands: The Pre-Sequel where using Moonstone in the weapon grinder would guarantee an increase in rarity. Nothing like that here).
- Some area challenges are impossible to complete unless massively over-leveled or playing online with other players. The online mode had about a dozen players active in it every time I started the game, so not an impossible task.
- Some level challenges are mutually exclusive, meaning you are expected to re-play levels.
- Some grinding for better gear required if soloing. No worse than in Borderlands, but expect it.
- Armor is tied to outfits, which are only awarded via chests and level-up bonuses. That means the best plan is to kill the enemies fast and have a good stock of potions on hand. Worry about armor later. There are passive bonuses which can help.
Overall, the looting, combat and level design are the most attractive features of Victor Vran, but unless grinding and completing challenges for loot is why you play games (not that there’s anything wrong with either!), you could get bored with it quickly. A good effort by developer Haemimont with franchise potential. Hopefully, future installments will showcase refinements of some great core systems.

A smaller scale sandbox city builder with an emphasis on year to year survival. It's fairly difficult to learn so your first few cities will probably result in everyone starving or freezing to death come winter, if you've ever played Dwarf Fortress you already know the fear of the first winter. It's scale is comparable to the Tropico series, you can see individual citizens with their own names and relations, you can also see a little tombstone appear in your graveyard when they die because you didn't build enough food buildings. It's also a sandbox, there's no specific goals other then the various achievements, and there's no specific scenarios or maps, they're all randomly generated from a seed.
So if you need a story, in-game goals, and don't like a steep learning curve, then you'll probably want to stay away from this one. But on the other hand, if you enjoy the likes of Dwarf Fortress you'll feel right at home in Banished.

I really enjoyed this game, but it's definitely not for everyone. The game thrives off of you failing. It's a game of trial and error. Cities get harder and harder to manage as the population climbs. If you're not comfortable spending hours on a city only to watch it crumble after a plague, this game may not be for you.
The way I think the game was designed to be played was for you to build it up to the point of your society collapsing so that you can say "okay, here were my mistakes, this is why it was unstable; I won't do that next time." In this sense, the game is immensely rewarding as you're constantly able to learn from your mistakes and get farther each time. That being said, this can make the game more frustrating than rewarding for some people. You're constantly faced with small and large failures that can make the game seem impossible. But, when losing is part of the game, you're not really losing.
Anyway, if you want a city-building sim and you like them to challenging, complex, and deep, this is a great game and you'll probably spend a lot more hours on it than I did.

Prior to it's release, I heard absolutely nothing about Valley. Didn't even know it existed. A friend of mine raved about the game the day it was released, and I got it the next day.
I can't believe there wasn't hype for this game.
The graphics of this game are gorgeous. Unfortunately, they are also a bit hard on some computers. I am stuck on a laptop that, even on medium settings, lags a bit with the graphics.
The music is also beautiful. If you are into game soundtracks, I highly recommend this one. The soundtrack is also on Youtube, if you want to check it there before committing to it.
The gameplay is so, so satisfying.
The game incorporates some physics a lot of games don't, such as accelerating you if you are moving downhill, which in turn has an enormous impact on your flight distance if you jump. As a result, you get to soar through some very gorgeous scenery.
The life/death mechanic is something I haven't seen before in a game,
, I rather liked it.
Combat is not particularly challenging, as this game is more focused on story and atmosphere. If you need a game to punish you to like it, Valley may not be for you. For those of us who are not masochists, this should not be a problem.
While I am not finished with the game, if you explore as you play, this could be a longer game (I had some friends try out the game, so my current play time is a few hours shorter than what is listed). Someone who speed runs this game could potentially finish in only a couple hours. Take that as you will.
---
Overall, if you like exploration games with fun gameplay and story, I HIGHLY recommend this game (and soundtrack). My only warning is to make sure your computer can handle the graphics.

Never heard of this game? Let me tell you a story.
While roaming around in this game I came upon some enemies. Rather than walk up to them and shoot or snipe or bazooka them, I got into a trash truck, loaded it with C4, drove it off a cliff over the enemies, jumped out, and parachuted to safety. My only concern would come attached with the excitement I have for Just Cause 3's release. Regardless of future games, this one is exceptional and still well worth it in my opinion. I have seen it for as low as 2.99 during holiday sales.

I happened to play this game back in 2005 when it came out. It stood out with it's great horror element, tough puzzles and the outstanding incorporation of the Lovecraft universe. For a huge Lovecraft fan, like myself, the latter was the reason to pick up this title once more, after ten years.
Now, there are a some cons to point out:
- The game hasn't aged well when compared to other games of 2005 like Call Of Duty 2, Battlefield 2, Doom 3, GTA: San Andreas, Splinter Cell: Chaos Theory. On 1920x1200 display the graphics gets pixelated and the low-resolution textures start to hurt the eye.
- The AI is crazy stupid. If you're far enough, enemies won't react to you shooting at them. If you shoot enemies from close distance, they rather react to the sound of the gun than taking damage. At times enemies would fail to shoot at you because there's some obstacle in their way, blocking the gun.
- The depth of field is so low that enemies will see you before you see them
- Dark Corners Of The Earth was designed to be a stealth game. You've got the 'crouch' option, the 'sneak' option and the game also tells you to hide in the shadows, to avoid detection. The reality is much more simple: if the enemy is turned towards you, he will see you and if he's turned the other way, he won't. Being in sneak mode or in shadows won't affect detection at all. The only differece is between walking or crouching, as one makes more sound than the other and that's the only part of 'stealthiness' that they did get to work.
- Lengthy unskippable cutscenes right before some of the toughest places of the game, which you then have to endure over and over every time you die.
Having said that, the pros are still there as well:
+ The atmosphere is still damn gloomy with absolutely superb looking Innsmouth and it's degenrate citizens.
+ The way you go from being a sneaky mouse to having the upper hand with considerable firepower carries the idea of remarkable character evolvement.
+ The horrors are revealed to you piece by piece, delivering the expected theatrical effect.
+ The story is typical Lovecraft - you stumble upon something unpleasant and get pulled into unimaginable horrors. Then it's your duty to struggle to stay alive while not going completely mad from everything that's being exposed to you.
+ Voice acting was one thing that echoed in my mind through all these years. I don't think I'm overstating when I say that the voice acting was perfect. The way the 'affected ones' struggle to sound articulate and finally fail to do so as the game advances, is an experience of itself. 'Halt stranger!' will be something, that will ring in your ears for a long time, shouted in a robust, disturbing voice.
+ Dark Corners Of The Earth is not an easy game, you have to struggle even with the lowest difficulty, getting shot or falling from a height will hurt a lot and health packages/save points are scarce. Fortunately you're packed with considerable firepower, so you've got the teeth to bite back.
Verdict:
Throughout the years Dark Corners Of The Earth has stayed one of the most memorable and bright horror survival experiences. They've nailed it with atmosphere and it definitely deserves the attention.

You also don't have to worry about noobs on your team because there are separate servers for beginners and pros (ranks 1-12 and ranks 13-84). The only requirement for the pro servers are that you have to be rank 13, which took me about 9 hours of overall playtime to get. Maneuverability is a strong point of this game. You can assist teammates up a large wall, you can crouch, you can lay down, and my favorite: you can slide. My favorite class is the engineer because they get smgs, which have a quick fire rate in case you didn't know. They also have mines which they can plant almost anywhere, and can plant and defuse the c4 (in plant the bomb mode) quickly. The only disadvantage to this game is that there is no loadout screen before you spawn. You have to select your class and loadout before you do a match and it can't be changed once the game has started.

the biggest issue ive seen is the spawns at times, there are just spawns in some maps where you cant even reach the trench to defend it because you have to go out in the open, and you will die most of the time, but when you get to where you need to go it can get pretty good.
my favorite is the fact that it forces the use of trenches, world war 1 games typically include trenches but dont force you to use them, at least not from what ive seen.
the use of gas is also good, nco calls it in and it affects your gameplay in more than one way, first one being the obvious,♥♥♥♥♥♥s deadly, use your gasmask. gas acts as a smoke screen as much as an area denial weapon as well so unless you plan to spray, you wont be firing into it or running blindly into it until it fades. relative to the player there's a few changes as well, the gas masks have a first person overlay, more or less, you can see the lenses and if you're german, they've got frames over the lenses, obscuring the view. the british masks are better becuase they lack them, but your view is still limited.
artillery and grenades can be a little wonky, sometimes you'll die and sometimes you wont. its something you have to call from a position you can actually see, not just pointing it out on a map on games like ro2, so i guess that helps a bit.
biggest difference from a lot of games. damage tables 100%. very few guns will just hurt you slightly, most you encounter will kill you damn near instantly, automatics will do about 2 hits before death, and pistols 2 to 3. most firearms are just simple bolt actions of their respective nations, and they're all instant kill.
as a whole i really like verdun, its a great game, just needs better spawns and some netcode improvements.
id recommend to someone whose not really into fast action but doesnt want really slow action, and also wants a historically accurate experience.

I would recommend this game because I found it to be relaxing, though it can be quite stressful at times. This is very true if your like me and don't read about how the game works and find out that children can only be created in seperate homes by a man and a woman, and never with your aging parents. Thus I had to watch as my small town age and die rather quickly, then to add insult to injury a tornado had to come through and destroy my only forestry, and just when things were going so well. I was soon left alone with an old fisherman whom I sat with until he drew his last breath and froze to death on the very docks he worked. A sad story but true, and I believe that it tells what the game is really about, survival of the town. Through out Banished  your people will die, from old age, starvation, drowning, trampling, natural disasters, and every once in a while a priest gets stabbed, yep even when everyone is happy my priest was stabbed to death, I blame the nomads I let in for that. Survival, and managing your towns survival is still the name of the game for as people are lost, depending on how important they are to the needs of the town i.e. food and shelter they may need to be repaced quickly to provided you with the resources need for the winter. The gameplay is simple and descriptions are provided for the buildings (except the baby making details), farms, domestic animals, and orchards will be your biggest food supplies while your people will hunt and gather your recources. Some things that could be looked into further would be crop usage there is not much that can be done with them, at least when I last played in the summer, and people's living locations, I know that people will move into a house or change occupations depending on what job they do to be closer but it could be nice to place people in certain areas rather than rely on the AI to move. Lastly specialization of people would be a nice touch especially with the school if you could teach the groups of kids to do a certain task, or tasks, better rather than  giving an overall boost, which is not very apparent, to the adults who leave the school. These are things I would like to see in patches or later if a bigger and better Banished comes out. If your looking to have fun and build a town while trying to keep your people alive during the brutal winters while avoiding unforseen situations then give it a try.  8/10

Not sure why I bought this. I didn't like videos of this and what they did too my precious mercury, too, I didn't.
But yeah, first about parts I actually enjoyed.
The setting of Falcon Empire Era is pretty neat, with all that skulldruggery, old ways of Ilath, orcbros, oceanic weaboo empire, necromancers not as power-hungry cartoon villains, but bizarre keepers of balance (more like it was in Diablo II). Story is good enough too. The split dynasty, the rise of Railag, the crazy adventures of Crag Hack (though I found this one quite boring, but then again, I was playing this for a while at that particular point) and a little fanservice with Sandro cameo (OHGODIT'SREALLYHIM). Dunno about vampire campaign though.
Sanctury is a good addition to the world, it's unlike anything you saw in Ashan before and I hope we'll see more of Naga Samurais and Sharkmen in the future.
The system of unlockables through seals is decent. Provides a bit of stimulus to play it if you feel you are bored here (and it happens pretty fast).
Now, the bad parts.
Soundtrack. Quite unremarkable.
The balance. The problem here is not overpowering something, but making it too difficult to figure out (the same mistake devs did in HoMMIV with cross-classes and tons of perks). See, there are just too many perk combos you can't really predict, because spells are perks here. In HoMMIII you could point your finger at a guy playing Necropolis or Conflux and call him an a-hole, In HoMMV you could point your finger at Kaspar starter, here...well...you can't. And it's not really a good thing (but it may appear so). Still, if you like overcomplification, you may just ignore what I said.
While devs created complications, they simplified the resource part. Which feels...unfair,
Ah yes, map layouts. Region - based map isn't a good solution for me. You can't raid mines behind enemy lines, now you have to sabotage them or keep you secondary hero there all the time. This is a huge problem when we come to next point...
Overuse of town portals. No really, this is a big issue. While they provide mobility, they are, well, too damn essential. You can easily evade encounter with enemy via it. And...everybody gets it for free. No spell, no perk, you just need enough mana to cast it.
Oh, about Conflux service. It wasn't down at the time I played it, so maybe Ubi fixed it. Maybe. Still, I'm okay with being online to play.
Still, the review is "mixed", so I have to claim "non-recomendation" here is gentle here, not strong. You wanna your 60 hours (well, I lasted nearly that amount) for that price - fine, go for it. If not, or you have bad experience with Uplay - better save the money for sale or whatever product on Steam you want more.

Never heard of this game? Let me tell you a story.
While roaming around in this game I came upon some enemies. Rather than walk up to them and shoot or snipe or bazooka them, I got into a trash truck, loaded it with C4, drove it off a cliff over the enemies, jumped out, and parachuted to safety. My only concern would come attached with the excitement I have for Just Cause 3's release. Regardless of future games, this one is exceptional and still well worth it in my opinion. I have seen it for as low as 2.99 during holiday sales.

Valley is a fun and exhilarating first person adventure game that really hit the mark for me.  If you're a casual gamer like myself, this game will be sure to be a hit!  I just completed my Let's Play series and it's available
if you'd like to check it out - including the Medallion Temple reveal!
On to a bit more thorough of a review.  On my first playthrough of the game, it was very easy to get engrossed in the storyline.  Any enemies you encounter are fairly easy to dispose of, but add a level of stress to the game that makes it just a little more challenging - and really embraces the thoughts of the characters you read about in the notes along the way.
I felt particularly taken in by the way the main story is told in a narrative, at critical points in the game and it was done very well.  At points, the sound effects alone are enough to get the heart really pumping!  All of that being said, I did have to go back and re-play a majority of the game to get some of the medallions, and it was still a riot.
I think I developed stockholme syndrome and a touch of paranoia in doing so, though.
The only thing I didn't really like about the game is that there are certain things that are generally anti-climactic.  When you expect to finally have reached a point in the story line, it gets pushed back just a little further out.  No big deal, really.  It added a little suspense.
I logged 20 hours on this game and ended up with 25/30 achievements.  There's still room for some replay, but I'm a bit burnt out!
For the $20?  A+ game, and Blue Isle did an incredible job.  Thank you for your hard work, and I hope that it has paid off for you guys!

Valley is a first person Action Adventure game where you play a faceless and nameless Archaeologist who has set out to discover the Mythic Life Seed, an object so powerful it could destroy the world. To aid you on your journey, you find a L.E.A.F Suit, a powerful Exoskeleton with a wide range of abilities.
Through the course of your journey you uncover a long-dead experiment surrounding the L.E.A.F project that was underway the same time as the Manhattan Project in order to help the Americans win World War 2 in a story that is delivered in combination between Text and decently performed voice acting.
PROS:
-	Beautifully done world
-	Well-crafted levels
-	Interesting story
-	Fun gameplay
CONS:
-	Lackluster Combat
-	Yet another game with Wendigos
-	Short (less than 4 hours)
-	Low replay value

Outlast is like the texas chainsaw massacre meeets one flew over the cookoo's nest, expect theres more blood, gritty sadism and  geunie terror. I can honestlty say I've never♥♥♥♥♥♥my pants playaing a video game, however....well ok that didn't happen but still there were some seriously dodgy moments. My advice? don't play this game in your sunday best... just in case. In fact if you suffer from a heart condition I wouldn't play this game either, I jumped out of my stkin atl least twice on the first playing. Ofcourse like all horror games you eventually desensitise to all the scary scary♥♥♥♥♥♥my pants geniune terror moments, but Outlast did a very good of keeping me immersed and emotiontal attacthed to what was going on.
One reason for this is the atmospheres the game gernerates is supperb, every sound, the floorboard creakiong the broken glass underfood the psycho eske soundtrack, which by the way is perfectly timed to suit the mood of the moment, it all rachets up the tension and keeps it there, making yoiu allways worried about whats around the corner whats coming up next? what new saddistic horror have the twisted minds that made this game got in store for next? At times itf feels more cinema than game. The graphics are no let down either, with alot of the game veiwed with a infra-red camcorda it all looks eerily real.
Another cool aspect of the game is that way it is played, this is no hack'n'slash where you are the triamphant hero wading through yet another pile of freshly made corpses, oh no, in this game when you come against on of the macrabe monstrosites that are lurking in the shadows you can either run, or hide, or die. Watching attacks miss on both sides of a turn-based RPG battle system for turns on end quickly turned any enthusiasm I had for this game to nothing very quickly. This is one of, but not the least of, many deep flaws that Science Girls has. Let's get some positives out of the way first, though.
Pros:
-The idea of female protagonists in a video game is always a welcome change for me. That I can respect, even moreso when it's done right and holds up to other "good" games. I can't fault games for trying, and won't overlook that for a second. More on that later however.
-Within battling itself, each character has a specialized role that they basically fill, akin to a class in most other RPGs of this nature. Giving attacks and spells to each character's "class" in this case allows you to find a relatively niche use for probably five of the six girls, the sixth only having a scan ability and not much else of use. The rest, however, are all viable picks for battle. Which is good, because you have all six of them within the first hour and will need a good balance to survive this game. Additionally, each girl learns a "finisher" skill at level 6 that will grant them extra exp at the end of the battle if they killed an enemy with it. All of these help phenominally with leveling and the idea itself is unique and pretty cool. I wouldn't mind seeeing it in other games, at that.
Unfortunately, that's where the positives stop for me. Let's move onto cons.
-Everything about this game feels so slow. The pacing of the game itself, the movement, the progression of the plot, and especially the battling. I would go through one battle and it would feel like fifteen minutes had passed. In one instance of a boss battle, it actually did take that long and felt more like half an hour. More on why battling is bad in a minute.
-The plot itself is tolerable at best and hollow at worst. You follow six girls fending off an alien invasion who seem to be after...people's hair? For some reason? That's really all I got. There isn't any more than that. It's weird, kinda creepy, and probably isn't taking anything seriously in the least minus the scientific concepts. Speaking of...
-This game throws around scientific concepts and the like like there's no tomorrow. Expect half of them really feel like there's no meaning to them. They talk about wormholes briefly, except nothing about wormholes is ever explained. They come up with different ways to cross paths that might be dangerous, but who cares? I just want to cross a ♥♥♥♥ing bridge, I don't need some complicated solution on how to do it carefully. I most certainly didn't learn anything from it, and it just didn't feel like it went outside the box to make it really interesting or even remotely fun.
-The art and sound are absolutely atrocious. I played the whole game with my sound muted because it was driving me up a wall to hear one of the characters cry out like a stereotypical anime girl every time they attacked something. Every. Single. Time. The music is lackluster and carries no sense of urgency. The school is the most generic school you could possibly see, consisting of empty classroom backgrounds and occasionally a storage room or cafeteria. The alien homeworld is no better, just feeling like an empty landscape that I have to trudge across for minutes on end in between the constant battles I have no chance of avoiding. The only thing you can do to tell the girls apart from one another is their hairstyles; oftentimes I would confuse them, even though I've been staring at them all for the past five minutes in battle. The only other NPC in the game is a bald teacher, and the entire cutscene he was in just made me cringe. Just...take my word for it.
-The characters themselves are also bland, uninteresting, and have little personality. Each of them is a student in a specific scientific field and... ...well, they do scientific things related to that field. In their profiles, each of them have three "likes" of completely mundane things, like horses, or pizza, or movies. That and their interactions throughout the game is all you get on them. Their humor isn't even cheeky. It's doesn't make me laugh, or even giggle. It falls flat in every instance. The protagonists here are one-dimensional. This isn't what I want when I say female protagonists. I want female protagonists with depth, an interesting personality, and a valid reason for doing what they do. "Let's save the world with the power of sicence lul" doesn't count. It's insulting.
-Oh boy, the BATTLING. Battling is many things. Battling is slow, unrewarding, trudging, and the worst part of the game. Maybe, possibly, it was because I was playing on the harder difficulty, but let's still go over every little thing that contributed to me wanting to throw my computer out the window in detail. First off, attacks will miss. A LOT. On both sides. Battles will drag on and on because neither side can land a hit on the other for possibly turns on end. Damage is always between two numbers, a low end and a high end. So when you finally do connect, you could do fifteen damage! Or you could do two. To get a higher low end, you have to level up a skill when you level up. However, that also increases the amount of SP you need to use the skill. It is ridiculous how much some of the higher level skills will costs. Upwards of 2/3 of your total SP.
Items are finite. The only HP and SP restoring items you get are the ones you find on the map. There are no places to fully restore your health, except through level up. If you run out of SP, you have to defend to gain two back per turn (that character's ENTIRE turn) and an extra bonus one if everyone in the front row is defending. Characters in the back row do nothing, not even gain HP and SP back, unless they're brought into the front. Yet, they're still susceptible to attacks. Why? You can't attack their back row. Enemies will always have stronger attacks than you. Certain enemies will counterattack EVERY attack you throw at them, miss or not. Bosses are extreme damage sponges unless you've invested a lot into your attacks or exploit the system in very specific ways. It's impossible to tell how much of a chance you have to actually hit an enemy unless you raise your accuracy stat, but then you're wasting skill points. The amount of exp you need to get even past level 10 merits battles and battles of grinding even with the finisher moves. And you know what? Those aren't even guaranteed to hit. One character in particular, had a 9/25 success rate of hitting random battle enemies with her finisher. That's nearly a third. Yes, I counted. Strangely enough, in every boss encounter, she seemed to hit every single time.
I am just. So worn out over this game. I didn't expect it to be great, but I figured it could be worth the time playing. It wasn't. Hardly any of the game was enjoyable to me, and if I was so tenacious in getting all the achievements, I wouldn't have bothered. Spare yourself the purchase. The people that made this have made much better games than this.

Jumping is a new feature on ARPG games, at least it is for me. This brings a tactical side to combat in the form of dodging and moving around, other thing it contributes to is the secrets.  Just like Doom, and other classic shooters that hosted secrets within their levels and giving you that much needed ammo with them, this game also has hidden chests within it's levels to give you gold or loot. Sometimes you have to make a jump or two to get past an obstacle to the secret area. I loved uncovering secrets as a kid in Doom, and it's equally as fun in here.
Maps aren't big ones, but they're filled with enemies and challenges. You might have to kill a certain type of enemy with a certain type of weapon, avoid taking damage (these are sometimes annoying since the cheap attacks/bad luck), killing xx amount of monsters in xx seconds and many others. They don't need to be done on one run.
Being a classless ARPG, your attacks consist of the normal one and two special attacks per weapon with the Q and E button. Each weapon type has it's own attacks and effects, they can't be changed. You also have two slots to potions, potions include standard healing potions, buffs and attacking-potions and two slots to Demon powers which are basically spells. Then there's the destiny cards which you can hold a maximun of five at the same time/as much as you have destiny points. Lvl 1 card uses 1 destiny point etc, and the cards are passive skills, increasing damage, armor, critical chance, moving speed, cooldowns, item drops etc.
All of that together forms the build of your character, so there is a lot of customization. And you can basically start all over again and do another build on the fly, without needing to start the game all over again and choose a different class.
Since you don't have any traditional skill points, leveling up increases your max destiny points/hp or other things among the way, and gives you always a choice to select one free item out of three. I was a bit skeptic with this system at first but it seems to work just fine.
So, the crafting system! Simple but interesting. Weapon can be enchanced pretty good as usual, cards can be upgraded, but keep the destiny points in mind, you might craft a too powerful one that you can't use for a while/you have to give up on others. Spells can be enchanced. But do you use your spells/cards to strengthen your weapon or your spells/cards? Since the amount of customization, and the rareness of spells it requires a bit of thinking and planning (or a lot of farming...).
Shuold you buy it?
YES! This is an awesome ARPG, main story is short, but the challenges and the interesting development system is well worth the money. Secrets in the levels are fun to look for, the jumping mechanic adds much to the combat. I hope we get a sequel, or more maps to this one. It's awesome, definitely a game to own.

Banished is a city-building game with a heavy focus on survival. From humble beginnings - just a few families exiled from their past lives and a handful of supplies - you will have the opportunity to build up a thriving community.
While Banished has all the footprints of a typical city-building game, it sets itself apart from the rest by including a diverse pool of resources to manage, each with impacts on your villagers’ happiness, health, and productivity. Each citizen adds to your total consumption, meaning you cannot afford to be complacent; you must always be planning ahead lest famine or disease wipe out most of your population. You must also manage your labor force (working adults), and should do so as efficiently as possible in order to minimize their struggle to survive.
The setting and the art-style compliment the survival theme quite well. There is never any doubt that you are building a barebones medieval-era town - all the buildings are made from wood and stone and the whole thing feels very quaint. The seasons change, which has both a visual effect as well as creating a growth cycle for plants and crops (can’t farm during the winter!).
As the years progress, your population ages, has children, and eventually passes away leaving the newer generations to repeat the circle of life... that is if they haven’t suffered any misfortunes along the way. Merchants will periodically visit and trade crop seeds, farm animals, and all kinds of goods once you’ve built a trading post. Wandering nomads may choose to settle in your town if you allow them.
There is a healthy variety of crops and buildings, and there is also Workshop/mod support. Although the modkit for Banished is only fresh out of beta, there is already a significant amount of additional content that improves the base game immensely. For example, the Colonial Charter mod provides a complete overhaul of the game with tons of new resources, buildings, and production chains.
If city-building games are something you enjoy, I cannot recommend Banished enough. This was one of my most anticipated releases of 2014 and it has definitely lived up to my expectations (and then some). A word of caution though, there are many hardships ahead; this is in no way an "easy" game.

I have played Demon Souls, Dark Souls 1, 2, and 3. This is absolutely the worst one. Instead of listing everything wrong with this game I'll just give you a few bullet points.
-Fireplace Teleporting
Instead of traveling the vast interconnecting world that Dark Souls 1 had, it's now scrapped for teleporting into a starting area bonfire, killing a boss, reaching the end bonfire, then teleporting to another starting location and completing its end bonfire. Makes the game feel very uneven. And while Demon Souls did this it was done a lot better with specific areas corresponding with each other until you killed the final boss. And these "bosses" are so freakishly easy and unintersting. Also take a look at any other review and see they have hitboxes listed as their grievance, and that's because rolling out of the way doesn't necessarily mean your going to survive a boss' ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t attack because their attacks don't line up with their area of infliction.
-Soft Caps
This is what pretty much ruined the game for me. Instead of watching your stats build with the points you put in them, skills have "soft caps" where you get a certain amount of points per level until reaching a higher specific level in which your points are now decreased for every level beyond that soft cap. For instance the Endurance skill gives you 2 points per level until level 20 in which you get 1 point per level. Now this may not sound so bad, but every skill has these random caps and pretty much every person who makes a build guide will tell you to never input points beyond the soft cap of some skills because otherwise you would just be wasting your level up. It makes pretty much every build conform to a certain linear progression system due to these caps and it doesn't reward you for investing points heavily into one skill. And yes, Dark Souls had soft caps too but they were pretty high and didn't take away too many points for reaching these caps. Dark Souls II wants to punish you for using a particular skill too much and it doesn't feel innovative or fun.
-tl;dr
Dark Souls II takes 1 step forward and 2 steps back. It is frustrating playing this game after loving Dark Souls I so much. Avoid this and pick up Dark Souls III which is waaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaayyyyyyyyyyyy better.

Decade old first person stealth. Trial and error gameplay. Clumsy first person shooting. Game breaking bugs that were never officially fixed by the developers, making the vanilla game you just purchased all but completely unplayable. The only way to (currently...) make the game run without crashing that I found was to download and install a fan-made patch
, download and run video capture software called Bandicam
, and also go into your video card settings to turn native V sync on. You probably want a walkthrough handy as well
to make sure any problems you run into aren't bugs, and there are some solutions to puzzles that are not so much too difficult or counter-intuitive as you'll walk past key elements a hundred times due to muddy graphics or poor signposting. I say that as someone who is very anti-walkthrough in most cases, but trust me... unless you want to turn a ten hour adventure into forty hours of walking in circles use the ♥♥♥♥ing guide when you're stuck.
Still with me? Call of Cthulhu: Dark Corners of the Earth is an excellent survival horror/adventure game and I highly recommend it. I had to start off with the negative points to put it into perspective: to get to the good parts of this game you're going to have to swallow some♥♥♥♥♥♥ but it's worth it.
You play the game as Jack, a hardened, somewhat stereotypical detective of the Elliot Ness variety. It's 1930's American prohibition era New England, so take the tough guy attitude and film noir/Dragnet speak to the extreme, calmly making strictly factual observations about the world around you, even while being tortured with a car battery by J. Edgar Hoover or staring into the unspeakable eyes of fish monsters and ancient gods. In a game explicitly about Lovecraftian horrors and utter madness, the one note voice acting of Jack provides endless comic relief. Whether it's intentionally funny or not is up to debate. Nothing phases this guy...
Jack is on the case of freeing a prisoner from the eerie, not-quite-right town of Innsmouth. The few sane inhabitants of the town warn him of cult activity and that the fishy smell that permeates the streets might have a more malicious point of origin than the cannery. What follows is quite an adventure into increasingly alien, hostile environments that is surprisingly ambitious in scope. While the first third or so of the game takes place in Innsmouth, you'll be boarding a Navy vessel under siege by Dagon's minions and exploring impressively sprawling, twisting caverns as well as an underwater city. If you just gasped and muttered, “Spoilers...”... The game is called Call of Cthulhu. Read some Lovecraft.
The game is a true eclectic mix of genres: stealth, FPS, old school adventure and puzzle solving, exploration, what would be considered some light modern “survival” elements. You can converse with NPCs and complete optional side quests. This is a true jack of all trades, and like most times that cliché is used not many of the gameplay mechanics are “good” in the traditional sense. Stealth is unreliable and usually frustrating as enemies seem to spot or hear you when they feel like it. The weapons you get early on feel almost useless with either a random spread pattern and/or a cockeyed aim down sight perspective, but there are instanced where you are forced to fight. Good luck. The most consistent thread is the adventure elements where you're using items from your inventory to solve puzzles and combing the playspace for clues. Though, with some poorly placed checkpoints combined with the aforementioned shaky stealth and combat you'll have to repeat in many instances... see above for a walkthrough link.
There are a few standout systems, most notably how the game handles health and sanity. When you take damage it is represented both by the bodily location of the wound and the type of injury. You might get grazed in the chest, which can be fixed by applying some bandages from the inventory of which you usually have plenty. Something deeper might require sutures to close a gash, otherwise you'll bleed out. If you fall from a good height you will break a leg (or two), and you'll physically limp, causing a sickening crunching sound and snail paced movement until you attach a splint. The healing items are all tracked separately so there's no Cure All to speak of save a shot of morphine which won't actually heal you, just provide temporary pain relief while you desperately search for a medkit. I really like this system: yeah, it's kind of goofy that Jack goes from a bloody mess with exposed bone and torn clothes to a-okay in five seconds, but it's the perfect compromise between nitty gritty hardcore micromanagement survival and typical hording.
When you get injured or see anything particularly unnerving (which you will), Jack starts to lose his mind. He's no longer the monotone detective; as his vision distorts and he loses control he sounds convincingly terrified as he mutters to himself, questioning his sanity and his purpose and his will to go on. Sanity effects aren't new or rare for these games, but whatever filter they are using to convey being disorienting is extremely effective. Something as simple as looking down while descending a ladder brings out Jack's vertigo, and let him freak out for too long and you'll get a gut-churning empathetic feeling yourself.
Again, I may sound overly negative when picking apart certain aspects of the game, but overall it rises above it's shortcomings. The janky, low budget nature can work in it's favor; you don't entirely trust the game to play by the rules. While not a jump scare/gorefest, it's does not shy away from generally taboo subjects: dead kids, an upside down take on beastialitality, torture, sacrifices, all that good stuff. Just when you're laughing at Jack's oblivious take on fishmen, you'll bear witness to something genuinely unsettling. When the game hits, it hits hard. And it's paced impeccably; curse repeating the same chase sequence all you want, once you go further down the rabbit hole there just seems to be a reason for everything. It's one of those games that you question why you're playing, but you can't stop. You have to see it through to the end, whether it drives you mad or not. Even the very last sequence took me many, many tries to the point where I was ready to give up and just watch the ending on YouTube and write a damning review about how broken the game is (and I already wrote one before taking the time to patch it), yet I persisted. And then as the credits rolled I just sat back and though, “What a great game.” It's fitting, I guess.

Valley is a First Person Adventure game created by Blue Isle Studios, the developers that brought us Slender: The Arrival. In this game you play an archaelogist (able to choose gender) who goes on an expedition to the Canadian Rockies to find the mythical Lifeseed, a mysterious artifact. When you arrive at your destination you discover you aren't the first one there. There are remnants of an old American WWII science team and WWII army units who used exosuits called the L.E.A.F. suits. Able to run incredibly fast, jump incredibly high, able to manipulate life & death itself, there is a lot you can do with the L.E.A.F. suit.
This is a game that's best played without knowing much about it going in. I didn't spoil anything in my description that you wouldn't have figured out in the first 5 minutes of playing or from the store page trailer. Part of the appeal of it to me personally was all the mystery and wonder of the game world Blue Isle Studios built. I won't talk too much more about the story but I will say that this game has a ton of platforming, secrets and suit upgrades. The game is also beautiful to look at and the soundtrack is perfect for it. The best words I could use to describe the soundtrack during some parts of the game is "enchanting" and "whimsical". The music is adaptive, meaning it changes with your actions. During certain parts, if you're running and jumping the music will change to reflect that. Lastly, this is NOT a walking simulator. There is a combat system in place that you will learn how to use fairly early on, as well as some really fast paced sections that are a treat to play through.
I highly recommend this game and it's definitely one of my favorites this year. It would have totally been out of sight, out of mind if I didn't watch Jim Sterling play the first 5 minutes of it so credit to him for turning me on to it. Game length averages anywhere from 4-6 hours if you breeze through it but it can last a few more hours than that if you look for all the secrets and go for all the achievements. You can return to any previous area you've been through via fast travel so there is absolutely nothing keeping you from going back and collecting everything. Whether you feel that length of game time is worth $20 I'll leave that up to you but I do not regret my full price purchase.
