Call of Cthulhu was an experience I will never forget. It was difficult, unforgiving, and unfair for the entire game. It was very glitchy, had a crash or two, and was full of aimless wandering. But it was all worth it in the end. As with most psychological thrillers, the game liked to toy with you in every way, by forcing you to endure absolute horror, figure out impossible puzzles, and continue living knowing that everything around is both a lie and is out to get you. CoC DCotE was grandly successful in using Lovecraft's style of horror, by making you wonder whether or not what you are seeing is real. Did a Deep One just kill that guy? Or did the protaginist kill that guy and only imagined the Deep One? With how often you are alone and surrounded by myths and crazy people, how can you be sure that what you're seeing is really what is happening? You face Fishmen, Deep Ones, a Shoggoth, Flying Polyps, Dagon, Hydra, Servants of Cthulhu, and other such creatures found in Lovecraft's tales as you play through a fantastic reimagining of Shadow Over Innsmouth.
Because of how this game tortured me with constant insanity, endless questions, aimless wandering, failure, difficulty, bugs, and doubt, I probably won't play through this again for a long time. It was a terrifying journey but it was worth it just to finish the game and experience the atmosphere that is Call of Cthulhu.
I go now, for the images that haunt my dreams are too much torture to handle. Everything this game had forced me through was too much. The questions, the wonders, the idea that there may in the future be a sequel, I just cannot handle the stress. So after I have cataloged my experience, I will throw myself to the streets below this home, before the creatures can find me and pressure me into attempting to aquire an A rank through the game. I hear them now. Buy this game, see what I have seen, and you will finally understand. They're at the door now! Scratching! Pounding! I just want it to end! The window! The window!

Magic mouse companion is back, it's basically a projectile that travels along most surfaces, allowing you to reach unreachable buttons and on some levels you can swap places with it (which doubles as a weapon, since it kills some enemies and destroys some blocks while you travel towards the mouse).

Napoleon: Total War was an interesting addition to the Total War series, created in hopes of improving upon the mechanics of Empire: Total War. On it's own, the game is not remarkable at all, but with the right mods, it suddenly becomes one of the best strategy games out there.
NTW obviously takes place in Napoleonic times and features prominently a series of campaigns that mirror Napoleon's wars from the 1790s to 1815. The main campaign of the game is his European war effort from 1805 to 1812, beginning with the War of the Third Coalition and ending around the time Napoleon was trapeezing about the Russian steppes. The campaign, like all Total War campaigns, features elements of economy, infrastructure, and regional control that bring about challenges to building your empire and maintaining control, as well as feeding, paying, and supplying your troops. In addition to this and the usual mess that is diplomacy, NTW features weather prominently, with zones of attrition existing across the map, in places where weather and terrain  demoralize men while also killing them off. Spend too long in one of these zones, and you will have no army.
You can also play the parts of Russia, Britain, Prussia, and Austria, in this European campaign. It should be mentioned that without mods, you cannot play any other nation in this or any of the campaigns (which include an Italy-centered campaign and Napoleon's expedition to Egypt. In both of these, you can only play as the French). This totally take away from the fun of ETW, in which you can take any nation that existed at the time and turn it into a dominant power. And, because the game mechanics sevearly tilt the odds in favor of Napoleon (which is both fair and unfair), playing as any of the afore-mentioned powers can be a fruitless struggle in futility and swarms of French soldiers.
The battles themselves are where NTW, as all other Total War games, truly shines. commanding vast armies of a thousand soldiers on the field of battle in real time is exhilarating. NTW did a particularly good job with programming for soldiers (it is a step up from ETW, which is a relief to many), and especially with artillery. Spectaular graphics make the battles all the more incredible, but this has always been a hallmark of the Total War series. And of course, there are some problems with battles in NTW:
-1) You really can just sit there in a defensive starting position while the enemy AI bayonet-charges you. It's like Pickett's charge every ♥♥♥♥ing game.
-2) Shooting mechanics are not accurate for the period. There is no firing by rank, and light infantry, which have the same weapons as normal line infantry, can shoot as far and as acurately as most riflemen.
-3) AI controled soldiers are prone to fire towards you, no matter if there are three units of their own men in front of them. Again, it's not much of a fight.
-4) Battles seperate from campaigns have the added benifit of a complete lack of variety in maps, most of which seem to be geared towards tournament play.
NTW does offer compelling battles, when fought against other players in Multiplayer mode. They even tried to add in multiplayer mode for campaigns, which was a brilliant idea and could have been wonderful but instead is a poorly-programmed piece of♥♥♥♥♥♥
The only way to have fun while playing a campaign, or to add fun while playing multiplayer, is to use the mod known as DarthMod. There is a DarthMod made by independent sources for every Total War game, and in NTW it is almost essential to have this mod in addition to the game. The mode enhances the sound quality, texture quality (smoke lingers in clouds, and blood splatters when soldiers are shot), melee fighting programming, the number of soldies per unit (from around 160 to about 360!) and most importantly, AI programing. Soldiers now fire by rank, and the AI is a cometent and worth opponent, both in battle and in campaign. Additionally, you unlock every availible nation with DarthMod. I've gone on rampages as Hannover, Portugal, Bavaria, and many more.
In short, if you are looking for a good Total War game, this is probably not the one to get. However, if Empire was your favorite Total War game, or if you prefer guns and cannons to spears and arrows, then get this game and the DarthMod for it.
Without DarthMod, NTW is a 4 out of 10.
With DarthMod, I give Napoleon: Total War an 8 out of 10.

I'm a few hours into this game so far and am thoroughly enjoying it. I'll try and list the pros and cons based on my opinions. I'll start with cons.
Cons:
-Everyone plays as the same character, hence, Victor Vran. The individuality comes from how you build your character.
-Lack of diversity as far as weapons and abilities go. This is crushing when combined with how everyone is already Victor Vran. There are only a handful of weapon types and demon powers.
-Lack of customization of Victor Vran himself aside from changing the color of entire outfits, and there are only seven or so in the current state of the game.
-Legendary weapons don't seem to be much better than properly built rares at the moment, but that is my opinion.
-Not many uses for currency seeing as any equipment you buy would be rapidly eclipsed by any loot.
-No trading.
Pros:
-Local co-op! My favorite point. It is very difficult to find games on PC with this. Note that local co-op players use other save slots but you will share a stash and most rewards you both will recieve. You can use two controllers or one player can use  keyboard and mouse.
-Adequately challenging. I have been playing on hard mode as a personal preference due to loot and exp effects.
-Controller support. Woot.
-Fun.
-Card System. I recommend reading up on this system before you play, as it is very important and also a very awesome mechanic. Essentially you equip cards to your character to uniquely build him. These cards have varying effects that can define what type of player you are.
-Transmutation. You can upgrade weapons, powers, cards, and such through a system and even gamble them to make different ones. This is where the vast majority of your currency will go and I like this system.
In conclusion, I do recommend this game. It's worth its price but maybe not by a large margin. If I hadn't purchased it without the intention of the local co-op I maybe wouldn't praise it as high, but I certainly don't regret buying it and I will continue to play it.

My second problem: when I try to start a new game the game crashes, solution go here and download it   [

Once you have the file downloaded put in the Fallout 3 folder.

4. Select compatibility and choose windows vista

7. Select 1 cpu not all of them.

2. Find the line: bUseThreadedAI=0 (you can use ctrl+f to find it faster)

I have a love-hate relationship with this game.  I have spent many hours building up a humble town, doing what I can to grow the economy and population, but then ultimately it all falls apart.  At some point, my population's demand for food outstrips the supply, and my once overflowing surplus of firewood becomes depleted.  When my town enters the death spiral of starvation and a stagnant economy, I can only play so long before I accept defeat and start over again.  The experience reminds me of boom and bust cycle of animal populations, when abundant resources lead to explosive growth and then swift demise once the food runs out.  But make no mistake:  The ever-present reality of defeat is what makes this game addictive.
However, there are some issues that prevent the game from being more enjoyable.  First off, citizens will often be assigned to jobs that are far away from their home, resulting in a long travel to complete a small amount of work before they return home for food or shelter.  This is especially troublesome when your town expands outward.  You will find that a building is taking forever to get built because by the time a worker reaches the site, they can only complete a few units of work before needing to walk back.  This adds inefficiency to your economy, which ultimately increases the changes of the town unraveling.  I feel that allowing citizens to move to homes closer to their work would be realistic and reduce a lot of frustration for players.
Another issue is that mines and stone quaries are not worth the investment of building and supplying them with laborers.   The output is far less than what you receive from just trading firewood and using those workers for forestry and wood cutting.  Coal, iron and stone are essential for growing your town, so this has a huge effect.  While you could argue that this is part of learning a good strategy to have a successful town, the ineffectiveness of the mines and quaries prevents alternative strategies from being worthwhile.  A balanced game allows the player to chose among several effective, yet different, strategies to reach the common goal, and in this instance Banished comes short.  So yes, if you play this game, be sure to keep the firewood supply flowing and trade it for other essential resources.  I was able to reach much higher town populations after learning this.
These are the two largest issues I can think of at the moment, which really stand out to me whenever my town enters the dreaded "death spiral" phase.  It's not that these issues merely make the game more difficult, it's that they make the game needlessly more difficult.  If these were addressed in a future patch or expansion, I would enjoy the game much more.

First review: Mixed feelings, some nice surprise and some major dissapointement...
Well, overall I would not recommend this game at it's current state, definitely not... OK, I admit, I am not a big FPS player even so I had my hours on CS, Duke Nuke Them, Battlefields and others but I like realistic simulation. So when I read about Verdun being a very realistic FPS happening in WWI trenches I was hot and I got it... too early maybe?
Let's start by the pros, and there is quite a few:
-Really accurate and historical uniforms/weapons/battlefield render
-Impressive ballistic and accuracy
-Quite a few different type of soldiers available with each a few variations in weapon types and action type (melee/distant fight)
-Nice set of maps, quite balanced
- Very interesting gameplay recreating trench warefare with assault/hold/retreat movements based on score/kills
Now the cons, and that is where it's gonna hurt a little.... a lot.... too much?
-Graphics : Well, for a 2017 game I am definitely not impress by the lack of fluidity of the players, the hard edged terrain depiction and most of all the hue/color choice of the dev is weird... I guess to give it a "realistic" feel they kind of greyed/low saturatated colors... it s overall looking nice but can be a bit confusing and not so realistic (Early French colonial troops were decimated while charging wearing bright red uniforms...just to mention this well known historical fact).
- Gameplay: That is where it is gonna hurt guys, sorry... Well for a realistic WWI FPS, I give the gameplay 3.5/10...
Straight to the point: I was expecting something more like Vietcong ( a realistic FPS developed by Pterodon back in 2003) where:
+++ when you die, you die... till next round your team gotta do without you and your skills, fair enough, you dead...and if ou gonna have respawn, maybe not in the middle of the fire fight just becuse your CEO is there... usually reinforcement are sent from the BACK, Mr Spoke does not just teleport them in the middle of the fight objective...
+++ when you kill and enemy of find a friendly KIA you can switch weapons/amo/nades, just like in real life guys cause running out of ammo in trench warfare surrounded by dead soldiers/ weapons /amo case and  is most unlikely to happen...
+++ Barb wire can kill you and his resistant to nades/mortar/ flame thrower... That is some really good quality barb wire, must be german made :)
So overall I am a bit confuse as I can see how the dev s are trying to take a realistic approach to the gameplay and yet seems to be missing the core of it, but that is only my OWN opinion.  Realistically in WWI, every shelling of an area would litteraly terratransform it to a brad new battlefields with new craters, barb wires being destroyed or moved by the blasts... only trenchs would remain as static point...every assault then having a random new cover/high points... Nades and mortar should definitly have an impact on crates/barb wires/dead bodies... com on guys, a mortar shell on a dead horse body and the dead horse is still there to offer protection? Dam, that is some tough meat we have right there!
At the end I wished it was more time spent on developing realistic gameplay and less time spend on nice unrealistic graphic elements (ok for the post card look but ...) like running out of ammo in front of a amo box in a trench full of guys and nobody can give me amo???? That got me that bad review to be honnest!!!!
Conclusion: At this stage, this game did not meet my expectations. Yet I reckon the devs are trying to give it a realistic feel that is really nice and unsual in this genre game. I am not giving up on this game and I look forward to see how the game will develop popularity among gamers with the new expansion coming soon...

So far, the most complex and the most difficult to learn global strategy game about the World War 2. Choose some (any of known at moment) country, and prepare it to the unevitable bloodbath. You may not be the one who'll start it, but in any scenario you'll have to deal with it somehow. Generally - by warfare means, as this series, unlike some other Paradox games, is certainly lacking proper diplomacy. However, there are spies, who alone can provide quite a challenging game on their own! I am so missing them when playing Hearts of Iron 4 now...
So, you run a country, choosing what you'll be producing and researching, what allies you'll pick, and what goals you're hoping to achieve at the aftermath. You preparing grunts - providing them with technically advanced weaponry, making drills - and then sending them to death. To make sure the score will be at your benefit, you gotta learn many details of operating the armies, and, the most, the logistics. Logistics! It can burn minds, but, if you'll master it, you are ready to pass the exams at your local HQ school. Which seems a nice achievement for me.
However, to answer a general question, if the game is worth buying... I don't think so. Especially if you're new to Paradox strategies. There are too much info to master, and too little in-game measures to ease the pain. Tutorial is just a cameo for Shekelgruber, who seems to be one of the gamedev's favourites. And what Adolf can teach you? Yeah, nothing good. There are, of course, some helpful youtubers, who are willing to get you going... But even with them, HoI 3 is basically a nerd's stuff. If your general field of expertise is shooters and racing games like NFS, I seriously doubt that's the game you need to buy. I'm tired of reading all those stupid negative "reviews", where people blaming HoI 3 for being too difficult for them. I agree, it's hard to learn, and there are some questionable mechanics like using of artillery or air/naval forces... and diplomacy is far from perfect as well... and interface is so lame... and dlc's are total crud, basically...
The list of negative features is much longer, but, all in all, Hearts of Iron 3 is still a biggest and arguable the best strategy on the given history period. And it's rivals are - Hearts of Iron 2 and 4! 2nd is so good, but so old, that not every PC will manage to run it. And the 4th is much more oriented on multiplayer, than on single-play. So if you look for really deep game with thousands of outcomes and countless possibilities for replaying - that's the right stuff. Just come prepared and don't whine about, if it's too complex for you.

It's been a while now since this game has been released and the sequel is already well on its way. So this is a short review as of November 2017 Including the most recent DLC.
The Crew is a sort of Hybrid between classic 'linear' racing games like NFS and open world titles like Fuel.
For everyone who is not a fan of the 'always online' gameplay: You can pretty much turn off all online notifcations/invites etc. and essentially have what comes close to a Single Player Experience.
With the most recent Expansion Bikes where added and I have to say they are lots of fun. Be it a Racebike for zipping around in an urban environments ( especially between cars ) or  a Dirtbike for really going off grid and doing lots of jumps, finding creative lines through the environment and even stunts - it gives the game a cool new perspective.
The open environments are visually impressive - combined with complete day/night cycle and weather it's one of the best looking open world driving games i have played.
There surely are more Hardcore Simulation Titles Like Forza, Dirt, F1 etc. The Crew combines relatively easy/casual gameplay with a great open world. And if you are looking for it there are many races/challenges that can be tough.
The open world is a scaled down and somewhat 'morphed' version of the real continental usa. All places however look and feel good and give you a real sense of experiencing a specific region of this big country.
It should be mentioned that Microtransactions are included in this title; to complete your car collection you are incentivized to purchase ingame Credits for actual currency. Some cars can only be bought for real currency.
However - If you follow the main campaign and upgrade your car throughout you have a relatively solid machine at the end.
All in all i think it's a good game and might even be worth a look for open world fans who are not necessarily racing fans - just for exploring a beautiful looking big gameworld.
Give it a try.

It's not flawless. The forced stealth sections drag on far too long in the beginning and toward the end. The chase sequences, while initially being very spur-of-the-moment, absolutely punish you for taking literally more than two seconds to figure out what to do next and will require a lot of redoing it once you fail. The save system is archaic in that you can only save at certain areas and not with simple quicksaves. The biggest nail in the coffin is that the game could be outright impossible to finish depending on a graphical glitch about 75% of the way into the story, and you cannot progress without looking up a walkthrough on what to do or just using a save file from someone who made it past that part in the game. And the game can be difficult when it comes to gunfights.
Still, this game is great. A great Lovecraftian story, great atmosphere, great voice acting, logical actions throughout, some tense firefights, a great health system, and some good puzzles. Just give it a shot until you get weapons and see if you like where it's taking you.

Puzzle-platformers are a dime-a-dozen. *Great* puzzle platformers are rare. Games starring a goat are even rarer.
Which makes Escape Goat 2 a rare beast indeed. It is an *excellent* puzzle-platformer, predominantly because it feels so novel. It doesn't resort to the same hackneyed puzzles that you've solved a hundred times before. The suite of mechanics, which are steadily drip-fed throughout the game, provide scope for truly surprising puzzles with solutions that might well make you giggle and clap your hands when you figure them out.
Fair warning, it gets hard. The difficulty ramp-up is steady, but the game leads you in gently. The latter half of the game will challenge (and probably frustrate) you, while still being solvable, albeit after 15 minutes of staring the screen and shaking your head.

This is certainly my favorite total war game to date.  It features several different campaigns that take from the beginning to the end of the prestigious general's career.  If your computer is capable, the visuals are gorgeous, especially once the combat starts and smoke covers the field and blows in the wind.  The AI is decent for a total war game, and much better than Empire's AI, which could never seem to correctly fight line battles.  I love how tactical the gameplay can get, and this total war emphasizes on positioning and formation to win battles, not just charging everything in sight.  There have been several instances in custom and multiplayer battles when my smaller or less experienced force defeated a much more powerful army simply by being in better formation, and I love that.  I feel like each unit in this game is useful and can succeed when commanded well.  The game itself is crisp and clean and relatively bug free, and local multiplayer games have been a blast.  I highly recommend this game to anyone interested in the time period or fans of the total war games, particularly empire due to the simularities.  What I expected to be merely a $15 mod for Empire total war turned out to be a much more polished and enjoyable game all around.

Might & Magic: Heroes VI is a turn-based strategy game from Ubisoft Entertainment. It is another installment in Might & Magic franchise.
Might & Magic: Heroes VI has kinda unique gameplay, you start with one castle, develop it, build a barracks, train troops in a turn-based gameplay, but to move your troops around you will need a hero. When you move your hero and the troops he command around, you can engage random enemy, found resources or found something that may upgrade your heroes, increase experience or even someone to join your troops. When engaged in battle, you will enter the battlefield view where you will play the battle in a chess like gameplay. It's kinda fun. But in terms of hardcore strategy play, well, this game is not that hard. In fact even though you can create many heroes, using only one hero is enough to win the game.
Might & Magic: Heroes VI graphics are good, not great but good. The detail and the model and texture are beautiful enough. The performance of the game are also good, and the game runs smooth and stable without any issues.
Might & Magic: Heroes VI is a good game that if you like turn-based strategy game, Might & Magic: Heroes VI can occupy you for many hours. I recommend this.

TL;DR: Cool atmospheric hack'n slash looter with refreshing mechanics and satisfying combat but a pretty boring story
Surprisingly good game. Got it in a bundle a while back, decided to try it out. Didn't expect much, but I ended up liking it. You control the character directly with WASD. At least, that's the default option, you can choose to play with the mouse.
You can jump, walljump and roll all the time. The game has some cool hidden spots which utilize the jumping/walljumping mechanism well. Pretty soon you recognize some ledges which need some wall jumping to get to.
The character building and combat is pretty straight forward. I loved it for its simplicity.
There are no skills or attributes. Instead, every weapon type has its own 2 special attacks available right from the start.
You'll find your favourite weapons pretty soon, as they all have a slightly different play style... Well, the core mechanic is still hack'n slash, but you'll see.
Instead of attributes, you can equip cards. These cards can be changed at any time to give you options in different situations, if you're looking for a more tactical approach. I just dumped everything in as much crit damage as possible, but then again.. I'm not really that tactical.
The missions are 100% linear. You just follow the 1 quest you have which is shown under your map at any given time.
You're free to explore as much as you like, clear caves, get l00t, but there won't be any side quests etc.
There are no classes, but there is some sort of costume feature. Every costume gives a different kind of perk and have their own pros and cons.
For these costumes also applies the fact that you can change it whenever you want.
Gameplay-wise I'm very pleased. But the story is kind of boring. I just ended up skipping everything, just to get back to the fun gameplay.

There seem to be a lot of mixed reviews on this game. If you loved Heroes 5, you'll probably like this one as well, but I can see why some of the die hards would complain.
Pros:
-It's Heroes. I've played the incarnations of this game since the original, and have enjoyed every version (except for 4, seriously what were they thinking).
-Every creature has a special ablility. I like that, because it means if you only have low level guys, you can still use stratagy to outwitt a larger army.
-There's a bunch of new creatures to explore.
-All of the town types are evenly matched. I found in the previous games Necromancers (my favorite) had generally weaker monsters compared to other towns, but would make up for it with numbers as you fought. The Necromancy skill has changed in this one so you don't mass up a swarm of skeletons from your enemy's corpses, but your army can hold it's onw anyway.
Cons:
-U-Play. I've never liked using U-Play, and this game is the best example of why. Aside from the bulky and unecessary U-Play shell that runs, you have to have a connection to their server to access most of the game. Also, if you're not connected, you can't access any of your saved games. And most annoying is the autosave. I found that after about two weeks of in game play, my computer would bog down to the point of freezing the game. I was able to fix the problem by not allowing the auto save, but that means I have to save my game myself often.
-Skills. I honestly don't know what I don't like about the new level up skills format, but something about it rubs me the wrong way. I do like that you have to earn your spells by leveling up, but there is something about the new system that just feels .... blah.
-Enemy Heroes are really tough. In a custom map, you can spend a couple hours building up your castle and hero. You'll find that the random map monsters are fairly easy to dispatch, but then an enemy hero will show up. "Holy Crap, where'd he get that army from?" or "How did he vaporize my stack of creatures with that one lightning bolt?" I find them wickedly powerful. The campaign though, which I havn't yet finished, seems much easier.
-You really only need one hero. You beef up one guy and go smashing. If an enemy is sneeking up on your castle, no problem, just use your town gate spell and you're home. It's also too easy to get your hero back every time. While I get nobody wants to loose their big main hero, I find this takes away the stratagy of defense for your castles.
Overall, I do enjoy the game and would suggest it to anyone, both fans of the series and newcomers alike!

I strongly recommend you play this game if you love turn based strategy games, RPG games, or are a sucker for a good story. Easily one of the best strategy games I have ever played (and I have played a hell of a lot!) - don't be scared of UPlay and Conflux (more on this later).
The game is at its core a Turn Based Strategy game, but also has strong RPG elements - levelling up, skill points, hero inventory, reputation points, faction variations etc.
I would strongly suggest watching some YouTube videos to see how the game plays out.
Briefly speaking you have a game map where you move your heroes around, collect various items/dynasty weapons for your hero's inventory as well as wood, ore, crystal, gold and fight neutrals. There are also various structures you can interact with which confer various bonuses, or grant units for your army etc.
On this map there are various towns and forts which you fight to capture, and once captured you build up to allow you to recruit more units, higher level units or get bonuses for your battles.
Battles involve moving stacks of units around on a grid, destroying enemy stacks in a variety of ways. There are a large variety of units in the game, roughly 7 types per faction - each with an upgraded version so really 14 per faction. Units often have special abilities, like being able to puppet enemy units to do your bidding, or charge through stacks slaughtering ally and enemy alike. All the factions have very different units so it never gets boring.
In addition to units being moved around, your heroes can also use various abilities each turn, you can unlock more by spending skill points as you level up. There are loads of hero skills split in to Might types or Magic types, and these are futher classified into many sub-groups, too many to list here, but for instance for the Magic branch you have separate skill trees for Fire, Water, Light, Dark, Earth, Air, Prime (not all are accessible for each faction)
Hero Dynasty weapons can also grant more abilities, as can items - many items come in sets (Diablo style) and wearing the full set can give you some very nice bonuses.
There are Five factions in the main game (Haven, Inferno, Sanctuary, Stronghold, Necropolis), and a Sixth faction (Dungeon) in the expansion Shades of Darkness - which I also strongly recommend you get! Each faction has completely different units, different available skill trees, faction specific abilities, reputation abilities, different game play and look very different too.
Sound and music in the game is awesome, the battle sound track is stuck in my head.
Graphics are amazing too; the detail on the maps, on the units, structures, flora is great. Even the main menu has switchable themes - all of which are great (personal favourite is the dungeon one).
The loading screens have some really nice drawings too, I had the Haven one as a wallpaper for some time.
Units have really nice animations, and even have idle animations - Dungeon's Assassin starts spinning his daggers above his head like helicopter rotor blades and gets lifted off his feet and then drops down headfirst (all an animation - has no effect on gameplay..!), Vampires start playing rock music and using their swords as an electric guitar - really shocked me the first time it happened -"where is that rock music coming from..?"
The storyline is amazing - I was eager to learn more just after the intro video!
The game is split into many different campaigns - each campaign has up to 4 missions. The core game has one tutorial campaign, and then one campaign for each of the five core factions. The expansions add four more campaigns.
The story is great but as the core campaigns all run simultaneously in the story chronology, it is possible to play one mission in one campaign and then ruin the story for yourself as you now know the outcome of another mission for another faction that you haven't played yet.
I would recommend you play the Custom games and Campaign missions in the following order:
Heart of Nightmares (Custom game accessed via the Custom game option in the main menu!), Prologue 1, Prologue 2, Stronghold 1, Sanctuary 1, Haven 1, Inferno 1, Necropolis 1, Stronghold 2, Sanctuary 2, Haven 2, Necropolis 2, Sanctuary 3, Stronghold 3, Inferno 2, Necropolis 3, Inferno 3, Sanctuary 4, Stronghold 4, Haven 3, Necropolis 4, Haven 4, Inferno 4, Epilogues, Pirates of the Savage Sea Campaign, Danse Macabre Campaign, Dungeon Campaign,  Necropolis Campaign 2.
Maybe copy-paste that list into a text file somewhere and delete missions as you complete them!
The only issue some people have, is with UPlay. Upon installing the game via Steam, you may have issues launching the game. Just install the latest Uplay off the Ubisoft site, see this link:
Another issue is that fighting neutrals can get repetitive as they are often so weak. Turn on Quick Battle in the options menu, and if you have a decent army, the battle will be resolved for you automatically.
Gameplay tips - The Reinforcements skill is the key to victory in most scenarios early on- use it on stacks that are going to attack / get attacked and you will never have any losses from your main army.
If you have other issues, just ask in the Steam Forum for the game, there are plenty of people that can help there!
I'll say it again, I strongly recommend you play this game! Or you can just wait for Heroes of Might and Magic VII which is currently in development - can vote on factions to appear in the game etc on the developer's website!

Let me open with some brutal honesty: Banished is probably not for you.
Now that the honesty is out of the way, let me just say that this game is spectacular. The design is flawless in it's ability to drop you in the wilderness with a few people, some houses, and barely enough resources to get going before winter hits you square in the crotch.
Banished is a sandbox simulation in which you attempt to keep a group of villagers alive as they start a new town. They will not make this task easy for you. From the beginning of the game you are given essentially zero hints and you have minimal resources, but you have access to the construction plans for every building in the game. This makes the learning curve very steep indeed. And to hinder you further, much of the vital information you need to keep your village from being wiped out completely by plague, starvation, or even natural disasters, is hidden from you in menus that are difficult to parse. Once you do finally figure out the bare bones of how the game works your villagers will stil die because their neighbors are greedily hoarding all of the food and firewood for themselves due to unfortunately scant AI.
But if you can get past all of that, you will sink hours and hours into this wonderfully deep, rich simulation of just how brutal life on the frontier could be.

Personally I find this to be the best HoMM game since the 3rd, don't really get the bad rep it got which seems to be aimed mostly towards uplay rather than the game itself, it's a shame.
Unlike HoMM 5 the maps aren't nearly as linear (which was my biggest issue with the 5th entry)
Neither have I run into too many bugs other than the camera-bug which makes me unable to look around with my mouse and having to nagivate with the arrow-keys instead (only a reboot seems to fix this from my experience) but fortunately it doesn't occure too often.
Unlike the 3rd one you don't have the whole RNG randomness of skills whenever a hero lvls up, instead you get this RPG-esque option to put out talent points into either Magic or Might. The balance doesn't seem to be all there neither, might is a far superior choice over magic from what i've seen and the factions seems to be a bit unbalanced as well. There are less resources to think about, etc. You can also not steal mines in the same way you could previously since they are all connected to the owner of the nearby town so it's a bit less micro-heavy than previously as well. For some this might be a big issue.
While the overarching story might not be anything amazing (neither was any of the previous installment's stories) I still enjoyed the campaign a great deal, playing from the different perspectives of Duke Slava's children, one for each faction.
And honestly if you are into the story that much I'd recommend going for the Might & Magic series instead.
All in all, It's a fun game if you can look past the whole double-DRM thing and some changed core features such as less resources and how the whole territory-war works.

I didn't like this anywhere near as much as DS1, and it had some major problems for me. The primary one was that there's absolutely no way to use mods of any sort with this version of DS2, even basic texture replacers, so if you don't have a controller, you're stuck with mouse and keyboard but the game still showing the Xbox button prompts. This was supposedly a better port job by Fromsoftware as compared to DS1, because this one doesn't need DSFix to be playable, but the issue with the button prompts is almost game-breaking for me. I had to go out and buy an off-brand 360 controller so I could play, and while that was a good decision because now I have the controller, I
. I see now that the Steam page says an Xbox controller is strongly recommended, but I'm mostly of the opinion that if I wanted to use a controller, I would be playing on console.
The game's "story" was another sticking point for me. Dark Souls as a series is known for the fact that what story there is isn't super clear or easy to find, but in this one it seemed mostly throwaway. Details seemed to be mostly hidden in item descriptions, bosses had no real lore connection to their location (that I could see, anyway), and it was never clear to me at any point why I was actually there. It turned out I beat a thing and got to sit on a chair forever? But then I just kept playing anyway and went into NG+ and did some similarly unconnected DLC content (that I found SUPER hard to find, by the way), and yeah.
Location and geography was the last big problem I had. I was sort of expecting it to be at least loosely related to Lordran and Firelink Shrine, but nope. Additionally, places with totally disparate times of day and weather were situated right next to each other, and things I absolutely should have been able to see from afar were instead magically hidden behind a wall. I'd go from daytime in a foggy forest to nighttime and pouring rain just by going through a tunnel; an enormous lava lake with a castle situated in it was reached via the top level of a big structure in an area that was not volcanic
. There's impossible stuff in DS1, where you go down through Blighttown, down through the the Great Hollow, and then you end up on the shore of a lake that appears to almost have sky over it; that was always deeply unsettling to me. And then there's this, where volcanoes and arctic areas and forests and night and day are just jammed in next to each other like in a Mario game. Place names that NPCs were from were tossed at me and never mentioned again or explained. I just got more clarity about the story from the wikia page about Dranglaic than I did from doing 2.5 playthroughs of the game for achievements. I will say that there were more places that felt like good old Legend of Zelda type video game levels, though. Sen's Fortress was about all that DS1 had that felt like that, but this had several, most notably the Shaded Woods that had fog, giggling jars, cat people, and enemies that looked like player specters.
I don't know, it just didn't feel as cohesive to me as DS1 did. Enemy and boss designs, overall, were still excellent. It seemed like a lot of things were just human variants, but I also know that I went "what are YOU?" an awful lot on seeing new things. There were also some things that made zero sense, like the inexplicable lion warriors. Locations felt like they were not only randomly placed but also just remixed from DS1. There were improvements to the physical gameplay, compared to DS1, including a number of things I've seen from watching LPs of Bloodborne; being able to use multiples of an item all at once, for example, the ability to put three weapons on each hand (and two rings per hand, thank you), and the use of shortcuts that DS1 had some of but definitely not on this level. There was a lot of reward to going through an area and then finding a door and recognizing what was on the other side of the door, because it was the start of the area. Armor and weapon designs were very good too.
Actually, another problem that I had was that unlike DS1, this one didn't handle my playing in offline mode at ALL well. I play offline because I really have no interest in ever having to tangle with another player (and also the sheer quantity of notes/specters in many areas was getting on my nerves), but doing so in this one kept Steam from both letting achievements pop and from tracking my play time. I racked up almost 60 hours and did get all of the achievements, but clearly my stats still say only about 12 hours played, and I had to use a third-party manager to manually trigger the achievements.
- I do recommend this, but it's definitely not Dark Souls 1. Gameplay was solid, graphics were good, sound and music were both good, but story and location were muddled and the inability to change even game textures was a real hangup for me. It's remedied by getting a controller, but then you can't remap those controls either (when I was looking up the Xbox controls, I saw there's a thing you can switch jump to, but I had no power to do that and get it off of L3). Basically, DS1 is staying installed because sometimes you just want to kill some stuff, but this is getting uninstalled because I'm through with it, I 100%'d it, and I never want to play it again although it was fun at the time.

I haven't played much, so I might be wrong on some of these. If so, you can blame the game for not keeping my interest long enough to learn, or for not having taught me through gameplay or tooltips already.
For the price, I expected a lot more. The core concepts are derivative of other games (Red Orchestra and Battlefield mostly) and Verdun does almost nothing to improve on any of these stolen mechanics. It's a mish-mash of good ideas that are never fleshed out independently, and so fit awkwardly together. For example:
It has a progression system similar to how other shooters have leveling systems. When you earn enough points, you level up and earn a sort of currency that you can spend to permanently unlock new loadout variations of any of the game's many, MANY classes. The game is extremely generous with these, so you're always guaranteed to have enough to fully unlock all loadouts for any class in the game. It makes you wonder why they bothered at all. It doesn't feel rewarding to unlock anything. It doesn't force you to understand the core concept of the class before offering you advanced forms. It's just meaningless, menu clicking busywork.
It has an emphasis on working in 4 man squads, much like Battlefield and other successful shooters. it attempts to incentivize players into doing this by offering buffs to anyone who's worked to level up as a squad. You level up as a squad by playing with the same person/people over and over again. This sounds like a good idea for all of five seconds before you actually start to think about it. What are the chances that you and three friends are all going to be up to playing at the same time consistently? It teaches players to seek out already successful high level squads and piggy back off of their effort. If a fresh install newbie squads up with two other dudes who spend a ton of time playing together, that new player is going to have advantages that four players who haven't played with each other but have played the game a long time won't.
But let's say that's okay, and you have three friends who are in to the game and can't wait to start leveling up as a squad and reaping the rewards. How do you level up? As near as I can tell there is only one way - by sticking really close to the squad leader. That's it. The game actively incentivizes you to play badly, and favors the type of classes that travel together in close quarters. So if you want to try a sniper class, you're out of luck. Want to not get wiped out all at once by a well-placed mortar or grenade? Too bad. Think you're all focused on one area and are about to get flanked? Don't travel too far away, or the game will yank your lease and scold you for having an independent thought. Because don't forget, those buffs you want to work so hard to earn? Many of them are only in effect when you're near the squad leader.
Let's talk about the classes. There are 18 types of squads, each containing 4 individual and unique classes in them. Most of them give you a bolt-action rifle. if you're like me and love one-shotting people from a muddy, bombed-out foxhole then this probably isn't a problem for you. But if you do dare to try and branch out and try out something fun, chances are that slot is taken by another player. Sure, it's realistic to have the battlefield consist of mostly this one type of weapon, but since each class is only available to one person per squad, you might end up getting shafted and forced into a class you despise. If you do manage to snag a "fun" class, prepare for constant notifications of people offering to trade you slots. Maybe you're like me and don't mind and so accept one of these offers. The game acts as if it's killed you, which means a potentially very long respawn time. Yes, it punishes you for your generosity.
I was really excited to see how the game handled artillery. No game has ever handled indirect fire in a way that satisfied me, and people touted this game as very realistic. I was disappointed. Instead of actually manning mortars, or even clicking on a 2d map like other games, to call in mortar strikes you have to 1. be a squad leader 2. point at the ground and right click. Humongous let down. If you're like me and will give any game with artillery a chance, give this one a pass.
Aside from how boring this is, it also creates a conflict with the other abilities of the squad leader. Since each squad leader acts as a mobile spawn beacon for his squad, it incentivizes him to be sneaky, get close to the enemy, infiltrate, and hunker down. But to lay down mortar fire, you have to expose yourself. If you're close to the enemy you're trying to mortar, you're going to bomb yourself. The lazy click-on-a-map solution is looking better and better.
Now a rapid fire list of things that will eventually annoy you to the point of regretting your purchase and wasted time:
-There are many places on each map where it would seem you could go prone, but can't. You will die many times because you couldn't dive to safety before someone gets a bead on you and puts a bullet in you. If you're like me and panic, hitting the PRONE button over and over, you might accidentally toggle it, meaning your character will drop to his knees, the ground, then back to his knees, then standing again. The enemy team will most likely reject your challenge to an Impromptu Dance Contest and just shoot you.
-Very rarely, because the game tries to spawn you by your squad leader, you will spawn in barbed wire. Slowly bleeding out is your only option in this scenario.
-if you want to mount a ledge without standing, you're out of luck. So much for the immersion of stepping up onto the fire step and carefully leaning over the top of the trench with your rifle, nope, you have to do a cartoonish mario jump and hope you can mash the CROUCH button fast enough when you land before someone takes your head off.
-Limited Spawn points. The game likes to spawn in waves, meaning half of your team is going to spawn in the exact same place as you at the exact same time. This gives people who know the maps well what I feel is an unfair advantage (you'll agree the first time you and half your team spawn into machine gun fire), and punishes the people who are brave enough to take off running and push out by ensuring they're the first to fall and start that respawn countdown all over again.
-getting caught "deserting" will eventually drive you mad. In the main gamemode, if your team has a failed attack, you are forced to retreat. The screen turns grey and a countdown begins, much like some battlefield games. You have something less than a minute before the game kills you and tells you you were executed for desertion. I can't tell if the game means to only incentivize you to retreat, or if it means to present you a choice, because MANY people like to maintain their location and catch the enemy team unawares as they think they have an entire minute to advance unabated. It's suicide, but you'll probably end up taking a hell of a lot of the enemy with you. It's something of an immersion killer when you hear someone say "go on without me, I'll hold em off for you" and then they're given a magical, telekinetic summary execution for being a traitor. Bad for morale, really. If you're less heroic and more derpy like me, you'll end up being executed because you got stuck in barbed wire and the timer ran out. I like to pretend it's a mercy killing when that happens.
Positive things:
-Most of the guns feel great to shoot, and the TTK is refreshingly, and realistically low. When you shoot someone, they die.
-The environments, maps, and sound design are all on point. If it wasn't for the wacky aforementioned mechanics, I would claim it's one of the most immersive games out there, and debatebly the best WW1 game in existence.
All in all it's a disappointing game that I would only recommend to die-hard history buffs who are okay with a clunky, watered down Battlefield/Red Orchestra.

TL; DR Game hasn't aged well, play TF2.
Let me start by saying I wanted to like this game. I had a positive bias before I even played it.
I tried many times to get into this game, and every time I gave up.
The problem with this game isn't that it's old, it's a combination of little things that make it a chore to play.
You can't tell when you hit someone.
You can't tell if you killed someone or if someone else did.
The grenades have such horrible physics you might as well just be throwing a laggy pillow.
You also can't tell when a grenade hits someone.
The classes are horribly imbalanced and bland, pyro's MAIN weapon has almost no hit registration and is given a rocket launcher to compensate.
The spy is nearly useless since you need to open a menu and USE YOUR MOUSE to disguise.
Nearly all the classes have some kind of shotgun.
The scout's nailgun never hits.
The demoman's detpack is useless except in extreme circumstances.
The pipe bombs have the same fluffy pillow technology as the grenades.
You can't tell any class apart from each other.
Everyone sounds the same.
There's no personality, it's a bland brown shooter.
The skill levels between players differ so greatly that trying to start out is nearly impossible because you die every 2 seconds.
Bunnyhopping.
I can see why this game would have been great 15 years ago, but now so many games outclass it there's no point in playing it. If you want a fast paced shooter that has fixed almost all of these issues, play the sequel Team Fortress 2. It's free.

I'm in two minds as to whether I actually recommend this game or not.  Very frustrating.
Pros:
Very comfortable, minimal 3D platformer.  I don't usually like first-person platformers but this game was (like Portal and Portal 2) very comfortable to jump around in.
Lovely atmosphere - the game is minimal but still has a feel of its own.  I enjoyed the ending (which was also minimal).
Cons:
This game has huge unrealised potential.  It is cheap and it is worth the price, but it is so frustrating to see a successful concept that doesn't realise its full potential.  What would it take to do that?  A few more levels and a couple more gizmos in addition to the elevators/pipes(under-ulitised)/bounce plates.  Maybe a few weeks of development time and this game would be 10x better.  I completed the game in 50 minutes - this game could easily supply four or five times that length with minimal investment.
Bottom line: Worth the cost, but you might be left frustrated by what this game could have been, but isn't.

After Amnesia, Outlast is another quite good Survival-Horror game developed by a small team of indie developers. It shares many features of its "older brother" (would that make Penumbra its Grandfather?) - you are some poor ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ (a freelance journalistst), stranded in a rather disturbing place (a psychatric hospital, to be more precise), and surrounded by various creatures that may or may have been humans at one point but, for the time being, simply want to eat you, cut off your fingers, or otherwise terribly maim you.
The catch is: You can't fight back. All you can do is run as if the Antichrist himself is behind you (and it's close enough, really), and hide. Ideally under a bed, or inside a locker. And ideally not while the monster is in the same room as you. Should the latter be the case anyway, the monster will drag you out of your hiding spot and hook you right in the goobar. Only to let you run again. Thanks to Regenerating Health(tm) you don't even need to look our for medkits anymore - one can't be a good journalists if he can't survive a couple of bonesaw slashes to the face, nowadays.
To make matters worse, the lighting in the mental hospital is rather lackluster (which effectively means that most places are darker than the inside of a black hole), Luckily, the protagonist is not a whiny pansy like a certain other person and won't go stark mad if exposed to complete darkness for even longer periods of time, but you still need a lightsource to navigate through most parts of the institution. Said lightsource is your trusty camcorder with built-in nightvision mode; an invalueable tool that eats through batteries as if you were actually using them to power the Deathstar. Fortunately enough, batteries seem to be more common than straigthjackets in the asylum.
So far, nothing new. Yet the question is - do you really need new stuff to be scared? Outlast says: "Nope". A fair mix of shock moments, atmosphere and fitting music are guarenteed to rev up your heart rate quite a bit, particularly if you feel that the next nude cannibal coming after you is long overdue but just won't show up. Only to show up just when you started to think he probably called in sick this morning.
As with all things, there are some downsides. The story, even though I don't want to spoiler anything here, is not exactly something to write home about. The monster variety is also a bit lacking (there are different . . . things . . . after you, but they all follow the same basic schema, without individual tricks or such). And especially in the later parts of the game it often seems predictable where the next baddie will show up due to a selected series of obstacles.
Still, Outlast is arguably one of the better Surival Horror games out there, especially in times when publishers feel the overwhelming urge to transform veteran games such as Silent Hill or Alone in the Dark into plain old action games. It can't be helped I supposed. Or actually, it can, so long as we have Indie Devs.

When it comes to puzzle platformers, my first thought comes to mind that "platformer" is merely a tool to present those deliberately designed puzzles ---- I think, therefore I jump.
Oh boy, I was wrong.
Escape Goat is an excellent puzzle platformer that offers great balance between platforming and solving puzzles.
There's a regular way to beat each level, but you can find lots of alternative routes with your platforming skilz ---- this happens in most platformers, however hard to find in a puzzler.
The original game Escape Goat is brilliant.
However the main campaign is too short, those extended levels (Room of Insanity) are hard platforming levels that loses the main purpose of the game. If I seek rage, Super Meat Boy is a much better way to go.
Here's how sequels should be made:
In every aspect better than the original, while preserving the main idea.
In short, Escape Goat 2 is a masterpiece.

Everything is 100% perfect except 1 thing....there is not enough of it and not sure of any sequels. With all indie games, they are genius ideas, but little content. Why, well, it does have shock value, and jump frights, and still manages to set the mood correctly. The best feature is, it doesn't feel guided, or that your on rails. It walks the line between guess work and obvious routes, they achieve this by making a plain "plan", like "get to 3rd floor" or "find the key", which allows you to discover areas and search at your own disgression. Although they lacked many key antagonist in the game, there are 4 special guys who you don't forget which is actually quite a lot for an indie game, the important is covered cause they leave an impression..........and you leave an impression on them. Bottomline, it is a must play game for any Indie or Horror fan, with plenty of action, horror, night vision, running, and most importantly, HIDING! I think every gamer should at least play through the first part, it is as amazing.

Heh, I recommend this game, but only barely.  My biggest issues are it's really short and offers no replayability.  The timer says I clocked 7.3 hours in the game, but I beat it in about 5 hours or so.  I ran around for a while after beating it to try to find the rest of the upgrades and get achievements, but got bored and quit without finding all the "acorn doors."
What the game does right (mostly):
- The story idea is interesting.  It's not really all that fleshed out in the game, and some plot points that are hinted at never really turn into anything.
- The controls for jumping and running feel decently fluid.  The grappling hook was a little buggy/imprecise for me.
- No game-breaking bugs at launch.  I fell through the world and got stuck once, and some geometry was a little glitchy, but nothing major since it takes no time at all to run back to where you were.
- The voice acting is not terrible.  The guy doing the voice-over for the Fallout-esque "L.E.A.F." videos is pretty bad, though.  He's not fooling anyone with that accent.
- Fall damage?  YOU are the fall damage.
What could be better:
- The game could use actual combat*.  Your toughest foe is water.  This is a walking simulator with some running and jumping.
- Because there is no combat, the game is laughably easy.  There's a reason why there is no difficulty setting.
- It would be nice if the map would indicate when you had found all upgrades and "acorn doors" in a particular zone.
- Too much of the game is underground and/or in tunnels, and it's so dark in there...
In conclusion, I guess I just wish there was more to this game.  The first time you do a downhill momentum running jump, it's actually very cool.  Unfortunately, after the novelty of that wears off, you're left with a pretty bare bones game.  Is it worth $20?  Well, I don't regret buying it, so I guess that's a yes.  If something else really good was on sale right now, I might feel differently.
It should also be noted that $20 will get you 40 of the best/worst tacos from Jack in the Box.  Good luck beating those in 5 hours.
*Yes, I know you "shoot" at "enemies" but let's be real here, okay?

I actually don't understand why this game is so highly rated.
It is an RPG that tried to do things in a Visual Novel style.
What I have garnerd from my limited time playing it is this:
The VN portion of the game is pointless and has no agency within the game. It's their because they wanted to do an RPG/VN. It serves no purpose.
The RPG protion of the game is sloppy. You have no way to gain consumables outside of combat. You have no place or way to rest/heal. The combat is slow, tedious and poorly designed. The basic attacks are worthless, so you end up in a ring of defending and healing just trying to get your party ready for the next fight. The character sprites could have used some variation other than hair.
Even on the hardest mode, their is no challenge. It just requires you to spend more time in the defend/heal/use special loop.
Moving the character on the map works best with mouse. Using the kyeboard is clunky.
Going through combat is best with the keyboard as using the mouse get tiresome quickly and you can accidently misclick quite easily.
Controller support might as well be yanked. Moving is sluggish, accessing menu's is unintuitive, and using special attacks sometime breaks it so that you can't do anything until you use the mouse/keyboard.
And finally the biggest question for a game: was it fun? The anser is no. It was slow, had no real story to speak of, troped characters and tedious combat that monopolizes the majority of the game.
I loved other games by the publisher, specifically LLTQ. So this game came as quite a let down.

I realized early that Heroes 6 is the weakest installment of the series. It has an utterly generic story that has nothing to do with the events of the previous titles and a gameplay that lacks any inspiration. But I could have ignored that, since, despite being not a very good title, the game still has some solid entertainment.
What really killed it for me is the "always online" issue, even if you really just want to play a single-player game and don't even care about multiplayer. While being always online in Steam is usually a non-issue, having to be always online on the notoriously unstable Uplay network can be a pain.
Also if Uplay servers are down for any reason and you try to work around that by starting the client in offline-mode the game will begin giving you trouble. For example it will refuse to let you load any of your savegames, because games you played while you were online are not available when you are offline. And if it has a particularly bad day it will deactivate completely, tell you that your version of Heroes 6 is "unregistered" and demand that you go online to register your already registered game another time before you are allowed to play the game again. So that's my real issue.
However, if you need another reason, then here is a word for those of you who just happen to be die-hard fans of the series like me: please take my warning. This game does NOT continue the events of Heroes 5 and/or Dark Messiah of Might and Magic. It is a prequel that surrenders the previous story-line completely.
I mean: Bloody hell! It's not like Ubisoft left us with a cliffhanger after Heroes 5, where the dark messiah, possessed by a half-naked, smoking-hot succubus, stopped the necromancers and their alliance of the willing from dropping weapons of mass-destruction on the underworld, destroyed the skull of the seventh dragon to free the demon-lord and open the gates of hell. So that the dark lord would rise from the abyss speaking the magic words: "I am your father". You know - introduce some global warming: the lucifer-way. And right before we found out if the world was going to end and if beelzebub actually can be a picture-book daddy... curtains dropping! The end.
And here comes Heroes 6 and it starts with the words "2000 years earlier"! Wait a minute, Ubisoft: I thought we just had some serious armageddon and succubus-action going on here! What happened to good old: smash skull first, eat brains later?
So honestly: unless you are really desperate for another Might and Magic title, just skip Heroes 6 and wait for Heroes 7. You won't be missing out on anything at all.

I bought Victor Vran in a Humble Bundle some time ago, though it was featured in a $1 tier recently.  According to my final stats, I finished the game at level 36 after 15 and a half hours, also after dying 44 times.  I cleared 92 of the challenges and found 44 map secrets.  I played the entire game with the Xbox 360 controller, in offline/solo mode, on Normal difficulty.
Zagoravia is your typical fantasy 18th century European castle town--brickwork, festivals, housing districts, demonic invasion...  Victor Vran is here to save the day!  With his fancy hat!  And this voice in his head that keeps making comments and taunting him?
Victor Vran is a different kind of Diablolike.  I don't have a console so this was only the second one I've played with controller support ever, though there is a growing number that have it as an option.  There's a large emphasis on movement and evasion.  Levels are not 2D planes with built-up structures to give it depth--you can actually jump over low walls and wall jump into different areas, or just jump to evade attacks or free yourself from getting cornered.  Victor only moves at one speed, so the dodge roll is essential to get a small burst of speed because it by default confers no bonuses, like adding defense or letting you use invulnerability frames to pass through attacks.
One thing that sets the game apart from others like it is the lack of classes.  After the tutorial, you're given your choice of Outfits which affect how your Overdrive (mana) is generated/retained along with some provided stats like Health and Armor, but you can freely switch between them once you've found or earned a second set of threads.  There are no stats to put points into or skills to waste points on to boost another further down the tree.  When you level up, you gain a specific reward, like unlocking the second weapon slot or a bump in stats like HP or Destiny Card capacity, and so on.  You invest in just your gear as opposed to both character and gear this time around, and that's where the diversity comes in--you eventually have two weapons to instantly switch from, two Demon Powers, two consumable potions/bombs, five Destiny Card slots, and your Outfit--all of those combine to make your build.  And you can freely switch from a cast-heavy mage to a melee tank or whatever so long as you have the gear to support both of those roles.
But the diversity feels shallow in a way.  Every weapon has three attacks, a basic and two special attacks with cooldowns.  Every weapon of the same class has the same three attacks--a Scythe will always have the basic swing, the stunning wave, and the spin attack, regardless of its rarity or affixes.  The only exception is Legendary items and they only put a spin on some attacks.  The only Legendary weapon I found, the Chicken Cannon grenade launcher, fired three basic shots at different distances in short succession but the other two attacks were just like every other grenade launcher in the game.  Same with spells--Boomerang will fire a medium-range projectile forward and have it return to you, with the only variations being its damage per second and its effect radius.  It's not entirely bad--you get used to a weapon's attacks and the comparison between two weapons of the same type comes down to solely stats.  It's always stats.
Each map has their own optional challenges, like killing X many monsters in Y amount of time, or using one monster's self-destruct feature to kill other monsters, or killing a boss with Hexes active without using Demon Powers or shrines...or just finding all of the hidden chests in the map.  Each map challenge awards gold, EXP, or items when completed, so they're worth at least attempting.  You can easily reset the map and unfinished challenges from the menu, so that was a nice feature.  You also unlock Hexes during level up, further optional challenges that alter enemies while granting you more EXP and items.  One makes them hit harder, one makes them move and attack faster, one gives them enhanced defenses and natural HP regen...  Some maps call for one or more Hex active for some challenges, and you are given rewards for using Hexes after so many kills.  Having all five active makes the game pretty difficult, though I stuck with three almost the entire game.
You know how in most Diablolikes, items rain down and it's your job to pick through it all and make repeated trips to town to sell the junk?  I didn't have that experience in Victor Vran.  Because of the page-based nature of the inventory, I never figured out what the maximum you could carry for any one category was.  I only returned to town when I finished a map and I either transmuted or sold off everything below Rare in quality on equips and I never touched Demon Powers or Destiny Cards.  I honestly bought quite a bit of stuff from the vendors--my final melee weapon of choice came from a store even--and in my past experiences with other Diablolikes, I usually stop checking stores past the first part of the game because their offerings are meager versus what monsters drop.  I have to say that it was actually kinda refreshing to not have to stop the action every few minutes to sort the keepers from the crap, but then I also didn't have any +item gear equipped apart from the Hexes.
Controls for the most part worked out well.  Left stick to move, right stick controls camera (no zooming unfortunately), camera largely didn't hamper me at all.  I only had issue with a couple of wall jumps because it seemed like if I tried it on a wall that wasn't fully solid or angled right, I'd just jump against the wall and not rebound.  It was a little temperamental but it was the exception as opposed to the norm, thankfully.  I had trouble with using the inventory with a controller, especially with shops.  Trying to check your currently active Destiny Cards without the cursor deciding it wanted to check your inventory was a bit of a chore--one of the times where I'd use the mouse instead.  The currently-targeted enemy has a glowing mark under them, but I found that I had to steer Victor towards my intended target in melee a few times because he seems to prioritize by proximity.  Ranged combat is also a bit of a chore if you're facing multiple targets and want to focus on one since you have the same glowing circle to go by.  I imagine those using keyboard and mouse wouldn't have as much an issue.
I had a couple of slowdowns even in the hub level safezone, so I wound up bringing the graphics to Low early on.  I don't think it really affected anything, and you're zoomed out enough that you can't check out details anyway.  Game ran at 60FPS except when I got mobbed hard in a few zones, and the cutscenes run at 30.  They're of the "slightly moving still image" variety as opposed to full FMVs.  And since I'm already kinda talking about it, the story's pretty basic.  There's a demon invasion--go kill everything and get loot.  The narrator and Victor will make comments at certain points, but nowhere near the frequency of Bastion or Transistor.  There isn't a lot of voicework overall especially considering the small cast, but you're here to kill things, not listen to the townspeople.  The music was pretty ambient, nothing terribly memorable apart from the town theme, and it wasn't anything I was muting either.
I enjoyed the game, a few hiccups aside.  It's nice to have such an active take on a genre I'm pretty familiar with, where instead of just clicking and getting into the fray and kiting, I can actually jump and roll and rocket jump out of harm's way.  And actually clear those insurmountable waist-high fences for once!  There's currently an expansion based on Motorhead in the works, so I think I'll come back to see what all that adds.  And maybe try multiplayer or the bonus dungeons, or maybe a few of those challenges I didn't clear the first time?

I realize the game is still in alpha, but the game is playable enough and their design choices are clear enough to write a review.
For starters, they have improved upon the original quite a bit. Grouping is quite a bit easier and generally handled pretty well. The grind, while still pretty redundant (again--it's in alpha), is much less annoying. Pets are much easier to get, and leveling gear is more than just a money sink (kind of). Many of the game play aspects (such as pets) have much deeper design.
Now for the bad...
I do not know any of the Trendy developers, but I have been repeatedly disappointed with their business model. Time again, it seems they have put money over development. Now it could be they're hard up for cash and need the money for continued development, but my impression is otherwise. For instance, in the original, Trendy continued to release new DLC (that understandably cost money) where they improved the game mechanics, while the original levels stagnated without an update. A good deal of the DLC (mostly the holiday) even reused the old maps and only added minor, themed changes.
Then they announced DD2. Awesome. But a couple of months later, they release a "new" edition of DD1 with new and improved features that fixed a bunch of the issues with DD1. Great, right? Yep. Except rather than release it as an update, it was released as an entirely separate game that required a new purchase.
So now they're charging for the pre-alpha of a soon-to-be free-to-play game. That makes some sense. Gotta pay developers. Sure. I get it, and I'm willing to support it. But then you get into the game and you realize just how "freemium" they're making it. Sure, they say it won't affect gameplay, and I think I believe them. But it's really annoying that the costumes are absurdly expensive (the only ones available now are $50 for the set, I believe). Even worse, one of the item drops in-game is a character-specific chest that requires a key to open...or you can pay $1.50 for a single, random accessory. Did I mention you can get the key for free? Yep, but it'll take you a couple of days using in-game currency that you need to buy stuff that will affect the game play.
Oh, and their introducing a wait time. Pets take 8 hours to hatch. In general, I'm not opposed to something like that...but not on a PC game...maybe mobile. You can (currently...though I'm seeing costly upgrades all over this) only hatch one pet at a time, and your eggs rot after 48 hours. And who knows? After 8 hours, you most likely have a worthless lemon.
None of these are deal breakers by themselves, but put together, it paints a picture I'm not sure I want hanging on my wall. I love the game concept, and it really is fun to play. But the business and design choices leave me wondering if I want to invest any time (or money) in a game I know will be wrought with frustrations down the road.

How to differentiate a bad Free to Play singleplayer game from a good one? Well, a good one definitely was made to be enjoyable and it also doesn't have this hogwash microtransactions. Furthermore, it's even better if this kind of game is rewarding and gives players a reason to play it again. OLDTV fits in this image of a perfect free game very well. In my opinion it's one of the best indie games in a zero-budget class that are available on Steam.
In this game you become a guy sitting in front of TV and surfing through different channels. Doesn't sound very interesting, does it? Definitely not, but a simple mechanic made this process entertaining and somewhat challenging. When you start a game, on your screen appears a word indicating a color (e.g. Green, Cyan, Red). If a color of a given word is the same as a word idicates you have to click your left mouse button, if it's different – right button. Simple. Simple yet diverse, because when you get to the next levels it becomes harder. Game starts to flip your screen upside down, makes your controls inverted or creates different screen distortions that disturb you while you're trying to identify if it's a right color or not. "Campaign" is divide into few levels (so called continents) which get increasingly harder, introducing you to new mechanics. You can also unlock an endless mode, but I won't tell you how to do that. It's a secret.
On a technical, side this game looks pretty cool. The menu as well as the rest of the game itself it's stylized to look like an old TV. Sounds are well matched and music gives you this special vibe which is hard to compare with something else. When it comes to rewarding players it has several dozen achievments that give you in-game bonuses and while unlocking them in a game menu they give you a special sound effect which is related to this achievment or something from a real world. Some references are droll, like for example Trump's speech.
For a Free to Play game OLDTV it's a very well made product, it has potential for mastering your reflexes and getting all of the achievments is satisfying (I will definitely try to 100% this piece). Probably the biggest flaw of this game is a fact that it can cause an epilepsy, it's quite flashy and jumpy. If it's not a problem for you, then you should definitely try it. It's free, the only thing that you will pay are few minutes of your time, if you won't like it, you can always uninstall.

When I saw that a game like this was published, I really enjoyed the thought of having the possibility to play an Anno again. Building a town, furfilling the needs of my population, trading etc. After playing a few hours I just felt betrayed. There is no real enemy but the AI. Villagers do basicly what they want, even if you give them another order, people die of ridiculous reasons (my chicken sheperd got trampled to death...), plagues or tornados nearly have no effect on my population and even on the highest difficulty the game bored me. Why? Here are some reasons:
- Most of the time I waited for the children to grow up, time I was forced to do nothing but watch the poorly animated people
- There is absolutly no progress. Yes, your town grows. But unlocking technology through building schools? Nope. Getting better buildings because your builders get more experienced or receiving a better education? Nope.
- Any competition against another AI? Nope. You are absolutly alone. Without any threat. So what's the point in building and enhancing your city?
- It is too easy. Even without any alien danger, there could have been something. Maybe an economy you have to keep going (things like a currency for payments, work time, trading special rescources for happyness etc)  or citizens leaving your town to form a own community. There is enough potential in this game to furfill those things...
These are my main reasons why I don't recommend buying this game. If you are looking for a challenge, don't buy this game. If you just want to build a town without any difficulty, without any point and just wait for things to happen, then this game is really a thing.
