This isn't the main game that I play, usually I just jump on this game with friends to have some fun and relax.
With that in mind, the most important part for this game is the developer involvement:
DEVSTREAMS: Every week the developers stream for an hour. The stream has gameplay in the background, a camera that has two developers answering questions from the chat and forums, and another camera with a game developer working on game assets (designing weapons or making animations).
DEVLOGS: These are a bit more informal and usually just a sentence or two. But every developer posts what they have been working on that week. At the very least it lets you know what is coming up soon.
INFLUENCE VOTES: For logging into the game (and the forums) you can get influnce points, then the team has public votes for different systems that the community prefers (how loot drops work, how to acquire certain items, etc). So you can just save up your points and actually make quite a considerable difference in something you feel strongly about.
All of this in addition to other videos for events and whatnot featuring developers answering questions on the forums or emails. They also have a department dedicated to going through every bug report sent through the in game system, the game is going to be in early access for quite a while, so it is nice to be able to follow along.
The game has bugs and isn't too terribly rich in the content department right now, but it's still pretty early in development.

The game definitely disappointed in this respect, alienating it's core by changing too many things unnecessarily and making it fairly easy to play. The deaths and challenge felt cheap and forced rather, the stage and the props were there, but the magician was fumbling his routine and you could see him trying to sneak the dollar bill into his sleeve right before your eyes. Hey From! This game isn't hard, it's BUGGY, the fans said. But they ignored this completely and made expansion after expansion because people kept buying them.
Then came this Scholar of the First Sin, a sort of "game of the year" edition to a not so stellar game which changed... well it didnt really fix any flaws or bugs, but it did add a bunch of nonsensically placed enemies everywhere. I guess they also added an item that limited your soul intake as an apology for their failed experiment of PVP balancing system.
Say what you will about DSII and much has been said, especially at release. But I actually grew fond of the PVP, it comes into it's own after a while. DS1 may be the popular one, but DSII is the new one and it's the one fans played, even the hardcore ones. There is defiinitely several skill ceilings to pass and even arenas with (broken) ranking systems.
It's kind of a broken mess of a game in the same way every Souls game is but it has strong qualities. Introducing the player with a fight like Pursuer made a much better impression on me than an easy cheap fight like Taurus Demon in DS1. They are similar in that there is a environmental/cheap puzzle solution, but Pursuer was engaging while Taurus Demon was a bit too chaotic and relied on glitches and bad camera for challenge.
This does not keep up, most of the Bosses in the game rely on the DS1 Taurus Demon type challenge, of bad camera and terrain glitches, sluggish controls for challenge rather than tactics or something like this. Especially the famous Smelter Demon which had a bug where you would get stuck in a wall and the AI actively pursued this glitch and tried to set it up. That's too meta, Dark Souls, just too much.
What is once known as "challenge" in Souls, in DS2 becomes cheap insta kills for cheap laughs and more annoying than difficult or tense. I am annoying dying and having to run through again rather than a sense of horror I would feel in DS1 or Demons, slowly creeping around the corner against unpredictable enemy AI. Everything is cheapened, from the graphical problems (hey at least its playable on PC now instead of just being on PC like DS1 was, thats a lot for podunk game company From.)
Oh wait no, From is actually a AAA developer at this point and this is a major release with marketing maybe tv commercials? Nevermind.
Scholar is the better version of Dark Souls II which is arguably one of the worse games in the series. It does not necessarily elevate it above any of the games, they are all about the same if we're being completely objective. For me the PVP presence was much stronger in Scholar than in DS3, but I get that Bloodborne/DS3 fans play these games for PVE which I cannot fathom at all and PVE is really bad, predictable, unmemorable and repetative in DSII particularly.
It seems that people being charmed by DS1's low budget and cheap design gave them the go ahead to make DSII downright appaling, only to embarass themselves at how stupid that is when the game got panned by critics with high expectations. Scholar does not fix this or anything really, it's just working on PC now with all the DLC included and now there is a ring that lets you cheat the broken online matchmaking system. This is probably the longest Souls game with all DLC, not including BB, maybe even longer than that.
When I played through Scholar in one sitting, I still had awesome immersive PVP moments that I could only dream of when playing Demons back in the hayday. DS3 failed me in this respect and I cannot forgive it for that. If you played DS3 and loved it and it was your first and you want more, Scholar is not the worst place to continue before you are ready to completely drop all your standards and play DS1 or Demons as they did not age well at all (ds1 barely playable on PC and Demons is not on PC at all.) Also the Souls games are kind of a one-trick pony, the psychological and massochistic aspects of the gameplay lose their value as you play through more of them.

Everything is 100% perfect except 1 thing....there is not enough of it and not sure of any sequels. With all indie games, they are genius ideas, but little content. Yeah the game is a good length with little repeition outside a few things, but overall experience is beyond commenting on, besides to say it is the best horror game of the year easily.
Why, well, it does have shock value, and jump frights, and still manages to set the mood correctly. Even though it is a guided tour, they still allow us hardcore gamers to get rewarded for searching nooks and crannies with extended content in the form of notes, and reward you with more in your supply of batteries. The best feature is, it doesn't feel guided, or that your on rails. It walks the line between guess work and obvious routes, they achieve this by making a plain "plan", like "get to 3rd floor" or "find the key", which allows you to discover areas and search at your own disgression. The only problem is, your in a facility crawling with lunitacs, and the problem with that is, most are set free to do whatever they want.
Although they lacked many key antagonist in the game, there are 4 special guys who you don't forget which is actually quite a lot for an indie game, the important is covered cause they leave an impression..........and you leave an impression on them. I have to admit, the first 20-30 minutes of the game, are some of the scariest moments in gaming. In real life, no one in their right mind would ever enter......but you have to, if you find a way!!!
Bottomline, it is a must play game for any Indie or Horror fan, with plenty of action, horror, night vision, running, and most importantly, HIDING! I think every gamer should at least play through the first part, it is as amazing.

This game starts out exactly as you'd hope for a Lovecraftian game - you're sneaking, looking for clues and exploring Innsmouth. It both looks and sounds very atmospheric; if it had kept going on in this vein, Id've been a happy man. However once I hit (what I believe to be) the halfway point of the game, the gameplay took a drastic swerve into different territory, and not for the better. I'd already muscled my way through several technical problems - not as bad as the constant crashing many players experience, but a crucial 'escape' sequence had been bugging out horrendously - and I eventually lost my patience with it.
What was the sudden change I mentioned? The introduction of guns, and lots of 'em. While the storepage's description mentions "combat" and "guns", I still didn't expect to be mowing down packs of fishmen with a tommy gun in what had hitherto been a stealth horror game. Furthermore, while I hadn't expected the plot to follow any one Lovecraft story exactly (it's named after one story and set in the town from another) things went from spookily bizarre to unfortunately silly when
. Pardon me for not realising I was playing a Syfy Original Movie.
It's a real shame, as I had high hopes for this game and I was genuinely enjoying it up until that point. I may play some more of it eventually in the hopes that it improves (if it does, I'll either edit or remove this review), but I've a sinking feeling that it doesn't.

Escape Goat 2 is a 2D puzzle platformer. It's very clever in it's puzzle and platforming. Having enjoyed Escape Goat 1 i was really looking forward to this game and it delivered. It's very much improved from the first title. There's plenty of content in the game and added stuff such as mutators will keep you coming back for more. I have really enjoyed this game. During this review i'll compare this to the first Escape goat and give my opinion on if it has improved or worsened.
Graphics:
They've totally changed the art-style of the game, from the pixel art style to much sharper clean looking art-style. In my opinion it looks gorgeous and runs buttery smooth. The FPS are locked to 60 FPS, i even turned off V-Sync but still locked to 60 FPS which isn't bad at all. All in all the game runs and looks very good. The first Escape goat also had a pretty good art-style but i think this one looks much better.
Sound:
If you have played the first game you would expect nice music from this game. The music indeed is very nice. The music still gives that same creepy vibe which the first game gave. Each level has it's own soundtrack and all of the ones i listened to were very good.
Gameplay:
Gameplay of this game is very similar to the first one, they've added some nice new abilities to your rat friend. The puzzles are very clever but not hard. It took me 3 hours and 55 minutes to beat the story missions. There is still some stuff to do so this game is easily a 6 hours game, add on top the mutators mode and you can have even more game time. The story is similar to the first one. You go in the castle and save your sheep friends. Still got that creepy satanic vibe from the castle. In addition the the sheep you get these ghosts from corpses of dead animals which give you some story information from time to time.
New abilities were added to the rat like a mini hammer power-up which turns your rat into a block, duplicate rats ability which lets you have 4 rats instead of 1. New abilities really give the game new life and makes things interesting and fresh. The game is not entirely puzzles as it involves platforming as well, you need to time jumps/drops, move with an object at the same time to avoid being electrocuted, etc. in order to complete some levels. The goat still has that same double jump and dash abilities.
Conclusion:
This game is very good, if you liked Escape goat 1, you would love Escape goat 2. If you have not played the first one and you like puzzle games, you will love this game. There's plenty to do in the game. It’s addicting too as once you start you keep playing. I beat it in one sitting. Not that expensive either so if you wanna wait you Can pick it up during a sale though in my opinion it's even worth it's full price.

Sigh... what a disappointment.
There are some new mechanics here, but not a lot, and a lot of the new mechanics go underutilized. The cape sees a very rare amount of uses and that four mouse thing happens like, twice in the entire game.
There's some fresh ideas with the old mechanics, but not enough. There's a lot of retreading old ground here, needless to say.
There's a lot higher focus on execution over puzzle solving, which I'm honestly against. This is way more of a platformer than a puzzle game, at this point. Especially true in the secret areas, which are basically just lost levels from the For All Intensive Purposes level set in the original game, that I intentionally did not play because this game's engine is not very good platforming-wise, but it kind of knew that in the original game and kept the focus on puzzles.
There's also just a fair number of puzzles that are downright stupid or broken. Enjoy your mouse randomly falling off walls using the cape, enjoy having reapers walk onto spaces you don't want them to be when going up or down platforms, There's one puzzle in the second half of the library in particular that's just... really stupid and kind of luck-based. There's also a ton of "gotcha" moments, some easy to see in advance, others not so much, A lot of switches, you don't know what they're going to do until you press them, and sometimes they'll trap you and you'll just have to deal with it.
Graphically, it "looks" better I guess but the game feels like it has less personality. The music's still great though. The story is still not really a thing, but it's not important.
This game does toy with decent ideas from time to time, and it's overall not an awful game, but I can't recommend it, especially in comparison to the first game. It's just kind of mediocre and disappointing, with a fair number of really frustrating moments.

Escape Goat – a gaming franchise named after a pun. Who’d have ever thought that the gameplay would be addictive, the controls tight, the puzzles super challenging and the overall presentation emitting as much charm and bravado as both of the games do? I didn’t always feel this way about that game or many of the better – more challenging – games in the genre. It’s taken me time to truly appreciate these games for the great works of art and entertainment that they are. A few too many rage quits at the hands of Super Meat Boy had me cursing this genre. I never wanted to play any of them again. I’d rather cry in the corner and pray that my mother was still alive so that she could give me a cuddle as I wrap my arms around her legs and she’d tell me that everything would be alright. Well no, god damn, it wouldn’t be. The genre kicked my♥♥♥♥♥ I was supposed to own it.
Or was I? Are the games in this genre intended to kick your♥♥♥♥♥ Is that what makes them so memorable when you either have had enough to the point where you delete a game from your hard drive never to be played again – or certainly until the next time you feel as though you must punishing yourself. We live in a sadistic world when one gains pleasure from torturing ones self but that’s exactly what these types of games do. Then you have your self-obsessed freakazoids, otherwise known as gaming masters, who are able to complete games such as Escape Goat 2 within the allocated 30 minutes to achieve that mighty achievement. I shake my head at their mastery. I am certain that it can be achieved – I’ve seen it with my own eyes – but not by a mere mortal.
It makes me think back to when I was a younger gamer. I used to be that good. The jokes about being like The Wizard and the deep family discussions – especially with extended family – that there wasn’t any money to be made in just being a gamer and you needed to do something more real with your life. That I needed to get an education. I did great throughout elementary and dropped off during high school. It wasn’t that the work was too hard. I’d get B’s when instead I should have been getting A’s.  I had a real lazy bone and if I was sent home with homework I simply wouldn’t do it. Home time was all about spending time outdoors with friends playing sport and if nobody was around to play sport I’d be honing my hand eye coordination playing whatever was the latest and greatest on PC, SEGA or PlayStation. It didn’t help that I was a little bit spoilt as an only child and didn’t have a sibling that I had to outwork or outdo.
But back to Escape Goat. Great game. When I put my mind to it I found myself finishing the levels relatively quickly. Thankfully it’s not as excruciatingly tough as Meat Boy but it’s challenging enough because all of the features of the game are immaculately executed – it’s supposed to be a challenge. It probably didn’t do as well critically as what it probably should have but the market is constantly flooded with games within the genre that try and do different things – most of them failing – so other games tend to suffer as a result of the whole rather than taking a deeper look at what the individual title is trying to achieve and how well they’ve done it. Although the concept and the gameplay isn’t unique this one does it about as polished a job as a small indie company could make. It’s graphics are exactly what I would hope for from the title and everything works in the fashion that it should. Oh and special mention to the glorious stained glass window on the level select screen – a touch of imagination and pure brilliance.
If you’re wanting a smart and intellectual challenge in the form of a puzzle platformer and you have yet to play this great franchise then I’d recommend that you start with the original and build your way up to it. However, that’s more personal preference – I like to start with the beginning game – and yet the developers at MagicalTimeBean have done such a marvelous job that you really don’t need to do that. You’re not going to get into “OMG this is insanely difficult for the start of a new game” if you don’t. It teaches you the core mechanics extremely well. The puzzles gradually climb once the developers have expected that you should have gotten the core gameplay components down. It’s well balanced in that regard – again much better than many of its peers.
For a game that began its life as a pun it sure as hell plays like a champ.

Heh, I recommend this game, but only barely.  My biggest issues are it's really short and offers no replayability.  The timer says I clocked 7.3 hours in the game, but I beat it in about 5 hours or so.  I ran around for a while after beating it to try to find the rest of the upgrades and get achievements, but got bored and quit without finding all the "acorn doors."
What the game does right (mostly):
- The story idea is interesting.  It's not really all that fleshed out in the game, and some plot points that are hinted at never really turn into anything.
- The controls for jumping and running feel decently fluid.  The grappling hook was a little buggy/imprecise for me.
- No game-breaking bugs at launch.  I fell through the world and got stuck once, and some geometry was a little glitchy, but nothing major since it takes no time at all to run back to where you were.
- The voice acting is not terrible.  The guy doing the voice-over for the Fallout-esque "L.E.A.F." videos is pretty bad, though.  He's not fooling anyone with that accent.
- Fall damage?  YOU are the fall damage.
What could be better:
- The game could use actual combat*.  Your toughest foe is water.  This is a walking simulator with some running and jumping.
- Because there is no combat, the game is laughably easy.  There's a reason why there is no difficulty setting.
- It would be nice if the map would indicate when you had found all upgrades and "acorn doors" in a particular zone.
- Too much of the game is underground and/or in tunnels, and it's so dark in there...
In conclusion, I guess I just wish there was more to this game.  The first time you do a downhill momentum running jump, it's actually very cool.  Unfortunately, after the novelty of that wears off, you're left with a pretty bare bones game.  Is it worth $20?  Well, I don't regret buying it, so I guess that's a yes.  If something else really good was on sale right now, I might feel differently.
It should also be noted that $20 will get you 40 of the best/worst tacos from Jack in the Box.  Good luck beating those in 5 hours.
*Yes, I know you "shoot" at "enemies" but let's be real here, okay?

First off, you may be considering to buy Fallout 3 due to Fallout 4 almost being fully released. But if you actually want Fallout 3 for a different reason, like the nostalgic feel, or just because why not. In this review I will be discussing many topics, so grab your pencils and start writing!
STORY
The story line in Fallout 3, may not be the most interesting, but it is deffinetly worth the time. Now on the other hand, side-quests are another thing that come to play in Fallout 3. Side-quests, some fun, some creepy, and some even borning, are EVERYWHERE. To anyone who can do every single side-quest in the game without getting bored, or just go insain, I salute you. Story rating: 4.7/5
GAMEPLAY
Gameplay is... well, gameplay. There is not much to say about the gameplay of Fallout besdies, it's good. Let's look at this in a broken-down fashion. Weapons are a big part of Fallout, they are what get you through the entire game, you can not go without any sort of weapon. How many weapons are there, you may be asking. Well, let's just say... over 110. Armor and Clothing is another part of Fallout, wearing armor will incrase the ammount of damage resistance you have, some armor peices even add special stats (such as +5 int). There are also junk items, and some other items, but it would take too long to list them all. Gameplay rating: 5/5
AUDIO
Fallout has very good audio. That is, if you can hear it all. Some audio in Fallout is not able to be heard, unless you either have a decent headset, in the perfect area, or by Radio signals. There are mods which can even add better audio quality to the game. Audio rating: 4.6/5
GLITCHES
Ah, Bethesda... what Bethesda game can you have without glitches? There are your regular minor texture or sound glitches, but usually nothing too serious. There are, or atleast was, gamebreaking glitches. These glitches can ruin your game in a good, and funny way, or in a more.. bad way. There are mods that fix most of these though.
(Additional) Running Fallout 3 on a system that has Windows 7 or later.
Fallout was never ment for Windows 7 or any later versions, so if you do own Windows 7, or any later version, you will probably have to dig through the files of the game, and download some mods so the game will run properly.
FINAL RATING: 4.9/5

Dark Souls II: Scholar of the First Sin is the definitive version of the game, and the additional DLC makes the bundle much more enticing.
If you played Dark Souls 1, then I definitely recommend this game. It has some strong boss battles, immersive environments, excellent combat, and an intriguing story.
However, this game is very different compared to the first game. The combat is a bit slower and less forgiving than that of the game's predecessor. In addition, while the game does have some very strong boss battles, most of the bosses felt more or the less the same to me. In addition, there will be some changes that veterans to Dark Souls and its spiritual predecessor, Demon's Souls, would not appreciate. These include the fact that once you die, you are not able to summon other players to help you in-game, and your maximum health is reduced by a small margin with each subsequent death. (Until you use a human effigy; not by burning one, but by using one as any other item.)
To me, Dark Souls 2 is bogged down by the implementation of artificial difficulty, and regrettably causes the came to not provide as good of an experience as Demon's Souls or Dark Souls 1. However, the increased polish and accessability within the game, along with the vast amount of content that has been included in it, definitely justify the $40 price tag in the Steam store. (You may want to wait until the game goes on sale, as in the most recent Steam sales, the game was only $10.)
In short, if you enjoyed Dark Souls 1, and desire for more of the Souls experience, then give this game a go.

I'm generally not a big fan of ARPGs. But I SORT OF liked Van Helsing - with which this shares some obvious similarities. For me though Victor Vran is a better game despite a few minor flaws. Having to manually alter camera rather than a standard directed camera angle is a little bit distracting and takes a bit of getting used to. It's not overly annoying but if you aren't careful it CAN get you killed now and then.
The game works off your standard hub questing with mobs strewn around locations on the way to your next challenge. Each challenge area has a series of tasks that will afford you bonus items, gold or xp. Whilst they are optional I'm sure most people will want to complete every challenge in each area rather than just breezing through the story. Your loadout is your customisation and the variety of weaponry and power cards you can find will radically alter your build and the way you play through the rest of the game.
Okay it's not rocket science and those looking for a serious RPG need to look elsewhere but it IS very enjoyable and perfect for when you want to while away an hour or so without too much headwork on the minutea of traditional character building. The graphics are reasonable, the NPCs are well characterised, the voice work is great, and the music is pretty decent as well. An ARPG fan might give this 8/10 or more but for me it's a solid 7. Lightweight but absorbing fun.

Strategy is my genre. I don't have any problem with Paradox. If you look at my hours played on Crusader Kings II, I've put more than a thousand hours onto the game. I've been playing grand strategy games for a long time, and Hearts of Iron III is just unplayable as far as I'm concerned.
I picked this up during a Steam Sale, though I've since forgotten when I bought it exactly.
I've attempted several playthroughs as different nations, and it's a long hard monotonous grind until Germany makes you take it up the pooper. Maybe I just suck at this particular game in general, but it's just not fun. To illustrate this, let me give a timeline of events for each of the factions that I've attempted to play as.
1. Sweden - The biggest problem that I have with playing Sweden is that it's basically balancing on a knife's edge. You can't make Germany mad, because they'll invade, and you can't friends really very quickly at all. I spend a lot of time building up border defenses and units only to have the Third Reich plow over all of my carefully laid plans by about 1943... usually it's earlier than that. My earliest loss occurred in 1939. As best as I can tell there was no way to overcome Germany's technological/numerical edge, so after four or five plays through as Sweden, I thought to myself: "Let's try another nation and see if we can't change things."
2. Belgium - I was kind of going for a vaguely historical playthrough here. Maybe I could hold out a little bit longer than Belgium and France did in the real world... turns out... no. You can't. I assembled gobs and gobs of troops and fortifications, but the Jerrys were able to pull off the Schliefen Plan even earlier than in the real world. Yeah, I knew that I would probably get taken pretty early, but the fact that I didn't even put a dent in things on "Very Easy" difficulty was just frustrating and ridiculous.
3. Brazil - If you're noticing a trend here, it's that I like to play factions that aren't particularly strong so that I can build them up to face bigger obstacles. While I didn't get invaded or anything like that, I got to a point where it was just a multi-decades long stale-mate. It finally ended when I attempted an invasion of Southern Spain only to have my massive army repelled by a dozen or so German infantry units.
I'm so done with this Hearts of Iron III, it's just not a worthy playthrough. The graphics are just a map with strategic unit cards that look like Xs for infantry and Os for tank units, so you're not missing anything there. The only exception that I can think of on that score is that in the production screen they have some black-and-white photos of WW2 era ships and vehicles. If it weren't for the fact that I could literally do a google search for the same pictures, that might be passable.
The game has great potential to just drag on forever while not allowing you to actually do anything to cause change in the gameworld.
The intelligence system is a hindrance because if you want to attack anyone that's not already at a high threat level you have to sink all of your leadership into spies while sacrificing research and officers and diplomacy. All four of these things cause a trade-off that makes exactly zero sense.
You start the game not knowing what tech that you need to research... then thirty hours into game play, and you still don't have a flipping clue as to what you need to research. The tooltips don't really explain what the different techs do very well, and there's not any way to divine exactly what you need.
You can assign your units into AI groups. The problem here is that the AI that helps you coordinate troop movements is about as smart as a bag of sand - which is funny because the Enemy AI easily encircled my troops without a second thought. The end result is that if you want to keep track of a massive invasion of Fortress Europe, you have to monitor the movements of every unit card and every transport... you could spend several hours just lining up an attack only to have the Germans tear your carefully laid plans into very tiny pieces without much effort on their part. Your AI will force you to orchestrate an invasion by yourself, because it can't figure out how to boating.
I spent the last 6 hours of my gameplay trying to get my Strategic Bombers to work to no avail. They just sat on the runway taking up space. I'd order them to bomb targets in mainland Europe and they'd just hang around... I kind of wish there was a mini-game where you can guillotine disobedient flight crews.
I played through the tutorial of this game 2 times that I can remember. The second time I very carefully read every single word of the tutorial and it's complete BS. It's absolutely unhelpful. You get an idea of how to move your units manually, but there's no instruction on some of the more difficult things... it may be because the devs didn't even really understand it.
There was a period about ten years ago where every First Person Shooter that you could pick up was set in WW2. Some were passable - most notable is Battlefield 1942 - but most of the rest were basically like video games of movies were during the 90s: just a ploy to make a quick buck off of parents that were looking to buy a game for a kid, and they thought "Hey, Jurassic Park, that was a cool movie. I bet my kid will love this game!" <cue sad trombone sound> There may be a decent WW2 grand strategy game out there, but this one is not it. I'm a little curious about Hearts of Iron 4 (just because I love Paradox), but if HoI3 is any indication... I just don't want to think about it. Save your money and avoid this one unless your cash is just burning a hole in your pocket.

Well, how do I start this... maybe with the caveat: for me, this is a "Do you recommend this game? - Yes, but...".
Now, let's try to get a few more details. The game itself is set in an interesting world, and while the characters might be a bit childish at times, they are still recognizable and likable characters. Plus. a game set in "Gamindustri", referencing games and gaming and stuff, and constantly nuking the 4th wall -- that has to be fun. As far as I'm concerned, I liked it.
Don't misunderstand, though. The game may be set in "Gamindustri" and the 4 nations may represent 4 console manufacturers, but the actual story is a standard fantasy-type story where some bad guys want to topple the good guys. "Gaming" is more a of general world theme, not so much the theme of the story.
You may want to be careful though. The visuals are nice but somewhat dated, the story is told in a visual novel style with endless streams of text boxes giving a lot childish dialogue that can be tiring. Some of it is voice acted, but many scenes are not.
Also, the game is very repetitive. Like they only have a handful of dungeons (which is where the gameplay happens), and reuse them again and again and again. The same applies to monsters, although those might at least get a color change :-) And they have more boss fights than bosses, so expect repeats there as well, even for story bosses.
Some aspects of the game might feel a bit grindy, like having to walk through a dungeon again and again until it gives you the item that you are looking for. Upgrading lily ranks or challenges to get the char upgrades attached to some tiers is just pointless grinding as well.
In addition to the actual story the game also gives you quests... which are forgettable, to say the least. Not only are they just standard fetch/kill quests -- I've stopped reading the texts pretty soon as those made no sense at all.
The game can also get annoying with it's inventory, since there's no sorting. If you want to check whether you have a certain item, select the category, and read through the list until you find it, or hope that you didn't miss it if you didn't see it. I'd also like to sell off the tons of garbage materials for some extra cash, but it feels too tiring due to the lack of useful sorting options.

Long story short: Best online arcade racer on pc at this time. 8/10 in my book.
If you want to know why, read on.
-Let's start with the most important aspect if you love racing games: This is NOT a sim! It is an arcade racer, but a very good one at that. You can expect taking corners at 200 km/h. Drifting with lambo's and jumping for hundreds of meters. Each car handles slightly different depending on it's type, not much though so if you are looking for a sim kind of racer, this will probably not appeal to you. However if you love cool cars and go insanely fast on the regular roads this is your game.
-You start with the story. The story is good, not too short, not too long. You can skip it but that would be stupid. During the story you get a feel of all the different types of cars and you unlock people for your HQ later. Each person will give you a selection of "abilities" that you can upgrade. This goes from a discount in the shops to gaining more xp to car upgrades like a visual race line and faster top speed, accelleration etc. Needless to say, you really want this. So you start with the story which is often very challenging and it gives you a good view of what the game has to offer.
- Cars: There are around 100 different cars & bikes. Expect most of the cool cars you know to be there. But.... that's only the standard versions you can buy. For each standard car, you can install upgrades and modify it to a different type. The types are Standard-street-terrain-sport-raid-circuit. ¨This gives you an idea of the race types you can expect. On top of those you can also unlock extreme upgrades and make your car a drifter-dragster-monstertruck. Each "class" is very different and not all classes are available for every standard car. However, let's take one of my favorites, the Mustang, you buy 1 standard mustang, and you can then multiply your vehicle to a drift mustang, monster truck mustang, street race mustang at the same time. So now you bought 1 car, but you have 4 different ones, which you can (and must) upgrade each one seperately.
-Bikes: yes, there are motorbikes too, and everything that applies for the cars, applies for the bikes. same classes, same upgrades. it's often easyier to do certain missions with a bike instead of a car, so make sure you have some.
-Police vehicles. Since the last update of the game there is another game mode introduced. It's basically racers vs cops. Think of Need for Speed (Most wanted, rivals, hot pursuit...), but much much better. While you are just cruising the streets, depending on your car (cop or regular) you will be invited to a pursuit. If you accept, you either help another racer or you try to bust another racer. You do need to buy and level your police cars first though. at least if you ever want to have a chance of busting other players.
-Online: This game is online only. You can play perfectly well solo though. The only thing where you actually need to play with others is PvP. the rest is simply random encounters with no impact unless you want it. You get to choose how you play this game, but honestly it's the most fun with some friends online. Either way, the entire game is online so make sure you have a stable internet connection.
-Tuning: The most addictive part of this game is ofcourse to upgrade your favorite cars and tune them. Now, let me dissapoint you first if you expect Need For Speed underground content. It's not like that. This is RNG. Is it a grind? Yes it can be, but you get to choose how and where you grind. Which means it doesn't have to be lengthy and boring. For each race (and that is a wide word in this game, but we'll get to that later) you do, you get 3 rewards: credits, xp and a car part. Each car has 11 parts, and each part has a level. Like gear in other MMO's. However on top of that, each part has a random affix. One of four: accelleration, top speed, grip and brakes. So basically you are looking for the top level parts, with your desired affixes. For example, a dragster has no use for the brake affixes. But, according to your playstyle it's possible you desire an overwhelming fast car to have more grip for example, so you look for those parts. The cool thing about this game is no inventory, you can keep ALL parts you ever collected, and should you one day want to change loadout of your car, you can. The downside though is RNG, it may take you a while to get all the perfect parts. On the other hand, remember it's arcade, you'll win without the "perfect" set too ;)
-Visuals: This game is graphically still top tier. The cars are stunning, and the open world just the same. You can modify the look of your car very well. You need to earn the visuals first though, or you can buy them with credits or real money.To be honest I have the coolest looking cars from all the racing games I ever played. Needless to say, I'm impressed here. Again, it's not Need for Speed grand, compared to those games the options are rather limited, but I feel there is plenty to change your looks. If we move towards the graphics of the world, this game is unmatched. We're talking a huge open world with weather cycles and day and night cycles which affect the traffic on the roads. Rain, snow, mud, you name it.
Once you finish the story, or during the story you are confronted with all the content this game has. And there is lots of content.
-The Summit. Once a month there is the summit, but before you can enter there are weekly mini summits in which you must compete. In order to enter those you need to have a rank 3 in stunt races. This is easy, you get a quest to complete (like make a wheelie of 150m or drive 1km on the wrong side of the road) and only then you can enter the mini summits. A summit is a collection of challenges, where you get good rewards. All prestations are stored and measured against other players. So you are playing against other players prestations, but solo. Your rewards depend on how well you do. This is probably the fastest way to earn upgrades for your car, and you can basically do this 24/24, 7-7. You compete in events like monster trucks, drag race, drift race, time trials, jump challenge etc. As you can see, it is very wise to have a own car for each class/event. So you really want a monster truck, a drifter, a dragster, a street car, a circuit racer etc. If you do not have one of the classes needed in the summit, one will be provided to you, but it will be a barebone piece of crap. If however you own one of the desired classes, the rewards will go straight to your car. Some summits have additional requirements, like a US muscle car, or japanese car etc. This encourages you to buy and upgrade new cars ;)
-PvP: pvp is pretty well done, unless you expect to choose standard races. Pvp in The Crew is very diverse. Each contestant chooses race type (like capture the flag, crown, regular race etc), then after that type of car and it all ends up in the RNG machine. One racetype/racecar will be chosen by RNG, and after each round it is the same. It's a very fair system imo, and it again stresses the importance of having at least one car of each type that is maxed in any aspect. If you have that covered, PvP is very fun here.
-Faction races. You get to choose your faction, and race for them. These are actual races with a specific car class requirement. Ideal if you love a specific race style like all terrain or circuit.
-Challenges: All around the world there are challenges you can pick up. You can pick them up during other missions too, or when you are travelling from one place to another to maximize rewards for minimum effort. You do that in a multitude of styles: slalom, speed, collect (the hardest imo), jump, follow the raceline, precision. Depending on how well you did, you'll get a piece of gear for your car. This is the go to when your car is too low level for anything else. It only takes like a minute or two to complete and you can rince and repeat.

Having played the this game's predecessor: Dungeon Defenders 1 it's great to see Trendy is trying to fix some of the issues that plagued the previous title, while staying true to the great foundations of the Defenders series.
Combat is easy to get into and unlike the previous title the hero abilities feel like they make a difference in combat, not only does this make battles more exciting it also gives you a compelling reason to invest in ability specs instead of heading straight for hero damage and health like in the previous game.
Tower placing has improved vastly since the previous game, and feels more balanced in terms of green mana being available - in the previous title towers were able to reach their maximum upgrade level fairly quickly, however in DD2 mana is more scarce so upgrades need to be more tactical and always repairs are essential at all times. Some towers in the game have combinations but the squire class seems to have been left out of this equation - something I hope the developers are planning on addressing.
Loot is more fair in this title, in the previous game loot was dropped and visible to all players, this would lead to a mad scramble as everyone abandoned their posts to try and snatch the loot before someone else. In Dungeon Defenders 2, loot is instanced (players can only see their own loot) and means that people focus more on the battle than watching for a nice drop. Nice drops are also alerted to so people don't have to stare at the map all the time.
However a lot of the game is still missing, I'd like to see:
* More bosses
* Improved pet system
* Higher level cap (as content comes)
* More game modes
* Balanced uber spec spheres
* A way of selling unused spec spheres
* More adventure maps

is a hack and slash game from an isometric perspective. It is not a  proper ARPG. The character is directly controlled, there is an option for it to control as a traditional ARPG in that the character follows the cursor but the default is that of direct control.
There is almost no character development inherent in the stats themselves. All damage, abilities and move sets are directly attributed to the loot you have equipped. The only thing leveling actually nets you is increased health and overdrive pools (used for demon powers).  As well as destiny points or card slots. The main things you'll be deriving stats and abilities from are outfits, weapons types, destiny cards and demon powers.
Destiny cards are the main modifiers of gameplay other than traditional loot. They drop from enemies and also at times are awarded for leveling. You have a specific number of slots for cards as well as an overall point limit and these cards will grant things such as increased movement speed for a short duration on kill or increased overdrive gain and other things in that same fashion.
One of my main complaints is that there are not that many types of weapons. Melee has only a few types of swords. There is only one type of weapon for casting and a similar number of types for ranged weapons as melee. Each type has a set of 3 moves that are specific to that type and do not change at all throughout the type despite having different stats.
Now, the game is very active and requires use of an active dodge. The game can feel a little odd especially if doing a lot of melee. Notice I did not say
as the game also seems to advocate for switching between weapon sets at a fairly rapid interval to be able to continue doing damage whilst waiting for cooldowns to end. Additionally, I felt throughout the game, as in combination with the active dodge and ability to wall jump, there should have been some system in place to at least to do some basic combos such as X,X,Y just to give the game some much needed levity from the rather monotonous enemies strewn at your feet.
Furthermore, there are not that many enemy types either. Within a few hours of play you'll have seen them all. Which in turn does not aid in alleviating the tedium.
The game has location based challenges that can be a fun distraction and can get you extra loot. There are also Hexes that behave very similarly to the way Idols in Bastion did.  Turned on or off at the entrance of any new place, they feature things like faster moving and harder hitting enemies in exchange for better loot drops and more XP.
On a side note, Doug Cockle is the voice of
. You may have heard of his work in the Witcher series. Odd thing is, his natural speaking voice sounds nothing like Geralt; But he is doing that exact same voice in this game. However, I cannot think of anything more appropriate for a monster hunter than to have the same voice as the legendary White Wolf. The Butcher of Blaviken.

I had little knowledge of Victor Vran before I got it from Humble Bundle. I knew basically that it was an top-down action RPG and nothing more. On the other hand I have plenty of experience on other arpg:s, mainly Diablo 1, 2 & 3, Torchlight 1 & 2 and Titan Quest and also some other 3rd person ARPG's like Dark Souls and Darksiders. When I launched VV I was expecting something very similar to Diablo/Torchlight and that expectation ended up being one of the reasons I didn't enjoy this game.
Although the game looks like a Diablo-clone, if you allow the expression, the game doesn't play like one. The core gameplay is closer to 3rd person ARPG even though the camera angle is high up. The problem for me was, that when choosing the control scheme, I chose the one that felt normal for top down ARPG, the mouse control scheme. If you can, imagine playing Dark Souls with Diablo's controls. Fair enough it's not the games fault that I didn't know what I was jumping into, but then again the game should have a clear warning, that the game was not meant to be played with this control setting.
So I was about 12 hours in the game when I finally realized that I should've chosen the WASD-controls. That was about 2 hours before the ending, so I didn't bother learning new way to control the game. But the reason why I mention all this is the fact, that I want to give the game a "chance" in a sense that I'm judging here only one aspect of a game, that could've been totally different if I had played it right from the start.
So what is so wrong when playing with 'just' mouse? First of all moving around in a 3D-environment is pain in the donkey when the environment constantly blocks your vision or your mouse clicks. Tall buildings, cliffs, mountains and even trees could block vision that either leads to death by swarming or Victor trying to reach out-of-reach places. This is especially painful when fighting a enemies that teleport around the map. I had several situations where holding a mouse in one place meant that Victor started walking back and forth, and the place where I tried to go wasn't even close to his path.
While the character can leap over obstacles, he cannot leap over all obstacles, and it's not clear which one he can and which he cannot. Sometimes Victor jumps over, sometimes he doesn't. As if this isn't enough, the game presents certain situations where camera rotation is a must, otherwise jumping to a required space is almost impossible. All this results in a very clunky movement, with a lot of errors just because the game is not sure where you want to go and you're unsure where you can go.
But I could easily recommend this game if controls were the only problem. From the screenshots and gameplay videos one can quickly see that the game is filled with ARPG cliches: skeletons, spiders, wraiths, elementals and vampires. Landscape is the typical farmhouses, villages, caves and tombs. Plot is even more cliche; pact with the 'devil' and a cursed queen. It is typical fantasy setting with some technology involved, but not used(see comments). On the top of that the maps are always the same, so the replay value is really low even if you happen to like it. Item progress is also very vague, compared to other similar loot-rich games and I felt that there was little progress in characters ability to do more damage. Victor gains no new skills while leveling so what you find really defines how you play. So in long run the game got really tedious, just spamming 2-4 skills from the beginning to the end. Neither Destiny Cards or Demonic powers gave nothing new to the genre and were just another way to clutter inventory.
But there are some features that are worth mentioning. All the areas in game have five challenges that give out rewards. Although the rewards are somewhat lackluster apart from experience points, the challenges were something that got me playing few extra hours in early parts of the game. I guess the voice acting can have a minor positive mention although I can hardly understand why they wanted Geralt of Rivias voice actor to play the exact same role on Victor Vran. Also I liked the hidden secrets in maps. If one doesn't count the problems in screen cluttering, I didn't experience any major or minor bugs, so in a sense it seemed very flawless product.
In short, if you didn't get this game from Humble Bundle like I did, I cannot recommend buying or playing this game. It's not horrible, but it doesn't really shine in any aspect. Unless you're a huge ARPG junkie, you better spend your time replaying Diablo/Torchlight or Dark Souls/Darksiders.

The black sheep of the entire series, Dark Souls II is the sequel to the critically acclaimed Dark Souls I and as you might expect, it didn't satisfy all of the fanboys when it came out.
You might have played 1 or 3 and haven't bothered even touching 2 because of all the bad things that have been said about it by the community, reacting to it like the game murdered their families and stole their cupcakes. With all of that being said, just play the damn thing anyway. It may not be the best Souls game but it's still a great game and gives you a sense of adventure, and most of the hate just come from vitriolic Miyazaki fanboys that can't adjust to a different way of playing.
Now I will elaborate on why you should still play this game, and keep in mind, this game is not perfect (just like any other Souls game). The combat is expanded on greatly from Dark Souls 1 and allows for much more customization. Power stancing, a wider range of hexes and spells, unique weapons that call upon cool effects and status buffs, expanded item list to accommodate for many playstyles are some of the many things that help with creating your own unique build and playstyle in this game. Even if you feel like you screwed up your build, DS2 introduced the ability to respec your character with a fairly common item.
Another reason to play: the covenants and online activities actually work, they're not broken and buggy like in the first game. You want to PVP constantly? There's a covenant for that. You want to help others through the level by fending off invaders? There's a covenant for that.  Want to be a TMNT member and defend Master Splinter's rat cave? There's a covenant for that (no, really) You want to defend bells from the tall man that oppresses the midget overlords? There's a covenant for that. (No, I'm not high) You want to praise the sun with your brethren? Of course there's a covenant for that. Want to rub sandpaper on your crotch and make the game harder than it needs to be? First, you need a therapist. Second, there's a covenant for that!
I could go on and on about the good qualities like the length of the campaign being longer than 1 and 3 or the levels of fashion souls on display being unbelievable, but this is when I tell you of the bad aspects of the game. Keep in mind though, that these aren't deal breakers but they are annoying to most.
The level design sucks for most of the game. Bonfire placement has been increased dramatically for the sake of the developers not knowing how to make the level connect as well as it did in 1 or 3. The tension of exploration doesn't really exist since you're likely to trip over another bonfire after straying away from your original one for 5 minutes.
Most of the bosses aren't great; in fact some just feel like they were thrown in to fill out a quota. Prowling Magus, Najka, Twin Dragonriders, Covetous Demon etc etc. There are some good ones though and once you get to the DLC, they can even be awesome.
While the lore is very interesting, some of the smaller tales feel unfinished.  Also don't get your hopes up for any of the loose threads to reach any resolution in DS3. The lore of that game almost pretends that Drangleic didn't even exist.
So there are a million other things I could nitpick or praise, but that would take way too long. All in all, ignore the negative nitwits and just try the game for yourself, you might actually like it. It takes things from DS1 and expands upon them for gameplay and lore without ripping off characters and inserting them for nostalgia value.
It's not like DS3 where it's on its knees with an open mouth, looking for DS1 senpai's approval the entire time.

A good game in a great franchise ruined by a bad company.  You can see that I have a lot of hours logged into this game.  What you don't see is that a tremendous number of those hours are idle; I simply refused to log out because I thoroughly distrusted uPlay to the point of not believing I would ever be able to log back in if I logged out.  Previous experience justified that fear.  Subsequent experience validated it.  I finally had to reboot my machine.  Once again, I cannot get into the game because of uPlay.  The latest "update" to uPlay upgraded my experience by once again denying it to me entirely--as in, where I once could log on, I no longer can.
When I was in the game, I was able to get through the first campaign and part of the second.  The game is a respectable member of the HOMM franchise but nothing truly revolutionary (the primary new element, dynasty weapons, is a good concept and I hope that it appears again, but it isn't exactly series-defining), and there are definite power balance issues among the factions.  Fortunately for beginners, you start playing the easiest (most powerful) faction (Necropolis), but the balance issues could be serious in multiplayer with random factions.
The bottom line is simple: Not only do I not recommend this game for as long as uPlay exists, but I personally will not buy another Ubisoft title of any kind until they abandon or dramatically reform that system.  There are many excellent publishers out there that treat their customers with more respect, or failing that, if they force you to use proprietary portals, at least they function.

Loot is varied and randomization is well done. Indie ARPGs don't always get this one right but they nailed it on their first try.

A surprisingly disappointing and strangely conflicting follow up to one of the best games I have ever played. Dark Souls 2 did not live up to my expectations for a big chunk of its main storyline. Only when I reached the end game and the optional DLC content it finally delivered an experience worthy of its predecessor.
The camera feels jerky when compared to other Souls  games and the combat has issues with hitboxes and some enemy models do weird swivels that suddenly lock them onto you - which can be frustrating. My biggest complaint, however, is that the world lacks its organic feeling of 'place' that made DS1 such a standout experience. Some areas seem to be stitched together from whatever was left in the fantasy leftover pot and lack any kind of streamlined design philosophy of idea behind them. Many levels simply look dull and, worst of all, they are boring to play and do not present you with interesting challenges. Instead of improving your skillset you are basically looking for a bunch of tripwires (dudes in blind spots or overwhelming numbers popping up in small spaces) that will kill you once when you do not know that they are there - when the surprise is gone, so is the difficulty. Way to push the death counter through cheap tricks rather than challenging fights.
The boss fights have mostly been a similarly disappointing experience. Some, at least, are atmospheric and aesthetically pleasing (Last Giant, Chariot, Demon of Song, Looking Glass Knight, Guardian Dragon), but almost all of the bosses are pushovers and lack the challenge I expect from Soulsborne games. The Smelter Demon is basically the only hard non-optional boss fight in the main game, otherwise there is only Darklurker to pose a real challenge after finishing quite a long and obscure quest line.
Not to be too critical: DS2 is not a bad game per se, the basic gameplay is solid, of course, it just is a very uneven and overall mediocre experience that does not hold up to other FromSoft titles. However, after playing some more through the game, I have to add that the final stretch of DS2 is a huge improvement over the early and midgame stages and finally gives you some quality areas that are both challenging and atmospheric. Especially Drangleic Castle is an absolute blast to play through.
Here is also a look at the content from the three DLCs, because it differs quite significantly in quality from the main game:
The Brume Tower is a bit of a mixed bag. The area looks great and houses some very challenging bosses, but it relies heavily on artificial, one-off difficulty with a platoon of clown cars opening up and spamming enemies at you once you enter a room - Sir Alonne and Fume Knight are worth the hassle though, absolutely the two best boss designs in the game. I did not care much for the Iron Passage, it most certainly is a brutal challenge - but once more for all the wrong reasons.
The Sanctum City/Dragon's Sanctum is my favourite area in the game, with intricate puzzles and pathways, interesting and tough mechanics and some challenging bosses - even though the Gank Squad Trio is a pretty cheap design. Both Elana and Sinh give you pretty cool fights, especially if Elana invites the VIP to the party.
Frozen Eleum Loyce is the third great area in DS2 and like Sanctum City and Drangleic among the best in the series. Its eerie atmosphere is haunting, the enemies present a tough but fair challenge and finally, FromSoft managed to get the bonfire economy right again. This is what Dark Souls is supposed to be like. The bosses are no slouches either and make this a very well rounded area.
To sum up: The strong ending and the great DLC content can not make me forget the twenty-something hours of "meh" I had to wade through to get there. For every Anor Londo, you get two Lost Izaliths with lots of Demon Ruins in between. All while most of the bosses you encounter are either Pinwheel or Capra Demon. However, if you have made it through the main game, I highly recommend looking into the DLCs - they really show what this game could have been to begin with and I really had a great time playing through them. They made me even consider changing my review to a thumbs up, but the fact remains that I can not recommend a game that bored or annoyed me for the majority of its main story.
For people looking to get into the Soulsborne games, I can only suggest playing either DS1, DS3 or Bloodborne first - they all are better entry points to start your journey. DS2 clearly is the runt of the litter and nowhere near as refined as the other titles; it is a slightly above average game, thanks to its base mechanics, that does not deliver on its promises with the exception of some moments of genius shining through at the very end. Fans of the series, lusting for more, should still consider picking up DS2, simply because of the great content that is provided by the DLCs and Drangleic Castle. For everyone else I can only recommend to at least look somewhere else for first impressions.
If there is one thing to say about DS2, it is that quantity over quality is not a good approach to game design. This game could have been a lot better where it about twenty to twenty-five hours shorter.

Some platformers pride themselves in being tooth-pullingly difficult, just as some puzzle games seem to do the same in being unnecessarily oblique.  "Escape Goat 2" finds the magic middle ground, requiring no more from a player than he or she is likely able to contribute.  The platforming is just hard enough to be challenging, clearly not trying to be Super Meat Boy Redux.  The puzzles will make you scratch your head, but won't make you scream aloud or hurl your mouse at your monitor (or your controller, as it is fully controller-compatible).  I couldn't put this game down once I'd started playing, and once I did successfully put it down, I spent a lot of time thinking about that last room that I was having trouble clearing.  Tim Schafer ought to be proud of this puzzle-platforming masterwork he's created.  Eleven thumbs up!

Science Girls is an RPG where six girls that study different scientific fields come together to stop an alien invasion.
This game is not good. Really, the only notable things about this game is that the protagonists are female scientists. It's nice to see media that supports women in science and technology. That's it, though. The protagonists are shallow, and offer very little personality beyond their chosen field. They look very similar (uniforms don't help), which makes it tough to remember which one is which, and after a while, I no longer cared. Sadly, the player-controlled character is just as interchangeable as the others, with the only difference being that she wears a dumb mask. Couldn't I have at least chosen which of the six to control? Also, most of the science the girls use is either basic high school knowledge or completely fictional, and I think the dialogue is actually a bit disrespectful to the scientific fields represented (though, as a CS graduate, I have spent time in a computer lab playing Nethack before). As for the story, I found it uninteresting and a bit too padded out with all the battling.
As for the gameplay itself, it's boring and horribly unbalanced. Your characters' basic attacks are worthless. I found I just kept relying on multi-target skills, with the occasional heal. It's awkward that there's no place that I could find to just recover HP/SP... I kept having to do it in battle by putting one enemy to sleep and defending/healing repeatedly. The battle and level up system are really pretty inelegant. This game would've benefited by keeping things simpler (like the Mario RPGs). Also, I hate it with a passion when skills in RPGs become harder to use as you level up. The saving grace is that all six characters are usable in battle and they all receive XP... at least that's one pitfall avoided.
The art is not very good. The pixel work is okay. The illustrations do a poor job of making the girls distinct. The alien homeworld looks particularly bad. As for the sound, well, apparently there's supposed to be some sound? There are options for sound, but I didn't hear any. I turned the volume way up and made sure my speakers were working, but no sound or music. The controls try to work for keyboard, mouse, and controller, but the keyboard controls were crap, and for the mouse, the buttons were a bit small and all over the screen, making it tough to use the mouse comfortably. I also found a number of small graphical bugs as I played through... this game really needed a bit more polish.
I was really hoping to like this game, especially from the publisher that brought us Long Live the Queen (which was great) and Magical Diary (which was not very good, but I still enjoyed it), but for me, this game was pretty much a miss on every level. I wouldn't recommend this game to anyone. If you know a small girl who is aspiring to study a science/technology field, have them play a good game instead. I wouldn't want her to think that science is as boring as this game is.

Victor Vran is an equipment-based ARPG with a sense of humor and a campaign that can last around 14 hours. It features the same VA as Geralt which creates a strange atmosphere since he plays a Hunter in this world, only without Geralt’s sense of humor or sarcasm, a sort of grim Geralt. The game features some interesting ways to customize your character, decent gameplay, great co-op functionality (I play the entire thing with a friend), and more. For me, it stumbles in the replay value department, but that’s okay. I had a good time going through once and not forcing myself to continue.
The gameplay consists of using WASD for movement and the mouse to attack. Your left hand will be very busy since this control scheme also uses Q and E for weapon abilities while Shift is your dodge roll, Spacebar is your jump, and 1-4 activate potions and Demon Powers. There are also two other control schemes for the controller and mouse movement. You can rebind keys too. The combat didn’t exactly amaze me, but I did have fun using everything at my disposal.
Combat is greatly affected by the items you choose to equip. Each weapon type has a distinct feel to it and some require more learning than others. Most of them are very straight forward such as swords and hammers, but a lightning gun favors mobile players that understand positioning for laying down traps and running away from your homing lightning ball if nothing else is around (your own lightning skills can kill you). Every weapon comes with a basic attack and two abilities. Victor Vran can equip two of them at a time which can result in interesting and useful combinations. You can also have two potions and two demon powers each. Both can be defensive or offensive. I preferred a healing potion and a fire bomb with a Sanguine Aura (armor and healing) and a Boomerang.
There are no skill points or stats in play that you can allocate points to which makes fun dependent on finding the right combination of items that suit you and changing them around occasionally. There are destiny points which allow passive card abilities to be equipped. At level 41, I had around 18 of them for five card slots. The cards can grant more armor, life leech, explosions on dealing overkill damage or crits, thorns for melee attacks, and even enhance weapon styles. They also come in three flavors from normal, Divine, and Wicked with the last two granting an extra effect on the card. Every single thing you can equip has a rarity except for outfits. Whites are commons and purples are highly coveted.
Crafting and exploration are both present in this game. Remember how I said Spacebar lets you jump, well you can also jump off of walls twice. Most of the time, wall jumps are used to reach higher places hiding secrets which is another word for chest in this game. It’s generally worth your time to keep an eye out for them, but I wouldn’t recommend backtracking often to find them all. The crafting in the game isn’t too interesting. Most of it is just increasing the stats on a weapon that you like. They did make it convenient by having all the recipes easily available. There are some hidden ones that you can look up that aren’t very important. Sometimes you can end up disappointed with the results when turning a normal card Wicked or Divine.
The co-op aspect is great and slick. You can play with strangers or friends via the lobby system or if you have your game set to online, friends can just hop in and smash demons with you. You do have to add each other first. All the loot is instanced so no one has to share. On the other hand, you can’t trade with other players. You can also cover for each other’s weaknesses by having loadouts that complement each other. I’ll mention that I found to UI to be well designed and easy to use.
While the game does feature a story, I thought it was ordinary. Where they did do well was in the narrator and humor department. There were plenty of dumb jokes and references that made me shake my head. It’s not a game to be taken seriously, especially with those dancing skeletons. The Voice’s comments are mostly entertaining. He has a condescending and sarcastic attitude with some lines failing to amuse due to the writing.
Victor Vran did feel like a “one and done” type of experience. I didn’t find myself caring about the challenges very much on normal and after I beat the game, I didn’t care about the Elite challenges. You also have no need to roll a second Vran since the gear-based gameplay means you can have different styles at Vran at any time. The fatigue also sets in when hunting monsters for bounties and looking for treasure due to the handcrafted maps. They have a daily dungeon which changes daily which isn’t enough for me. I didn’t find the wave-based map to be that great either, especially if a co-op partner dies and they’re stuck waiting around until you make it to the next platform.
I’m not complaining about the level design. They did a fine job except for a single map that I thought was just confusing to navigate. It just doesn’t have that procedural aspect like Path of Exile or Diablo 3’s Rifts that can keep me playing over and over. Keep in mind that it’s a smaller game and they seemed to have made the right decision when it comes to my tastes. You don’t want a half-baked random map generator that produces boring environments.
Other aspects I didn’t find appealing were the Demon Soul prices and the effectiveness of armor. Demon Souls are a rare currency that can drop. I only ever found two of them in 14 hours which tells me that it must be for players that stick with the game for a long while. Armor for Victor Vran himself did not seem very effective.
I chose the outfit with the highest armor and even used a Knight card that bumped me to over 110 armor. I would still receive an incredible amount of damage during the later portions of the game. The only solution I found was to stack even more armor with Sanguine Aura for another 100 which finally allowed me to stay alive much more often. I’d say I died under 30 times so the count wasn’t too bad, but I don’t know how other builds could do it without becoming glass cannons. It took 200 armor for it to feel effective and deflect damage while maintaining a good damage output.
Victor Vran is a fun time that will not break your wallet, but don’t go in with the expectation that you’ll extract 200 hours of gameplay. You can grab it for $1 right now for six more days at Humble Bundle which is a steal and what I did. I think it’s different enough to warrant a purchase and it doesn’t have severe flaws. Get huntin’.

Might & Magic: Heroes VI is a bit of a mixed bag in my honest opinion. Right off the bat I’ll say that, overall, the game is decent with enough content and unlockables to keep you occupied for a while. The various factions each focus on their own unique theme and due to this they also have different units to go along with it as well as heroes that can be adapted to your playstyle with the use of skill trees and reputation. This works just as well in the different campaigns where the reputation you choose for the main character will actually influence the story potentially giving you two different endings for each one. As good as this may sound the game isn't without issues that potentially ruin the whole experience (at least it did for me).
Firstly it's worth mentioning that the game uses Uplay (a platform made by Ubisoft) as opposed to Steam meaning you have to register the game on a Uplay account as well. This was more of a slightly annoyance rather than a problem so I won't get too much into this point but I have heard that this has caused problems that seem to involve Uplay not accepting activation keys provided by Steam.
The main problem I have with this game is the way the multiplayer was handled and how disappointing it was. I bought this game to play with a good friend but in our first game we quickly discovered that you couldn't watch battles being fought by other players (including allies). This means that every battle that your friend will take part in is another 5 minutes of having to sit there and watch the map as nothing happens (unless you both make use of the quick fight feature which I would recommend doing).
This also means that you're forced to miss out on any significant battles between your friend and enemy heroes which may decide the outcome of a match. What? You actually wanted to see these two mighty armies clash? You wanted to laugh at your friend as he makes a bad move and gets a stack of his units killed or even see what his faction plays like? Too bad. You can't.
The only way I can really recommend this game is as a single-player game which it seems to do well enough but as a multiplayer game it just feels like most matches (under normal circumstances) take longer than they should and even when you do finish it you look back and realise that the experience could have been much better. Regardless, if this game ever goes on sale and you are a fan of turn-based strategy games then I would still recommend it even if it's just for the campaign and the occasional skirmish against AI.

I've mixed feelings about this game. Ever since spending countless hours playing Heroes of Might and Magic III and it's expansions/mods years ago,  I've been a fan. I love a good turn-based tactical combat based game. In fact, it may be my favorite genre. A strong strategy of collecting resources, helpful items and building powerful kingdoms backed by a solid story, good character dialogue, with outstanding art and soundtrack all mixed together, it's my opinion there is no topping this genre of game.
Might and Magic: Heroes VI though falls short of legendary status for many reasons. Many avenues of this series have been simplified such as the resources, additions like the caravan options from HoMM IV and NPC monsters on the map being able to attack you during their turn if you are too close are missing. The story is nothing that held my interest and the dialogue happening in the pop-up screens was pretty horrible in many instances, and the in-game cutscene graphics are pretty generic. I did enjoy the map art and the soundtrack was okay.
The gameplay is decent, though at many times not challenging. I had to crank up the difficulty to hard for any real strategy. On normal it can be difficult in the first few levels, but once you amass some powers/items/armies it's pretty much a steamroll. I played through 3 of the campaigns and towards the end of the 3rd I was getting bored and just selecting auto-battle and having minimal to no losses.
I did like the inclusion of dynasty weapons, dynasty traits and having to open further slots and options by playing more and earning the achievement points. Again, there wasn't much of a challenge to the achievements other than just playing long enough to rack up enough kills/battles won without losses/ etc.
Uplay is another barrier. Online activation to continue your game, if you do need/have to be offline you have to play a game started in offline mode.  I don't like to open my steam purchased game in two menus. Not a deal breaker for me, but annoying and unnecessary.
I doubt I'll go back and play another full campaign. Perhaps, a random map here and there. Overall, it's just okay. Nothing spectatular that a turn-based strategy lover must have, but a worthy buy if you come across for cheap.

I initially wrote a positive review, but the more I played, the more glaring the problems with the title became (which seems to be the general pattern if one reads the rest of the negative reviews).
So while I was initially sucked in by the games atmosphere (and my own hopes for a realistic WWI depiction) the cracks soon appeared. So I had to write a new review, because I simply cannot recommend this game any more.
First off; The community for this game is dwindling. The developers seem to have let the game go and care little about maintaining its fan-base or player-base. Instead they have opted to use moderators who constantly shut down threads pertaining to suggestions and feed-back.
According to the moderators, the developers have no interest in differentiating their game from the rest of the bog-standard shooters, instead going for an arcadey feel, but with a thin veil of realism tacked on to it (so not at all realistic as it's advertised). If that's a bad thing or not is up to you. So if you're looking for a more realistic approach to WWI than Battlefield 1, this sadly, isn't it.
Also be aware that the developers rarely engage with the gaming community directly.
Not to mention the bugs. But you can read about them in a lot of the other reviews.
In short, if you don't mind people killing you with well aimed fire while jumping through the air, if you can stomach being shot through walls or from behind obstacles, if you have no problem going up against opponents with aimbots, wall hacks etc., and if you don't mind the dwindling player-base or the lackluster interest from the developers in maintaning the community, or if you feel like paying for a product that cannot compare with the glossy packaging of Battlefield 1, yet does very little to differentiate itself from it when it comes to actual game-play...then I guess this game is for you.
I myself will be moving on to other games with a more vibrant community and responsive developers whilst hoping that we some day get a game worthy of depicting WWI. Going by this title, however, I cannot see their next game, Tannenberg, being any different.
