is a first-person action game with little bits of other genres woven in.  For instance, it almost reminds me of a walking sim early on, and then when you get a L.E.A.F. suit it's a bit more exploratory.  The suit itself has some nice capabilities, like taking and giving life to creatures around you.  The running and jumping is a really nice aspect to the suit, which feels very free and invigorating to me in a sense.  You can also essentially "live forever" as long as you have energy to replenish the life around you as you take life from the areas you are in.  This is key for collecting the acorns as well, since trees tend to drop acorns on a regular basis.
It's not a very long game, but the areas are fairly sizable and vast.  There is some really nice equipment upgrading as you continue on, and several types of collectible items to collect for acorn doors, which are locked without the proper amount of acorns, and some mysterious medallions you find in certain boxes with a slight shiny glint you can see from afar if you're in the right spots called pendulum cases as you travel different areas.  You can go back and forth as you please with the Travel option in the pause menu as well, if you gain new upgrades and want to explore around some previous areas.
When hostiles start to appear on the map, you have some very slight FPS elements involved in targeting while being attacked.  This is extremely light, and I don't find the difficulty to be a problem at all in this game.  I find it a little short, but compared to other games at this price range, the grapics and music and complete package make it one of the better games on Steam I have played in this price range.
One gripe I have is the look sensitivity was extremely fast!  I had to move it all the way to about five percent from the lowest setting in options to use it with my controller.  This probably should be updated.  I also fell through rocks a few times while exploring out of the way areas, as well as some ceilings that I went above.  A few times I was completely stuck, and I had to restart the area.  Things you collect are still accounted for, so you don't have to redo everything again and again, aside from getting to the spot where you need to be.  In this suit, that's not too hard to do, generally.
As mentioned, the time was a little short, but I'd rather complain a good game was too short, than play a bad game and constantly hope the next part is the end of it.  Most people don't even bother in the latter case, but I can be a bit of a masochist in that respect...  Sometimes bad games are so bad they end up good, and sometimes they are so bad they have a lot of humor along the way.  It's refreshing when I find one of those that bring something to the table, intentional or not.
Great graphics!  I really loved the colors as I went from area to area.  It kind of speaks for itself in game photos and video, or some of the screenshots I took as I travelled around.  It's beautiful!
The music is really relaxing on relaxing parts, pretty intense on intense parts, and overall fits your surrounding scenery or goals.  It's what I would call "world music" if I were selecting a style or genre, but the use of instrumentation reminded me of the Uncharted games a bit.  It's not constant, but will change or calm down.  It is not overpowering, and I liked not feeling like I needed to cut the volume down or anything while playing at any point.
The L.E.A.F. suit is a lot of fun!  The jumping and running around is very freeing and you can almost feel it as you traverse landscapes.  I won't go into detail on this one, but they have some really good upgrades too, especially later on as you move through the game's story.
The creatures you encounter are awesome too!  They are called, or rather nicknamed, daemons, as you learn, and the bigger ones don't really have a name.  I won't talk much about that, since that is something the story will eventually get you up to speed with.
Collecting things along the way to unlock other things.  This is something you can go back through to balance out some of the shortness factor that I kind of complained a bit about, sort of.  Going back with all the upgrades can help you find a lot of what you may have missed earlier, or just focusing on finding the rest of the items, if you choose to do so.
I liked the text that would come up here and there of your own thoughts.  As you entered an area that sparked a thought, you would see something on the sides of the screen as you went along.  Simple concept, but it worked, I thought.
The length of the game could be a little longer, but honestly, this is not a huge complaint for me.  It fit the whole story well for me, but in a way I always want games to be longer, even a game I spend 100 hours or more on, if it's good.
Glitches where I was stuck in rocks, or fell through and couldn't get back into the map.  I only fell a little, but I usually had trouble finding a way back, especially when I only had the basic suit.
I would like to see difficulty created.  It was very very easy for me.  I'm not so much complaining about my own experience as much as for some that might like a more challenging experience.
A map.  I couldn't find any sort of a map feature.  There is a small bar, like many Bethesda games have, where it has the compass kind of thing near the top, and the "point of interest" is marked as a red spot, but I would like one where I could see the layout of everything. Wasn't able to find this, if in fact there is one.  Would love it if there ever is one!
The story is... a bit generic in some respects, but in others I like that it sort of makes you wonder and question things as you're going along.  There are some twists that make it more interesting than your average story of this type of war and madness-driven power.
I think I stated it all in the original few paragraphs, but for this price range, this is one of the best games I've played on Steam.  It's an experience all its own, and I recommend this at full price if you're looking for a single game on Steam you want to spend $20 (or whatever your currency may be).  I personally love sales, since I have a big frugal side, but this game is something I doubt anyone purchasing will regret playing!  Amazing game!

Ah another World War II real time strategy game? What could this one have in store? Lets find out! Get your Comrades together, grab your commander's baton, and put on a monocle! Were gonna take over the world!
Pros:
+ Amazing Detail in the combat, some of which I've yet to understand even to this day!
+ Great Soundtrack, it really sets in the mood that the world is at war and that you're fighting for a big cause.
+ The AI is pretty intelligent, I mean its not unfair amounts but its atleast self aware... unlike other games.
+ Each nation can play a part in the war, even small countries like Bulgaria, Denmark, Belgium, ect.
+ You can change history in many different ways, making this game a playground of new alternate scenerios.
+ National and Global events give you multiple choices that impact the world and history it self! Choose wisely commander!
+ You can sit down and create your own battleplans; now hear me out... what if I told you that sitting down drawing arrows and lines in this game can some how... boost the fun? I know I know, its weird right? Well you can draw out strategic battle plans across the many nations and continents for your amusment and of course strategy.
Neutral:
/ Creating armies and going through the logistics is tedious and often VERY hard to micro manage but on the flip side it feels SO good to sit in the boots of a real Commander's job of working with the huge military forces of WWII.
/ The Military Research is bland you go from "Infantry I" to "Infantry II" and so and so on. However its easy to understand and grasp, so its not exactly all bad.
Cons:
- DLC out the rear end, I could understand like... one big pack for the Sprites and multiple for the bigger DLCs but the Sprite Packs are all seperate for different nations such as Germany, America, Italy, Russia, ect. Which is ridiculous.
- Diplomacy is a joke; Diplomacy is useless unless you're allied or friendly with the nation you're speaking to its practically a waste to even use it as most responses otherwise are "No" even if you present a gift.
- Politics is also similiarly a joke; politics boils down to one of two things, you're either replacing ministers to give better stats, or you're creating puppets/liberating puppets. Thats it, no massive change to certain ideologies or anything.
- Naval and Air combat is a bit lack luster, nothing is really gained nor is there a sense of urgency when using the navy or airforce.
- Some nations are ungodly powerful two that come to mind are the US and Germany; don't get me wrong both were super powers but they seem unrealistically buffed and over powered; for nation that suffered greatly under the great depression.
DLC Specific Parts:
Pros:
+ Their Finest Hour's additions are quite great with the Custom Mode being my favorite; you can litterally rebuild a nation from the ground up as you see fit!
+ New units and abilities! Fun Fun Fun.
Neutral:
/ Some of the content from "For the Motherland" and "Semper Fi" I don't even use often, but the abilities are there I suppose.
Cons:
-♥♥♥♥♥♥tons of Skin packs that really don't add that much to the game.
- They could've just bundled Semper Fi, For the Motherland, and Their Finest Hour
Conclusion:
I love Hearts of Iron III, great game for the Commander in you! I give it a 7/10 without DLC and with all major DLCs a 9/10. Its just simply a game any WWII History Buff or hardened RTS Commander needs.

It's been a while since I wanted to play a translated version of this game as I own an actual cartridge of the game and played from start to finish. The cost and negative reviews came off as rather off-putting for me at first but I waited so long for this and decided to get it anyway...
... And what I got is an absolutely playable version of the game and I've been having a blast right off the bat. If you only worry about whether the game is playable or not, it is easily accessible through a keyboard and mouse (the game manual tells you about the keys) and there are ways to make controllers work.
GAMEPLAY & STORY
Romancing SaGa 2 is a jRPG that, much like most SaGa games doesn't play like a standard game of the genre. You do not gain EXP from killing enemies but you (semi-)randomly get increases to your stats and expertise at using whatever weapon or spells you're using. You also get stronger by getting new attack skills which you get randomly by "sparking" when you do an attack with the weapon of your choice. Your chance to learn is higher as you fight more powerful foes. The game also has the advantage of allowing the player to escape (only through the emperor) which isn't a feature available in all SaGa games.
Speaking of foes, your enemies grows stronger as you fight more and more and yes, this can make your enemies way, way harder if you treat this game like a traditional jRPG. Personally, even when stuck with overwhelmingly powerful enemies I've been able to progress but it's a matter of patience which is an element common to the series. Escaping is not a bad move at times as it'll allow to avoid enemies with resistances to your attacks who'd make things much harder for you.
The game is also non-linear which means you can travel to various areas at your own pace (especially as you go further in the game) and you have choices that can affect the game such as enabling new classes to use, get new magic, etc.
The game is one of the hardest in the series but if you take the time to get used to the game, you'll eventually be able to handle fights you'd find difficult at first and carry on with a sense of accomplishment from learning the mechanics of the game and defeat the challenging seven heroes. The story by itself is very simplistic and so are the characters but paying attention to the dialogue bits and character actions will allow the players to notice various themes that makes some characters a little more deep than they appear.
MUSIC
The game has the exact same music you'll find in the SNES version. It is a phenomenal soundtrack with a mixture of powerful, beautiful and sometime even emotional music at times. Music during events gives a good idea of the mood and even simple dungeon themes gives a powerful atmosphere at times. The various battle themes are all fantastic and it all culminates with one of the greatest final boss themes ever. It easily ranks up there with the all-time greats among other jRPGs.
PORT
Controller issues, seemingly incoherent keyboard setup, screen size issues, etc. are common complaints but a keep look at discussions will reveal that there are ways to solve many of those problems.
. The answer to this is that
. The game responds perfectly fine with a keyboard and mouse and checking the actual game manual will show that the controls aren't even so bad and they become intuitive within a few seconds or minutes.
The game also comes with all the fun and neat addons and unlike the Final Fantasy ports, the visual changes are not a detriment to the game as they give a nice enhanced look that makes the game more lively. If you played SaGa Frontier before, you might get an idea of that sensation.
Is the game worth it's cost? I'm inclined to say yes, especially while it's on sale as the game is lenghty and if you like non-linear gameplay with challenging enemies, there's a chance you'll enjoy it despite the odds being against you at times. Romancing SaGa 2 truly is a classic and anyone willing to forgive the current faults this port has might potentially get a chance to enjoy this series since most of the games in it have a lot to give in term of fun and longevity.

Well, I finished it in under six hours, so it's not a long game. However, I didn't 100% it, and I intend to go back and do more.
But value propositions aside, I got this game after seeing Jim Sterling play it, and the running and jumping, the sense of speed and momentum, looked so fun. It is. I did not get tired of it at all. This game does speed excellently. Perhaps perfectly. Thus, it was worth the price to me. Whethe it provides enough value to you, well, is up to you.
In addition it solves the problem of first-person platforming by both letting you see your feet, and always providing platforms big enough you can judge your positioning with no problem. Thus, the platforming is very fun.
The shooting, too, is quite good. It's minimal, but where it shines is when you find yourself soaring through the air and shooting things (to life or death) before you land. That is quite satisfying, and almost makes me want a challenge mode or to try speedrunning it.
There are two other mechanics: a grappling hook and magnetic boots. The magnetic boots, in my opinion, feel awful. The transition from walking on a wall to jumping off or vice versa is jarring and not at all smooth. In addition, twice it bugged out and gravity still applied to me, so I just fell. The grappling hook, however, I quite liked, once I got used to it, though it can be fiddly remembering to hold down the button to keep it attached, which killed me a couple times.
Then there's the fact it is gorgeous and the soundtrack is amazing. My only complaint with this is that about half the game isn't in the gorgeous valley but often rather dull interiors, which is quite a shame. They could've easily been designed better to solve the dullness problem too, but I shant spoil how.
The soundtrack, meanwhile, has only one problem: the running tracks are too good. Too exciting. And when you're just wanting to pause and find collectibles or read notes in a speedy section that can be a bit jarring.
Lastly, the story's good. It's not remarkable, but it's solid. And it is told all through environmental notes scattered around and audio logs, in very much a walking simulatoresque style, which some people will have a problem with, but I found myself engaged in it.
Really, in many ways this game feels like it owes much to walking simulators like Everybody's Gone to the Rapture, except they then made it a proper game. They added gameplay. I don't hate walking simulators, but really, they're not games, they're digital art pieces, and can only be judged by their story and beauty. This has those as well as being a great game.

Though dated, Fallout 3s good writing and survivalist atmosphere more than makes up for the technical and visual issues. A good 100+ hour world to get lost in, and would recommend DLCs too.
The year is 2277 and it has been 200 years since the Great War that consumed the Earth in nuclear fire and radiation. You are a resident of Vault 101, one of many underground shelters built before the war. The door to Vault 101 slides open for the first time in 200 years, and you emerge into the ruins of Washington D.C, now known as The Capital Wasteland.
This review is written from the perspective of a fan of RPGs and story-driven games, who hasn’t played any other Fallout games.
Fallout 3 is a massive open world sandbox RPG that can be played from a first or third-person perspective. You are thrust into the world and given a goal, but it is up to you to decide how long you want to take to reach it. The Capital Wasteland is a harsh and sprawling land that lets you go wherever you want, whenever you want. The map is absolutely huge, consisting of downtown DC and all of its surrounding areas ranging from sewers to suburbs. The absolutely huge amount of approaches to the land can be overwhelming for some players. You may struggle with knowing where to start, especially given the fact the game offers very little direction. Just doing quests would probably only uncover a quarter to a third of the entire map, so players that prefer independent exploration and spontaneous discovery will get a lot of more value vs. someone who follows the quest markers.
The progression system is fair and you start to feel more powerful over the course of the game, however by the end if you play your stats right you can literally have a jack of all trades, master of all character. Being able to cap every single stat on one character can eliminate some replay ability meaning the only reason to start another character would be alternative morality choices. On the other hand, it does eliminate the annoying factor of not being able to see what’s behind that door because I’m one point too short in this specific stat for people who don’t have time for 5 different playthroughs. Enemy difficulty adapts to your character level rather than the areas. This means that no matter where you go, the enemies will always be at your level. This is good as it keeps the combat fresh and evolving all the way to the very end, but bad because you can't stomp early game areas. It also allows players to explore freely at any point in the game without the risk of being suddenly disintegrated by some level 30 mob and losing 3 hours of progress because you forgot to save.
I really like the way the game handles the exploration and looting systems. You can fast travel back to any area you’ve discovered. This sparks the age old argument of immersion vs. quality of life, but hey, you’re not forced to use it. As you work your way through the game you slowly progress from picking up as much useless crap as you can carry to analysing the environment and cherry picking the most relevant and valuable stuff. For example, I didn’t see the point in lugging around a motorcycle gas tank until I found out you can build a flaming sword out of them and began hunting for them. I hoarded seemingly useless scrap metal until it paid off because it turned out some guy in a city was willing to pay for it to fix some pipes. I felt a wasteland junk expert by the end, as my approach to every new room became systematically rummaging through filing cabinets and desks for valuables that extend beyond money vs. not money.
Fallout 3s story is essentially structured into the main quest, side quests and DLC quests.  The main quest itself is a pretty mediocre story about finding your dad. It has its moments, but ultimately just serves to give the game a beginning and end. The middle portion, you will spend getting lost in the sometimes great, sometimes bad and sometimes plain weird side quests. The side quests are few in number (given the games size) and you won’t see 4 or 5 people with floating question marks on their heads asking you to fetch 12 bear asses. The role play aspect plays a big role in these side quests, allowing you to morally be the second coming of Christ, a boring stoic neutral dude, or Lucifer himself. This can cause quests to branch a few different ways (your stats can come into play during conversations too) but ultimately it usually ends up resulting to being good or evil. The excellent DLC packs definitely present a lot more ambiguous choices where you really have to think about things beyond being good or evil. Every DLC adds something to the game both story and gameplay wise, and I whole heartedly recommend getting them all (or the Ultimate Edition) if you can.
The other side of the story telling is more subtle than speaking to townsfolk and being explicitly told what’s going on. A lot of the locations in the game contain stories that you figure out, rather than being told. For example, I entered a motel room with a bunch of long dead skeletons, some guns and pre-war cash laying around. Some people would just loot the joint and move on, and that’s fine. Other people will look around and realise through the way the bodies and guns are positioned and seeing the pre-war money was leading back to a briefcase in the middle of the room, that a standoff after a bank heist took place in this room over 200 years ago. Bethesda put a lot of TLC and work into deliberately laying places out this way. It’s not just a random composition, there is a reason why everything is the way it is. You may think it’s a shame that so much work was put into things most players would miss, but I prefer the think that the fact that so many players miss it makes it much more special for the players that catch it.
The voiceover work can be a bit hit and miss, with the stand out performances being Ron Pearlman’s narration and Liam Neeson as your dad. Everything else is ok, or sometimes outright embarrassing, but I suppose that’s fair enough given the sheer amount of people there are to converse with. Your character isn’t voice acted, which of course gives a lot more freedom to the writers regarding conversation options. The writing is the real star of the show in this game. The game also offers a couple interesting radio stations to listen to whilst you roam the wastes, but in a game as long as this you will run into a lot of recurring dialogue and music that unfortunately gets old fast.
Fallout 3 was released in 2008 and it shows. It is by no means an ugly game and the scale of the world definitely makes up for the lack of eye candy.  The scale of the world also results in lots and lots of bugs. Some can be game breaking (albeit rarely) and others are just irritating or sometimes humorous. Ultimately I would say it’s worth powering through them to play the game. The game also has some major stability issues, especially on newer hardware. For instance I was having issues because for some reason this game was having issues with an OS newer than Vista and a processor with more than two cores. Almost everyone falls under that blanket these days and although these have easy fixes they are still annoying to deal with. The game used to have GFWL but thankfully it’s been removed. I would normally mitigate the ugliness of older games with mods, but I had issues with those here as well. Your mileage may vary, but I couldn’t go over 8-10 mods without constant crashing and FPS drops. In depth complicated mods are also much more annoying to install than something like Skyrim so I had to settle for more minor visual and quality of life changes.

Lastly... the more we buy this, the more likely the already confirmed RS3 Remaster lands in English. BANISHED is a city-builder that will make you question everything you think you know about survival, life, and humanity. It will take you on an emotional journey and force you to confront the idea of meaning in the face of an indifferent universe.
The game is deceptively calming and Zen-like, with its peaceful music and pretty landscapes. But you can't play the game with a casual mindset, because things can go horribly wrong, horribly quickly. Starvation, fires, disease, and lack of resources are ever-present dangers. Things can be perfect for 50 years, and then collapse in a matter of weeks.
Every time I play, I undergo a drastic change in mentality. At first, I'm very emotionally attached to my villagers, watching them live their lives and raise their families. As my village grows, I become detached and cool -- I no longer know my villagers by name, and I no longer become concerned when one (or two, or twenty) are homeless or starving. "This must be what a god feels like," I think to myself as I roll my eyes at the death of a villager apparently too stupid to walk ten feet and grab some firewood from the marketplace.
As you can tell by the number of hours I've played BANISHED, I absolutely love this game. I'll go a few months without playing, and then find myself missing it and open it up to start a new game. Every time I do, it's the same lovely, immersive, sometimes frustrating but always satisfying experience. BANISHED scratches some sort of existential itch in my soul, and I know it's a game I will continue to turn to for years and years.

As far as mechanics go, I absolutely love that the villagers of BANISHED are "smart" enough to perform routine tasks without being told. If you want to build a house in a forest, you don't have to tell them to clear the forest, gather resources, and then build the house -- they will perform the necessary steps to achieve your ultimate goal. This alone makes the gameplay superb to most city-builders.
I also enjoy playing this game with some of the many mods that other players have made. I love the new content and how easily it integrates into the basic game. But I think I'll always prefer to play it un-modded, because its very spareness is part of what makes it so real and so addictive.

To be fair, you have to have a very high IQ to understand Dark Souls 2. The lore is extremely subtle, and without a solid grasp of theoretical physics most of the story will go over a typical viewer's head. There's also the protagonist's nihilistic outlook, which is deftly woven into his characterisation - his personal philosophy draws heavily from Narodnaya Volya literature, for instance. The fans understand this stuff; they have the intellectual capacity to truly appreciate the depths of these lores, to realize that they're not just interesting- they say something deep about LIFE. As a consequence people who dislike Dark Souls 2 truly ARE idiots- of course they wouldn't appreciate, for instance, the humour in Maughlin's existencial catchphrase "I'm rich," which itself is a cryptic reference to Turgenev's Russian epic Fathers and Sons. I'm smirking right now just imagining one of those addlepated simpletons scratching their heads in confusion as Hidetaka Miyazaki's genius unfolds itself on their screens. What fools... how I pity them.

It's a very satisfying, and at times quite challenging puzzle game that I would highly recommend to anyone who enjoys the genre. The level design is done well enough that anyone can pick it up and understand the basic rules of the game. The developer, Ian Stocker, took notes from Egoraptor's Sequelitis video on Mega Man X, and has done a great job at creating the level of conveyance necessary for a good puzzle or action game. Every time there's a new element, it's introduced to the player in a safe way where the player is not in danger of dying (or is very unlikely to die), then is immediately used in several different and creative ways in the following puzzles.
I completed it in about 4 hours, 26 minutes of in-game time, and I'd say for $10, plus Workshop support for custom user-created levels, it's well worth a buy.

The SaGa series is one of the most experimental and intriguing RPG series out there. Romancing SaGa 2 is no exception. Nonlinearity and branching choices absolutely make this game wonderfully replayable. I would recommend jumping on the forum to find out all the secrets and mechanics going on in Romancing SaGa 2, but it wouldn't necessary for a first playthrough. Just be aware, SaGa looks and plays like a typical JRPG, but it's not.
The HD visuals look great, the sound is top notch, and the use of a controller is so comfortable in a game where enemies appear on the field.
Romancing SaGa 2 is a great entry point if you've never played a SaGa game before. Just be aware that levels and grinding play out very differently. SaGa really wants each battle to feel special, and honestly it doesn't want you to neddlessly grind. The game would rather you completing scenarios, finishing side quests, taking on difficult bosses, and if you die, your lineage inherits everything you've done, so you can go right back at it again! A one-of-a-kind series worth picking up and realy delving into. High replayability with checking out different paths and seeing new scenarios!

This is an English port of a jRPG from 1993 that didn't get a worldwide release until 2016. Romancing SaGa 2 does not hold your hand. It rarely tells you where to go, instead giving you the general objective of "build up your empire and gain strength so you and your descendants can someday stand a chance against the villains". This is good.
Having the freedom to explore makes the world feel very open. Sometimes the chancellor of your castle notifies you of crises happening in various parts of the continent that you can investigate. You are free to follow his leads or go wherever you please depending on your priorities.
The sheer variety of characters means you'll have a good time customizing your party in each generation to suit your needs. Even though there is perma-death, Game Over screens are exceptionally rare (mostly occuring in the beginning and around the end). Death usually means learning from your mistakes and passing your knowledge down to others, a theme established early on. This also means that while you pick up new characters throughout the game and lose old ones, the new ones will never fall behind.
Pick this up. There's a fantastic amount of replay value due to not having a set order in which to do things, experimenting with magic combinations, and events potentially having multiple outcomes.

A great Squaresoft game from the SNES era of the Romancing SaGa series that never found it's way to North America when it was first released. Strangely enough the GameBoy SaGa games (called Final Fantasy Legend 1 & 2 & 3 in NA), SaGa Frontier 1 & 2 and Unlimited SaGa all were released, yet we somehow missed out on Romancing SaGa back in the day. (except for Romancing SaGa: Minstrel Song for PS2in October 11, 2005 which was a remake of Romancing SaGa 1)
The most important thing to understand about this game is your guys are gonna lose LP (Like HP but get taken off after you are incapacitated from losing all HP) and eventually die when your LP runs out.  Replenishing LP isn't something easily done, expect your guys (including your main character) to die, especially on your first playthrough because you might just not get the hang of it all at first.  Guess what?  You just replace them...
Don't attempt to play this game like other JRPGs.  For one grinding isn't needed like most games, in fact the more fights you engage in the harder you make the game.  It takes a tight balance, if you don't grind a little you'll wind up too weak to beat the bosses, if you grind too much the monsters will get too tough for you.
The game isn't for everyone, but anyone who is a fan of the SaGa series should feel right at home with it's quirkiness.
People seem to be complaining over a few "problems" about this port.  First and foremost this is infact a mobile game, there are infact parts of the game that clearly were designed for mobile and weren't changed.  Get over it, those things don't mean anything.
Then there's the much whining about things that are so easily dealt with.
Alt+enter for fullscreen.
Turn on Steam's controller settings to get your controller to work perfectly fine.
I haven't needed to use mouse/KB for anything in the game to work other than fullscreen and it stays once you set it.
I grew up using DOS, there used to be a lot of things you needed to mess with to make games work.  You kids today couldn't handle that, you'd just whine and complain that things didn't just work without trying to figure anything out yourself, and then when somebody told you how to do it you'd just whine some more about having to do it.

The single-player campaign takes, at most 5 hours, if you are either terrible or love looking for secrets. You finish it and go, "is that i?"
No, that isn't it. There are plenty of maps the main game didn't take you to, there are multiple challenges on each map (use a certain weapon, don't use potions, use demon powers, etc) that provide in-game rewards. There are outfits to collect, legendary weapons to find, destiny cards to collect so you can switch up your build. There are transmutation recipies to discover.
There are bounties and treasure maps that you can find and that other players can share. After you go through your bounties or maps, go ahead and share yours; sharing is encouraged and there is no penalty for doing so.
Then, after you do all of that, you can start using Hexes. Hexes either hinder you or boost the enemies and you receive extra rewards for using them. Turn on all five of them and discovery a new land of challenge and reward.
Basically, this game seems really simple and light-weight, but it actually has many options to keep you interested and entertained and encourages communication among the player-base. The story is just the beginning.

Banished is the best city builder I've ever played (and I've played a lot, having been a fan of the genre since the original Sim City and the old Sierra historical builder games). The game is deceptively simple, you start with a few settlers and minimal supplies and you build a thriving settlement. Sounds easy enough, but it's probably one of the most challenging games I've played.
There are a variety of crops, animals, and natural resources. Your setttlers will plant and gather and use these to build a rustic town. Steel tools and stone houses represent the pinnacle of your settlement's technological advancement. You can barter goods with a few visiting tradesmen and some nomads may periodically ask to join your settlement, but that's the limit of your outside contact. Peace reigns, you won't need any military (or even police) here. The only hostile forces you will encounter in Banished are tornadoes, fires, diseases, starvation, and cold. And you will encounter them, a lot.
Although the game is relaxing to play, it can at times be incredibly difficult. Your settlement might be going along nicely for 100 years, with plenty of food and lots of citizens available to fill all the jobs that need to be done, and suddenly everyone has cholera and you're closing down the schoolhouse to free up some child laborers to expand your cemetary. Banished is brutal that way. But it's also beautiful. The music and graphics and effects are really appealing, and the immersion factor is high. It's definitely one of those games you can sit down to in the early afternoon and play for hours and hours and then be surprised to find your stomach growling and oh hey when did it get so dark outside?
The developer is very active and involved in the community, and new features are added often. Now the game offers modding capability and Steam Workshop. So far the community has responded with some amazing tweaks and additions which only make the game even better (also a little easier, if you find the challenge a bit much).
I can't wait to see how Banished continues to evolve, which it seems to do in much the same way that my tiny settlements grow and evolve, with all of the little details coming together to make something really satisfying and enjoyable.

(also sometimes referred to as
) is a free-to-play indie game developed and published by Creability. The game consists of the player switching through different "channels," which are all accessable within 5 different "regions." Each region has different channels that present different gameplay mechanics. The main mechanic in the game is the method in which the user must switch between the channels. If the text displayed onscreen matches the color of which it is describing, the user must left-click to go to the next channel. If the text does not match the color of which it is describing, the user must right-click to go to the next channel, all of which must be done in rapid succession throughout the game. If the user makes one mistake, it is game over, as the game does not contain a stock/life system. The game is more of a test in how fast the user can process and react to information being rapidly thrown at them, but ultimately mastered in a clever and artistic and creative fashion, which results in an astounding gameplay experience.
+ Well-designed interface
+ Easy to learn, hard to master
+ No ultimately steep learning curve, jump in and play
+ Free-to-play
+ No in-game microtransactions - the full experience is there from the get-go
+ Achievements that take effort to earn
+ Amazing artstyle and aesthetic feel
+ Smooth, quick, responsive gameplay
+ Addition of new mechanics mid-game work very smoothly, and take little to no time to understand fully
+ Fantastic soundtrack with music from multiple artists, fits the feel of the gameplay and the artstyle
- Replayability after unlocking all achievements and completing the game fully is lacking
10/10

I bought this game in March and played it for about 64 hours, then abandoned it for a while. Then I picked it up again today and realized why. Re;Birth 3 is a valiant effort at revitalizing the series, but it just doesn't do enough.
First off, the battle system has been substantially modified. Now there is no EXE gauge - instead, your SP gauge does double duty. Suddenly, Rush attacks actually matter. No longer can you half-heartedly assign some spare points to somewhat-decent Rush attacks; now you have to think carefully and balance between all three types. Now everybody has to worry about Rushing. It adds a little more strategy to the gameplay - though I will say that grinding your SP back up after a boss battle can be quite a chore, especially when your fastest characters keep killing enemies before the slower ones even get a chance to touch them.
Inside dungeons, the hidden treasure system has changed slightly. Now instead of using that annoying radar, you look for shadows of invisible blocks (think Mario) on the ground and hit them. They all give you credits, but only one per run of a dungeon gives you an item. So basically, it's the same as before, but they're easier to find. Heck, in some dungeon layouts, you can even see the box shimmering in the air. That said, though, the developers continued their infuriating trend of hiding important items in them. Plans, weapons, armor, even
. The cooler the item, the lower its spawn rate is, with costumes and accessories reaching nigh-impossible levels. To give you an idea, I spent three hours doing nothing but going in and out of Ario Plateau (or was it Luji? Screw it, I can't be bothered to remember), waiting for Blanc's school uniform and accompanying hat to spawn. And apparently I'm one of the
ones. If you want to unlock all the cosmetic options in the game... may Noire have mercy on your soul.
Another thing that got a spit-shine is Stella's Dungeon. It's much more straightforward now, and the DLC bundled with the game (the base game, mind you - for once, they've decided to give you the non-cosmetic DLC for free) makes the first several areas go by pretty easily. Uzume hasn't left my side in... well, forever, actually. It eventually becomes hard to lose at Stella's Dungeon, assuming you exercise a minimal amount of caution.
Dungeon layouts are, again, recycled. You'll see a lot of familiar places that pervaded the first two games of the series, though - like Re;Birth 2 - this game adds a couple more to the mix, some of which I found greatly enjoyable. The Luji Plateau layout is full of whimsy, and I found the Lowee Castle layout's myriad winding corridors to be a joy to wander, confusing as they may be. That said, there's still a lot of recycling. There's a lot more dungeons in this game than in the other two games, meaning you'll be running into the same layouts perhaps even
than you did in them. Plus, all the layouts from the first two games are laughably hostile toward the new hidden treasure system, as their floors are too detailed/dark to see the shadows. There's a plan that shows the treasure spots on the minimap, but still. When you're grinding for that Noire weapon you absolutely HAVE to have, it gets painful to just bounce around like an idiot hoping you're close enough to the box for it to register a hit.
Which brings me to a new feature: "challenges." There are certain "challenges" that can increase characters' stats, grant them plans, and so on. These range from "jump X times" to "spend X battles outside the party." The vast majority of them, though, require the character to be the leader. And with one, two, three... 28 characters in this game, this gets painful FAST. Heck, I've had Nepgear as my leader for pretty much as long as I've had her, and I'm still nowhere near maxing out her jumping challenge. Oh, and did I mention? Each character's standard EXE attack is locked behind a "use skills X times" challenge. So you have to do some grinding before anyone becomes worth using. And once your first few characters do get their EXE attacks, you won't want to use anyone else. Looks like Histoire is gonna be a permanent member of my lineup.
Then there's the story. It's nothing as good as the second game, but it's still pretty competent. There's ups, downs, and so on and so forth. Even the villains get comfortable amounts of screentime. The second game had a hard time striking a balance, but this game - despite having more villains - gives each of them enough time to feel like they were worth including. I will say, though, that the recycled boss fights get old fast. Come on, even the second game had a few fights that weren't Underling or the Four Felons. Fortunately, there's only three endings this time, so you don't have to undo the Change Dungeon on Millennium Labyrinth five thousand times just to get 100% CG completion.
And last up... the translation. I'll come out and say it: it's just as bad as in the second game. Fortunately, the most brutalized characters (Nepgear and Ram) are background characters in this game, so it's not as noticeable. The memes, though, are in full swing. More so than they were in the second game, since Neptune is the main character again. Be afraid. Fortunately, there's a fanmade patch for this game, too, so it's playable. Then again, IFI shouldn't be forcing us to resort to these extremes in the first place.
However, it really cannot be understated how much stuff there is in this game. Not content -
. There's a zillion dungeons to mindlessly wander in search of that dag-blasted LASOU Uniform, there's a zillion different characters to buy weapons (and make accessories) for, there's a zillion different plans to make and challenges to complete, there's a zillion different enemies to get item drops from, the list goes on and on. Re;Birth 3 is by far the most egregious of the trilogy in terms of mind-numbing grinding time asked of the player. Never has any other game - even the other Neptunia ones - so thoroughly crushed my desire to complete it - or even finish it. That's right. I haven't even finished the game. I'm sitting around in Chapter 8 right now because I've come to see the game as a chore. The rewards I get for farming enemies and making plans are meaningless when they're just the exact same things as in the other games. Why bother buying all these weapons, accessories, and costumes when I already have them in Re;Birth 2? This game recycles almost every item that it contains (except for, obviously, the Plutia- and Peashy-specific ones), making them worthless. And the story isn't bad, but it's nowhere near good enough to keep me engaged.
This is why I said the game tries to improve upon the formula, but doesn't go far enough. If you've played either of the first two games - and if you're looking at this game, then I'm assuming you have - then you aren't missing anything. There's really no reason to buy this one. The second one was worth buying, despite the repetitiveness, because of its story. This one has no draws. Just ignore it and move on to something else. I hear that Megadimension shakes things up a bit - maybe you can try that.

I got the game last week, and beat it last night.  Not going to discuss how long it took, because I don't believe games should be rated on the amount of time it took.  Not to mention, times vary depending on if you want to 100% it, get all achievements, or create and play through community levels.
I really enjoyed this game, and anyone who enjoys semi-casual puzzle platformers will like it a lot, as well.  The main puzzles for completing the game to a bare-bones ending are not bash-your-head-against-a-wall difficult, while still maintaining a good level of both creative thinking, platforming, and satisfaction for solving.  The music is stellar, the art is gorgeous, and the "story" is sparse.
Some minor issues: the controls feel a tad too floaty, hit-boxes are a bit too broad, and it took me over half an hour of avoiding any contact with Toragos before realizing that you can touch (ride) him without taking damage if you avoid the head.  That last part could have been better demonstrated, because a gamer's instinct in a game like this is to not touch any part of the enemy, lest they perish.
I, for one, will not be 100%ing this game because it would take me WAY too long to find all the invisible keys, and that's not as fun as solving puzzles I can actually see.  But for what it was, I really enjoyed it, and I might even play around with the level creator, and/or speed-running.
I recommend this very much, and look forward to future titles from MagicalTimeBean.

Pros:
Amazing map. Throughout detailed and extremely large.

Decent graphics (I've found that anti aliasing can kill fps if you don't have a ton of VRAM)

Most of the glitches (cutscenes in particular) are super fun to mess with
Cons: (big breath)
Graphics can look like crap in some places (crank up that demanding anti aliasing)
Most of the cool cars are dlc or extremely expensive
Very hard to get money (I'm talking 1k-2k each race)
The physics are really wierd at slow speeds (but they do get better as you start getting into faster cars that can handle the speed)
Sometimes the map feels TOO big, like when you have to do a long road trip and it takes you half an hour to an hour at 200 MPH on highway to cross the map
The physics (yes I'm mentioning them again), while they eventually start to make sense and become intuitive, are EXTREMELY difficult to completely understand
Connection issues with multiplayer
THE GAME IS ONLINE ONLY SO IF YOUR PC IS IN A CRAPPY SPOT OF THE HOUSE WHERE THERE IS NO CONNECTION GOOD LUCK PLAYING THIS GAME (fr tho)
Overall, I loved the game, even though it has ALOT of quirks. The vast amount of places to visit and things to do really make up for the faults that this game has. The physics can be wonky, but make almost perfect sense in faster cars at high speeds. The only thing that drives me nuts is how hard it is to get money in this game. This is NOT Forza Horizon 3 where they throw money at you constantly, AT ALL. It is hard to get the fast cars because of this but not impossible.
So, in short:
Physics take a while to master
Game is absolutely massive
Decent length story
Difficult to get money
Basically, if you've got alot of TIME to play, then get this game. But if you can only hope on every Saturday or something, go find something that doesn't need you in it for the long haul.

Sit down boys and girls, and listen to an old man's yarn. I've played this game since its earliest build, when it was still a free beta download on the internet, with two maps, a handful of guns and only four squads. I still can't believe how far its come in the years since.
-------------------------------
I get back on after several months of inactivity. Its christmas time and the game is hosting its annual Christmas Truce event (MUST credit the game for doing something no other wargame has ever done, annually commemorating a truce event where we all just play soccer and write digital christmas cards instead of killing each other). Of course, for us veterans, we know that each christmas brings new players.
I join a Stosstruppen unit on an Ardennes match. I spawn in a trench with a fresh batch of newly converted BF1 and Call of Duty fanboys who bought the game on a one off this christmas because its WW1 like BF1. They go over the top in a twitch shooting induced frenzy and get cut to pieces by a machinegun. I joyfully listen to the screams of their dying characters as I weave my way up the trench towards the area with the most cover between lines.
I cross over and with my MP18, clear out the first line trench, allowing the newly respawned pubbies to finally cross noman's land and cap the trench. The match switches us to the defensive and the Allies start dropping heavy arty on us. The pubbies line up on the line and start pouring out fire while the shells and mortars start dropping on us from on high. Then someone calls in gas.
The pubbies have never seen something like this before. They freak the ♥♥♥♥ out and start running around like chickens with their heads cut off. Some jump out of the trench and are cut down by MG fire again. Others run away and are exectued for deserting. Most just suffocate in the cloud of mustard gas engulfing our trench.
I calmly don my gasmask and crouch down among the bodies as the enemy starts to creep into the trench. With the low visibility and natural camoflauge I manage to kill three before someone drops a grenade at my feet and I get gibbed. By now the pubbies are starting to rage quit and the team has become heavily unbalanced.
I know the match is effectively over, especially on Ardennes, we can't win without at least equal numbers, especially from the German start. Then, a miracle. The Almighty ZAB, twitch shooting jesus of Verdun, descends upon the German team. Armed with only a Kar98AZ and the speed of his OP twitching BS, he quickly kills over 60 enemies in two minutes without suffering a single death. The enemy team starts to rage quit.
Ten minutes later we win the game. Afterwards the game shifts to Truce mode, ZAB leaves immediately for the next killing field and the few remaning pubbies that stuck around start wandering around in confusion as I go to send a christmas card to a friend. Later I sit around the fire with some NPCs and a pubbie comes up to me. "This is so weird", he says. "This is history", I respond, "this is Verdun."

Just Cause 2 is an open world blow'm-up simulator in the same vein as a Grand Theft Auto or Saint's Row; half the fun is messing with the physics of the world.
The major success of Just Cause is that it gives players the tools to explore the world to its fullest extent. Your character's grappling hook is the most obvious of these, giving you the ability to traverse terrain at high speed, rope in enemies, or tie objects together. With a little imagination, it's the best thing since the Gravity Gun of Half Life 2... and both can be used to overturn vehicles!
Furthermore, the protagonist is rather agile in his ability to manoever. While his ability to safely hop on top of a moving, swerving car makes little sense, it also makes him able to do fun things... like throwing delicious explosives at pursuers. He can ride anything, grab on to anything, and jump anywhere, and it results in a very liberating experience once you get the hang of 'the rules' of these manoevering abilities.
As a car-jacking game, there are a TON of vehicles, and excuses to use them. Even when you acquire air travel and fast travel, there are many reasons why you'd use land vehicles; either they're more practical for quick getaways, have weapons attached, or you just want to ride on an occupied vehicle to keep your hands free to blow things up.
There are only two minor downsides to this game. First, the story; it takes itself a bit too seriously for a game where you can tie someone to a jet as its taking off, and it doesn't relax its tone until the end. Second, this game lacks the ability for multiplayer - yes, there is an awesome multiplayer mod, but it's pure free-roam and without NPCs; the game proper does not support multiplayer when it feels like it should (having one player driving, another car-surfing, and another para-gliding would be an awesome way to make a getaway).
However, these flaws are minor; the gameplay is satisfying, the world is gorgeous, and the price is right. Heck, the price may even be too low; Steam Sales have pitched this game as low as $2 when it is easily worth much more. Unless you really don't like gunplay and violence, this game is an absolute blast and recommended for anyone looking for some creative destruction.

Press F11 for fullscreen mode.
Go into Big Picture and check the boxes next to Xbox Controller, PS4 Controller, Generic Controller, and "Home opens up Steam" in the controller options (Thanks Oretachi for that!)
Now go and enjoy this fun little JRPG that we English speakers missed out on 24 years ago!
As for the game itself, the plot is not bad, and has some unique quirks, but it also seems mostly like an excuse to delve into dungeons and fight baddies.  And given the SaGa series' excellent combat system, that's totally ok with me.
This game seems like it might deviate a bit from other SaGas though... there's no seven characters at the start to choose from, the world so far is just a town, a menu, and dungeons.  And then, once you get through the initial portion of the game, it opens up and you can do some side-quests and, unexpectedly, a lot of X-Com style base-building.  Given that I prefer traditional RPG style gameplay over a strategy game... I actually consider this kinda cool.  It lets me experience some of those strategy game elements without being a full-blown strategy game.
But I am absolutely having fun with this game and recommend it if you can get over it being a barebones port without a lot of the bells and whistles that come standard on most PC games these days.  The actual gameplay is great and IMHO that's what matters.

The survival horror genre is a genre that is hardly seen anymore in gaming and that is why I consider Outlast a breath of fresh air. You are Miles Upshur, an investigative journalist that travels to Mount Massive Asylum in the hopes of exposing an evil corporation. Once inside however you will encounter unimaginable horrors and will need to think some things up on the fly to survive. Instead of using an array of weapons your only option is to run and hide. You can hide pretty much anymore like under beds, in lockers and behind piles of junk. However be wise about where you choose to hide as the enemy AI are very clever and will actually check around in an attempt to find your hiding spot. You are also equipped with a camcorder that can be used to record certain events to help you gain a better understanding of the nut house. There is also a night vision add on that can help you explore dark areas but be careful how much battery power you use. You will need to recharge it by picking up any stray batteries you may come across. As you progress through the game you will come across many documents explaining what is happening around you. Outlast is a gorgeous game and I will go far as saying it's one of the best looking PC games I have ever played and the good thing is no frame rate drops, the game runs as smooth as butter. The sound is chilling, especially when you're hiding and you can hear an enemie's heavy footsteps nearby and their crazed muttering and the story is gripping, it honestly had a Resident Evil 4/Silent Hill vibe for me. I was also never bored with the game as it threw a totally different situation at me every time I turned a corner. I really hope we get more survival horror games like Outlast in the future because with games like this, the future of the survival horror genre is looking bright.

I gave this one a go despite the poor reviews, as it was a game I always wanted to try having played several of the other Saga games and enjoying them.  And it's as a bad a port as everyone is saying.  No settings at all, mobile control UI, poor controller detection.  Which is a crime, because it's a good game if extremely unusual as typical jrpgs go.
The game makes you THINK there's actual characters, but in reality there's just classes.  Even the main character.  Like other Saga games there's potential permadeath.  Unlike later games, you can't avoid it.  Some enemies will attack LP directly no matter how careful you are, and you will simply run out of LP at some point.  You will then recieve an heir character with similar stats and a different look.  There isn't much of a plot, basically you're dungeon crawling to build up loot and stats until you're strong enough to start knocking off the Big Bads.  And that's all fine, not every RPG has to have deep writing; it's fun and it's actually challenging.
The sticking point is the pricetage for such a relatively simple and old game with a shoddy port.  And Square does NOT have a good reputation for supporting these mobile ports after release.  This is in no way worth the current asking price on Steam when it's cheaper on other platforms for the exact same port, or can buy some excellent modern RPGs with far more depth for similar prices.  If it were $10, maybe even $15, I'd say it's worth a go.  As it is I will be refunding this as I cannot support this lazy effort.  Hopefully Square learns their lesson when it comes the eventual port of RS3.

I'm a fan of the SaGa series, but this port is not perfect and with that in mind I will provide pros and cons for people on the fence about purchasing the game, with that said, let's go!
The Pros:  The story is great, the inheritence system is interesting, let's you foster your abilities and develop your characters over time, not having to focus on the main bosses the entire time and instead strengthen yourself for the evnetual curbstomping that only the 7 Heroes can provide.
You don't have to beat the game to access new game +, you can carry over all the abilities, magic, weapons, armor, accessories and items you had in your playthrough.  The newly added content also provides you with some pretty good loot, new classes and tough enemies.
The music is nothing short of masterful, the laid back town music to the intense as heck Battle with the 7 Heroes theme, every peice of music is a pleasure to listen to and I'm so glad that they stuck to the original OST and didn't opt for a more updated one.
The spritework is excellent, the moving enemies breathe some life into it, but I think the game could of gone without it, except the 7 hereos of course, they're awesome.
The Cons:  The controlls are a mixed bag for me, I don't hate them, but they're nothing to write home about either.  The games doens't recognize your controller untill you enable steam controller.
The menus are the exact same as in the Android version, this makes the game feel like it was rushed before giving it the polish is needed.
There isn't a way to change the display in game unless you force it full screen yourself, these kind of things should be handled the way the Final Fantasy XIII ports handled it, opening an app that lets you determine screen size for yourself.
The backgrounds aren't too impresive, they're not so bad it's destracting, but it looks like they rushed that, too.  I hope the port of Romancing SaGa 3 will learn from this in some capacity.
My Rating:  I give this game a 4/10, it's playable, but it doens't get a complete pass because they didn't change anything to optimize it for PC.  Just buy the console version, you don't need to worry about bad controlls or screen resolution problems.  I will be refunding this game effective imediately.

I'm making this review after my first playthrogh, 65 hours-long.
Okay, out of the three Re;Birth games this is the one I feel I havel to review. Why? Because it's awesome.
I'll assume here that you know about the Neptunia series and know what you're getting into. If you do not, I strongly recommend that you start with either Re:Birth 1 or 2, and check gameplay videos first. This series is notoriously low-budget, so many might be put off by how the game feels.
TL;DR: Gameplay is mostly the same, though there are a few nice balancing changes and some great quality of life changes. Story-wise, in my opinion Re;Birth 3 is miles ahead of 1 and 2. As a Neptunia game, this is a solid 9/10.
Pros:
+ Awesome story. It's like the devs were like "this is the 3rd game, how about we make an actual story?" and they did it. Some surprises, some plot twists, stuff that I didn't come to expect from this series.
+ Plutia. Amazing new character! Her being in the story is part of what made it so awesome.
+ Different dimension, different versions of known characters. Noire, Blanc and Vert behave mostly the same, but they feel more interesting this time around. They also interact more with each other instead of mostly Neptune, something that bothered me in past games.
+ Lack of Uni, Ram and Rom. Okay, I know this is a personal opinion but they were very uninteresting and I'm glad they barely showed up here.
+ EXE bar is now the same as SP and EXE skills now cost more bars. Now the tough fights aren't about you spamming EXEs anymore, and you don't have to spam rush attacks every time you go into a dungeon to build up EXE, since SP doesn't diminish on its own.
+ I feel like I should mention Plutia again, for being so awesome.
+ By pressing Y (Xbox gamepad) on quests and plans, you can now see where items drop, where monsters are found, if the dungeon needs to be changed or not, and etc. Extremely useful.
+ Stella's dungeon is more polished. The stuff she finds can really help you out.
+ No more scanning for hidden items in dungeons. Now you look for shadows and jump on them to reveal a hidden box with stuff, there are around 4 to 6 boxes in dungeons and only one has items. Unfortunately, in dark cave dungeons it's literally impossible to see the shadow. And fortunatelly, around halfway through the game you get the plan that lets you see them on the mini-map.
+Challenge system. You get certain in-game achievments for each character for things like damage dealt, enemies killed, skills used or how many times you jumped. Each challenge has multiple levels and each level will award you with permanent stat gains. In short, the more you play a character as a leader or in the main party, the stronger she'll be.
+ Shares no longer necessary to get different endings (or plans, that I know of). Honestly, shares were just a bothersome requirement in previous games.
+ A few dungeon bosses have nasty surprises prepared for you. I'm looking at you, Nurse Binder and Gargoyle.
Comparing this to previous Neptunia games, I can't think of many cons. But there you go..
Cons:
- Nations in the other dimension are separated from the world map. Now you have to click on them, go to their screen and then you see their respective dungeons. Visually it looks great, but now there's more loading time.
- Most playable characters aren't actually on your party. You get every Maker character plus the Oracles but they're just add-ons, none of them are really with you, which means they don't take part in the storyline. Most people won't care about it, but it made me refrain from using them on my first playthrough.
That's about it, I guess.. IMO this game is better in almost every way compared to the other two. If you liked them, don't hesitate to get this one.

TL;DR: More like Boreface.
A very run-of-the-mill shooter with some pleasant and quite detailed environments.
Warface has great scope for some cool co-operative gameplay, and delivers on some of them where it allows players to help eachother up ledges, heal eachother and give ammo to eachother; however, as far as the co-op elements go, that's where it ends.
The painful reality for Warface is that the team-based play is so weak and shallow that it reduces the different classes to nothing more than the type of support item they give - health, revives, ammo or armour - and is not robust enough to provide agency to players outside of their chosen class. It would benefit from having some universal abilities that allow you to help other players, or avenues in the level design that forced you to split up and help each other from afar.
In this sense, Warface is an unfortunately middling attempt at a dated type of gameplay that we've all seen before in older, admittedly less-polished games from Korea and the like. That's obviously a shame, because the game looks pretty good visually and you can tell they put the effort in.
Regardless, this has perhaps the most damning knock-on effect for a game of this type: The lack of decent co-operative gameplay turns this into a linear corridor shooter with mentally-disconnected team members who, in lacking any way to meaningfully assist you as part of the gameplay experience, barring shooting at the enemy, will just focus on killing and then killing some more, ignoring you outright. You can tell that this is where Warface has its focus, given the importance placed on completion speed, enemies killed and the general audio-visual response - hit markers, EXP pop-ups, etc - that Warface uses in the same vein as CoD4.
Naturally, that attracts a highly uninteresting and anti-social playerbase that could play this game without you. Don't expect to strategize unless you're with friends and have a healthy imagination; the levels and gameplay are formulaic and are designed for the lone wolf player, not you. Naturally, if you choose to play Medic, you will find yourself to be both the most sought-after component of the team, as well as the most accountable in the event that your team fails a mission.
Warface players do not have any concept of protecting the medic, staying close to the medic for heals or standing still during heals; the revive cooldown is also an absurd concept to the average Warface player. This is due to the aforementioned points: Players, lacking agency, are therefore blind to teammates until they need them for something, and woe befall anybody that fails to address the needs of a 19-year-old European kid typing up a storm over chat because the team wasn't following them head-long into machine gun fire.
3/10. Play it with friends for an hour, tops.

This is a mediocre port, but it's not a bad one. Biggest problem is the lack of proper gamepad support without screwing around with your settings in Big Picture. That said, the best way to control this game is with WASD and the mouse.
As for the game itself, Romancing SaGa 2 is an old game, but still a very unique one in its framing and execution. Many games that have multiple generations of successors tend to be either linear with few differences, like the oft-maligned Phantasy Star 3. In Romancing SaGa 2, the game (and series as a whole) makes the story take a back seat in favor of a heavy focus on gameplay. If you want an epic story with depth spanning centuries, you're not going to find it here. The core mechanic of the game is that your emperor's gains are passed on infinitely until you vanquish the Seven Heroes who are bringing chaos and death to the world. At his disposal, the Emperor has masses of wealth even from the beginning, and an infinite supply of elite warriors from all over the region ready and willing to perform this task.
RS2 differs from most RPGs in that you should consider your units
main character completely expendable. They can and will fall in battle, and will often get beaten while they're down until they are killed off for good. Don't bother getting attached to any of them, even if they do survive the whole way they will retire with each generation shift. You are not building up a party, but rather the statistics, spells, and skills available to you.
The game is entirely nonlinear, with huge amounts of the area open from the get-go, and a huge amount of sidequests that translate into loot, more available classes, and more income and territory for your empire. SaGa as a whole isn't for everyone, and games in the series tend to be very polarizing. If you want a straightforward RPG, run away very fast, because this is anything but. It is difficult, has a lot of depth, and explains very little. As a saving grace though, even if you screw up royally the game has New Game+ unlocked from the very start so even a seemingly unwinnable situation can be salvaged by starting over and retaining a large chunk of your earnings.
At the same time, I don't consider it worth buying at its current pricetag. Though this is a good remaster of an old game, it comes off as primitive in areas.

Sadly you can´t see any of these sorcerers and you are not able to shoot them. There is a program to fix this problem though. I will post the link to it down at the bottom of my review. So, it´s a bugfest mkay, why am I still recommending this game to you? If not the steam version, or if it is the steam version why am I still recommending it? Because it´s a ♥♥♥♥ing fantastic game if you have patience, a sense for atmosphere and if you are able to use that brain of yours. Because you might need it.
You play as Jack Walters, private detective. One day you get called to help out in a serious nutcase shootout. You enter the building and you find the nutcases talking to you like they know you. You find something very dark and menacing deep down the house in the basement and you turn insane. You are now in an asylum, you get cured and can continue your work as a detective. You still look for answers what happened back there down in the basement, but of course you still have to continue your work as a private detective. Making a living. You get a new case, a boy named Brian Burnham is gone missing in a dark creepy fishermans town called Innsmouth.The story is told very well, it´s very immersive and the characters are good. It does a good job telling an actual adventure and letting you feel like you went through an adventure at the end of the game, just like the metro games. Really, really great. I intentionally shortened the prologue. I personally dislike getting too much info even if it´s just the prologue by reading reviews.
This game is unique... and if I say unqiue, I mean unique. The health system is based upon real time healing. Meaning: If you get shot at the leg, you have to go to your inventory and pick the spot you got shot at and leave the inventory. Walters will bandage himself then for couple of seconds. You have to be careful and manage to get as little damage as possible or else you run out of medical supplies or you have to bandage yourself and pursuers are going to hunt you down quickly. This also means real life effects and insanity effects. White and black screen as soon as you run out of blood (blood loss). Or you get shot with a shotgun in the legs, meaning you walk like a cripple until you fixed it. You have an inventory but it´s not annoying unlike Fallout 4 or such crap, you don´t have any inventory management at all really. You have your tiles but there are always enough as each tile is for one thing. The inventory is for applying medicine and checking ammo and such or taking certain things and use them for progress. It´s kept simple and useful.
Too much psychic stuff makes you wanna do suicide if you are unlucky. You need to maintain your sanity at some scenes and you are a slow walker, meaning you can´t run in this game.... for the sake of the few script sequences and tension. It doesn´t affect immersion that much. Even though walters running animation is slow as ♥♥♥♥ it´s fast enough to be able to make it past all the faster sequences.
GUNS! Well, the guns recoil tends more into the realistic category, you have no HUD, it´s a purist game. Arm sway, weapon sway, etc.. No HUD, no ammo counter, no health indicator. You know you have 31 rounds left? Better count your shots, cause realism is often meant to be taken seriously in this game. Lots of arm sway and delay during aiming, the aiming with mouse is still smooth and accurate though. You have to play carefully. To understand what I mean, it´s like in Red Orchestra. Everyone who played Red Orchestra, knows what I mean with arm sway. Spongy controls. Or like in The Darkness I. Games who take a more realistic approach in gameplay have this. Mirrors Edge, Red Orchestra, etc. The game paces very nicely, it´s overall a mix out of stealth parts, which not always work, and shootouts. There are many riddles to be solved in order to advance. In one mission you have to get a car working and while "he" fixes it, "you" get your♥♥♥♥♥moving trying to get that "special item" for him from the police stations safe. You have to combine many things or use things you acquired earlier in the game in order to progress. The game was complicated in the ending riddles and it gave you some options, either you sneak or you go in guns blazing, either you rescue her or you let her die. These decisions have no impact on the story though. The game really wants to force the detective out of you and uses many mean tricks in order to make you go batshit crazy. It really is hard sometimes. The game is not for casuals at all! It´s very challenging and overly complicated at some points and you need to have patience. There´s one scene in this game I want to mention though: "the marsh refinery end sequence". In this sequence you have after easily 30 min progress, no checkpoints or saves. Mark my words and make sure you look it up before playing any further. Right after you burned the entity and you can finally go to the secret shrine, look at a playthrough and remember the place you need to place the pillar with the gem on it in order to open the door before the time runs out. You will know what I mean as soon as you experienced that ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥scene once. ^^´
