The great dilemma: should you support this subpar release of one of the biggest titles the west missed out on two decades ago?
Why is it even a question when there are so many flaws here? Allow me to explain.
Sadly, it is another Squeenix hatchet job of a port, straight up from the android/IOS release with little to no improvements, but I imagine this one wont get away with reaching a "mostly positive" rating like FFV/VI.
The internal resolution is set by default in the likes of the vita screen and there are no options to change it in the menu, you will have to use Alt+Enter and F11 for proper fullscreen or stretch the window to your desired resolution, controller is limited to Ximput or Steam Controller, so you might have problems depending on your setup. Big Picture is your friend here, try it if you controller refuses to work. [UPDATE: Seems like they fixed it at the time of this edit.]
Graphics wise the improvements are not stellar: Some of the backgrounds look like they came from an RPG Maker game and the new animation in some of the bosses is jarring, but at least they kept the sprites, those burned by the steam ports of FFV/VI will find some solace here.
The translation itself is pretty dry and awkward in places, it gets the job done, but it seems they didnt revise it from the smartphone version, which is a pity.
Some users report crashes, so far I have not experienced any.
But what about the gameplay? Almost untouched from the original Super Famicom release, along with bugfixes to polish up some of the problems present in the old days, there is even some optional extra content and New Game+, which is a nice addition.
That being said, SaGa games are a tricky sell, the best way I can describe it is that these games are the furthest you can get away from classic JRPG standards while still remaining a JRPG at its core, there is nothing quite like this series out there.
There are no levels, no random battles, character growth is determined by the actions you take during combat and by the gear you have . Enemy encounters are represented by sprites roaming the maps and scale in power according to several factors, and they are not afraid of surpassing your party with several steamrollers hiding in a seemingly harmless little dog colliding with your party.
Theres also no world map, well, at least not in the traditional sense, you can fast travel anywhere on the map but you cant roam around in a big overworld like in other titles, just roll with it its SaGa.
Your Characters can gain access to special commands in the middle of battle at seemingly random times, one moment you are attacking with your meager sword and the next your little guy briefly unravels the secrets of the universe and pulls some sick moves out of his♥♥♥♥♥♥that then get added to your repertoire for later use. These also depend on the weapons and abilities you are using, if you want to get the best you cant be a jack of all trades.
The health system is divided in two: your normal health and Life Points, if a character is down you dont need to revive them with a special item, you just pop up a potion and they are good to go, they also go back to full health once the battle is over. the catch? every time they die they lose LP, and those are fixed with few ways to recover them, if they run out, thats it, they are gone Fire Emblem style.
There is also an inheritance system, you wont make it with your original party to the end of the game, by that point you will be controlling their descendants, how cool is that? and its a lot less linear than you might think considering its a JRPG, with tons of replayability and plenty of challenge. (and by plenty I do mean plenty)
Speaking of cool: the music is what you should expect from any great JRPG of the SNES/SFC era, the SaGa  series has managed to have great music even in the Gameboy days and this is no exception, there are no rearranges or remixes here, but honestly the original music is pretty great in its original form.
If any of this sounds interesting you should know there are many systems working under the hood, part of the fun is peeling away at the layers and understanding them, if that sounds like your cup of tea or you are seeking something different, you should totally give this game a shot.
You are going to hit your head against the wall big time, its a tough journey, but you know what? you can save anywhere, BIG plus right there, not enough JRPGs do this even to this day.
Just remember: sometimes its better to let it go, after all there is always someone ready to take up the mantle, let them have their revenge.
Now for the great question, should you support this release?
If you have a console maybe get it for your PS4/Switch/Xbone/Vita, the steam version is not the end of the world, its fine as a means to play such a wonderful little piece of lost JRPG history, but it is a big, BIG wasted opportunity and should be counted as one of the biggest crimes against PC gaming since the steam release of FFVI.
Well, Im exaggerating, but lets say Im not happy with how SE treats some of its biggest classics with ports like this, somebody should slap some sense on the higher ups.
If you dont have an alternative, then by all means support this game on steam, Its still one of the greats along with Chrono Trigger and FFVI, and until recently perhaps the holy grail of classic untranslated JRPGs, and the series director, Akitoshi Kawazu, has expressed his desire to bring Romancing SaGa 3 to the west, along with Scarlet Grace, the most recent entry on the series. Lets pray to the fickle localization gods that the next port has some more effort put into it, and lets pray tenfold for the slim chance of a western release of Scarlet Grace.

Victor Vran. You'd at first think of it as a cheap knockoff of some other Dracula-stealing-protagonists named Helsing. Well, yeah... You can't talk about vampire hunting without making a reference to Bram Stoker's work in some way.
The story here is very hammy but somewhat original. Without going into spoilers, the one named Victor Vran is out to clean a massive infestation unlike any other in an isolated region and eventually faces his long-time nemesis. If narrative is what you're looking for, turn away now.
The game's strength is, in my opinion, the simplicity of the weapons and magic skills you use in combat. There isn't a terrible lot that you can do at any time because you can equip two weapons at a time and switch between them and you can use a dodge roll to avoid enemy attacks. And also jump. You control the camera angle if you want another viewpoint, which helps in finding some of the secrets, and each weapon type has multiple unique versions that greatly change up the playstyle: this is a blessing and a curse, as some are clearly better than others of the same category.
There's also a form of passive bonuses via tarot cards which is really fun to experiment around to find your ideal niche to support the weapons you like the most or to go all in with tactical choices to counter the issues you may have with the weapons you want to use but don't like. Basically, these cards are what constitue what in other games we call "builds". The garments you wear also affect some passive stuff so you can further enhance the way you'd rather play, and you can colour parts of them if you find dyes and dislike their base colour.
And then there's the free DLCs, which are all great. The Cauldron of Chaos in particular is a good place to spend your time once you've "done everything" in order to unlock more stuff or to get unique weapons you might not have.
The game is also much more interesting with others, and there's plenty of people who play open so you can join them (or you can just ask in the global chat channels if anyone wants to join you instead!). There's also a PvP arena if you really want to do it but it's kinda pointless in my opinion.
Should you buy this game? Yeah, on a discount. Just keep in mind that your enjoyment of the game will depend a lot on if you enjoy the base combat mechanics and are cool with at least 2 of the weapon types.

Hearts of Iron III is like a once-beautiful Victorian mansion that's been abandoned for twenty years, and haunted. It's a beautiful, well put together game with a robust simulation, but it is aging poorly, and there's nothing Paradox can do about it, having somehow managed to lose the source code and with it, their ability to fix bugs. For instance, this fullscreen-only game has extreme difficulty making connections via multiplayer, crashes when you alt+tab, and frequently crashes in the middle of gameplay as well.
This, combined with a somewhat outdated, clunky interface and a very poor tutorial, results in a game where you can't tell what's a bug, what's a feature, and what's user error. And it's never going to get better. It can't. Paradox can no longer fix or develop this game, because again, they managed to somehow lose the source code.
I've never given a negative review for a Paradox game before. Do not let this dissuade you from buying games from them in the future. The bizarre and apparently unique blunder that led to HoI3's problems are very atypical for who are otherwise developers of VERY high-quality grand strategy games.
Get Hearts of Iron II or IV instead of III.

Basically, it's a platform puzzle game where you do standard platform puzzle game problem solving, except it doesn't feel that way.

I really hope whoever made this gets some work for this, because this is some of the best level design I've seen in a long time.
The graphics are simple, but still nice.

It's short, but not too short.
To sum up; if you're looking for a good, solid gaming experience where game play is the only thing that matters, this is a game for you. This is a game every gamer should play at least once.

A platforming puzzle game with a large bundle of interactive features, this game succeeds at two goals. First, at being a good challenge that causes you to think about your approach to dozens of levels instead of just roaming through and pressing buttons. Secondly, and here’s the catch, also at being fun whilst doing so.
Whenever you make a mistake in this game, you know it’s usually your own fault and you mutter unmentionables under your breath before you willingly try again – because it’s fun.
There are times when, in levels with multiple buttons all being required to be pressed in order to activate something, it’s not very intuitive as to letting you know what it will accomplish and you’ll need to find the solution behind pressing all the buttons before you’re thrown into a second task in the same place. I think this was actually the idea behind the design, but I can’t say I’m incredibly fond of it. Sometimes, things move simultaneously at multiple points on the map and it can be a bit much to take in. It feels like the workings of the level aren’t entirely in your control, which is something the game is otherwise very good at not doing.
There are a few times here and there where you’ve made the right decision and have been thrown off the trail by chance bad feedback, either through a Reaper facing the wrong way at the wrong time, or your button press being just a miniscule portion off where it should have been. As such it’s a good idea to try an idea a couple of times before you give up on a notion.
Not to throw you off though – these things only stand out as bad because they’re the odd ones out in an otherwise great game. The puzzles never seemed completely beyond me, but never did it feel like it wasn’t challenging. For the most part, the only stages that don’t cause you to stop and think about your approach are the ones that are introducing new ideas, and you can be sure that that means more interesting challenges ahead. Occasionally, you can find yourself overthinking a puzzle because extra bits and pieces were placed for the sole purpose of throwing you off the scent. Toward the end of the game, there’s a set of levels designed to make you react very quickly, and the true challenge is being able to work under pressure.  It’s a refreshing switch-up.
The whole theme is friendly. You’re a goat with your sidekick (occasionally magical) mouse, out rescuing sheep in a big castle with scary monsters. What on Earth isn’t to like about that?
Oh, and allow me to just throw this out there. You will die in this game. A lot. This will bring you back to the beginning of a level (which are never incredibly long, but it can feel frustrating to have to redo that thing you finally did right after trying and failing at least ten times first). There’s even a hotkey for making your Goat explode and die to restart the level quicker. You’ll be using that button a lot. Several functions rely on your trial and error because they’d be impossible to figure out the first time. Try not to let it get to you.
The music is fitting and blends into the background well. It keeps you from getting bored and doesn’t feel incredibly tedious. Otherwise it’s unremarkable.
I’m pretty sure that whoever is behind this game must have played Pokémon Silver & Gold as a child, because I drew correlations between three particular puzzles in this game and puzzles from The Underground, Cianwood City Gym, and Ice Path. I thought that was interesting.
I completed the game in 7h40m over the course of about a week (apparently mine was a slow playthrough), but like a frickin hour of that was on the last level. Just finished that one now. Sheesh. I died 625 times overall, which I believe averages a death every 44 seconds.
There are also apparently secret puzzles which I haven’t discovered, so I look forward to trying them out and scraping up all the (majority of) achievements I didn’t achieve through my playthrough.
If you like puzzle games, I have very little doubt that you will love this one to death whist you occasionally pull your hair out. Highly recommended for fans of the genre.

This is a fun, turn based Strategy RPG focusing on controlling an Empire and the Heroes that you recruit.
(CATEGORY) "Poor/Sub-Par/Average/Great/Superb" 1-5/5 - Description
(OVERALL)- My personal rating for this game is 85%. My average rating for this is 71% (3.5/5)
(GAMEPLAY)  "Superb" 5/5 - Battles are turn based tactics using a grid system, similar to games like Final Fantasy Tactics, Poxnora, Disgaea, Ogre Tactics, etc. Each turn you aquire resources depending on what mines/ect you've captured, and can spend those resources to upgrade your town(s). Your Heroes gain levels, and new abilities which are both passive, affecting the Army of Monsters you recruit at your town, or directly doing damage or providing some various effects (slowing down enemies, speeding yours up, summoning monsters to fight for you, etc). You end up fighting Neutral monsters that are stationary on the map, usually blocking your path as your armies are too weak (at first). Armies are formed from Monsters/Units that you pay to recruit (with gold) at your town/village. Each unit bought will represent a "Stack" of units. You have around 10 slots to have different types of creatures in your army, and you can have as many "Stacks" as you can afford / create to build up your forces. There are a huge variety of ways to play this game, all of which are really fun. Many elements of this game are comparable to a 4X game.
(STORY)  "Sub-Par" 2/5 -There is a storymode to this game, and infact it is one of the best ways to get strong gear for your Hero. Gear aquired during those missions (and some other ways) allow you to make your Hero stronger, earlier, in any form of gameplay. The story isn't insanely good, but I found it to be very well done as far as being creative. Depending on what DLC you buy changes how much story you can access. This is one of the greater faults for the game. The story itself is something I like, however limiting it by DLC is not something that I favor. (Note, without some of the DLC (IE you bought Shades of Darkness, not the original) you will get a lot less content, which is why this is a 2/5)
(GRAPHICS)  "Average" 3/5 - The graphics are quite good, but not amazing. There is enough going on in the world that it can draw you in, as a fantasy world. There are all sorts of odd buildings, and interactable objects. Exploration is one fun factor in the game (as there is Fog of War) and the graphics help tie in the feeling of exploration. Seeing the units in 3D during battle is always nice, and fun to watch (though if you have a slow-walking unit, try speeding up how fast your units move)
(SOUND)  "Great" 4/5 - At first I was going to rate this a 3/5, but I realized that several of the songs in this game had gotten stuck in my head. Remembering that, it was a lot easier to rate this a 4/5. The Gameplay was addictive, and so is the music. Although it isn't anything over-the-top, or mind-blowing, it is still a fitting sound track.
(ONLINE)  "Sub-Par" 2/5 - The games worst issue, by far. MMH VI has to be connected to the internet at all times to play the game. DRM-Stuff. This is a huge deterrant for most people, and thus have rated this section quite low. However on the flip side it has a great single player mode (which you still need to be connected to the internet to play) which you can setup your own matches against the NPC's and either destroy them, or be destroyed! It is a lot of fun learning tactics for certain maps, and for certain factions.
(RE-PLAYABILITY) "Superb" 5/5 - This game is truly addictive. While I only have 40 hours in the game right now, it is because I haven't been able to re-install it and to get it working (with an issue others have had, a black screen) I haven't tried re-downloading and installing since I tried last. The game has a great sense of addictiveness to it. You earn new equipment to use on your Hero. Your hero gains new levels, and you can re-do it every match. You can play all sorts of different tactics, take your time or not, and generally, do what you want.
(COST) "Average" 4/5 - This game costs either 30$ USD or 20$ USD (Depending on if you get the base game or Shades of Darkness) My review is based on Shades of Darkness. At 20$ USD, this is a steal of a game, as long as you don't mind staying connected to the internet.
(OVERALL)- My personal rating for this game would likely be a 4/5. My average rating for this was a 3.5/5 or a 70%.

Honestly one of the better games I've played so far, although with a good few flaws of course.
From the beginning of the game it'll certainly have a weird feel to it, as it tried a lot of different things compared to DS1, mainly the way movement is handled and infact the first ''real'' area to explore is one of the worst parts of the game unfortunately, however there's a good lot better things on DS2, like being able to warp between bonfires right away, builds being allowed to be a lot more flexible (I'm SL 270+ before beginning NG+), magic being an easy fit into the huge majority of builds, covenants not being as restrictive, being able to respec your entire build, and a few other upsides to DS1.
Of course, there's still some bad things like not being able to have *full* control of your movement to go in all directions with a controller but this is offset by the fact you can now dodge in all directions compared to how DS1 only allows dodging in 4 directions (when locked on), also needing to go back to the main hub to be able to level instead of using the bonfire directly (however we got some really nice NPC to do the leveling for you) and some attacks feeling slightly unresponsive every so often.
Then there's bosses, which is the biggest part of the franchise. Unfortunately this is where DS2 most falls short in a way, where most bosses are either pretty easy, horribly unfair, or simply uninteresting. Most boss music tracks are also extremelly forgettable specially since they're pretty quiet and have very little impact, except for like 4 boss fights. More than half of the bosses in the game aren't going to feel that intimidating, and this all makes DS2 an easier game in general compared to DS1.
As for the content for the ''Scholar of the First Sin'' version, it is certainly better than the base game with DLCs built in. Graphics are bumped up slightly, but that's one of the last things to take in consideration. Firstly, you won't have to worry about missing out on anything in the game and there will be no obstacles. Then there's the fact the devs went out of their way to ''tweak'' some of the lore, placement and other things of the like of the base game to fit properly most of the time, along with a few new things around some areas in the base game that you wouldn't get with the original version otherwise.
DLCs are pretty nice by themselves, however the Sunken King DLC is simply horrible, to where it's like the Lost Izalith/Demon Ruins of DS2, except instead of just being mediocre, it's both mediocre and extremelly unfair specially since people like to camp it as invaders to get really easy kills because of how dangerous the entire area is, so you may see yourself trying to ''negate'' invaders temporarily with a certain item. Iron King is great, though not *as* polished as I hoped it could be, it includes the hardest boss in the entire game that provides a real challenge to where even summoning a player won't be enough to sweep it at all, as it'll require some serious effort to actually get through. Ivory King is my favorite, with a very pretty and interesting area all around, however the last boss of that DLC is pretty damn bad, sadly.
For playtime, it definitely just depends on what your playstyle is like. You could be done with the game as soon as a week or a little more than that, or you could take over a month or so doing absolutely everything possible in the game and getting your build as complete as you could want it. In the end, you'll definitely get your cash's worth in playtime.
You should only buy this game during a sale, however. I probably wouldn't enjoy it as much had I gotten it at full price. If you can buy it at 10$ or 15$, absolutely get it (as long as you've already played DS1, otherwise get that first).

The survival horror genre is a genre that is hardly seen anymore in gaming and that is why I consider Outlast a breath of fresh air. You are Miles Upshur, an investigative journalist that travels to Mount Massive Asylum in the hopes of exposing an evil corporation. Once inside however you will encounter unimaginable horrors and will need to think some things up on the fly to survive. Instead of using an array of weapons your only option is to run and hide. You can hide pretty much anymore like under beds, in lockers and behind piles of junk. However be wise about where you choose to hide as the enemy AI are very clever and will actually check around in an attempt to find your hiding spot. You are also equipped with a camcorder that can be used to record certain events to help you gain a better understanding of the nut house. There is also a night vision add on that can help you explore dark areas but be careful how much battery power you use. You will need to recharge it by picking up any stray batteries you may come across. As you progress through the game you will come across many documents explaining what is happening around you. Outlast is a gorgeous game and I will go far as saying it's one of the best looking PC games I have ever played and the good thing is no frame rate drops, the game runs as smooth as butter. The sound is chilling, especially when you're hiding and you can hear an enemie's heavy footsteps nearby and their crazed muttering and the story is gripping, it honestly had a Resident Evil 4/Silent Hill vibe for me. I was also never bored with the game as it threw a totally different situation at me every time I turned a corner. I really hope we get more survival horror games like Outlast in the future because with games like this, the future of the survival horror genre is looking bright.

Call of Cthulhu is a really interesting game, captivating, challenging and very dark.
While the game has graphics that weren't even good by the standards of the time in which it came out, and also has certain elements of the gameplay that lessens the experience, the story alone, and the frustration and occasional fear that follows is what makes it worth the money you pay for it.
I believe this game might have caused many people to take an interest in the work of H.P. Lovecraft as it is a very good representation of his little creepy universe.
The game is somewhat linear, but does offer up some "choices". Set before WWII, don't expect a hectic shooter with machine guns and tactical gear. In this game, you play as a private detective, and your main mission is to figure out what is going on. Especially with your own head!
If you go in, expecting a game similar to resident evil or silent hill, you're going to be disappointed. It's an FPS game with controls very similar to, say, half-life. The game has dialogue and narrative on par with some of the best RPG's out there and the setting is truly excellent.
While it's definately an FPS on first glance, the truth behind Call of Cthulhu is that it's more like an FPR (first person runner). You find that you're constantly outmatched by your enemies. Crawling around in the dark, armed perhaps with nothing, or maybe with nothing more than a handgun and a few bullets and maybe a knife, you pray you won't have to fight again.
The health system is quite advanced, and I reckon it's probably an attempt at mirroring the pen&paper roleplaying game that it's based on, though I wouldn't know as I've actually never played it. I can say that the game perfectly captures the essence of the original H. P. Lovecraft books.

Call of Cthulhu is a First Person Survival Horrror game developed by Headfirst Productions. It takes inspiration from the works of H.P.Lovecraft and as a result melds together an engrossing stroy-driven adventure with intense First Person Shooter mechanics that still stands the test of time, 9 years after it's original release.
You play as a detective looking for a missing person in the gloomy and mysterious fishing town of Innsmouth, you will have to talk to many people along the way, gather clues and even run for your life in certain scenarios. The FPS mechanic doesn't pop up until an hour so into the game, where monsters and humans pose an equal threat, and taking them down can be challenging and intense.
Call of Cthulhu is an story-driven adventure not to be missed and comes highly reccomended!!

Without a doubt the clunkiest, most awkward, least enjoyable and most tiresome FPS I have ever played in all my years. It feels like an unstable mod from the old Return to Castle Wolfenstein, with suspicious hit detection resulting in numerous deaths at the hands of people you just shot twice without it registering. If you want to lie perfectly still for several minutes waiting for someone to walk around a corner so you can oneshot them, this is the game for you.
If you want to do literally anything else, you're out luck.
Almost every weapon is a one-hit kill with a few exceptions being two-hit kills, and the game includes massive aiming penalties on movement. You also have to "hold breath" as an additional layer of time needed to aim properly. This allows a camping player an insurmountable advantage over a player whose moving, since they can easily 1-hit-kill anyone who enters their LOS long before their opponent can prepare and take their own shot. The game has three environments; narrow corridors, narrow trenches, and open fields, all surrounded by "desertion zones" which you die upon entering, ensuring their is no way to flank a camper. There are also no vehicles, ensuring their is no way to overpower them.
The entire game has been designed to revolve around making camping the strongest option in the game bar none, with massively favourable K:D ratios awarded to those who lie on the ground with a sniper rifle and wait for someone to walk around the corner. This apparently causes people to hail it as a masterpiece of historical game-making, but World War 1 was not actually an enjoyable experience that I would advise accurately recreating as a leisure activity.
A man can only deal so many times with "veterans" who demand you follow their every instruction, switch places with them if you're playing the class they like, then proceed to insult you and/or ragequit if they don't get their wishes fulfilled immediately. And that's without considering the ones on the other team who believe waiting at the end of a long unflankable tunnel with a machinegun is somehow highly-skilled, or that spawncamping with grenades is a feat worthy of praise. To be fair, I suppose a superiority complex is inevitable when you have access to unlockable air support systems that give older players access to long-duration, moving-area airstrikes capable of clearing entire trenches, or aerial scans that mark the location of all enemies.
I've never encountered a game that makes me feel this way, but I actually hope this game fades away to the point where its' small, religiously loyal, blind-to-all-it's-flaws, unforgiveably elitist fanbase are left alone with eachother (and their unique sense of fun) and not inflicted upon any hapless new arrivals.
Which is all a shame, because the different styles of squad and their varying weapons and bonuses are actually kinda cool. But "kinda cool" ideas cannot carry such demoralising gameplay.

I am generally upset about the fact that there is no possible way to restart your game save. I contacted Uplay and talked to them about the issue and even asked if they could just wipe my uplay account and start it from scratch considering I do not have any DLC's. They said they did not have the ability to do so. Here are my pro's and cons.
Pros:
1. Huge map
2. Good graphics
3. Enjoyable gameplay
Cons:
1. Campaign was a let down. The ending threw me off and I was fairly unhappy.
2. Terrible NPC AI. That being racers and police or street traffic.
3. Lack of performance modifications. If you come into the game thinking you can upgrade parts like in need for speed then you are wrong. While the visual mods are nice and can add charactor to a vehicle you dont have the same luxury when moding the performance. I have spent several hours grinding for parts to upgrade my vehicles performance through challenges. (Tip: Salt flats are your best friend for grinding)
4. Not gaming wheel friendly. While yes you can hook up a G27 for example but the force feed back is a nightmare. Found myself playing 99% of the time with force feedback off.
5. Lack of money earning after campaign. Yes if you fork over the money to get the DLC's you will have more missions. But without the DLC's you will find that you can't earn money without doing factions mission, etc.
6. Way overpriced vehicles. This brings me to part of the number 5 issue. After the campaign you can't make money easily. If you want to get a new vehicle that is relativly quick or a classic your going to have to fork over 100k+ in game. The quickest way to get this kind of money in game is doing faction missions. There are a few races that will give you around 130k but they take 1 - 4 hours to complete.
7. Missions are so repetitive that it's almost hard to play.
8. I time playthrough, No restarting campaign.
I'm sure you get the point. Without DLC's the game ends for the player relativly quick and is no longer fun. If you have a couple buddies that are interested in getting the game then I would recomend getting it. But on your own it gets very boring very quick.
I give the game a 5/10

Heavy with atmosphere, light on fun. Outlast is a well presented horror game which doesn't quite work. While I very much enjoyed the aesthetics (night-vision being done spectacularly well), I found the actual gameplay very mundane, and this distracted me from Outlast enough to ruin any sense of terror. This isn't a completely negative review, but more or less this grumpy Steam-user's thoughts on why he didn't enjoy it as much as he thought he should have.
As an investigative journalist, you take it upon yourself to prod around a horrible asylym. At night, no less. Without the common sense to bring a flashlight, ofcourse. As though that weren't the silliest of ideas, the protagonist seems incapable of picking up many of the objects which could be used as weapons to defend against the horrors he stumbles upon (such as a handy length of pipe or a brick). While I completely understand this fits the context of the game, it doesn't quite fit the context of the story. As such, I felt the lengths of running around, avoiding enemies were forced and clumsy. Were the enemy AI or level design more solid this may not have been a problem, but often the game asks you to run circles around slow-witted enemies. Paths are conveniently circular, and oponents will rarely block a hallway, making it easy to plod ahead. There is such little threat of dying, and such little penalty if you do, that encounters become bland very quickly.
Did I feel anything for the story? Well, not really. You know very little about the protagonist (I suppose we are supposed to put ourselves in his shoes), but the little pieces of information that can be found on documents around the asylym paint an ugly picture. While falling to cliche in a lot of ways, the setting is appropriately spooky. I just wish I cared more about these happenings, but aside from a few neat flourishes, it is a fairly run-of-the-mill romp.
So no, I didn't enjoy this enough to recommend a purchase. If you want a truly scary game, have a look at the original Silent Hill.

Oooh boy... where to start. I want to recommend this game, it does some horror stuff quite well. I bought this game and finished it in about five hours a long time ago. Too many jumpscares and predictability of gameplay. The monsters never actually look where you're hiding, so the risk factor is reduced. The game is fairly linear, with some paths hidden quite well that make survival more about knowing where to go than how to avoid monsters. As for game mechanics, they're all a step down from Amnesia a Dark Descent. Never do you actually control the full animations of opening doors, instead it does it automatically with a character animation that wastes a lot of time. This is very bad when you're standing at the wrong side of the room, you'll close the door trapping yourself with the monster due to a silly mistake. Running is completely overpowered, you cannot get tired and you're never actually in any direct threat.
As for the story, the ending makes absolutely no sense. Spoiler alert, your whole objective was to escape and in the end, it turns into a Kill Bill sort of objective. Clearly there's an elevator near the end where you're able to escape, but the objective is "You must kill Billy," thus ruining your chance of survival. In the end, you do kill his physical body, only for him to enter yours and use it. Then killing Billy was a terrible idea after all? Couldn't Billy have just used any host then? It makes absolutely no sense and makes your effort in prolonging your entire survival a waste of a time. It's also a huge departure from everything else in the game, the idea that all your enemies are psychotic deranged humans. Game should have ended right after the man dies in the stake.
It's good for a one time experience, but I recommend Amnesia the Dark Descent for the mods and better gameplay mechanics.

I thought about getting this game in early 2016 after I first heard of it, but after I saw it being advertised at the Farnborough Airshow on a school science trip in mid-July that year, I was sold on it, and bought it just days after.
I'm pleased to say that, one year later, I've got over 100 hours out of this *without* mods (despite the enormous amount of mods available), and that this game is also regularly updated by its developers. It goes from strength to strength, and can be as simple, or as complex, as you like. There is an enormous amount of freedom with what you build and what you don't, and if you don't have the creativity, time or know-how to build your own car/plane/boat etc, there are thousands you can choose from made by the community. There are also LOADS of different locations to explore and discover in the sandbox.
It's also good fun to try and challenge yourself and try to make something to beat the various races and challenges.
There's lots more I could say, but I think my stance on this game is pretty clear regardless - it's brilliant.

The game is essentially Empire without the crippling bugs and more tasty unit variety. Where in Empire, most of the mainstay European faction units were painfully generic, thankfully there's much more unit types and looks now.
The main campaign is a close knit and somewhat scripted affair, it doesn't detract from the experience, as you are retracing Napoleon's footsteps. If that doesn;t strike your fancy, there's also Campaignsof the Coalition in which it is more open ended but still on a smaller map than empire, plotting Napoleon's downfall.
It's not entirely historically accurate, an inevitability in such a game like this. However, it tries its best to stick to period authentic tactics and effects.
The battle effects are very lovely to look at although the Warscape engine is starting to show cracks what with wonky animation sync and sound clipping as well as some atrocious balance in some engagements. However, it works and is a decent engine for representing Napoleonic combat.
I am a bit biased as I'm a monumental Napoleonic and 18th century history enthusiast and if you have a love of history or total war or any other strategy 4x title, I recommend this game highly.
Tl;DR thank god it isn't Rome II.

Edit:  So it has been almost a year since my last review and since having taken a hiatus I came back to this game to see how it was getting on and give it a fair crack of the whip.  Turns out it has made a lot of changes and feels like a much fuller and complete game.  At this point it is worth it based on just the fact it is not free to play and offers a lot of content.  This game has found its own charm and balances the tower v player aspect very well.  Progression feels so much better and lets you play through without getting stuck or wondering what to do next.  They seem to be keeping up with monthly events and things like the carnival to keep people interested, and to give them the opportunity to own unique skins and items.  Pets are in FINALLY and have improved significantly but I still feel like they don't do as much as they should and they don't feel unique at all.  I'm still confused as to whether or not the only difference in the pets is the skin and the active.  The pets in DD1 were a lot more useful, offering a wide range of abilities.  Pets don't seem to change much upon levelling up.  It would be nice to have something more like the engineer that helps you repair or increases tower attack.  All in all good game.
As of right now the game is very much incomplete feature wise, with a completely different feel from the original, kind of more professional but that was what the original has as a charm aspect.  The second game focuses more on the player taking part rather than the turrets doing most of the work.  This somewhat takes away from the strategic placement of turrets in the first game to where the player is instead.  The game is fun to play and has a bright future ahead of it.  However right now it is missing most of the important parts which make it a fun tower defense, collect em all, achievement heavy, grind festy game.

This game features quite a bit of rather intrigueing gameplay mechanics that weren't very common back in it's time which shocked the gaming community. The environment takes time to get used to and this game is nothing short of stressful chase. This game starts off on a strong note and immediately throws you straight into the action. Stealth, creativity, innovation and keen detective skills are necessary if you are to survive this Lovecraft-inspired menagarie. Never stop for anything, never turn around to see where they are. Check to see you blocked off every entry point possible. You will have allies along the way to push you through this story-rich cult classic (emphasis on 'cult'). But be wary, not everyone in this game is here to help you. Especially what lurks below the city and in the murky depths of the ocean.

Basically, it's a lovecraft-themed first person survival horror game with Fish-men, the Occult, Sanity (or, insanity), Cannibalism, Necromancy, and overwhelming odds. It is the Dark Souls of first person horror games. You have no HUD (sorry, FPS gamers), almost no ammo, and will eventually have no sanity.
Yes, before Amnesia, this game implemented a Sanity feature. As you are... *exposed* to certain things "
" your sanity depletes. This has some rather interesting effects on gameplay that shall not be named.
The game is pretty linear, if you were expecting multiple paths, you will not get them. However, if you were expecting suspense, horror, and a fun gaming experience, you will receive. The game is neither combat nor stealth-based. Although there are times where the player lacks weapons and must resort to stealth, or cannot avoid enemies and must fight, for the most part, there is always the option.
The combat system is in parts very realistic, and non-realistic, for reasons you might not even think. As I explained before, there is no HUD, no ammo counting, no crosshair, no health meter. You can aim your weapons down their sights, but sustained aiming tires your arms and unsteadies you. You will fight enemies that really will only die by headshots (Mutated Fish People, or the Part Fish/Part Man people that you encounter early on). Sure, on "Boy Scout" difficulty you might be able to kill a cultist with five shots to the chest, but ammunition is scarce, largely due to the fact that, unfortunately, and unrealistically, enemies do not drop ammunition or weapons. The only reward for eliminating an enemy is the satisfaction of removing an unholy terror from the earth.
Health is determined by the current state of your player. You can get injured, and much like Snake Eater, you will have to resort to surgery. Thankfully, you won't have to worry about complex military surgery on yourself, it is simply application of bandages to light wounds, splints for broken bones, surture for deep wounds, and antibiotics for poisons (Don't worry, this happens rarely... unless you aren't careful). Instead, you will probably be worrying much more about the mental health of your character. Those overwhelming odds can drive a man insane. So can the adrenaline from killing so many people in so little time. So can peeking down into a window and seeing a swarm of rats drag a rotting carcass into a room. So can... (you get the idea). What's more is that your decreases in sanity can cause hallucinations, schizophrenia, and even the strong desire to commit suicide.
You will play as a private detective who has had his mind♥♥♥♥♥♥♥by a Yithian. I suggest you read up on Lovecraft if you want to understand what any of these things are, otherwise, you will probably think I have been smoking something. You find out about the Esoteric Order of Dagon, who you seem to♥♥♥♥♥♥off while to try to find a runaway store manager. Basically, they want to kill you. (Read "The Shadow Over Innsmouth") So you have to escape. Upon escaping, the Government decides the people they have been watching kill hundreds of non-converts and worship Elder Gods for the last decade, are a threat to America, so they make you do all the work, since they have never read any Lovecraft, much like the Call of Duty, FEAR, and Resident Evil fans complainng how hard this game is.
Although, even if you are Lovecraft fan, this still may not be the game you are fhtagn about. It is flawed, even to a diehard fan's standards. It has bugs and problems. Bugs can be overlooked by anyone, but this game is also extremely difficult, even on the lowest difficulty setting. If you are unsure of what you are doing and don't take the game seriously, you will fail. Although it has difficulty, it lacks the replay value of a game like Dark Souls does. You may enjoy replaying this game on higher or lower difficulties, and there are collectibles, in the form of mythos relics and stories, to discover. You will definitely enjoy some of the relics that provide backstory to the game and information on the mythos. It isn't going to provide hours of entertainment for bookworms like Skyrim or Oblivion do, but it is a fun aspect of the game.
All in all, the game is a very good, if not excellent survival horror game. It is fun, albeit difficult, with a compelling story and gameplay. If you are seeking a scary game, this game delivers. Although there are jumpscares, it uses those sparingly, instead relying on atmosphere and suspense build-up. There are some pretty disturbing scenes and images in this game, not quite Outlast-type stuff that this generation may be used to, but certainly enough to horrify. There are moments, that if you have your eyes open, much like in FEAR, will be visible, and you may take time exploring the area to find them. I myself find the game to be one of the better survival horror games, but it is too hard to compare to the majority of horror games. It is a different experience. It is not for everybody, and not everyone will like this game, but definitely worth the price, and above the price.

Some missing or broken files prevent it from running on many computers, but after reading of an easy workaround on Steam forums I managed to play this game just fine. In the end I decided to rate it positively and not let that initial défaillance influence my opinion.
This is the second game in the series starring the archeologist and adventurer Samantha Swift. Despite it being a sequel, the story is self contained and only minor references from Samantha Swift and the Hidden Roses of Athena are present, which is a nice touch (maybe even... golden? Okay, that was terrible). There are even microscopic references to the protagonist of a different game/series from the same developers, Angelica Weaver, but nothing that would spoil the enjoyment of the game to those who haven't played that one.
Overall Acquista Samantha Swift and the Golden Touch slightly improves everything from its predecessor and offers a medium-length HOG with a relaxing but catchy story, beautiful art and a decent selection of puzzles. One minor nitpick I have is how the story initially seems to show information about Samantha's father and his mysterious disappearance (something only briefly mentioned in menu notes in the first game) but it quickly reduces itself to an excuse to gather recurring items (Swift tablets) without any actual progress on the search for him, although one might speculate this could lead to bigger development in third and fourth episodes of the series not yet on Steam (spoiler:
).
Aside from that detail it's still a good casual game, and just like I said in my review for its prequel I'd at least recommend it if bought during a sale or from a bundle.

That being said, I'll review the game content itself although this bug should cause some concern for people who'd buy it at full price on Steam.
It's definitely an improvement from the first title when it comes to gameplay. The difficulty went up a notch, the objects now more obscured using shadows. The puzzles were a lot more well-developed and the background had extra animations that made the environments more pleasing and entertaining. The items you find in the HO scenes are used more often to progress to the next room.
The art has changed to a higher more polished quality although the resolution itself is stuck at 800x600. This made it difficult to pick out some objects, and it required a bit of pixel hunting. Basically, if the item was a string, the clickability is limited to that thin strand which means you'd be clicking frantically at it until you perfectly hit the string. It was a major struggle to click on rings, tiny bugs, and the like.
There's a bit of gripe with repetitive objects, and mixed quality again. Some objects look real while others looked hand-drawn. I'd really prefer one or the other since it sorts of breaks the immersion and makes the game itself look messy and cheap. And I don't know how many times I'd need to seek 'sack' and 'knife/dagger' in every part of the world. There are a lot of things in the world, why limit to so many similar items? And they're not even hand-drawn.
Unfortunately, the story was a lot less interesting than Hidden Roses of Athena for me, I just didn't resonate with the dialogue and found myself glazing over it. I really liked the bar area, it was a different take on HO scene interactivity but the story itself felt quite condensed in comparison to its predecessor.
Overall, it was playable and I still had some fun with it. I liked the puzzles a lot more this round but the countries chosen maybe not so much. Buy it only if you'd like to experience the continuation of Samantha Swift's journey (since it picks up where you've left off) but as a standalone game, I don't particularly feel enthused about it.

Its not terrible I suppose but for the price I can't recommend it. This is more like a neutral review but note these things:
-Low resolution, seems to be locked at 800x600 with no way of changing it.
-Very few options.
-Cursor and detection issues. I frequently click the correct area and it doesn't register.
-A lot of the scenes include a sort of "round 2" in the scene using tools you just collected. Some of them are logical but a lot of them aren't so you just sweep the screen with the tool searching for the area you're supposed to use it.
-Few added added puzzles. HOG scenes and using a tool after completing a screen is mostly all there is.
-Music is okay but nothing special.
-The artwork isn't great. It's probably passable but at such low res I found myself squinting at it more than enjoying it.
Basically this is a short, easy HOG and yet its still somehow frustrating instead of relaxing. It also seems a lot more dated than it actually is, it feels and looks older than something released in 2009.  With all this in mind I'd also say it has very low replay value. I'll honestly be glad when I'm finished with this one.
I'd say pass unless you're an avid collector or fan of HOGs, or want to buy the Samantha Swift combo pack. You could get a more modern HOG with better art that supports higher resolutions, has more content, a better story and a much better interface for the same price or less.

Very accessible, streamlined ARPG. For some veterans it may be too arcade like.
Victor Vran aims to experiment with innovation in the genre of ARPG. Do you want to jump?, even wall jump?, well you can. Do you want to merge some of that repetitive loot, well you can, sometimes a gamble, but you can.
Victor Vran is very polished, smooth with great graphics. But it doesn't follow the formula of games like Grim Dawn, Diablo 2, Titan Quest. It scraps the class system and allocating points into skill trees. Instead it focuses on different abilities from the gear you use. I think what the developers wanted to avoid is where the player reaches a stage where they just steam roll everything or being trapped within a class they hate. I find the game very flexible in terms of abilities and various gear offers plenty of abilities, yet also consistent challenge andl fun.
It is not an open world game, instead there are various areas, where you can go and complete challenges. You can use hexes to up the challenge, there are timed challenges also and bosses, these can earn the player stars. That is not to say that there isn't some exploration, there are dungeon like areas and mansions within the areas to explore and further challenges. What I'm trying to say is that quests are very simple, go there and find this person. But the challenges offer something different and give you a chance to get good loot and level up. In this way Victor Vran has arcade like elements. You can return to early stages to earn more stars if you desire, or complete challenges you may of missed.
The voice acting is excellent. Victor Vran is Geralt from The Witcher series, and he is taunted by a voice in his head, kind of like a Gladis from Portal type character. I'm enjoying the story, characters have depth. The game does not take itself too seriously, it really mixes up humour, with tragedy, which is actually refreshing.
Overall, this game is fun and online seems to be picking up, I can join others in their games easily enough. Anyway, I'm going to get back at it.

Hyperdimension Neptunia Re;Birth is back for the PC with its third installment and it heavily leans on its two predecessors and their accomplishments. That being said, while it heavily relies on premade assets and basic gameplay ideas, it still delivers on new features for the game. Sadly it falls completely short in the stability department.
I joked about it for part two, but this time, if you know the first game, you really know most of this one. It copies every map of Re;Birth 1 and some of 2. As the maps of 2 were sometimes lacking in depth, this is a welcome rebrand for Re;Birth 3, if lazy. And of course nearly no new enemy types are added, just rebranded - if at all - and sent out. You will even remember some of the quest texts. While this could draw the ire of many players, the story theme of "A world in the Past" actually makes it an irony in itself. So if you can adopt it to your game's storyline, you might let them get away with it.
The story is set in another dimension, the Ultradimension, and has Neptune being exiled to it from her own home the Hyperdimension of Re;Birth 2. Yes, this game is an actual sequel! In her first days in the Ultradimension, Neptune quickly realizes that not all is as she remembered... and the future has yet to be written for her and others. In this setting, the game excels in its most important asset yet again, the meta-story and its jokes about the console wars of the past. Many of its easter eggs, secrets and jokes make more than up for its grindy gameplay and exhausting repetition even for those that don't follow Red's wifey fetish or like to play dress up with digital assets. All of this is delivered in the now common format of a novel-rpg hybrid.
Within this genre, this game is as casual or hard as you want to as it continues the trilogy's idea of "play like you want". You quickly get the plans and choice to craft harder or easier enemies, to get more experience or to just play the game normally. That being repeated even from Re;Birth 2, much HAS changed in terms of gameplay to its two predecessors! The old % grinds have been replaced with them being tied to the story and are only part of the actual immersive gameplay of the quests. Further the eternal button mashing to scan for hidden treasures in maps has been replaced with the "Super Neptune Sisters" blocks you can see hover in all treasure locations in a ghostly outline. While only one of them offers treasure like before, all offer a small monetary benefit for hitting them. And it saves the liftetime of your X button.
The biggest change to gameplay though is the removal of the party shared exe drive and the variable status of SP, this games type of mana. Now its maximum is always 1000. While it was feasible to have heavy-hitters before with characters like Falcom with immense hit counts collecting your exe drive, your rush attacks now actually refill your own SP and only those. This bar works as your exe drive as well as your mana pool per character. So slow characters tend to fall behind in refilling their abilities unless you switch to defending for them to catch up. This also devalues the super exe attacks, which are far less rewarding than a traditional guard break combo before unleashing the necessary amount of SP with a normal SP skill on the enemy. The gameplay has truly been changed.
Stella's Dungeon also makes a return, this time with 20 floors of one dungeon to clear. The gameplay has been streamlined and flavored with side-characters you in the past only talked with. They can do the scouting work for her and new ones get added per cleared floor, offering up new abilities or rare items and monsters to find. It also takes less time than before, at least with the DLC plans. As in Re;Birth 2, even sped up, the last dungeons took A DAY, none will take more than half an hour with it.
The game's crafting system still focuses most on clothes and outside changes on the CPUs. Unlike Re;Birth 2, though, the developers could reuse all assets from Re;Birth 1 and thus the immense long list of accessories from Re;Birth 1 makes a resounding return. Don't expect anything new, but if you loved some in Re;Birth 1 or 2, the chance is high you can recreate them in Re;Birth 3 all over again. There will be no lack of recipes to grind for, unless you cheapen your experience so far with the easy mode recipes, that you run out of MB.
Sadly, the greatest problem of this game is THE EXACT SAME Re;Birth 2 had. It tends to crash during repeated transmissions between zones in speed grinds in medium to long play sessions. And while before it could also happen in battles with graphical glitches in components of characters warning you about an impending crash, this time it has hit the novel-rpg sequences instead. Once one of the story assets turns into a weird cut out black blop or the background disappears, abandon all hope. Before the sequence ends, the game WILL crash. Unlike Re;Birth 2 there is no chance you reach a savepoint by then. Save often and restart your game at least every two hours to prevent bad surprises. This game was not polished or properly ported. Long play sessions will risk your current advances in the game at any moment. While the lack of graphics in the sequences can be funny, the loss of a hard fought boss might not. At least restart before a boss fight at the save point and make sure to never do long grind sessions without going out of the dungeon or to a savepoint to keep the data.
Like with its predecessors, my main interest in the game still stems from the light humor of it and the quirky story. And it delivered well, despite or especially because of some darker themes in this new installment! It might have been one if not the best of the trilogy I played. I can only compliment the author of many of the jokes. While not all work all the time, I found myself enjoying and laughing. And in the end that is what matters.
The gameplay has been diversified a little and the minigame actually became a proper minigame to enjoy. Before I called the gameplay solala, now it can be considered average. So the game overall is already better than any of its predecessors, of which it heavily borrowed in assets and gameplay anyway. As always, the fun lies in the characters and story, if you love to break the fourth wall, have some wifeys or a digital dress up party... or a nostalgic grind.
Play it your way, and try to enjoy the insanity of our Hyperdimension's Neptunia. But if you are reading this, you surely had some fun with its prior installments and thus you can't go wrong here. Just consider the stability issues past the two hour mark per session!
My final verdict for Hyperdimension Neptunia is finish it, including the Social Games DLC storyline, Stella's Dungeon included!

If you've played EG1, then EG2 is the logical sequel: it's bigger and shinier while keeping what worked with the original.  The graphics, lighting and sound are great.  Controls are very responsive (I used a 360 controller).  New gameplay elements include a couple more superpower-hats for your sidekick.  Generally I found the levels more varied and entertaining than the original game's.
Here's why I can't rate it a 5-star:
- while "if it ain't broke, don't fix it" applies to some extent, I'd have liked to see a couple more enemies added.  The sawblades and the reapers are back, and that's it - apart from the snake-boss (whose levels I didn't enjoy, because they were too fiddly).  How about some different classes of reapers, at the least?
- some of the levels are way too tricky, while most are plain sailing (can be done within a couple of tries).  I wonder how many of those really tough levels were beta-tested?  Because the timing required on some of them is outrageous.  A couple involve your goat being stuck at the bottom of the screen on a platform which is decaying or otherwise moving out from under you.  If you jump too soon, you die; if you hesitate, you fall and die; and, if you jump incorrectly (by not hitting a high-enough jump or by brushing against a tiny pixel) you are blocked from completing the jump (and then you fall and die).  In desperation on those levels, I looked up how the YouTube experts did it, but replicating the same feat is another matter.  I always say it with puzzlers: if you can see how something is meant to be done yet can't replicate it within an hour of trying, the game has failed.  Or should be labelled: only for kids with catlike reflexes.  :(
Niggles aside, I had a blast with the majority of the game, "finishing" it in around 7hrs (87% completion, it says, but more than enough to get to the outro).

So, I now have about 100 hours in to this game. I've played multiple games, with my best reaching a population of approx 900 people before the wheels fell off. I've played easy, medium and hard. I've read all of the guides  on the wiki, the forums, and even Reddit. I really, really wanted to love this game. I waited for it to come out for what felt like *ages*, stalking this guy's FB page for update info. And I am just so sad that I can't love it.
Why? The inconsistencies. I am a creature of habit. I place all my buildings  in a predictable pattern, and I'm a hoarder by nature so I'm very careful about pathing to ensure maximum efficiency of the workers. And yet, despite my consistency in behavior and detail, there is no consistency in output. In one game, 2 woodcutters will provide enough firewood for a population of 120 with firewood to spare. In another game, 14 woodcutters cannot keep the same population afloat, despite over 4k backlog in wood. Woodcutters placed directly beside stockpile containing 2k logs. Woodcutter (A) will cut 42 logs in a season, while Woodcutter (B) will cut 298 logs in the same season, and Woodcutter (C) might cut 3 logs that season. All three are educated, and are situated in homes very close by. Their food is supplied by the gatherer and hunter that are always paired with foresters on my maps. They want for nothing, but they do not work.
This is a problem that I find repeatedly throughout the game. You want a field of about 40x40 cleared, so you free up  100 or so laborers, prioritize that field and wait for them to get to work! And you wait.... and you wait.... and you wait. You re-prioritize the field. You de-select everything else on the map for clearing. You wait..... 8 seasons have passed, and your field is not cleared. 8 seasons of 100 laborers that could have been doing any number of other things.
This is a randomly occurring problem within the game. You could go 50 seasons without a hitch, before you get a spike of random unproductiveness. Whole fields can produce less than 50 food per year, woodcutters that just dont show up for work, miners that idle the entire season away in the Cemetary.
Oh! And for funsies, when you get a disease outbreak, and the diseased persons refuse to go to any of your multiple, fully staffed hospitals for treatment! They just wander the map, going about their business like Typhoid Mary from Hell. Every town center I make gets a hospital, and the sick folks generally find their way to them in short order. However, every now and then, you will get a Typhoid Mary who will inflict their disease on 100+ of your population before they finally die.
Yeah, inconsistent.

So now that i have played the game for a decent amount of a time, i want to go into deeper detail about the game, share what i love about it, and stress the things about the game that really rub me the wrong way, first i wanna talk about the akward stuff since its still fresh in my mind.
1.Hero DPS/Tower DPS
Ever since dd1 the end game required that you have buildings which are built by characters which are speced for tower stats. which is totally cool, if it didnt make you feel like your character himself did less damage.
The problem:
Say i love to play the huntress, and that im the number 1 huntress fan who wants to run around doing alot of ranged dps and at the same time feel like my traps were optimal, and that they are helping out my team to the best of their ability. I would have to make a huntress that was speced for defenses, place traps, and switch to a completly different huntress who is speced for dps for when combat starts.
Why do we have to have to limit a certain aspect of our character and have to make two? it feels like i have to make two halves of a huntress instead of focusing on one super bad♥♥♥♥♥dps dealing & traping machine. some might say that it lets you play specific roles within your class and look for certain gear to help you play that role better, but it can be done without having to fall short of the other roles.
Solution:
why cant certain gear contain hero damage and other gear contain tower specs? it completly removes the need to have two characters of the same class. lets say that weapons contained the hero damage stat and that those special extra stats that you might get only contained damage buffs. Armor could contain hero health and resistance stats and the extra special stats could retain to tankyness. and lastly relics could contain tower stats, and the extra special stats(like ones that buff your towers) could enhance towers.
At the moment all hero stats are spread across all items, if these were more organized to certain gear we wouldnt have to make a builder and a dps. only one singular character.
How this translates in game and why this is a huge problem:
lets say things are getting heated and i fell like i need to throw some more geysers down and it also needs to be upgraded, sure i could do so, but instead i have to worry about them not being efficient, why put down geysers on my dps huntress when i can save the mana for a builder huntress. who could put down a geyser 5 times better then my own. i could just throw down the geyser and upgrade it, then sell it next round for the builder huntress and lose out on mana, but this really disconnects me from the game. I should be able to have a good dps character, throw down a situational trap, and not be worried about wasting mana and building units that my other building speced teamates could use alot more optimally. The way stats are speced right now encourages linear and repetitive gameplay. Lets say a new set of maps comes out with a new max character level to go with it. and i wanna be able to experience the new end game content with all characters and all their towers. instead of saying "Wow i cant wait to level and gear my huntress! i bet there will be cool new weapons for her! ohh i cant wait to see what *insert squire/ tower here* could do on this level, i bet  leveling him up and gearing him will be a blast!" and so on and so forth. instead i think " time to level up huntress 1 and find gear for her, then level up huntress 2 and do the same, and the same goes for squire 1, squire 2. monk 1, 2. wizard 1, 2, 3.(you can see where im going with this). this system is especially ridiculous if the game is going to have alot more new classes. as somebody who wants to experience the game on all the different classes, it feels like a chore just to gear and level a single class.
If dungeon defends prides itself on being action/tower defence, why do i feel like i can only play one at a time without handicaping my team because i wanna throw down a quick defense on my dps character?
2. difficulty scaling
This progression system ties in very badly with the way difficulty scales, which i dont even know how is supposed to work.
so difficulty depends on three things, the map, the playlist, and the actual difficulty you set in game.
which makes really makes it complicated as to how you play through the game, sure after beating the game in one playlist you could play it again on hard mode, but when you progress to the next playlist where does the difficulty and item drop quality increase? is the first level in the game supposed to be harder then the last level on the playlist before? i wish this were the case, but no. so where do you pick up? do you replay the last three levels on the next playlist for better loot? the last 5?6? who knows, the game doesnt tell you, this just leads to alot of confusion and will probably just make players accidently join lobbys they arent ready for, and if they are indeed ready for the hardest level in the next playlist, then are we just suppossed to play the last level on each playlist? if the game simply just made level 1 on the next playlist harder then the last level on the playlist before, if would be simpler, and give reason to actually re play maps, but if the whole idea of the wyvern den being easier then level one of the next playlist, then just dump the whole playlist system and turn that difficulty scaling into just setting the difficulty in the tavern. The way playlist are labeled is campaign mode, 20+(you hit level 20 around the time you beat throne room) 25+,25++ and incursion. since the first map of incursion isnt harder then the last map of the playlist before, then does that mean the item level that the playlist recommends is for the first level? obviously not so, why even have that item requirement? if you are gonna have the requirement could you tell us what map that item level recommendation applies too?
all in all the difficulty settings and playlists are a huge mess in that sense, and despite me typing an essay about what i hate about those two parts of the game, i actually love the game, and recommend it to anyone. the game is truly special and hear is why.
What i love about dd2.
for the most part, it feels like a proper sequal to dd1. character combat feels smooth and engaging, skills are all unique and fun, and each class feels like it has something to bring to table(combat wise, and defense wise). the game actually rewards you for using towers of every class, and even rewards you for synergizing them (new players try electric aura and water geysers :)). the new towers encourage teamwork and diversity, and thats one of the things i really enjoy about dd2.
For those of you returning to the series, dungeon defends is a game that combines tower defense, and action rpg elements. each class has stats that make their combat special, along with their own abilities and defenses. using each class to its strengths and using other classes to cover its weaknesses (and vice versa) is where the strategy and team work comes in. After you strategize with your buddies and strangers about what you should spend your very precious tower mana and building units on. you drop your tools and pick up your weapons, because god knows those arent gonna be enough for the hordes(and i do means this to its full extent) and armys of the old ones, which includes but is not limited to : rampaging groups of goblins, armored orcs( and their lady friends) who laugh in the face of your petty physical attacks with their massive amounts of armor and health, spearmen who love to sit behind the carnage and snipe your defences, ravenous kobalds who would love nothing more then too charage into the heart of your defenses and detonate the TNT straped to them(continued v)

I'd say I'm a part of the concensus that says that while Dark Souls II: SotFS is the weakest in the series, it's still a masterpiece in its own right.
Needless to say, it's hard. Every game in the Soulsborne series is hard but still retains a sense of fulfillment and enjoyment. That's all there in DSII but there are times where it starts to feel strenuous and your frustrations meter will rise and the fun meter will drop. In other words, this game can feel like a chore more than the other. I feel like some of the areas in this game had the cards stacked against you just for the sake of difficulty. Some of the zones were unimaginative and inflated with infinite poise enemies to mob you just to make it hard. This applies to many of the boss fights too. They definitley went for quantity of quality.
The good thing about DSII is that it starts out less linear. Some people didn't like this but those of you who played Demon's Souls on the PS3 may welcome this feature. If one zone is frustrating the hell out of you, don't worry. You can always warp out and explore another. On the downside, this can create some confusion on where to go next but this Dark Souls. You are both punished and rewarded for exploration.
While playing through DSII I missed the mysterious dreamlike atmosphere of the first game but in retrospect I appreciate the setting in this one just as much. I think this is the most dark and depressing Dark Souls yet and I mean that in a good way. Being hollow carries more weight as your health bar decreases each time you die. Hopelessness is in the air and I still gain much comfort when I see a new bonfire or when I return to the Emerald Herald to level up. The soundtrack is great and very fitting for some of the bosses and locations.
Some may call this game the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ child of the series but I think it has a rightful place and deserves "Dark Souls" in the title. If you want to play through the Soulsborne games, don't skip this one.

The deeper you dive the more you'll find.
Victor Vran is a unique take on the ARPG while still feeling "old", comfortable and just how a ARPG should. The emphasis is definitely on the action as the builds and loot deceptively appear to be shallow. The main quest line is very approachable and beatable, especially if you take advantage of the co-op feature. There's reviews on here of people beating it with friends in just a handful of hours with some asking for more. But, there is indeed oh so much more to the game than those simple first glances and impressions. Everything gets much more depth the more you try to accomplish. If you set out to complete the 205 challenges and find the 116 secrets you will soon discover everything this game has to offer.
All sorts of fun features unlock as you level up. Special dungeons, an endless dungeon, more customization, PVP arena, etc. etc. A "transmutation" system makes upgrading items and melee/ranged weapons to your playing styles possible. The "destiny cards" allow you to build traits via a passives system. And the amount and strength of the cards you can use continues to grow well into the leveling up. Your "demon powers" and consumables will make your fingers fly around on the keyboard and mouse during the hardest of challenges. Plus there are difficulty modifiers called "hexes" that take things to yet another level. I will say that outfits are definitely lacking and just one piece. But they do control the way you power your demon powers (useful options to have depending on your other gear) and have some modifiers, color cosmetics, and the ability to be slightly upgraded in the later character levels. There's just always something new around the corner! So much so that even I had to call it quits at a certain point. I was not at all surprised to find out that the list of things to do didn't remotely end with those 205 challenges I went after... I just didn't have it in me to push on again! But I most definitely got what I wanted out of it all. And then some.
Victor Vran really does strike an amazing balance of being approachable as well as having depth. The amount of things to do for those wishing to jump off the deep end is staggering. And I'd argue really well done to keep things as fresh as possible in a genre known for the end-game grind. You can beat the game with a single weapon you like on the lowest difficulty over a weekend. Or you can take up the challenges that will require you to discover the depth of what you can do with character builds and get nearly 30hrs out of it like me. Or you can go even further! Much much further. And all of it either by your lonesome or with a friend(s). Then when you consider steep sales and bundles and well, my goodness is this a bargain.
Looks good, sounds great, controls great (WASD/mouse, mouse movement, OR gamepad), and you get out what you put in. Couldn't really ask for much more. I very highly recommend checking it out if you want a ARPG for your next gaming adventure!

And perhaps that becomes true at some point in the game, but the parts I've played over and over aren't that way at all. Perhaps it's an unskippable tutorial and that hasn't been made clear, but whatever the case, any time I veer too far from where they want me to be, I am penalized and reverted back to an earlier checkpoint, despite everything I'd managed to accomplish up to that point. The furthest I've gotten is an "on-rails"-esque escort mission where I have to ride atop a guy's car while he escapes and make sure he gets out alive. If this were Fallout or Skyrim [two truly open world games], I'd have the option of failing at this, and they would just say that it sucks to be me, and move on from there. Whereas in this, if I do what I can to keep him alive but he dies anyway, I get to replay that whole section again. This is the sequel to Samanth Swift and the Hidden Roses of Athena, and it follows exactly the same formula: you visit different countries searching for separate components to a myserious object that will save the day. Each place you visit involves a number of hidden object scenes, finding things that are lying around, and using tools in mostly obvious (and sometimes extremely unlikely) places. Occasionally there's a mild puzzle to solve, such as solitaire, match 3, jigsaw puzzles etc. It's all very easy, the cartoony style makes the objects stand out quite clearly, although in each scene there's usually one or two objects that are hidden a little better than the others. However, the game really falls over itself to give you hints, clues and not-so-gentle nudges, so you're unlikely to get stuck for more than half a minute.
