Generally good but those expecting Diablo or PoE may be disappointed. The addition of an action roll and significantly reduced focus on character building gives it more emphasis on the A and less on the RPG.
There's still a serviceable crafting system and weapons with randomized prefixes/suffixes, though the variety is fairly limited. At any time you have 4 skills to use, two based on the type of weapon you're using and two from spell cards you carry. Between those, having two weapons to switch between on the fly(meaning 2 more skills), and two items(potions or bombs) you do generally have a good number of possible actions to perform so that's good. The drawback is that there just aren't that many different spell cards, weapon types, or items so there just isn't the variety you'd expect. I ended up switching weapons fairly frequently but settled on the same two or three spells and two potions for 90% of the game.  The enemy variety feels a bit lacking as well.
Some of the voice acting was excellent, though the writing seemed pretty lacking. Maps were all hand crafted and good looking rather than repetative procedurally generated stuff. There were quite a few humorous bits thrown in, though only some worked while other attempts fell flat and just hurt immersion by breaking the 4th wall with bad meme references.
Having said all that, if you treat it as a 10-20 hour beat'em-up, rather than a Diablo/PoE/Torchlight competitor, it's by no means a bad game. I generally had a good time. If this were a full price AAA I wouldn't recommend it, but as a $20, frequently discounted title? Yeah, it's a solid game. If you think the trailers look like fun and you're not expecting skill trees and massive loot variety then you'll probably have a good time with it.

i recommend this game, it's a fresh take on the ARPG genre and i personally really loved it. However, i'll list some problems i personally had with it in case anyone considers these deal-breaking.
-not a lot of enemy types (you wouldn't think this would be a big thing but enemy variety is something that's really needed here and something that games like torchlight II and diablo 3 do better.) even though the enemy types featured do reward the player for being skilled enough to know how to fight them properly
-legendary weapons scale with level. this doesn't sound like a problem considering it means you get to use your favourite legendary longer, but considering how rare legendary drops are, it can result in you using the same weapon even after you get bored of it because you can't justify using a rare one instead. i would suggest a system that allows you to pay either a large amount of gold or a transmute option to bring a legendary weapon up to your level rather than having it automatically scale. this has become such a problem for me that i started a new game (not ng+ as you keep your weapons in that) so i would have an excuse to use different weapons.
-not a lot of end-game content (unless you're a crazy person who likes 100%ing every area and getting every star) and a fairly short campaign. zagoravia is a cool setting but i thought it would only be like half the game and the other half would be in the demon world (especially how they built it up) but the game is actually surprisingly short. the end game content consists mostly of once a day runs of the cauldron of chaos, a randomized dungeon filled with random endgame mobs, bottomless pit, which is an endurance/survival mode thing that gets boring pretty quickly, and doing either bounty or treasure hunts, which are largely unrewarding and only very rarely drop legendary weapons. also new game plus because it's an arpg.
-bad drop rates. the game seems to want to restrict top tier gear by having it be locked away behind low drop chances for legendary weapons. i'd be able to forgive this if they didn't go the opposite direction with demon powers and cards, as it's very easy to get a mythical demon power or card to drop.
-no expansions. i hear a lot of talk about the game being set for an expansion about the game motorhead. i heard about this and got excited, thinking the game would be receiving some much-needed content. then i looked up "victor vran expansion" and found out that it was announced in august 2015 and hadn't been mentioned since. the prospect of content updates is dead, folks. i'm grateful for the tome dlc, highlander outfit and the cauldron, but this game desperately needs more content.
despite all of this, i really do like the game. i play it very often and it's one of my favourite arpgs, and i highly recommend it.

Let me get this straight, you want me to tell you a review about this game? Whoever you are, you might as well go to the curators, because if you've come for a review on this game, you've come to the wrong place. However, if you have come for an outstanding chocolate chip cookie recipe, you've come to the right place.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Ingredients
1/2 cup (1 stick) unsalted butter
3/4 cup packed dark brown sugar
3/4 cup sugar
2 large eggs
1 teaspoon pure vanilla extract
1 (12-ounce) bag semisweet chocolate chips, or chunks
2 1/4 cups all-purpose flour
3/4 teaspoon baking soda
1 teaspoon fine salt
Directions
1. Evenly position 2 racks in the middle of the oven and preheat to 375 degrees F. (on convection setting if you have it.) Line 2 baking sheets with parchment paper or silicone sheets. (If you only have 1 baking sheet, let it cool completely between batches.)
2. Put the butter in a microwave safe bowl, cover and microwave on medium power until melted. (Alternatively melt in a small saucepan.) Cool slightly. Whisk the sugars, eggs, butter and vanilla in a large bowl until smooth.
3. Whisk the flour, baking soda and salt in another bowl. Stir the dry ingredients into the wet ingredients with a wooden spoon; take care not to over mix. Stir in the chocolate chips or chunks.
4. Scoop heaping tablespoons of the dough onto the prepared pans. Wet hands slightly and roll the dough into balls. Space the cookies about 2-inches apart on the pans. Bake, until golden, but still soft in the center, 12 to 16 minutes, depending on how chewy or crunchy you like your cookies. Transfer hot cookies with a spatula to a rack to cool. Serve.
5. Store cookies in a tightly sealed container for up to 5 days.
For a Rocky Road Bar:
1. Lightly butter a 9 by 13-inch baking pan. Make the batter as per cookie recipe and fold in 1 cup chopped walnuts along with the chocolate chips. Spread batter in prepared pan. Bake until the edges are light brown and the batter sets, about 45 minutes. Cool slightly and cover surface with 4 cups marshmallows and 1 cup chocolate chips. Broil at least 8 inches from the heat until marshmallows turn golden brown, about 2 minutes. (Keep an eye on the marshmallows, and turn the pan frequently--they go from golden to char in a wink.) Cool, cut and serve.

"The Amazing Adventures of Ash - Afterparty" is a game developed by Z3roram Studios and developed using the RPG Maker VX engine. The game is a horror-style one if you will, and is mostly puzzle-based but has a few RPG elements to it, such as the casual RPG fighting. The game stars a girl named Ashlee who gets invited to a party, but later needs to escape the house which the party took place, with everyone vanished and unable to help her. Only to discover the shocking truth behind who owns the house, and why souls are present within the house.
I have just beaten the game as I'm writing this review. If you know about the other RPG Maker games "Witch's House" and "Five Nights at F***Boy's", you would say gameplay is like a mix between the two (Without the sexual themes of FNaFB, obviously). Most of the game is about solving puzzles within the house, and sometimes you'll come across a monster which you must fight and defeat RPG-style. So this game involves leveling up and gaining new abilities. But it's a bit cheezy how the minor combat feature mixes in with the major aspects.
This game MIGHT also be a "Choices Matter" type as I have been given feedback from the game after doing a specific set of actions. Such as taking an item only to realize I was accused of stealing it later in the game. But I'm pretty sure these choices don't matter as much as other games like Undertale.
People were complaining that the game was poor for its puzzle solving, how it wasn't as difficult and convolluted as other puzzle games, which kind of make you think logically. But overall, this game is a pass for me. It's the kind of game you would expect from paying $2 for it, like something out of a dollar store.

Before starting the review, I would like to point out that my long playtime is because at one point I put my computer on hibernate and went to sleep without closing the app. Now let's move on shall we~
The Amazing Adventures of Ash is an okay game. It's not the worst game out there but I can't recommend it either. It is supposed to be a puzzle game, however it fails to deliver good puzzles as most of them are just running around and interacting with everything. The most you are going to get is finding passwords which is easy because you do not need to figure them out yourself, they are simply given to you. There is a lot of looking around as sometimes the items aren't obvious at all. I had to look at the screenshots to actually figure out that I can get a candle. Most of the time you are clueless about what you need to do because the game does not point it out to you. It's like giving a pear to a baby and expecting him to turn it into a key and use it on a door. You get what I mean :P
There is barely any character development. We don't know much about even Ashley's personality. We know very little about Emily and his dad too, it's like they are just there to fill in the plot and nothing else. They don't feel real. But there are also some things that never get explained. For example, who is the lady with the blue hair? A friend of Emily? Another person the dad sacrificed?
There are also quite a few things in the game that never get explained. Why are there spirits in the house? Did some one die there before? Why are there weird places like a playground and a maze in the house? What about the ''He Watches'' message?
The mapping in the game was not too bad. Larger rooms were a bit empty and some tiles were used incorrectly, but overall it was pretty good. The art was pretty weird and looked like something in MS Paint(in cases like these I actually prefer games without custom art). The battles are way too easy. I was able to get past them just by mashing the attack button. Even though there were only 3(I'm sure there is more but maybe I noticed to avoid them)I still thought they could present a bigger challenge.
The game is poorly made in cases too. You can interact with things even when you aren't facing them and that seems to be a common bug in newbie devs' games. It's really really easy to fix. There are also unwanted options in the menu which the developer didn't get rid of, such as equipment. I feel like for a game that is planning to go commercial, the developers would at least bother to google how to do it. In fact there is a forum post with a tutorial on how to remove them and it's literally the first thing that shows up when you google ''rpg maker vx ace removing menu options''. There are even scripts to do it!

There were things I did enjoy in it too. The length was just about perfect(BE WARNED, the game takes 1.5 hours or so to beat. I know some people consider that short. Overall, I cannot recommend this game. While it could be a good first game it shouldn't be commercial. For the developers, try uploading some free games and getting feedback on them before going commercial. I heavily recommend Rpg Maker Net or Rpg Maker Web as there are a lot of rpg maker experts that would be willing to give feedback to help the game improve. This developer clearly has potential but needs to improve. I'm sure Episode 2 could be better since the dev will be getting feedback for this game.
For the dev: I'd be willing to help out too whether it's giving feedback or helping with eventing. I'm sure you will improve so please don't take my review harshly :)

Allow me to ask you a question. What can purchase for $2 these days? Now, I’d like you to narrow that list down and ask yourself what you can get for that $2 that will provide you several hours of entertainment. That is one way of looking at games such as The Amazing Adventures of Ash – Afterparty, Z3roram’s debut game on the Steam platform. To be even fairer, the idea behind the game came from one of their team’s first time developers, Lisa, and this is the very first game that she has developed. But my gosh, what a fantastic first effort.
My expectations weren’t high entering the game. Thoughts of ‘meh, just another crappy RPGMaker game,’ ‘good grief this is just a cash in for the female gamer crowd,’ and ‘It’s so cheap that it has to be nasty’ filtered through my mind. I couldn’t have been further from the truth. The game immersed me into its creepy little world almost immediately. The puzzles kept me firmly entrenched. I struggled mightily early on trying to work out just what I had to do.
The lone negative review on Steam to date pinpoints the problems that some players have with RPGMaker — the technology is old and games have a tendency to look generic. However, I find that there is a certain charm that helps build immersion in the good or better games built in the engine. I do have an admission to make. I was not a fan of the engine before the creation of this site. I didn’t appreciate the games that were made in them nor the developers who made them or the publishers that published them. Steamified have now featured several games in the engine and those games have shown me that if you put your heart and hard work into the creation of your game that there are a number of different intricacies that you can make. I wont forget the unique battle system that was a huge addition in Pale Echoes, for example, or the delicate manner in which Beyond Reality handled important issues relating to science and mankind. I can say again with ease that The Amazing Adventures of Ash utilizes the RPGMaker software with bravado. It’s so much more than a generic RPGMaker game if you’re willing to give it an opportunity.
The narrative, the story and the puzzles are just flat out fun. The game had no right to suck me in the way that it did. A lot of hard work and thought went into its development. It’s a shockingly debut game for a single developer. I have to think that at some point in the future we could be hearing a lot more from Z3roram’s Lisa. There’s not much to criticize and there isn’t much to point out other than the superlatives that I have offered herein already. It’s just a really good game and at $2 you owe it to yourself to pick it up – or at the very worst pick it up when or if it ever sees itself added to an indie bundle.
If I could offer some advice it would be much as it always is. Please take full advantage of Steam as a platform. You would see sales rise if you were take advantage of adding Steam achievements and trading cards. Further, you would further gain monetarily through the Steam community marketplace with people who sell the cards. I do not understand why developers and publishers fail to take advantage of Steam. I would happily play through the game again if it allowed me to unlock achievements. As a badge collector I would certainly play more to unlock trading cards. As an open question to developers reading this, why do you not utilize what Steam offers? It seems like a no brainer from a monetary perspective and selling your games, regardless of whether or not they are a passion project (which I would hope for most indie developers it would be the case more often than not), is a business.
It is my genuine hope that Z3roram give Lisa the time and the freedom to complete more episodes in this series. Although it wont appeal to every gamer there is a player base for this game and that audience will appreciate what this game has to offer.

Review changed from negative to positive. Originally, the functionality of online play was so ridiculously awful that I and plenty of others found it impossible to play a full game without at least 50 random failures first, but a lot of work has been done since then. I still have trouble connecting to servers sometimes, and I occasionally can't move after an online game starts, but it's nothing too major anymore, and the developers are continuing to work on it.
The actual game itself? It's absolutely wonderful. Half platformer, half stab-your-friend-in-the-back-with-cheap-tricks simulator, and fully hilarious, it's easy for anyone to really get into the game and have lots of fun with it. It's the first multiplayer game I've found where I don't even care in the slightest who wins at the end, because every round, every increasingly impossible setup of objects, and every trap placed by a player in a mean spot all works together to give me a good laugh, so much so that I'm too busy cracking up to even pay attention to the scoreboard most times. How someone can make a platforming game all about competing for the finish line without the overall 'feel' of the game being competitive, I'll never know, but it's truly refreshing to find a game that's so simple and easy to get behind, and always so entertaining.
It's also pretty fun to build deathtraps out of conveyor belts, honey, and sawmill blades.

Stop it! I see you reahing for that "ADD TO CART" button. Stop it! I know what you're thinking: oh man, a survival horror game based on stories by Lovecraft? I love survival horror games! I love Lovecraft! And oh man, every survival horror nerd online is gushing about this game! I have to get it!
But if you just listen to me for a moment, you can save the 10$ you would waste on this awful game, and maybe help me repent for giving money to (some of) the people responsible for its existence.
I'll try to make this quick and mostly spoiler free (I'll tell you when spoilers begin). DCotE starts out great, with a tense atmosphere and impressive attention to detail as you play Detective Jack Walters, sent into a mansion where a cult is holed up, engaged in a shoot-out with the police. It's really great talking to the cultists and picking up clues to what's going on in the mansion, going from room to room and witnessing the madness and the horrors involved.
And then you try to go down a ladder, and the game crashes.
OK, no problem. A lot of games crash. Hell, even AAA titles have crashes. Not a big deal. There was a save point a bit back, I can start over.
And then you try to go down the ladder again, and the game crashes again. And again. And again.
So you check the internet for fixes, and whaddaya know, this is a common problem with running the game on modern computers that no one made any effort to let you know about! But oh wait, no big deal, all you have to do is keep pushing forward as you move down the ladder. No? Game still crashes? OK, they say try a different resolution. OK, it seems like it's going good now aaaaand game crashes. And crashes. And crashes.
No kidding, this complete game-breaking bug kept me from playing this game for 9 months, because I couldn't figure out how to get around it. Eventually, I got a workaround which involved getting a save file from past that point.
That's not the only place where I had to do that. There is a bug where if you jump where you're not supposed to, you're launched all the way to the ceiling and get stuck there, forcing you to restart from a save point. There's a particularly nasty point where you're supposed to target enemies with a cannon and hang on to cover when they counter attack, but you can't see the enemies, the cannon barely moves, and worst of all, no matter how you position yourself relative to the cover, there is only about a 1 in 3 chance the game will register that you pressed the key, meaning you will often get hit and maybe even die and have to start over, all because this game is so badly programmed. The final game-breaker I encountered was after one of the last boss fights, where for some reason, the jump key would only work about 1 out of 10 times, and this was pretty bad because of a short but deadly platforming section, wherein if you die, you had to do the boss all over again. After failing to get through this about 5 times, I tried changing the controls, reasoning that maybe the control mapping was the problem... at which point the game crashed. And this is all just a sample of the hell I had to go through playing this game.
So OK, it's buggy as all hell. But is the game any good in-between bugs? Well, yes at first, but not in the long run. Like I said, the game has a good atmosphere at first, and it's really cool seeing all these Lovecraftian horrors coming to life and having to fight them. However, combat is one of the worst aspects of this game. A lot of people say this is a really hard game, but it is in fact ridiculously easy when bugs aren't involved. It's only difficult if you try to be stealthy, because the stealth system is completely broken. This is one of those really bad stealthers of the early 2000s, when everyone tried copying Metal Gear Solid without any of the craftsmanship or charm of the original. Enemies are near-sighted to the point of blindness when you're sneaking, but then, when you are discovered - and you will be discovered because at some point someone will notice you regardless of what you do - there is no way to shake off your enemies. That's not stealth, that's just running and hoping not to get caught.
Luckily, enemy AI is so terrible and most enemies are such bad shots that you can often run through a gauntlet of enemies without getting hit by a single bullet. Not only that, but the game has so much ammo and enemies fall down so quickly that you can almost always just clean out entire sections of a level and never have to worry about enemies again. From the moment I got a gun in the game (which is kind of a funny moment, because the protagonist gets really excited, saying something along the lines of "yay, finally, a gun!"), I only ran out of pistol ammo once, and I still had plenty of rifle ammo. This is all on the highest difficulty level available on a first playthrough! Nevermind that once you get the game's final weapon in the last stage, you are basically death incarnate. This means that DCotE is less of a survival horror game and more of an action game with scary enemies - kinda like Resident Evil 4, only bad.
OK, survival horror with bad AI and bad controls, what else is new? Is it interesting? Is the plot any good? Well, let me start by saying again that yes, the game's plot does start out good, with you uncovering slowly the horror behind the case you were sent to investigate in Innsmouth, this despite really bad voice acting delivered by a very small cast. But then -
*SPOILERS BEGIN HERE*
Hoover comes in. Yeah, you fight the hordes of evil with J. Edgar Hoover in this game at some point. Hoover forces you to basically go it alone against the Order of Dagon on pain of sending you back to the Asylum*, and refuses to let go of you even when it is clear that a horror from beyond (a Shoggoth) is roaming the area to which he is sending you, a lone ex-detective with no special training, holding nothing more than a pistol and some medkits. After this, you head to the underground city of Y'ha-nthlei, where you kill a bunch of human-fish hybrids, a bunch of deep ones, fight a polype boss, and finally, to top it all off, you KILL MOTHER HYDRA. Are you kidding me with this? Isn't the point of the Cthulhu mythos that there are terrible creatures beyond our understanding that we have no chance of destroying? You might as well have a final boss fight with Cthulhu.
*And seriously, what is it with video games and the FBI trying way too hard to get pretty mundane people to do its dirty work?
It never gets that stupid, but it might as well have. We find out that Jack's amnesia was actually caused by his mind being switched with that of a Yithian* for six years, and the Yithian who tells Jack all this also tells him that, in a very Star Wars kind of twist, I AM YOUR FATHER. Seriously! And uh, realizing he was a Yithian and all the dark♥♥♥♥♥♥he saw drives Jack bananas and he kills himself.
*Ancient alien race that can switch minds with people, even from different times. Don't ask.
*SPOILERS END HERE*

With Call of Cthulhu (COC) appearing in so many "Top 100 Games Of All Time" lists, and as a huge Lovecraft fan, I was eager to play this game.
Many people have discussed the game's instability and bugs, particularly on newer systems. This is all true, but the game's most major problem is poor design, pure and simple. The game commits numerous cardinal sins of game design that make the whole experience a frustrating mess for the player.
When the game works, as it does occasionally, it is extremely eerie and atmospheric. In particular, the hotel escape is an excellent recreation of a sequence from Lovecraft's writing. Some of the gameplay choices, such as the sanity system, are also quite daring. Unfortunately, the game's moments of brilliance are all too few and do not make up for its horrendous failings.
Additionally once you acquire weapons the game attempts to become Half-Life, but without Valve's finesse. The shooting destroys the game's tension and the dialogue and design also seem to go downhill from this point. That parallel is not accidental by the way - if you know Half-Life, you will see some *very* similar areas and puzzles in COC.
Here are some of the major flaws with this game that will make you tear your hair out:
> Poor level design: A non-intuitive mess that will leave you wandering around levels aimlessly for hours. For instance, doors that you have previously tried and were locked will suddenly become open-able after you complete a seemingly unrelated task (e.g. turning the gas on in the next room).
> Poor game design: Jumps that can only be completed from a precise angle. Objects that take five clicks to be picked up and added to your inventory. Traps that require in-human micro-second timing to avoid and are instantly fatal.
> Poor puzzle design: Puzzles frequently require items to solve them. That sounds simple, but the game doesn't tell you what items you need, or even that what you are looking at is a puzzle at all. For instance, you might come across a heavy grate. If you have missed the crowbar earlier in the level (easily done thanks to poor level design and muddy textures) then you cannot open the grate. You will simply think this route is a dead-end and have no idea you need to find a crowbar, unless you read an FAQ. It's even possible to progress to a point where you cannot backtrack to get an item you need, making the puzzle unsolvable!
To illustrate just how appalling these design problems are, here's an example of a typical COC experience. At one point in the game I spent about two hours trying to move past a street with several enemies in it. I tried sneaking. I tried fighting. Nothing worked. The reason? One of the enemies was invulnerable. Deliberately. This was how the designers chose to stop the player progressing in that direction. Instead of blocking off the street, they created an invulnerable enemy that looked like any other. As a result, many players will literally be throwing themselves against a brick wall. It turned out that I needed to pick up a certain object earlier in the level and then progress through a different area - but there was nothing to tell me this - no hint that I needed the item and no sign that the other route was the correct one. Welcome to COC!
Add to these issues a waypoint saving feature that forces you to replay large sections when you die, unexpected game crashes and plenty of unavoidable "instant death" moments and you have a recipe for pain and frustration that will test your sanity more than your character's.
All this leaves you facing two major irritations. One is that you will simply become lost, not knowing where to go or what to do next, and wander aimlessly until you stumble on the way forward by chance. The second is that you will know what you need to do, but the game's poor control systems will not allow you to do it. For example, you may need to crawl under a broken fan with split-second timing that takes 7-8 attempts - and each attempt requires you to reload and replay through the entire previous area.
Bottom line: COC is not a diamond in the rough. It is a diamond in the septic tank, and I wish anyone who wants to try it the best of luck digging it out. If you are eager for the plot, watch a play-through on YouTube. Avoid this game at all costs.

Refunct is a calming, short gaming experience. The 3-D platforming and parkour elements are enjoyable, and there is a bit of strategy and puzzle solving to it, as you do need to think a little to make it from point A to point B. That being said, it's not at all difficult or overwhelming.
The graphics are lovely, with a soft color scheme, making it a welcome change from the neon, flashing, strobe effect in so many recent games. The soundtrack evolves with game progression and accompanies the scenery nicely.
Full controller support is offered, and the responsiveness of the controls is very good. The game itself is intuitive in the sense that it doesn't require a tutorial or complicated instruction to complete. The open world envirnonment includes being able to venture underwater, and the game can easily be completed in one sitting.
This is not a game with a high degree of replayability. However, I would recommend it to casual gamers looking for a relaxing or minimalistic game that can be completed in a short time. The game also offers easily attainable achievements, so this may very well be your next 100% game.

A diamond in the rough, Victor Vran offers everything an ARPG should: The combat is frantic and brutal with enemies abound that can make your life very short with poor preparation. The challenging combat paired with fluid player controls and mobility makes for a fun fast paced slasher that's even better with friends. The co-op is done well, allowling players to play with their friends as they tackle hordes of spiders, skeletons, dancing zombies and vampires.
The character customization, while very simple in its approach allows for a multitude of play styles and setups as your characters are outfitted with 2 weapons each with 3 skills, two individual demon powers that you can mix and match to compliment your weapons and playstyle and 5 (or 6, depending on your outfit) "Destiny Cards" that give you passive bonuses that will enhance your abilities as the difficulty climbs. It's definitely one of those "easy to pick up, difficult to master" kind of things, with dozens of cards to pick and choose from there's hours of theorycrafting available here for all the hardcore players.
With a safe dose of humor injected in for good measure, this game also sates my desire to laugh while I'm slaughtering my enemies.
The graphics and visuals are smooth, very artistic scenes and environments help bring the game together with an atmospherically dark sound track, 10/10 on the sound design.
While the story is somewhat short allowing probably only 5-6 hours of straight through gameplay, there is, however, the potential for dozens of hours of replayability. You can revisit maps to attempt challenges and find secrets hidden in every nook and cranny.
Overall, an easy 8.5/10. Definitely recommended, and even moreso on sale and with friends to play with.

There are 2 types of ARPG. One that requires many many hours of grinding items to min/max them and the other where you play a game once or twice and you have done it all.
Victor Vran is the later.
It's pretty unique ARPG. You can roll and jump and double jump from the walls. There is a pretty decent amount of verticality . You can rotate the camera (even tho I would still have prefered ISO over free camera - it's more annoying than helpful). Gear system feels fresh and quite to play with. I've read that's also good to play with a controller, but I'm a fan of "keyboard and mouse" so I played the game with this set.
There are no skills like in Diablo or Path of Exile or Grim Dawn, but every single item type has 2 individual skills. You can choose to play with sickle, sword, rapier, magic book, shotgun, lightning gun and grenade launcher + you can quickly switch between them for some pretty awesome combos. And that's not all. There are "Demon Powers" too which you have to charge by hitting monster. They can vary from offensive ones (meteors, earth tremors and so on) to defensive ones (hp regeneration, damage absorption, etc.) And when you play with this whole package the gameplay feels very fluid and fun and sometimes even challenging.
The one thing that kept me playing this game - the objectives. Victor Vran has many different areas that you can play in. Every area has 5 different objectives (kill x amount of monster with that type of gun or with demon power, or avoid taking damage while killing monsters and such). Those objectives reward you with xp or gold + you feel awesome when you complete them too ^^. If you fail one or two - you can just restart an area and try to complete those failed ones once again. Pretty simple. Most of the objectives are moderately easy, some are really annoying and some of them require to move your butt quickly because of the timer ^^.
Overall - it's a great simple ARPG, with good graphics, good voice acting, forgettable music and fun gameplay.

Having cut my teeth on hundreds and hundreds of hours of Heroes 3 and Heroes 5, I really wanted to like this one.  It looks great, no doubt, but I'm afraid the magic is gone.  Enemy AI cheats to a game-breaking extent, so the only way to really experience this properly is to only play with other people.  Unfortunately, that's not generally desirable or workable online, due to UPlay's instability and the general unreliability of anonymous players in general, and 1v1 hotseat (or the like) is itself pretty limited and unsatisfying.  I miss the days of playing cooperatively with one or two other human players against the AI.
The mechanics have also become problematically distorted, leading to too many unwinnable games where the growth of map creeps outpace your own troop production, or how suffering even incidental losses in too many map skirmishes can permanently doom your long-term war effort.  The idea of local forts/castles serving as the control point for local resource generators in the area was kind of nifty, and I could be okay with that depending on how it was implemented, but it feels too much like everything that formerly made this series great (particularly in HoMM3) has been gradually stretched, squashed, and otherwise mashed into some cheap imitation of its former glory.

Incase of TLDR: Game gets a 7/10
Combat's nice, enemies a'many, weapons a'ton, dastardly invaders, helpful phantoms, story's stale, graphics beautiful but slowly declining. A great game but has it's flaws. If you're planning on getting the game, be sceptic about full price but do a tiny leap when it's on sale. Like on the autumn sale when I wrote this review. Thank you, I'm gonna have a sandwich.
Foreword:
Another entry in the Souls series. Like it's predecessor, it's gonna whoop you, homefry. Dying, and psychologically yourself, will be your mentor in teaching you the dangers of the distant future land of Drangleic, said to be the same land as Lordran but with a couple of kingdoms rising and falling on the same oceanic rock in between.
Story: 5/10
So you're this traveler. Been through stuff. You're ragged, hollowed and somehow led to this portal-like water vortex. This leads you to Drangleic. It's never mentioned if this character of yours were from the times of Lordran or the likes and the vortex warped time or whatever. Now you have to, instead of linking the dying fire thus prolonging the age of fire, you must become the new undead monarch since the previous King Vendrick was tricked and f**ked up his kingdom, leading it to ruin by the giant dudes. You will must wander Drangleic, collect gear along the way as well as friendly/unfriendly faces. Either with a phantom friend or a bloody invader, you have your task before you to become the next monarch.
But you're probably gonna die and try again a couple of times.
The story itself is way too widely stretched. Sure the land of Drangleic has rich lore but I didn't recieve it too well and just focused on the gameplay. It felt generic and nothing emotional that made your neckhair stand or something. I think the DS1's story was better and I'm a twonk for thinking so, let's move on.
Graphics: 6/10
Sure you could call it stylized, but even if you drop the graphics to their bottom values, the game felt like a downward hill visually. As soon as you've punched your death-v-card, you've probably made it to Majula, the hub area. This area is, imo, the prettiest area in the game. And it slowly goes downhill from there.
Gameplay: 7/10
A third person hack-n-slash with your handsome self as the star of the flick. As with a revamped, shinier and smoother combat style of this new adaptation: you can slice, cut, stab, pierce, impale, backstab, swash, buckle, block, parry and all them there actions with a new array of weaponry as well as plenty of reused weapons from DS1.
The enemies however have have a new weapon up their sleeve however. Magnetic weapons. Many master strafers have fallen and more will along the way. Rolling aside, blocking or just striking first's gonna overshadow strafing in most situations. But aside from some insane magnetic enemies, the combat feels really nice.
Two new features include more potent hollowing. The more times you die without going human, your lifebar will slowly resemble being cursed in DS1 having it capped at half it's original value. The other feature is that you can only farm enemies so much now. Kill an enemy and reset the area enough times and the enemy stops spawning. Play around with burning stuff in your bonfire if you intend to prevent this.
The variety in enemies as well as weapons are great. Both in the aspect of quality and as a measurement. Find your pick, pick your foes and you can pick your noes before the day's over.
Oh. And uh. Get a controller. Really. Like DS1, the keyboard is for sadomasochists only.
Performance: 9/10
Forget about DSfix. With the required specs you're in for the smoothest souls adventure yet.
Oh yeah, it's SotFS so the game's prettier and revamped compared to the regular DS2.

A short, scary, and beautiful game. The first thing that struck me about this game is how good the visuals looked. The lighting looks better than most big titles today. The environment itself is really well done. The actual asylum has a realistic design that makes you feel like you're actually inside a real place. Most horror games have you going through hallways and rooms that don't make any design sense. Like most horror games lately, this game forces you to take a different approach to enemies, pure stealth. You can't fight back at all, the only thing you can do is sneak around the halls and hope you don't turn a corner into something scary. One really cool feature is the ability to lean and peak around corners. When facing a wall close to an edge, your character will place his hands on the wall realistically as if you're really carefully looking around the corner. It gives the game that much more depth. In addition to peaking and leaning, you're also given a camcorder with a night vision mode. This is probably the coolest part. You need to find batteries to keep the night vision mode on, and you have no hope of surviving without that night vision. Don't worry about the night vision being incredibly bright and make it less scary, this night vision is more realitic and has very limited range, so you'll only be able to see a few feet infront of you. The game took me around 3 hours to complete, which is great because it gives you the chance to sit down and play through the entire game without taking a break. Putting a horror game on pause can really pull you out of the experience and ruin the flow. Thankfully this game doesn't overstay its welcome and it makes for a really cool game. I hope we get more games as unique as this.

: In this game you ultimately sit and watch statistics of your food production and make adjustments accordingly. In the long run it just feels like you are trading on a stock market.
: The most similar games  to this one that I've played are Dwarf Fortress and Gnomoria. The thing that piqued my interest in this game was the serene looking gameplay, modding support and be able to build pretty villages :3.
Yes; the game felt relaxing at some times.
Yes; modding is awesome.
However, this doesn't help me from feeling that the core gameplay is lacking and even contrasting with the aesthetics of the game. You are constantly trying to make your village as efficient as possible and to expand it, carefully planning what buildings to place next. Although the graphics are decent and fits the game, the necessary placements of buildings and farms often makes the village look like crap. Furthermore, the placement and rotation of buildings are fixed by a static grid, making the villages look stale and industrialized (which they clearly aren't). The "prettyness" is damaged even further as everything is placed on the same altitude, flattening the ground beneath as you place your buildings.
Although the modding support at this stage seems promising, none of the mods that are currently out there add something more gameplay wise. During my playtime I couldn't feel that there was a endgame worth fighting for and that was ultimately the thing that put me off from continue playing.
: Music. Setting. Interface. Aesthetics. Modding support.
: No vareity in gameplay. Contrast between Aesthetics and gameplay. Lack of descriptions and information in-game.

This game has a long way to go before it surpasses the first Dungeon Defenders.
Now, with this being said I'm not going to say its a bad game, and that doubles for the fact that this game is pre-alpha. Something that I don't understand why people complain about. Pre-alpha means that there are so many more updates that they want to do, they aren't even considering launching the game as an alpha game yet. That just shows pure dedication, and show's exactly how far they are striving for this game to go.
So, let's start out with some of the positives----
Graphics. I play on low graphics for almost every game (What can I say, I really like seeing big numbers next to my fps, and I'm not exactly rich.) so graphics don't mean a whole lot to me, but when you look at the difference from the last game to this one? Just wow. It's so much better looking all around and that deserves at least some praise.
Upgrading Equipment. So, a lot of people will disagree with me here (See "Needing to use items and gold?? That's Dumb!" and so forth.) but I personally love this system, it makes so much more sense to pay someone to fuse other gear with your gear to make it more powerful, as opposed to just cramming some crystals into it and calling it a day.
Animation- Yeah, this applies to the tavern mostly. Upgrading and the like, some really nice looking animations for a game of this type.
Currency- There are three different types of currency in this game, a big upgrade from the last where you used gems for everything. There are blue gems, used as you'r character's mana to use your abilites. Green gems, used to build defenses, up and re them, so on and so forth, and finally gold. Which is used to buy/upgrade weapons. I think that is much better than just one currency to rule them all.
Noooow to the negative...
Matchmaking- This is posted in the to-do list for trendy, as anyone who reads their updates will see. But I cannot beg you enough to get that update live. Matchmaking is really hard on everyone, not just high or low levels, but everyone. I can almost never seem to find a group to play with.
Defending in Single Player- Towers took an arrow to the knee in this game. They are so nerfed that they can hardly stand their own without someone there to kill enemies at the same time they are. Towers just aren't strong enough to hold themselves up and if you are one person you can't be everywhere at once. So this can make single player really difficult
Javelins- Enemies that outrange your towers. Okay, I see what you wanted here trendy, you wanted to make the game more balanced so that people cant just set up towers and afk farm to their hearts content. And I praise you for that, that is not a bad idea... But once again, if you are in single player, or even if your allies don't see one of these guys? You can expect to lose. They will utterly dominate your towers since your towers have no hope of retaliation. It's a good idea trendy, but this just adds to the nerf that towers took, at this point it's just kinda adding insult to injury.
Resistances- Please, no. Just no. My squire has to use an ability that has a ten second cooldown just to deal normal amounts of damage to this enemy? This is like saying "PLAY MONK OR PLAY ONLINE". Sure you still deal damage to enemies that are resistant to your damage type, but it gets so annoying to watch the enemies just soak up the reduced damage and still deal their normal amount of damage to you.
My overall advice for this game, if you are looking for an awesome game that you want to play online, make some new friends or just bring your friends in to play with you. This is without a doubt a good game for you to play. If you are looking for some quality single player action, look elsewhere, this game will not do you well.
Keep up the great work nonetheless trendy, I love playing this game online so I plan on sticking around to see what you plan to do and how far this game makes it.

Some horror games stand above all others in delivering a polished, terrifying experience.  Call of Cthulhu: Dark Corners of the Earth...is NOT one of those games.  This game is the definition of a buggy, terrible, unintuitive nightmare.  You will be scared, but not because of the lovecraftian nightmares chasing you, but because of the crap game itself.
I picked this up on the recommendation of many people, who cited it's atmosphere and story as the selling points.  And, to be fair, the atmosphere is oppressive, nightmarish, and very unsettling, while the story is pretty decent, a nice introduction to lovecraft for those who haven't or don't want to read his writings, for whatever reason.
HOWEVER!  This game has far too many problems for anyone to want to play.  First the control scheme is terrible.  For an FPS it's decent enough, but the controls require you to be nose to nose with an item or enemy before you can use it or attack it.  Also, the game is built like an FPS, but in the first half of the game, you are completely weaponless and defenseless...not very smart.  Second, the game is incredibly unintuitive.  Almost nothing is explained in terms of gameplay and nothing that you need to do is made clear.  Passages to the next section are buried in crawlspaces or hidden so well that 30 minutes of searching is required to even dream of moving forward.  It feels like a point and click adventure that was badly shoved into an FPS.  The gunplay and healing is different, as the weapons are from the 1920s and require manual reloads, like the shot gun which can only fire two shots before being reloaded.  The healing happens in real time, so you have to plan the where and when to heal.  That would be fine, but you die so easily from even the most minor of wounds and the aiming is so awful that enemies will FREQUENTLY kill you.
And that's another thing.  The first time you try a section, your pulse will pound, your heart will race, and you'll feel really exhilirated because of how tense and scary it is.  The fifteenth time you try a section, you will want to scream at the screen for how buggy and unintuitive the section is.  The game loses its mystique of horror when you have to constantly reload saves to redo a section over and over again because of a mistake where you don't know what to do or don't know what you're doing wrong.  This game is so frustratingly unfun that I had to quite at one section where the glitches and poor game design just broke me.  One section of the game requires that you fire a cannon at 3 blue lights to trigger an event.  Problem.  There are NO BLUE LIGHTS.  The game's graphics are buggy and glitched so that sections like that are nigh on unplayable, and those are only for starters.  The platforming, yes there is platforming, is equally unplayable and unfun.
The only reason at all to play this would be for the story, and for that, you can go to the youtubes.  Greatest horror game of all time my butt.  This game is a buggy mess.  Cthulhu and Lovecraft deserve better.  Stay far away from this piece of gargabe.

Hearts of Iron III, in general, more of a wargame than a grand strategy game, and it is EXTREMELY HARD to get into, even for a grand strategy game, for a few main reasons:
1. The Order of Battle (OOB) system. It is very intimidating, and it's not unusual for you to spend half an hour or more organizing your army.
2. Poor UI. The UI for Hearts of Iron III is quite far from perfect, an example being there being a ton of mapmodes, with few even being useful, and a lack of shortcuts.
3. Relatively railroaded gameplay. Bringing up my wargame point from earlier, Hearts of Iron III has few sandbox elements outside of your country, and becomes extremely predictable very quickly, following the order on how the war begins, and the same people joining the same teams every time without player influence.
4. Terrible tutorial. The in-game "tutorial" is basically ignorable and a complete waste of time that teaches you very little about the game; you're better off just watching a few YouTube videos as a new player.
With it being an old game, there's also quite a few bugs. You will probably experience crashes, freezes, and other game-breaking bugs. On top of this, the AI is also very poor; once you develop basics for the game, you can basically just beat all of the AI.
Because of all of this, I do not recommend this game, since it's just too hard to get into, and requires you to devote long amounts of time into learning the game. However, if devoting a lot of time and doing military roleplay is more of your thing, then you might enjoy this game, provided you don't experience too many crashes.

Thought this game would be similar to Van Helsing, well its not.
Quests are alot easier, you dont have to look around the whole map to finish it. Every quest is bound to a specfic dungeoun, and is not hard to understand.
Typical quests:
Kill 10 monsters of certain type within 4min
Kill 10 monsters with a specfic weapon
kill 10 monsters with a specfic hex active
find 5 hidden chests
dont take damage or use potions
and if you fail one of these quests, you can either start again by exiting the dungeon and re-enter, if you have completed some quests you dont have to do that one again. Or you can just leave that quest alone, its not like you have to do it, but all those quests have rewards of some kind.
Hexes:
These are negtive traits in a sense, game gets harder when you active them, but they also give you better loot and xp, so you can adjust the game to get harder if you whish. Some quests require you to activate specfic hexes.
Movement:
This is new for me to see in a arpg game, you can jump, even jump against a wall, and when you hit wall you can jump again. Also you can dodge sideways, backwards or forward.
Skills:
Each weapon has 4 diffrent skills, and theres a lot of diffrent weapons to chose from. not all are good, but some quests requires you to use a specfic weapon. Also you can set up 2 charged skills, these comes in form of a gem, and charges while you hit enemy, most of those gems have interesting effects, ex. rain of fireballs. And there are potions, like healing potions, firebombs and more.
Traits:
These are actually cards you slot, and cards are loot and rewards, can also be bought from merchants. Slots for cards unlock as you level.
There are no classes, but there are diffrent types of armor that will boost something, personally i prefer the one that increases critical damage, but has low protection. You can get a "normal" armor too, but it only protects you, dont have any special effect, the other armors has low or no protection.
Oh, you have endless space in your inventory, have a storage space in the city, also endless space. Auto-sort buttons are there.
Conclusion; if you like arpg games that has alot of details, and your the kind of gamer that like to go slow and explore every little secret in games, then this would a good game for you. Personally i love it, havnt played alot, and i hear it gets quite alot harder in the end of the game. But im now playing the game on normal with all hexes active, and ive played alot of arpg games before, so im looking forward to it.

This was the biggest letdown of it's year. I expected a great new arc in the genre.
But it's failed in so many ways, some up to personal opinion others less so. My opinion is based off of a comparison between this game and the games before it, Heroes III and V especially.
The first and the defining failure in this game is the lackluster abilities and function of the heroes. In it's predecessors Heroes III and V, they could gain great power and spells that both were and felt awesome, as well as unique for their factions and style.
Now, their abilities are all the same in the TWO different classes, and you'd be hard pressed to find any real difference between one hero and the next. They're called "Heroes" of Might and Magic, not Peasants of punches and fairy dust. Half the fun of the previous games was customizing a build with different schools of magic, but when all spells are "balanced" and every hero has the same there's no difference.
The game was littered with bugs upon it's release, since then it may have received updates that have fixed them.
There are only four resources. Once again, diversity and resource mechanics are taken out only to be replaced by a bland "everyone uses the same" resource called gold, wood stone and "crystals". Apparently, having different resources for different things is too hard.
As for personal opinions which is a matter that must be taken with a grain of salt:
The game seems very balanced to the point where similarities between the factions become too strong, and once again the diversity and innovation of the game is lost.
The gameplay is decent, although occasionally slightly sluggish.
Story's good, although very long. But that wouldn't be a complaint if one likes the game.
Heroes VI is terrible because it has taken exactly what was fun about it's predecessors, the customization of Heroes and gaining immense powerful units, and made them all the same, fair, balanced and utterly boring.

Stay clear!! If you own the original Escape Goat, don´t buy this. If you don´t own the original, buy that instead of this downgrade.
By all means an inferior game than the original Escape Goat, which i absolutely adored. From what i can concern, there is absolutely no new features what so ever. Calling it a sequel is actually misleading, since it´s the exact same game but with LESS content. You read that part correctly, Escape Goat 2 is LESS of a game than it´s predecessor. Why? Because the developer (s) removed the Level Editor! The original boasted an easy to use, yet extremely powerful level editor that allowed you to create anything the original campaign could offer. You could even create your own campaign by chaining the levels together. Escape Goat 2 have no level editor what so ever.
That´s right, they removed the ONE feature that allowed a wonderful community to grow up around this game. Maybe they realised that a level editor would make any DLC obsolete. Worse yet, well no not worse, the omission of the level editor is the main offender, but the new graphics aren´t really up to snuff.
The original had pixel perfect, atmospheric and gorgeous sprite art. The sequel is still made out of sprites, but it is all convoluted in an unnecessary comic look. The original had a sense of mystique, an omnious almost gothic vibe. This game looks like your random, kid friendly iOS game. To add insult to injury, the lightning effects obscures the playing field. It´s not always clear what is what, and while it certainly ain´t no big problem, the new graphics diminished the enjoyment of the game, at least in my case. It´s also unnecessary demanding! The first game i could run on my MacAir with perfect framerate and hardly any CPU usage. This game chugs even at the lowest graphics setting, and is setting my fan on fire.
So there you go. Take a game with a wonderful premise, because the basic gameplay behind Escape Goat is truly amazing, disguise it in less beautiful and more demanding graphics. Remove half of the content. (One could argue the level editor was more than half really), and up the price. And there you have it folks. Escape Goat 2.

This game has a great sense of atmosphere that really captures the sanity-shattering cosmic horror of Lovecraft's writings, and of the Call of Cthulhu paper-and-pencil RPG.
The story itself does a good job of using Lovecraft's original stories, combining and expanding on his works. It's not a typical FPS that solely focuses on killing lots of enemies. You don't even get a weapon until quite a while through the game!  The latter acts become more heavily combat-oriented, but the focus is always on the narrative. The play experience is pretty linear, but it still manages to create the sense of exploration, mystery, terror, and fun of the old-school RPG--and the immersive atmosphere (e.g. no HUD, storytelling journal entries, puzzles that require talking to NPCs and checking notes to solve, sanity effects that alter your character's perceptions of reality, occasional insane muttering from the protagonist) really makes this game shine.
There are some bugs in the retail release, but don't let that turn you off of this purchase. There are community-made patches that fix the game-breaking bugs, and also let you tweak and enhance the gameplay. If you're a fan of the Cthulhu mythos or of survival horror in general, I would highly recommend this game.

Nep-nep is back and this time with more characters than ever! Overall this iteration of the anime JRPG is the best for me so far. The story takes you on a fun ride with lively characters and great humor, without jeopardizing the integrity of the overarching plot.
1. The characters get a lot more action in this game compared to previews iterations, with more dialogue even for the side characters. Plutia as a new characters really brings another dimension to the whole trope theme, and, although unfamiliar at first, quickly became one of my favourites of the series. Even the bad guys seems a lot more real compared to the typical conquer the world villain, and all of them are redeemed in the end.
2. The UI is improved greatly, with a whole new menu, great new battle UI, and separate maps for the different nations. Access to an improved Stella's Dungeon early in the game really helps with collecting materials and completing plans.
3. A lot more dungeons this time around, together with an improved Stella's Dungeon, make completing plans a lot less tedius. The new change dungeon plans also provides an access to challenging bosses a lot early in the game.
Overall this game is a really fun ride, and I recommend it to anyone who is a lover of JRPG and anime games. Definitely check out Re;Birth 1 too, as it establishes the characters and makes this game a lot more enjoyable. If you haven't played the previews games, this game is not completely unrelatable for new players too.

I absolutely loved Escape Goat, and I am happy to see more of it now. Escape Goat 2 is basically more of the same, which is not a bad thing. It offers a nice balance of platforming and solving intelligent puzzles. The controls and mechanics are just great. Really nothing to complain about here.
The difficulty is very low in the first few levels and always gets a little higher from level to level. Nobody should have any problems getting into the game. And yet it is quite challenging later on. Escape Goat 1 offered some high difficulty levels after beating the campaign. I expect the successor to offer the same (I didn't beat it yet, so I just can assume it will).
The main difference to the first part is the graphics style. Instead of the basic pixel art we got in Escape Goat 1, this game now uses a new high definition graphics style, which many people will like. I personally prefer the old art style, but I am fine with either of them. The most important thing for me is, that the controls didn't change at all. Despite the new graphics the game feels absolutely like the first part. Not all games manage to do that.
I like it a lot. Both Escape Goat games are real indie gems. You will enjoy your time.

DISCLAIMER: I recommend the game, but do NOT get this version.
So, long story short, I think that this game is really good if you're able to look past the fact that it's a bit dated (I think it shows more age than games that were actually released before it). However, the biggest issue is that this Steam version is terrible.
I played the game when it first came out and loved it, never had issues with it. Then I bought this Steam version to experience it again. But things are broken in that the game crashes at just about every corner, lags without FPS drop (and it lags WITH an FPS drop--two different symptoms) despite being such an old game, and drops sound occasionally.
I've tried patching the game but to no avail. So, I'm incredibly irritated at the moment, as I'm currently only like 1.5 hours into the game really (despite having played for like 4) and currently my game keeps crashing and exiting when I'm trying to finish a level. Each time I walk through a doorway, the executable crashes.
The game itself is good in that it is atmospheric. There's no HUD (and to my memory, it was one of the earlier games of this type to ditch the HUD) and tries to really draw you in. And you don't really get weapons for a good while, so you're mostly meant to sneak and be afraid. Your character can go insane too, so it makes things even more difficult but also fun. Plus, I like Lovecraft.
Anyway, the game is good but dated. If you're going to give it a try, however, do not get this version. Look for it elsewhere.

Napoleon was done brilliantly.
The land battles are a major upgrade from Empire. That I could coordinate my line, light, and grenadier units and position them in accordance to the terrain as opposed see that they have guns was nice. Oh, and Horse Artillery units are a blast when they zip all over the battlefield. In comparison, Empire felt like an add-on to the end of Medieval II when you start mass-producing gun units. With Napoleon, I felt like my understanding of battle tacics was actually important and being tested as opposed to simply trying to outnumber my opponents.
The naval battles at least ran smoother, a bonus for me since I like the novelty of them early on. A lot of my friends say it's just another thing to autoresolve, but I like finally having the ability to coordinate my outnumbered and outgunned fleets into capturing massive enemy vessels.
There aren't nearly as many options in the campaign, but I'll live with that. I played the Great Britain and Prussia campaign's and neither was overly disappointing. One of the things I didn't like about Prussia though is that you should have the power to join the Coalition or ally with Napoleon, but the game steers you against France the entire time. C'est la vie.
Now, Napoleon's mini-campaigns and the like were where the real brilliance of the game shows itself. You play through his conquests of Italy and then Egypt much in the style of Medieval II's Kingdoms expansion, where it's only in one theatre of Europe itself. Egypt got surprisingly tough early on; I had to settle for wiping out the Mamelukes instead of taking only what I need in order to get the Bedouin raiders to leave me alone, and I never did take the deserts from them. After those, you go to the traditional map for taking on Europe as a whole. It was difficult, but not impossible, and I enjoyed my series of battles with Wellington.
However, the best part is the very end. After that, you need to play the battle of Waterloo. I sat down, cracked my knuckles, and thought long and hard about what I should do. I know my history and why Napoleon failed, as well as his opening moves that carried into his defeat. I tried 300 different strategies. I set it on easy. I lured Wellington into the plain and smashed him to pieces in time for the Prussians to attack me from behind. I waited for the Prussians to arrive and wiped them out first. Every different move I could make, I made it. And I lost. Every. Single. Time.
The game is about Napoleon, about one man and how in both victory and defeat he changed the course of history, and it grants you the power to be him. It wasn't until I lost for the 300th time at Waterloo when I released something; I was thinking the way he did. The game and my past victories conditioned me into believing that not only was a better general than Wellington (and a computer-generated one at that), but that my knowledge of Napoleon's own defeat meant I wouldn't make his mistake. And in doing so, I walked right into his greatest failing, being blinded by my pride and thinking I would win. I've never had a game deliver that specific brand of experience before, and it was incredible. Props to The Creative Assembly for that.
Overall, I give it a 9.8/10. My only complaint is that certain generals like Napoleon and Wellington are unkillable in the campaigns. I get that it's supposed to emulate history more than any other of the series, but I'd have liked to be able to change the details. It's one thing to send Napoleon packing back to Paris, it's annoying to have to fight him for every single inch every turn or so.
Also, I had no internet access at the time of playing this, so don't be decieved by my hours of game time.
I hope that in the near future I can get the Peninsular Campaign and other add-ons to continue the experience.

Let me give you the TL;DR right now. Worst game ever.
I played a single race (yes I made it that far, so I earned the right to judge the game). I immediately remembered a really funny parody of the FPS games of that era. Duty Calls. Now for those who aren't familiar with this name, let me describe it briefly. Duty Calls is a parody of many FPS games, based on Call of Duty franchise. It was made as an advertisement for Bulletstorm, whose trailer played at the end of this mocking game, with the message being "nowadays FPS are like the one you just played, here is what it is supposed to be like (Bulletstorm trailer begins)". Flatout 3 felt exactly like that. "Here is a crappy racing game to depict everything wrong with racing games today, and now, real Flatout 3 begins where you get to have super fun just like you had in the previous games, even ultimate carnage, which was basically flatout 2 re-sold to you suckers, but turned out to be pretty good anyway". Disappointment begins... It was no joke, no "real" Flatout 3 started. Flatout 3 really is the horrible.... ummm..... I can't really say that it's a game.... It's...... a software...... where you control...... no not control........ more like........ watch a car that was based on the drawings of a drunk newborn...... cruise in a city designed by a band of autistic apes...... and think that you contribute to its behaviour by pressing certain buttons on the controller.
Ok jokes aside. Graphics are extremely unfinished. Simple and undetailed, but not intentionally, just due to lack of skill and/or effort. Just look at the screenshots. At the first glance they look pretty decent. Now look closer. Inspect details. Don't tell me it's a 2011 game. Compare it to DiRT or just Flatout UC. You will see it has horrible graphics.
Controls just don't matter. You don't feel in control of the vehicle, not even a little bit. The car just goes vroom vroom. No realism, no control, no fun. For those who will bash me for looking for realism, just go play the previous games. You will see what I mean. Junker cars used to slide, drift, bump, etc. Now they just perfectly hover over the asphalt. When you try to turn, it either doesn't turn enough (if you're too fast), or turns successfully (if you're slow enough). It doesn't drift, slide unless you pull the handbrake. But if you use nitro when your car is aligned with the road, it just immediately and magically stops sliding and continues it's hovering over the road. Here is a short list of games that offer a better and more realistic driving experience: Asphalt 8 (iOS and Android), The Need for Speed (1994), FIFA '96. Also, I'm using a Logitech F710. When I set the controls to the gamepad, it stops working. If I set them to keyboard I can use my gamepad with xinput mode. ♥♥♥♥ logic!
Sounds. There are 4 sounds in total. One of them is the menu sound "click". Three in game sounds are "vroom", "bfffttt", and "dufff". Now "vroom" is the engine sound made by the cars engines. The sound was produced by a pair of bored game devs, that just made the sound with their mouth. I can almost hear one of them saying "screw the consumers, they will buy our games anyway", in the middle of the sound recording session, faintly hidden behind the sound of the engine. "bfffttt" is the sound nitrous makes, and the artistic creation of this amazing sound was most likely based on an air refresher spray. "dufff" is the collision sound used in every single collision to every single combination of objects. Again, it was probably made by devs dropping a heavy pillow from a distance.
Music. Literally non-existent.
Car tuning. Do you remember the simple, yet fun car modification system Flatout used to offer? It's gone. Here is the new system. "Would you like to tune the car?" [Yes/No]. If you choose yes, then the car is "tuned" by standards seen fit by the devs. I swear to god, I am laughing at the stupidity of this, as I'm writing, while crying on the inside because it isn't even slightly exaggerated. Ladies and gentlemen, a new era of modification begins where cars are either "tuned" or "aren't".
Please just watch a single gameplay footage from any source. Even the official game trailers give you an idea of how ridiculous this game is. Don't take any of my word for it. Just look it up on youtube yourself. Watch some videos and see for yourself that every single sentence you read here, is describing that video.

I haven’t played the original version of DS2 but, having played and loved DS1 i can say that this game didn’t disappoint. That said, this is not exactly the same as ds1 in terms of some mechanics that you’ll need to get used to. The online presence of this game is still decent and you’ll be able to invade and co-op without too much trouble for most of the game if you don’t farm too much.
I’ll list below some major changes of this game and what i think of them.
It’s a hard action gdr in which you’ll need to learn your attack patterns and enemies attack patterns in order to be able to progress, while it might be very hard at first i think that the beginning of the game (mainly forest of the fallen giants ambushes and ruin sentinels) is the only major difficulty spike of the game, while the rest of the game is more linear in terms of difficulty. You can also play with a friend, with some restrictions, if the game gets too hard and while some boss battles become way too easy this way, others become really fun.
While the pace and action feels slower (stamina recovers slower, for example) than the first game this is not a bad thing, and once you get used to it it won’t be a problem at all.
In this game you can be invaded even in hollow form, but each time you die you lose a part of your max hp until you use a human effigy (this game humanities), this change  is not welcome by many players, I think the base idea was to punish players for being reckless, i personally didn’t like it but after some time playing it became just a minor nuisance than a real pain to deal with.
is a new addition and it works for multiplayer, it keeps track of every soul you get and in multiplayer you will get paired up with players with a sm similar to yours, this means that actual character level has no effect and it’s very hard to manage. You will need a special ring that prevents your sm growth by taking away every soul you get in order to be able to get paired up with player in early-midgame zones. I think this was made to prevent high experienced players invading newbies at the start of the game but is overall the worst change in the game in my opinion.
What is the best thing that this game offers? the answer for me is
. There are a lot of different weapons (even if many share the same moveset) and armors, 4 types of magic and 9 different infusion types for weapons and shields and this, paired up with the ability to respec your character, offers a lot of possibilities for viable and fun builds.
are, in my opinion, the best element of the game; they allow you to respawn a boss and upgrade the area near the bonfire they are used in into ng+ difficulty, allowing you to get access early to many new ng+ items that drop from bosses or from particular invaders/non respawning enemies, or simply to farm more souls.
After you kill enemies many times they’ll stop respawning, this is another change that many people hated. I have to say that I think this helps new players a lot especially early game when they are trying to figure out how to beat certain bosses and they keep dying because they simply can’t reach the boss without being hit by generic mobs and the healing items are scarce. If you wish to farm mobs however, you simply need to join a specific covenant that will prevent mobs from despawning.
Compared to ds1
is a lot less interconnected and the world feels less desolated, the plot also is radically different with the monarch succession theme as its core, if you care about the lore I think you’ll like this, especially the awesome dlc already included in the game.
is simply better than ds1 in every way, with more covenants and less lag. I have to say that even when i was starting to learn the game and i got invaded I felt like i had a chance to win even when i got defeated, a feeling that in ds1 simply isn’t there until your build is ready for pvp, in ds2 it’s more difficult to parry and to backstab.

This is a long one bois so bear with me.
Dark Souls 2 is the most "unique" when it comes to the DS trilogy, this is no wonder, because it was developed by a different team instead of Hidetaka Miyazaki. Because of this differences, a lot of people dislike the game, but most just hate it because new peoplehave bandwagoned the hate train, of course this has affected the game.
But despite all this, Dark Souls 2 (both versions) has better mechanics than 1 and 3, (in some ways not all) it lets the player have more freedom of creating builds for all playstyles, and of course, powerstancing. But Dark Souls 2 should NOT be your first dark souls game because of some complex and unnecessary systems (looking at you soul memory).
The better mechanics are mostly on movement like sprinting, rolling and jumping, they are vastly different from 1 and 3 but once you know how they work, movement and battles will be easier and be more thoughtful since you dont have a lot of stamina.
The build variety i mentioned is ver self explanatory, while there IS a meta that tryhards use in the arena, there is not much of them these days. In this game even greatshields can serve as powerful and capable weapons, you can also infuse staffs and bows for even more variety, theres a lot of different catalysts, even some shields server as catlysts and this gives them some very good damage, and Dark Souls 2 has A LOT of weapons, more than 1 or 3.
And lastly powerstancing, in its most simple explanation, its the ability to dual wield different weapons and getting a unique moveset with them. This mechanic also helps with build variety.
Now lets adress one of the many issues with the game. First of all, the story, Dark Souls 2 story is bad, and sometimes the lore just doesnt make sense or isnt developed like 1 or even 3 did, with the player not caring much for breaking the curse, the only factor for me to care for the story was the Emerald Herald, since you level up with her you hear from her a lot, but overall not great lore and a bad story.
Next issue that is also tied with the story is on how the game wants you how hard it is, with most characters saying how you're gonna die over and over again, making the player feel like the focus is on them, one reason why dark souls 1 story is praised because the world makes the player feel insignificant, it lets the player know that even if theyre gone, nothing changes.
And lastly soul memory, unless you look on the 'help' menu (not sure if even that tells you what SM does/is) on your first playthrough, you ignored completely how and what soul memory is, in short its all the souls you ever had, and this affects summoning and invading, to a new player wanting to play with friends may have issues if he/she doesnt know about the engraved ring, although this helps with less twinks and overleveled people (unless they hack) but this good thing doesnt cover that they didnt teach the player how it works.
Conclusion: Dark Souls 2 is a good game, very fun to play PvE or PvP but not remembered for story and lore and not so beginner friendly (for a souls game). If you have played any souls game I recommend this game but if this is your first option, I insist for you to play 1 or 3 first.
Now I know I didnt cover EVERYTHING, simply because there is too much to cover and i cant remember everything, I just covered the basics and explaining why this game gets hate.
Thank you for your time. :)
