Written review below:
Q1: What is Escape Goat 2?
Escape Goat 2 is a puzzle platformer by the indie development studio Magical Time Bean.
Q2:What is the main draw of the game?
In this game you play as a purple goat who must escape a fortress by unlocking and exiting through the door in each room. Along the way you meet various friends like a mouse, who travels along with you and is a crucial part of gameplay, as well as sheep, who have gotten lost in the fortress and need to be rescued.
Q2.5: What is the gameplay like?/Is it fun?
The gameplay of Escape Goat 2 is phenomenal, calling upon both your reflexes and problem solving skills. The controls are fairly simple: the goat can jump, double jump, and dash. Dashing is used to break boxes or push blocks, or simply as a quick traversal technique. But what really makes the gameplay shine is the mouse character. When you release the mouse, either by throwing it upward or in front of you, he sticks to the wall and climbs around the walls until you call him back. This is incredibly useful for hitting switches that are out of reach or for baiting enemies. The enemies also play a large part in the puzzle solving, the most common enemy type throwing fire at the goat or mouse when they see them, which can be either a hazard or a tool to open new pathways. But the main new gameplay feature of Escape Goat 2 in comparison to its predecessor is that you can obtain various powers for your mouse. I don’t want to spoil all the powers, but the first one you’ll encounter is the Magic Hat, which allows the goat and mouse to switch places. In addition to being able to access areas which are too small to enter as a goat or have been closed off by the fortress’s mechanisms, you can also destroy enemies or boxes in a line between the goat and mouse as they swap places. And that’s just the beginning of the puzzling possibilities. Escape Goat 2 is a game that encourages experimentation, giving only the bare minimum of tutorials; that is, at various points in the levels it suggests you press a button and then you just see what happens. Everything else is left up to your skill as a gamer. It’s rare that there’s only one way to solve any given puzzle, and that freedom is very refreshing, if sometimes a bit frustrating until you figure out what to do. But those are some of the best moments in gaming.
Q3: What is the graphical style/presentation like?
The graphics of Escape Goat 2 are great. When compared to the original Escape Goat, they’re on a whole new level, going from rough pixel art to hand-illustrated art. The graphics are fairly standard as far as modern 2D platformers go, but the characters are very smoothly animated and a lot of detail was put into the mechanisms and gears in the fortress. Each zone in the fortress has its own unique visual identity as well, from the Woods of Duplicity to the Halls of Gleaming Crystal. The entire game somehow manages to give off a “mysterious” vibe. The music in the game is also appropriately atmospheric for each zone, and it’s pretty catchy too.
Q4: What control methods does it allow?
The game can be controlled with either an Xbox 360 controller, which is the recommended control method, or with the keyboard. I didn’t get the chance to try it with a controller, but the keyboard was definitely usable enough with the default settings, and the keys are fully remappable, so that’s really all I can ask for.
Q5: What kind of replayability does the game offer?
I beat the main game, that is, escaped the fortress, in just over 2 hours. However, that was after only discovering 45.45% of the rooms, or so the results screen told me. Any level in the game can be replayed via the map system, and extensions to each zone are unlocked as you progress through the game. And boy, are these extra levels tough! I haven’t been able to beat all of them yet, but I can already tell that all of you puzzle-platformer fanatics are in for a treat!
In addition, a level editor will be added post-launch, with which you can create and share your own levels, for potentially infinite replayability.
Q6: Is the game worth a purchase?
If you’re a fan of platforming and puzzles, and you’re not afraid of a challenge, I highly recommend you pick up this game. It’s available on Windows, Mac, and Linux on Steam, Good Old Games, and The Humble Store.

I found the first game to be fun but felt like the main campaign was over as it was just getting good. This game isn't baaaa--ad at all. Yes, I went there.
Escape Goat 2 has quite a bit more to offer. The story is richer (especially for a puzzle game), the gameplay is a lot more varied, and the puzzles offer even more profound "Ah ha!" moments than the first game.
The system for moving between levels is much better this time around. If you get stuck you can easily pull up the new overworld map system and go back to any other puzzle--no more need to start rooms over at the first puzzle just to get to that fifth puzzle again.
Regarding story, the original Escape Goat didn't have much--which was part of its appeal. You won't find anything too deep here but there is more this time around. If you talk to all of the animals you'll get quite a bit more backstory and world history. I found myself feeling excited to beat the next section of levels so that I could see what would happen next; the game did a good job at keeping me coming back for more.
The art is fantastic, I enjoy the attention to detail and the new lighting engine adds a lot of depth to the feeling of the game. The soundtrack is great too; I didn't find any of the tracks to be repetitive and didn't feel the need to use my own music while playing the game.
The original Escape Goat had a few secrets. This game has so much more to offer. I was floored the first time I discovered a secret room. The mechanics for getting into that particular secret room were so clever. I don’t want to spoil any of the fun though, so I’ll leave it at that.

Re;birth3. Wew. This was a fun experience. Introduced another new dimension (The Ultradimension) 2 new waifus (Peashy and Plutia) and a ton of new things to do. Let me begin on the improvements from the last 2 games
1. The menus now looks more vibrant and better to look at. The old one was fairly bland and not much, but this one now looks stunning and nice too look at every time.
2. They removed the search system (couldn't use that at all without a plan) into a hidden block type deal where the blocks are fairly easy to find but could be missed in a quick glance
3. Stella's Dungeon has been improved a ton, now including a partnering system
4. THE END GAME DOES NOT MEAN YOU RESTART. FINALLY. There are multiple after-game things you can do, like fight bosses and such.
5. Nep-TV. Adds a bit more depth and connection to the games in my own opinion.
6. The map system is now divided up into sections (You have to go into a world map then choose, for example, Planeptune, just to enter an area).
7. It's not as much of a grind to finish the game.
Also, unlike Re;Birth2, this game actually has a good story that isn't 100% doom, gloom, and all serious. Plutia being my favourite character for how many times she makes situations better by doing horrible things. Nepgear also gets an improvement, seeming to be more of a comic relief type character and not the serious younger sister as before. Neptune may be a bit more mean spirited in a way, and even was lazy to do some fairly important and life threatening things, but I didn't note it and forgot about it.
All in all, this game is how the original Neptunia 3 helped the series. Made improvements on things that needed fixing, and overall was good. One of my fav J-RPGs of all time, and I will soon not forget this journey. Well, depending on how Megadimension treats me.

This is the third subjective, unbiased and totally unfunny review yet again but for HyperD Nep VGen. Nothing has changed. It’s still a JRPG trough and trough. For the third time you play teenager girls having an adventure by visiting dungeons, fighting monsters while they attempt to break the 4th wall to make fun of popculture and videogames.
And this time the writing is back to form. The girls take nothing serious and get sidetracked a lot by talking nonsense even in front of impending doom. And It’s gloriously entertaining! Some of the situations the girls find themselves in are so hilariously stupid that they become good again.

The same gameplay pattern too? Yes! Follow the story as visual novel, go to dungeon, fight monsters, beat boss, continue, Repeat! New is that instead of a single overhead worldmap, the world is separated into small subscreens. Some of them get unlocked by going into a dungeon from one side and leaving trough the other. Clever!
Stella’s Dungeon, the spelunker mini game, is also back. And unlike the previous version (which forced me to not 100% the last game) it’s fast, more complex, yet simplified. There is still a gigantic amount of items to craft, to loot and use but it won’t bulldozer over you because the devs finally added a feature to check which monster, in which dungeon drops which item: Making the constant alt-tabbing to a browser window to check the games wikipedia obsolete.
The combat system got changed a tiny bit as well. You can’t spam superattacks anymore, cuz actionpoints don’t automatically refill when leaving a dungeon. Actionpoints need to be gathered by attacking monsters with rush attacks. Makes the combat much more challenging. But overall it stays the exact same. Yay for animation-skip-button!
Shares of the nations no longer come into play to progress the story. The 3 possible endings will be triggered by watching optional VN-events. There is more details to it, but please check one of the dozens guides that explain how to get the endings. Thanks!
The humour is marvelous, all characters loveable, all essential DLC’s are already integrated into the game without any additional purchase. This is the game Rebirth 1+2 should’ve ben from begin with. Without second thought, I recommend V Generation to those that like the prequels or JRPG's in general.

Alright: Call of Cthulhu: Dark Coners of the Earth.
In itself it is a pretty good game. It's creepy in parts (not very scary, but a tad creepy), good atmosphere
good soundtrack, story is alright but nothing too fancy.
However... The game is starting to get a bit old, so graphics aren't exactly phenomenal. There will probably not be too much you haven't seen before as well. It suffers from a slow build-up into the story and that is great - sometimes. I actually got pretty bored before I started enjoying it. With this comes danger of quitting before the game starts to get better. The guns feels abit awkward and unnatural to me, people complain about ammunition being scarce, but when I played on medium difficulty I never REALLY had any ammo-emergency. Maybe 1-2 times.
The dialoge is decent, but the voice-acting is just downright BAD, especially the guy YOU'RE playing as, of course. A few of the creepy guys you meet early on does some alright voice-acting, but on the most hand, it's rather bad.
But at least I suffer from a great deal of dialogue-cuts. Like, the audiofile stops playing 2 seconds before the sentence is finished at times. Not always. Thank God (...or Cthulhu?) for subtitles!
This game also suffers from a lot of glitches and bugs. Most of them you don't really notice, but some of them actually makes it almost impossible to get further into the game! ...at least without cheating. And that's pretty EFFIN' annoying.
Game crashes. ALOT. So do yourself a favour and save often.
It terms of gameplay itself, the controls are OK when you set the keys for your personal preferrence (Default you move with WAXD and S is "Use", like wtf?). You hide alot, but you have the option to fight as well. You get a variety of different weapons throughout the game, but they all feel a bit weird as mentioned before.
There are puzzle upon puzzle as you progress through the game, and most of them are pretty neat and makes sense, others just suffers from glitches. F.ex when a diary says that you start turning the thingy clockwise first on the safe when cracking the code, and it in reality must start counterclockwise... C'mon...Other puzzles are just a pain to do. That's life.
So all in all:
Audio: 3. Varied level of voice-acting talent, breaks mid-sentence, but other effects are up to standards
Music: 7. The soundtrack is good.
Plot: 5. It's OK, maintains a certain string to the Cthulhu-lore of H.P. Lovecraft.
Atmosphere: 6. It's good, but not superb.
Gameplay: 4. Clumsy but workable controls, weapon-awkwardness and BUGS! Good variety between hiding and shooting.
Overall: 4. The glitches is what really ruins the game for me. That and all the sudden crashes and other unpleasantries. If they'd spent more time fixing the tiny flaws and details and not making the game so damned long, they'd end up with a much better gaming-experience for the consumer.
I also should mention that I still haven't completed the game. (8hrs ingame at the moment of writing)

This is a hard call between recommending or not, but at the end I think it is worth the money if you find a good discount.
To make it easier I split the review in pro and against.
Pro:
This is very much like the original games, the ones that got very popular, with the addition of a relevant achievement system.
There is this extra layer to the game where you create your heroes and give them the habilities, and as you play you do not only level in game but you also level your profile and acquire in game coins. This profile leveling allows you to expand the set of options for your heroe and the coins to acquire more habilities and other stuff for your set.
It's interesting and fun developing your profile as if it as an in game character, and it gives extra game hours.
The game itself is pretty much like the series, you have castles, armies, heroes and resources and you are in a row for conquering it all. The AI is decent enough, the creatures have a nice variation of habilities and magic is interesting although narrow.
If you like the series, this is a good call. I personally didn't like the Heroes V, but this one I did. There's plenty hours of game in.
Against:
Ubisoft have been showing a tendency to shady business in recent developments, and this seems pretty much it.
The games have loads of bugs that will probably never be fixed, it crashes, hangs, etc. also the Uplay is mandatory for this game, but there are bugs syncronising content making the loading a pain. Almost every time I open the game I have to wait for a long attempt to syncronise content with their server, eventually it fails for time out, and only then I can play.
Another hint that Ubisoft do not really care much for fair play is that this is not a full version. You'll not find the Dungeon available, the only way to get this is to buy another fully independent game by a price way above a game pack. I'm also not sure if this is the only thing missing as I originally bought two game packs along with this because of a sale.
Bugs and shady business aside there's one more annoyance, if you are a fan of multiplayer or stand alone, to take the most of the game you'll have to at least play one campaing with your favourite race, aside the introductory campaing. This is the only way to unlock some special items that will be attached to your account.
The introdutoring campain is boring like hell but is "short", the race campain I can only tell about the Undead which is not bad.
All in all, there's no other game like this. Falling Enchantress gets close to beat Heroes, but it misses some fundamental stuff. Others are too simple to be interesting for long... so in my opinion this is worth for the simple reason that there's no competitors for this game style, specially if you want to play with friends.
If you are looking at games at random and not after this game style in specific, then stay away.

Awful in every sense of the word, ESPECIALLY when you compare it to its predecessors.
But, before I begin, there's something you must know - The first two FlatOut games were made by Bugbear Entertainment, and they were phenominal racing games, especially FlatOut 2. This game? Totally different company that completely misunderstood everything Bugbear had done right.
First things first, the AI is pitiful. I know the name of the game is destruction, literally, but it's a RACING game, and I'd rather have people using force to win the race than veering off the track in the first lap to wrestle in the grass like kittens.
On this note, *everyone* targets you. I went into one demolition derby round, and it was hilariously stupid the way it worked. As soon as the countdown hit zero, the twenty-or-so other non-player racers veered to the opposite side like the Persian army and all ganged up on me at once, with the exception of, what, like, two motorists smashing each other's bumpers in. I mean, I played FlatOut 2's derby mode religiously, and it sometimes feels like the AI prioritizes you over their brethren, but even in it worst state it was nothing compared to this insanity.
Now, it's time to compare it to its predecessors - Yes, Flatout 3 was made by a different company than the first two, but being a sequel by its title, I have to rate it in comparison to its past successes in the franchise.
The other NPC's -- The way this development team tried to recreate Bugbear's non-player character gimmick is awful. If you haven't played FlatOut 2, lemme give you the jist of things - There were seven NPC's that were the only opponents in the game. They all had distinct driving styles, color schemes, and skills in different racing areas. They were so memorable thanks to this that you had those names ingrained into your brain after your first couple of races and figured out very quickly whose names to curse every time you launched out of your windshield.
Well, 3 messes this all up. There are something near 15 characters, and some of them are so similar that you have no hope of remembering them. The character models are all very idealized, if you catch my drift, and there's one fully anonymous man wearing a motorcross helmet with practically full-balanced stats that you'll choose every time if you're sane. That's another thing, too - Unlike the original, where you were your own identity, you have to choose one of these punks.
Anyway, 2.5/10, because it technically functions, I guess. Go buy Next Car Game instead, it's made by the same company that made the other FlatOut games. Speaking of which, go buy the other FlatOut games, too, they're super cheap and also on Steam. It's a shame those two don't have online multiplayer anymore, because if they did, I'd force you to buy them at gunpoint.

Was apprehensive if I'd enjoy this - first time playing this series, and I just couldn't imagine tower defense and RPGs joining hands and singing kumbayah. But holy crap, they joined hands, made out with each other and had a precious gosh darned baby that is this game.
Combat is great - a simplied, more action-oriented "WoW" style system with 4 special attacks (that you unlock through leveling - and leveling goes by fast) that have rather negligible cooldown. There are also four towers which are similarly mapped and aren't just elemental recolors of each other. The Monk's towers specialize in auras - Lightning Aura shocks any enemies repeatedly as they try to barrel past, and I have some Buff Aura tower that buffs nearby towers all around (sorry don't remember the actual name offhand).
As I've said, I've only played the monk, but the game really encourages teamwork. You could theoretically win on your own, but it's a lot easier if you have a few teammates to fill in what you lack.
Definitely would recommend. Only problem is too many towers 7.8/10 - IGN.

Single player experience definitely lacking in this one, level design is bland, bosses are weak both in terms of design and difficulty, I can't really name a single memorable boss, DLC improves the situation a little but still they are pretty unsatisfying to fight against. Story still vaguely tied to the first game and even somehow inherited a lot of items from vanilla (like dark knights weaponry or Havels armor from the first game although those characters are completely absent in this one), I guess someone on the dev-team though it would be cool to stuff DS2 with vanilla items for some reason. PvP on the other hand is the best among "souls" series games: less laggy, moderate speed, no backstab fishing (backstabs have an actual animation now instead of being a 1-frame nonsense in DS1), estus chugging is not as fast compared to DS3 and weapon balance is pretty decent although I think STR-weapons could use a slight damage boost.
The other thing is the lack of Red Eye Orb from vanilla which enables infinite invasions, the only way to invade in DS2 is by using Cracked Red Eye Orbs (CREO) and the best way to acquire them is to fight in the covenant named The Brotherhood of Blood in which you'll fight against a covenant member in the arena and the prize for winning each duel is one CREO. People fighting in this cov are abusing most powerful builds/weapons and if you want to win then you'll have to adapt. What's wrong with that, you'll ask? In the end PvE players are the ones who suffer since the game literally forces wanna-be-invaders to fight in the arena for CREOs and it makes them much more skilled than the average player. When I started playing I just wanted to invade people and fight them with my spoon or a plow and see how it fairs versus their weapon of choice, I died a lot but it was really fun. And then when I ran out of orbs I started the endless arena quest, now I can eradicate a group of 4 PvE players with little effort... And it becomes really stale unless I bump into a good player. Of course repeated invasions from Red Eye Orb would make players better as well, but experience during any invasion is so much different than what happens in the arena, so in the end PvP encounters would be much more friendly and winnable for the average player.
And yeah, the infamous Soul Memory (SM). Didn't get this mechanic at all. So every single soul you acquire stores in your SM and online matchmaking is determined by SM-tier (total amount of souls you acquired). Let's say you got 100,000 souls, forgot to level up, died, died again occasionally while trying to pick them up and BAM, you lost 100,000 souls yet they still recorded in your SM and you're up one tier in matchmaking now anyway. How's that good for new players? The idea behind this was that you gain souls, you spend them, get stronger, more experienced and can only play with/vs equally strong players regardless of their Soul Level, but what if you just lost a lot of souls or bought a bunch of consumables and you're still at level 70? Well, according to the game you should be playing versus high level players who played better than you and spent their souls more adequately, seems fair. And not to mention the Agape Ring which let's experienced players to negate souls acquisition and stay in any SM-tier they want, that is just bs in my opinion.
Yeah, I wrote a lot of negative stuff, but I really like the game, don't get me wrong. It just has it's issues which I wanted to highlight, but combined (PvE+PvP) experience is quite superb, I'll give it 5/10 for single player content and 8/10 overall.

Refunct is nearly the perfect chill-out game, and one that I've completed dozens of times over. The mechanics are simple, immediately intuitive, and rewarding.
Where Refunct really shines is in giving the player the space to create their own game. Some people opt for speedruns while others imagine their own challenges: beat the game without touching the same surface twice, never fall in the water, or touch as few surfaces as possible. While some players may rightfully prefer a story or direct narration, Refunct should appeal to those who just want a beautiful sandbox to play around in for awhile: parkour off some walls, slide under platforms, or go for a swim just because you want to.
To be critical, the game's default sensitivity feels pretty low; I had to bump mine up to 150% to get it to feel "normal." I'd also love to see a larger reticle option (basically just a large circle around the center of the screen) for those that are prone to motion sickness. Other than that, this is the perfect game for just chilling out and playing around for awhile -- or scratching that OCD itch with minimal effort which to me is well worth a few bucks. 8/10.

Well, this was a pretty decent game. Beat it via co-op campaign in roughly 16 hours of playtime. I'd say it is comparable to Torchlight II in some basic ways but with some major differences. This game has a dark, broody atmosphere thanks to the Eastern European setting. There is a tighter, more linear storyline than games like Torchlight. The weapons, specialization and customization all make for a satisfying experience. Controls are tight and combat is fun, even if most enemies pose little threat to you. Your character can use different powers easily and it is easy to appreciate the overall design of the game. Levels and enemies are of decent variety and things rarely get stale.
One small disappointment was that in the co-op campaign the other player doesn't play as a different character. So...for 16 hours I had another Victor Vran running around in a different costume. Another is that while you can choose the order in which you beat levels, there really are no choices that are presented to you that have any meaning beyond your own character customization.
In summary, a fairly bare bones hack 'n slash with low to moderate replayability (imho) that gets pretty much everything right. Fun co-op and an easy recommend as an 8.2/10.

In general, Victor Vran is a great ARPG, with fairly easy controls and a hilariously sarcastic narrator. The ability to change between your "class" and skills really suits me, as I usually spend half an RPG regretting my class choice.
In more detail, some pro's and con's:
+ Silly, sarcastic humour in the form of a narrator not unlike "The Stanley Parable"
+ The ability to switch between classes and skills at any time
+ Uses WASD-controls, instead of clicking to walk and controls are very smooth
+ Possibility for multiplayer and joining a game is easily done
+ Enhancement of abilities through the use of destiny cards (this to me was a very new and refreshing feature)
+ Temporary bounties and treasure hunts, shareable through chat (both ingame and internationally)
+ Enemies level simultaneously with the player, so returning to an earlier area is still as challenging as the first time
- Poor, cheesy story. To me, this is was very crucial
- Mediocre voice acting
- Overdramatised game, making it hard to feel sympathy for some characters
- Victor Vran's attitude is perpendicular to the narrator's, breaking immersion more than once.
All in all, I'd say the pro's outweigh the con's and especially when playing with others, I would really recommend this game, either at full price or on sale.

After putting in over 30 hours into this wonderfully crafted strategy game during the era of the Napoleonic Wars I can say for sure without a doubt that any tactically player or historical player will LOVE this game! Imagine managing any one of the multiple major nations at the time such as Russia or Britain, allowing you to make any decision from controlling your government, trade, industry, research, diplomacy and of course your most important is your military. Now not only are you given objectives to complete within a certain time period but also it gives you the chance for European domination as any one of those major nations. Plan your nation's expansion across Europe allowing you to pick any strategy possible from either destroying large nations to annexing smaller nations into your unstoppable empire! Once you're tired of playing Napoleon's 3 campaigns (Italy, Egypt, and Europe) you can play as any of the coalition nations against Napoleon's France or play multiple different battles that were decisive turning points in history from The Battle of Waterloo to The Battle of the Nile. Finally once you've completed all of that there is multiplayer that is quite entertaining when playing campaigns or battles with friends or anyone else too. Overall this is a pretty good Total War game to buy for you and a friend to play sometime together as a team or as foes.

When it was first released, Napoleon was being charged for at full price ($60 US)... when it has no place being charged at full price. It was released a bit under a year after Empire: Total War and plays almost exactly the same. In effect, it's a standalone expansion for Empire that Creative Assembly and SEGA tried to pass off as "the next major Total War game." It certainly has a number of technical improvements over Empire that make it not run anywhere near as badly, as well as some additional features, but I have issues recommending the game.
The lack of content compared to Empire is the chief issue I have. It seems at first like there might be quite a bit, as there are 4 campaigns to start with. Two of these are based on the actual historical events of Napoleon's Italian campaign and the French invasion of Egypt during the era. The other two are the French "mastery of Europe" campaign and the Campaigns of the Coalition, which are basically the grand campaign limited to France and the Coalition in a campaign to defeat Napoleon's France, respectively. All four of these campaigns feel incredibly limiting compared to what we're used to from the previous Total War games. There are eight playable factions, compared to the 11 that were in Empire, and a few of those factions are only playable in certain campaigns (ie. Portugal and Spain are only playable in the Peninsular campaign). Each faction does have its own units, but they feel pretty much the same across the board due to the nature of warfare during the Napoleonic era. They attempt to supplement the game's shortcomings in variety with a
of DLC that makes the game seem more like a cash grab than anything else.
Like I mentioned before there
some improvements over Empire. The AI is
better than it was in Empire (which isn't saying much... the AI in Empire was pretty stupid), but it's a pretty negligible degree that you really only notice if you played a lot of Empire. It runs quite a bit better (probably in no small part due to the lessened amount of content), they improved the battle simulations a bit, and they tossed in some additional multiplayer features like the multiplayer campaign. So that's nice to have, of course. The only real problem with that is CA never really sorted out the netcode all the way with their engine so issues that popped up in Napoleon still persist even in subsequent games.
I could go on about how I personally find the warfare of Empire and Napoleon to be rather dull (line infantry squaring off under artillery barrages with cavalry charges to break up the monotony seems cool the first few times you do it... then you realize that's how
goes... it wears thin incredibly quickly), but that's just me. I'm well aware there are plenty of people out there who find that incredibly interesting. If you liked Empire, you'll probably be able to get something out of Napoleon. Had CA & SEGA released it as an outright expansion to Empire rather than a full sequel (ie. a "Napoleonic Campaigns" DLC), I feel like it would've been better as a whole. As it stands, we have a full standalone product that is basically a stripped down version of Empire with some slight improvements in certain areas, and I just can't recommend it based on that.

Lets keep it "short"
Probably the Best Fantasy World you will ever enter.
Why? Story is - lets say classic- but with its own twist, dark humor, unique side quests and challanges and overall: it feels like a world filled with People, not NPCs. Everybody has his own little Stories to tell, and the Design of the Map makes you fall in love with it. To conclude this part: The Divinity Universe is very Unique, follows classic scenarios, but in a very unique and characteristic way , while other RPGs always play the same (Gothic, Risen, TwoWorlds, Skyrim etc.)
Graphics: 2009 basiclly BUT it looks stunning. The Designers made what you can see in WoW for example: a very pretty and different Graphic Style that looks- well lovely maybe? Divinity has a Mix between Realism and Fantasy.
Probably the Ideas of visuals where better than the actual textures, but still just look at the screens, its old-ish but looks awsome (if you dont have a fetish for every visual Nvidia effect youll love it)
Story: Well as said above: The thing youd expect: You are the Hero, you need to kill something evil and you sometimes get to decide whether you are evil or not. But where Witcher 3 is like " we are an awsome game, we have sidequests" Divinity consists out of them: There are probably more than 100 Side Quests, some bigger setted than others but written insanely good. Or to say it in another way: you do them because you are interested in the Story of the Sidequest, not because you want to 100% the game or cuz you want the Loot (also the riddles are challangeing as♥♥♥♥♥sometimes). Eventhough the game is 12+ it really has some dark dark Humor, and often feels like 16+ or 18+.
Overall its a game where you can enjoy every single part of the Story, and dont fast click through every Conversation.
Gameplay:
Awsome. Finally i can Combine Mage/Fighter/Necro. I usually run around with 2 Creatures (1 Taunt Demon, 1 Multibodypart-Thing) while I have my Shield and my Sword, Shooting fireballs, Magic Missiles, Magic Blasts, Firewalls.
I usually hate games where you are a Fighter OR Hunter OR Mage OR Necro, but this game lets you combine at least 2- and if you do it well even 3- Skilltrees. Its not like you are the OP-Goodateverything type of Character, but you can Build pretty flexible (Try Mage+Hunter its Op)
It is challanging at first, but it gets easier as soon as you understand what you are doing and what you enemies are capeable of doing.
Fighting is pretty simple: No blocking (but dodging), Skillbased (mostly around 4-5 you usually use), Attacks are targeted (you gotta aim at least a littlebit)  WASD+Space+Leftclick+12345678 is bassicly whats going on.
You can go everywhere you can Jump (or Fly).
Flying is also Pretty easy: Press Q to become a dragon (you can only fly to keep the ground interesting for mantoman combat) again leftclick+camera+12345678.
The complexity of the fights comes with the Skill Combinations (which makes replaying the game pretty cool with another class/weapon combo)
Overall, its a beginnerfriendly Game with Mechanics for People who love: Story and Sidequests, Skillbased RPGs (for example NOT Skyrim), replay potential, a HUGE viarety of Weapon and Armor Types, and a lovely designed Open World with an own character, and not a Boring Everyday RPG world.
Would buy it again for 40€

I wasn't expecting much from Refunct when a code invite popped into my inbox, but I wisely looked up (and downloaded) the developer's previous game, Refunktion
and saw that this simple but gorgeous sequel was a response to some saying that first game was too difficult. Refunct didn't take long to complete (I took my time and spent about 45 minutes, but some players clock out at between 20-30) and while incredibly easy, manages to be brilliantly conceived and executed.
No instructions needed here, just intuitive controls using k+m or a controller, some surprising jumping (that should be adopted into other first-person games) and a payoff that brought a smile to my face (and a bigger one after that when I was able to get 100% after completing the game when I tried to better the 98% I ended with).
If anything, creator dGrieshofer should expand the game into an entire series of puzzles on the same map and keep the same enemy-free, death-less approach. The feeling of finally playing wall-climb sequences in a game that aren't frustrating series of trial and error runs was exhilarating to say the least. Now, I want more. You will too. Go get this and have a blast.

Wow, so the developers of this game should seriously think about careers in hollywood movie making. They really know how to set the tone. The motif is a silent hill-esque investigation style horror. You play as an investigative journalist armed with only your video camera and a tip that leads you into the abyss of a psychiatric asylum.
I love the creativity behind this game. It can be difficult to conceptualize survival games this isn't basically a never ending quest for resources, dulled by knowledge of predictable mechanics and action points. Outlast breaks the mould, and excells in these areas. Admittedly some parts are predictable and the motif, although not a widely used one, still gives you an idea that can't be too far from the truth without adding aliens or sasquatch.
Having said that, the game itself is far from predictable. You'll quickly learn you can't play this like other games, with the exception of reload which are batteries for your camera. You find documents along the way which lays out the story. You have an assortment of maneuvers that allow you to negotiate your environment, my favorite being the ability to slide through narrow gaps... that one will literally save your life ;)
Movement doesn't feel sluggish however there does seem to be some slight hangtime when jumping. The graphics aren't the best in the world as post processing elements are basically stereoscopic and there is a constant, migraine inducing noise overlay which worsens tenfold during the use of your cameras nightvision. The textures aren't spectacular but they aren't distracting either, they do the job just fine. And in all honestly, you'll likely be too immersed in the game to notice many of the lacking elements, post processing and overlay excluded.
Now as I understand, this game isn't optimized for 32bit systems and requires a workaround.
In summary I'd recommend this game to friends and horror genre fans. Happy Gaming!

This is a fun, atmospheric, first-person platform/parkour game that looks good and sounds good as well. It's not very long - it can be finished in as little as 30 minutes - but it's a must for people who prefer some abstraction in their games.
All that you do is jump from area to area as you raise a city, or really a collection of pillars and platforms, from the ocean depths. It's easy to start and gets progressively more difficult but not to the point of being annoying. There is no story but for something like this a story isn't really necessary. The graphics are gorgeous with a continual day/night loop and the electronic music is very soothing and atmospheric.
This game isn't going to be to everyone's liking, and people who complain if a game doesn't last more than a few hours (fools that they are) probably should stay away. But if you like atmospheric games and light platforming/parkouring, you could do a lot worse than to throw a few dollars, Euros, or whatever at this indie game.

What is Victor Vran?
An action RPG where the player controls a single character from an overhead perspective in real time hack and slash combat.
Is it any good?
Its a decent game which could have been even better if the developers had made a couple of different design choices. I had some fun with it, but I wouldn't say its a must play, unless you're a fan of the genre. I'd rank it below Grim Dawn but above Path of Exile and Torchlight 1&2.
Combat system
You can use melee and ranged weapons, and you can have 2 weapons equipped which allows you to quickly switch between them during combat. Each type of weapon has 2 special attacks which are on cooldown timers. You can dodge/roll to avoid enemy attacks. As you deal and take damage, an "overdrive" bar charges up, which will allow you to activate your choice of demon powers, which are Victor Vran's equivalent of offensive magic. You can also equip destiny cards, which are passive buffs.
There's plenty of variety in the weapons, demon powers and destiny cards that are available, so you can build a character that suits your playing style, and this is the game's biggest strength.
For example, after a while I started to realise that its hard to avoid getting hit, even if I constantly roll around like a crazy person, so I designed my tactics around health regeneration. I found a warhammer and a shotgun that both had a "vampire" ability, restoring some of my health every time I hit an enemy. I equipped a vampire destiny card and a slayer card (restore health when killing an enemy), and other cards to increase my maximum health and armour, plus a card that creates an AOE explosion when you "overkill" an enemy by doing massive damage above their current health. And my favourite demon powers were boomerang, which is exactly what it sounds like - does damage to all enemies in a straight line ahead, and then comes back towards you, hitting everything a second time, and diamond, which is like a protective shield which absorbs all damage for a short time.
You don't find individual pieces of armour, but you can choose between different outfits which have their own stats. They mainly affect your armour rating, and how fast your overdrive meter charges up. By default, overdrive charges fairly quickly, but the bar empties between fights, which means you can waste the charge. After a few hours I unlocked an outfit that makes overdrive charge slower, but the bar stays filled outside of combat, which allowed me to use powers more often, and I could save it for when I really needed it.
The negative aspect of the combat system is that there doesn't really seem to be any penalty for the player's death. When you die, you just respawn at the last checkpoint, or the start of the level, with all your progress saved. Monsters that you've already killed stay dead, so you can just run straight back to where you were. Death is a momentary inconvenience, and this made the combat feel less intense.
Story and other stuff
The story had potential to be really good. Victor is a hunter who is trying to the save the city of Zagoravia, which has been overrun by demons, monsters and undead. There's a couple of neat twists involving the city's queen, and Victor's mysterious past. Victor is also voiced by Doug Cockle, aka Geralt of Rivia. Unfortunately, it doesn't fulfil the potential because the player never gets to make any dialogue choices, and this is also one of those games that has NPCs talking while you're in the middle of combat. Seriously game devs, stop doing this. I'm not listening to the dialogue because I'm busy trying to not die, and afterwards I feel like I might have missed something important.
I finished the main quest in 16 hours, but there is some replayability provided by the challenges on each level, which require you to perform specific objectives such as "kill x number of this enemy with this weapon" or "kill x number of enemies in y seconds". I didn't notice any bugs, and controls work fine with mouse and keyboard. Everything is fully rebindable.
The music is quite good. This is actually the second part of the game that reminded me of the Witcher, because one piece of music sounds very similar to the Vizima night track. However, I didn't like the sense of humour. There are lots of jokes, but most of them are annoying, including an "arrow to the knee" meme, a reference to GabeN, and several mentions of hats.
Recommendation
If you like action RPGs, you'll probably enjoy playing Victor Vran. There's enough content to justify a full price purchase.

The concept is good. The horror and the atmosphere is there, especially in the first half of the game. The are some ideas that were quite a novelty back in 2005, like the sanity, no hud, lack of weapons and general fragility of your character.
Unfotunately, the game is broken in many ways. First of all, it didn't age well. Unless you're playing on XP, It's impossible to finish without unofficial patch that can be found on the forums. It does not support widescreen properly, and since it is a port from the first xbox, the graphics are so-so even by 2005 standards. Being a hastily port, it has many bugs. There are bugs that force you to reload from the last save game, and bugs that manifest themselves *when* you reload from the previous save. And a bunch of minor bugs, that are simply annoying.
But it's not only technical issues that spoil the fun. Many parts simply don't work as the creators intended. You may call it 'hard' but I call it 'badly designed':
- Some of the stealth sequences are next to impossible to pass unnoticed and are much easier if you simply 'run for it'.
- Some puzzles give absolutely no clue what to do next, and you wander aimlessly around the level searching for that one object that can be picked up, or interacted with.
- Some levels are trial-by-death type. You'll die at least several times untill you finally find out where exactly you have to go or what to do next. Given that save points are rare and can be missed entirely, plus many scripted secquences are unskippable, this quickly gets frustrating.
The combat, when you finally get some weapons, is difficult, but that's fine. Your character is not a Rambo (even though he can carry eight weapons, several books, medkits and a diary at the same time).
To sum up, only play this game if you are deep into Cthulhu mythos or you're out of horror games.  Otherwise, there are many better ways to spend 10 hours of your life.

I’m not too sure how to review this game, so i’ll just point out what you can find here.
Hyperdimension Neptunia Re;Birth3 V Generation is a good game and it doesn't require having played the first two games to follow the story. If you're new to the franchise, this game is a good starting point, well, actually any game is a good starting point.
For how I see it the games of this franchise provide not an excellent game, but a fun experience overall.
Combat is very simple but it works and it's been a bit tweaked to make it harder to spam ultimate attacks, making those special abilities more likely to be used in battle (in the previous games those were almost useless).
Storytelling uses a visual-novel style like the previous games and there are a ton of anime and games references (some very obscure, like the pineapple salad for macross). The scenes tend to be veeery long, and while the dialogues are well written sometimes they drag on for too much, but you can skip them.
A peculiar feature is the remake system, basically a crafting system that lets you create new items, gain new abilities and change the monsters in dungeons, it ends up being very simple, but it's a good addition to boost the replayability of dungeons.
If you like anime games, I'd say either nep1 or this are a must buy.
Most of it is pretty much more of the same classic nep, with an arguably better story, fun characters (all of the nep1+2 team) and dungeons and some small improvements. This time the story is a continuation of nep2 and is not set in an alternate universe.
The exe drives now require sp (and many of the classic ones need to be unlocked via character challenges) and you'll probably have to initially rely on the normal special abilities, which I found great, because in previous games I ended up not using these normal ones at all, with the exception of compa’s healing.
Dungeons are more diversified and the new ones are really cool, but there are pretty much no new monsters introduced in this game.
The other two main additions are the character challenges from Fairy Fencer F (basically little stat bonuses you get for doing stuff with your characters) and a post game state where you can choose if you want to jump into NG+ or keep playing.
This game usually gets huge discounts so you should wait for one of those and then you're guaranteed to have a game worthy of 30+ hours of fun with neptune and her friends.
I recommend buying the DLC since it helps in the most frustrating rng part of the game, the Stella's dungeon.
+ Well written wacky story
+ All the characters from nep 1+2
+ Character challenges
+ Remake system
+ Fair price with regular discounts
- Stella's dungeon (but it's way more useful than in nep2)

For the obvious, Call of Cthulhu is a game inspired by Lovecraft. It's called Call of Cthulhu, but that's more of a marketing thing, as Cthulhu actually plays a very little role in the title. The game is more about a few of Lovecraft's other novels, the most notable one being Shadow Over Innsmouth. However, if you don't know the difference between a Cthulhu and a Dagan or a Xa'ligha, that's okay as the game doesn't expect you to know these things, as you play as a character who knows nothing about these things either.
Call of Cthulhu: Dark Corners of the Earth is a first-person horror-adventure game. It has elements of a first-person shooter, an adventure game, and a survival-horror game. It's also a really tough cookie, it's not an easy game, and there is a legitimate survival element, as well as a few tough puzzles, and some pretty fantastic atmosphere and scares.
You play as a man named Jack Walters, who's a detective. The game starts with a prologue section when Jack helps a local police force he's acquainted with break into a house run by a group of cultists. They're shooting-up the police... However, when Jack infiltrates, the cultists don't seem to be hostile towards him, but rather actually welcome him with open arms, as they commit a mass-suicide ritual. And when he enters the basement, he witnesses something strange, and everything becomes a blur. He becomes conscious six years later, when he finds out he spent the last six years in a mental asylum. He has no memory of this time, and to him he was just at the cultists house. He of course is really curious about this time, but tries to resume his detective agency. He receives a letter and takes on the requested case to investigate a missing persons report of a Brian Burnham, a man who tried to start a grocery store chain in a nearby coastal town of Innsmouth. He goes to investigate.
Gameplay has a lot of variety, and fantastic pacing for the most part if you can accept it moves at a bit of a slower pace, a more slow-burn type of game (which benefits it rather than hurts it, I feel). The game has sections of exploration and interaction with townspeople. You actually have a big portion of the game at the beginning when you're defenseless, and have to master skills of stealth, evasion, and survival with taking advantage of the environment and lowly tools you have that are hardly murder weapons. There's puzzles, both in the on-the-fly gameplay sort and the 'need to solve this puzzle to continue' variety. And the game isn't full of scripted scenarios either (though a few do exist), so a lot of the survival has to be taken from your own wits and cleverness.
Survival is important. Gun bullets don't graze you, they can seriously damage you. The game has a mechanic where you bleed when shot, as well as where you are shot effects your damage reaction to being shot. You heal it with limited healing items you get, some to stop bleeding or mend wounded appendages, others to recover blood and health. You also need to be careful as some weapons can inflict poisoning on you to recover from. Eventually you do get a gun though, but the game hardly becomes a run-and-gun, you have to be really strategic and know when to let-go of being undetected to fire, and which enemies are really worth taking out. You have limited ammo, and the enemies can seriously kick your♥♥♥♥♥if you're not careful.
But the game isn't all about combat and stealth. There also are areas and levels with almost no enemies at all, and some fantastic horror scenes, strange sanity moments, and just some atmosphere and sequences that go in very different directions. The character also has a sanity feature, which makes it so the more he's around unpleasent things, the more weird things may become for him. Certain areas, imagery, and the like help his sanity, while others break it.
The game also has some memorizing music, graphics are obviously a bit outdated but do the job, and as the game continues, situations open up a lot more to how you can approach them. And the game continues adding new elements, additions, and set-piece like moments all the way through to the end to prevent it from becoming too much of the same, and leaving you to continually wonder what might be coming next. It's pacing can be argued is slow, but I think works very well for the title and what its trying to achieve.
I also can mention that this game I would label as a scary game, it is absolutely tense a lot of the time, and some segments legitimately scared the crap out of me. But part of the way it pulls this off is that they're not over-abundant or consistent, and don't rely on the same few tricks or overly on cheap scares.
There is some jank here though, with some bugs, sometimes you may be detected by enemies when they really shouldn't of detected you, and there's a few frustrating parts of the game that are kind of trial-and-error, where basically you need to do what the game wants you to do or you'll die. There are some fan patches to address some of these issues, however. On a similar note, the game has some bugs for Windows 7 users, as the game was designed around Windows XP. I suggest doing some homework before you play the game to find some fan patches that fix a number of issues on newer machines, make some trial-and-error parts of the game easier, and make the game look better graphically.
It's not perfect, but I do think it's a good horror title, and worth checking out if you either have interest in horror games or Lovecraft mythos (as its mine and many others personal favorite Lovecraftian-inspired game). It does require some patience though, but there is an excellent experience here if you enjoy this sort of thing.

The story is amazing, but that's about it.
All computer controlled units (including neutrals) scale so fast such that it becomes impossible to engage in any combat unless you have all your units/resouces pooled onto your main hero, meaning that any secondary hero you happen to get is nothing more than a glorified unit courier; a feature that was absent in all other games of this series. Consequently, losing a single unit on a single stack is enough to warrent a reload. The game has been out a long time and still the final 'dynasty perk' slot hasn't been unlocked for use; even at max level and with all DLC. Finally, the game has a random crashing issue that has yet to be resolved; the crash may occur within five minutes of starting or after six hours of play.
Despite all this though, the game is surprisingly balanced (again, assuming all your recources are pooled to your main hero) and the units are refreshingly diverse across all races.
TL;DR
If you're a fan of the series and have played one of the predecesors this game is a big disappointment. If you're new to the series or the genre in general: wait for it to go on sale.

I played this game on the PS4 for 100+ hours so don't be fooled by my playtime hours of this game from Steam. It's really dissapointing that even with it being the same online-only game and spent so much time on the PS4 version and so much progress, that I can't transfer my save to PC. So now I have to start ALL OVER again.
--SHORT VERSION--
PROS:
- Huge map
- Good amount of car custimization
- Fun multiplayer with good variety of game modes
- Neat car showrooms with car testing before buying
- Free-cam mode for making cool looking screenshots
- cloud-saving
CONS:
- Terrible, disjointed, and condensed copy-paste map of the U.S.
- Graphics look terrible at times with low-poly textures.
- Clunky vehicle physics
- Very grindy part leveling
- Unrealistic vehicle topspeeds
- Frustratingly slow money earning that can take hours upon hours of racing
- Special multiplayer events with exclusive rewards that are not at-your-own leisure and expire within real-world times, mimicking time-based mobile games.
- Can't transfer saves from platform to platform.
- Third party app required to play on PC.
--DETAILED VERSION--
PROS:
- Huge map that is bigger than Test Drive Unlimited's Hawaii, 1:1 scaled map and Test Drive Unlimited 2's Ibiza, 1:1-scaled map combined with different veriations of environments. Cool landmarks to visit.
- Good bit amount of vehicle custimization options and fun to watch a standard street car turn into a monster truck or an offroad vehicle.
- Fun multiplayer competition with different gamemodes and co-op missions.
- Neat car showroom visuals that let you look at each vehicle by opening and closing doors, honking the horn, looking at the inside of the car from first person, freely moving the orbit-camera and test driving any vehicle before purchasing.
- Free-cam mode with many options that lets you move the camera around freely and take awesome screenshots for showing off to friends and uploading.
- Progress loss is impossible with your saves constantly being uploaded to the servers
CONS:
- Instead of having a really cool fictional map to drive around and explore in, the developers decided to design this wierd condensed, disfigured map of the USA. It gets really akward when driving from like New York City to Chicago in 10 minutes and gets really comedic at times watching how small and close together cities, towns and highway systems are. Residential areas especially look VERY close together and look extremely artificial. Parking lots and back alley streets look hilariously disjointed and have small pillars installed with tall invisible walls to keep you from exploring and discovering more of how terrible they look. Also the cities and towns in this game look about the same and only have a few unique land features and structures such as monuments but that's about it. Driving around in these cities and towns are also very limited when it comes to freedom because just about every shopping plaza, town home, and generic copy-paste business building and strips have these wierd looking short shouldn't-be-there pillars with invisible walls that keep you from driving up steps and their alleyways that totally look like you should be able to drive up on. Even most of the ramps in this game that you should obviously be able to drive up on have these invisible walls that even keep monster trucks out. Hell even most of the parks in the cities and towns in this game are strangely off limits! As badly put together the map looks, alot of the areas literally look like a custom map you would make in a Far Cry game trying to mimic a big city in real life. It just doesn't look right AT ALL. All this just so the developers can brag at E3 saying that the "Whole USA map is at your hands to explore". WTF.
- Even after the Wild Run update that gave the game a graphics and color boost, it still looks really terrible at times, especially in the cities. Player vehicles and country environments can look very screenshot-pretty, but when it comes to generic civilian cars, pedestrians, buildings, and landmarks, it reminded me of when I played those Need for Speed games in the mid 2000's. Low-polygon textures and absolutely low details made me wonder what the hell the developers were thinking when it came to quantity over quality.
- Clunky car physics that are wierder than Midnight Club L.A.'s. Going offroad and want to climb a rock with your monster truck or drive over a car? Good luck with that. Hitting a wall at 200 MPH barely scratches the front end of your car but driving into or through small bushes and brush absolutely destroy your car. Your car slowly "heals" over time, so it becomes laughable watching your car's damaged body artificially correct itself and transform as if nothing ever happened as your driving.
- Extemely grindy trying to get higher level car parts. And I mean it is soo grindy, it will drive you up the walls if not literally. It will feel like you are playing a mobile game like NFS No Limits when it comes to car progression.
- Very unrealistic and unfair top speed when you have just about all of the highest level parts for your cars because whether you have the slowest or fastest cars in the game, they will all have THE SAME top speeds and acceleration which makes ABSOLUTELY NO SENSE. No point of spending 700,000+ credits that took 50+ hours for you to get when you can spend 16,000 on a slow car that will have the same power as that Ferarri when you have all the highest level parts.
- Takes a VERY LONG time to get money in this game if you don't want to spend real money for in-game credits, hence the microtransactions they throw at you all the time. Even with money-earning perks maxed out and exploits you may find to get more money quicker, It WILL STILL take you LOTS and LOTS of racing just to get a decent amount to buy a Mustang and that's not counting custimization parts and such.
- Real-time multiplayer events that require you to not have a life because they are in-sync with real world time that expire after a certain day or time just like a mobile game does. Not really an at-your-own leisure friendly game when it comes to engaging in special higher-reward events with exclusive car rewards and parts. Really dissapointing if you have a job and can't make it when you come home and find out that you missed an event with that exclusive car you wanted to win and will never get.
- Can't transfer saves from platform to platform, despite being able to link your Xbox Live Account and PSN to your Ubisoft account which is useless to do with this game. Each platform has its own servers for online which can be frustrating if transfering.
- Required to have a seperate third-party app, UPlay installed and running on your computer which can take up valuable hardware. So now not only do you have shortcut keys for and overlay of Steam running in the background while playing The Crew, you ALSO have an overlay and shortcut keys for UPlay running in the background as well while playing.
*This game is OK. It can be really fun at times with HUGE jumps to make, driving 300 MPH+ in drag car builds, playing around with friends and showing off each other's vehicle builds and paint designs, going into free-cam mode and taking awesome screenshots, but the negatives feel like they just totally outweigh the positives for me. Especially with games that I have that are far more interesting and fun to play than this one.
** When I had this game for PS4, I really liked it because it was kind of an alternative to Forza Horizon because I didn't have an Xbox One nor gaming PC at the time. I didn't have college and had alot of fun playing with friends. Now that I have a gaming PC and have college, I would rather play Forza Horizon 3, which has WAAAY more cars, more custimization options and parts, more beautiful graphics with better optimization for PC and overall just much more enjoyable to play than this game. I would rate this game a 2/5 for PC.

I got this for $2 during a sale, and this game is definitely worth the price. Originally, I played Divinity Original Sin 2, and wanted to get more into the franchise. At first, I didn't expect much from this title, but I was pleasantly surprised as the dragon mechanics are reasonably well done, combat keeps you on your toes, and the graphics are rather good for a 6 year old game.
However, the game seems to continuously throw you a ridiculous amount of mind-numbingly boring side quests that involve "Oh no I lost my earrings, Dragon Knight please help me!" or "Oh no I forgot something while fleeing from monsters, Dragon Knight HELP!", that sort of thing.
Despite all that, for some inexplicable reason I just couldn't seem to put down the game, but instead binged the entire game within 3 days. For its age, the plot, mechanics and general RPG elements are pretty good (although I might say there are quite a few plot holes nontheless).
Hell yeah.
That would depend on how tolerant you are on old video game mechanics, graphics and UI. Since I've played numerous old titles, it didn't bother me. However, if you are branching out from a newer Divinity title like Divinity Original Sin 2 and is used to the more modernised UI and/or graphics, then I wouldn't recommend you buying it on full price.
Now onto Divine Divinity!

One of only two Focus Interactive games that I actually like. This is an almost unique blend of action, wonder, well thought out gameplay and even a bit of humor that allow the player to immerse themselves in the story, the lore, the thrill that you get when you finally beat a really tough stage. This is an example of what can happen when the devs listen to the players and adjust thier games accordingly. You see this was one of the products of what I call the Golden Age of gaming 2007-2013. If you look closely, this does not have, lootboxes, pointless DLC's, paywall content, microtransactions or just about any moneygrubbing tactic used by the likes of Unbisoft or EA these days. This does not try to be a Dark Souls wannabe, it is its own game. Yes there are a couple of niggles, early glitches were common, and save corruption ruined many a game. Also the steam version does not have Controller support because, well I really don't know why exactly. The point is that the devs, wait for it, fixed the bugs! They did not just say "Deal with it"-Farcry 2 or "The problems were addressed in the new DLC we are releaseing"- ME3. Yes the graphics do feel dated to us now but this is the best you will get for some magic hack and slash action without having to pay through the nose. Look, don't take my word for it, buy the dang thing. Keep Larian liquid so they can save the world from EA.

Well, once again I haven't done the DLC (with the exception of Operation: Anchorage, which I liked; as a matter of fact, I haven't done the final ending choice for the main game because I'm waiting on Broken Steel), but I feel I've done enough to get the essential experience, as usual. Anyway, I'm going to do something different this time around and review this one twice, once as a game and once as a Fallout game, because THERE'S a contentious issue.
As a game: It's a bit clunky, and the mechanics are often broken, but the story, atmosphere, characters, and immersion completely make up for it in a way that I've never seen before and almost didn't think possible. It was Yahtzee Croshaw that once said, "Immersion can save the life of a bad game, and inversely, a lack of immersion can be a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ bullet right between the eyes." I wouldn't call Fallout 3 a bad game, per se, but the flaws are clearly there. The weapon degredation isn't entirely necessary, as you'll run out of ammo far sooner than your gun will break, and there really aren't enough non-combat options for...anything, except getting bosses to stop being♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ Overall, though, it completely sucked me in, and I highly recommend it to anyone who can handle what is probably the first game I've played that truly deserves an 'M' for Mature (as opposed to WHEE SHOOTY SHOOTY EXPLOSION).
As a Fallout game: Let's start off with the good. With only one exception I can think of (the T-51b not being 'powered,' which I immediately created a mod to fix), it fits in with the lore perfectly, so no complaint there. In addition, it builds on the Fallout universe in a way that makes it seem even more truly alive, and does a lot with what already existed. I like what they did with Mr. Handys, Deathclaws, Harold's story, Fallout's trademark crazy people who'll start a cult over anything, the music (good God, I LOVE what they've done with the music), and several other elements. As for the bad, or what is popularly concieved as disowning it from the franchise: well, the tone is definitely shifted, into a more desperate, lonely experience, but people often forget how often that was often present in the first Fallout, too, what with the Glow, the invasion of Necropolis, the whole Boneyard situation, etc. Secondly, the gameplay is obviously completely different. It's certainly necessary for this particular game, but was it necessary for a new Fallout game? Countering a question with a question, is it really that different? You can still target individual parts of enemies, increase skills and earn perks, the SPECIAL system is still thankfully there, and you can get companions to help you out. Despite the 3D gameplay, this is still the same Fallout world with the same Fallout situations that you solve in the same Fallout ways. Yes, it is a Fallout game. I personally would put it below Fallout 1, but above Fallout 2. If you're an original Fallout fan, I recommend it even more.
No, you want a game that seemingly will deviate to a large extent from the originals, look no further than Fallout 4...
P.S. I find it interesting how Dogmeat shifted to a tank, instead of the ally who knocks enemies down so that you can get 95% criticals to their eyes. No complaints on the new version, though.

I picked up Victor Vran after I got a little tired of playing Grim Dawn over and over. Found an ARPG very similar to the likes of Grim Dawn, The Incredible Adventures of Van Helsing, Torchlight, Diablo 3 etc, but also very different.
I like the approach taken regarding character classes (spoiler, there are none) and skills. I haven't played a WASD ARPG before, but Victor Vran makes the implementation extremely intuitive, and the dodge and jump functions are again a unique addition to a standard game genre.
Honourable Mentions:
- Pop culture references abound. I found myself having to pause the game to finish laughing over the Monty Python and Gangnam Style references.
- I like that even the tutorial screen tips update whenever keys are remapped, even to non-standard keys on my gaming mouse. It's little additions like this that help keep me immersed in the game.
- The integration of hubs, overworld and dungeon maps is great, and really helps for short gaming sessions.
Highly recommended to anyone wanting to play another dungeon crawling shoot 'n' loot that happily wears its changes.

It has it's technical flaws, but I'd highly recommend it to any fans of Lovecraft and the Mythos.

This is a *very* tentative recommendation.
Verdun is a multiplayer-only FPS set during WW1. It aims to recreate the clunky brutality of the era with far more attention to detail and realism than something like Battlefield 1, for instance, and where it sacrifices a certain degree of playability, it adds a niche appeal that rewards thinking outside the box.
This is not a run-and-gun game. If you get your history lessons from BF1, you won't realise that most weapons in WW1 were bolt-action rifles or revolver pistols. As such, the game puts most players on an even-field in regards to gunplay. The weapons aren't perfectly accurate and thus the game doesn't reward twitch shooting, in fact any movement directly before firing, especially if you fire just after running, will mean that ADS doesn't actually aim down the sights - the weapons takes a few seconds to still and this can make all the difference in a close-quarters skirmish. Thankfully both you and your enemy will often be in the same boat, and coming out of a fracas alive will often be down to blind luck, and whoever didn't panic.
Because it's a one-hit kill situation with most weapons here, which has both its pros and cons; yes, it makes it easier to nail an enemy from a distance, but if at any point you allow someone to get a bead on you, you won't be celebrating Christmas this year, and 7 times out of 10 you'll never know where you were shot from. And since Verdun mostly features trench warfare with stretches of no-man's land in between, you will be getting killed a lot. You can't outrun a bullet, and trying to creep makes you an easy target. Advancing requires either luck, incompetence on the part of your enemies, or accurate cover fire in support. It's thrilling stuff, and dropping into one end of a trench when the enemy doesn't know you're there makes you feel like a fox amongst the hens. The flip side of this is that modes like Team Deathmatch devolve into a camping trip each and every time, and it's a truly enraging experience to spend 10 minutes in a game and not lay an eye on a single enemy and still die half a dozen times.
The sound design is worth a massive commendation. Fighting in the trenches at night and hearing the report of pistol and rifle fire nearby is terrifying. You can follow the action by following the sounds, and after a battle the area will be filled with the screams of men shot and dying. Rifles are *loud*. The sound of a shot will give away your position as much as anything else, and this knowledge just sits in the back of your mind every time you feel like a boss, sniping on the enemy from afar.
The game also looks quite good, although a tad dated, and certain tactics like watching for muzzle flashes and skylighting your enemies are very effective, and at one point I managed to effectively camouflage myself in the foliage to the point that I killed two soldiers staring right at me before one of them could even get a shot off. The movement, however, is awful. Clunky and fiddly controls aren't aided by very rough terrain. You can get stuck on barbed wire without knowing it was there and not know which way to move to get out, resulting in a cheap death. You can get stuck on terrain and get shot. You can get stuck behind friendlies in trenches and not be able to get past. If the game played smoother I suppose it wouldn't gel with the intentional clunkiness of the weapons, but god it'd be less frustrating.
And so this is the part where I talk about the bigger flaws with the game itself. Firstly, short of reading the manual, there's no way to teach yourself how to play - selecting a game type throws you straight into gameplay. The half dozen or so in-game menus are all clogged with info that the game doesn't tell you the relevance of. There's no option for training or bot-matches just on your own, so when the game hurls you into the middle of a match for the first time, you're gonna get your butt handed to you time and time again. Oh, and about that, in my first play-through I was spawn-killed no less than 6 times. Because sometimes it'll pop you in or behind your line, and sometimes it'll pop you right at the forefront of the attack and the enemy will kill you before you can even get your hands on the controls. You never know where you're gonna show up, and you don't have a choice. This is straight-up inexcusable. I also ended my first playthrough with a crash to desktop. This is apparently not uncommon for the game, and just highlights a certain lack of technical polish that shouldn't exist.
The weapon loadouts are lacking as well. Again, this is all part-and-parcel of the realism aspect, but if you're playing as the rifleman, for instance, you get one weapon only - a rifle. You can spend points on getting one or two different versions of said rifle, but the rifle is all you have. Which means that if there's only one spot left on a team, you're stuck with one weapon and one weapon only, and you don't get a say in things.
Verdun is a mixed bag. This is clearly just a first impressions review, but I immediately found there to be a few glaring issues with the game, as much as I enjoyed most of my time with it. Once you come to grips with and start getting kills there's a certain bitter joy that comes with laying down some of the punishment you've been going through yourself. It feels authentic to a degree (I mean, they can't make a game about sitting in a bunker and getting shelled for three straight days), but there are also points where it feels clunky beyond the realism. It's not a perfect multiplayer game, and the distinctive WW1 setting doesn't set it apart as much as it would like to, but the balance of difficulty means that it skirts some of that frustration awaiting new players entering an older MP game. I recommend it for super cheap - when I last logged on only 148 people were playing, and while my game was more-or-less full, that points to a rather short life span.

I got it for $1.99 during a Steam sale, and I feel like I got more than my money's worth.  Easily 50 hours of entertainment.
It is a bit older than it looks on the store page.  Release date says 2012, but it's a rerelease of a 2009 title.  It does need the 4gb patch to run well on a modern system.  You can read more about that in the forums and guides.
There's a lot of solidly built open world fantasy games out there, so I'll focus on what I feel sets this one apart from the others.
+At a certain point in the story, your character gains the ability to transform at will into a giant, flying, fire-breathing dragon.  It's pretty cool.
+The game rewards the kind of players who like to ignore the main quest, go looking everywhere for side quests and loot everything that's not nailed down.  Your character is a mind reader, and most of the characters you meet have something to discover, whether it's hidden loot, or a minor quest.
-The game expects you to notice some very small things in your environment, but the problem is the graphics aren't that great, even on max settings.  Sometimes, even reading an online walkthrough, it's hard to find a tiny square button you need to press that's barely distinguishable from its surroundings.

While Dark Souls 2 is by far the weakest entry into the trilogy, it is still an absolutely solid game and the Scholar of the First Sin edition only adds to that. With re-worked enemy and item placement, new story, a new final boss and all the DLC inculded this makes SOTFS the definitive version of Dark Souls 2.
Improving over the original Dark Souls in many aspects, such as allowing for better build diversity and improvements on the magic system that has more unique spells instead of multiple versions of the same basic projectile, or the addition of powerstance, which allows dual-wielding builds to be fully viable, instead of almost useless in the first game.
However DS2 has some serious flaws in it that cement it into the worst game of the trilogy for many people, The new adaptability stat was a terrible addition in my eyes, as it causes your roll invulnerability frames to be dependant on a stat intead of armour weight, causing you to get slaughtered early in the game if you can't nail your very small roll window in certain situations.
The enemy placement, while better than the origional DS2 still has a fair sare of problems, such as dropping you into gank encounters often, where you must fend off against multiple strong enemies who can easily overwhelm you, or the much worse world desing, instead of the almost seamless feeling of DS1, you instead almost feel like you teleport to certain locations through tunnels that are much shorter than makes any realistic sense.
However what absolutely carries my opions of DS2 into very positive is the content found in the DLC, which in classic Souls tradition can be wildly considered to be the best part of the game, with incredible boss fights, level design, a ton of new items, spells and weapons almost makes the DLC feel like something from the other entries of the series, which is something base DS2 definately needed.
Dark Souls 2: Scholar of the First Sin is flawed, however it absolutely deserves a place in what is arguably the most influential trilogy of the decade.
