Game Review
The game, as directed from the title is a dungeon based defence game in which the player builds towers in order to stop enemy minions from destroying the main base. As well as the main objective on the harder maps, are side objectives which the player needs to defend otherwise it will allow for more enemies, often flying types to be able to access the map making it harder especially without certain classes.
Logical thinking is required by the player to complete for ever changes and more difficult maps. As the game calls upon the player to think through the use of their 'Tower Budget' whilst building defences to stop the enemy minions form reaching the main base, the better the tower the higher the cost. Along with the budget, the player has the choice of class types, which impacts the levels massively, as depending on what characters are on the team during the missions effects the difficulty as some cannot attack air units or some are not able to take as many hits as others.
Along with the thinking required is the effect of the choices made, as in the game they are able to have a very negative or positive outcome as for example having a Mage try to tank hits from enemies would be a poor choice compared to having a knight tank the hits. But there is a lot more than just deciding what person defends where, each player chooses their class each one having different abilities or attributes that can help the team and as stated above the choice of towers will be one to rule all or end all within an instant.
Considering these whilst looking at the game play allows you to see that things are coming together well, the game entices the player into what is called a 'one more round' mood, in which if a player is enjoying the game by winning or by having or rethink the same map several times to pass. As well as being able to invite friends to have a more cooperative team and a more thrilling experience as everyone will be able to have a laugh no matter what the outcome.
Overall my experience with Dungeon Defenders 2 was a good experience and produced a lot of good points, however with every game there are a few things that can be tweaked. Such as the enchantment system as I never truly understood it whilst using it and the glitch at the main hub (tavern) where players fall through the floor.
Overall i give DD2 a 9/10 rating.

First of all i have to say you've done an amazing job at making the sequel to dungeon defender, its everything i hope it to be and more. Firstly lets go over the game play, dungeon defenders two is a 3D tower defense game basally but more vamped up than you typical td game. You play as one of 4 characters that is available at the moment due to the game being in pre alpha, which is the apprentice, monk, huntress and squire. The apprentice a ranged fighter and is useful for placing down extremely high dps towers that deal aoe dmg but is quite squishy and has low base dmg. The huntress is a high dmg sniper with medium dmg traps they can place down, useful for taking out flying monsters. the squire is a tank with towers that deal a medium to high single target dmg, but makes up for the single target problem by tanking while his towers takes down mobs. Lastly is the monk, who is a melee fighter who deals aoe dmg and also has medium dmg aoe towers but he has extremely hard times dealing with flying enemies.
The game play that is available at the moment is both challenging and fun at the same time, along with that all maps are beatable with the right strategy which is necessary to have in more higher level maps. The strategy element in the game has been quite nice at the moment,  to be able to win any map you need to use a certain amount of strategy by coordinating with your team mates, for example having the tank take multiple lanes and drawing agro while the towers kill off the enemies. This level of strategy in placed is at a good balance where you can easily pick up how to play properly and the learning curve is quite gentle to newer players to jump right in and not feel way out classed.
The texture of the game is quite nice with no eye sore images where its to bright or to dark, and doesn't require a high end computer to run the game at a nice medium quality. so far the game has no bugs to be found and from my experience has a smooth game play experience and is really enjoyable to relax with.
overall the only aspect of the game which annoys me is the enchanting system in place, it clunky and slow as well as costing way to much gold to the ratio that you earn per level you win. in my opinion i would make an option to fast enchant the item you're trying to upgrade along with reducing the cost of enchanting slightly or increase the gold income per round or income for selling items
Other than that i would highly recommend the game to all players that are into this type of game.

Quite a unique ARPG - which I commend it for. It's also a surprising amount of fun.
It differs from most other ARPG's in several ways. Firstly, the control scheme is more skill based - using the WASD keys to move and also features dodging and jumping. Combat is also much more skill-based, rather than build-based. At any point in the game you can swap out destiny cards, weapons and demon powers (more on these later) to completely alter your play-style (a bit like Diablo 3's skill system in that regard).
Loot has a great importance in this game (perhaps even more so than most other ARPGS). The reason for this is that how you equip your character determines your "class" (as such) - there are no attribute points or skill points to be assigned at level-up. Instead, you are given health and destiny card boosts as you level up, allowing you to equip more powerful items and further customise your build to your liking.
Each weapon type in the game (Scythe, Hammer, Sword, Rapier, Shotgun, Lightning Gun, Tome) has its own unique attacks and skills associated with it. Swapping a different weapon in gives you instant access to these skills, regardless of how you have otherwise equipped your character, offering a fair amount of diversity.
Destiny cards are items that you can equip in special slots that can dramatically alter your "build". Some increase attack damage, critical chance and armour, others can dramatically alter the way your character works. Each card has an equipment value - so you can only equip cards that stay under your maximum destiny card amount. You can also upgrade cards to increase their potency at the cost of more points to equip. It ends up being a juggling act, getting the cards you want equipped at the same time while not exceeding your total.
Demon Powers are the "super move" you can activate when your overdrive bar has enough charge. Overdrive is built up in different ways depending on the armour (outfit) you equip. You can have it build up over time, when you attack or even when you crit. You can eventually equip two demon powers at a time - with effects ranging from buffing (health, armour, regen) to attack damage "spells". These, like destiny cards, can be upgraded and swapped out at will.
Graphically it looks good enough - and it also has some very well done music and sound effects. It also features the voice actor who did the Witcher games - Geralt, which was a pleasant surprise. Story-wise it's nothing to write home about, but then people don't usually buy ARPG's for their story anyway. It also features multiplayer co-op (internet) and even local co-op, which adds a great deal of value to the game as these are so much more fun with friends.
All-in-all, it's a well polished and enjoyable ARPG, which strives to mix up the formula a bit. This makes it feel fresh and fun, with some great combat and fluid gameplay. It suffers from being a bit short and lacking in certain customising aspects.

Hi there! This game is Fallout 3, a post-apocalyptic game from the wonderful developers of Bethesda Softworks. This game is over 6 years old, but despite the short main story in the game, there's still a good amount of content to go about. The game world is open, the Capital Wasteland is inhabited by many things, some friendly but most things you'll meet are going to want to tear you apart and use your skull for decorating. But how about the DLC? Well I'll tell you. The only DLC that I have currently is called "Operation Anchorage", the story of the DLC is that in broad strokes you're helping fight the Red Chinese in the American Reconquest of Alaska, it gives you an insight into how a soldier lived before the Great War, daily putting his life at stake for the greater good of America, and the defense against Communism! You also need a DLC to continue playing after you continue the main storyline though... I don't know, I don't mind myself, but of course the DLC also gives you an expansion to the story, which I won't really go into, because it would spoil some... Things... Let's keep it at that, I guess you may have already had it spoiled anyways but I wouldn't wanna be the person that does it.
Beware though, multiple people are complaining about the game being unstable on Windows 7 and even more so on 10 I've only had it crash twice, one being because I messed with the game files... I only had one glitch as well, and it wasn't gamebreaking.
Questions I'd like to ask myself if I had no idea about Fallout:
Q: Why wouldn't I buy Fallout 1 and 2 or Tactics first?
A: You can do that, but the three first games are different to 3 and New Vegas in the sense that it's isometric top-down view in those games. There are also major graphical glitches on some system, but they should be fixable with an unofficial patch somewhere I believe... In comparison to newer Fallout games, which can be played either as 3rd person, or 1st person, I personally play as 1st person because it's more immersive.
Q: Is there/what is the levelcap of Fallout 3 without any DLC and does DLC make a difference for the levelcap?
A: In comparison to Fallout New Vegas where the levelcap can be 50 with all the DLC (30 without any at all) Fallout 3 only has a levelcap of 20, however this can be raised to 30 if you have the Broken Steel DLC, which is also the name of the DLC that allows you to play on after the end of the main Story.
Q: What are the main differences between Fallout 3 and New Vegas?
A: There's a number of them, mainly the factions system that they included in New Vegas, and also the removal of percentage chance to have a successful special dialogue option in favor for the more simple "Have X amount of points in Y skill, and you will be successful in this special dialogue." There are mods however, that allow you to switch it back I believe. Also that Fallout 3 by default has a color filter that makes everything look greener, whereas in New Vegas it makes the game look more orange-yellowy. There is a mod to turn this off called Fellout for both games, and I highly recommend it as I like being able to see specific colors instead of them being tinted either green or yellow. The locations are also vastly different as Fallout 3 takes place in the bombed ruins of Washington D.C and New Vegas takes place in the Mojave desert at Las Vegas (New Vegas in the game, surprise surprise) also the ability to disguise onself as a faction is New Vegas... It's something I don't really use but it can definitely be helpful in some situations, like when you don't wanna cause a shootout, and need to stay stealthy.
This has been my review for Fallout 3 and I hope you liked it, patient reader. At first I thought I would just adress that the game is far from unplayable with Windows 7/10 as some people claim that it is, but it may vary from system to system I suppose.
Thank you for reading, and I hope I convinced you somewhere along the way to buy Fallout 3.

Banished is one of my favorite games in recent years. Thus I recommend Banished wholeheartedly, but I want to help you understand what you're getting. You're not getting a broad game with whiz-bang graphics. You're not going to get something that's going to get your pulse going. You're not getting something that's going to give you the feeling of dominating the world.
You're getting a software toy in one of the purest senses of the word. You're getting a suble, refined and elegant experience that allows you to build a simple medieval village. And once you've done so, you sit back and take pride in your handiwork in crafting that village. That's it. That's the entire point of the game. It does this marvelously.
There's no invading goblin forces. There's no magic. No gold to give to the king, no Robin Hood, no mysterious cave to explore. There''s no foozle to kill. There's a lot of things Banished is not. It is a narrowly tailored game about staying alive and sheparding your village towards being a vibrant and sustaining place to live. Your principle opposition is the environment itself, creating a balanced ecosystem and trying to maintain that balance as simple factors like weather, village width, population aging and a bad havest try to throw it out of balance. It's both simple and complex at the same time.
The game is complete and the developer is done with it. From my standpoint he crafted a thing of beauty. Personally, Banished is one of those games I revisit from time to time and I always have a great, relaxing experience doing so. It's like putting on your favorite sweatshirt. It fits well and it feels great.
Now for those who want more, there are Workshop Mods including the comprehensive Colonial Charter mod that add so many different options to the game. So if you like buildilng games with an attention to detail then Banished is for you. It remains one of my favorites in my ever-growing Steam library.
PS - Even over a year later I keep coming back to this to play it.

Being quite a big Disney Fairies fan over the years, I quickly bought this upon its arrival on Steam. Are my experiences with it enough to recommend it?
It plays a lot like the DS games based on the Tinker Bell movies. Manouvre around a 2D map of small locations, collect things, talk to people, and play some minigames. The flight mechanisms feel wonderful to fly around with. Most of the scenery looks nice. But the story mode, which is the only mode that feels like a proper mode, feels like a collect-a-thon in almost every level. To fulfill deliveries, or to begin with equipment repairs, you need to find specific items scattered around.
And those are for the very most part flower seeds, other seeds, and berries, scattered around on specific (or sometimes random) screens; except for a few items that can be only gathered through minigames. But collecting items is what virtually every level of the game is about, in their essence. Each level takes place during a season of the year, or rather, in-between when they change the seasons on Earth a few times a year. Though, each season-themed level only really consists of one task that needs to be done, before they pretty quickly skip forward to the next season. Thankfully, there are still more than just 4 levels in the game.
I do like calm games. I do like games where I can just play around. This game completes that task, although it had big problems keeping my attention after a while, due to the repetitive feeling I got from most of the game. New areas are continuously discovered during gameplay, but the map screens aren't all that much bigger than they were in the DS games, where they were really tiny.
The graphics deserve a paragraph by themselves. For everything in the world, you will want to click the High Quality button in the settings, and not even then does it really reach even 720p (My bet is more on 1024x600, but my eyes could in theory have deceived me). The intro sequence's use of very low-quality footage from Tinker Bell 1 is also a bit of an oddity to behold.
Canonwise, despite the thumbnail's use of Lost Treasure clothing and scenery, the game goes better along with Tinker Bell 1, from which many in-game locations and some characters hail from.
I have been uncertain as to whether to give this Thumbs Up or Thumbs Down. It has given me a Disney Fairies non-DS game at long last, but the long-term gameplay, and the graphical quality (which for one time's sake actually is complainable about), does not deliver. At €17 at the time of purchase, I felt like I had overpayed even when I did like the feel of the game. If it ever gets somewhere below €12 (the further down, the better) and you're a very long-term Disney Fairies fan, then it could qualify as "More content. Yay!". But I have to stoop down against one of the franchises in my life that has meant the most to me, and say Thumbs Down.

Public opinion of this game is that it's a VERY well done "Souls like" game that just happened to be made by FromSoft so they could get away with calling it Dark Souls 2. And there's definitely a lot in there to support that notion.
- There is hardly any overlap with the lore in Dark Souls 1 (Drangleic instead of Lordran, no demons, what's Lindelt?, only some vague references to the gods of the first game). This wouldn't have been so bad hadn't Dark Souls 3 turned 180 degrees and went right back building on the original's game's lore and characters, barely acknowledging DS2 even existed. Had the third game ALSO been a completely different setting Dark Souls 2 would seem right in place. But the public was too enamored with Lordran, Onion Knights and Gwyn. So now Vendrick and company stick out like a sore thumb.
- Everything works a differently enough to make switching between the games feel awkward. Parries are slower and need a break between the parry and the riposte. Drinking your Estus heals a LOT slower. Greatswords don't swing by lock on. You need adaptability for good invincibility frames on rolling. Weapon durability matters a LOT more (where in the first game it, as long as you were even slightly aware of it it might as well not have existed).
- Level interconnectedness is "off". Going from Undead Burg to The Depths to Blighttown to Demon Ruins to Lost Izalith was almost seamless in Dark Souls 1. You could often SEE the next zone from the previous one. Going from Aldia's Keep to Dragon Aerie is jarring to say the least. Not to mention the now legendary transition from top of Earthen Peak taking an elevator UP to the sunken in lava Iron Keep.
But this is all comparing to a game that was practically revolutionary at the time. Fact of the matter is, it remains a game VERY well done. The lore is deep. Levels are rich and often winding. Weapon variety is unparalleled and you can almost use anything with anything and succeed. There are a LOT more ways to make gameplay easier if you're struggling and to make the game harder if you think you've mastered it. And once you do, start to master it that is, you'll wonder what everyone's fussing about.
With the release of Scholar of the First Sin technical issues are non-existant making the only barrier of entry having a decent controller (I heartily recommend an Xbox360 or Xbox One controller). That the game remains popular is shown how every Steam sale the there's a resurgence in popularity. Summoning help is easier, forums are alive and suddenly you can get invaded again!
Now if only my PC Gaming Friends would hop on :)

Quckly things get out of hand and you end up trapped in a grisly asylum with nothing but your legs to carry you through. Hang on, because this ride gets bumpy.

Sound: 80% of what makes this game creepy is the sound. You'll actually want to use the sound to your advantage. Most of the times you'll hear a cue that tells you that you better haul♥♥♥♥♥to a hiding spot. Your character also breaths very heavy when danger is lurking which adds a nice effect to the horror.

OLDTV is a mental reflex simulation game. You have simple test, left click when the word and the font colour matches and right click when they don't. E.g. Left click on White but Right click on Red. All of this is done within a limited time frame and with increasing difficulty. As the game progresses, the screen will flicker, the images will blur and the screen will become grainy. These are all visual effects that 90's children would have noticed on their old CRT televisions.
Conclusion, not my cup of tea. The whole match-colour-match-word idea is a silly simulation. There are other variants that were used to test children and adults. Sadly, this is all that the entire game hinges upon. It just can't make it interesting enough to play. Flickering screens are seriously a bad move.

This is one of my favourite multiplayer games.
It works like this: every player picks a part-- a block, a moving platform, a spinning sawblade, whatever-- from a random selection.  All at the same time, they place these parts on the map.  Then, everyone must try to find a way through the platformer obstacle course they just built.  You get points for making it to the end (and a couple of other things); a game usually takes many rounds, with the map and your strategies evolving as you go.  There are other modes, where you can always choose your piece, and you race one-by-one, but you should probably just stick to Party.
By default, the game ends after a certain amount of rounds, even if no-one scored high enough.  I would recommend you turn off max game length, because the true UCH begins about twenty rounds in, when all the sawblades and projectile launchers are attached to moving parts, when every black hole has a cloud of burning tennis balls in orbit, when there are so many portals on the map, you lose track of which goes where.  There are times when the spawn zone is no longer safe, and everyone needs to sprint as soon as the game begins to survive.  There are times when a level is literally incompletable, and everyone acknowledges it's incompletable, and instead of putting stepping-stones across the unjumpable gap you all just add more crossbows.  And there are times when you just sprint headlong into a whirling heap of machinery, and make it out the other side, and don't really understand why.
The game has some technical issues.  It bugs out sometimes: occasionally a moving piece will fail to move for all players (usually starts moving the next round), or a pair of portals will fail to connect for all players (usually stays that way all game).  Often there are tiny desyncs between people's games, and you'll see a player floating next to a platform, or getting shot over and over without dying (any damage kills instantly, normally).  These bugs tend to be "fair", in the sense that that other player is completing the course properly ON THEIR SCREEN, just not on yours.
The platforming itself feels good, the controls are fairly responsive, and I've never found myself annoyed at my character failing to move the right way.  Never needed to use a controller.  I've lagged out occasionally, but I think that's more my internet than a failure of the game.
Anyway, this game is entertaining and rewarding, and worth full price, as long as you can get a bunch of friends to buy it as well.

The Napoleonic age was by far the most ironic era for warfare in terms of beauty and romantisism but its very opposite relation with the brutal afair of war times. CA did do right to extend the 18th and early 19th century warfare, and with it, they were able to get the uniforms pretty close to what they wore... well... not quite. Some uniforms are a little cartooney in nature and some of it fantasized, which when i found out kinda made me loose interest. But i eventually found myself going back to it. (Explain later). one big thing about this game is that a large modding community is owned by it and they are, in my opinion, very decent historians for the skins and even custom units that arnt even in Vanilla or the DLC purchassables.
So, after modding it with Darthmod, Napoleon total Combat, and Napoleonic total war 3, all very prestiegous and respected mods, i found myself clining to this game and settling on NTC, and Napoleonic 3. One for having a broad 40 unit Army factor, and the other having a very to-Earth tatical over veiw.
The game in Vanilla in my opinion, is kinda poorly done. I remmeber when i was facing thr AI, which became very perdictable and famous for just making the old 'form a huge line of the army' strategy and either approach mine head on and inevitably be repulsed dozens of times, or i flank both their sides in my attack and eventually let them cave in. I Even tried Expert difficulty to get a thrill going, but later i found it just makes it impossible to beat the AI by terms of being buffed up in Stats only. abotu 2 to 5x that of the players army and its ability to have less upkeep/recruiting costs.
I did, though, have a fun time with the annexation of countries and how the people were either somewhat reluctant or very repressive, and trying to restore their own country again when im not looking. And i mean it quite literly, they did do it when i wasnt looking. Sometimes i got away with the tax exempt tatic to calm the masses, but other times that just hurt my economy and myself in slowing my campaign against a neigboring country.
In terms of what the battle looks like, id say its really dazzling at some moments. To See huge clouds of smoke gather with the vollies, and the gleam of cavlary sabers in a massive charge, and the rotation of the day made quite a spectacle. And i then found myself addicted to the old Russian 4 movie series of War and Peace, Napoleon 2002 series, and Waterloo. Even watching unoffical Napoleonic war videos and movies and even reenacting clips.
So i would say in a finally answer:
Vanilla mode = 6.5/10 : the reason being is that ive been a fan of the TW series for a while, and i knew they could do better than this. A very large 16 to 20 stack enemy army jsut forming a huge line became rather boring and very easy to beat, and left me concluding that using expert just to beef up an already lame brained AI's army, was a very lazy way to go.
However, i am very impressed with how the people want to be heard, no matter how powerful you are or how far away you are. Id be quite♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥too if someone looted my home town,♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥for possibly 20 more turns maybe.
The multiplayer, is a completely different experience in my opinion. The Revoltionary idea of having multiple players for a campaign map game is very engenius of CA to create, and it was very enjoyed to replace the AI. (unlike Rome 2 which is only 2 player campaign) And sometimes it made a very difficult struggle just to forge an Empire for yourself whilst just annexing minor states.
As I said before, the dazzling scene of the battle is breathtaking, and it even jumps a mile and a half away from the dullness of the secene of battle such as in Empire TW or its predessor Medieval 2. It does have a way of keeping things fresh, nice looking, and colorful whilst having a strong dose of destruction with it.
Though my final verdict isnt all to great, my final verdict of the game WITH mods, is a strong 8.7/10. Though most mods, large and small, are rough around the edges, they are not all created equal. I once thought that Darthmod would be my only choice of a true, realistic experience, but then i decided to broaden the horizens with other mods like Order of War and things of that nature. And even the refined mod Napoleon Total Combat has its own MP set up on the way to jumpstart it up again, in a more clear way it shouldve been, and the AI is none the less smarter than vanilla, save the sucidal generals an occasional light cav.
Thankyou for reading my reveiw, and by all means message me for whatever reason in contrast with this awsome base game. See ya then

Please treat with caution before you purchase this game. If you need an epic musket line battle simulator then this game is spot on. The battle aspect of the game has very epic battle scenes and astonishingly satisfying graphics. The naval battles are also really enjoyable to watch with top-tier ship of the line models. However, eye candy as it is, the player might spend the majority of their battle keeping the general alive and tweaking formations. SInce there is no chain of command, the game is pretty demanding for the player as he has to micro each line as well as the whole battle. Simiarly in naval battles, the player is offered an interface more suitable to command each ship, instead of a fleet. The grand strategy aspect of the campaign has little synergy with the battle part, and is flawed in various ways. The player cannot make any significant decisions like when to start a war and make an ally, but are given timed mission to capture certain places. Decisions the player made, like teching and build infrastructures, hardly make any differences. The game also didn't represent Napoleon well. In this game Napoleon seems nothing more than a power-hungary prick eager for land. If you want to learn more about Napoleon, this is not the place to go.

No contest (with me) this is my game of 2014.
Extremely well designed and has the best customizable UI that I can think to come up with.
This is a city building game with its emphasis on survival, set in a low tech age. What you can build is based on resourses and better buildings are always available. It is a matter of collecting rather than unlocking. To restate, this is a survival game rather than a build your dream town style builder.
The main part of the entertainment is coming to understand the interconnecting systems. What is good to trade, what should I focus on each season, how to produce the most food, etc.. The only thing I think that isn't well signaled is villagers aging. While the rest of the game is set on a yearly system, the town folks seem to age at 4 to 6 times that, and at a certain age they no longer move out to couple and breed.
Overall: If you think survival town building sounds fun, and direct your play with the achievements, you'll get much enjoyment out of this title.

It really makes me sad to have to do this, but I would not recommend this game. Let me be clear, I'm not a "Dark Souls is too hard" person. I have beat DS 1 and 3 on xbox and ds3 on pc. I love Dark Souls as a franchise.
However, this feels way to, for lack of a better term "Video Gamey". I come to Dark Souls for fast paced and tight combat. I come to Dark Souls for rolling, open landscape and dense lore. I come to Dark Souls for the merging of mechanics and narrative in a way few other developers can capture.
Dark Souls 2 is a perfectly servicable game. It's just not a good souls game. Miyazaki, the director of DS1, DS3, and Bloodborne wasn't in charge of this one, and it really shows.
Pros:
-Runs amazing right out of the box (looking at you DS1).
-A lot easier than DS1 or 3, so if your new to the series, this might be a good place to start.
-Weapons repair at bonfires. Thank God this carried over to DS3.
-More active servers than DS1 or DS3
-You can wear more than 2 rings
-Ladder sprinting
-PVP is more balanced and learning the nuances and complexity can be fun.
Cons:
-(This may sound dumb, but this broke the game for me) The art design of the levels is terrible. Traditional dark souls designs the level first then figures out how the player will move through it (Anor Londo, Blighttown, Sen's fortress)  This game is exactly the opposite. Every set piece feels inorganic and unreal. You could never picture anyone living here, and it breaks immersion. I'm always hyper aware that I'm playing a game.
-The game is designed to be intentionally unreasonable to the player with enemy placement. It's obviously trying to capitalize on the "Dark souls is a hard game" marketting. It's not hard, it's just irritating. I played recklessly for an hour and a half with no deaths.
-Combat is slow and far too easy. Inevitibly comes down to hitting first.
-Invincibility frames are variable, so it's always a guessing game about if your roll will dodge the enemy attack.
-Enemies attacks track the player during the attack animation so you have very little time to dodge.
-Art design feels very generic fantasy (see female bandit and smelter demon armor)
-Levels are unintuitive and hard to organically figure out. Invisible walls (The kind you can't pass, I don't mean illusory walls), unclear signposting of which direction is forward, and generally chaotic and amatuer design.
-Breaks the traditional monomyth narrative iconic to dark souls and makes the story about the player rather than the world (Not a bad thing for most games, just not great from dark souls)
-Bland soundtrack.

After being somewhat apprehensive about the Divinity series, I'm very glad to have started with Divinity II: DC.  A good bridging point for those who are curious about the lore/setting, but are more comfortable playing action-adventure RPGs with simpler but effective combat of the late '00s.  Think of the first Witcher game, SW:KOTOR, Jade Empire and the like, that will give you a good idea of what to expect.
A nice engaging storyline, plenty of decent voice acting and plenty of in-between content aside from the main quests. Don't expect any realistic physics though, as it is neither present or important for this game.
Bought this game on sale for a bargain at $2.  I believe it is worth the asking RRP ($20 as of this review) but a half-price discount would still be a great jump-in point for the uncertain.  I'll be giving the turn-based and more in-depth Original Sin entries in the series another look once I'm done with this.

This is now one of my top favorite competitive multiplayer games of all time. It offers some unique experiences compared to other multiplayer shooters: The assault-occupy-and-counter-attack structure of the trench warfare system is engrossing and fun, plus everyone is forced to follow the structure or be executed, which prevents everyone from running off on their own and doing whatever to ruin the system, which is a good thing to me. The WWI-era weaponry and the fairly realistic implementation of it adds depth and strategy that the typical run-and-gun bullet-spraying shooter doesn't have, and adds tension to every encounter. And the squad and class systems add tons of additional strategy and experimentation as well. The game also has experience points and ranks that unlock additional loadouts for each class, so it can stand with the best AAA multiplayer shooters in that regard too. In my opinion, Verdun does WWI better than the big budget EA-release Battlefield 1 did, so I highly recommend this game to anyone curious about what a WWI-themed shooter should really be like.

(Before reading further, realize that my hours logged are not accurate as I was in offline mode for most of the time I played this. In reality I got a few hours in.)
Call of Cthulhu is a good adventure game that was killed by the malignant tumors of terrible action and terrible stealth. My attempts at playing showed me something important about videogames: the enjoyability of a game's story will be bottlenecked by the enjoyability of the gameplay because one must play the game to progress through the story.
The game starts out as a first person adventure game that gives you interesting puzzles, environments, and notes about the world. Everything this game needed to be great was more or less present in the introductory stage.
But everything falls apart once fishmen start trying to kill you. It took me several tries to escape the first room where the action starts. The game requires a fairly specific sequence of actions in a limited time, and if you don't divine what the developper wants you to do, then gameplay can devolve into trial and error. Trial and error is the arch-nemesis of immersion, and immersion is all too vital for horror games. In other words, I didn't so much get a scary horror experience as I did a fishpeople themed level of McPixel.
And there are stealth sequences. The problem with those are that the stealth mechanics flat out don't work. If an enemy sees one square centimeter of you hiding in the shadows, then everyone knows your exact position. Moving quietly is so slow that it is impossible to cross the distances you need to cross without getting spotted. Your trials and your errors will once again make you try the same section over and over and your immersion once again is broken.
Of course, the game compensates for these issues by making fishpeople have aim that makes stormtroopers look like elite marksmen by comparision. A fishpeople with a double barrell shotgun five feet away has a good chance of missing you standing still. So if you are anything like me, you will probably be finding yourself dawdling circles around armed fishpeople because it is often the path of least resistance.
And guns. I will admit that the handguns and the rifle feel kind of nice, but that is kind of irrelevant. The game claims you should take cover during combat. The problem with that is that when you lean around cover, your sights don't line up right when you aim. And there is at least one level where I am certain that enemies were respawning.
There are more nitpicks I can make. Like how enemies disappear as soon as they die, further damaging your immersion. Or that the health system makes it such that if you get hit, you will become too crippled to get yourself out of danger.
I didn't make it too far into this game. I reached a point where I continued only because I hoped the game would start being enjoyable if I stuck with it. I've learned that if I ever reach such a point, I should probable stop wasting my life on such a game.
There is promise in this game, but the problems are so annoying and so overhwelming that I can not recommend this game to anyone. The promise of Lovecraft's world being made real is bundled with some truly awful gameplay that would take extreme tolerence to plod through.

Every time I play an ARPG I inevitably compare it to Diablo 2, which from my point is still today the best and most influential ARPG ever created. Somehow thinking about Diablo 2 usually makes me look down on other games, but Victor Vran is different game. This is a great game for one simple reason: it's tremendously fun to play.
Just like in a few other modern games, you don't get to choose among different classes. Instead, your skill set depends on the weapon you use, which I find pretty cool. That means that when you're tired of a certain play-style you can just choose a different weapon and that's it. That's also good for another reason, which is that each level has a number of challenges you can complete if you want and some of them require you to use a specific weapon, which you can all do with the same character.
As for customisation, or what makes your character different from others, there's only gear. You've got a transmutation system which is quite similar to Diablo 2's Horadric Cube, where you combine some items and get a new one. This way you can upgrade your weapons.
Something I really like playing with is Destiny Cards, which you can equip and obtain certain passive abilities. I like using different ones depending on the situation, e.g. boss fights or aoe fights.
Overall I think it's a complete game with lots of things to do thanks to challenges and it's certainly not too complex, so you can actually start enjoying it right away.

Please treat with caution before you purchase this game. If you need an epic musket line battle simulator then this game is spot on. The battle aspect of the game has very epic battle scenes and astonishingly satisfying graphics. The naval battles are also really enjoyable to watch with top-tier ship of the line models. However, eye candy as it is, the player might spend the majority of their battle keeping the general alive and tweaking formations. SInce there is no chain of command, the game is pretty demanding for the player as he has to micro each line as well as the whole battle. Simiarly in naval battles, the player is offered an interface more suitable to command each ship, instead of a fleet. The grand strategy aspect of the campaign has little synergy with the battle part, and is flawed in various ways. The player cannot make any significant decisions like when to start a war and make an ally, but are given timed mission to capture certain places. Decisions the player made, like teching and build infrastructures, hardly make any differences. The game also didn't represent Napoleon well. In this game Napoleon seems nothing more than a power-hungary prick eager for land. If you want to learn more about Napoleon, this is not the place to go.

I only have 6h so far, so I cannot say much but I would like to share a little.
TIP: For the BLACK SCREEN BUG - go to your "my documents" folder and look the "The Crew" folder. Inside it, you will find a file called "PCScalability.xml". Open it up with notepad, and look up for a line that contains the word " Appearance= ". Now, after the equals sign, you will have a number (usually 2) and all you have to do is, change it to 1 and save the file.
What this does is change the game from fullscreen mode into fullscreen borderless mode. I hope it helps.
Now for the review. Actually its more like a tiny story, but for me it tells a lot about the game and what it is about. But before all, mind that this game is NOT A SIM. In a scale of 1 (arcade) to 10 (sim) I would say 3.5/10.
I was driving around, trying to reach one of the missions on the map, then I got a call to support a package delivery (help someone to transport a package from point A to B, blocking cops along the way). I was like: allright, bring it! And all the suddend I found myself jumping from NY to LA in the middle of a crazy car chase. A few minutes later it was all over, the package was secure. Then I had to get back on track with my missions, and I was on the other side of the country. We always have the option to fast travel into places we've already visited, OR drive all the way. Instinctively I opened my map and started clicking for a fast travel. But then I realized: "That's not what it's all about. That's how I drive in other games, not this one." I grabbed the ultimate edition of the game and it comes with one of my favorite cars ever built the Nissan Fairlady Z. It was around 9pm in game when I started it, my tip back to NY and I drove that car in cockpit view for the most if the trip. I went thought the beautiful nevada desert, some snowy parts I have no idea where (I'm not from US sorry folks), and it was an extemely enjoyable 45min trip. Just me, my Z240, the night sky and some nice trip music.
Pros:
-Quite enjoyable driving.
-Tons of cars, with cockpit view.
-Tons of car kits that change the whole driving model of your car.
-Bikes!
-Amazing scenery!
-Awesome interface (I like it)
-Nice police chases.
-Seamless transition to join other player's match or persuit.
-Tons of micro events that you take part on the fly.
-Tons of hidden stuff to find.
Cons:
-Netcode can be problematic sometimes hahah.
-Crash psysics are a little inconsistent, sometimes crashing feels like hitting a wall of butter the car just slides off. Others you hit some invisible walls (only in very rare occations though).
-Controls -keyboard- can be a little rough, sometimes I have problems to make small adjustments and keep a straight line, making the car feel unstable.
-Drift is not as enjoyable and overly simplistic. It feels like your actual speed is dictated direcly by what gear you are (it feels clearly faster even though the indicated speed remains about the same).
-Drag is the same story, I missed a bit of the sim mechanics for tunning.
Wishes:
-More old school Rock music for long travels.
-More prominent engine sound.
If I would recommend it? Damn right I do!

I see myself sinking many more hours into this before getting tired of it and will certainly need that time to polish my building strategies.

This is now one of my top favorite competitive multiplayer games of all time. It offers some unique experiences compared to other multiplayer shooters: The assault-occupy-and-counter-attack structure of the trench warfare system is engrossing and fun, plus everyone is forced to follow the structure or be executed, which prevents everyone from running off on their own and doing whatever to ruin the system, which is a good thing to me. The WWI-era weaponry and the fairly realistic implementation of it adds depth and strategy that the typical run-and-gun bullet-spraying shooter doesn't have, and adds tension to every encounter. And the squad and class systems add tons of additional strategy and experimentation as well. The game also has experience points and ranks that unlock additional loadouts for each class, so it can stand with the best AAA multiplayer shooters in that regard too. In my opinion, Verdun does WWI better than the big budget EA-release Battlefield 1 did, so I highly recommend this game to anyone curious about what a WWI-themed shooter should really be like.

Medics don't heal but cap points and heavies are completely useless.
Despite all of this it's still a game I cherish. Today there might not be any people left playing but once upon a time this was the premier game for skill and teamwork.

Perhaps one of the most criminally overlooked RPG's to be released in the last decade, Divinity II is a unique entry in the Divinity series with much more action-oriented gameplay than any of its siblings. The class-building system is much simpler than Original Sin, but deep enough to be satisfying for the real-time action-based combat, with immediately noticeable impacts on each skill point spent. It has an excellent sense of player progression, starting you off feeling weak and frustrated with entry-level mobs and eventually being one of the most powerful and respected people in Rivellon: A Dragon Knight. That is, someone who can transform into a dragon at will and destroy anything by looking at it. Make no mistake, this game is a proper "power fantasy" RPG, complete with your own fortress and cast of servants eager to do your bidding and please you in any way they can. You start off collecting herbs for alchemy, or gems for enchanting, and suddenly find yourself telling one of your minions to gather them for you instead. Any of the tedium of resource collecting and crafting that Western RPG's are known for can quickly become a task delegated to someone less than yourself, with more efficiency than you ever could on your own, and it's just as awesome as it sounds.
Divinity II is often described as an open-world game which I really don't think is accurate. Open World implies a certain non-linearity and encourages the full exploration and travel of the world without loading screens separating specific "zones" aside from say, cities or dungeons. However Divinity takes the latter approach, with each zone distinct and seperate from one another, a loading screen between each one, and one specific path you take from zone to zone on every playthrough. Enemies aren't scaled to your level, but rather to the area they're in, making it very obvious which area you're expected to progress to at which point in the game. Once you clear the monsters out of the zone, they're gone, making it easier to traverse and explore as you play, which I actually found very rewarding. None of this is a bad thing, it's just more like "Fable" or "Zelda" than "The Elder Scrolls" and there's a lot of misleading information on the store page through tags and user reviews calling it "open world" when that's not at all what you're going to be getting into.
The game, like every other entry in the Divinity series, excels most in its NPC interaction and conversational dialog. The writing is very sharp and witty, and each NPC has its own distinct personality and motives, which means you'll be playing for the sidequests just as much as you will be for the main story. There's an obscene amount of voice acting in the game for all the characters, and it's amazing that a game like this can maintain the quality that it does across all voice actors and characters in the way that it can. Whereas many fully-voiced RPG's suffer from having every NPC sound dull, bored, and void of personality, Divinity II very obviously puts individual effort and care into crafting every character you meet. You can compare this to Skyrim, where everyone has the same robotic, empty projection using a small handful of recurring voices and feeling less like real people and more like quest vendors.
Unlike some of the other entries in the series, which certainly had their fair dose of humor, Divinity II seems to put its goofy, bonkers demeanor on center stage, rarely pausing for a moment of somber reflection for the world or its characters. While the story tells of an impending doom, entire cities and provinces being destroyed throughout the course of the game, it never uses it as an excuse for melodrama and instead embraces the wacky nature of Fantasy RPG's in a semi-satirical, wholly self-aware, and absolutely hilarious fashion, without ever stooping down to lazy attempts at 4th wall breaking or mocking tropes that it actively takes part in but acts like it's okay because they acknowledged it. Rest assured, it has the same wit and intelligent writing that the series is known for, and doesn't skimp on lore or in-game literature.
The game has tons of content, with lots of sidequests, skills, dialog options, and secrets. I certainly didn't do a completionist run by any means, though I did take my time in each city to do as many sidequests as I could be interested in doing and eventually completed the game at about 33 hours. Compared to other RPG's of this type, such as Fable, I think this is very generous and those with more motivation could easily go beyond this number if they wanted to. For me personally, I don't see much replay value in the game unless I wanted to play through the game again as a different class, since the zone-to-zone progression would make every playthrough feel a little too familiar for my taste. But if you're really keen on discovering how each sidequest and conversation plays out due to different decisions, I'm sure you could get another play or two in. Regardless, even as a single-playthrough experience, I thought it was well worth the time spent and hope more people discover this game after playing more popular recent entries like Original Sin 2.
NOTE: The game is not playable on Windows 10 right out of the box, you'll likely need to download a small patch file from Nvidia to use more than 4GB of RAM, otherwise it will give you an infinite loading screen when entering a building. In addition, the game is locked at 30fps, but emulates 60+fps by displaying the same frame twice. It's a cheap tactic that's very noticeable but I didn't find either of these issues inconvenient enough to prevent from enjoying the game.

Outlast, also known as "I'm not coming out of this locker until every enemy in the game dies of natural causes" simulator 2013!
It's been a long time since anything that even remotely resembled "horror" was implemented into a game properly (I'm looking at you, downward spiraling Konami/Capcom!) and for the first 2 minutes of the game, I thought it would be taking exactly the same route as the other "appeal to all audiences" horror-fluff experiences...
Well, my nerves beg to differ past that.
Not only is this an extremely beautiful game considering it's dark tones (which it captures perfectly), but it's game mechanics are absolutely solid.
Throughout my entire playthrough, I felt alone, helpess and completely exposed... and it felt great!
Each corridor, every pitch black corner, even doors left slightly ajar felt like a mountain to cross with each footstep building almost unbearable tension.
But even with it's unrelenting horror, curiosity pushed me forward. The story is extremely gripping, every room has it's own story, every creak in the floorboards whispers it's secrets to you, every abomination you encounter shares it's suffering.
I
enjoyed my time with Outlast, even if it was spent in 30 minute increments (half of those been spent hiding under tables with the last flicker of battery on my handheld video recorder barely lighting the flicker in the monsters eyes that were stalking me.)
If you're looking for a real horror experience, I guarentee you won't regret picking up this amazing game!

WOW .... I just paid £2.49 for three RPGs.  Two are a wonderful old school throw back to games such as Ultima and Fallout, and Divinity 2 is just brilliant.  I am hooked.  It reminds me most of some of the MMO games I have tried ... Conan, Guild Wars.  Do not come here looking for originality, but the mix of traditional fantasy with elements of Japanese MMO rpgs is superb.  It runs perfectly on my 1.8 GHz laptop - not gaming rig here (yet).  Divinity excells at colourful landscapes and light touches of humour, but clearly, from what I have just witnessed, they can also go very dark.
I am only seven hours in, but already know where the rest of the next few weeks will lie.  Or do I --- I expect there will be a few twists and turns to come.  Really great fun.  And I am also finding a lot to like in the earlier titles, too.  Divine Divinity is clearly a little gem.  It is fascinating to quest in the original Divinity world and then to see how the ideas here carry forward into the newer games.
This is my first experience of Divinity and its lore.  I am just thrilled to be in somewhere completely new and fresh, to me.  As others have mentioned, I would have been happy to pay £20 for Divinity 2, so three titles for less than £3 is insanely good value.  Thank you to all involved ..... "Victor Vran ARPG"
The title itself is implying that it is an action role playing game. I See action, I see the role my character plays in this world that I have no control over whatsoever. But I Dont see too many of the traits of a game I have described as RPG. Things like "What level am I", "What is my defence", "How much experience do I have", "How much damage should I be doing?" and more are just arbitrary for this game. Your level restricts the zones you can play in, And the zones scale to your level. The level restrictions seems only to be in place to keep you in the story zones, A "Story" which isnt very good. And you will never reach the level up of "wow I feel powerful" revisiting older levels (they scale up to you remember?).
The weapons of the game really do delagate how your character plays in the game, Next up would be the Destiny cards which put a buff on some stats, and sometimes a short term buffs, Finally your outfits have a set list of effects with pro's and con's. These 3 things are literally the only level of control over your character you have besides mashing X button, occasionally pressing Y, or B. And pressing A to jump for reasons of jumping over barrels that you have broken several times before in this "mission"

What is Victor Vran? It's basically an Action-RPG with direct controls, meaning you can use a controller and it feels more like a brawler than your typical ARPG, or maybe this IS the new definition of ARPG, I don't know. What I DO know is that it works rather well and the addition of a jump feature makes it even better.
In Victor Vran you take on the role of the titular hero trying to save the world. Of course. The story is more or less run of the mill, but the presentation is nice and there are a few twists here and there. The meat of the game, however, lies in its combat. You're not gathering loot and swapping for the best in slot items in the traditional sense, no, rather there are fixed "types" of weapons like swords, hammers, shotguns, lightning guns, etc. that you can equip as main or secondary weapon (doesn't really make a difference, but you can only carry 2 weapons at a time, so 1 melee and 1 range seems like a good idea). Each weapon type has its own skill set consisting of an auto attack and 2 active skills. The character itself does not have any skills, but you can equip potions and bombs, etc. to vary it up. This means that different weapons are best for different scenarios. You have to find that out yourself. Slow and heavy? Fast and agile? Single target or aoe?
This makes the game feel rather unique. Other items are so called demon powers, of which there are also different kinds, for example a living laser, a meteor shower, a shield, etc. Of these you can also equip 2 at a time. And then you can add some passive bonuses in form of destiny cards. You can equip only a certain number of cards and only a certain number of "points", so if you have 15 points available, you might equip 3 5-point-cards or maybe 5 3-point-cards or whatever.
There is also an upgrade system in the game, but I found it rather clunky and useless, as it increases certain values by just single points, so....waste of time. Once you get legendary weapons and items there is also no need to even gather any more. At least in the first playthrough. This is where the game's system really has an issue. Why should I swap out my legendary sword for my rare scythe? Yes, the scythe might be better suited in terms of skills, but it does way less damage and the sword has great attributes making up for it. For the last third of the game I used a sword which reduced my skill cooldowns to almost zero...there was no reason to ever use another melee weapon. Likewise with the ranged weapon which had a high amount of life return. I wished to use other weapons as well, but they were just not worth the bother any more...
Armor doesn't exist in the game by the way. You only have "outfits" and they have certain stats and features...that's it.
Getting through the story should take you around 12 hours, but the main reason to play the game is to 5-star each level. This means that you have to fulfill certain challenges like "kill 20 of x in y minutes" or "defeat x of y with weapon z" or "kill x with hexes y and z active". Hexes are difficulty modifiers that you can activate or deactivate to make the game more challenging. Some stars require the activation of 1 or more hexes. The challenges usually also can't be completed in 1 sessions, meaning you have to restart the level multiple times to get 5 stars.
After you have beaten the game you can complete even more challenges and an endless dungeon as far as I could tell. There is also a PvP component, but I'm not sure how many people even play that. If you have 3 friends, you can also take the enemies on in coop, which sounds like fun. If you're looking for long term motivation Victor Vran can offer that in the form of challenges and endless runs. If you just want to experience the story, get it during a sale. And also grab at least the weapon DLC, because the tomes are pretty cool ;)

Ok, I was honestly expecting that the latest release of Flatout will be the best so far. I have never been so wrong in my entire life and yet they got the name right: "chaos&destructrion" which fits perfectly to my hopes and dreams about this game. But here it goes, allow me to start with the good parts of this "masterpiece":
+it has steamworks
+it has achievements
+it has multiplayer and works well with the steam incorporation
+it gives you a good reason to appreciate the classics and your life in general
+it has wacky looking characters and vehicles, always good for a good laugh (since this entire game is a laughing matter)
And now...for the long and tedious negative list...I could probably just sum it up to: "It sucks!", but I will mention just a few of the downgrades (in comparison to it's predecessor it seems lesser of a game) and downfalls of the game:
-it crashes, sudden unavoidable and uncontrollable exit of the game (I have everything up to date, but not only for me, but also for others...it just gives an error and crashes)
-bad handling (not sure if this game was supposed to have handling that you would only see in those old car games, really rudimentary and quite disappointing)
-bad graphics (I know I played it on low, but I wasn't expecting to look worse than the first title)
-no community (hmm, I wonder why? *sarcasm* )

-it was not worth the price I paid at the time
And the list can easily continue for a lot...this is my experience from only an hour or so of gameplay...but, I will still recommend this game, because it really helps you to learn to appreciate what you have and, heck, how knows, you just might enjoy this game while you are drunk or feel like doing something really dumb, so why not keep it close for just those special occasions when you "dare to be stupid". This game really deserves it's metacritic score 2/10 .

This game gets a lot of♥♥♥♥♥♥for not being Dark Souls 1.5, but this is a terrific entry into the souls series with some great inovations and mechanics unfortunatly not found present in the future games sequels. Even tho the movement and fighting feel a bit slower they still have the same mechanics and pasing in other souls games which is the best in the genre, with the best build diversity in the series with more stats that matter allowing you to make a character the way you wish with multiple builds being the most effective they have been in the series, such as tanky armory builds, shield reliant ones, and even dual wielding with the very fun powerstancing mechanic. And of course the 4 schools of magic. Pyromancy, faith, inteligence and hex builds are all effiecient and viable which this series has struggled finding a balance in magic before, whereas in this game all of them feel satisfying in both pve and pvp. Speaking of pvp all the build diversity and options you have carry over, making it the best pvp in the series with fuctional arenas and hotspots, alongside invading mechanics and covenants that actually work allowing for invasions that feel almost as different minigames, such as protecting an area in a gaunlet type fashion with traps and mobs, or honorable duels that the victor gets closer to becoming a dragon.
In short anyone who played ds1 and enjoyed it will definitelly love this game all the same, at most the movement and combat will feel a bit floaty but the wordbuilding and variety is there all the same!

2. The tutorial ought to be a little longer. I presume 'inverted controls' means click the opposite button to the correct answer, but that seems to cause me to lose the game too, so I've ended up holding down the mouse button to skip the inverted controls parts. I don't understand why the game doesn't take you aside when you fail these sections and teach you how to progress- perhaps extend the tutorial as you unlock continents?
3. Again, issues with clarity. When buying a new continent for example, I eventually had to Google search what to do, since when buying other skills you just clip on the skill, but buying a continent requires clicking on the continent and then the price of the continent. The game seems to make the most basic things very counterintuitive- why not just have a 'click to buy' button or something?
Overall it's a very well polished game and the mechanics and ways it tries to trick you are very clever, but in a skill-based game that relies on player speed the player should never fail because they were cheated, e.g. the game displayed information after the player had made a decision, or because the player was unaware of what was required to progress.
Despite the crashes, this game is the bomb!

Being a DD1 veteran, I expected something deeply engrossing and fun. A game that would let you eventually break the game and feel mighty, a new wave of epic that you could never hit in the past game. What I got was an experience that ripped out half the turrets from the original, made all 4 characters feel samey rather than unique, and worst yet... brought enemies that can stand completely outside the line of fire from your turrets and just wreck your defenses completely.
Gone are the days where you set entire halls of traps to cover you while you held one side by yourself with some light defenses... No, in this game, you have to be all over the map at once, punishing solo players happily. I really hope you didn't enjoy solo Glittering, and sharing epic strategies, because this game has been so watered down in it's scope, chasing the "almighty perfect balance" that every character now feels rather bland. I'm sorry, but this doesn't feel like Dungeon Defenders. My defenses in DD1 were sturdy as heck, and allowed me to solo a lane while my defenses cleaned up the other. I am incapable of this at all in DD2.
The game also desperately pushes the idea for you to level multiple characters, rather than have a favorite. Don't like Monk? Tough, you better learn to love him and his itty bitty lightning aura that covers a small part of a lane. He and the Huntress are the only way to outdo the range throwers other than spamming upgrades on your turrets and hoping for the best. So far, I give this game a gigantic thumbs down, especially when compared to the game it came on the heels of. They promised me a deep, fun experience. All I got was something that made me feel like a quarter of a hero that I was in DD1.
TL;DR, if you're one of those guys that prefers tiny defenses barely doing anything, and feeling constantly weak to push that "omg so hard!"  button, you'll probably like it. If you liked feeling like a badass with turrets that fired halfway across the map, with giant explosions, rolling orbs of death that ran off gravity, and characters having unique styles that were colorful and epic... buy DDE.

Call of Cthulhu Dark Corners of the Earth is a game released back in 2005 on the original Xbox and PC in 2006. The game follow Jack Walters, a police detective who finds a manor in Boston filled with deranged pychopaths where he then finds something mysterious and terrifying which causes him to go unconcious. Six years later Jack is then a Private Detective who recieves a missing person's case in the town of Innsmouth, when investigating he then stumbles upon something more sinister and horrifying than anything he has ever seen which ultimately makes him start to lose his sanity.
The game's atmoshphere is by far one of the most atmosphereic games I've ever played, I was always paranoid thinking that something would pop up behind me, especially when I hear voices and Jack's rambling as he loses some screws. This is accomplished due to the lack of HUD (Heads up display) and well done sound design. When I think of atmosphereic games I always think of Call of Cthulhu.
The gameplay is a mix between adventure, shooter and horror. As a shooter it often trips and stumbles due to clunky shooting mechanics and inability to sprint. Which can make it needlessly difficult to shoot enemies.  As a horror-adventure, it does almost everything right. The mentioned masterful atmosphere, foreboding locations, horror sequences and unpredictabilty.
On your journey you can find med kits, ammunition and quest items littered around areas which are vital for your survival, this game isn't easy. In fact it may be too hard even on medium difficulty, many times I have died due to the fact that Jack cannot sprint and not get hurt from falling a few metres down, which makes things more frustrating to the point that it can almost ruin the brilliant atmosphere. Another problem with the game is the lack of navigation, don't get me wrong, I'm glad there is no HUD, but on more than a few occasions I had to look up a walkthrough to know what the hell I had to do, this lack of navigation can get so bad that a friend of mine actually ceased playing. The things you have to do can go beyond cryptic
When Jack witnesses horrific events (Alien beasts, dead corpses, screams) he will start to go insane, the more insane he gets the less control you have over him which can ultimately lead to him killing himself with his own gun, which can be pretty stressful in situations. Aside from early cutscenes, you almost never leave the 1st person view which helps immersive the player in this brilliant atmosphere.
The graphics of this game, for it's time, were very well done if a little dated with great textures and models as well at good animation. Sound design is again well done, with good voice acting from everyone in the game, especially Jack Walters himself, who has a real sense of panic.
Call of Cthulhu is not really a short game, it's more lengthened by the fact that there is no sense of navigation and the really difficult set-pieces. overall it took me roughly about 11 hours when trying to not use a walkthrough.
Last thing to mention is that this game is unfortunatly plagued with technical bugs, such as most of the dialogue being cut out at the end of the person's sentence, getting stuck in geometry, to even game breaking stuff such as this part where you're on a ship and you got to shoot down 3 towers, but if you're running on an operating system higher than windows XP, you cannot see the towers, if you want to fix this download the unofficial patch that modders managed to create, which resolves this issue by changing the script to where the game believes the towers are destroyed.
Call of Cthulhu is a game I can see that has poetential of being one of the greatest horror games of the past few years, but is held back by techincal issues and questionable game design choices. If developer headfirst managed to squash all the bugs and fix those issues, we would probably have one of the best horror games of all time.
As it stands though, Call of Cthulhu Dark Corners of the Earth is a game that you should check out if you can endure it's many bugs and issues and lose yourself in the game's brilliant atmosphere.

- Although I played Heroes V for some time and recall some improvements implemented before, the overall gameplay overhaul in Heroes VI is, for me, its greatest advantage. All the flaws of the Heroes III (which I am very fond of) are fixed and remade into intersting mechanics. I could name many examples, but I will focus on the two selected, the first being the Town Portal mechanics. In H3 all you ever wanted from your Hero was to have Earth Magic on Advanced level and a single Town with Town Portal spell to learn. If you could get it, you practically won the game, as you could jump around the world to collect your units and utilize a devastating mobility advantage. In H6 all units from given faction can be purchased in a single Town, provided it has all the necessary dwellings so there is no need to jump from town to town to accumulate the army. As for the mobility advantage, Town Portal is no longer a spell you have to learn - its a building you can create in any of your castles. Level 1 Town Portal allows a visiting hero to teleport to any other town or fort of his choosing and Level 2 Town Portal allows any here to teleport back to the city (nearest with L2 Town Portal) from any place on the map. As you can use only one of those spells on a single turn, Town Portal becomes a commodity and a feature of its own. The second noteworthy feature is the complete revamp of unit tiers. In the past units were categorized by 7 tiers, first one being the cheap weaklings and the last one being an all-powerful destroyer. Now you got pretty similar units but reworked into 3 tiers: Core (three first units), Elite (the next three) and Champion (the old Tier 7). All Core units are comparable in their usefulness and so are the Elites, but they got their traits that would work best for certain heroes (as the rule of a thumb, there is a Might unit, a Magic unit and a shooter in both Core and Elite tier). This makes creating your army more flexible and greatly increase the basic unit performance in comparison with Champions. Unit reclassification was the real gamechanger and a very welcome one.
+
- The environment is pretty amazing, especially in the campaign maps. The world is filled with random magical objects or unique decorations that really help to maintain the magical character of the world of Ashan. It is also very well optimizes for older graphic cards. Unit design is top notch and campaign posters (images seen when loading a campaign map) are simply fantastics.
+
- The world of Heroes has always been ridiculous and over-the-top with its magical theme, but I think this is the first time the main story actually embraced it and used it so effectively. The dialogues form a suprisingly coherent narrative for the main plot, which might not be written that greatly, but sure as hell is well voice-acted. I was very positively suprised how well contrived the world of Ashan is in the dialogues, so the story has its value whatsoever.
+
- The game, even without DLC, provides you with a very decent amount of content to go through. Core game has 22 campaign missions, clocking at about 5h each, so you can easily go over 100h just enjoying the single player mode. DLC add another 14 missions (2 in Pirates, 2 in Dance Macabre and 8 in Shades of Darkness, so the two adventure packs ain't worth the price), with similar amount of gameplay within. And of course the multiplayer, especially the couch one, can provide you with another Infinity hours of gameplay. If you buy the Gold or Complete edition on sale, the price to value ratio is pretty damn good.
+
- Lots of the tunes are remakes of the H3 score and everything else really complements the graphic design. Soundtrack is what you would expect from a Heroes game, but thats a good thing!
-
- Ubisoft bloody DRM will turn the game off when the Internet is down (less often) or UPLAY servers are unresponsive (very often). It also forces itself into the game in the form of CONFLUX orbs - something similar to chatrooms, placed near boss battle locations. Their Mission/Reward system is stupid and the whole software is simply annoying as all hell. Still, its not Origin, so I guess it could have been worse.
-
- Why did the developers of Heroes decided to go from classy hexgrid battle to obviously inferior square tiles? I know it was the same with H5, but why? Hexgrid is million times better!
-
- Although units on their own are very well balanced when comparing factions, the Hero bonuses are not. Faction powers of Haven and Necropolis are far better then those of Sanctuary or Stronghold. Blood/Tear bonuses also vary from totally worthless to grossly overpowered.
-
- After few missions and some skill experimenting, the game gets pretty easy and repetitive. Reinforcement skill almost break the game, as it allows you to go through most minor battles without a single lost unit. You don't have to change your tactic that much to win with different enemies.
Overall, I recommend this game very stronly. Unless you hate UPLAY more then I did or you want to play this game competitively againts your friends, you gonna love H6 if there is any affection for turn-based strategies in your heart. Is it better then H5? HELL YES! Is it better then H3? Arguably yes, but even those that treasure H3 as the best game ever will say that H6 holds the solid second place on the HoM&M podium.

If you were looking for a review, then keep looking. If you're hungry, this is the place for you
Grandpa's Dutch Apple Pie Recipe
You need a Pie pan, a fork, and some sort of Apple peeling device
-----------------------------------Ingredients:-------------------------------------------------
5 apples (Granny smith, crimson crisp, etc.) (Decently sized)
A stick or two of butter, depending on if you made your own crust
Some cinnamon (To Taste)
Some sugar (To Taste)
Pie Crust
3/8 cup of flour
---------------------Recipe----------------------------------------------------------------------
Preheat oven to 225 Degrees Celsius (437 Farenheit)
Peel, Core and Cut all 5 apples in small cubes or thin slices (Soak in water with a bit of lemon juice to prevent browning)
Mix together a stick of butter, some oatmeal, a third cup of sugar, a pinch of brown sugar, a dash of vanilla extract, and a little under 1/3 cup of flour. Mix it together until you end up with a crumble-y texture.
Precook pie crust at 225C for 4-5 minutes
Mix sugar, cinnamon, and apple slices
Pour apple mixture into crust
apply crumble on top of apples, they should be piling over the top of the pie pan
Bake at 225 degrees C for 20-25 minutes
Add whipped cream or vanilla sauce to your hearts desire.
Note: I prefer to mix apples in a colander, then move them to a bowl after they've been sufficently sugared, so that they don't soak in the apple-sugar-cinnamon juice for too long. Just long enough to give it some flavor.
