I picked this up in a multi-pack with several other games as I had played previous games in the series before.  Honestly, I think I might have been better off paying more to buy the rest of the pack separately without this one.
Avoid this game and here is why:
The graphics are at best mediocre.  However, despite this expect to find the game stuttering and struggling to keep up (especially when turning corners).  This quickly becomes more than a minor annoyance when you find yourself losing control because the game has stuttered on a corner.  Textures applied to the walls around the track (such as graffiti on the concrete) will flicker.  (Keep in mind this is on a PC with an i7 CPU, 8GB of RAM, and a GeForce GTX 670).
The car handling is distinctly fishy.  Half the cars will stick to the road like glue.  The other half will be sliding all over the place.  There is nothing in between.
The AI is even fishier.  When they go around corners expect to see carnage as they drive straight in to walls.  To make up for this the AI will quickly catch you on the straights – passing your car with no problems even when you’re burning nitro.
The damage modelling on the cars is all or nothing.  Where Flatout Ultimate Carnage slowly added damage to the cars depending on the impacts in this game your car is either brand new or has been completely crumpled.  There is no damage in between these two options.  As soon as your car scrapes against anything expect to see the whole car appear as if it has been squashed by an 18 Wheeler.

This game has a fun and interesting premise marred by a variety of less-than-great design choices.
Having listed a number of complaints, I'll conclude with a few positives: the gameplay itself is generally pretty solid. I didn't actually have too much trouble navigating thin ledges or narrow tightrope-like areas most of the time due to the responsive controls, and had a lot of fun when it worked. Actually navigating around in the levels can be quite fun, though the "tiny islands and narrow catwalks floating in the void" school of level design means that you rarely get a chance to stretch your metaphorical legs and go all out as you're frequently in danger of overshooting your next target. More levels or bits of levels where you're navigating a larger plane or structure with less imminent fear of falling to your death at every step would be nice. Some of the level bits where you're being shot through loop-the-loops are pretty cool too. The graphics are pretty (although the level geometry is a bit boxy) and the game itself is solid on Linux, with no issues or crashes that I've come across so far.
I think there's a fun game to be found in here, one that unfortunately isn't currently living up to its full potential due to some poor design choices that mar the experience. But if you enjoy this type of gameplay and practicing things over and over to get good, this might be the kind of game for you.
After going back and playing some more, I've realized that my complaints really have a lot more to do with the individual levels than the game as a whole. The next level after the two that made me compose this review was on a giant mountain where you could move around, fall down without instantly dying, and had to go searching for hidden switches to advance, and I really enjoyed it. I also unlocked a new ability; instead of an "instant brake" ability I had the abilty to set a  checkpoint and teleport back to it instantly, which kinda aleviated my issue with the lack of checkpoints and made redoing a tricky bit a lot easier.
It's still not a perfect game, but it does have its fun parts.

It's just busy work, The lot of it.
You won't get anything new from this, at the end of the day it's just your bog standard open world racing game with performance upgrades locked behind skill challenges.
The driving model is simple. it's not quite an assetto corsa, and it's not even a forza. It has more in common with Grand Theft Auto 5 which is to say the driving is approachable and welcoming to all skill sets. However, due to this it is also lacking in challenge and the blatant and rubber banding in the game only serves to alienate the hardcore driver even more.
Despite how large the world is you don't have very many single player races to attend to, it's especially odd considering how many real-world race tracks are in the game. Don't think this is a wasted oppertunity though, the tracks are especially innaccurate and are more like cartoons of the tracks presented rather than the actual tracks.
The cars are the real stars of the show and the selection, while passable, does not showcase too many obscurities or cult classics. The car selection was more to please the crowd rather than actually shed light on cars that people have forgotten about. I mean it's fine having your R34 GT-R's and your Chevy Camaro SS's but after countless games with those cars featured surely it'd be nice to feature something else, something historical, something new, something borrowed and something blue.
The story is Need For Speed Undercover crossed with the 2005 cartoon series Acceleracers crossed with Fast and the Furious. It's a world where everything revolves around street racing, especially crime. It's the dumbest thing I've ever watched in a long time where everything was conveyed so seriously. I honestly feel like all of it would've made more sense in french.
It feels like it was written from the perspective of someone who doesn't really understand why people like cars but really likes the fast and furious films but doesn't speak english so they had to watch it subtitled and really didn't pay attention to the subs half the time. In addition, it's very noticable that the main story of the game is just a patchwork blanket of 'things-that-happen-that-don't-really-matter-that-we-put-in-cus-we-need-gameplay'.
Everything is contrived. The entire setup for the game is contrived. Theres no setup TO the setup of the game. It's a bit of a mess. I mean, yeah, I don't expect shakespeare but I also don't expect dry oatmeal as the story to my trippe A racing game. There are NO plot threads that are interesting. There are NO characters that are interesting. They set up something and it's payoff is so flaccid I would've rather had no payoff. In parts it feels like the writer thought they were being really hard hitting with their drama but without anything to really get me invested it just made me feel embarrassed on behalf of the people who made this game.
The characters really aren't characters, they're just plot devices used to justify reasons as to why you're doing a certain task at a certain time. I can tolerate it but the games serious tone just sucks the joy out of it. I was left longing for Forza Horizon's justification of: "it's a festival" for everything you did because that had a tiny bit of joy to it, this is just miserable.

Spectraball is a short but neat marble game, similar to something like Super Monkey Ball or Marble Blast. This game stands apart from those games by having larger/longer levels. The main campaign took me a little over an hour and contains 7 levels and a tutorial - all of the levels felt unique and had a good balance of platforming and simple puzzles. There's also a mechanic where you have a charge ability that stops all your momentum, it helped me a few times but it's an optional ability so the level design doesn't really use it.
The presentation hasn't aged that well but for an indie game in 2008 I think it looks fine, it doesn't hurt my eyes or anything. The music isn't really catchy or memorable, it's mostly ambience, but it fits the levels well and it didn't annoy me, so that's nice!
The big issue with the game for me is that unlike the other marble games I mentioned I can't really see myself replaying it. All of the levels have leaderboards, which is nice, but the levels feel too large for me to optimize them. A casual playthrough of the game was enough for me, I would recommend you pick this one up on a sale if you're interested.

Verdun is an amazin game for someone who's looking for an immersive experience, and a well-crafted tactical squad shooter to boot. People familiar with faster paced games like Battlefield, COD, and Titanfall will want to be aware that the pace and tactics of this game are on the other end of the spectrum entirely. You both die easily and kill easily, all weapons are viable and deadly.
This is one game that it is very important to learn the progression mechanics and find some friends to play with (or make some!). The leveling mechanics are entirely based on playing with the same people repeatedly, and the different squads in the factions all have specific playstyles with their own weapons and differing sets of perks and officer abilites.
All in all a super-fun game that I highly recommend to anyone who is looking for a unique shooter to play with thier friends.

Historical, measured bolt-action warfare, but with a few irritating hiccups.
-----
Bit of a mixed bag, this one!
Verdun is excellent at creating moments. The weapons have limited clip sizes and lengthy reload times, so when your trench is getting swarmed and you run out of bullets there are plenty of moments of panic as you have to decide whether it would be better to reload or smash someone's face in with the butt of your rifle. Sitting in your trench staring into some smoky crater-scarred landscape and seeing the shadowy figures of approaching enemies dashing from cover to cover is also quite memorable.
The gunplay is generally good. Inaccuracy is highly punished so taking a little extra time to line up your shots is a good idea. There's a variety of weapons to use all from the same period, with various advantages and disadvantages, from a range of different wartime factions.
The movement is a little clunky, particularly the kneeling and going prone animations. They just feel a bit 'off'. But it does at least add to the weighty feel of the combat.
My experience was that the game comes a cropper in three key areas though;
1/ The game is prone to freezing up.
2/ The impression I get is that if it wern't for the recent humble bundle, there would be no player base.
3/ There isn't any variety. You'll be in a trench defending or in no man's land attacking and that's pretty much the whole game. There are different maps in different locations, but it still all feels the same whether you're knee deep in mud outside a ruined fort or behind a tree in a grassy forest.
Overall, if you're interested in the historical period then there is definitely some fun to be had here, but just be aware that it might not always be a smooth ride. And in a couple months time after the bundle hype runs out you may find that there is nobody to play with again.

Banished is a great sim game!
On the surface, it is somewhat simple compared to the masterpieces of old such as SimCity (any version prior to 2013), essentially because there are fewer buildings and resources to manage simultaneously. However, that doesn't mean it lacks depth, as there are other aspects to think about such as population aging/birthrates and resource consumption versus production capability.
This is what makes the game really shine in my view, there is depth if you wish to explore it, or you can simply build as you go and have fun with it.
One down side to this game is that once you have acquired all the resources and built a huge town, there really isn’t much else to it. That’s not to say there isn’t re-playability, as every new map is randomly generated, inviting you to approach building new towns with different strategies.
All in all, it’s a fun time to be had, weather you’re casual or an armchair general. Just enjoy it in short bursts rather than a binge.

Also known as Kino's Journey Simulator 2014.
Banished! You and your sect of friends, family, feeble, and rabble have been banished from your home kingdom/city-state/fuedal village for whatever closed-minded reason, and have decided to settle your own hamlet/city/empire.
Now, Banished is an attractive, medeival-looking city building game where you construct a small town out of the landscape around you, and then
stay in that simple stage until the Netherworld (read:hell) freezes over.
Sounds a bit boring, right? If not, go back to watchin' that paint dry.
If it does sound slightly... bland, that's because you've not heard the terrors provided by nature. Remember the Oregan Trail? Dysentery is going to look like gold once you're done being Banished.
The cold kills, diseases kill, idiots can't harvest enough crops to feed themselves, nomads will flood your town, the mines and quarries kill, mothers die in childbirth, there's a stabbing at the market!
Hope you built a hospital to quell that plague, or some wells to keep your wooden shacks from burning like the Cleveland river. The stabbings can't be helped, people are just evil, sometimes.
That's all just the general layout, too. Really, anything could kill the villagers - even themselves.
the game also gives you all sorts of chances and options to thrive. Most basic needs are easy to access, and come in that wonderfully stepped system of mine, build,
, profit. And people are resilient and happy if they're given the right help, so build that school! Learn 'em up!
And now, my personal experience with Banished:
Had the luck to spawn on a large lake where a river emptied out, so fishing was a quick way to grab food. Forests all around, and not many mountains, so plenty of supplies at the ready for my town. Soon, was running a village of happy, healthy people and managed to have it grow beyond the lake and into the wilderness, with nearly sixty educated people.
Seeing a large, flat stretch of land close by, I set farmland out and began growing a crop of pumpkin. Life was good.
For atleast five years, that system worked. Until, one day after building a long-awaited chapel and town hall, everything hit the fan with the full force of an atmoic detonation. I made the horrible, awful, absolutely terrible decision to close the school, believing it would benefit me for the time to produce faster rather than in larger yields.
The now-moronic people of The Land of Equals couldn't create tools nearly as efficiently or quickly as their past relatives, and even with full fields from good weather, would not harvest enough to feed the nearly-120 person population. And the great decline into starvation began, until a decade later, when there were only 17 survivors who'd managed to stay alive
get through schooling.
And, as I type, the educated remnants of that Banished pilgrimage are rebuilding with stunning succes thanks to their teaching. But the town hall's charts will forever show the great decline into Idiocy, and the impact it had upon The Land of Equals.
So, TL;DR short, Banished is amazing. It can be calming, or stressful. It can give you a warm feeling of care, or a cold feeling of despair. If you take the challenge, be prepared for anything. AND NOW THERE'S MODS! =D

Outlast, also known as "I'm not coming out of this locker until every enemy in the game dies of natural causes" simulator 2013!
It's been a long time since anything that even remotely resembled "horror" was implemented into a game properly (I'm looking at you, downward spiraling Konami/Capcom!) and for the first 2 minutes of the game, I thought it would be taking exactly the same route as the other "appeal to all audiences" horror-fluff experiences...
Well, my nerves beg to differ past that.
Not only is this an extremely beautiful game considering it's dark tones (which it captures perfectly), but it's game mechanics are absolutely solid.
Throughout my entire playthrough, I felt alone, helpess and completely exposed... and it felt great!
Each corridor, every pitch black corner, even doors left slightly ajar felt like a mountain to cross with each footstep building almost unbearable tension.
But even with it's unrelenting horror, curiosity pushed me forward. The story is extremely gripping, every room has it's own story, every creak in the floorboards whispers it's secrets to you, every abomination you encounter shares it's suffering.
I
enjoyed my time with Outlast, even if it was spent in 30 minute increments (half of those been spent hiding under tables with the last flicker of battery on my handheld video recorder barely lighting the flicker in the monsters eyes that were stalking me.)
If you're looking for a real horror experience, I guarentee you won't regret picking up this amazing game!

Bought for 1,99$ during sales
I must admit, the Very Positive reviews on Steam and the studio's two recent succesful games made me purchase this game, but the lack of reviews (Angry Joe, MMOhub etc.) and this being my first time to ever hear or read about this game made me a bit suspicious from the start.
Nevertheless, having finished Witcher 1 and considering it to be one of the best RPGs I've ever played, I thought I'd give this one a try aswell, after all I've learned to value older RPGs and 1,99$ is a joke.
And thank god it was 1,99 and not 20$ because that would have been a big joke indeed!
The game started in an odd and unexplained way where you get to change only 3 aspects of your appearance and you are greeted as some super important Dragon Slayer and you are being commanded to do some things. After running ahead to find this important NPC to progress your story, you notice the graphics which are mostly... underwhelming but it's a dated game so we'll excuse that.
During your first quests you are made aware of many cute female faces strolling around you which will most likely (at least for me) make you sit comfortably on your chair and hope that all the quest givers are females in this game. The voice acting is good in this game too and they've really hit the spot on the first area. But, oh well after you move to the second area women become mostly extinct and you are greeted by tons of soldiers and priests. Way to go Larian, good bait there.
It seems I forgot to mention the music by now... well actually I didn't, there was just nothing to say about the music. It's always the same 2-3 songs being repeated over and over and ove... just turn the slider to 0 and let your ears thank you.
So by now you are still trying to make sense of the story, you are sent into some catacombs to kill a ghost and then run out of town, meet some dying girl who transforms you into a dragon, A DRAGON!!
Which last for 3 minutes only....
You are still wondering who the hell that ghost was and then you suddenly meet the end boss who casually kicks you unconscious and throws you out of his fortress. This is one of the most cheesy stories in any RPG I've ever played it's just impossible to care about it. Literally everything revolves around your character, the rest are dull and unimportant people who you just Mindread for useless information (more on that soon) and they just act as quest puppets.
Mindreading! Yes you can do that here and I found it aswesome at first too, but guess what! Mindreading costs exp. Do you want to mindread that cutie who taught you how to be a Dragon Slayer? Pay 100 exp. Mindread the barkeeper to see what he's been hiding? Pay 200 exp. Mind read some random guard who looks drunk? Pay 300 exp. This is so dumb it just plainly kills the role-playing aspect in this game. PAY EXP to experience the story, lore and to embrace the role-playing part of the game through NPCs!!
Just... why?
But there must be something good in this game worth buying for! Let's see... the combat?
If you are lucky and decided not to play melee then the combat would be a simple "average" for you.
Ranged: kill almost all mobs from miles away before they even get to you, using "poison" or "explosive" arrows.
Mage: Summon a Demon (which was fun) and spamm Fireball, Firewall or Missiles, because charm and fear are so useless you are just wasting your mana. Mobs who need to be charmed will always resists the spell and those who can't resists it will die in 2 hits.
Now this was the good part. Here is the bad part... Do you just like me enjoy melee and like to get in and personal?
Well I'm sorry buddy, it seems that Larian forgot about "balance" there. Enjoy chasing every single freaking mob in the map, where you could just snipe it instead, enjoy having to stop moving in order to attack, enjoy getting to the mob, attacking but having the mob move away while you do all of that just so you will hit thin air instead. Oh and of course enjoy having 2 healers and 2 rangers in every multiple encounter spamming heal and poisoning you and kiting you around while you try and chase them like chickens.
The only few things which I really enjoyed and made me forget the bad aspects were the cinematics and the Dev Tools.
No Cooldowns so you can spam Rush and no more mob chasing? Check
God Mode for these annoying bosses who 1 shot you even if you are over-lever? Check
Unlock every skill so you won't have to start a New Game every time? Check
I'm sorry Divinity 2, I really wanted to finish you, but when I activated Super Sayain whatever it's called mode and started running at triple speed and then you suddenly decided to throw 3 Dragon Citadels filled with puzzles and levers in my face, where precise stepping is OF UTMOST IMOPRTANCE... well then I just had to quit. At least add a /mode off command.
I even tried to watch the videos to see the story, but it was so uninspired and filled with terrible combat that I gave up.
This game is nothing like the Elder Scrolls series or the Witcher series as some people here say it is. These are games with plot, with interesting characters and with proper combat. I've even read some comments about Kingdom of Amalur... that game's combat is MILES ahead.
Anyway, I'd only recommend this game for free or for a huge sale and only if you don't play as melee and if you have finished all the top RPGs out there. Because once you've witnessed quality content, this game will just feel like an Alpha test of an actualy game.

Even though film and literature are absolutely thriving with good Lovecraft stories, video games seem to be lacking on this front. Sure, you'll fine Lovecraftian elements and tropes in some games, but few of them ever deliever on the real feeling or experience you get from reading one of Lovecraft's stories.
Enter Call of Cthulhu: Dark Corners of the Earth. This is a game that captures the feeling, aesthetic and terror of an HP Lovecraft story perfectly. The slow, agonizing descent into insanity, the strange monster who are indifferent if not outright hostile to your existence, and the eventual revelation that humanity is just a fart in the wind in the hideous grand cosmic scheme of things.
As a survival horror game, CoC:DCE does a fantastic job. Being hunted by crazed villagers and bizarre monsters, watching chaos fall all around you, trying desperately to hide from the horrors that be and struggling to stay alive. In terms of survival horror, these segements of the game are up there with the greats (Silent Hill and Resident Evil spring to mind.)
However, this game has a major hinderence that's hard to ignore. Although the first two acts of the game are fantastic, the final act decides to try and turn the game into a full blown action shooter, which is where the game becomes absolutely awful until the satisfying ending which justifies the slog.
The shooting mechaniscs in this game are really bad. There's no hud, no crosshair, the protagonist cannot hold his gun steady, enemies don't drop ammo, the hit detection is wonky, the enemies are bullet sponges with tons of health. This is all great for the first 2/3s of the game, as they add to the feeling of helplessness a horror game is supposed to give you. But when the game tries it's hardest to be Call of Duty, these crappy shooting mechanics make it feel absolutely miserable to play.
Lastly, and this is downright inexcusable - the PC version of this game is broken and cannot be completed due to a graphical glitch that affects ALL modern systems. You need to download a fanmade patch for the game to work properly, or you can never complete it. There is no excuse for this, and if the game were not so good, I'd have to give it a non-reccomendation based on that alone.
But even with all these problems, the game is a fun and entertaining experience and well worth putting up with all the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t. If you're a Lovecraft fan, or just a fan of horror games in general, you have to check this out.
But seriously, this glitch needs to get an offical patch, it is completely unacceptable.

The best Heroes yet!  I think the designers have finally removed most if not all the issues with the Heroes of Might and Magic series.  (I have been playing since 1 back in the day).  I have enjoyed this one the most so far.  Let me list the issues with the last games and how they have been fixed in 6...
1) Crossing your fingers whenever you hero goes up a level, hoping you get the skill you are looking for.  In 6 you may select any skill that you want.  Of course some of them require other lower level skills  and some have hero level limits.
2) I have 3 town and they are so far apart, it is going to take me a week just to combine my armies.  In 6 the number of creatures you can buy per week is shared with all towns so as long as your town can build a certain unit you can recruit all of them.  (Works with special building that give you bonus units as well).
3) Gosh the enemy took all my mines again and if I retake them I cannot get back to defend my town. (Not enough movement).  In 6, you can take a mine for the turn if you leave your hero on it, but as soon as you leave control returns to the player who has the closest town.
4) Issue I have with 5 - Gee that phoenix has taken 3 moved before my Earth Elemental ever got a 1.  How unfair.  I lose no questions. (Unless I am the phoenix, in this case I hope you enjoy cheese).  In 6 they do have the initiative bar but each unit only gets 1 move a turn.  Much better, so yeah all my units might take an action before yours but only 1 action.
5) Wow that is the 3rd chain lightning in a row, magic is so much stronger than might...  In 6 each spell has a cool down time, so no more chain lightning each turn until my 3000 units are toast. Most spells are every 3 turns.
6) Alright I am going to build a magic tower, cross fingers...  Oh crap I already have all those spells...  In 6 spells are hero abilities so you can pick whatever you want, no randomness.
7) (Not a issues but a cool new thing in 6) - Units have a might and magic attack and defense.  Not just 1 value for attack and 1 for defense.  So you can have the magic user who gets destroyed by the sword but spells / magic attacks do very little to him.
My only complaint so far has been the difficult, not that it is too hard but it is out of balance.  90% of the fights I can just hit auto combat and go have a cup of tea.  But the "boss" battle at the end of the map usually requires my hitting next turn for a  few weeks to get enough units to win. (This is after I exploed the whole map.  Perhaps it is my style of play.  I am an explorer not a rusher).

Napoleon Total War is one of the best games I have ever played. It is like the classic wargame but all the toy soldiers out there are able to move, to shoot, to reload, to skirmish, to form an infantry square, to throw grenades and to die. It is so fantastic and amazing.
The game engine works perfectly in every line battle. When you order you infantry to advance and your cavalry to charge, you can really feel the excitement inside you. The Creative Assembly did a great job of designing. Everything is so realistic. The military costumes are realistic and every soldier and every horse is detailed. You can even hear them talking, screaming and cursing in the middle of a fight. They are not little plastic toys anymore.
In terms of campaign, Napoleon total war is pretty similar to its predecessor Empire total war, but adding more features into game, such as cold/heat attrition makes invasion more challenging and stronger rebel forces requires you to put more attention toward town management.
If you're a big fan of Napoleonic era, line battle and 18th century history, Napoleon Total War is the very game for you!

Hearts of Iron III has been such an amazing game and is a good representation of what grand strategy games should be like. The game is defintely not for the faint hearted as it has a decent learning curve and can be very hit and miss with whether or not you enjoy it. The game is defintely aimed at fans of the grand strategy genre and the second world war. For a game made in 2009 its definitely aged well and still has a fairly active player base with around 200-800 players at any one time.
The game itself involves you controlling any nation in the world from early 1936 through the second world war up until 1946. During this period players mostly control the production and operations of their vast militaries. However diplomacy, espionage and trade does play a role (albeit a small one). Players control units right from Brigade level up to Theatre commands and Army Groups. I highly recommend purchasing all of the expansions for the game as they expand upon the games great model and bring some really useful additions. You dont need the skin pack dlcs but these can be useful for those wishing to increase the level of immersion, but I know that I personally tended to just stick to using regular counters.
Once you've had enough of the regular vanilla game there are also many many community created mods which allow for endless oppertunities to experiment and game. These include such mods as the WW1 mod, Black Ice mod and the Modern Warfare mod.
While this game does have a large learning curve and does not sport the most interesting of user interfaces it defintely does the genre proud. I would rate HOI3 a solid 9/10.

Although I have only played about 8 hours so far, this is by far my favorite game in my collection at the moment. It is very addictive and extremely fun. It's the kind of game you want to have when you're sick of getting shot at or dismembered. This is one of the few games I have enjoyed with no story, no stunning graphics, no main characters. You yourself are the protagonist and antagonist. It is up to you to help or hurt this makeshift society.
Pros +
- Fun and engaging gameplay that anyone from 5-105 would enjoy.
- A nice getaway from games like Skyrim or Battlefield.
- It doesn't pull any punches. What I mean is that if you make a few bad decisions, your citizens will die. As Eddard Stark so wonderfully puts it, "Winter is coming."
- Better graphics than expected, this is the first game I've played on Steam that I can with out a doubt say that the pictures don't do the game justice.
- Worth the price. Right now $19.99 USD, worth it, although I got it for $10 in a Humble Bundle Sale.
Cons -
- Still needs work, the game is not perfect. The AI is a little buggy, and the timing on the weather is very predictable. Sunshine, rain, sunshine, rain, sunshine, snow, sunshine, snow, sunshine, rain, sunshine, rain,  and so on...
- Not exactly a CON, but the dev is one person from my understanding. Great game designed by one person, but it could be even better if designed by 2+.
- Very hard to play now that Borderlands 2 is $9.99, but that's a personal problem.
All in all, I give this 4 out of 5 stars. To put in prospective, I give Sims 4, a LOOSLY similar game, a 2 out of 5. Unfortunatly I can't compare it to another City Builder game, as I have none. Hope some people get something out of my  very first review, thanks for reading!

Tuesday, April 28th 1914
Western Front, Champagne
Belgian Squadroon, 5th Division Infrantry
It was a rainy day, the trenches were overflown with mud and blood and it was almost a miracle if you didn't find a rat hair in your soaked food.
All of a sudden the alarm went off, the German troops were invading our trenches, we leave everything behind, grab the rifles and run out in the open.
Machine gunners deployed their weapons on the sand bags for cover fire, we hid behind the corners, waiting in fear as the germans moved towards our encampment. We could only hope that the other side of the camp was as prepaired as we were, so we wouldn't be surprised by the enemy from behind.
Waves and waves of them approached, all deflected with heavy losses on both sides, when some of them decided to take a different route, and travelled above the trenches, where noone expected them. A screaming body fell besides me, and I quickly aimed and shot the scum that killed my squadmember.
Soldiers of the Central Forces retreated, and we were commanded to invade their trenches. I ran with my squad leader and another comrade from the army. We reached the frontline, and threw our bodies on the muddy ground, we were shooting our rifles everywhere, killing the opposing men, but not enough. I heard the haunting sounds of a machine gun, and my friends fell before me, dead on the ground. Our charge had lost momentum, before we could even get into their camp. Scared for my life, stained with friendly blood, eyes watered from the loss I ran as fast as my feet carried me back to our base. I crouched by a barrel, aiming my rifle down at the long narrow corridor between camps, shivering from fear and cold, expecting the next wave...
Those men... their wives are widows now, and I fear Margaret will be one soon... Margaret, my son, I miss them so much...
God is my witness I will see them again!

A bright and pleasant 3D first-person platformer. It's fairly minimalistic as 3D goes, but the textures are enough to make me feel like I'm not playing a demo. The palette is nice and the day/night cycle makes the game feel more alive.
In Refunct, you walk & jump around on a tiny island, stepping on a series of buttons. Every dull grey platform you set foot upon will have its color restored. Every time you step on a button, more platforms (and more buttons) rise up out of the sea around you. The objectives are pretty linear, and the game itself is quite short. As you unlock more areas, the buttons become harder to reach, requiring more precise jumps and more retreading ground if you miss a jump.
The platforming is somewhat satisfying, but I don't feel that the wall-jumping was presented in a very intuitive manner. There is a part wherein you drop down into a boxed-in area to press a button and there is no apparent escape. I assumed that I had pressed the buttons in the wrong order and broke the game. This space was actually designed to encourage you to jump around haphazardly until you realize you can wall-jump (My recommendation would've been to present 2 parallel walls with water instead of a floor, leading up to an obviously-too-high ledge with the button). That said, the wall-jumping is actually pretty satisfying in certain parts.
The water is kind of a strange factor, and I have mixed feelings about it. It actually put me a bit on edge, because there's just something about being underwater in a game and not being able to see how far it goes or know whether there's something coming for you. You can't really do anything in the water except jump up onto a waterline platform. It's interesting to see not-yet-risen platforms beneath the surface, even if you can't interact with them.  It seems like it's possible to play through the entire game without ever touching the water (I think there may be ONE button that truly requires it, but I may have missed an alternate access route), which seems strange, but it makes me wonder if perhaps the water was a late-development addition.
It's short, pretty, and uncomplicated. It feels very much like it's a dev's proof-of-competence project, and I'm looking forward to playing the dev's next 3D platformer, should one occur.

Oh boy, this game. Where to start, where to start... Let us start with the world and atmosphere.
This games atmosphere and world is something that can't just be replaced. It's both bleak and beautiful at the same time. You can stumble upon an old school, half destroyed, but still filled with childish drawings of the pre-war world, like there isn't a care in the world. You may come across an old house where the family and pet dog remain lifeless and dead, and yet, their robot servant still sings soothing tunes to the decayed skeleton in the bed that was once a laughing child, and going to walk the now dead dog, thinking that he's only being a stubborn little brat.
Main story wise, it's about you, The Lone Wanderer, growing up in Vault 101, where nobody ever enters, and nobody ever leaves. However, at age 19, your father (played by Liam Neeson) leaves the vault inexpliciably, and you also exit the vault in a search to find your dad who mystyeriously vanished without even telling you. Along the way, you meet many differint people, ranging from Lucas Simms, the Sherrif of Megaton, all the way to Dr. LI, the lead scientist of Rivet City, an old Aircraft Carrier repurposed as a city. You work with the Brotherhood of Steel, to repel against the Enclave, and its sinister leaders, Colonel Autumn, and their president, John Henry Eden.
Gameplay serves its purpose. You can play in 1st person, 3rd person, or the V.A.T.S system, which allows you to stop time, and carefully place shots at the enemy. However, it's a percent chance, detemined by certain S.P.E.C.I.A.L skills.
All in all, I wholeheartedly recommed this game, as it's atmosphere, world, and immersiveness, is unmatched by most other games.

is a game that utilizes a well-known mind quirk: if you write the name of a color (like 'Red') in a different color (like blue), we become all confused, unable to quickly tell which color the font is and which, the semantics. In this game, however, you'll have to do precisely that, quickly judging color names written in various colors as they flash at you on the screen. This is more or less it, save for various additional challenges like words being written upside-down and so on.
You can actually finish the game in half an hour if you're a fast learner, but it also has a bunch of achievements that probably require honing your skills for a while. And it does as every point feel fair. Nothing in the game wastes your time, it's just a straightforward challenge through and through.

Pretty good game if you like the FpsSurvivalHorror (Amnesia/penumbra) type genre. The game kinda falls apart near the end since the developer went under mid development, but it actually manages to still make it worth slugging through the publisher/dev mess to see some of the most frightening moments in any video game to date.
To get more in depth, as previously stated this game is legitimately scary and that is honestly something that is hard to achieve in a video game. There is one specific instance where you are frantically trying to escape and barricade the path behind you as you flee from the Gilman Hotel. This specific moment is a recreation of an exact event from the short story "The Shadow Over Insmouth" by HP lovecraft. The game is set in his universe and most of it takes place in the town of that story Innsmouth, a New England port town.
If you are looking for a shooter or a Triple A game look elsewhere now.
This game really excels in the first few hours before you obtain a weapon to defend yourself. Jack(you) struggles to find out what is going on in this very desolate port town, talking to some of the more sane residents etc.
Now I am no game historian but its possible this game may have had the first sanity meter (mechanic now used in Amnesia for example). Either way the first thing you will notice when you launch this game up is the lack of a hud, everything is dealt with in a debatably more engaging way. Your character starts to visibly freak out if you stare at a rotting corpse, the screen might start turning a shade of grey if you are bleeding out. All of these work to immerse the player into the game's world.
The gameplay is a combination of puzzles and action, I cant really say the puzzles stand out but I mean they didn't in Amnesia either and people love that game to death. The gun play on the other hand is pretty awful, the hit registration feels very floaty sort of similar to the first metro 2033. The enemies die in a seemingly random number of bullets also registered hits feel sloppy and like there is weight behind them. While a person looking at this game is probably not interested in how good the gun play is, I have to warn you the second half of the game really does force it upon you.
On the topic of sloppiness, this game is buggy as all hell. It was to my knowledge finished in some devs basement after the studio went under. Bethesda did end up publishing it, although they didn't really update it after launch.
The town you explore around, the frantic set piece moments and the hp lovecraft world make this game from disaster into a buggy gem that deserves way more recognition that it ever got. Oddly enough PC Gamer did manage to sneak it onto their top 100 PC games of all time list at #87, so maybe people wont forget this game after all.
To wrap this up. If you are a fan of the first person perspective horror game genre, HP lovecraft or you like a gamble pick this game up. For others you might want to watch some gameplay videos and judge for your self.

I would recommend this game overall but this is not one of the best games out there. This game exhibits great RPG elements, and mastering an expertise in battle requires dynamic strategies. However, there are many issues that I have with the game as well. For example the AI is stupid; there are two settings: aggressive and defensive. If you play against defensive then the AI only stockpiles units, which means you will eventually win by sheer force from taking over the map. If you play against aggressive then enemy heroes will only engage in battles that they win in, but only return back to base if forced to. This means that (1) you won't enter in any battles unless your slated to lose (which sometimes means that no matter how resourceful and strategic you are, you will lose); and (2) if you reinforce your main hero then you will eventually overpower the enemy. However, this tends to just end up the AI playing chicken to take your city and you just sitting there until you abuse bad AI scripting to, for example, make them miscalculate. While this makes players think, this doe not make for interesting or fun gameplay. The campaign offers relief from this type of AI stupidity but only sometimes; however, the campaigns did contain some maps that were definitely a puzzle. To be honest, the only reason I recommend this game is because the combat system is engaging, and by abusing the computer's stupidity of amassing units; can reach battles of epic proportions. The hero powers become essential in achieving victory and is the best way this game hands control into the player's hands: all units are balanced among the different races, but it really is how you build your hero that defines a win from a loss. If I could make an ideal 4x game, Heroes of Might & Magic IV would be the type of combat that my game would emulate. That's how fun and different it is from say CIV or SC. However, there are many better strategy games that offer more meaningful experiences where the player has much more choice, not just in hero customization but in building a kingdom. I bought this game thinking it was a strategy game: let me be clear; if that's why you would buy it then do not. This game is an RPG game with strategy elements. Find loot, defend your bases and points of interest; and win by sheer force. If you want a game where you get to control massive and visually epic battles then I'd recommend this game for you.

This is probably way overdue; but here it is. Along with every other total war fan I became hopelessly obsessed with NTW from the moment I saw the trailer and felt the tingles of empiricism run down my spine. We'll start with the campaign. Although I liked the fact that historical accuracy was kept intact with the coalition against Napolean, I found the campaign interface seriously lacking in my expectations. Having become accustomed to the layout of ETW I struggled initially to adjust to NTW and navigating my way through the campaign. Eventually I got the hang of it, but I found that everything took far too long, from ship building to unit replenishment, everything cost too much as well, making progression very difficult. However; what the game lacked in campaign dynamics it completely made up for in battle realism. I always found cannon shot on infantry in ETW to be a little, "underdeveloped" as it were, only killing one or a few men everytime. But in NTW it couldn't be more realistic; anyone with a brain stem can figure out that an 18 pound cannon ball hurtling towards a body of men all tightly bunched up is going to rip a hole through them! I find this is perfectly incorporated into the battle aspect of NTW. Along with this, I find the unit variety much more inclusive of the period, and my particularly favourite touch that was thrown into the battle sequence was the fact that unlike in ETW; when the troops fire their muskets they all don't fire at once. NTW truly is my number one game for battle realism, with brilliant detail, such as when you zoom in to view a unit up close, the screen shakes to signify the marching, you get sun glare, and music plays, which to my amazement is indicitive to the regiment. This is a masterpiece in strategy gaming, and I would reccommend it to any serious gamer looking to delve into strategy gaming. 9.2/10.

It's a pretty fun game. It's a place where you can let your mind be free and create anything that you want, and that's something that's hard to find. I appreciate who made this game, because they've changed a lot of people.

- No POW related mechanics. Pocketed or shattered divisions will vaporize without a trace. A 'military' POWs were the central type of irrecoverable losses during the war.
- No HOI2/4 alike casualties stats counting system. I know about the 'moral side' the devs were talking about, but this game isn't for 6+ kids. It's a Second World War - brutal, bloody, mercyless. Moreover, this feature was implemented in HOI4, so 'wtf' anyway? Where is your so-called morality now?
- Armies and manpower pool are much lower than it was in real life. Soviet Union had 5M active personnel when the war started, but in the game you'll be lucky to have 3,5M at a peak. Same goes for other countries.
- Also, if you are good enough, you can drain enemy's manpower to 0 within few large operations. E.g., Germany at the end of 1942 without any manpower to make up for losses is a crippled kid ready to get beaten by anyone. I had to create custom event, giving Germany and its allies manpower when it's less than 5k men. Cheat, basically.
- No AI-held/scripted invasions. Yep, no D-Day for you, kid.
- At the end of the war, even if the game went as much close to be historical as it can, there won't be a possibility to finish it correctly. No special wargoal for the UK, the USA and other countries. You either puppet or annex them.
- Many start dates, especially 1944, are undeveloped. UK will fail in Italy and in Normandy; Soviets won't start the operation 'Bagration'. AI will be just senselessly moving divisions along the frontline.
- Stupid AI. For battles, for allies, for production and research. AI ruins most of the fun.
- Lack of units. Lack of depth for divisions creation.
- Lack of historical events and decisions. No variability for most of the countries.
- At some point there's no challenge. And that gives you two options: either pump the AI-ruled countries with cheaty buffs (+100% to manpower, +20% to IC) by adjusting the difficulty, or... See the next line.
- Using the mods after some time (for me it was 200 hours) is just inevetable. For me it's BICE. You can pick Downfall, HPP and so on. Units, AI improvement, more depth, events and so on. Rely on mods.
+ Still, this game is unbeaten example of what the global military real-time strategy about WW2 should look like. Its rеtardеd younger brother by the name of "Hoi4" isn't even close to that. Yet, even the 4th game has some mechanics that are the way better than in the 3rd game. Stats, deeper (not better) production system, alternative countries.
After all, I love this game. It's not for a casual gamer, it's not for 1-hour "play a little, Bobby, and then go the bed". For me, with BICE installed, Hearts of Iron III is a hardcore deep representation of things that were happening in special rooms ~75 years ago. Marshals, tired and frightened, are standing around the map, whispering carefully to each other, sometimes moving the figures of infantry and tanks. Air is filled with sigarette smoke and fear. The enemy made a breakthrough through our well-prepared defence line. No reserves left, no tanks are coming to stop them. Only the perfect military planning may save our homeland now. Maybe, you are the one, who'll stop the enemy at the gates?

Banished is a game I waited for a long time ... all the way back since the glory days of Settlers II. Yeah, that's right, back when the only mobile phones were ones with a two mile long cord and your computer was larger than your dishwasher. The problem with most citybuilders and games alike (for me, personally) is that I don't enjoy great measures of micromanagement and I want to focus on the citybuilding instead of the constant warmongering that the later Settlers-games & Co offered. Banished delivers.
This isn't really a citybuilder thou, it's a survival game with a citybuilder/management-game wrapped around itself like a warm cosy blanket. Your people are banished from your homeland (about 20-50 of them to start with) probably because bad poetry or whatever and you need to settle in a new land. So you build houses to live in and start producing food to eat and materials to build with, maybe trying to produce a surplus of something to trade with. Your people will (hopefully not die horribly but instead) start making families and producing
babies that will grow up to become workers. You'll also need to worry about sustainability of natural resources. If you just cut the forest down you'll be living in a barren land with nothing to heat your houses with come winter.
The survival aspects of the game is what makes it intense. It feels like where other games had combat to bring that intensity, Banished has substituted it for infants dying of hunger and old ladies freezing to death while logging. And all the people in your town live their own lives; you can check any house and see how Joshua the farmer (aged 40) just married Maria the woodcutter (aged 12) and feel utterly disgusted, but at the same time you feel ashamed when their daughter Zara (aged 2), who by the way was about to marry that sixty year old man at the market (just kidding; it's not THAT gruesome), dies because you fail to produce enough food. The people that live in your town really matter. And children are really children (until they're married off way too young to their cousins mind you) - they don't work, they just eat your food until they're old enough.
Your job is just to balance everything out, and the larger your town grows over the decades the harder that gets. Not farming enough during the spring and autumn seasons can lead to a potentially devastating winter where half of your population starve to death because your largest food production is your farms and they just harvest crops once a year.
Oh, I've gone on for far to long... but that's just how captivating and addicting Banished is.
Just to finish it all off; if you're a fan of the RTS-type citybuilders, or the very micromanagement:y-type, this might actually not be a game for you. It's quite slow paced and actually is more about retaining a perfect balance in your infrastructure. It's about surviving, and at the same time your town is growing, that survival-element never disappears. A large town is 300-500 people, so we're still at "personal"-level.
But for me; this game is absolutely amazing!

Victor Vran is a really beautiful, massive Action RPG, which has a pretty unique gemplay style and method of building your character's skills & attributes.  There are many weapons to collect, ranging from swords and hammers to magical tomes and lightning guns.  Your character (Victor Vran) can run and even jump, which makes this game so brilliant.  Many areas in the game will require Victor Vran to jump (sometimes against cliff walls and other objects) to gain access to.  There are many seceret areas also.  After 125 hours play there are still a few that elude me.
Victor Vran can carry two two-handed weapons, one of which can be used at any one time - and each weapon has three attack methods (standrad attack + 2 special).  The controls works so well with an xbox 360 controller.  Character animation is excellent.  Victor Vran also has two demon powers (powerful weapons or auras) which are powered by the use of overdrive. Overdrive is accumulated by method defined by your outfit, which may include, among other factors, attacks on enemy and kills.
Victor Vran can change outfits, which vary attributes, such as the number of Destiny Cards you can carry/armor/overdrive gain, while the amount of Destiny Points you can use is related to character level.  Destiny Cards can affect attributes such as critcical chance, or health regeneration and so on...There are lots of nice loot drops to find - legendary items and special power stones that can upgrade demon powers, destiny cards, your outfit and weapons, in the transmute section back in the hub (Castle Zagore).
Overall, Victor Vran is easily one of the best games I have ever played.  Very possibly the actual very best.  The combat gameplay is so satisfying and character's power building is so absorbing.  The size of each in-game area is simply astounding, the detail incredible, and the sheer number of them immense.  The game is set in a really beautiful world, which is so huge.  The single player story line (I say single player, although the main story is also playable in co-op mode) is really excellent and maintains interest in the game, while the challenges set for each area, while not necessary to complete, provide an extra level of challenge and an extra incentive to replay each area time and time again, (especially in multiplayer).
Multiplayer is excellent, with players being helpful, and you can filter whether games are visible to just your firends or everyone.  Online multiplayer players will often share treasure codes, which can be redeemed, by clicking on them in chat, or entering them in the options screen.  The treasure codes provide details of Treasure Hunts and Bounties, with bounties spawning Epic monsters in the relevant game areas, providing nice loot and xp gaining opportunities.  This also provides an excellent post-campaign end-game for teaming up in mulitplayer (or singleplayer).  Players can play local Co-op also. There is also a Bottomless Pit, PvP brawling arena, and Cauldron of Chaos with new challenges daily providing even more replayability, online or offline.
Even at full price, this game is a bargain.  It really is so massive with so many cool items to collect and different character 'builds' to explore.  And the combat is truly unique -  players get a real sense of controlling Victor Vran's movements and attacks, with sword attacks slashing and jolting, lightning bolts and massive explosions on crit (if applicable) etc...so easy and fluid to play with controller (while at the same time providing adequate challenge).  Full controller support/Steam Trading Cards/Steam Achievements/Online Multiplayer...and the sound track is really truly beautiful music also.  Highly recommended.  10/10.

As someone who started with the Hyperdimension Neptunia Victory on PS3 for the first out of the Neptunia series, I was really on for a treat. I also played the previous two Re;Birth games, and I can only tell this was going to be a great game overall.
For starters, this was based on the best Neptunia game I played back overall (the two Re;Birth games were fun, but not that much fun), meaning that I was going to enjoy the upgrades for this game. It included an extra chapter (which was ridiculous), some extra scenes that were pure fun (but not as fun as a certain side quest) and even characters the original Victory did not have (being the four Oracles of MKII/Re;Birth 2). And with messing around with the Plans, you could just do stuff like skipping battles (given you're a much higher level) when you Symbol Attack enemies, make the game relatively easier/harder, double EXP/G obtained and much more.
If you want a game that is comedic with serious moments and you just want to beat this game, you can absolutely get this. Just be warned; there is fanservice here and there. A LOT OF FANSERVICE. (Especially when you get to meet Iris Heart the first time...)
Also, this game comes with the DLCs of Victory; new characters, new weapons/armor, Level-limit breaks (now it's up to 999 instead of 99), and if you try the DLC dungeons, be sure to grind a lot. And when I say a lot, I mean nearly 400~800 Lv will suffice...(?)

In some ways, better than Oblivion. Based heavily upon the
(DRM-free) release of Divinity II: Developer's Cut, which I've sunk a ton of hours into.
PROS:
+ Much better and more open-ended story than Oblivion, with quite a bit of 'moral ambiguity'.
+ Combat, especially ranged combat, puts Oblivion's combat to shame.
+ Decisions have real effects on the main story, especially later in the main story.
+ Dragon arial combat, which is also enhanced with Dragon form skills and armor.
+ Tons of variety: side quests, potion mixtures, weapon and armor enhancements, allies to enlist...
+ Allies are plentiful. From Summons to Necromancy to various factions, you'll make lotsa friends.
+ World is huge and opens up dramatically with main story progression.
+ Alternate realms, similar to Oblivion Gates, appear mid way into the story.
+ A good sense of humor at certain points.
+ Modest hardware requirements.
+ Priced accordingly for the amount of content that's included.
CONS:
- Character customization isn't as robust as Oblivion's.
- World isn't quite as big as Oblivion's, with areas being a bit segmented.
- No Mac or Linux versions as of this review 2017-10-30.
BOTTOM LINE: I'm thoroughly impressed by what Larian, an INDEPENDENT developer, has done here. Some may pass off Divinity II as a mere 'ghetto Oblivion', but I firmly disagree. Larian took a fraction of the resources Bethesda has to work with and managed to craft a AAA (for 2012) game. Divinity II made me a fan of Larian Studios.

Good Sides:
- Great atmosphere, dungeons don't give the feeling of repetitiveness.

Bad Sides:
- Limited variety of weapons. Would like to see more weapon types.

- Diablo 3's Rift idea could be implemented with randomly generated dungeons. Would love to see randomly generated maps.

What do you get when you take a simple colour test, add in some distracting mechanics, multiply it with some adrenaline-fuelled pumping music and use an everyday household that's been around for years? You get OLDTV.
While the gameplay is super simple and easy to learn by left-clicking if the colour's matching the word, and right-clicking if it doesn't match the word, you may think that it's going to be easy, but it isn't. As you're faced with a decreasing Frequency counter (timer) and a large variety of distracting mechanics, you'll need to think as fast as you can without making a mistake as one wrong move will just simply end your TVenture. Can you quickly find the signal, or perhaps can you figure out the answer if the word is upside down, jumbled up whilst the screen's in a different colour and your controls has been inverted?
It's a really fun game with an endless plethora of channels to flick through, as if you're actually watching some TV yourself! I do recommend it if you're interested in a simple, but challenging and intense, game.

A solid, long-lived and intense action RPG, with some interesting introduction in gameplay and a good level design.
Victor Vran is by no means perfect, but it's fun, ensures hours of play in the hack 'n' slash genre.
The game has a very dynamic combat system and is - in my opinion - superior to Diablo 3. In D3 it always felt like "I am doing DPS to the enemies". Here, it feels like "I am slashing the enemies with a sword".
Each weapon requires a different playstyle.
There are no character points or skill trees associated with Victor because each weapon is a self-contained class of skills and strategies. There are a lot of weapons, and between rapiers, broadswords, shotguns, mortars, and lightning guns, there’s a lot of skills. Spells and bonus passive cards, to enrich your character even more
Each level has a lot of objectives that can take quite a while to accomplish, but they're optional and you can just plow through the game in a few evenings if that's your style.
Given that it costs less than $20, most of the criticism can simply be ignored.
Victor Vran highly recommended for action RPG fans!!!!!!!!!!!

pros:
-imagine if the people who made the old mx vs atv games decided that they were going to branch out into open world racing games, thats what we have here.

-the driving physics while pretty arcadey are still a lot of fun
-theres a decent amount of variety with all the specs
-the map is ♥♥♥♥ing huge and theres tons to explore
-there was an attempt at a story other than "start as some nobody, become god", it certainly isnt the best story, but better than any racing game ever
-i really love that they took the time to put other types of vehicles into the game, im lookin at you pickup trucks, the buggy, and all the different motorbikes
-you can be a cop
-the graphics could be better, but are still decent
-it is so much fun to play with a friend, the crew system is real awesome
-monster trucks, there needed to be a special note for them
-ignoring the limitations on parts depending on what spec you choose, decent customization options
-you can literally go anywhere, and theres activities wherever you do choose to go, or however you choose to play
-friendly to new players, you get one of each spec for free
cons:
-the after story activities can get a little grindy
-its a bit pay to win, bucks are a little too hard to earn, and you can buy a special currency if you are too lazy to earn said money, i understand they need to maintain the servers, but cosmetic only next time, and no exclusive paid vehicles
-the release was terrible, and it took 2 years to add stuff that should have been in the game right from the beginning, and we had to pay for dlc for them to do it
-the pc version is plagued with issues, i cant see my friends when were in a crew, the game crashes lots, i dont have a wimpy pc and its still a bit jittery at times, stuff like that which should have been fixed by now
-pathetic limitations on parts depending on what spec you choose to use, if i dont want ♥♥♥♥ing carbon fiber on my perf spec car dont make me put carbon fiber on my perf spec car!
-we should have been able to design our own stickers for our cars
-disregarding all the different specs for a moment, it could use some more cars/trucks/bikes
-it took them 2 dlc to improve their ♥♥♥♥♥♥ release graphics
- the driving mechanics were fun, but at times lacked logic, a drift car should be able to maintain a drift, not just slide for a bit and slowly lose power, and why can my monster truck not drive over other cars
-why does my hq look the same in every location that i go, and why do i not get a say in where its located, let us pick next time, and design different interiors
-while a good start, the mmo/rpg mechanics need to be more refined and interesting next time
-while the map size is impressive, key landmarks still seemed pathetically small in most circumstances, it took me less than a minute to drive the lake pontchartrain causeway... thats not right man
despite all of its shortcomings the crew is still one of my favorite open world racing games ever, the decent mechanics, huge map, and the fact that it reminded me of the mx vs atv games i used to play as a kid have helped it greatly in achieving this, the instability on pc upsets me because i spend less time playing which makes me sad

I have been a fan of Heroes of Might and Magic since Heroes II The Price of Loyalty.  Heroes III is arguably the best in the franchise.  I really enjoyed Heroes IV though.
And then came UbiSoft...
It seemed their mission was to destroy the beloved franchise.  With Heroes V came lame, watered-down spell-casting.  The graphics were good in 2007, I had no problems there.  The inability to divide your troops in your army was bad.  I had all but given up on Heroes of Might and Magic.
Then I saw Heroes VI.  The graphics are fantastic.  The animation is good.  The storyline is interesting, if a bit underdeveloped.  I like the ability to convert towns, forts, and dwellings.  I have played this game for over 240 hours, and beaten all of the campaigns and expansions.  I like the hours of playability it provides for one player.  It doesn't hinge on multiplayer like so many other games do these days.  I love the Necropolis in this game.  The Altar of Eternal Servitude provides a deliciously twisted advantage as your army never dies, depending on if you have enough resources.  The Haven is excellent despite only one shooter.  I'm better with the Sanctuary than even the Necropolis.  The Stronghold is just impressively strong.  I like the Dungeon expansion.
Now for what I don't like:
1.  I don't like how you have to go through UPlay whenever you turn the game on or off.  "Synchronizing Your Saved Games With The Cloud" takes a very long time, and only works maybe 12% of the time.  It is highly frustrating.  I want to be able to click on the game and have it load.  When I quit to desktop, I want the game to quit.  This is the first game I've had to deal with these issues.  The benefit UPlay seems to provide does not outweigh the cost of time and sanity.
2.  I don't like how I reached Platinum level before I completed all of the campaigns.  On paper, I should be one of the best players in the world.  Once you max out on experience there really isn't much to play for.  On campaigns the maximum hero level happens too quickly.  The maps are epic in scope, and there is so much to do, but if you max out your levels one-fifth of the way through the map then it's not fun anymore.  I understand that the experience keeps going into the dynasty weapons, but you really don't see that happening.  Let us players continue to grow!
3.  I don't like the Haven's faction ability.  They are pretty much the antithesis of the Necropolis except for the faction ability.  Necromancy heals troops, but Guardian Angel doesn't?  At least until level IV.  No, the Haven faction ability should be healing.
4.  The Necromancers differ in this game in that they don't raise skeletons after each combat.  Other than that, I love the Necropolis.
5.  I do not like that troop growth is centered around your overall kingdom.  I miss having a lot of troops.  Instead of only getting 8 Core creatures a week, for instance, you should get those 8 Core creatures from every castle you own plus every creature dwelling every week.  That is one upgrade I do not like.  At least you have the ability to divide your troops in your army, and among secondary heroes.  Give us more troops!
6.  I have a very nice gaming computer, and Heroes VI still glitches to where I have to just shut the game down and start back at the last save.  And that takes forever because I'm waiting for Uplay to sync.  Glitches happen, I know, but I haven't heard of any patches in months.
7.  The Inferno has been completely castrated.  It's so hard to look at.  I get the Chaos aspect, but still...Inferno has been done better.  Get rid of the Inferno and bring back the Sylvan elves.
8.  I absolutely hate spell recharges.  The whole point of having a Magic hero is to be able to obliterate enemies with spells.  Casting Lightning Bolt once every three turns sucks when in previous games you could cast it every turn.  The mana is mismanaged in this game too.  Your hero may have 200 mana, but each spell costs 45, 37, or some other random amount of mana?  No, take some lessons from what 3DO did correctly.  Unleash the spellcasters again!
9.  Though I like having the skills and abilities options Heroes VI provides, the levels are few and far between, so it's hard to take the path you want to take when you level up.  That's just a minor issue with me though.
10.  I hate how the Boss fights give you a pre-set number of troops.  What is the point of building an army for the whole map if you can't use all of your troops in the final Boss fight?!  I understand the need for a challenge, but there is something so satisfying in having an overwhelming army that you just spent 3 hours running around assembling.  I like the introduction of Boss fights into this game, but please let us bring in our full army and wreak havoc!
11.  Maybe it's just me, but the AI is super hard on the Scenarios.  I can barely beat a single AI on Easy let alone levels with multiple enemies.  I have no idea how the enemy assembles such a huge army before I do, etc.  Maybe I just suck, I don't know (I don't think I suck that badly).  That's just another issue I have.
Overall, I love this game.  It has given me hours of playability, and for that I am grateful.  It is a visually-stunning and beautiful game.  The Inferno is so hard to look at, but the beauty of the Sanctuary makes up for it.  If they make a Heroes VII I hope it is a lot like Heroes VI, but with the changes I have suggested.  Take away a cliche Demon threat and give us some other storyline.  Let the armies grow like they did with 3DO and Heroes V so the Might heroes can thrive, and take the recharges off the spells so the Magic heroes can thrive.  I recommend this game highly, but with those caveats.

It's kind of hard to rate this game.  It is a part of the M&M Heroes series, which alone makes it worth playing.  However, there are some things about this game that I just really don't like very much.  Probably the biggest complaint I have is the rushed feeling that this game has about it.  Unlike the other games in the series where you were given more time in each level for exploring, this game comes at you fast and furious.  It seems like every level you are simply trying to just stay alive long enough to finally build up an army which you can use to rush toward the enemy.  There are quite a few areas that you want to explore, but every time you start going toward them, suddenly another large enemy army is marching towards your city(ies), and you have to turn around and defend yourself (there's no way that you can produce a generic hero strong enough to defend yourself, only your main hero has a chance to win.)  Even on the easiest level this game just doesn't want to give you the chance to explore and discover all parts of the map.  Plus, the longer you take to explore, and look around the enemy quickly becomes so strong that you can't possibly win.
There have been quite a few changes to the actual gameplay and interface as well (some good, some not so good), which is probably more of an individual preference as to whether one likes them or not.
The story doesn't seem to be nearly as strong as was that of HoMM V, plus you have the option of choosing which campaign you want to play, rather than having to unlock the campaigns as you go along (which also kind of takes away from the continuity of the story).
Another huge problem with this game is having to use UPlay to actually play the game.  UPlay and Steam just don't want to work well together, and normally I have to try to launch the game 2 or 3 times (sometimes even more), just to get it to actually work.  Once I turned Uplay's sinchronizing feature off, it did help a little, but only a little.
If you are a big fan of the series, then you will want to play this game (even with all of it's irritations and quirks), but just don't expect the same epic experience that you got from HoMM V - it just doesn't compare.

Scumbag developers that have known about game breaking bugs and crashes to desktop for years across many of their games using the same engine, but have done nothing to fix or patch the problem.
Meanwhile, they're happy to sell you more cosmetic DLC and release new games leaving the years old game breaking crashes unfixed since they were first reported well before that.
I bought a bunch of their games in a sale months ago (so well beyond the refund period) and Pure Pool, Pure Chess & Backgammon Blitz seem to crash constantly between 5-25 mins. What's worse is that it won't save your progress during a game, so when you restart you've lost all your progress for that match.
PS - Changing graphics settings - like lowering resolution, windowed mode, etc, do seem to remedy the problem slightly, but it really just just seems to delay the inevitable crash, rather than stop it.
I've bought many of their games on console, too. Whilst all very basic in functionality and options, they do work perfectly. It seems to be just another case of a lazy PC port that was an afterthought for some quick cash.

It seems this iteration of the game is completely obsolete now and will never be patched, so avoid.  I haven't bought Chess Ultra due to the neglect across multiple of their other games, but I'd be very wary of it also having the same crashing issues and getting abandoned, too :|
Edit - After messing with every variation of graphics settings to try to get this to work; it turns out you can fix the "Mantis APP crash - please attach debugger" issue better by disabling the Steam Overlay.  Solution will follow below if you want to persue this, but I still experience crashing after, albeit a lot less.
This problem dates back to 2014 & was never fixed, which is completely unacceptable on the part of the developers.
So top left Steam tab, settings, In-Game sub menu, then untick Enable the Steam Overlay while in-game.  This means you won't be able to Shift Tab whilst in-game, but you can play windowed mode instead and switch between Steam & the game if you need to use/check any Steam features.  The game still crashes for me though, just way less.  Probably works on the other mentioned games, too, but frankly I've given up at this point to even try testing.

The physics work well, and the puzzles are good. I have just a few gripes with the game:
1. Checkpoints aren't placed in spots where they absolutely should be placed. This leads to replaying easy areas that lead into trickier areas, sometimes over and over to the point of annoyance.
2. The camera has some wonkiness (which is actually poor level set up) and leads to situations where you can't see the ball. This is less of an issue than #1, but from time to time, it's still annoying.
3. You can easily screw up on loops by pressing in the wrong direction (which is actually the direction you start the loop on). In most games that change your direction while moving, the movement continues in the direction of momentum as long as you keep the movement button pressed in the same direction you started with, which is what they should have done here.
4. Level size is much larger than one would expect starting even from the first level. Smaller levels up front, longer levels as you progress should be how it goes.
Overall though, a decent game. I would prefer if this was more of an RPG, as the levels are long enough to support some kind of progression for the ball (more speed, better control, etc.).

Is this game bad? No. It's decent. It's a better performing Dark Souls 1 with a graphical upgrade, more areas to explore, and more undead things to slap with oversized weapons. Sounds good right? So, why the no recommend?
To me this game is a lot like Skyrim. You get a big, huge area to explore; but instead of that area being largely full of anemic timewasters, Dark Souls 2 fills that area with scores and scores of anemic monsters that shamble towards you! To the point where the entirety of game balance is predicated on how many enemies are in you immediate surroundings.
Remember the part in Dark Souls 1 where you had to take out your bow to snipe enemies so that you wouldn't get dogpiled on after turning a corner? Me neither. Entire bosses are are nothing but unit spam. This how Dark Souls 2 does difficulty.
There can be too much of a good thing, believe it or not. I'm sure Dark Souls 2 can be fun if played in short bursts. I certainly had fun with it my first time around, but this game seems like it wants to put in the minimal amount of effort, rehashing so much from the original without any shame at all; like its going through some sort of checklist. Yeah, gargoyle fight? Check. Dead thing made of other dead things. Check. Tag team fight. Check. Etc Etc.
Its not a bad game. But it certainly can't live up to the high watermark set by the original. I think even the die hard fans of this game can admit that Dark Souls 1 had more personality in a finger than Dark Souls 2 has in its body. So, what do you call a not bad/ not good game? Average. And for my money, there are plenty of above average games more worth your time.

Who would imagine a game this simple and minimal could be so enjoyable? One of the most beautiful games I've ever played, Refunct is definitely my video game Zen/Massage. It's everything you might come to expect from reading the descriptions. The gameplay is short and basic: jumping/swimming around platforms activating buttons to spark more platforms until you reach the end through a gradual day/night cycle. That's it. There's no story, no explanation, no complexity. Just this simple and brief design.
What makes it so enjoyable? Probably the fact that the game does what so few do these days, and that is stay simple and know what it wants to be. The developers clearly understood what kind of game they wanted to make and didn't try to push beyond that. Obviously this is not the only factor in its quality, but it's still significant.
But even then, it's worth giving honorary mentions. As a PC Gamer I find the controls to be among the smoothest ever experienced. Having played through the game twice I can't recall any moment where I experienced frustrating trial-and-error. The peaceful and relaxing setting is a joy to behold, accompanied by perfectly executed sound design and music score. The atmosphere of the game is always calm, and changing a block from grey to more earthlike is very satisfying for some reason. And I certainly can't remember the last time a first-person game included wall-jumping. Also wait till you reach the game's end. I guarantee it will make you feel good about yourself!
Believe me, I can be quite picky about a game's overall length and replay value. Therefore the fact I highly recommend this game despite my currently low playtime should say a lot. Get it now!
