Quick Summary: Victor Vran is a “simplified” action RPG in the same vein as Diablo, Torchlight, and Incredible Adventures of Van Helsing. In terms of art and level design the game is extremely similar to Van Helsing, fighting spooky monsters in a sort of steampunk world. The game does have some different mechanics though, that will take some getting used to if you’ve only played the previously mentioned ARPGs:
*You can Jump. This is actually not as big a deal as you might think since jumping doesn’t really dodge enemy attacks very well. It’s mostly used to cancel your channeling spells and wall jump into secret areas.
*There are no character “attributes” or “skill tree.” You don’t get points to distribute on level-up to customize your character. Instead, each level-up gives you a predetermined bonus, such as +100 life and a random loot item. Combat skills are either associated with the weapon you’re using, or “demon powers” (spells) which are found and equipped like items. They don’t level up, you just find better versions of them.
*There is no “mana” in the game. Instead you build up “overdrive” by hitting enemies, and when it reaches a certain threshold you can use your equipped demon powers, kind of like super meters in some modern fighting games. This can be changed however by equipping certain outfits (kind of like character classes). For example one outfit might make you generate overdrive passively, but you no longer gain it by hitting enemies. An outfit like this is good for “spellcasters” since you can just wait for overdrive to fill up before jumping into battle.
*The randomly generated weapons you find don’t really get that much stronger throughout the game. In Diablo or Torchlight, a high level weapon could be 100x more powerful than a level 1 weapon of the same type, but in Victor Vran, an end game weapon may be less than 2x as powerful. Weapons in Victor Vran don’t have levels or stat requirements (because you have no stats). Because of this, and the predetermined level-up bonuses, every character is generally the same at each level (except for the equipment you’re using). That means there’s more player skill needed in this game than in other ARPGs.
*One of the loot types that you accumulate is “destiny cards” which are like mix and match bonuses. There are about 25 different card types (and multiple levels of each type), each with a bonus such as +armor, +life steal, +range damage, etc. You can have up to 6 cards equipped at a time and can customize your bonuses to each combat situation.
*You can increase the game’s difficulty using “hexes” that are given to you at a certain level, and stored in your inventory. At any time you can turn on one of these five hexes for a predetermined boost to difficulty. For example one of the hexes might make enemies move faster or hit harder. Another hex might make more “champion” monsters spawn. Turn on all 5 hexes simultaneously to make even the starting areas of the game a challenge. Of course, you’re not doing this just to make life harder for yourself, the hexes also give noticeable bonuses. Each active hex gives you +10% experience and +5% magic find (better loot).
As for the game’s story, you play the title character Victor Vran, a demon hunter with a mysterious past. Your current quest is to free the kingdom of Zagarovia from demonic infestation after many of your fellow hunters have failed. The game has a central city hub from which you can access any area in the game as “missions.” This means that unlike a lot of other ARPGs you don’t actually need to run through the entire map looking for the next area, most of time you can jump to the next main quest from the main city hub (optional areas may still need to be found though). Also, since each area is a standalone mission, they all have “challenges” that can be completed for additional loot or exp. For example in one area there could be challenges for “find all secrets” or “kill 30 spiders without taking damage” etc. You can replay each area as many times as you want to get all the challenges, they don’t need to be done all at once (many of them require more than one play through anyway).
I mentioned earlier that skills are bound to your weapons, and what I mean is that each weapon “type” (for example sword, hammer, sabre, etc.) has 3 skills that you can use when it is equipped. The first skill is the basic attack, possibly with some small random effect. The other 2 skills have cooldown timers, but may be significantly more useful. For example swords have a skill for high damage to a single target, and a daze skill for stunning an enemy. Shotguns have a skill for high damage to a single target (instant cooldown when you kill any enemy) and an area effect blast skill. The game pauses (in single player) when you open your inventory, so feel free to swap weapons as needed to adapt to enemy types. You may find though, that most of the time you’re just smacking enemies to build up enough overdrive to unleash an awesome demon power on the hordes. There are some truly powerful damage per second demon powers that can clear entire rooms (sunray, boomerang, etc).
Pros:
+Interesting game mechanics that rely more on skill than on having godly equipment.
+Co-op multiplayer, though there aren’t that many people playing nowadays.
+There is a transmutation system to build/upgrade your weapons, but unfortunately I didn’t really know to keep my old loot until near the end (apparently inventory space is infinite in this game). You need to sacrifice weapons/items for transmutation, and I had already sold all the stuff I thought was trash. Transmuted weapons can be more powerful than “legendary weapons” because of the ability to boost specific traits.
Cons:
-The story is kind of lackluster, possibly because the game seems to be adapted from another language. Maybe it’s just bad voice acting though. The voice acting from the main antagonist is pretty good though.
-The ability to jump around can be a little annoying because it’s not always clear whether or not you should be able to jump a gap. There are a lot of “invisible walls” that block your progress when you’re trying to jump.
I was kind of hoping to come back after beating the game and just breeze through all the areas again, completing all challenges and getting Steam achievements, but because of the way the game works (you’re not that much stronger in the end) I wasn’t able to do it. I guess I’m not patient enough to replay levels over and over trying to meet specific criteria. Overall, the game is fun and worth the 16 hours or so that it takes to beat every level at least once, especially if you enjoy action RPGs. Unfortunately I wasn’t able to do much multiplayer, due to the low online player base.

Local co op review. So I have sat on this since December 2015 awaiting the local co op patch, so thought it should get a co op specific review for anyone purchasing for this feature.
The way local co op has been implemented is outstanding. Easy to set up from the main menu, no fiddling around just press A on the second pad when prompted.
Gold, XP, even loot are all shared. Its so refreshing to see developers implement every aspect of local coop that I enjoy and leave all the niggles out of the game. When you get a chest the items are duplicated so each player gets to choose whether the item is useful to them.
Players are clearly labelled on screen so even if you opt for the same outfits its easy to spot who's who.
Game play works really well with the extra player onscreen, menu screens are separate though so you do have to wait for each player to finish their build.
To sum up, perfection. Only Diablo 3 comes close in terms of perfect execution.

This is the first good chess game I've seen since the chessmaster.
Game: The recent problem with developing chess games hasn't been getting very good chess engines but dumping them down to the casual chess player, say 800 to 1200 ELO. Chessmaster's lower ranking players were playing like grandmasters for several moves and then doing something stupid like sucrificing a queen just to justify their low rating. Pure Chess isn't like that. I've played through levels 1 to 7 and they all seemed pretty good simulations of how a human would play. I'm playing levels 6 and 7 regularly now and I'm enjoying every single game.
I don't get how the rating system works. It includes ELO and some PureChess rating number. ELO is stuck on 1000 since day one while the PureChess rating gradually changes but not after every game. There should be more explanation about that.
Graphics: Great! Yet, double check the system requirements: there're ridiculusly high for a chess game and there's not much choice in terms of graphics settings. You may think that a 5 year old laptop capable of playing COD4 will manage this... Well, it may not.
Learning: There's nothing, just a joke set of courses about learning the basic moves et cetera. Get chessmaster for that (if you can find it).
Multiplayer: Not worth it principally because there seem to be people not willing to make a move. If you're playing with your steam friends it's probably good (I haven't tried it)

I think 33 hours playing this game is enough to write my review.
This game placed in a World War 1 setting. For me, this alone makes it worth to try, because, as we know, there are very few FPS games in this period.
The Gameplay in Verdun is quite fast-paced which makes it quite arcady but because of the map layouts, there is still a lot of positioning you have to do in order to be successful. The maps themselves are incredibly interesting representations of what a battlefield would look like during those times. The environment seems realistic as you traverse the long trenches or charge through the no-mans-land. You can see the numerous objects like ammo boxes, crates, artillery pieces in the trenches and near them, you can see tents, crashed airplanes, tons of craters, barbed wire.
The arsenal in this game is quite large and I think there is a "class" for everyone - one can use the cool old rifles, charge to fight in close quarters with bayonets, trench knifes, clubs, pistols. There are cool machineguns with which the player can lay down supressing fire or just snipe the enemy. You can use snipers which have the ability to use both the scoped sight and the iron sight. There are two semi-automatic rifles and one submachine guns but I have seen them very rarely.
The last thing I wish to say is that this game is a good one. If you are a fan of FPS games and desire to fight in a WW1 setting, this is the game for you.

First off, I love this game, and it's constantly being updated to become just as addicting as its predecessor.
Genre:  Tower defence with loot finder elements.
Pros:
(- Level up system:
* Ability points.
*  Different towers.
*  Stat increases.
*  Gear level Requirments.)
- The combined genre of TD (Tower defence) and Loot Finder make this game extremely unique.
- Up to 4 player coop which might be increased to 6 or 8 player on select maps in the future.
- Great graphics.
- Four different hero classes.  Some might complain about this in comparison to DD1, but again, there will be more hero classes in the future.
Neutral:
- Non boostable leveling.  This is something that I can't quite tell if I like or not.  Allow me to exaplain...
- In the first game, if you wanted to level up a character very quickly it could be done easily by setting up a defence with multiple high level heros and then switching to your level one to instantly hit around level 70 after maybe 4 waves, depending on your setup.  In DD2 this is not possible, your character level is capped with a maximum level difference between both characters of 5.
Cons:  Last time I played the game was still in Pre-Alpha, might be in Alpha now, and these cons will repesent the game in Pre-Alpha.
- No kicking system.  Nothing grinds my gears more than when someone ques up for coop and afks.
- No Pets.  I miss my treadmill buddies.  Maybe we'll get some elliptical pals this time around.
- No survival mode as of yet, I'm sure they'll get around to it soon though.
- No outfits yet, not much of a con.
It's very difficult to think of cons for this game.
Eventual pro:
The game will eventually become free to play with microtransactions for cosmetic overrides.  If you buy it now you'll recieve in game credit for what you paid!
I highly recommend this game.  I love it.

At first, Banished seems like an ordinary, go-to build-your-city-and-that's-it game. That is, until you actually start playing it. Behind the Stronghold-ish outer shell lies a game of immense size and difficulty. It is quite unlike any settler game I have played, and even though the UI is simple, the buildings few, and the goal simple, I have never needed to start over as many times as I have in this game. It challenges you, but reaping the rewards of a well-built city is so much more rewarding in this than in any other game like it.
After several years with plenty of food and resources, even a single mistake can tip the scale and annihilate your entire city in a matter of a single summer. As deceptful and tricky this game can be, as great will it be when things go right.
However, a few things seem to still be missing:
- Multiplayer, for one. The option to make a map where you can play with a few friends would rocket-toss this game into orbit, and I, for one, fear I'd never leave my room again.
- Minor tweaks to things such as clarity. I want to know just WHY my labourers and builders are prioritizing certain things, how many people a single market can cover - stuff like that.
- Minor bugfixes. Prioritizing a certain area doesn't seem to always work - and sometimes that is a really crucial thing. I need my workers to build a fishing hut instead of laying down road, and it sucks to lose 30% of your population due to this.
Overall, I rate this game 4.5/5, and I'd recommend it to each and all. It's a great game, doesn't take up much space, and can easily be the game you play when you have a few minutes before you have stuff to do.

As with any Early Access game, make sure it is a game you are okay with it being changed as development goes on. As it stands, the game plays very similar to the first, with some minor changes. So far it seems to be living up to the greatness that was Dungeon Defenders 1.
Understand that because it is early access, I know a lot of my concerns with the game will be fixed, and I will update my review when that happens.
Pros/Cons:
+ The AI seems to be smarter, and more dificult than those in the first game.
+ The ability to move your hero while in place/repair/upgrade defense mode is amazing.
+ The Dual Mana system is also an awesome addition. You now have mana for abilities, and a separate mana for towers.
+ The new defenses each hero has are either upgrades from the first game, or new all together, which is good.
+ The ability to vote for the next addition into the game is an awesome early access feature, and should be done more often by developers.
- The gear upgrade system is lacking, and confusing at first.
- There has yet to be added a proper tutorial system for new features.
- The small amount of maps gets old quite fast, and the game tends to get boring after a bit.
- Costumes and pets are nowhere to be found, and is one of the things that made the first game a favorite.
- The gear shops are barely useful, as the only reason I use them is to get junk gear to upgrade my current stuff.
All in all, the game is damn good, and can only get better from here.

Hyperdimension neptunia Re;birth3 is the sequel to MkII/Re;bith2 Sister generation, rather than being set in a different universe, Re;birth3/Victory is a continuation from MkII

The Gameplay has been kept the same as Re;birth's 1 and 2, so only slight differences may vary, for example, a character's EXE attack can only be used if they have a bar filled in their SP bar, so instead of having 4 EXE bars, you could have 16 EXE attacks depending on if you use them, non-CPU characters have access to an awakened state, which powers them up, and of course, we have the challenges, from staying out of battle to jumping "x" amount of times in the areas
Re;birth3 has really great jokes and solid writing (IMHO), though i would still suggest jumping into the series from Re;birth2 if you want to make sense of the plot (especially for Megadimension)
Overall: Re;birth3 is another great remake of the mainstream neptunia games (This is Victory BTW), buy it if you like Neptunia, or if you want Sadie to spank you at night

Its atmosphere, art and narrative make this the most successful adaptation of H.P. Lovecraft's Cthulhu mythos to date; in terms of game design and programming however, it's borderline unplayable. Atrocious collision detection, poor enemy AI and line-of-sight, a stupid quadrant-based health system, useless stealth and an overall mess of bizarre bugs break what is essentially a great game. The only mechanics that work involve exploration and environment interaction which brings it closer to a first-person adventure game than a shooter (a rare type of game even today). In fact, were many of it's bad mechanics dropped or reworked you may very well have something exceptional. In terms of story it's adaptation of Lovecraft's mythos is pitch-perfect. The locale and many of it's characters are word-for-word from the short stories. The characters invented for it are so close to Lovecraft's vision of a malign universe that it brings a level of genuine cohesion to stories that were sometimes more of a sketch. From the haunted detective Jack Walters to the thuggish J. Edgar Hoover and the scheming Marsh family it sets a tone of fantasy horror and noir where every character measures up. You search the damp, decaying port town of Innsmouth unearthing every horror imaginable and eventually lead a charge with the FBI and military against the brood of Cthulhu... And if you can get through all of that without crashing once or dying for no reason you'll enjoy it. Hopefully in the future games like it will get all the bugs worked out.

Call of Cthulhu is an astonishing game, unlike anything you have every played before. It's a psycho-horror game from 2006, and what it lacks in graphics is tens of times weighted up by the gameplay. This game creates a thrill on the same level as Amnesia: The Dark Descent, and some of the levels are even more intense and makes you even more scared. You dont have any weapons half of the game, or bullets scattered around to help you. This is why I find Call of Cthulhu so much more enjoyable than games like Dead Space and F.E.A.R. Those are all "jumpscares", and in these games, when you first have spotted the enemy, you can fill them up with bullets. This is not the case in Call of Cthulhu. In this game you have to sneak around, and if you're spotted - you're ♥♥♥♥ed. The only option left is to run as fast as you can, and to barricade the doors behind you. And oh! Did I mention that if you get hit in your legs by the enemy, the ability to walk is restricted? If you dont heal up, you will bleed to death - unless the enemies gets you first. As if that is not enough, this game makes you think you're actually in the game. The heartbeats of our hero, they are like your own. The breathing of the hero when he's scared? They are like your own too. This creates a tension unlike anything I have ever played before - I forgot I was sitting in my room at night. ♥♥♥♥, this game makes you believe you're there.
As stated before, the big plus in this game is the gameplay. However, the storyline is abit odd, based on the literature of H.P Lovecraft. You play as a private detective in the 1920's, looking for a kid in a town where everything seems abit "odd". As you talk with the people to get clues where to go next, everyone are calling you "stranger", and they seem rather suspicious to you. As you walk around to discover the city, you realise that you're, mildly said: ♥♥♥♥'d. You're looking down a basement in the house nexdoor to the inn where you're staying, and you realise theres a dead guy lying down there. Before you're able to react, theres this "huge" shadow dragging the dead person away from your sight. A few moments later, when you're thinking what the ♥♥♥♥ is wrong with this city, theres a guy walking out of the front door. Isn't that the innkeeper?♥♥♥♥♥♥
This is what makes this game absolutely perfect. It creates a cosmic horror of the unknown. You never know what comes next. You get clue upon clue that this place wants you dead, and you cant do♥♥♥♥♥♥to prevent it. Even better, the sanity of our "hero" is mentally broken down. He tends to hallucinate, and what you think he sees are "only" a dream. Or is it? You dont know. Sometimes its just an hallucination, and sometimes its "real". Only one thing is certain: you're ♥♥♥♥ed.
However, there is one feeling you get in this game which makes you scared ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, and makes you coldsweating. The feeling of helplessness and hopelessness. You're isolated, and your victories are only temporarily, and they often come with a great price. This makes you think: was it all worth it? Did I do anything wrong?
To sum it up: this game kicks major♥♥♥♥♥ The psycho-horror thrill this game creates is unbelievable. If you play it alone at night, you forget its just a game. This game makes you think it's real. It creates an hostile environment who expands around you. You never know what comes next, but you know its going to be bad. Thus, it makes it one of the best, if not the best game I have ever played in the horror-genre.
Play this game. You wont regret it.

Napoleon: Total War
+ Relive key battles from history in the 19th century playing as Napoleon Bonaparte, fighting against the Coalition.
+ The campaigns of Napoleon focus specifically on particular geographical locations, like Italy and Egypt. Interesting to play on.
+ Real-time battles where you command thousands of soldiers, artillery and cavalry at once.
+ The Grand campaign map spans Europe, so it's a decent size. However, it's definitely smaller than most Total War games and is therefore less enjoyable.
+ Nice diplomacy system.
+ DLC packs (The Peninsular campaign) are fun, but be prepared for a challenge.
+ Graphics are a step up from the previous title in the series, Empire: Total War and look acceptable, but they're not fantastic by any means.
- Napoleon: Total War is less complex than its predecessor, Empire: Total War. It's missing a lot of features which would enhance it and seems a bit too simplistic at times. This is an issue which greatly detracts from the potential of the game.
Overall Score: 8/10
Napoleon Total War offers many gameplay options to players and is downright fun. It could have been a 10/10 like Empire: Total War was, but it falls short. I recommend you grab this at any opportunity when it's not expensive.

Looks lovely and does basic computer chess well.
Others have reported issues with piece selection and camera control. Personally I have had no issue with either - I simply drag to the camera position Iwant and let go, then it stays there whilst you play. Of course the pieces are so pretty that it's hard to resist flying around them all the time! Admittedly you don't have full 360 degree movement (you just swing around your half of the board), but in my opinion it does the job. I haven't had many issues with alt-tab either, though I do have to tap Tab twice in order to get out and occassionally it doesn't work at all.
This is not a serious chess programme: it doesn't import/export games, allow you to set up positions, rate your play, train you (beyond basic move rules), play FICS or any of that. And the online isn't up to the job (you just press 'auto challenge' and it sets you up with a random, if any are online). But you have got Lucas/Arena/Fritz/Jin and the rest if you need those things.
What it is, is a satisfying way to play a few games against a competent AI or a friend (locally or online). I've played a fair bit of chess and it's far better than I am. If could play properly then it may not be up to snuff, but for 90% of people I'd guess it was more than adequate. And because it's so damn pretty, I reckon it'll encourage me to play more.
I do hope that the developers will consider adding some tutorials, maybe classic games (preferably with commentary) and allow game import/export. With such an attractive set-up, it would be a great way to step through a recent game on FICS, for example.

When it was recommended to me by my Brother, I had no clue what to expect from Verdun. Awaiting the outcome of "Battlefield 1" I however was interested in the subject and curious enough to give it a try.
Once I got in the game for the first time I was not disappointed about the interface at all but it was somehow complicated to find a way into battle. It made me think right away I was in some sort of a single player mode.
As soon as I found out how it all worked the game surprised me more and more every battle. So far I only had tried the Death-match mode, and I felt other game modes would have even many more surprises to me.
That's when I made a very appreciated discovery. ...Well actually, I had seen the possibility earlier but I hadn't tried it out yet. So I decided to try the TDM mode which is more than a usual TDM  mode as we know it from most shooters.
Verdun managed to lift it to a higher lvl. The way they implemented the famous WWI trench-war tactics made it even more realistic and it requires more tactical and combined thinking from the players themselves, instead of lone wolf hero-actions.
New to the concept of TDM is that you can choose your preferred (players-created) division, or put up your own. So u can play either as a French, German, Belgian,... soldier in a one nation battalion. Each battalion you join you have to work your way up again. To know that all sorts of Battalions fight their own type of weaponry means that you have to upgrade your weapons per battalion, not per weapon type. That does stimulates you to fight in the same battalion each time. It also means that you have to join a battalion representing the nation of the origin your preferred rifle was used in back in that time in order to hand you favorite weapon.
Beside an overwhelming range of authentic rifles and even light and medium machine guns with each their advantages and disadvantages, the game also showed me very detailed uniforms worn by the different nations that fought in WWI. Also the details of the maps are surprisingly great, well thought out and teach us something about WWI warfare and living conditions.
To me there is only one thing missing making the game as if you were really there; the cold and the smell of gas, sweat, death, explosion-fires.
- In short:
Look & feel: ++
Realism: ++
Graphical details: ++
Gameconcept: ++
Sound & vocals: ++  (original languages and accents per nation)
Can I think of any negatives? Movable objects may be more interactive, so is the way soldiers move.
I definatly would recommend u to give it a try. To me it scores way higher in realism than BF1 does for example.

All in all, I recommend it for a good price.

There is alot to like about this game. But there probably is more to hate sadly.
The good.
-Great visuals(textures), and realistic gas effects.
-Maps have been mostly fixed so that spawn camping isn't as bad as it was, or as bad as some games.
-The wave-based respawn system is in line with alot of realistic(ish) FPS games.
-The historic locations look great, and the
trench based warfare makes way more sense than whatever BF does.
-Lots of different factions to select from and each has different available weapons usually unique to that particular
faction.
The bad.
-Viewing distance is atrocious even at max settings. The image at any distance past 50-75 meters is so aliased and
blocky at 1080p that it's almost impossible to get kills at range unless you have a scoped rifle. FXAA is the only in-game
AA option and it does almost nothing to the image. I've tried DSR but the game just crashes, and forced MSAA results in
constant crashing and unplayable framerates(I went from 90FPS to 20ish at 2xMSAA).
-Guns do not fire in straight lines if not held in iron-sights. Repeatedly dying after shooting enemies point-blank(with no
hit indicator) from the hip(chest?) shows that either the guns don't fire straight, or the hit boxes are jacked. This is a
common issue in most FPS games due to a design choice for balancing purposes but shouldn't be for a realistic shooter.
-There is no cover system. For a game that is focused around trench warfare, the only weapons that allow you to setup
behind cover are MG's(but not all of them).
-The suppression system is not effective. It simply changes your screen color to black and white.
-Hit-boxes on terrain is bizarre. Sometimes you'll get shot through the same piece of cover you just tried to shoot
someone else through. Or you'll be standing next to a wall and shooting down the trench and the bullet will hit
perpendicular to the end of the weapon.
-Weapon balancing is insane. 90% of the time ANY bolt-action rifle will kill you in 1 shot, regardless of position on body.
The Reichsrevolver M1883 has similar lethality. The issue I have is that unless you get a headshot, every other gun that
uses a similar caliber is much less lethal. Machine guns regularly take 2-3 shots to kill(even ones using the EXACT same
cartridge as bolt-action rifles that 1-shot), SMG's are a joke taking 4-5 shots to kill and have insane recoil. Most other
pistol variants seem fairly balanced however at 2-4 shots depending on location.
The odd.
-Squads are made up of 4 unique unit types. Squad leaders get 2 abilities(depending on faction) a pistol(sometimes there
is a rifle or SMG option), and maybe grenades. Machine gunners usually get a single weapon(either a bolt-action or 2
different MG's). Sniper's get a bolt-action or 2 different scoped guns. Grenadiers usually get 2 pistol variants(or a bolt-action) and grenades. There are only 4 people per squad though, leading to too many of some unit types in battles.
-Grenades have similar AOE to artillery. And you can throw them insane distances(easily 100m) but you have no way of controlling the distance. They also seem to have rag-doll physics making accurate use almost impossible.
Overall I feel pretty conflicted about the game. While unendingly frustrating with it's flaws, I find myself drawn to play the game with friends(because the server populations are so low). There is much potential to this game, but I think it's been too long since it's release for it to recover. Unless some expansion or major boost in sales occurs, I'd stay away and save your $25.

As with any Early Access game, make sure it is a game you are okay with it being changed as development goes on. As it stands, the game plays very similar to the first, with some minor changes. So far it seems to be living up to the greatness that was Dungeon Defenders 1.
Understand that because it is early access, I know a lot of my concerns with the game will be fixed, and I will update my review when that happens.
Pros/Cons:
+ The AI seems to be smarter, and more dificult than those in the first game.
+ The ability to move your hero while in place/repair/upgrade defense mode is amazing.
+ The Dual Mana system is also an awesome addition. You now have mana for abilities, and a separate mana for towers.
+ The new defenses each hero has are either upgrades from the first game, or new all together, which is good.
+ The ability to vote for the next addition into the game is an awesome early access feature, and should be done more often by developers.
- The gear upgrade system is lacking, and confusing at first.
- There has yet to be added a proper tutorial system for new features.
- The small amount of maps gets old quite fast, and the game tends to get boring after a bit.
- Costumes and pets are nowhere to be found, and is one of the things that made the first game a favorite.
- The gear shops are barely useful, as the only reason I use them is to get junk gear to upgrade my current stuff.
All in all, the game is damn good, and can only get better from here.

This is an actually
WW1 First Person Shooter. If you are interested in the western front of WW1 and the weapons of that era; you should really check the game out. However the game has it's negatives. The maps are not that many (although they are HUGE and well disigned), the learining curve is steep as hell and the game is limited the thed west only (if you prefer the eastern front you should check their new game: Tannenberg). Also the game is VERY buggy. I do however really like it.

Finally, we have a nice, but affordable little chess game on Steam (without annoying advertisements, Simply Chess!), a necessity that was missing for a long time. I appreciate that I have the choice to play against humans, play against the AI or solve little problems with an increasing degree of difficulty. I feel a comfortable, relaxing and somehow noble atmosphere, brooding over my virtual board while listening to Mozart.
The controls are something one has to get used to, and the game does not do a good job explaining itself in this regard.
- Sometimes, it is hard to distinguish the different kinds of (glass-like half transparent) pieces from the default perspective; left-click and drag moves your camera though, and you can check wether this is a Queen or a Bishop...
- Moving your pieces with your mouse does not work well sometimes, because the hitboxes are not set right; you can however solve this with your arrow keys.
- Setting the volume of music and sound effects is explained ingame, but not in a helpful way; again, clicking the value and dragging the mouse (up or down) is the solution.
- Finally: Leaving the game temporarily with ALT-TAB is not possible; if you want to read tutorials or do something else without quitting the game, you have to choose "fullscreen off" in the launcher menu.
Such difficulties are more than unnecessary, and I hope the developer will fix them with patches!
Nevertheless, the game works as it is, and I love chess, therefore I give it a 6/10.

So, this is often billed as the scariest game ever.  Well it isn't.  Is it scary?  Sure.  A little.  The problem with this game is that any seasoned horror film/game fan (primary audience) will recognize it as a collection of cheap scares and a mimicry of the countless, absolutely horrible, found footage Blair Witch knock-offs.  Most horror fans wish that sub genre would go and die a slasher's death but it just keeps coming back to life.  Outlast doesn't feel any different to me than watching one of those horrible films.  You can't see all that well.  You spend most the game looking through a horrible green, nightsight lens and the "scary" parts are reduced to simple "something jumps out and makes a loud noise" moments.  There is no real genuine scare here for one big reason - I have absolutely no investment whatsoever in my own character or the meager plotline provided.  The hiding tactics are rarely used and most often trumped by simply running away.  And you have absolutely no real decision making power at all.  You go through the game as they intend it - very linear - and then it is over.  If Outlast lacked the simple mechanic of me being the one who presses the button to make the character move, this would be a subpar horror flick that went instant to video.  Now... all that said...  This is the best presentation the "survival horror" genre may have seen save State of Decay (a different spin).  If you have played other survival horror, this is merely the most polished version of every other game in that genre.  What Outlast and this genre needs is a more emersive plot, game mechanics that actually matter, decisions that the player can make that actually affect game outcomes, non-linear levels, a geniune attempt at character development to make me care whether I live or die, and some less cookie-cutter enemies.  There is only so many times I can see fatty fatterson and get scared.  His tenth presentation in the game was sort of tired.

Victor Vran is an isometric, free camera, action RPG set in a fictional vaguely 19th century Eastern European country that's been infested with all manner of evil creatures.
While it's an ARPG at heart, it separates itself from it's peers in several key ways, most of which are a welcome breath of fresh air. If you've played Diablo, Torchlight, Fate, Titan Quest and games simlar to those, you know the drill, so I'll list the things that make Victor Vran stand out:
- skilled gameplay: You'll need to dodge, charge up, move and strategically retreat in order to survive. This is not a click to kill sort of game. In this regard it has elements of a twin stick shooter and character action game mixed in the control scheme.
- Less loot, but more focused loot and loot improvement: for better and worse, it's a good shake-up that won't really let true loot ♥♥♥♥♥s down, you'll still be sorting through your inventory comparing stats and looking for upgrade properties.
- Many maps and lots of challenges. "Curses" and hard mode add an additional level of challenge that left even an ARPG veteran like myself feeling like I had to fight for progress rather then sleepwalk through the enemy hordes.
- Level up system: stats are locked to levels, but you can earn rewards and custom gear. Destiny cards add a further level of customization.
Now on top of that:
- The graphics are crisp and detailed depicting a wide variety of environments from city streets to swamps, to dungeons, to rural villages.
- Controls are precise and feel intuitive once you get the hang of them.
- Enemies look great, mostly with a gothic or classic horror feel, but there could be a little more variety.
So in conclusion: Victor Vran is a solid action RPG that relies on player skill and treats you to a short, not particularly amazing story, but provides hours of great gameplay, challenge, and atmosphere.
I reccomend it!

Victor Vran is a solid enough action RPG. It is by no means the best action RPG ever made, but it is different enough to carve its own niche.
The combat is more dynamic and action oriented than your typical action RPG. Victor Vran is fairly mobile as he can both jump and manually dodge attacks. This works reasonably well, even if the controls could have been slightly more responsive.
There are no classes as such, instead your active skills are determined by your equipped weapon type. There's a decent variety of weapon types and they play quite differently, too. In addition you have access to demon powers which are pretty much traditional spells, just under a different name. And finally, you can collect destiny cards which provide various stat buffs.
Apart from the weapons, destiny cards and demon powers there's very little loot to be had. All in all the loot system is frankly  not very exciting. Leveling is also rather underwhelming, as you mainly unlock additional destiny points and get a few bonus items.
The main story is extremely bad and forgettable even by the rather low action RPG standards. At least each map has various bonus challenges that offer fun ways to get extra loot and experience.
Despite its flaws Victor Vran is an enjoyable enough experience. It's little bit shallow and the story is rubbish, but I would still recommend the game to anyone looking for a new action RPG, especially if you have grown a bit tired of the traditional Diablo formula.
I completed the main campaign on normal difficulty and went back afterwards to do some of the map challenges. I'm unlikely to keep playing, however, as the endgame doesn't sound particularly enticing to me.
The good:
- Combat is much more dynamic than your typical action RPG
- Each weapon type plays quite differently
- Scythes as weapons
- Map challenges are a fun addition
The bad:
- Fairly shallow gameplay
- Rather limited item and leveling system
- Terrible story and forgottable characters
- Some annoying enemies
- Enemy scaling can be tedious at times
The ugly:
- Initially I was suffering from a really nasty crash bug that made the game basically unplayable. Latest patch seems to have fixed the issue

Out of all Re:Birth games I've played so far, this is my second favorite after the first Re;Birth. There are also some good features that make this one a little better:
-The new SP system, which needs a bit of effort to fill up without items at first (Unless you have drill, which makes you god-like), but gives every party member their own exe drive, so you can use multiple ultimate attacks in a row.
-Using four characters at once instead of just three. Not sure why they didn't do that with the first one though.
-This time you're allowed to choose between keep playing after finishing the story or start next game cycle instead of pulling you straight into the beggining of the story again.
-They added a feature to let you track which monsters have that specific drop you're looking for
-Those little plans to customize your game that make playing it all the better with your favorite character.
-Good soundtrack, from awesome battle tracks to funny or casual music during cutscenes.
-More Nep...what's not to love about that?
Now as much as I love this game and could keep going on and on about it, it has it's flaws:
-Some 3D scenes or battles can get laggy when fighting with everyone in HDD mode, especially around the ending.
-The game and grinding might get slow and repetitive after a while, especially around the last levels.
-The true ending can be complex to get without a guide to help you. And even then you might have to do a few game cycles before getting it.
-In Re;Birth 1 and 2 they added Processors to give Noire's HDD form her pigtails hairstyle from Victory, but didn't bother doing it the other way around in this game...not really a flaw, but fans of her original hairstyle (like me) would have loved it.
-A lot of people wanted a DLC that let you have Rei Ryghts as a playable character, but that never happened. Again, not a flaw. But indeed something that would have made a lot of people happy if added.
Conclussion:
As a fan of the franchise, I might be overlooking some flaws. And this game isn't really for those searching for a dark, serious story. But nonetheless, it's a fun and entertaining game to play, and I recommend it for everyone looking for a good RPG-Visual Novel hybrid coupled with a few laughs.

Call of Cthulhu Dark Corners of the Earth (Aka Call of Cthulhu: DCotE or CoC:  DCotE) is a truly amazing game. Yes the graphics are old and outdated, but this game still manages to create a sense of horror and panic. The story is inspired by several of H.P. Lovecraft's short stories. Though I won't ruin the plot I can say that this game is what got me into Lovecraft's terrifying mythos. CoC:  DCotE didn't innovate any new mechanics like Portal, but it did take mechanics from old Adventure games, First Person Shooters, and Stealth games rolling them into one terrifying mystery that feels like the work of H.P. Lovecraft. The game did manage to innovate one thing, the simulation of going insane. Through out the game as you encounter the horrors of the world, your sanity will drain causing you to see blur effects, and hear your self whispering dark things. The game suffers horribly from glitches, and I'm not talking about seeing a flying cart, I'm talking about game crashing glitches. I don't know if it's because of my new and up to date computer or because they were simply in the game to begin with, but there were two points where my game crashed. These points can't be passed at all. There’s literally no way passed them unless you do what I did, find a computer from that era. No, I didn't go out and buy an old computer, I happened to have three computers. My laptop can still run "Doom 95", my old computer runs Windows XP, and my new computer runs Windows 7. I found for me at least, that the game ran best on my old computer. This dilemma may not happen to everyone though, and once I started on the right computer I didn't encounter any glitches. If you have the money and the right computer you will find your self in one of the best horror game experiences out there. On a scale from one to ten, I would give this game an eight over all.

There is a lesser focus on loot. The loot you do get is useful for transmutation, the games crafting system, which isn't a neccessity at all. End game seems to have plenty to do. Hundreds of challenges to complete and secrets to find that all give rewards. Time limited treasure hunts & bounties to kill certain elite mobs in certain areas, a wave based arena, and an area that refreshes with new bosses and challenges every day.
Overall a solid experience, I'm definitely looking forward to the Motorhead themed expansion.

I'm just gonna be outright, I love this game. You should just stop here and go buy it so you can truly experience it for yourself.
Regardless, people want a review, not 1+ thread, so here:
VVVVVV (Pronounced like a singular statement of the letter V [Vee]) is a slightly older 2D side-scrolling platformer (2010) by Terry Cavanagh, who is also known for the game Super Hexagon released two years later. The main gimmick is the forsaking of a traditional jump for the ability to flip gravity.
The art direction is reminicient of Comodore 64, due to it's clever use of blackspace, limited yet vibrant color pallet, and simplistic yet recognizable sprites. Foreground and background are well differintiated, as are hazards from terrain.At times the speed of the game can be disorienting, but the drastic color pallet allows it to be of minimal issue, as things can be very easilly recognized and dealt with, without fumbling through same-y textures. The soundtrack is nothing short of fantastic, and needs to be experienced for oneself to truly respect.
The gameplay is supurb: The game is hard, as death is quick, but so is respawning, so you are back on your feet almost instantly. The controlls are tight and simple; move left or right, or flip gravity. There is an accelleration to movement, but it is fairly minimal, it is very nessecary to take into account regardless.
In terms of length, it took me around four hours for my first playthrough, one hour of which was spent exclusively on getting one very difficult to acquire trinket. I died 1800 times, 1000 of which was on that same trinket. I did not complete the game in this time, as there are also time-trials, special modes, and other post-game challenges to take on.
The game does run in 30 FPS (at least for me), but it was of little issue for me, as it was incredibly smooth and playable even at such a framerate.
As to avoid spoilers, I will be stopping here. I wish you all well, and hope you look to pick this one up.

Bought the complete edition on sale @$9.99 USD. Few installation problems with Uplay and Steam but I found a way around it.
PROS
Very long and illustrious franchisewith its ups and downs. Up to HOMM6 now.
Certain classes of heroes (Sanctuary) can swim without a ship if all units in the army are amphibious. Similar to Disciples but a good addition. Would also have liked a hero that can fly. Makes each faction less generic.
Pirate race of neutrals sounded great (Crag Hack campaign) until it became all Orc Class / Stronghold Faction. Good attempt.
CONS
The game feels like it is incomplete. After playing Might and Magic : Duel of Champions and seeing all the different creatures, spells, classes, buildings and heroes, Heroes feels like it is still in alpha.
Diplomacy mechanic has not been changed. It is is still very weak and almost useless. It only increases the number of creatures that join you and only affects neutral creatures. Creature stances are fixed in stone and do not change e.g. Hostile creatures stay hostile all the way throughout the game.
Minor issues like illogical campaign speeches e.g. Orc Campaign : Acama speaks on your side when you have yet to convince him to join you.
Campaign choices for Tears vs Blood may always favour Tears since letting neutral creatures run away without a fight gains +10 Tears.
Dynasty weapons take way too long to grind up beyond Level 2.
Logging into CONFLUX before the game starts is getting on my nerves.
Edit:
Story is pretty boring for all factions, except the Necropolis. Only Anastasya's story is somewhat interesting.
Faction abilities are not of an equal level.
1. Having the Necropolis have the most powerful faction ability to resurrect AND heal is quite overpowered. Not to mention. Having the Altar of Eternal Servitude makes it even worse with an immortal army.
2. Gating ability for Inferno takes too long to activate. It has to first gain points then wait in queue to be summoned. Although being able to summon anywhere on the map seems enviable, it is quite easy countered. Gating units does not help to prevent unit loss since gated units do not stay. While the L4 gated ability (instant gate + copy of original stack) is ridiculously powerful, it takes way too long to activate.
3. The Haven "bubble" is not very useful. Enemies almost always have another valid target to attack. The main benefit is being fast to cast and preventing your range units from being targetted in the first round of combat.
4. Castle architecture is very bland. They resemble coloured boxes. You can't differentiate a barracks from a market.
RECOMMENDATION
Bring in all the stuff from MMDOC into Heroes. E.g. Wizard Class/Academy Faction which already existed in previous versions of Heroes, Tier 4 creatures like the Ghost Dragon, Wyvern Riders for the Stronghold.
You can even bring in unique creatures to prevent classes from turning stale.g. Al Betyl Ghoul is a way more powerful ghoul compared to normal Ravenous Ghouls for the Necropolis.
For Diplomacy, allow it to change the stance of the creatures towards you. e.g. Diplomacy makes Hostile to Aggressive and Agressive to Passive and Passive to Friendly. The ability to bribe safe passage. The ability for Diplomacy to work on enemy heroes not just neutrals.
Flying heroes. On dragons.
Co-op campaign maps.
REFERENCES

Before I get to the game, I should point out that I play on Mac only, but due to the poor coding of the game some of the content (like achievements and online leaderboards) won't work natively despite the game clearly being advertised for all platforms. Because of this I have to run the game through a Windows environment. When I have to emulate the game on a platform I'm not normally supposed to play in, that's a not a good sign.
I will give the game credit for its appealing visuals and super cool marble skins, but for the gameplay itself? It's highly lackluster and in some cases poorly made. The marble you control is slippery as all can be; trying to maintain your footing on platforms is a jarring task itself because of how bad the marble controls. There's also a severe lack of control when the marble is in mid-air too. 50% of the time when I'm trying to move while in mid-air the marble is just stuck almost in a straight, vertical line, and I end up undershooting a ton of jumps. The final unlockable you get in the game is a double jump for use with the power-up button. This should have been selectable by default because without this ability the level exploring is atrocious and ultimately an unpleasant experience. This game could have been something really impressive if they took more time to fine-tune the controls, make the acceleration less slippery, and overall make the movement more fluent. I would dare say this game is enjoyable only after you've gotten perfectly used to the awful controls, which is not good.
Apart from the main 7 levels (yes, there are only 7 levels in the game) are 3 different mini-games you can play. Arena is a poor-man's survival game where you can hug the center chain and last hundreds of seconds before the enemy marbles knock you off, Laser Jump is a basic jump-rope game with no real strategy to it, and Crate Chaos is an abysmal "air-time" game that is infuriating to try and last 100 seconds on due to the aforementioned poor jumping controls. One cool feature I will admit adds more replay value and is somewhat enjoyable is the addition of a custom levels archive, which can be downloaded in individual sets for more action. They're shorter and surprisingly better designed despite most of them not being as aesthetically pleasing to the eye. As of this review, it's the only portion of this game that is bringing me back to play it from time to time.
Overall I found this game to be a disappointing experience. Poor Macintosh compatibility despite clearly being advertised on all platforms, slippery physics & controls, disorientating motion blurs, convoluted level design, and unfair achievements that test the raw sanity of its players. I do not recommend getting this game, even if you are an avid marble platformer game fan. I recommend playing something like Lost Marbles, Switchball, or MarbleBlast Gold instead.

As a gamer who likes platformers and multiplayer party games, Ultimate Chicken Horse was pretty much made for me. I loved the concept from the second I saw it on Steam’s list of upcoming games and I knew I had to give it a try. After playing the game for a few hours, I can already tell that Ultimate Chicken Horse is a game that I am going to come back to time and time again to spend a fun hour or two. It isn’t a game you are going to play for five hours straight but in small doses, it is a very fun time.
There aren’t very many negatives with Ultimate Chicken Horse but let’s just get the few of them out of the way right away. First of all, while this isn’t really that big of a negative since it probably wouldn’t be very fun anyways, the lack of single-player still has to be on the list. Most likely the computer player would either be an idiot or an unbeatable force (it has to be really hard to program a computer player in a game like this) but players who have nobody to play with locally and hate playing online are out of luck in this game (I know that is a small minority though) and should not purchase it.
Other than that, the only negatives for Ultimate Chicken Horse are one small scoring decision I don’t agree with (I feel that underdog gives out too many points to the trailing player), one addition I would make to scoring (adding either a slight reward for finishing much faster than your opponents or a timer that starts once one player has finished and all their opponents must finish the course before time expires or they will fail the round), and the wish for a few more levels (though nine different levels is definitely a solid amount).
Unless you have nobody to play with locally and hate playing online, those negatives are not severe at all and everything else about Ultimate Chicken Horse is great. The presentation is awesome. The game has a very cute cartoony, almost hand-drawn like art style that I love. The characters are adorable and I can’t even decide which one is the cutest. The sound effects are cute as well and the soundtrack is pretty darn catchy. Everything about the presentation will definitely appeal to both children and children at heart (like me).
Also, for a game that lets you edit a level on the fly, Ultimate Chicken Horse is surprisingly easy to use. All you have to do is select an object to use, move the object to an acceptable location, and place it. Since you are building the level yourself, the difficulty of the game itself is very flexible. Kids can construct relatively easy levels that they can complete while masochists can make levels that can compete with Super Meat Boy on the platforming difficulty scale. If you really like to mess with your friends, you can even technically sometimes make a level that is impossible to complete just so your friends can’t get those precious points and steal your lead. The messing with your friends mechanics are very fun though if you are playing with an overly competitive person, they can relatively easily mess with everyone else so that nobody can overtake their lead (they can use a bomb to destroy helpful objects, set up nearly impossible obstacles and traps, etc.). A lot of the fun of the game is messing with your friends and making the most ridiculously difficult level that you can.

Flatout was one of those games that I found on GOG and decided to try. I didn't expect much, but there was a sale, and I picked the game up for $1.90. The instant I got into a race I knew that the game would be good. There was mayhem, car bits smashing everywhere, tires all over the road, explosions after colliding with barrels. The game was fun, and to this day the original Flatout is one of my favorite racing games.
So when I heard that there was going to be a Flatout 3 (Sequel to Flatout 2, which was also a great game,) I was excited. I waited the week until it came out, (I should've known something was up, they only announced the game a week before it was released!) and promptly bought the game off of Steam. Once it had finished downloading, I started the game up to see if it was a worthy successor to the game that I had loved.
The first thing I did was check out the graphics options. I have a fairly fast computer, so I maxed everything out. I headed into a race. There were several classes of cars to choose from, and one of the classes was Classic. The car looked decent, so I chose it. After a loading screen with an unmoving bar, I was in. From the start, I was shocked. I won't tell you the specifics of this race, I'll just break it down by category:
Physics
One of the best things about the previous Flatout games was the tight sense of physics. It wasn't quite a simulation, but it was realistic enough that you had to be careful not accidentally hit something solid and crash. It also had excellent car damage, and the cars dented and crunched realistically. With Flatout 3, all of this was thrown out of the window.
Cars in Flatout 3 handle like they do in those racing games at the arcade. When you're driving them, you don't really have a sense of control like you do in a real car. They feel way too fast, and also very light. They are also very difficult to control. The cars in Flatout 3 have all of these traits. They just don't have the tight sense of control that previous games had. Instead, they feel like someone modded the game files to make things more hectic. Honestly, it just feels bad.
Gamemodes
If there was one thing that I thought Flatout 3 had going for it, it was it’s gamemodes. It has a varied lineup that looks like it could be fun to play, but still manages to fail. The modes are: Race, Stunt Man, Big Battle, Battle Arena, Monster Trucks, Speed, Nightshift, Offroad, and Challenge.
Race is the obvious one. Race around a track, and the first to complete the predetermined number of laps wins. Nightshift is actually identical to race, the only difference being that all of the courses are at night. Race mode lacks depth, but this can be forgiven seeing as there’s only so much you can do with a lap race. Even so, the mode really isn’t very good. I wouldn’t say it’s bad as it is, it’s just kinda boring.
Stunt Man is the classic minigame mode from the previous games. In it, you launch your driver through the windshield to accomplish various tasks. An example would be the high jump. You would drive down a long track until you reached a high net. You would hold down the nitro button to adjust the angle, then release to see how high your driver would be launched. It sounds horribly sadistic, but it really was quite fun in the previous Flatout games.
Not so in Flatout 3.
The reason for this is simple, and this is essentially the reason the game is so bad: The physics engine quite simply fails. You just can't launch your driver like you could in the previous games. It feels cheap, kinda like a bad iPhone game. The physics just don’t perform like they should in the situation. It ruins it.
The next two modes are Big Battle and Battle Arena. In these modes, 8-24 cars are thrown into an arena. A car wins by destroying all other cars in the arena. This is essentially the Derby mode from the older games. This mode sounds fun when I describe it (and it was in the last two games), but it’s terrible in Flatout 3. The reason for this is (once again) the incredibly poor physics engine. Cars fly around as if they were made of paper. A car trading paint with you does 50% damage to you, whereas a T-bone collision only does 20%. And don’t even get me started on the explosions. Unfortunately, this gamemode feels like a cheap knockoff of the established mode from the other games.
Monster Trucks is unique, and it is the highlight of the game. In this mode, your only cars are (guess what) monster trucks. You can then choose from five gamemodes. The first is Search and Destroy, which is a timed dash to destroy 40 barrels on the map. The second is Bring the Light, in which the goal is to bring 5 objects into a container. The next mode is Catch the Bus. In this mode, you have to knock over 5 double decker busses as fast as possible. The fourth is Royal Flush, where players roll a mine into the sewer. The final mode is Dude, Where’s My Car, which is similar to Search and destroy, only with car wrecks instead of barrels. These modes aren’t terrible to play like the other modes, and can actually be enjoyed. Unfortunately, this enjoyment is short lived, and it soon falls to the mundaneness of the rest of the game.
Speed attempts to play like a F1 racer. All of the cars are Formula 1 cars, and the tracks are similarly themed. However, this simply doesn’t work. The combination between Flatout 3 and F1 2012 is a match made in hell, and the mode fails horribly.
Offroad is kinda interesting: The goal is to get from Point A to Point B in as fast as possible. Playing the game reminds me of an old game called Fuel that I once had. The premise is interesting, but there’s so much junk everywhere on the track that its a nightmare to drive, especially with the physics engine that stubbornly refuses to go away.
The final mode is challenge. This basically sets up specific scenarios in the previous gamemodes with goals you have to complete. This could be something like a time trial, or a race where your goal is to deal a certain amount of damage or wreck x number of cars. It fails to impress, just like everything else in this game.
Graphics
Sometimes graphics can warrant the purchase of a game. You may buy a game just to show off your computer, and that’s alright every once in awhile. This isn’t one of those games. The graphics are flatout terrible! (See what I did there!) The game just doesn’t look good. The cars always seem kind of squashed when you look at them, and they're low enough poly to be in a GameCube game. In fact, the entire game looks like a GameCube game. Here’s some examples to prove my point:
If the GameCube one were higher resolution, it would beat out Flatout 3 easily.
Sound
Er, no. Just no. This game has terrible sound. The main theme gets old and repetitive. Cars sound like RC cars. Collisions have no force in them. And just about everything else sound really bad. It doesn’t help that this game has no soundtrack, which means you’re stuck listening to crappy music that someone wrote in a day. Words can’t describe just how bad it sounds. It really is pathetic.
Conclusion
If you haven’t figured out by now, this game is terrible. Unfortunately for the studio that made this, the reason I feel it was so terrible was because of the Flatout label. Everyone who had played the original expected it to be the same. It just wasn’t. This game might have been decent it it wasn’t called Flatout 3, but because it was, it is terrible. There really wasn’t anything going for this game, and I’m truly sad to see how a previously excellent franchise fell flat.

Well... it isn't a lie when it says "Notice: Fallout 3 is not optimized for Windows 7 and later". I would recommend modding this with some performance and optimization mods before playing.
I really enjoyed this game. Unlike games similar to this such as Skyrim and New Vegas (Both came out after this, I know) this game is a lot easier to get into. I dislikes both Skyrim and New Vegas at first and found I had to play a few hours before getting into it, FO3 got me right from the start. The main story is interesting (not very choice dependent as it seems sadly).
The ruins of D.C gave me a great time while I explored it and fought of Super Mutant. The Metros were like mazes and filled with everything from loot and gangs to fire breathing ants and you can get lost in them, and that isn't a bad thing.
Make your way across the Captital Wasteland on the surface or in the extensive Metro system, both offer different experiences.
This game captures the post-apocalyptic feel and the stuggle for survival great. It can be a challenging game as supplies are limited and mutants and bandits are out to get you, as well as each other. The side quests are also interesting and plentiful (However I didn't get to do many). At the time of writing this review I don't own the DLC but I do intend to buy them so I can run the TTW mod for Fallout New Vegas allowing me to play Fallout 3 on New Vegas's modified engine (I would also recommend you do this if you own both 3 and NV with all the DLC as you can play with a lot less issues (But still some issues of course if running with other mods)).
If you're looking for a great story with a great atmosphere and characters, Fallout 3 if your game. If you're looking for a more open world (Not to say Fallout 3 isn't open world but it can be less open in cities and in the metros if you choose to go there) and/or choice making that matters to the game's plot then I would say get Fallout New Vegas. Personally I prefer Fallout 3 over NV especially with TTW mod to make it more stable (Most mods work as well if you use TTW's patcher).

Victor Vran is one of those games that broke my usual routine. I never was a fan of isometric RPGs, a heresy which caused me to dislike games like Diablo.
However, this game broke through my initial distaste for the camera with a fun combat system - which is based on special skills and dodges, dynamic difficulty - which allows the player to turn on/off runes that give buffs to enemies and debuffs to the player character and a sense of humour - narrator, enemies and the NPCs make me grin rather often.
On top of that, game looks aesthetically pleasing and doesn't have any glaring flaws or bugs. Story is written well, but isn't anything special.
Music is nice and fitting, but does not stand out much.
It has to be noticed that the glorious voice of Kevan Brighting serves as narration (mostly known for being a narrator in Stanley Parable) and the unquastionably gritty but amazing voice of Doug Cockle serves as a voice for the protagonist (also voiced Geralt of Rivia in the Witcher games).
Game seems to have some FPS slowdowns on occassion, but it is rare and subsides quickly in my case.
Overall, if you think that you would like an RPGs with an exceptional cast of voice-actors, good writing and fun combat, well, you found one.
I also have to note... it was about time that heroes of the isometric aRPGs learned how to jump.

Overall I highly recommend this to any fan of ARPG or hack and slash games looking for something with a lot of personality and charm!

I have always been looking for an ARPG where I can move my character with WASD and target with my mouse. This one delivers that wish, and much, MUCH more. Wish I had discovered this game before.
-----
Movement in this game is different; even though it supports traditional "Mouse Movement" control scheme that other ARPGs have out there, it shines when you use "Action" or "Gamepad" one instead. You can jump, roll, and if you are using "Action" have your movement unbound from your target cursor.
Customization may look bad at first; compared to the other ARPGs where you have a lot of item slots, this game offers very few. However, after playing for a few hours, I found out that customization is more complex than it looks. The "Destiny Cards" - as you level up, you unlock slots where you can equip destiny cards, passives that allow you to tweak your character - these cards allow you to set up different builds. Outfits (armor) mainly alter how you gain "Overdrive"; a special bar that allows you to use 2 special "Demon" powers, and this actually alters how you play the game as well.
Every weapon type comes with 3 skills, 1 basic skill and 2 with cooldowns, and you can equip 2 weapons and swap them at any time. In essence, you have access to 8 skills in total; 2 charged skills and 6 weapon skills. You cannot improve your weapon skills directly, but there are some cards that add bonus to specific weapon skills. Transmutation (crafting) is an essential part of the game, and has a lot of recipes.
It seems an expansion is on the way, which will add local co-op support. Online multiplayer is drop in-out at any time you want. The DLCs so far are free, and one of them adds an area with different challenges each day, and if you want to push your limits, you have an endless arena where you can test your endurance (and your build).
Graphics are great, with a lot of options to suit low-middle end PCs as well as push the limits of high-end ones. Art style is very nice, and sound effects complement to the general atmosphere of the game. Music may get repetitive though.

For the technical reasons I can't give this game a positive review. The game is pretty much broken at this point because of its age. If you want to buy a WW2 grand strategy game just wait for Hearts of Iron 4.

Let me preface this review by saying I am a huge fan of motorsports and racing games. I was a junior in High school when Gran Turismo 4 launched back in ’05 and it was the sole reason I bought a PS2 that I had saved for from my part time job working at the 99 cent store. On the weekends my friend and I would take shifts driving the 24 hour endurance races. Over the years I have spent many hours playing other “less serious” racing games as well, from everything with the title “Need For Speed” or “Midnight club”; after what I can only assume are thousands of hours spent playing racing games when I started playing “The Crew” I was a bit confounded. This may contain some spoilers.
The Crew boasts a wide array of vehicles and specs to choose from; everything from street spec tuner cars, performance muscle cars, bikes, dragsters, drifters, off road rally type vehicles and even the occasional monster truck. With lots of visual customization options to boot, on the surface, it seems like something very similar to midnight club.
The game starts you off driving an American classic, a ’69 Camaro, and for reasons I don’t quite recall you end up working for the police trying to infiltrate a gang, I think they killed my cousin or something? It’s not really memorable or engaging, but in order to really get money to get cars and unlock new specs you let the story lead you around Detroit, Chicago, New York and then Miami, and after about 13 hours in, I didn’t feel like I was really playing a racing game at all. Sure there are some races sprinkled in the story and they seem more like an afterthought as you spent most of your time trying to beat the clock in point to point missions to spy on your friend.
By this point in the game I had done some exploring of all the content the game had to offer including police chasing me in my ’67 Shelby GT 500 (yes it is silver) running crates to get car parts to unlock a Bentley and make some cash. I had replayed some story mode races, I even tried some PVP, which was not a race like you might think but a game of capture the flag , or king of the hill , I wasn’t really sure. While wondering around Key West, longing for the game to feel more like a race game then a badly written police drama I stumbled upon a faction mission; A race from Miami to LA! The info about the mission said it would take 2.5 hours! Would it feel like a real race I wondered? I accepted it and off to LA I was in my Dirt Spec’d Ford Focus (in retrospect, not a car I wanted to spend 2 hours in).
Fighting our way through Miami Traffic the race was on! And with really no clear indication of where I was headed other than north after about 20 minutes of racing I was in New York, I think. I didn’t really have time to scope out the landmarks while continually trading 1st and 2nd position with another Focus; however, even this fight for the lead didn’t really seem to matter, because in order to complete this mission you only have to place 3rd or better, and there was only 4 cars, you just couldn’t be last, which didn’t seem to be an issue, because the mini in last didn’t seem interested in holding any other position.
Another 20 or so minuets and I was driving past Mt Rushmore. Not really sure I felt like I was racing at all, but just investing time into the game to get the 160,000 purse from finishing the mission.
Turning south and driving through the South West badlands I was trying to come to terms with what this game really was, or find some justification for finishing this race, yet as I came upon the Grand Canyon and hit some seriously long stretches of dirt road I was having fun sliding my little focus around the corners trying to go as fast as I could. Heading north again, towards the Sierra Nevada Mountains I started to think, in spite of everything the game tries to offer it still does not feel like an actually racing game but rather a showcase of motorsport competitions, and tributes to various car movies, like the Fast and the Furious or gone in 60 seconds. Finally as I was blasting down the Pacific coast highway towards Malibu I released “The Crew” is actually a love letter to everything motorsport, unfortunately that letter is written in crayon and authored by Ubisoft.

Easily the worst FPS game I've ever played. The main reason for it being, the devs do not know if they want to make it a realistic or arcade game.
Imagine some of the most frustrating aspects of a realistic shooter such as Red Orchestra and some of the worse aspects of a arcade shooter such as Call of Duty. And you get this game.
Its "realistic" aspect makes it so that SOME guns can kill you with one shot, its arcade aspect makes it so that you cannot get out of the way of these shots and are killed. Its "realistic" aspect makes it so that you can choose a few loadouts, its arcade aspect makes it so that the guns you have in your position are not the standard soldier's rifle and bayonet but rather anything from a sub machine gun that a lot of people want nerfed because what are weapons that there were 300 copies of made three months before the war ended doing in this game? All the way to a shovel. That's it. Its "realistic" aspect makes it so that you easily die. Its arcade aspect makes it so that you get shot anywhere not in the head with a pistol and then walk off a half meter drop and die.
The game is not sure what it wants to be. And for that reason it sucks. Play a free game such as Fistful of Frags, play CS:GO if you like arcade shooters, and play Red Orchestra 2 if you like realistic shooters. But do not play this game.

Punishes every strategy except rushing. I did not like this iteration of the series.

- A bad physics engine means that often the game thinks you happened to bounce a fraction of a milimeter, which means that very regularly, your acceleration is non-constant, and jumps don't register (so you miss the last critical jump in that series).
- Jumps (both from jump pads and the jump key) have a seemingly random height.
- No way to tell your speed or where you're about to land, so often you'll overshoot or undershoot a platform, without knowing until it's too late.
- Camera gets obscured by world objects that mean you don't see where you're going.
- Checkpoints in illogical places.
- Levels where it's actually possible to get stuck by losing a key prop, which doesn't get reset when you go back to a checkpoint, meaning you'll have to start over completely.
- No real puzzles, just really annoying tracks you have to get through.
Not recommended.

Going back to 5th grade, where I discovered Resident Evil 2 at a friend's birthday party, survival horror has been a favorite genre of mine. Later on, in high school, I discovered Silent Hill, which generally set aside jump scares for the sort of horror that surrounds you, and gets under your skin, until you have to turn the game off because you're so inexplicably freaked out. Outlast opts for a different kind of horror - the type popularized by Amnesia, where you are the victim in a horror film, and cannot fight back. It's a different beast from Resident Evil and Silent Hill altogether, though in the case of Outlast, it falls much more into the "shock and panic" category. Unfortunately, like most horror experiences that rely on a select few mechanics, there are diminishing returns here. The first hour or so is fairly terrifying - I'll give it that. It reminds me of the first time I played Resident Evil 4, where I was mostly running for my life and dying every few minutes for at least the first two hours. After that, though - once you learn the game's mechanics - things get tedious fast. A typical segment of Outlast: "Okay, new area. Hm. Nothing's jumped out at me for a few minutes. Oh, there we go - there's the false scare. Can't hurt me, so I must be getting close. Hey, I need to find this or activate this to open that door. Okay, part one, dude's gonna start chasing me. Okay, time to run away and hide. Oh. He killed me. Darn. Reload." I don't know - maybe I'm just jaded, but Outlast didn't give me the self-soiling goodness I was hoping to find. Rather, I wanted to get through the game as quickly as possible. I'm also fairly certain the story won't stick with me like the Silent Hill series has. Still, it's a polished game (I only encountered one bug), and worth playing if you're looking for a brief descent into madness and gore. And who doesn't want that every now and then, right? ...right?
