If you didn't play Re;Birth 1 and 2, you probably should do so before playing 3. You're gonna miss a lot of humor referencing past games, involving characters like Nepgear and Arfoire.
So what changed? Not much really. Gameplay wise, the biggest change is the SP bar, that you now use to activate exe drive and recharge with rush attacks. I really like it, because I always felt the SP bar was quite useless. I never consumed all my SP in previous games, but now it's something you need to manage.
There are now Challenges (slay x foes, fight x battles, nothing hard really), that you'll need to complete to unlock bonuses - AND YOUR EXE DRIVES! - so be prepared to grind a lot.
A lot of people said this game is easy. I disagree. Boss battles can be unforgiving and you're probably gonna get oneshot by Badd... By Anony... By Yellow Heart... See where I'm going? Of course if you're gonna play with the 4 oracles (they are quite OP), weaken enemies and super exp up, then yes, it will probably be easy. I don't know why you would do that, but whatever floats your boat.
Just a couple of new dungeons: Lowee is gorgeous, but the "Blocky Pixelated Hills" should come with a vomit alert. Not because it's bad, but because it's nauseating to navigate.
Stella's dungeon works generally better, even without blast exploring and death insurance, but it's still your typical idle game that will save you tons of material farming.
You can now see from inside the game where the plans materials are.
Lily ranks are stupid once again. I played around 70 hours and I didn't even raise ONE of those. And the fact that there's about 20 characters is really aggravating in this regard.
Story wise, it's quite alright but be warned. There'll be A LOT of talking. I mean, WAY more than the previous games. I have mixed feelings about it. I like watching the characters interact, but I can't say that watching Plutia spend 5 minutes to finish a single sentence is fun.
And of course it's fun is its integrity. There are a lot of jokes, video game references, and a surprising amount of talk about boobs. Yes, there IS fanservice, roughly the same as RE;Birth 2.
There's no breaking the 4th wall because there's barely any 4th wall at all. Nepnep goes wild in this installment.
New enemies are quite memorable: Copy is one of the best things in the entire game.
So yeah. Buy Hyperdimension Neptunia RE;Birth 3 right now, it's quite cheap for more than a hundred hours of fun.

If I had bought Victor Vran for its full price, I might have second-guessed if I should, in fact, recommend it, but at this point in its lifetime it's not a matter of discussion – if you're even remotely a fan of ARPGs, get it, you can hardly find a better way to waste at least 15-20 hours than hackin' n' slashin' monsters with up to 3 buddies.
Soooo... Let's get down to it, shall we? I will try to break the game down into what's good (+) and what's bad (-) about it.
(+)
This is by far the best thing about the game – who knew that adding actual action controls into an ARPG could make it all that much more fun? I guess, if you're a fan of using 15 hotkeys to cast spells you won't be as enticed as I was, but as I'm not, it was perfect. Ranged enemy attacks, however, are largely homing and really high-ranged, so jumping is not valid and dodging is often a mundane exercize of dodging around one projectile for 15+ seconds.
(+)
Story is poor, yeah, but it
it's poor. So why not just go with the flow.
(+)
Although you'll be mowing 'em down the same way, different areas have different enemies, and a good chunk of them are randomized to possess same powers you have.
(+)
You have 2 potion slots (although I do admit I only used healing ones, since bomb cooldowns are ridiculous, 90 seconds for one use), 2 Demon Power slots (although I found my favorites fairly early one, rendering the rest useless) and 5 Destiny card slots, which give passive bonuses, but require a certain level of ingenuity to build properly (we did not venture into the endgame content, so min-maxing wasn't a necessity). You also have 2 weapons slots, and they have have 2 skills each, which let you combine them for maximum effect. There is also the outfit which is sort of like your class, but even if you pick one early one, you can find the rest as an item.
(+)
It's really well done, and as the story isn't too serious, it's hardly too weird to have 2-4 Victor Vrans running around in the same game. Story progress can be shared without any issues and challenges can be completed together as well.
(+)
Even now there are at least few dozen people in the global chat, and they are always ready to help. It's always nice of devs to go the extra mile and allow this to be possible.
(+/-)
Loot is weird in this game, so I can't decide if I like it or not. You do find plenty of items, and legendaries scale with your level, but as the game is tailored to depend 50/50 on both your items and your mechanical skill, the mobs don't scale too far and your damage remains more or less the same after 30+ level. I do believe that grinding out legendary weapons/cards could make a difference, but I don't think it's as big as it could be. Also, there could be more weapons, there are just 3 ranged weapons and 4 melee weapon types – 14 weapon skills total.
(+/-)
This is not yet in the game, so that's why I'm putting it here. It's promised though, and should eventually be released. When/if they do release it, I'll probably replay it at least one more time.
(+/-)
They do make up a large part of endgame, and I guess it's fine, but at some point you have to ask yourself: do I want to keep restarting this one cramped area to try and kill 40 mobs without them hitting me with homing spells?
(-)
It may just be my laptop, but frequent framerate dips really did a number on me. And as the game seems to be tied to framerate, it resulted in too many mobs knocking my framerate to low 15s, which resulted in 400% longer cooldowns, jerky movement and all sorts of shenanigans. My friend, however, had no issues whatsoever.
(-)
It pains me to say so, but bosses are really, really ♥♥♥♥in' underwhelming in this game. Which is ludicrous considering the possibilities of having an active movement system with the option to dodge AND jump. Last boss and endgame DLC boss are two of the most annoying things in this game: last boss is just a frustrating bullet sponge you have to walk out of range of every 30 seconds, and endgame boss is just a stupid oversized regular mob with 2 high-damage attacks and exhausting invincibility frames.
Got 15-20 hours to kill? Get it. Looking for a good co-op experience? Get it. Want a cheesy game that won't require your low attention span to work on memorizing the complex twists and turns of an in-depth story? Get it. Itching for an ARPG, especially one with a unique twist? Get it.
At the price this game goes for now it'd be silly not to try it, at least. And while there are many things the devs could've done to make it THE definitive ARPG, they always have another shot if they decide to make a Victor Vran sequel. They have my trust.

This is the game the original Two Worlds wanted to be. This game came out in 2012, when fantasy games were abound and stagnating. After Fable 2 and Two Worlds, but before Dragon Age 2 and Two Worlds 2, this game serves as a sort of time capsule, bringing you back to a time when game developers made gigantic worlds on shoestring budgets at the cost of refinement. In an effort to meet deadlines, this game sacrificed ease of control and balancing. The story is not the most original you've ever heard, but it will be completely serviceable if you're looking for traditional fantasy. In the end, Divinity 2 is a lot of fun, but it's also insanely frustrating. Imagine if Dark Souls was made in Belgium, was poorly balanced, and didn't have Z-targeting.
You'll die. A lot.
You'll be under-leveled. A lot.
You'll be quick-loading. A lot.
And if you love fantasy settings, then you'll love every second of it.
If you DON'T usually like fantasy games, this won't sway you. Go play Pillars of Eternity.

It's hard not to love a game that begins with its protagonist hanging himself in an insane asylum, but "Call of Cthulhu" never really realizes its potential. To be fair, it is a bit before its time. Some of its segments nail exactly the sort of "run and hide from the monsters" tension that later survival horror games like "Amnesia" ultimately perfected (COC even used the "insanity" game mechanic long before "Penumbra/Amnesia"). But for every effective sequence there are 2 or 3 that suck all tension out of the game and result in frustration. It wants to be all things at once: an adventure game, a stealth game, a first person shooter, and even a (terrible) platformer. But it only ever really nails the "adventure" aspect so when it tries to be anything else enjoyment stops dead in its tracks.
Which is unfortunate as ultimately the story is interesting (and you'll probably want to play this anyway if you are a Lovecraft fan). But mostly a missed opportunity.

To make a long story short, initially, I had
with this game. No matter what I did, including running the game with most, if not all graphical options off or at their minimum settings, running the game with command-line options, and even running the game in a significantly reduced resolution in a window, the game would insist on either giving me constant 'directx errors' or simply locking up my entire system, forcing me to hard-reset my PC every time this happened.
At that time, my PC's setup looked like this:
i5-2400 @ 3.1 Ghz
8GB DDR3 RAM @ 1333 Mhz
GTX 560 ti 1 Gb (Running Nvidia 344.11 drivers)
Windows 7 Home Premium 64-bit
Having logged roughly 23 hours in the game, a good deal of which was spent troubleshooting, tweaking settings, and re-playing and re-attacking places that I'd already finished before due to having lost progress from crashes, I finally gave up, after exhausting all the solutions I could find on the Internet in order to get the game to work, and buried the game in my library as a write-off.
---
It was only because I recently upgraded my GPU that I decided to give this game another try. My new configuration at the time of this updated review looks like this:
i5-2400 @ 3.1 Ghz
8GB DDR3 RAM @ 1333 Mhz
Windows 7 Home Premium 64-bit
The game ran fine without any need for command-line option tweaks, and was even able to run stable with all settings maxed out or enabled (including decals being turned on).
Considering the fact that the game still crashes, even on a brand new GPU with updated drivers, I'm hesitant to blame the technical issues I experienced entirely on a faulty GPU. I think the game has some strange problems that may or may not show up and that will vary in severity, depending on your PC's specific configuration. When I was originally researching solutions to the technical issues I was having, I found that all sorts of people with varying configurations had problems - even those with PCs that had more than enough power to run this game at maximum settings. For some people, the solution was as simple as turning off various graphics options (decals and bokeh filter). For other people (especially those with laptops), a certain command-line tweak was required to get the game to recognize the proper video card. Other people (initially including myself), kept crashing and crashing no matter what they tried.
---
With technical issues aside, I will say that the game itself is quite fun, although some may find it repetitive. Half of the game consists of killing enemy soldiers and destroying marked government facilities. The other half of the game consists of going on a scavenger hunt for various items and collectibles scattered throughout the game world. These collectibles grant various benefits like cash (required to order things from the Black Market), additional maximum health, and weapon/vehicle parts for upgrading things you purchase from the Black Market. I should add that most, if not all, of the DLC is completely unnecessary to get through the game, and is mostly only provided to find more amusing ways to kill your enemies (or little extra things to try out). The most useful DLC would be the
, though I'd still consider getting this on sale (or as part of a pack).
If you're looking for a story, then know that Just Cause 2 only has 7 story missions. There are 49 faction missions (factions are criminal organizations that you can work with). I found these missions to be varied and interesting. I also found the game's crude sense of humour and the voice acting of a certain faction leader, quite amusing.
If you're a completionist, perfectionist, or like accumulating statistics, then you'll appreciate Just Cause 2's record-keeping ability. Kills, headshots, and all manner of other records are continuously tallied throughout your playthrough of the game. Unfortunately, these figures don't mean much more beyond being simple records of your achievements. Supposedly, when you perform certain actions, the game tells you that certain things have happened as a result. For example, destroying a pipeline 'disrupts the Panauan oil-distribution network'. Killing a colonel 'reduces military morale'. Destroying a communications array 'disrupts military communications'. Destroying a propaganda trailer 'reduces the President's influence over the people'. While this seems nice, no matter how many pipelines, colonels, military communications antennae, military bases, or propaganda trailers I destroyed, I saw
It just didn't feel like any of these actions had any real effect on the game world.
The game also has an immersion-breaking way of spawning things. When the enemy calls for air support, enemy helicopters tend to spawn in mid-air out of nowhere, and quite close to you as well. You could be flying along in your own aircraft and see a helicopter just materialize out of thin air. Additionally, I once attacked a village in my own helicopter, destroying the troops and vehicles stationed along the roads, before clearing the village to 100%. Some enemy helicopters arrived to shoot me down. After taking them down, I flew back to the same village to inspect the damage, and noticed that all the troops and vehicles I'd previously destroyed had already respawned. I couldn't have been gone for more than 60 seconds, yet it was as if I hadn't even been there.
What the game does well is open-world exploration. There are plenty of places to find and destroy, and some of the major military installations are quite nice and believable in their design. The combat is also decent, and the grappling hook makes for some interesting gameplay mechanics (as well as downright trolling of NPCs). Pull people off buildings, hijack moving vehicles (even airborne helicopters), pull a soldier off his motorbike and tether him to your vehicle before dragging him along the ground to hear him screaming and crying. The list of creative things you can do goes on, but you will have to
in order to enjoy the game this way, rather than expect the game to give it to you via missions or a compelling storyline.
Just Cause 2 also has an impressive list of vehicles to steal and use, including various aircraft, ground vehicles, and boats, most of which are a pleasure to drive. The only complaint I have here is that helicopters feel like they are meant to be steered using a controller, rather than a mouse and keyboard.
+ Nice open-world exploration
+ Decent visuals
+ Large amount of vehicles to try
+ The grappling hook makes for some interesting possibilities
- Short campaign
- Some vehicle controls are awkward (helicopters in particular)
- Some actions have no real effect on the game situation
- - - Strange technical issues could make this unplayable
A decently fun, open-world experience, that may or may not give you technical problems. Play the demo several times to see if you'll have issues first.

The music in this game is good, too, especially the battle themes.

The gameplay itself didn't changed much, so for those who are familiar with this series can dive in instantly.
The battle system is fun, but you might need a bit of grinding.
Storywise it is packed with funny jokes, although the translation seems to be a bit off, noticeable on Nep's (the main character) lines. Her IQ seems to have dropped by several points through translation.
Some archievements take time to get, but with the right equipment it's not too much time consuming.
So, this game was a fun JRPG experience and a worthy sequel.

Napoleon: Total War is a strategy game from Creative Assembly and published by SEGA. Napoleon: Total War is a sequel to the previous game Empire: Total War.
Napoleon: Total War is set and focused on Napoleonic era while retaining almost everything from Empire: Total War, but perfected in this sequel. Features are almost the same as Empire: Total War but with more focus on their category. Troops will now replenish their losses automatically on friendly region, mostly decreasing micromanagement for the series. The campaign map is refocused back to Europe but still large.
Graphics doesn't seems to have some big improvements. But the troops animation now plays more smoothly than before.
Basically, Napoleon: Total War is a perfected version of Empire: Total War with a Napoleonic era focused. While the game is pretty similar to Empire: Total War, it is better than Empire: Total War. I recommend this.

Spectraball is not the typical platformer you would play, because it's quite unique with its power-ups and puzzles. There's a few other "ball platformer" games out there, but trust me when I say this, Spectraball is the best of them. The graphics are beautiful, but if it gets too rough for your computer to handle, reducing the graphics does wonders for your fps.
The game offers you 7 levels to complete, all in different biomes. Every level has its own biome, offering unique puzzles to solve. The first level is quite simple and easy to understand, but it gets ALOT harder towards the end. Some of the levels were quite confusing about where to go, but because of the fun ball physics, it's fun to explore the maps. However, the game is very short because it only has 7 levels, but the game has a level creator which you can create levels with and publish for the other players.
The first playthrough took me roughly 2 hours, which I felt was very short. But later when I found out some shortcuts, I realised the game is a pretty typical game for speedrunning. Alot of shortcuts to use to your advantage, the different power-ups etc.
Every level has its own global leaderboards where you can try to compete with the other times. Every power-up has its own leaderboard for every level there is available, which makes the leaderboards fair.
Even though i've completed the game about 6-8 times already it doesn't get boring. Sometimes you discover new shortcuts and think that "Heey, I could speedrun this map!" and all of a sudden you spend 1 hour easily trying to climb the leaderboards.
TL;DR
After you get the mechanics down, there's not too much to the game except expanding.  Entertaining for the most part.

Refunct had caught my attention some weeks before the summer sale, and it came as a great surprise when I got it gifted by a great friend of mine, thank you once again Danii!
This is the prime example of simplicity. The game's simple aesthetic with day/night cycles makes it a beautiful looking experience to screenshot dozens of times. it's definitely not a game for everyone, by reading the game's description you know exactly what you're going to play. Refunct has no story, and barely any sort of context as well, but is it good? Yes it is.
To put it simply, all you do is press red buttons in order to restore this island that's lost in the middle of a never ending ocean and every platform you walk onto turns green, so in a way you're restoring this island back to life. You also have these little cube collectibles scattered throughout the island to collect. All of these elements are required to reach a 100% completion on the game. There's gameplay mechanics that reminded me of games like Mirror's Edge, like sliding and wall jumping so you can reach certain platforms more easily. Beware that the game lasts only about half an hour, although it's definitely not a game that should had been longer.
One of the highest positive aspects in this game is it's soundtrack. Composed by Kristofferson, the album entitled Connections plays while you're restoring the island. It is definitely a very relaxing set of music, that improves the gameplay experience a lot.
It is hard to write much about a game so simple and so short, but all I can tell you is that if you're a fan of the so called Walking Simulator genre, which I am a big fan of, if you want to play something very relaxing and if you love a really good looking game, then you're in for a treat! Again I do say, Refunct is not a game for everyone, some might not even call it a game for some reason, but for me it's an amazing one.

I got this game when it was on sale, and I fully expected it to be about average quality. After playing it, I can say that if I had know how great it was going to be, I would have definitely payed full price for it.
Good, but not amazing, at least not until the second-half of the game. It's easy enough to follow, and there's lore abound, if you're into that stuff like I am. The story might not be the selling point of the game, but the writing certainly is. Side Quests and hidden secrets are positively everywhere, and you'll run into many interesting characters during your adventure if you venture off the beaten path a bit. Combining the compelling story and rich lore with the wealth of captivating characters, both those involved in quests and regular old NPCs, you're left with an adventure through a land that feels truly alive.
Moving on to the gameplay, which had to be my favorite part of the whole experience. The game handles well in and out of combat, with a cohesive UI and a neat, uncluttered inventory management system. Item stats are easy to understand, and there's a built-in comparison system to see how a new piece of gear stacks up against your currently equipped weapon or armor. Weapons and armor in themselves offer a whole wealth of choices in themselves, with several weapon types to choose from, each with their own unique skills that can be unlocked on the
skill tree. There's swords, bows, greatswords, axes, hammers, magic, shields, and even bare fists, all of which are viable. Dual wielding is an option, as well. And did I mention that all weapons and armor can be enchanted, granting additional stat boosts? If it sounds badass, that’s because it is. Combat is slick and fast-paced, and rarely feels sloppy. Skills unlocked from the aforementioned skill tree can be mapped to hotkeys, as can items, allowing for easy access during frantic battles, which often have you facing more than one enemy at once. By the end of the game, you’re facing small battalions of enemies, living out a classic power fantasy as you one-man-army them into oblivion.
The overall sound quality of Divinity II is very high. The voice acting is amazing, enhancing the aforementioned outstanding writing. Unlike in Skyrim, you don’t run into the problem of every other character being voiced by the same actor, which would easily break immersion. Instead, many characters have unique voices you only hear from them. The SFX are also well done, with the clang of your weapons against enemy armor providing a sense of weight and impact. The music, however, is probably the weakest part of the sound package. While fitting, it certainly isn’t the most memorable soundtrack out there. It’s not bad by any stretch of the word, but just isn’t something that will stick in your head for weeks after playing it.
The graphics are, well, kind of dated. It’s certainly not at the level of GTA 5 or NieR, but the game came out in 2009, so I would argue that it deserves a little slack. That being said, the lands you adventure through are bright and colorful, and the various dungeons and locales you find yourself exploring aren’t nearly as generic as some other games. The character models are fairly detailed, and the lip-syncing is well done. Having somewhat dated graphics also means that it doesn’t take a top of the line pc to play it in it’s finest form, which is a welcome change in a market full of games designed with only the highest specs in mind. While the graphics might not be the strongest point of the game, not once did I feel that it detracted from my experience.
Divinity II is a wonderful action-RPG, positively brimming with content and charm, offering a lively world full of quests to complete, secrets to find, and foes to slay. If you can find it on sale, I would wholeheartedly recommend grabbing it.

Never has a game both literally and figuratively earned the title of cult-classic than Call of Cthulhu: Dark Corners of the Earth. Adaptations of Lovecraftian themes, creatures and the idea of cosmic horror are nothing new to video-games as classics like Alone in the Dark as well as new titles like Bloodborne and Darkest Dungeon incorporate various elements into their own creations. Direct adaptations of Lovecraft, however, are too few and far between one another which often relies on adventure games for gameplay or they are failed experiments. Perhaps only matched with the popularity of the board game, no one game adaptation has captivated the experience of Lovecraft as much as Dark Corners of the Earth.
Beyond its source material, DCOTE is also largely responsible within its mechanics of first-person survival horror that would inspire the Penumbra and Amnesia games, which would cultivate in a resurgence of survival horror. Ideas like chase-sequences/stealth from insurmountable enemies, adventure-lite FPS mechanics, insanity effects and immersive puzzle/gameplay elements like the recreated Shadow Over Innsmouth chase sequence are the timeless qualities that make this game into a classic of horror.
Unlike these modern games, ironically, DCOTE does not always limit the player from fighting back much like Alien: Isolation; instead of creating a nemesis that chased the player to discourage combat, DCOTE would instead focus on making compelling atmosphere and situations to instill the desire to flee from situations rather than stay and fight. The result of all these mechanics playing with one another is an experience that feels more player-driven despite how linear it truly is, and that is the non-Euclidean madness in which the game excels in creating.
As one might expect from an older title, Dark Corners of the Earth is an FPS that goes beyond traditional conventions as far as how the game is structured as well as played. Within the first couple of hours, the player is completing adventure-styled puzzles and storytelling of the lore through the town of Innsmouth with some stealth elements every now and then. These elements would continue to be used throughout the game but after the Innsmouth Hotel escape is when the game begins to incorporate more FPS combat as well as more action and horror sections of each area as you solve a simple missing person case that goes into the depths of the earth best not uncovered.
Interspersed throughout the adventure, you play as Jack Walters, a psychically linked detective who uses his powers beyond his understanding as well as his improvisation skills to survive the horror of Innsmouth that takes him from time and space as he uncovers the secret history of the town. As far as the narrative is concerned, DCOTE is pulpier than the storylines based on Lovecraft as it combines various creatures, stories and ideas throughout the mythos into a consistent storyline of a conspiracy that relies on its exposition and the withholding of details to draw the player in further into the world. Some people may not like the obvious obfuscation of Lovecraft of his the unnamable, indescribable and unspeakable attributes that mark his writing style, yet in this adaptation it’s explained enough to the point where the questions you are left with give you something to think about while never knowing the full extent of the reasons behind why these creatures do what they do.
When the game picks up after the first quarter snooping the town, the game’s more interactable elements begin to show their promises and blemishes the farther as you play. The first of which is the lack of a HUD; instead of displaying meters, cross-hairs, etc. the game expects you rely on the visual and audio elements to inform you of the player’s condition as well as be cautious when attacking/fleeing enemies as the player is forced to use iron-sights and a steady aim. Perhaps what was ambitious of the time, a more complicated health system is ultimately a minor issue as it means you use a different resource to fix yourself. Insanity, another great idea on paper, amounts to a visual effect that obscures the screen when the player stares at something disturbing so long that can result in the player committing suicide if it lasts too long. These ideas, as well as various other little details that are Lovecraftian, are ultimately lacking as while they are stylistically appropriate they don’t always translate into making a true Lovecraftian experience as well as offer a fun game mechanic.
When it comes to creating a Lovecraftian inspired game, there comes the problem of how to translate the feeling of helplessness and insignificance into gameplay without risking the gameplay itself being tarnished by the idea that the game is not meant to be fun. Contrary to what Reggie from Nintendo of America believes, games do not always have be fun as experiences like XCOM as well as Darkest Dungeon rely more on the feeling of despair and hopelessness, and overcoming the odds for the satisfaction that would normally be described as “fun” in other games. Instead, gameplay that is compelling or rewarding despite the negative feelings they invoke is what games like DCOTE aspire to create in order to engage the player to continue seeing the end.
However, one issue of DCOTE that appears to be more lambasted with time for fans of Lovecraft, is the hypocrisy of its gameplay to make the player mechanically capable to fight against the Old Gods. Ignoring that the player never kills the Old Gods themselves, only that they forestall the inevitable demise for another time with the aid of Yith technology, fans criticize the game’s structure of being able to mow dozens upon dozens of Fishmen and Deep Ones as not resembling the feeling of Lovecraft. (There are also enemies like the Shoggoth who cannot be harmed at all by the player.) This is perhaps the fundamental paradox of creating a Lovecraftian game that creates a player-fantasy worth playing while also making the player feel insignificant.
Games can be created that are not fun; however, can games be created that are not structured to recognize the player’s actions as well as to disenfranchise the player’s role in the game? DCOTE attempts to handle this by having players overcome obstacles like the fight with Dagon or narratively with the ending that intentionally robs any sense of lasting reward, leaving the player feeling helpless because of everything that was accomplished up to that point. Even the ending is spoiled by the beginning, a classic Lovecraft trope of “I’m going to die in a moment, so let me monologue my whole life now,” which makes the intentions of having both the power-fantasy and the cosmic insignificance work within the confines of the same game. The result is neither is the ending satisfying for non-fans of Lovecraft nor entirely faithful for the Necronomicon scholars, and this is perhaps what prevents these games from being anything more than having cult-status.
With the canceled sequel, At the Mountains of Madness from the same developers, something more likely to succeed given the wider audience nowadays, as well as the new “Call of Cthulhu” (no relation) game on the horizon, the prospect of a financially successful and of a faithful Lovecraftian adaptation in video-games is something I remain skeptical will happen.
However, if you are willing to overlook the flaws of a great horror game, there is something bewilderingly unmatched in the fear of the unknown that Dark Corners of the Earth encroaches upon and remains dormant in the realm of possibilities in the future.

Question.
Do you like Dragons?
I ask this because your answer will also probably answer how much you'll like this game.
That is because the key selling point of this game is that your human character can transform into a DRAGON. Not for all of it (boo) and not everywhere in the game (BOO) but for a good chunk of it you can simply press a button and rain fiery, winged death down on anyone stupid enough to remain in the immediate vicinity. In this game you can assault vast flying fortresses as a dragon, tear their defences down, have aerial dogfights with flying demons, then morph back into a human and cut your way through courtyards until you kill the enemy general - all without a single cutscene. This can be a really fun game.
The writing is also stellar, striking a fun balance between humor and seriousness; this only gets better in the sequel campaign where your character almost seems to start channeling Deadpool. This is my first Divinity title, so I can't say much about how it compares to others in the series but I thought the world was quite well handled, sticking to a lot of fantasy tropes while still putting them together in a unique enough way, my only real regret is that I didn't get to see more of it. The music is really good too.
Sadly it is not without flaws. The combat, while fun and frantic in the later game can be frustrating early on (I highly recommend low level characters to always carry a bow). Your only method of avoiding attacks is to jump or dodge-roll, leading to you spending most fights rolling around enemies like a spiky, sword wielding barrel. Flying round areas in the late game is fun, but during the early game and the second campaign the amount of backtracking some quests require becomes annoying. I also encountered a few crashes during loading screens; nothing that couldn't be worked around but still annoying.
Divinity 2 is not as polished as the likes of Dragon Age, but play it for any length of time and you'll see the potential beneath the surface. It can be annoying, even frustrating at times, but those moments are brief. For the most part Divinity 2 is thoroughly enjoyable, and when it embraces the things that make it unique it becomes downright spectacular.

Might & Magic Heroes VI is a turn-based strategy video game for Microsoft Windows developed by Black Hole Entertainment and published by Ubisoft. It is the sixth installment in the Heroes of Might and Magic series, and was released on October 13, 2011, coinciding with the 25th anniversary of the Might and Magic franchise. Heroes VI acts as a prequel to Heroes of Might and Magic V, occurring almost five centuries earlier, and is set in the fictional world of Ashan. The story follows the five heirs to the Griffin dynasty in their quests to repel a demon invasion and assist or impede Michael, a legendary Archangel general plotting to revive an ancient war.
As in previous Heroes of Might and Magic titles, the player can choose between single-player or multiplayer modes of play, and controls a number of heroes and towns associated with various factions, commanding armies of creatures between tactical overland exploration and a turn-based combat system to satisfy each scenario's victory conditions. Heroes VI alters some of the series' long-standing conventions, overhauling its chance-based skills system and reducing the number of resources in its economics model, and also introduces new mechanics, including a points-based reputation system and the ability to convert one faction's towns to another.
Heroes VI has been received positively, attaining a score of 77 from the aggregate review site Metacritic. Reviewers praised the title's replay value, visuals and improvements to the Heroes formula, but were critical of the numerous bugs and glitches in the release version and its intrusive DRM system, which requires players to maintain a connection to the Internet to avail of several features.

Эта история началась в Нью-Йорке, когда два раздолбая достигли 10 уровня. Это было уже после двух часов игры и продирания через дебри интерфейса, слёз и непонимания. На наших внутри игровых счетах образовалась круглая сумма в размере 100К. В отдельной спец-валюте. И вот здесь и началось что-то непонятное. Здесь игра вдруг стала другой. У дилеров оказались разные ассортименты. Я смог купить Dodge 1969 года, а он… и я тогда ещё не знал об этом (а ассортимент для каждого игрока в один момент времени - разный) Chevy Impala. Два масл-кара, которые встретившись вместе собрались пересечь Америку от восточного побережья до западного.
Чтобы это случилось так, как случилось - мы послали к дьяволу игру отключив все возможные интерфейсы и клятвенно пообещали не открывать карту, руководствуясь лишь собственными географическими познаниями. Четыре часа мы не могли достичь желанной точки. Останавливаясь в отелях и заправляясь на бензоколонках (понарошку конечно). Приключение заняло три дня и две ночи по местному времени. Мы выехали из Нью-Йорка и описав петлю попали в него же. Проскочив Сент-Луис чуть не задели Канзас и «рухнули» в Большой Каньон. Его я вспоминаю с ужасом. Ещё ни в одной игре, кроме я не ехал столь долго. Он действительно велик. Не заезжая в Лас-Вегас (а зря!) мы забурились в Скалистые Горы и они полностью сломали нам ощущение ориентации в пространстве. Дорожный серпантин, определенно, меняет восприятие реальности. В совокупности с ночью это помогло нам проскочить Лос-Анджелес и потом полчаса гнать рядом со стеной… и, слава богу, что мозг таки сработал (что характерно не мой) и мы наконец осознали, что это великая мексиканская стена.
Порой картинка была уныла, но чаще она подкидывала весьма красивые пейзажи, поражая размером. Его хотелось бы заполнить многим. Необходимостью заправляться есть и выполнять курьерские миссии, разумеется выходить из машины и бить живых мертвецов по башке разными подручными средствами. Спасать прекрасных дам и пить за здоровье спасенных за игрой в покер или кости, прожигая кровно заработанные в клубах сигаретного дыма и запахе старого дерева. Всё это было бы очень здорово… и очень хочется... но не в нашей жизни ребят. Вероятно детки наши такое увидят. Чтобы и размер был ого-го, и качество сервиса. Будь это GTAV, да с таким, мать его, причиндалом... но нет. Увы. Проработать "по рокстаровски" мир такого масштаба на данный момент невозможно.

I find myself playing a lot of these small indie cult classics recently, and I'm immensely satisfied with the 2 or so hours I spent finishing VVVVVV. The game looks like it belongs on an Atari, but it plays like it belongs on Steam. You flip instead of jumping, you got Mega Man style spikes everywhere (don't even touch the sides), and a f*cking kickass soundtrack. Like holy sh*t, have you heard this? This game as a whole, but the soundtrack especially, makes me think of like an Undertale before Undertale - looks old, has fantastic music, and does something fairly unique and does it really well. Sure you'll die a hell of a lot trying to get that one damn trinket in "Doing Things the Hard Way" (endgame stats said I died 150 times in that initial room, 15% of my deaths for the entire game), but the half an hour or so that it took me to finally beat that piece of sh*t seven rooms of falling was totally worth it for the payoff of finally beating that thing back to wherever it came from.
VVVVVV is a lot like that, just satisfying to play. It's a lot of trial and error, and there are definitely some exceedingly bullsh*t parts, but on the whole it's a really enjoyable experience if you like platformers and aren't afraid of some serious difficulty compared to today's dumb handholding. You just get out there and explore this dimension, fallin' through space and looking for trinkets. Sounds fun, right?
I give it a 4/5.

Team Fortress Classic, also known as "TFC" is a remake of Team Fortress, a Quake mod which started off the Team Fortress series.
Team Fortress Classic, compared to it's successor: Team Fortress 2, has no customization or storyline whatsoever, instead being based purely around gameplay. Specifically, team-based gameplay such as Capture the Flag, VIP and Territorial control.
Classes in TFC have different abilities, and their own class-specific grenades which can be used in a variety of situations, creating a rock-paper-scissors form of gameplay.
One main point which makes Team Fortress Classic unique, and in some ways "better" than it's successor is that it has a massive amount of custom maps, plug-ins and content which usually goes on to be implemented in Team Fortress 2.

+ RPG & levelling elements; fairly standard in practice, but work well and mesh perfectly with the feel of the game
+ Myriad available perks add enormous flexibility to a player's role
+ Karma system is a lot of fun to play around with, and also goes a long way to showcase the consequences of one's actions
+ Combat is fairly run-of-the-mill for an RPG FPS; certainly not fast-paced, but is implemented in a way that rewards planning and preparedeness
+ V.A.T. system functions well-beyond a simple gimmick; functional to the point of being vital in its proper use, intensely fun, and sensationally cinematic (save for one minor scruple, outlined below)
+ Environment, while graphically aged, is nonetheless incredibly detailed; there are always interesting things to find off the beaten path, and the player is encouraged in (and often rewarded for) exploring
+ Map is expansive and populated with secrets and locations to visit
+ Voice-acting is largely excellent, with only a few minor characters standing out as being less than exemplary in vocal quality
+ Side-missions are well-detailed, fun & interesting to complete; the rewards for doing so can sometimes be extraordinary
+ Plot moves forward at a pace set by the player, and is interesting to see through to the conclusion; writing ranges from passable to excellent, and never strays from the game's established charm
+ Total freedom in the way problems are solved and obstables overcome
+ Extremely, stupidly mod-friendly (via third-party applications - I recommend NexusMod, personally)
+ Modular damage, for both the player and encountered enemies, is very well-implemented; damage to certain areas of the body will hurt perfomance appropriately, further emphasizing a sense of immersion
+ Boasts a seemingly unending variety of items and weaponry; the hoarding game is real
- Oddly enough, this game uses GFWL, but is easily bypassed (simply by exiting out); this won't be counted thrice against the game (as GFWL, in this case, appears bafflingly neutered), but it does pop up, so it should be mentioned
- Camera can sometimes prove buggy and unreliable during V.A.T. kills
- Character models and animations are below-average in presentation (easily remedied via third-party mods, of course)
- There seems to be a bug where GFWL asks for a nonexistent product key; this is easily bypassed by simply exiding GFWL within the running game

Best game EU. 210/5
NOTE THIS IS AN EARLY ACCESS REVIEW WHEN IT WAS A NEW GAME!! I HAVE NOT CAUGHT ON RECENT EVENTS OF THE GAME DUE TO PERSONAL STUFF.
//Simple review over
In all honesty the game is unfinished(heck that's why it's in early alpha), rubber banding all over the place. IN ALL TRUTH IT IS WORTH THE EARLY ACCESS BECAUSE GOD DAMN IT IS POLISHED. For an early access game it's really polished, chocked full with content and being continuously updated by a dedicated studio. I could not really fault too much apart from lag issues (both fps and internet) but really it's only my fps for some reason that's slugging. You will experience the occasionally lag spikes(sometimes leading to my doom) but it's usually fine. Do not get put off because it is different graphically from the original it has the same premise and same mechanics (a few mechanics have been taken away) but the sacrifice is for a greater good (more fluid and not too cluttered imo). The solo has been underplayed here as in slightly underappreciated and teamplay is more promoted which I cannot criticize too much since teamplay sometimes lacked in dd1 because solo building normally got through all the levels if you knew what to do.
Sound/ Sound effects
The soundtrack is very reminiscent of the old dungeon defenders with the melody slightly changed but you can still feel the sounds from the old dd's giving it that slightly humble nostalgic feeling. The Sound effect for combat is very crisp and smooth, hacking and slashing feels really great especially to big monsters I feel like I'm dicing their fleshy flesh bodies every slice as a squire. For ranged characters I can't feel the same oomph but the abilities for the ranged characters make me feel powerful as if I have a huge presence in the map.
Graphics/ Effects
The effects are beautiful and very colourful if not cartoony. This may appeal to a select audience but I haven't been put off by it at all infact it's a much fresher feeling from the slightly darker tone of the last games. Hyperdimension Neptunia Re;Birth3 is a light hearted RPG that doesn't take itself too seriously. If you're new to the franchise, that might be a let down if you want a mature  and serious story. Not a bad thing but it's good to say that in the very beginning so you will know what you're getting.
However, if you are acquainted to the franchise, welcome back! This is a worthy sequel.
It's not necessary but it would be good if you did. The story is set a few years after what happened in the end of Re;Birth2. There are some references and dialogues that you won't understand otherwise, and you will know and connect better to some returning characters. But that's only a small piece of the whole game and you will be fine if you're playing this first.
That said, lets begin the review:
It's a turn-based RPG, where you can move your character through a certain radius each turn, and his position in the battlefield determines his hit range and the amount of enemies he will hit with normal attacks. There are three types of normal attacks and there's up to five attacks in a single turn. Rush attacks fill your SP gauge faster, but are weaker. Break attacks are focused on destroying the guard of your opponent, and the Power attacks are what deal more damage.
The first attack is determined by the weapon and can't be changed. The other four attacks in each category are customizable, and you can attach different attacks in each of them. In Re;Birth2, there were up to four attacks, instead of five.
SP is used for skills and EXE Drives, that deal a lot more damage but are more expensive. In Re;Birth 2, the SP Gauge and the EXE Drive Gauge were separate things, but here they are united, and I really think is better this way, for you can't spam skills and EXE Drives anymore: if you use an EXE Drive, you will lose points to use skills, which requires a more careful planning.
There are many equippable weapons, armors and clothes, as expected in a RPG game.
The Remake System is back. Basically, is where you use the Plans you get throughout the game (by key events or exploring) to unlock items, weapons, attack slots, dungeons and more, and change some aspects of the game (like the Fortify Enemies plan, or the Jump Higher plan, Change Dungeons and so on). It's really fun, and necessary to get the True Ending.
The mini-game Stella's Dungeon is back with some nice additions. In it, you equip Stella with the weapon, armor, and amulet of your choice, and send her to climb a tower to the top. She climbs by herself and the game shows the amount of time it will take. She keeps climbing even if you quit the game. There are 20 levels with more than 5000 floors, and you can select up to what floor she will climb and then stop. You have to be wise to select the equipment and up to what floor she will climb. In each run, she gathers new equipment (for her and for the main game) and some itens you can use in the main game too.  The addition is that you can select a partner for her now. There are dozens, each with specific skills.
There are many dungeons, including many optional ones.  However, the game suffers from the same problem that Re;Birth 2 has: the recycling of dungeons and monsters.  Most of the dungeons are copypaste of others with different monsters and with one or two roads blocked or open, and many monsters and are the same of others, only with different colors. The dungeons, as in Re;Birth 2, are too small to encourage the player to explore it.
There are missions to complete in the guild, like killing specific monsters or gathering specific items. You get credits, items and shares in reward. Shares will be better explained in the Story section, but basically each nation has a percentage of them, and you have to keep a balance between them. The amount of shares gives a boost in the attack of characters of each nation and may give you some plans and unlockable story events, but the impact is minimum compared to Re;Birth 2, where specific amounts of Shares were necessary to achieve different endings.
You can unlock the Colosseum too, and it has dozens of battles. Each with it's own rewards.
The Lily Rank shows the bonding of characters, as you can pair 4 front-line characters with 4 back characters. The Higher the Lily Rank, higher the boosts and coupling skills.
The Challenges give permanent boosts to the characters if you complete them, like "Walk 100 meters with x character as the leader" and so on.
The whole Neptunia franchise is based on making a parody with the gaming industry, so expect a hell lot of references. This franchise takes place in a world called Gamindustry, and there are four nations, each with it's own Goddesses, called CPUs.  The faith in each Goddess is what give them power, and this is called Shares. In the beginning of the game, Neptune, the CPU of Planeptune, is throwed to another dimension, where a group called Seven Sages is acting and trying to create a world where CPUs don't exist. She, then, must try to go back home, and help defeat the group in that dimension.
The story is told in Visual Novel style in the dialogues. It develops well, not rushing the pace, but I felt that the pace was too slow sometimes. My main complain is about the Seven Sages and enemies in general: I know this franchise won't have a dark story, but I just couldn't feel any sense of threat from them. This happened only when the real enemy unfolded, but it takes too long. Re;Birth 2 has a real threat behind the context from the very beginning, and you can feel it throughout the whole game, even with the light hearted mood. But even so, the Seven Sages are very charismatic, and the real enemy of the game has a badass final battle in the True Ending Route. The new characters are very nice, and the returning ones, if you already know them, also get a place to shine.
I only got the True Ending, and it took me more than 50 hours. I was careful in exploring all I could, but I missed a lot still. Expect a long game.
If you get the true ending, there are tons of post-game content, and this is really nice. New dungeons and Colosseum Battles, and a post-game story that takes around 2 hours to complete. Even so, you can start a New Game+, keeping the levels and equipment to get other endings or leveling up the characters more.

It's, at first, somewhat difficult to get into if you are used to the other Heroes games. It's not your standard Heroes game, with random skills, yet I would not say it's a bad change. It got a pretty art style, and I would dare say it's rather satifying to build your own hero.  The sadest part of the whole game, is that there will most likely not be any more DLC, as Blackhole was sacrificed to release the vanilla of the game, leaving it without the Wizards and hippy elfs.
My major complaint about the game, is the online and offline system. Being two different saves, playing offline and online can be very annoying. Suddenly you find yourself without internet, eager to continue the amusing (Yet somewhat.. Unfinished) story of Sandro, and you can't. Why? Because it's not saved offline. That would be online, on Ubisoft's own servers. And of course, if they are having problems with their severs, that will indeed mean exactly that, you cannot continue your save. This is very annoying to say the slightest. You get rewarded for playing online, with weapons, achivs and a dynasty to level up, yet Heroes is the kind of game I've always felt was made for a offline hot-set experience, NOT an online only experience.  Combined with unstable servers... Just no .So, being somewhat punchished for playing offline is just silly, and I cannot see the problem with just having one save, and no limits on the online servers.
To sum up, I liked the game, having a brilliant art style, a fun ability system, and some good stories. Yet, I cannot help to feel the save system ruin it. It's just a bad system, though the dynasty and weapon level is a fun addition, it could just as well have been offline. Knowing there wont be any more, as Blackhole was sacrificed by Ubisoft to create the Vanilla, is sad, but yet, I would recommand at least trying it.

First and foremost, HOMM6 is steeped in DRM. If this isn't your thing, be warned. You have to use Ubisoft's highly lame login system which causes me overlay issues with Steam and is generally mildly and endlessly annoying. On the flip side, you earn Uplay points when playing the game which can be used to unlock Ubisoft rewards to the game, such as wallpapers, extra PC cards for avatars, and even a Hero PC.
The game has been a better experience in the past. Chiefly, the campaign story feels very rollercoaster; that is to say, you can't get off the rails. Each event leads to the next event, which in turns leads to the next one. In previous incarnations, the game almost encouraged exploration. I felt like I was exploring only what it wanted me to find up until the chokepoints. This made the game feel taxing.
Graphically, it looks good. A bit like The Frozen Throne though; cartoony, bright. Combat is very close to what one would remember from previous versions. For those who haven't played this series, combat is tactical. Once you engage an enemy on the larger map, a somewhat randomized battle map appears before you. On one side is your hero and your army. On the other, the enemies (possibly an enemy hero). Combat turns fall to whichever units are faster than others, thus making a hastened group a good group. Attack power, defense, and special abilities fall into the mix as well. As does your hero's abilities. The magical gear in the game is pretty cool overall, with a lot of variety to the pieces and plenty of set gear that offers bonuses when you combine them with other pieces of the set. Also a nice addition are the legacy weapons.
Where I found the game to be weak is in the enemy AI. It was far too predictable and at some points, just makes really bad decisions. So bad and so common, that I could predict exactly how the computer was going to attack. This detracts from the game. HOMM6 isn't a bad game, but it has been more exciting in the past. Whenever this game is $20 or less, it is a good purchase.

You start with just a handful of settlers, banished from their homeland. And perhaps a cow or two, depending on difficulty settings. Winter is approaching fast. Clear an area, build some houses, get some food production going in the form of a farm or fishery. Will you have enough lumber for firewood during the harsh cold of winter? Will your food stores last long enough until the next harvest? Or will a sudden disease, fire, or natural disaster wipe out your colony.
Banished is a pure sandbox colony builder. The only goal, aside from chasing a few achievements which can act as “missions” if you interpret them so, is to see how far you can get. Expand your colony too fast, and you might not have the food production to meet demand. This leads to starvation and a huge chunk of your population dying off. If your birth rate is too low (limited by population mood and available housing), there may not be enough future laborers to take the place of those that die of old age. A sudden cold snap, when you don’t have enough warm clothing to go around, causes people to freeze to death in their homes.
There is so much that could go wrong at any time in the randomly-generated wilderness, that simple survival has it’s own zen-like reward. When all the plates are spinning nice and balanced, somehow, and everything seems to be going well, the colony acts like a well oiled machine. One you built yourself, through trial and error. It takes a bit of time to learn how things work, like the interplay between the various types of resource generating buildings you can make, how close or far apart you should place things, when should expand, and so on. But each catastrophic failure becomes an important lesson learned to apply to your next attempt. The way Banished works, how its colony ecology functions, is very clear visually. Unlike, for example, SimCity where much happens in “abstraction” as numbers and the movements of the city’s inhabitants are visual fakery, Banished leans closer towards the likes of Theme Park or Theme Hospital. Every colonist matters. You can follow an individual, track their mood and thoughts, and watch them from birth until death.
There is so much quality in both the design and execution of Banished. The user interface in particular stands out as clear, functional and powerful without being overwhelming. It’s hard to believe it was all made by just one person. All the software development, artwork and audio is the result of one Luke Hodorowicz, whose debut effort outshines most of the recent city planning simulators by far bigger studios.

I can't say that the creator didn't put any sort of effort into it, but I can say it could easily be taken for some videogame school project meant to showcase your atmospheric and design skills, rather than a well-thought game per se. It really needed more polishing to even manage to be an intriguing walking simulator. That said, for 50 cents I don't really regret it, but still disappointed in the missed potential.

- Content (specially end game and higher difficulty)

There's a lot of info i want to give you about the game to help you judge it, but go ahead and watch the streams/videos and decide for yourself, i found myself getting the game a while ago, and i simply love it, love the game love the dev interaction, totally worth it, this game is going to rock for me. Very Fun and Engaging Game! Coming from somebody who basically mainly plays arpg's dating back to the Diablo 2 days, let me say that this game is truely a gem for what it is. I have played them all, D2-3, POE, Grim Dawn, Van Helsings, Torchlights, Titan Quest, Marvel Heroes ect.. and this game, although it doesn't have the longevity as other games with ladders/seasons and an online economy, it is remarkably well made.
I purchased this game pretty late, and frankly, I am not sure how I actually missed this at launch back in 2015. But let me say that when I first jumped into it, I was instantly engaged and hours just passed by. The game presents itself very well and has top tier combat, which you can use WASD keys, mouse or a controller. You have the option in difficulty by selecting CASUAL, NORMAL or HARDMODE. Be warned, this game will kick  your backside even on normal as enemies seem a little too overbalanced.
The game adopts the Guild Wars 2 style weapon combat system. Where a player can equip two weapons and have different skill sets based off of those weapons. Mixing and matching these is pretty fun. Along with this, it has a unique destiny card system, which allows you to use a variety of cards which act like passives. There are also demon stones, bounties, treasure maps, endless pits, and it goes on and on and on.
With all of its positives, I suppose there are also a few crucial down sides to the game. Firstly, the playerbase is very miniscule. I have been online playing and have never seen more than 25-35 people in chat combined. Whether the majority just play offline, is beyond me, but the game seems as if it didn't take off, sadly, because it is overwhlemingly good. On top of this, the servers are not secured, so people can modify files and cheat. Some call it a problem and some do not. I suppose it depends on what you look forward to in a game like this. There is also no trading and economy, which to me, hurts the longevity of the game.
TL;DR    Great game, diamond in the dirt! Worth the price.
PRO'S:
-UNIQUE COMBAT SYSTEM, GREAT FLUIDITY
-EXCITING AND ENGAGING GAME
-VARIOUS THINGS TO DO
-GREAT ART AND HILARIOUS DIALOGUE
-FUN ITEMS AND PASSIVES TO TINKER WITH, AND A LOT OF WAYS TO PLAY
CONS:
-LOW PLAYERBASE
-OPEN SERVERS WITH OFFLINE WHICH MEAN, PRONE TO HACKING
-NO ECONOMY/TRADING SYSTEM
OVERALL SCORE 8.5/10 for what it is, with the potential to grow immensely with the MOTORHEAD dlc and more.

I personally have not played the first Dungeon Defenders game, but I put a ton of hours into Dungeon Defenders Eternity, and saying I enjoyed the experience is an understatement. For something in Pre-Alpha, the amount of development that has happened in this game is extremely exceptional. What you get out of the game depends on what you put into it, and to be perfectly honest, I feel like I have put a decent amount into it.
Compared to Dungeon Defenders Eternity, this game offers a variety of ways to play, since one aspect I particular enjoy is the synergy that certain defenses can undergo with one another. To name a few, There is the Geyser/Storm Combo, which can keep certain targets in place (some argue the combo is broken, but I could not care less on that point), and another combo is something I call Magic Shatter (people may call it something else) where you freeze a target, then send it airborne. The result is when they come back down, the target shatters, most of the time instantly killing it. The point is unlike in DDE, The defenses all seem to have a particular place, and do not seem to make any single tower worthless. (except for maybe the Squire's Training Dummy)
The gear in Dungeon Defenders 2 is already extremely versatile , with unique abilities to a certain item type that can greatly improve a player's performance, meanwhile in DDE, gear just improved tower and player stats directly. An example of some gear affixes are improving a specific tower performance, such as "Increased Flameburst Tower damage by 5.03%" making the item effectively an apprentice ideal item to improve his flameburst tower damage. This allows items to cater to specific classes, and once again improving the depth of the tower and also the character. There are some rarer mods that are extremely significant, so if you want to get truly powerful items, you have to be ready to hunt for them to get the best performance. Another thing I believe is improved compare to DDE is that gear is still able to be leveled, but leveling gear does not break the game as hard as it did in DDE. When you upgrade items, the stats will go up by a fixed amount every time, unlike in DDE, where the amount that the stat will increase is dependent on the stats the item had when it spawned.
The next thing I will address is the leveling system. The leveling system itself is pretty straight forward, you get experience by completing waves and defeating enemies, as well as completing certain conditions to gain fixed experience points and gold. That is pretty standard, but it's a good system. The thing that I believe that DD2 has done amazingly is that instead of being able to allocate points to character and tower stats directly as a result of leveling up, the character and tower stats go up automatically, and once you reach level 5, you gain 2 points that you can put into passive skills to improve your characters performance in a series of ways. For example, the Squire is able to place points into an ability that gives his spike barricades a chance to stun enemies when they attack targets. The more points you put into a skill, the more effective it becomes. As you put more points in, the results will have diminishing returns, so a player can decide when enough is enough, and begin skilling other abilities. Furthermore, you can completely respec your skills for free at any time, so long as you are not in the middle of a wave, allowing you to test out various builds and find a setup that suits you. Each character has 6 skills you can invest in.
The next thing I will address is the enemies. A few of the classic enemies make their return, goblins, orcs, wyverns, etc. The enemies still come from a variety of spawn points, where a variety of enemies will come out of each one. Those enemies were great in DDE, and most of them return in DD2. The enemy cast also expands, offering new challenges to overcome. One particular subject that has received mixed criticism is that some enemies have the ability to attack towers from outside of the common tower's attack ranges. This makes the game a bit more of a puzzle, due to the fact that unlike in DDE, tower ranges can't be increased to such an obscene level to counter absolutely everything that the map may throw at you. This does not break the game, there are still measures that the player can take to manage the various enemies, both old and new.
The final subject I will touch on is the Co-op play. I never went to public taverns and went looking for people to play with, so I won't comment too much on public matchmaking, but I have friends I have played with, and this game is just as awesome in Co-op as it is in solo play. If you have friends that you know and can communicate with, the experience is far more satisfying. The enemies will scale with the number of party numbers, both in health and overall difficulty, making it a perfect game to either play solo, or bring in some of your friends to go beat down the Old One's armies.
To conclude, for a game in its Pre-Alpha state, I believe this game is exceptional, and will go far. The devs are working to update the game, listening to feedback, and working to balance the game. Some things in the game still need fixing, some things still need to be balanced, but the game is still very young, and I am certain it will develop into a memorable classic. It will turn into a F2P at launch, but to be perfectly honest, I don't mind having paid for the game. I'm actually glad to have paid, because it's a way people can say "thank you" to the creators, especially since the game will be free at launch unless something changes that. In a nutshell, if you enjoyed the first Dungeon Defenders, I would assume you would enjoy DD2, the same holds true for Dungeon Defenders Eternity.

At the time, years ago, when it came out I was incredibly hyped for this. Who doesn't want a good RPG? We still don't have many.
However I was only able to get it like I dunno months ago whenever I played it. The world is good and creative. Also taking good spins on the typical things you see in other medieval/knights worlds.
People bash the game for it's graphics, which to today's standards are incredibly poor, but at the time they weren't that bad. They were okay at best.
The game has good promise, but it's such a shame the company was so small and lacked so many resources at the time. I'd like a reboot of this to be honest. It lacks a lot of polish. For example I mean you can only choose between brown or blonde hair at the character creation screen. I'm not serious. They cut a lot of corners just to bring out a fresh and original world and game concepts. Such as being a dragon etc.
It lacks a lot but it's got such good heart. It's hard to recommend unless you are a diehard fan of RPGs, because then you judge purely on the story, characters and world etc.

So I briefly played this when it first launched on the 360 and never got more than 10 or so hours into it.  I decided to pick it back up and man was I plesantly suprised.  This is far from a perfect game but I've really enjoyed my time playing.  My biggest issue is just the combat system.  Its very clunky and just doesn't feel satisfying.  It's not unplayable, but it does hold the game back a bit.  What makes this game great is the writing.  I was constantly suprised by the dialogue both in the main quests and side quests.  Larian Studios are the kings of gaming comedy and if you have ever played the Original Sins series you will immediately recognize the humor.  Apart from the writing, being able to trasform into a dragon makes your character feel very powerful and cool.  There is a good bit of custimization you can do with your gear stat wise to make your character perform the way you want.  I would definately recommend picking this game up if you are looking for a fun RPG.  I probably wouldn't play through more than once but the game is fairly cheap now so I feel its well worth the money.

This game was appealing at first. It seemed like a fun little free-to-play shooter. So I got it and downloaded it. It was really fun at first. In the lower ranks, everybody is more or less a noob and are getting to know the game alongside you. You start out with basic weapons which you don't need to repair (I'll get more into that later). These weapons are somewhat well balanced, and each map has different strategies. This makes the game seem very well-made and fun to play at first.
Unfortunately, such is not meant to last.
The first problem that you encounter is the change from rank 12 to rank 13. This puts you in the higher rank-tier. At this rank, you play with people of all different skill levels. This is an issue, because the teams aren't always balanced well and you get killed by high-ranked players. As well, there is a big problem here in that the team balance suddenly becomes way unbalanced. This is an issue, but isn't in itself gamebreaking; it can even be seen as an opportunity to get better.
As you play more games, you get the currency called "Warface Dollars" Early in game people are likely to purchase weapons directly from the store. However, as you will quickly learn, it is better to buy "random boxes", which award random items from a loot table, with one major item that is the goal to obtain. These random boxes are relatively cheap, and opening them is exciting. Eventually, you will get a couple of items from these random boxes. It's very exciting, but the excitement runs short once you discover the repair mechanic.
The repair mechanic perhaps single-handedly ruins the game. Items that you use will over time wear out, and you have to pay warface dollars to repair them. The problem? The repair costs are rediculously high. It is unwise to have more than one or two non-basic items; otherwise you will have very high repair costs, often outweighing the amount that you get from playing games. This added costs makes it difficult to have real progression, and also then adds to another problem.
The worst problem, worse than the repair mechanic, is how pay-to-win this game is. In this game, there is a currency called "K". This currency is used to purchase a multitude of things, from cosmetics (character skins) to specialized random boxes. The biggest problem with this is that the items from the "K" random boxes are insanely overpowered. One is a shotgun which does burst-fire (2 shots every time you pull the trigger). Shotguns are already massively overpowered in this game, which is another issue (poor class balance). Another one is a semi-automatic one-shot sniper rifle. That means that you can spray and pray and still get kills the majority of the time. This destroys the game.
You can also use K to purchase warface dollars, which also breaks the game. This means that people who pay can have all the stuff they want equipped because they don't have to worry about repair costs. This means that while most people can only afford 1-3 items, they can have all 7 items non-basic. This makes paying way overpowered.
Essentially, this game is destroyed by the greedy developers. The game is horribly balanced, and the meta of this game makes certain OP strategies (sliding and proning) dominant. I wish that the developers weren't so greedy; this could have been a genuinely good game.

SimplePlanes offers quite a bit for a small package. It teaches the essentials of flight and gives you a very gummy build style with the core pieces to redesign quite a few aircraft and vehicles or come up with your own designs.
Gameplay:
Mostly a simple vehicle sandbox based around flight physics, it does feel almost like a bit of an actual simulation more then you may be led onto believe. One of the most beautiful aspects of this entire game is all of its user-friendly design, from crafting to flying, and most notably the GUI itself- You can learn it all in about 2 minutes.
Campaign:
It offers a quick set of GUI and gameplay tutorials along with challanges and also a sandbox mode, as well as a 'quick combat' mode of dog fighting and bombing targets.
I would recommend this:
To any one who wants to fly some planes/jets/VTOLS quickly, learn the essentials of flight most-accurately, and enjoy having some dog fights against AI or bomb some ground targets---- Or not bomb anything and just build, think and fly!

Spectraball is part of a very narrow subgenre which you may call “ball platformers” (they are also called "marble rollers"). These type of games usually are nothing more than glorified tech demos that showcase and engine’s graphical and physics capabilities.
In this regard, Spectraball is no different. You control a ball, have three possible unique powers to help you on the stages, and your goal is to try to reach the end of each stage as fast as possible.
Although the game says it has puzzle elements, in reality this is a pure old-school platformer on par of the most well-known ball-busting hard NES titles from decades before.
This also means Spectraball is an excellent game for those who like to speedrun platformers, especially since the game has online leaderboards.
Sadly, the game is short, with only seven stages and three survival challenge maps which each offer an achievement.
Overall, if you like challenging platformers and indie engines which utilise wonderful graphics, this game is for you. If you want a puzzle game though, you will more than likely be disappointed. If I had to add some numeric value to this review, I'd go around 60/100; the game doesn't really have many strong or weak points, it's just another indie platformer. A fun pasttime for a few bucks.

Napoleon: Total War.
Is the game worthy of the name "Napoleon?" That is an interesting question. In Vanilla, It does have it's issues. It is like a more atmosphereic version of Empire. It's campaign is shorter scaled, with a whole 2 cultures to take hold of. Either European (Prussia, Austria, Britain, Russia & France) or other eastern factions (eg. Ottomans, Egyptians, Mamelukes.) This game has, to be honest, a much better AI than empire did. If you enjoy Naval battles, Napoleon is better than Empire. BUT. BUT BUT BUT. The campaign is not anywhere near as wide-scoped as Empire's. With the Vanilla game, my conclusion is that Napoleon is better for a head on, Multiplayer fight. But Empire has a better, Longer and more open campaign. THERE IS A WAY TO MAKE NAPOLEON BETTER THAN EMPIRE ON EVERY ASPECT. This is acheived through "Darthmod". As many Total War junkies know, "Darth Vader" makes amazing mods for The Total War series. Napoleon is no exception. So if you do choose to get the game, which I beleive is worth the money, get Darthmod Napoleon. Thanks for reading,

First off, by the date of writing this review (January 24th), I had not successfully played this game on a windows 10 machine, or on any machine. Within a few days of writing this review, I tried it again, and it worked. Thanks GandalfsBeard, as it did not when I tried it on a machine that did exceed the minimum requirements, but now does on the same machine I tried playing it on.
The 21 hours GandalfsBeard is referring to were clocked by leaving the game's launch interface open on accident. I had spent about one of those hours trying to wait for the game to load and stared at a black screen. After the original post date of Janyary 24 2017 of this review, I did end up playing it to get the timer up to 25.5 hours, and it worked! It enthralled me so much, after such a long wait to finally play the game, that I was able to tolerate time elapse for a few years in about two games before I realized how terrible a game this is compared to HoI II in nearly every facet. From research, to UI interface and navigation, HoI III left a bad taste in my mouth. All the limitatiuons of HoI II were folded into HoI III, along with many new nuances that made this edition dul and feel more like a chore than a game. My expectations far exceeded the execution in this newer edition: the sprite animation is lacking, the information provided to the user is limited, troop navigation, diplomacy, espionage, research, all of these were built up from the previous edition in ways that deteriorated the appeal to HoI II. In HoI II, research was completed in one area once an area of technology was researched. I understand new methods build on old, but frankly making iterations of research based on historical year is too redundant and grossly misrepresents the strides in technological advancement these iterations achieve.
All in all, HoI III was not fun for me, possibly due to previous exposures to previous editions of this game. In total, despite what the hours clocked say, I have really only played 4.5 hours of this game, and frankly, that is all I will every play.

This is a super-super short game. It's also the very embodiment of "pretentious walking simulator", a genre I happen to like.
It ticks the pretentious walking simulator boxes: narrator revisiting past, telling stories, plinky-soft emotional piano music in the background.
But it's 30 minutes, tops. I was shocked at just how fast the game was over. The graphics are pretty good for an idie effort but they won't blow you away. If you're playing with a controller, you'll have to do battle with a forced setup window requiring mouse and keyboard before you get into the game.
It's hard to recommend this game. It's clearly a labor of love from the developer and it's definitely not some quickie trash thrown out there to collect money off an asset flip - some care went into this.
And yet, because it's so short and light, you really need to be in the mood and willing to pay (at this time, $3) for that experience.
It didn't do it for me, maybe it'll do it for you. Not recommended: 2.5 out of 5.
