Even though most criticized as a gaming genre - since it rarely contains an aim aside discovering the story presented - I do love a well-structured walking simulator.
was the first in the genre that I've ever come to experience, and I did fell in love with the game and the potential video games do hold for artistic expressions. Either its tone be humorous, melancholic or horrendous, great games followed the example to utilize video games as a medium of art and experience.
is another short yet elegant example.
It is somewhere in the American South in a warm morning, when we witness a singular, vibrant memory which belongs to the nameless narrator: “I remember when I was a little girl, waiting at the end of my driveway. I had already missed the school bus, but I stood there anyway… envying the birds.” From that moment onwards, we take her control and start exploring neighboring premises which consists of her childhood home and the countryside around. As we explore, the narrator makes some remarks, sharing her impressions of the time, presenting fragments of the story. As we discover anecdotes from her life, we witness her gathering courage and her raising exigency to redefine what "home" is.
Even though the experience is quite short - which can be completed in one sitting, within half an hour playtime - it presents a naively beautiful atmosphere of a perception, a self-defense mechanism of a young girl from a broken home elaborately arranged to preserve innocence. The ending - the intended one - reveals an incomparable sense of freedom, the start of a journey rather than an end. In means of symbolism,
is an exceedingly beautiful work. Items you stumble around are chosen carefully to portray the early years of a hard life, which battles to not lose the childhood magic. Atmosphere is elegant, the color palette is nostalgically gracious and the voice acting draws the outline of your fleeting feelings.
If you are in favor of the genre, this one is an experience worthy of your time. Yes, it is quite short, yet the clash between the realism and the romanticism, the age old battle of innocence and experience, in which fleetingly beautiful innocence is doomed to lose is presented to you. As the innocence is lost, one does embrace the courage to go out for the actual journey. So home is where One starts indeed...

This review is in three segements.
1: Mechanics
2: Visual's and performance
3: Story
Mechanically wise this is game perfect, there are no other words for it. The gameplay mechanics are so beautifully refined, it's just so fun, I find myself learning enemy attack patterns too better defeat them, I constantly make sure I am using the best possible weapon all while trying new ones, and same goes for Demons Powers and Destiny Cards. Mechanic wise this game gets a 9 outta 10. The reason for it not being a 10 is for one very minor, but still quite annoying detail is the camera, the angle for isn't quite right and sometimes I find myself running staright into a bunch of enemies that I couldn't see due to camera looking down to much. But other than that Mechanics are just fine.
*For details on some of the mechanics in the game, they are located at the bottom of this review*
For Visual and Performance this game isn't too bad for a 3rd person RPG, Hack and Slash. All though the higher graphics does seem to tank on my PC, but that doesn't make the game unplayable. I prefer low graphics to high, I'll happily sacrifice high quality if it means I get 10 extra FPS, It's just my personal preference. I give Visuals and Performance a 8 outta 10.
And finally for Story, I have only played up too the first major boss and so far it's not bad, it doesn't really hook me in, but I'm honestly here for the hack and slash, but it's so far it looks to be your generic 'Main Character Saves World and Is Undefeated'. But one thing I do like is the over head voice, he is absolutely hilarious... sometimes, and I love the little easter eggs where he talks about other games, for example he accidently calls the player 'Stanley' from the Stanely Parable game, as the voice actor from that game is the same voice actor in Victor Vran. So for Story I give it a 9 outta 10.
Overall this game is brilliant, this is my first Hack and Slash RPG and I am absolutely love it and will definitely play it too completion. I give this game 9 out of 10.
*For anyone curious on how the game works here is a quick overview, At the beginning you start off with 1 weapon slot, 1 potion slot. With all the weapons there are 1 primary attack and 2 secondary, the primary attack is a basic hit, the secondary's however are different depending on what weapon you have, a hammer can do a slam down type attack, or a charged attack, doing allot more damage, there are also shotguns with precise shots and scatter as well. Potions being things like health and some others as you progress. As you gain experience your weapon and potion slots can increase to 2 and can switch between the 2. Later in the game you can acquire Destiny Cards or Demon Powers. Destiny cards give you permeant passive abilities too aid you in the game, it can be more HP, more damage and bunch of stuff. Demon powers are incredibly powerful abilities, either being offensive or defensive and can be activated by chaining kills together in order to fill a meter, once the meter is full you are able to use the demon power, these are just some basic stuff, the game expands allot more in the future*.
*Discloser* This review is based on my own personal expirence and everything said here is of my own opinion. Diablo was the first arpg I played, and the game that left the strongest mark from my childhood. The atmosphere, the music, the inevitability of death, it was just great. Of course, I played plenty Diablo II through my teens, and most arpgs of note since then. No game came close to emulate the feeling I had when playing Diablo, surely not Diablo III, which was a massive letdown. I thouroughly enjoyed titles like Torchlight and Van Helsing, but even those, as good as they are, didn't leave a lasting impression.
Enter Victor Vran, and all of a sudden, I'm 9 years old again, smashing skeletons on a dark, mysterious setting again. This is not a Diablo clone, though, this is much more. It takes what made Diablo such a great game, and redifines it with twists of its own. English is not my native language, and I can't quite find the words to describe  how good Victor Vran really is. Let me just say this, if you're looking for an arpg, look no further, for this is the best one you can find today.

Maybe skip this one if you don't like walking simulators, but as someone who basically was this little girl, wilderness included, I found it both hauntingly familiar and charming.
It's a little bit like a lucid dream of an unpleasant memory you no longer recall the specifics of, the edges blurred by time and the actual unpleasantness long forgotten, but you know it was an awful point of your life and that knowlege colors everything about it. You can piece together what happened, but do you really want to?
You could, of course, rush through the whole thing in a matter of minutes if you look up a walkthrough, but that's not the point at all. Much of the charm comes from stumbling across things that, accurately to life, you really don't expect to find where they are. Pile of beer cans in the middle of the forest, far out of reasonable walking distance for the not inebriated? Sure, that's normal. Somebody's fancy dress shoe in an abandoned barn? Well, there's a reason you've been told to stay out of it, probably.
I felt it worth the price tag, and honestly might have paid more for it.

In short, this, game, is, hard. Even when you play it on easy, you get a lot of starting stuff, you find yourself with lots of food earlier on, then you population booms and you find your scrambling for food as winter comes. The randomness of each map punishes those who don't truely plan ahead and reaching even 100 in population can be difficult if not managed the right way and for those that managed 900+ congratz on getting one one freakin hard award. Also, difficultly REALLY affects how you start off. As with easy, they give you a lot, 12 people, a herd of animals, 2 kinds of seeds, a werehouse, houses, tools, food, everything. Medium, bumps it down, no animals, one seed choice, only 10 people, less food, stuff and so on. Hard, is for those who truely want to make it a builder as all you start out with is 8 people, and a cart full of stuff, no prebuilt buildings.
Overall, the game is simple when it comes to it's buildings. Collect the resources, spend the resources on buildings, man them, and what not. So building wise, it isn't that special. It's the planning of said buildings that will get ya. This game also doesn't work on large scale populations. The starting population being 8, 10, or 12. So you don't get a lot to start with. Makes that 900+ seem even more impressive now eh. Also, being disconnected from everything, means that if you want something new, like say, a herd of sheep, or some bags of tomato seeds, you gotta builda tradding port, and barter them. That's right, barter. There is no money in this game. It works on a give and take. I'll give you 100 iron tools, I'll take 20 sheep type of thing. Each item has a value and you want to match it up as close as possible. Which makes producing extra's pretty important.
The people and managing them is really difficult in this game, since you work with small populations for awhile, getting everyone onto a job that you want isn't easy. Oh, and you have to have laberors so you can't give everyone a specific job. Someone has to carry those logs right. The game does play it smart though. When a farmer is done with his crops at the end of summer/fall, he'll take on the tasks of a laborer. Or if the tailor has reached the maxium  number of stuff you want to make, laborer. Now, this is temporary as when spring comes back, the farmer will farm again, or if the tailor gets a new quota, start working again. A hint, early/mid/late winter is the best time for resource collecting and building. That doesn't mean you can't do those during hte rest of the seasons, but it is easier, cause those 10 farmers you have will starting carrying stuff now.
I could go on, but this is a game you have to play for yourself to find out, or look to a review that wants to list every little detail. I would suggest you buy the game and find out for yourself. Word of warning though, liking a city builder will make this game loads fun, not liking them, well, hard to believe you are considering buying one. If your unsure, there are easier ones out there, but, if you start here, you'll get a good grasp of how to build a city, from almost nothing. Some of my numbers may be off so it's worth checking other reviews as well.

Now, my real and honest opinion on the "game", after passing that literal game breaking bug(I could not play at all), this game is not bad, for supposed "early-alpha", it feels like a good base for the dev team to go off of.
Early access really explains itself in the title all its own, this "game", is really not much of a game; not that it is not playable, it just, is not there yet, and I am not mad about this or sad, that is just the way early access works. You are paying for what the development team is working on, you are paying for a sneak peak and basically a walk through on the development process of a game.
This game has had flak, I even gave it flak before, but I don't know how realistic I was being. They released this game into early access a little to early in my opinion, the word "early" is used very strongly here ladies and gentlemen, I am talking, you get 6-7 decent maps and around 50 or so different items, don't expect too much from this game, Yet.
Now I have this conversation with my friends all the time, and they are all avid gamers theirselves. "Is early access viable?", yes, and no. This game, and this dev team have a little bit further to go before this project they started really turns into something that is great, like its predecessor DD1. I wish this game was just done tomorrow, it really feels like it has very high potential, you can already tell by all the easter eggs that this game is built for greatness, like the child of a star athlete and a super model, that being DD1 and the super model that was the community for DD1.
I hope to see this game really figure it self out, and not just be a re-textured version of DD1, but add on to DD1, change some things that may have not worked as well; create a better server hosting gui, this was my biggest Con of DD1, hosting something was a simple two buttons really, join and create, nothing more.
Here are my list of thoughts on this current "game"
Pros:
- Good base for a big and fantastic game
- So far, I feel as though it is better than DD1 was in early-alpha
- Potential, potential & well, potential
Cons:
- Updates seem a little slow so far
- The game development company feels like they are leaving this game as a side project
- Feels sketchy buying it this early, this is a game company that is not that indie, but anything can really happen this early development
To expand on my con that is: "The game development company feels like they are leaving this game as a side project"
It feels as though they released it and kind of, just, slapped together like 10-15 monsters and 2 textures per tower, 4 classes and put a 28$ price tag on it, handed what was there to the community and went for a coffee break. This, is the one gamble with early access kids, you really don't know what is going to happen, but, I guess I can only hope for the best.
Rating: 3/5 Stars
For the time being, give it a little bit before purchasing, unless you really are a big fan of DD1 and you want to follow development, but know that you have been warned of bugs and not large bundle of content you would get from a full release game.

There are a lot of 'generic' things about Victor Vran, the title is generic cool guy name, he has a generic cool guy always gravelly voice/demeanor who always wears comic-book cool guy hats and is always in cool-guy poses where you can never see his eyes. He's so cool he even made some deal with the devil or something to get demon powers. The end result of course it the game isn't cool at all, it's super nerdy in a 15 year old boy way, right down to the inability to make non-creepy dialogue involving women.
If you can suspend your disblief about these things there is a lot to like. The setting, while generic, is a nice change from the nonstop gothic fantasy of other ARPGs. The combat is more like a twin-stick shooter than diablo-style ARPG, and seems originally intended to be played with a gamepad or wasd + mouse combo (both of which are options here). But there are a lot of ranged things to dodge as you muck about.
They do fall into some classic gameplay traps though where their attemp to polish things makes the game worse. Specifically the movement is animation driven, which means there will be a 0.5-1 second arbitrary delay on all movement input. This just makes walking around annoying and dodging projecties overly difficult. The other thing is an over-reliance on RNG for damage. It makes all the weapons feel weak and underpowered.
But the best thing they did was is in the implementation of the optional map challenges and 'hexes'. These are additional challenges and modes that make the game harder (similar to Halo's skulls) which encourage experimentation with the different equipment and play styles in a natural way. This seems to work very well in the ARPG context, where otherwise I tend to want to use my most powerful weapon at all times for way too long.
This is the definition of a 'Swimming in 7s' game. Not going to change the industry but will probably be some kids' favorite game.

I like the idea of the game... no where else is there a (still-active) trench-warfare based first person shooter game. The game gets that idea really well, with a great attack/defense system. Too the squad idea is really nice, and you can always create your own if you don't want to mess with someone else's.
The problems are with the actual gameplay and controls... it's all very clunky. I don't know if it's meant to be that way or not but that's what I feel and see. For example, if I'm in prone and I move a single centimeter, the crawling animation plays for like a tenth of a second, and it looks unnatural. When I aim down my gun, the sights wobble around a lot which I guess is realistic but not particularly enjoyable.
A lot of it too boils down to the different stances and actually just moving around. The game doesn't have any stance up/stance down controls, instead they have three separate controls for prone, crouch, and jump, which is not what I am used to. Often times I found myself jumping out of a crouch instead of re-pressing the crouch button.
And in everything I do, there always feels like there's some delay between when I press the button and my character actually starts moving.
There are also problems with the spawning system... once I spawned in the middle of a gas cloud and died before I could get my gas mask on. Another time I spawned right in front of an enemy. Sometimes too the whole wave of reinforcements spawns out in no-mans-land on the edge of the map, and at that point my only goal is to get into the safety of a trench and I accidentally wander off the edge of the map and am quickly "executed" for desertion...
I remember once an old WW1 Source-Engine mod simply called WW1 Source... perhaps the game wasn't as pretty and didn't have as many weapons, but the game was silky smooth and extremely responsive. There wasn't any disorienting camera shake or lag. Of course you don't want it to be too responsive, or else players could abuse the stances by quickly changing between them, but overall the game played well. Too bad that good game's community is dead...

If by now you have not played a Counter-Strike game, it might be time to. It is a great FPS, that has a single and multiplayer aspect. The single player being, playing against bots that are of a certain difficuly, and the multiplayer being against other players. Depending on the map that is chosen, depends on the what the opjectives are. There are 2 teams against each other, one being Terrorists, and the other being Counter-terrorists. If the map has a prefix of 'de', it is a bomb map. Bomb maps being that the terrorist plant a bomb and the counter-terrosits defuse it once it has been planted. The maps with a 'cs' prefix, are hostage based. Terrorists protect the hostages from being taken back, and the counter-terrorits try to get them back. All maps can be won by eliminating the entire other team. At the beginning of every round, you are able to buy your weapon of choice and grenades to go with it, so long as you have the money to do so. To get money, win rounds, plant/defuse bombs or rescue hostages, and kill your opponents. Kill teammates to lose money and get a round suspention (if friendly fire is on).
All and all, an awesome game to just have a quick round or two, or spend hours farming achievements and killing enemys and friends alike. (friends being on your steam list on the other team ofcourse)

I don't know how to recommend this game. By contemporary standards, it has very little going for it. The graphics are outdated (and were even at the time of its release), the controls feel strange, and the combat aspects of the game are frankly awful.
What it does have going for it though, is that it is the single best adaptation of the Lovecraftian horror genre that I've ever seen. For those unfamilar with H.P. Lovecraft's works, what you need to know is that he was basically one of the prime movers of our conception of the horror genre. Although a lot of horror films and books are influenced by Lovecraft (see: the Alien series, pretty much all of Stephen King's books), his original stories suffer for recognition since they're honestly pretty poorly written.
Dark Corners of the Earth does a damn good job of translating a classic Lovecraftian story ("The Shadow Over Innsmouth") into a videogame.
I'd strongly recommend this game for anyone who enjoys playing horror games :)

The first thing you should understand, if anything of the game. You will not always win. This game isn't designed to favor you.. though it is neither designed to destroy you. The world is at best, indifferent. As it -should- be. To your citizens, and your plans. One horrible winter can wreck your firewood supplies. Growing too fast can leave you with 20 non-working citizens to feed while your farms need the extra hands. Untold deaths filling gravesites can strike the town at any moment.
But then again. Succeeding, even for five minutes is rewarding. You don't see people struggling, you see them thriving.
Currently holding three savings of three different towns, with three different settings I love the game, even if I'm failing I love to just see how one idea works as opposed to another. Having three seperate towns with a variety of success due to the gamestyles I set for it, the replay ability is amazing. My best town approaching two hundred people, enjoys an excess of food every harvest. While the.. less educated town of my worst is currently starving, and laying scattered across the map. I will admit, the game requires a bit of immiedate attention and I can not stress ENOUGH how you want to either pause or slow down time if you need to take a break but want to keep the game up. You can very easily come back to find quite a lot of people dead on 10x speed.
The SECOND thing, and.. I will admit that I only thought of this now, after writing all of that. The second thing I should mention is that it is very much number crunching. If you have already bought the game and are having difficulties with food there are some things I should mention for you.
Certain buildings have yello circles surrounding them, what this means is that it will be beneifical to you to not quite rush the housing area inside them. Gatherers hut, herbalists and foresters benefit from trees and space to replant the trees. Remove stone and iron and for gods sakes keep those other buildings away from these areas.
Hunters cabin benefits greatly by the wild deer that roam the map. A nice open area attracts them, while a forested/rocky/city discourages them.
Fishermen... yea they can't support the population that well but here's a tip on how to use them anyway. You will never get their radius to fully engulf water, HOWEVER. If you can get more then half of it to cover water. It goes a long way to make sure you don't die immediately if you happen to spawn in an area that isn't quite large.
Another.. very useful might I add.. tool to help you is the Town hall. Once built it takes no human resources to function, instead it gives you all the spreadsheet tools you need. From having graphs to tell you the amount of food you're producing and consuming to even going the extra mile and -telling you exactly how much of both you're doing.- And in the same window let's you increase the storage cap (provided you actually have enough storage barns for it) for food and other goodies. Extremely useful if you can't seem to eyeball the production rate. It does take up a lot of resources and a significant chunk of land that could be used for houses/farms/woodcutters so be careful. However the information is invaluable when trying to figure out what resource to expand towards next is.

To be quite honest, I DO RECOMMEND THIS GAME FOR THOSE WHO HAVE PLAYED DD1 AND LOVED IT. It's great, but there are multiple problems that you would commenly expect when getting a pre-alpha game. Ignoring the fact that I have down voted this game, there are multiple aspects of this game that include DD1 gameplay style and newly intergrated styles in this new game.
Now for the main reasons I have (not) recommended this game.
- A lot of the features of DD1 have been removed/rehased/recycled. This means that some of the things have been kept, while some of these things have been reworked, while most of the other stuff has been reused.
-Style of the game is great, it is visualy appealing and very well textured/graphics are amazingly good for a pre-alpha.
- A lot of the classes have been reworked and nerfed heavily. Huntress's mines/traps and bombs area of effect has been greatly nerfed had has no were near the the effect they did in DD1. Squire's defences are while the same, have been heavily nerfed, and dont hold a candle to DD1's squire's defences. Monk and Apprentice are in the same boat, thus making the game a lot more difficult and challenging when progressing onwards in leveling. Defences are also quite weak, and you're forced to rely on your hero to do most of the cleaning of waves.
-Mana: Mana has been drastically altered and is no longer the main currency of the game. While you still use mana to build towers and use abilities, the new incorperation of a coin/gold system is now the new money of the game. Speaking of mana, there are two different types of mana. Ability mana (Blue) and Tower mana (Green) both drop off enemies, but in very LOW quantites.
-Online system: They have a very strange working of the Online/Server set up which at first greatly confused me. However it took a while to get use to. You are thrown into a recruitment tavern where you talk to a recruiter. This brings up a menu allowing you to pick from multiple different level groups. E.g. 1-5. 5-10. 10-15. This also stops boosting somewhat as if you were a higher level, (E.g. 15) and joined a lower level bracket, (E.g. 5-10), you would be brought down to level 10 for the remainer of your time in that bracket, once you leave, you are returned to your normal level. This also kicks lower level characters from trying to join higher level brackets.
Overall, the game is very different from DD1. I was expecting it to be a lot better than the first one, and wasn't expecting much of the workings of the characters to change that much considering they were perfect in the first game. However this is my opinion and that doesn't mean much on the internet.
The main reason I am not recommending this game is becuase it's purely a pre-alpha and the the fact that its $24, (from New Zealand), is not really ideal. However, in another case, if you loved DD1 and want to give it a try, by all means, i would recommend it to you just becuase its a great start to a game that has LOADS of potential. However, definately needs work, and lots of changes.
~~TLDR~~
If you liked DD1, get it and see for yourself. If you haven't played DD1 or didn't like DD1, don't get it, becuase it's simply not worth $24 or whatever its going for in your country. Especially when rumour has it that on offical release its going to go Free 2 Play.

Here's a fun fact for you: When I was little, I wasn't allowed to play multiplayer games. It wasn't because our internet connection was horrible (though it was). it was because we were a rather conservative family, and my parents worried about the language we would be exposed to (which, given kids I hear in online games nowadays, is a fair point I suppose). As a direct result, almost all games I played were single player.
After I finished the story in a game, if there were a multiplayer component, there was really nothing I could do besides play on my own with bots or with my siblings. When a mode with bots wasn't available, my sister and I would explore the map, traversing the jungles of Far Cry in an completely nonviolent, and likely unanticipated by the developers, way (another fun fact: for a time, we were able to play Far Cry, at first as long as we wore headphones (so our mother wouldn't hear the cursing), and then later with the voices turned completely off (and then later not at all)). Sometimes, however, I would explore the maps on my own. This didn't usually last for long, as I would get bored in a few minutes, but it's something I kept coming back to, especially once I discovered the wonderful world of modding.
One summer, or autumn, or spring, or even winter (to be honest, I don’t even remember the year. Kids, consider journaling), I bought Jedi Knight 2: Jedi Outcast. The single player was a blast, and the developers should be commended for their hard work, but at the same time, what I remember most were my adventures in worlds the fans made up. There were a few single player mods that I enjoyed immensely, but for the most part, the modding community spent their time and effort making multiplayer maps (I’m afraid I never joined in the creation itself- and that’s something I very much regret). These maps varied wildly. Some were true to the Star Wars lore, others had disco rooms that played the Hamster Dance on command, and graveyards where you might find a tomb labeled “your mom!” (being as incredibly conservative as I was, that last bit deeply offended me). There were tombs, giant space hotels, wild west saloons, beautiful beachside palaces where the song “Time to Say Goodbye” played endlessly, and so much that I just barely remember.
I downloaded map after map trying to explore as many of these wonderful places as I could. Each held little idiosyncratic pieces of the author's mind, tiny lovable quirks, and endless expressions of their creativity. All of them held little secrets- hidden doors and buttons, portals to completely new worlds where you’d least expect them- All of them had a soul. I still wish I could visit them again, to see what they were like, and how they hold up in my memory, but part of me worries I wouldn’t be able to find them, or that they’ve been lost completely to everyone but the authors (many of them were from FileFront, which seems now to be gone).
But why am I telling you all of this in a review of “Home is Where One Starts…?”
Well, friend, Home is Where One Starts is a lot like those maps in Jedi Outcast, except for the fact that it has a story (and a moving one at that). For the best experience, you should go into it looking to explore. You won’t find secrets put in by some devious modder, but you will find inside it a similar sort of love of one's work as of those modders; a love that also drove this author to put hours upon hours of time into creating this little piece of space. You won’t find the quirkiness I mentioned above, rather, you’ll find poignancy, delivered partially through narration, and much more through the environment that they’ve crafted. You’ll wander about, enjoying the sun and the wind, but also find that it retains a focus on a certain time, place, and story, that those maps I remember from the modding community lack. As with those multiplayer maps I explored alone, you have to go in knowing that this won’t be your typical game. Indeed, “game” is a poor word for these digital worlds we construct, and one we only use because we don’t have any other words that convey exactly what we’ve managed to achieve through video games (“interactive experience” just doesn’t have the right ring to it).
You have to know that it’s quite possible you won’t like this game at all, and that your reaction of dislike would be perfectly valid. My big brother loves Starcraft, and I don’t really care for the game. My favorite game of all time is The Beginner’s Guide, and he didn’t find it particularly engaging at all. We all have different tastes, and that makes the world a more interesting place. But if you realize and accept that this is “a walking simulator,” that the experience will largely be one of exploration and listening rather than action, and that it's an indie game, and that it’s budget was likely little to nothing… then maybe, you’ll like it too (not despite its approach, but because of it).
Sometimes when I tell people how much I love The Beginner’s Guide, I’ll tell them “it’s certainly not the best game of all time, but it is my favorite game of all time.” That was mostly my reaction here, too. Don’t come to this game expecting perfection or greatness (if possible, don’t come to any game with that mindset). Just…
. The author pouring their heart out to you in what they describe as “interactive poetry”. Maybe you’ll end up loving it as much as I did.
I’ve only played it once, and for less than an hour at that, but this game is somewhere I hope to return to again. It’s not my favorite game of all time, but if I still feel this way tomorrow, I think it will probably makes it into the top 10.
TLDR: The game’s got heart. Will play again. Thumbs up. Like & Subscribe or whatever.

November 2017 update: TFC is still my favorite game of all time.
This is my favorite game of all time.
This was my introduction into competitive gaming. I spent the majority of my free time playing TFC for eight years, and made friends that I keep in touch with to this day. So much of my late teens and early 20s had this game in the background (or foreground) that there's no way I can give an impartial review - TFC is the best game I've ever played.
I had read an article in PCGamer about a custom Half-Life map called Hunted, and had only played a couple rounds before a new patch for Half-Life added official support for TFC. I played Hunted almost exclusively for quite a while, as the combination of asymmetric teams, objectives more nuanced than 'get more kills than everyone else', and my first real introduction into online gaming started to consume the bulk of my free time in high school.
The core mechanic of HL:DM (and every other FPS I was aware of) was aiming: put your crosshair on the other guy and click before he does the same to you. I've never been any good at aiming. Starting with my experience in Hunted and gradually branching out into the Capture the Flag maps, I discovered ways to be effective and useful without having to be good at clicking.
I learned to air strafe and bunny hop, to be quicker and more agile than my opponents. I learned to use strategic spam to compensate for my lack of accuracy with explosion radius and volume. I learned to use grenades to launch myself (or others) across the map. And, eventually, I did learn how to aim a little bit.
Then I got into my first gaming clan, {GTO}. Over the next 6 years I built relationships with folks I played TFC with (and against), worked on improving my agility-based skill set, and trying to guide the clan toward higher rankings in the competitive leagues and ladders. TFC was my escape and diversion from the stresses of being a teenager, and the community and the online friends I made helped balance out my social awkwardness and introversion as I started college.
It's possible that TFC could have been replaced with some other game and the outcome would have been similar, but to this day I haven't found anything that compares to the unique combination of asymmetrical teams, diverse and nuanced mechanics, variety of maps, lofty skill ceilings, and opportunities to improve.
There are 9 classes to choose from, and although not all are used equally (Medic and Scout dominate offense while Soldier, Demoman, HWGuy and Engineer are the primary defense roles) there are times when a talented Spy or Pyro can turn the tide of a game, or a Sniper can dominate a zone of the map. Becoming proficient with each class means developing a variety of skillsets, and in many cases being good at aiming is irrelevant (Scout relies entirely on speed and agility since their weapons are so weak, Demoman is all about timing and distribution of explosives, Engineer is only as good as their Sentry Gun management, etc).
The offense vs. defense dynamics combined with the variety of CTF maps provided a deep well of skills to learn and develop for specific scenarios, while the movement techniques and other quirks of the Half-Life engine provided a broad avenue of applications for players to develop and leverage their proficiencies.
Compared to this depth and variety games like Counter-Strike seemed very bland and shallow in comparison; generic shooting contests where the best clicker tended to win. Team Fortress 2 was not what I had hoped for - the removal of grenades and increased emphasis on clicking skills felt like the striking landscape of opportunities to learn and develop skills had been flattened out to lower the skill ceilings and increase the crowd appeal.
Of course, CS and TF2 were hugely popular so obviously my opinion does not represent the general population. And considering the age of TFC and its dwindling player base I doubt anyone is going to have an experience similar to mine at this point even if you're like me and prefer games you can get good at without having to know how to aim.
That said, the current price is between $1 and $5 depending on sales, and many people already got this in one a Valve Pack or Half-Life Bundle. If you can get a few friends interested it's worth checking out, dive into a server together (or host a listen server) and play around a bit. Try a game of Hunted if you can get 5 people or more. Try openfire_l 2 vs 2 if you can only get 4. Even if you only find a small fraction of the enjoyment I got out of this game, I'm sure you'll get your money's worth.

I like the idea of the game... no where else is there a (still-active) trench-warfare based first person shooter game. The game gets that idea really well, with a great attack/defense system. Too the squad idea is really nice, and you can always create your own if you don't want to mess with someone else's.
The problems are with the actual gameplay and controls... it's all very clunky. I don't know if it's meant to be that way or not but that's what I feel and see. For example, if I'm in prone and I move a single centimeter, the crawling animation plays for like a tenth of a second, and it looks unnatural. When I aim down my gun, the sights wobble around a lot which I guess is realistic but not particularly enjoyable.
A lot of it too boils down to the different stances and actually just moving around. The game doesn't have any stance up/stance down controls, instead they have three separate controls for prone, crouch, and jump, which is not what I am used to. Often times I found myself jumping out of a crouch instead of re-pressing the crouch button.
And in everything I do, there always feels like there's some delay between when I press the button and my character actually starts moving.
There are also problems with the spawning system... once I spawned in the middle of a gas cloud and died before I could get my gas mask on. Another time I spawned right in front of an enemy. Sometimes too the whole wave of reinforcements spawns out in no-mans-land on the edge of the map, and at that point my only goal is to get into the safety of a trench and I accidentally wander off the edge of the map and am quickly "executed" for desertion...
I remember once an old WW1 Source-Engine mod simply called WW1 Source... perhaps the game wasn't as pretty and didn't have as many weapons, but the game was silky smooth and extremely responsive. There wasn't any disorienting camera shake or lag. Of course you don't want it to be too responsive, or else players could abuse the stances by quickly changing between them, but overall the game played well. Too bad that good game's community is dead...

I bought this game after watching some popular youtubers play it. (Markiplier and friends! :D Check out their videos if you're on the fence about buying the game.)
It's an interesting party game where you work/compete with some friends/enemies to craft a level with the goal being you want to be the only or at least the first cute barnyard animal to get to the flag. No points are awarded if nobody died so you have to make it challenging but not so challenging that you can't beat it yourself. The host gets to set the amount of points needed to win and the game modes are just a choice between letting the players place any object they want down or the game randomly picks some parts and the players have a quick time challenge in picking which part they want to place down. You can only place 1 part down per a round.
The Community is really nice and even if you don't have any friends to play with you can make new ones through the game's matchmaking which is decently alive. Not really super populated but not empty either. There is also a feature where players can build their own maps in a freeplay game mode and get a code assigned to it, then simply challenge people to type in the code at a certain menu to load the map.
My only complaint is the game is there is nothing to do in singleplayer other than make maps which are kinda hard to share with people since the only way to share them is to tell someone your code and have them enter it or host a game and vote for the custom map. A fun game mode where you just beat maps that you can pick from a pool of maps that other players have made would be cool! The unlockables are also werid because it's hard to unlock stuff for yourself since one person randomly gets an item when item drops happen. Item drops are just random locations marked on a map that you have to touch, the game will let you know which map has an item to earn on it.
Overall: 8/10
P.S: Try my first custom level: V7Z7-K5A2 :D

Absolutely love this game and can easily lose a weekend to playing it. As a WWII history buff, I appreciate the amount of detail and work that has gone into this game! I particularly enjoy the randomness of starting off with one of the preset scenarios (1936, 1939, etc) as a Major actor in the war and watching it evolve differently than recorded history with just a few policy or diplomacy changes.
For example, playing as the U.S. starting in 1936, I placed a large focus on my naval and ground power and gave mere lip service to production and development of my air assets. Though I was able to win the battle in the Pacific against Japan by 1944 forcing surrender without using Nukes, and able to neutralize Italy in marching from Sicily to Switzerland, I was mired in the battle for Fortress Europe as I learned quickly that not having adequate air power against the German Luftwaffe in France as well as the Low Countries was not a great strategy. My bombers were pummeled every time they lifted off, air support that I sent as escorts were being swatted out of the sky like flies and the Luftwaffe bombers made me pay for every square I took in battle.
My only wish was that there were a proper way to co-ordinate with the AI/Allies to achieve objectives to more closely simulate real operations (Dragoon, Torch, Overlord, etc.) as the one that is currently in place is pretty ineffectual. Aside from that, I will continue playing this until the next iteration hits the market.
Absolutely recommended!

And so it ends, Fallout 3, the first contact I've made with the saga so far. This was not about ending the game, it was rather about the journey itself. Lone wandering at its finest. Exploration, real time action, tinkering with your equipment, improving your skills. My classic favourite ingredients. All of this flavoured by a great post-apocaliptic and sci-fi background and scenario. And, on top of that, I totally fell in love with the karma system.
Bethesda never fails to satisfy me with their sandboxes, although I have to say, The Elder Scrolls still has my heart, it's a richer world.
But let's not lose objectivity here, these endings were quite anticlimatic and they don't really match the experience the game has to offer. The repair system actually doesn't make a lot of sense. And the combat should be balanced to let you reach more than level 20. But I guess it's okay. (You always have Mods to cover the details you don't like)
Now, next stop: Fallout: New Vegas (After a rest and some other games in the middle, just to enjoy my return to the saga even more).

One of very few games I've returned/had $ refunded for.  Graphics are pretty good (8/10), from the single player storyline/plot/character interaction I experienced, I enjoyed it (not going to give a numeral rating as I experienced very little of this due to quickly refunding the game).  Unfortunately, the driving physics and controller (wheel) support is garbage.  I have a G27, I'm quite familiar with *it's* issues (such as the ~18-20% hardware deadzone on the wheel), but I've managed to get it working properly in all driving games I've played that can natively support the wheel.  Having said that, I spent ~2 hours tweaking the controls in this game, as well as pouring over forums about the 'best' setups for the G27 in the game, and I could never get these two aspects of the wheel behavior correct; steering 'weight' (any amount of weight on the wheel, just from your hands, is enough to move it around without turning up the force feedback, which then *kind* of gives it a proper feel.  its not just a 'centering' issue, i couldn't find a way to sustain 'weight' to the wheel, i'd constantly and seemingly randomly go 'slack' and not when the front wheels were off the ground or anything like that).  the other aspect is the 'arcadey' feel many other reviews here and posts online have detailed; it is just very hard to 'organically' control cars in this game with a wheel, its more of a 'black or white' 'left or right' 'straight or smashing into a wall' control.
On top of the control issues, which definitely ruin what could be a phenomenal game, to me; there is the issue of the amazingly overaggressive and cheating AI - going ~180 in a 'street' upgraded mustang and the *normal* cop cars aren't having trouble catching up at all, in fact, they're so fast they'll actually surround you and start body slamming your vehicle.
I should probably just stop buying any ubisoft games, they seem to all have a common theme; pretty good gfx + decent concept + horrifically ruined by not polishing the gameplay properly. = ubisoft games.
If they ever fix the controls in the game, I'd *definitely* buy it; however, I doubt this will ever happen, I bought this in 2017, and these same exact complaints have existed in the community since its release at the end of 2014.

The Crew is an open-world MMO racing game where you can play either as a street racer or a law enforcer (DLC) made by Ivory Tower in collaboration with Ubisoft Reflections. The gameplay, in general, is like one of those classic old-school Need For Speed i.e. Need For Speed Carbon, Need For Speed Underground, etc. You can drive around in a scaled-down map of the U.S. freely and visit mission activation points to race.
Although The Crew is a MMO game, the game does have a single player element in it, meant to be played concurrently with the online play or used as an introduction of the gameplay. The online gameplay works similarly with Need For Speed (2016) and Grand Theft Auto V - you will be put in a session with several other players and you can interact with them in races/free-run. You will also occasionally receive racing invitations from other players.
1. Lots of car variation. Again, similar to old NFS games, you have tons of choices of cars. You also can switch cars you own on-the-street using a 'mobile garage'.
2. Strong MMO aspect. Grinding for money, parts, experience, skill points, crew skills, etc makes the game worth a lot of hours.
3. Customizable driving elements - sensitivity, handling control, etc.
4. The Crew is going for the niche of arcade racing, so don't expect realistic driving experience like in Project Cars or Asetto Corsa. However, this connects to point (1) in the Cons list.
5. Beautifully made map - not necessarily in the context of quality, the map itself feels much more alive than other racing games and I really do enjoy driving around for no reason at all. The variation of the terrain is generally accurate of the real geographical aspects of the U.S. and is definitely a plus for the gameplay.
6. Massive map. Devs actually created the entire scaled-down map of the U.S. It can take quite a while to get from point A to point B. IMO, this is gold for an open-world racing game.
7. Environment is alive. Unlike the dead city in NFS series, you actually have pedestrians, commercial airplanes, planes watering a farm, etc. You can use train stations and airports, too. This is one of the reasons I enjoy driving around in the game.
8. Complete day-and-night cycle
9. Challenging races - your car's power in general can't be too far ahead of your opponents.
10. Big variation in the gameplay: classical circuit & sprint street racing, off-roads, stunt tracks, police chase (DLC), time limits, impromptu open world events, etc.
11. Detailed, color-customizable car interior
12. First-person POV available
1. I somehow feel like I'm driving a toy car in this game, especially when I drift. It's just weird and off in general. I fiddled with the settings quite a bit and managed to make it a bit more realistic, but it's still...too virtual? This is a highly popular complaint by other reviewers and I have to say I agree with them. The physics of the game is just ridiculous - both in driving and in the environment. I know the niche is arcade racing but they should at least keep a good balance between easy and realistic instead of going full-on 'toy car mode'.
2. Graphical quality is not that great and inconsistent. In some areas, you can notice that the environment texture is very crude but some other places do make quite a scenery. This gives me the 'immersion ruined' feeling since I'm very meticulous on graphical details. (Played on 4K Ultra settings)
3. The voice actors are seriously bad and cringy from the start, but the voice actors in Calling All Units DLC are much worse. I can't help thinking that they made an arbitrary decision to use one of their own staff as an emergency substitute for the original voice actors who are not available for the DLC making.
4. Cliche, boring storyline.
5. They clearly didn't put much effort in texturing the background characters, both cars and people.
6. Performance should be more optimized. Games with this level of graphical details shouldn't ask for that level of specs. This issue is extremely similar with Ubisoft's optimization issue with Watch Dogs 2 - crude graphics, but highly performance demanding.
7. This one is purely subjective, but I find the radio songs to be very, very annoying. I am aware most in-game radio tracks are from new artists looking to promote their songs, like in GTA V and Watch Dogs 2, I can still accept the quality of the tracks. But in The Crew, I lost all of my tolerance to bad music. I finally made my own Classical musics and Lorde - Royal playlist, which doesn't go well with racing games but apparently, I have no choice.
8. Cutscene camera was clearly designed to be bombastic, dramatic, and fast-cuts-style - this makes me nauseous.
9. I'm not a fan of 'powers' (EMP, UI disabled, etc)- makes the game too arcade-y in an extreme way and definitely a killer of immersion. If I want powers, I would play Mario Kart. I do not expect these kind of things from The Crew or NFS Hot Pursuit.
Progress is a bit slow. Racing rewards are a bit too low for me and the mission points are too far apart. Some people prefer this method to keep them engaged in the game for an extended period of time. But as someone who don't have that much time to play games, this style doesn't fit me. This is a very personalized point, so you decide the value based on your own life schedule.
Is it worth the price?
Is the CAU DLC worth paying for?
. The base game itself offers a lot of hours of playtime with its massive content. If you enjoy arcade racing, The Crew is your ultimate-updated-graphics arcade racing game. The CAU DLC's police chase content itself is already worth it. It's a great newly-added gameplay variance where you get to be the law enforcer and chase actual players. The police cars are also very cool to have and worth grinding for.
I hope my review can help you decide whether to purchase this game!

Home is Where One Starts... is a walking simulator and with a genre full of games how does this one stand out from the crowd ?
The walking simulator genre is a very popular genre and a lot of the games are critically acclaimed, like Firewatch, That Dragon Cancer and others. So with the overcrowded genre Home is Where One Starts definitely passed by me without me knowing anything about it.
I only recently got a chance to play through this game and I still don't know how I feel about this title.
You play as a girl who lives in a broken home. She narrates about her life and how she deals with her drunk father and how she escapes her everyday life when she goes outside. You explore the surrounding area and you listen to her stories about things.
For example you find stuff like a shed with graffiti in it and she tells you about the times she comes by the shed and looks at the graffiti for hours and how she loves it. The game is pretty much just a walking simulator, there's no puzzles to solve what so ever.
Now in most walking simulators the story is what's most important and honestly this game isn't that great. I mean I enjoyed my time with it, but it was for other reasons than the story.
One of the reasons is that the game looks really good. Once you start the game the sun is setting and it sets the mood perfectly. Graphically the game looks quite good and it's one of my favorite aspects of the game.
The game is short. To fully complete it and get every achievement would take you around an hour. After that there's no replay value what so ever, so don't expect multiple playthroughs.
In the end do I recommend it ? On sale yeah it's worth checking out the game, but however don't expect anything amazing out of it as it's nothing too special.
Final Rating:
6/10

+ Great Visuals
+ Somewhat interesting story....
Cons:
- ...but nothing too special
- Incredibly short

Banished is not your average, run in the mill city builder. There are no tech trees, no money. You can build anything at any time... provided you have the resources. This makes the experience very, very free.
However, that freedom comes at a price: it's a ridiculously hard balancing act. If you run out of food, people start dying. If you have less people, your production chain break down. Same for tools: if you run out of tools, your blacksmith will start to work less efficiently. If he works less efficiently, your productivity goes down, so even less tools. Even several (dozen) hours into the game there may be a baby boom where one minute you had 25000 food (which is a LOT), the next you run out of food and people star dying on you.
That being said, it's a marvelous game. It's very fun to play, save the occasional frustration, and lets you create your own frontier town or towns. If you enjoy builder-type games, this game from a one-man studio does an awesome job and is definitely for you.

If by now you have not played a Counter-Strike game, it might be time to. It is a great FPS, that has a single and multiplayer aspect. The single player being, playing against bots that are of a certain difficuly, and the multiplayer being against other players. Depending on the map that is chosen, depends on the what the opjectives are. There are 2 teams against each other, one being Terrorists, and the other being Counter-terrorists. If the map has a prefix of 'de', it is a bomb map. Bomb maps being that the terrorist plant a bomb and the counter-terrosits defuse it once it has been planted. The maps with a 'cs' prefix, are hostage based. Terrorists protect the hostages from being taken back, and the counter-terrorits try to get them back. All maps can be won by eliminating the entire other team. At the beginning of every round, you are able to buy your weapon of choice and grenades to go with it, so long as you have the money to do so. To get money, win rounds, plant/defuse bombs or rescue hostages, and kill your opponents. Kill teammates to lose money and get a round suspention (if friendly fire is on).
All and all, an awesome game to just have a quick round or two, or spend hours farming achievements and killing enemys and friends alike. (friends being on your steam list on the other team ofcourse)

Not that I don't like the control I get over an economy, industry, diplomacy, military of a WW2 nation, but it's not for me.
For one, you don't really "manage" intelligence and politics, you just set a couple bars and hope it works out.
For another, not everything is explained...at all. Watch Youtube videos to better understand some of the mechanics.
Personally, if you want to just jump in and get experience, play America to practice controlling an economy and industry, then go Italy for some military experience. Diplomacy matters more to Italy than America, but mostly it's just historical events.
DO NOT GO AS GERMANY IF YOU ARE CLUELESS! THE WAR STARTS, AND LARGELY FOR THE FIRST 2 YEARS, RUNS ON THEIR SCHEDULE! YOU WILL BE OVERWHELMED BY HOW MUCH STUFF HAPPENS AT ONCE!
Also, managing armies isn't always straightforward. Note: if you're army has no supplies, it can move, but it cannot attack an enemy army (can still occupy territory I believe). You will take longer to move over rivers and in mountains without engineers (train lots). Finally, you cannot post any troops in terrritories with less than 2 infrastructure. Seriously, they are foot pounders...WHY DO THEY HAVE TO HAVE A ROAD SYSTEM!?
Also also, while commanders give bonuses, it's not an easy system to understand. FYI: you set the stars, or "seniority" of commanders (just dictates how high a command they CAN take).
Higher level: higher command since it'll take awhile to level up...unless they have an ability that's really handy to a particular army right now. Lower levels: tend to be front-line leaders, but not all abilities are useful (ie. supplies reduction is likely useful in Theatre (highest) command, since the most troops will be effected (even if the general is a lower skill level)
Overall, while the sheer ability to command all major aspects of a WW2 nation is nice, not all commands are created equal, not all features and mechanics are explained in useful detail, and at times there is simply too much micro-management for someone like me to enjoy.
Good effort, but improvement is definately possible and I'd argue nessecarry for this series.

Just Cause 2 takes place in South East Asia on the Panau islands. You play the role of a man named Rico Rodriguez sent to track down a dangerous American. However, in order to get the information you need you work with the 3 rebel/criminal factions, the Reapers, the Roaches and the Ular boys against the country's oppressive government.
Just Cause 2 is a beautiful game, sure, but looking back
honestly would want to take the over 100 hours I spent on completing this game to 100% back. It's a grind fest, all Just Cause 2 consists of is collecting weapon parts, vehicle parts and destroying a number of things to reach 100% completion in any given settlement. There isn't very much replayability once you've completed every settlement to 100%.
●
The majority of trees and shacks in the environment will come tumbling down if you use explosives or crash into them with a vehicle.
●
The idea of using a parachute while using your grappling hook to slingshot your way across the landscape it quite creative and exclusive to Just Cause 2. I often find this method of transportation superior to using conventional land vehicles.
●
Cars, bikes, atvs, boats, helicopters and planes are all in this game.
●
You often take licensed music in other open world games for granted but after playing through Just Cause 2 for over 105 hours, it makes you realize that it's the only thing keeping you sane. It couldn't have cost that much to license music from obscure artists or at least implement a feature where you can manually install music tracks and listen to them through your PDA while you're zipping around Panau, could it?
●
It's debatable but it can only be seen clearly if you have experienced a multitude of other products to compare.
, I see it better than Ride to Hell Retribution although Bolo Santosi and the npcs you have to escort through stronghold take overs are the cringe worthy.

Spectraball is told to be a puzzle and platformer game. While the platformer part may be right, it is not a real puzzle game as thinking is not required. The so-called puzzles are way too linear and obvious to be a challenge and the only hard thing might be beating your own timerecord.
The graphics may have a rather good quality compared to other games of the genre, but there are a ton of useless and weird looking shadersn that really throw me off. One of those shaders can be seen in the screenshots: Every surface reflects the magic shine of the ball, may it be stone, dirt or snow.

"I'll never forget that morning. I had already missed the school bus, but I stood there anyway…watching and envying the birds."
"Home is Where One Starts" is easily one of the most beautiful video game experiences I've ever had. The sad thing is that I imagine a lot of people will hastily pan this title as being trite and boring, while others will overlook it entirely. I believe a lot of people miss out on life. Either they are too afraid to gaze beneath the surface of it all in order that they should experience something of the profound depth of our existence, or they simply have never considered that there is a deeper meaning beyond the obvious. Eddie Cantor once said, "Slow down and enjoy life.  It's not only the scenery you miss by going too fast - you also miss the sense of where you are going and why." That quote sums up the subtle, yet radiant beauty of this game. You've gotta play it like that. By slowing down, savoring the details, and allowing for your heart to unfold with a vulnerable kind of tenderness so that you can see reality with a new set of eyes.
One of the key principles developer David Wehle utilized in his game is that of "less is more". Gaming, in my opinion, is a somewhat squandered art form in that a lot of it relies on the literal exploitation of violence, sensuality, foul language and the most ludicrously verbose set-pieces and storytelling imaginable to entertain its audience. I get it: it's what sells. And I'll admit, I've been very entertained by many games falling into these over-done tropes. But how refreshing it is to see a game stand so bravely against the tide as "Home is Where One Starts"! How needed it is to offer up something more, even while relying on so much less than what we have been conditioned to expect out of our steady diet of entertainment.
Although "Home is Where One Starts" is a very short and simple first-person exploration experience, it is in all of its poignancy which solidifies it as a truly great game. Certain objects have been placed strategically to tell a bittersweet, sentimental story as the player diligently explores the surrounding farmland -- one of vivid childhood memories, hopes and dreams, heartache and sadness....of just being human.
Guiding these snapshots into the past is the future self of the main character, reflectively narrating her experiences and feelings. It is to narrator Elise Wehle that much credit is owed to the game's emotional effectiveness, who brings a raw and tangible sensitivity to the script, flooding the game with the fingerprints of a real, genuine personality.
Second to the narration in effectiveness, the sadly tender music pushes this short journey quietly along like a soft Autumn breeze. The gentle cooing of doves and the lightly chirping birds as sound effects are so at home in this setting that they sometimes seem to be of primary importance to the entire experience; it is in these minute details that this game breaths and has its own kind of organic life.
Graphically, the game does an effective job bringing a kind of surreal tangibility to a lonely countryside. While the trees and swaying high grass, the pond and the pollen floating through the golden air are all slivers of the narrator's memory, somehow the overall presentation caused me to feel as though I had been there before, and that the secret, individual details of my childhood were just a threshold away.
Is "Home is Where One Starts" a perfect experience? No. But in these rare gaming instances I find that negative critique isn't warranted. Given the overall impact the game had on me emotionally, I would highly recommend this title to anyone who can see the beauty in subtlety, and who is not deaf to the heart-aching power of memory.

I've been playing Banished and Tropico 4 quite a bit, and I see a big difference between the games. For Tropico 4, after the intial growth period, you can get to a point where your economy rocks hard and you stablize your society and its cruising from then on. For Banished, you never get to a point where you can cruise.
Banished is a great strategy game because it constantly keeps the player under pressure. After a certain population size, you have to convert to farming or have an educated workforce, if you do not have any seeds at that point (Hard Difficulty), you'll have to trade for it, if you haven't got enough Tools or Clothes to trade at that point, tough. You're headed for a starvation crisis.
You're constantly having to balance between having to keep building new homes for your people to avoid a future population collapse due to your population not replacing itself. You have to keep an eye out for the age of your children, and build new homes as they mature. Obviously the people in this game are not Asians, because they do not reproduce when they are living with their elderly parents. So in order to keep up with the materials to build the houses, you have to divert your population to gathering wood, stones and iron, and that might leave you short of people to gather your food. See above for what happens.
This game is simple elegance. It does not have a whole lot of variety as you see in many strategy games, but the few tools the creator uses to keep us under pressure, he uses to an exquisite balance. A population collapse due to an aging population or starvation is always possible around the corner. This game does not need deus ex mechana events like natural disasters to keep players on their toes. Fulfilling the human needs is a natural disaster enough.
Simple things like people living far from the school takes longer to graduate just demonstrates the elegance in which the creator puts the players under pressure.

As a Pre-Alpha game, there's so much to do in Dungeon Defenders II. With the success of the original, I know Trendy will give us an awesome game especially since they're looking at fan feedback for balancing, etc. Hopefully, their team's morale is also a lot higher than what it was during an incident with their former president a few years ago. Anyway, currently, my hero deck consists of a huntress, apprentice and squire.
Unlike some players, the game can definitely be enjoyable as a single player game. I've had no issues in the later half of the game with my trio of characters. As the more difficult your characters become, specific gearing becomes a necessity to ease the stress of completing a map. My squire is built as a defense tank. All items consist of adding defense health to his defenses, but I only have him set spike blockades. My huntress is used as a damage dealer. I don't really use her traps other than for utility, so I decided to increase her own damage instead. My apprentice's defenses are the damage dealers and I found myself mowing down enemies effectively.
Each character has a set of passives you can upgrade as you level, so there's a variety of builds you can work with along with item passives as well. Items come in a variety of tiers like many RPGs such as Diablo with legendaries being the best items you can get. Each item can be upgraded a certain amount of times and can add to improve your character's stats.
The game will drop a lot of loot..Like a lot even in single player. You'll feel like a rich snob and become very picky about which items you pick up. The good thing is if you regret not picking anything up, there's a temporary item box that allows you to get items from previous maps you've done. This allows for selling and upgrading items without having to fill up all your item boxes. The chances of higher quality item drops increases if you're in a group.
Leveling isn't much of a grind either. It feels just right. It might take a while in a pug map, because people will take forever to set up their defenses. However, as a single player game, as you get used to the maps, you will set up your defenses quickly. As stated above, you can definitely play this game solo even in harder difficulties. As this is an early access review however, it will be difficult to see how this review scales as the game adds content, but right now, it's highly enjoyable. I recommend it.

Was a big fan of Dungeon Defenders, and I have been awaiting DD2 with much anticipation.
I definitely felt that there was more emphasis on player defense as opposed to the more tower focused DD1. Not that towers aren't important, but (so far) I haven't felt confident enough in a defense to let it handle it's lane while I focus on another, I feel the need to keep tabs on all lanes to make sure nothing gets through. That may be because it's early on, I'm not sure yet. Personally, I like taking part in the defense, some survival games in DD1 got dull after you upgraded, because the defenses largely took care of everything.
One thing you'll notice straight off is that there are few towers for each hero, and more abilities than before. Most of the abilities feel strong and useful, though so far I find the Squire's to be the least helpful. Huntress has some very strong damage abilities, and the Apprentice has a great control in Tornado. You'll notice some towers are missing now, since there are fewer tower slots, but staples like the Ballista, Fire Tower, and Lightning Aura are still there.
Another change is the mana system. You have two bars, blue and green, for abilites and towers, respectively. Corresponding mana crystals drop from mobs, and chests give green. Honestly, I don't see much reason for abilities to have anything except cooldowns. I've only rarely used abilities so often that I ran out of mana, and then it only took a few seconds to run over to pick some up. Plus, some armor regenerates the mana, so at higher levels it probably wont be much of an issue. I'd rather have the old mana system in place, but I'll touch on that below.
As for negative things, it's hard to say since the game is in pre-alpha, but two things have really been annoying me so far.
First, all melee attacks move the heroes forward a significant amount. This means you can't backpedal and attack, but instead always charge into a group. It's really just personal preference, but I hate it when a game moves for me, or adjusts aim (which also occurs for ranged attacks, but that might be able to be turned off).
Second, it's not as satisfying to kill mobs anymore. In DD1, mobs died in an explosion of colorful mana crystals, each one worth a different amount. Now, some mobs drop crystals, and there are only two colors, blue and green. They don't roll around anymore, and blend into the scenery since they lack the bright colors of DD1. Again this is more personal than an issue, but it takes a lot of the fun of seeing piles of mana everywhere, and rushing to collect it before it disappeared, or fell off the edge of the map.
I still recommend the game, for a pre-alpha it looks and plays great, but it's obviously missing a lot of content since it's so early. The final game will also be F2P, so if you'd rather not pay for the early access, then just wait awhile.

I can't belive i paid money for this tripe. Flatout 1 is worlds better than this. Do yourself a favor and get the previous titles to this series. For starters, the gameplay is absolutely broken with garbage physics,
nonexistant handiling, and incredibly bad AI there is no reason to try to play this game. The visuals are
late PS1 early PS2 quality, with way too much motion blur and bloom that can cause siezures there
should be a warning to those that have epilepsy; the courses themselves are unimaginative and
poorly put together. The cars look and feel like rejects from a Hot Wheels game along with some that
were foisted from the previous FlatOut titles to give some impression that this is a sequel.
There is no structure to the gameplay mechanics, for starters the damage calculations are randomly
generated so hitting an opponent can result in either doing little to no damage to you or taking most of
your health away. There are no boundries on the tracks so you pretty much can drive where you want
with no penalties. There is no way to regain boost except crossing checkpoints; hitting cars or objects does nothing here. If they want you to use boost to "heal" your car then they should have more ways to obtain it.

Just Cause 2 takes place in South East Asia on the Panau islands. You play the role of a man named Rico Rodriguez sent to track down a dangerous American. However, in order to get the information you need you work with the 3 rebel/criminal factions, the Reapers, the Roaches and the Ular boys against the country's oppressive government.
Just Cause 2 is a beautiful game, sure, but looking back
honestly would want to take the over 100 hours I spent on completing this game to 100% back. It's a grind fest, all Just Cause 2 consists of is collecting weapon parts, vehicle parts and destroying a number of things to reach 100% completion in any given settlement. There isn't very much replayability once you've completed every settlement to 100%.
●
The majority of trees and shacks in the environment will come tumbling down if you use explosives or crash into them with a vehicle.
●
The idea of using a parachute while using your grappling hook to slingshot your way across the landscape it quite creative and exclusive to Just Cause 2. I often find this method of transportation superior to using conventional land vehicles.
●
Cars, bikes, atvs, boats, helicopters and planes are all in this game.
●
You often take licensed music in other open world games for granted but after playing through Just Cause 2 for over 105 hours, it makes you realize that it's the only thing keeping you sane. It couldn't have cost that much to license music from obscure artists or at least implement a feature where you can manually install music tracks and listen to them through your PDA while you're zipping around Panau, could it?
●
It's debatable but it can only be seen clearly if you have experienced a multitude of other products to compare.
, I see it better than Ride to Hell Retribution although Bolo Santosi and the npcs you have to escort through stronghold take overs are the cringe worthy.

Call of Cthulhu: Dark Corners of the Earth is a very obscure game, yet one I hold very close to my heart. It is a shame that it's developer, "Headfirst", went bankrupt before they could put out a sequel, as they certainly did a fantastic job with this one. Call of Cthulhu is a mixture of first person shooting action set in the 1930s with period weaponry, tense (yet sometimes frustrating) stealth, mediocrely difficult puzzle solving, and good old Lovecraftian horror. As the title would suggest, the game is based off of the works of Howard Philips Lovecraft, a horror writer from the 1920s-30s, although the game is more based off of his short story, The Shadow Over Innsmouth, rather than his other titular short story, Call of Cthulhu. The plot is memorable and full of twists, yet for a full understanding of what exactly is happening, you will need to get the "A rank" ending, although I suggest watching it on Youtube, as it is hard to get an "A rank" for most people.

Call of Cthulhu is an absolute technical mess with mediocre gameplay, but it's story, atmosphere and music more than make up for the iritating experience you'll probably have. It has it's share of game breaking bugs and one particular nasty one that hinders your ability to progress, but if you're able to somehow continue on through the game (using unofficial patches or someone else's save data), then you'll not be disappointed by the end of it. Despite the problematic end sequence.
The game's enemies can be intimidating, they make for some nerve racking encounters and one intense chase sequence that is let down a bit by the gameplay. Level design is pretty good here, Innsmouth is more or less how you could imagine it to be, but there are some areas that can be a pain to traverse thanks to the iffy gameplay and many trial and error situations you'll find yourself in.
If you're a Lovecraft fan such as myself, you'll probably be more forgiving with this title. It's one of the few if not the only game that uses Lovecraft's stories very well. It's true to the source material and an overall entertaining experience, if you can push aside the frustration.
Do I recommend this game? If you can handle the bugs, then yes.

VVVVVV surprised me quite a bit. It was a very enjoyable game and the difficulty ended up being a bit less than I expected. That is NOT to say the game is easy at all. I still died over 500 times on my first playthrough. And if you are not that great with platforming or fast reactions, then the game can definitely beat you up. But I was efficient enough to make it through the game 100%  in a few hours (where I had originally expected like 10+ hours) and had fun during every second of it.
The art style is minimalist in most places, as you can see, and filled with some awkward looking objects here and there (e.g., the “YES” or “STOP” items seen in the trailer) that are actually obstacles. The audio is some great 16-bit sound - I really liked the music a lot.
The game's mechanics only give you 2 actions: move left or right, or flip the gravity. You never actually jump. Instead, your character suddenly flips upside down and flies all the way in the opposite direction until they hit a wall or an obstacle. The mechanics give the game its difficulty, as there are many places where you have to move quickly. For instance, certain platforms dissolve when touched, and it’s awkward to flip gravity many times in a row while trying to get somewhere.
Exploration is part of the game as you get around the space you are in, though the game fills in a map as you go along. Almost all of the map is entirely open from the beginning and you simply need to make your way through. No objects block your progress to finish the game, though there are collectible items which unlock a specific place once all of them are retrieved from around the map.
Further, the game has fast travel thankfully, as you find teleporters and can use them to get around to any other teleporter you have encountered so far. That is very helpful, especially when you are searching for the collectibles.
The story is that you are searching for teammates from your space ship after some teleportation happens and everyone is scattered around. Each member is almost in a “dungeon” on the map, because each area usually adds in a new mechanic to the gameplay. While your actions of moving and flipping gravity do not change, the areas do things like add temporary wrap-around screens or lines that immediately flip the gravity once you hit them.
Simply put, VVVVVV is an original platformer that is quite difficult to get the hang of, but if you are pretty good with platforming, you can very likely finish the game in a few hours. It is nothing like Super Meat Boy or “I Wanna Be the Guy” in terms of style or difficulty. I highly recommend.
