My mom grew up in a setting like this.
I bought it instantly when I saw it, thinking the game would make a good gift for her. Sadly, I left feeling disappointed overall for several reasons.
The setting was what drew me to the game, but it was also the biggest disappointment. The American South has a lot of unique cultural attributes, very few of which are in the game. There's no kudzu on the trees, the dirt is a generic brown instead of southern red clay, and the whole map lacks a sense of verticality that I associate with the south. The map draws you inside of its history, and it makes you feel boxed in, but things are subtly "off" enough that I can't get really immersed.
The interior environment also has some missed potential. There are mentions of oj, milk, beer, and mushroom soup, but nothing of actual southern food. A mention of grits, iced tea, chicken-fried-steak or something else could really help contextualize the setting as being distinctly southern. There's no mention of religion or the type of work the father does, which could have given him some needed personality. Lastly, the examinable book in the father's room is The Middle Parts of Fortune, which seems like an odd choice. It's a book about WW1 by an Australian author, does it have a special relevance to the author or setting? If not, Twain or something would have been a better fit.
Finally, a few things stood out as strange to me. The family lives in a two bedroom trailer designed for mobility, but there are two bathtubs inside, which is rare. There aren't many clothes in the closets. The rooms feel unusually barren, especially without the trash. I'm also a bit confused on when exactly the game happens. The protagonist mentions Princess Leia, and there are VHS tapes in the living room, which makes me think it's set in the 80's or very early 90's. However, the protagonist owns a computer, which is uncommon for that time, especially for such a poor family. Speaking of the computer, it's a bit out of character to leave computer parts strewn around the floor where they could get dirty or stepped on. It's one of her few means of escape, so she would logically want to take good care of it. Lastly, there are three identical gardening books stacked on the same shelf, and other repeated assets that don't really make sense in context.
A lot of my complaints here may be petty, and may be limited by the development time or the engine or something, but I think it's important to go into detail about what didn't work. This is a game about childhood, so people will be looking for things that trigger nostalgic memories. This is a walking simulator, so players will be pondering about the deeper significance of what's going on. In both cases, attention to detail is paramount, and it's where Home is Where One Starts lost me.
Having said all that, I still think positively about Home is Where One Starts. There's a beautiful idea for a game here, and a little more polish would have helped it really stand out. Currently, there are free games on gamejolt that are of a similar caliber to this one, but I don't mean that as an insult. Was I disappointed? Yes. Does that make it a bad game? Not necessarily. David Wehle exposed some of his humanity on this project, and I respect that a lot.
I look forward to your next game.

Victor Vran is a isometric role-playing hack and slash is a great game and one I would recommend but it's worth mentioning some of its faults.
This is poor loot game that makes Diablo 3 pre loot 2.0 look good. It has poor itemisation and not much variety in the range of weapons you get. Ignoring loot, character customisation is lacking featuring no character classes or no stat location. The game has a COD system levelling system where customisation is peace mealed level by level to you and you won't find your character’s potential realised until around 30 level (at the end of your first play though). There is no armour customisation besides clothing that you get providing different modifiers to Victor.
Victor Vran's strength lies in it's fantastic combat system. It's so good you can literally overlook its bad loot and character progression system. One thing I will say about the combat it got really annoying killing skeletons (especially with difficulty modifiers enabled) as you have to kill them twice as they reanimate. There is a jump and rolling mechanic that is rare to see in this genre and rolling is effective in closing the gap or moving out of harms way.
Voice acting and music where decent enough and Doug Cockle that voices Geralt from the Witcher series voices Victor Vran himself.
4 out of 5.

Home is where One Starts is a short memoir of a young girl who missed her school bus one morning. Developed by David Wehle, I bought this game for the low price and the high rating that it had, I had a feeling that I wasn’t going to be disappointed, and I was right to feel that way.
Home is where One Starts begins when a young girl misses her school bus one morning and decides to roam around the trailer where she and her father live, and the beautiful nature that surrounds it, while she recounts how she felt that morning, and many other of the days she spent there. The game is a soft and straightforward story of exploration and discovery, but the narration that you unlock as you walk around tells you of a dark past of a scared, lonely girl, and her alcoholic father.
In terms of the main character, not much can be said. Details are kept so minimal that she could be absolutely any girl, but it is her feelings and wishes that are made clear to the player, us. As the morning goes by, the early sun shinning through the trees, you walk around finding lost toys and forgotten things, sometimes throw away on purpose, amongst the trash that is scattered around her trailer.
The game takes about 20 to 30 minutes to finish, and there are a few alternative endings depending on the things you were able to find, on the aspects of her story she ends up telling you about, and the direction that you decide to take when everything comes together and it ends.
All in all, Home is where One Stars is simply what the title tells you, a story of self reflection and perhaps self discovery. It is a short but satisfying story, with beautiful music and amazing graphics I originally wasn’t entirely expecting. For a mere 3.29$ on steam, I would say that it would be completely ridiculous for you not to go buy this gorgeous and touching game, and play it in one sitting.
Small con: The game has no save button, but considering how short it is, it is very easy to finish in one sitting.
Big pro: Gorgeous graphics.

I bought the game at launch, or a couple days after, here's my take
WHEEL USER'S REVIEW (Sim racer's point of view)
The Crew does many things well:
-Endless driving across the US
-Decent feel through a T500RS (with the extraconfig.xml file you can find through ISR or Racedepartment)
-Lenghty game overall
-Though dated, looks nice
-CarPG
-Discoverables
-Useable physics for low level cars (preferrably street or dirt specs primarily)
However there's major things that this game does NOT do well:
-Lateral grip loss (bad for drifting, though drifting isn't impossible)
-HIgher level cars get more and more unrealistic, to the point where wheel users won't enjoy
-Cops are....well, they don't matter, until they unrealistically and impossibly DO matter out of nowhere
-The umpteen amounts of over-the-top "LOOK AT ME I AM STREET RACORZ" bling bling
-Cut-scenes for every single action
-New muffler part;  BRAKING BONUS!!!
-Users without Calling All Units have major issues with constant annoyance to buy DLC, as well as friend disappearing when cops give chase, or simply alert that you have a slight bounty against them
-Occasional drop-out of co-op missions
-Honestly lame sound overall
It's a game I recommend to wheel users but ONLY if you're ok with using only half the content.  For wheel users specifically, once you get cars to a high enough level, or start using the higher specs of tuning, it becomes more and more arcade and unuseable for wheels.  It's not completely useless, but it definitely makes it more bland the more you progress.  The game's FFB (even with extraconfig.xml) strength is determined by vehicle weight, so the lighter the vehicle, the less FFB there is entirely.  Trucks and heavier vehicles naturally have more strength in the wheel overall.
The FFB on the GOOD side, is pretty decent.  There's communication going on, and opposite lock (catching slides or drifting) is, in fact, there.  It's redeeming in itself, for a CARPG.
On the BAD side, well, I've already mentioned the weight, but on Dirt, those forces nearly double overall.  It's rough on Dirt.  Some might complain due to lack of consistency, some might like it actually.  I kind of like it.
The physics are....arcade, with a slight touch of realism.  At the lower levels, cars feel mostly natural.  On the higher levels, they float with total disregard for gravity and grip limits (HANDLING BONUS!!!).  Breaks are way too strong and acceleration is too fast.  The tires spin wildly, trying to impress somebody, yet nothing is happening on the driver's point of view.  Just generic wheel spin.  Still, there's a level of conservation needed to keep yourself from dying.  Snow is more fun to me.  I spent the entire game making sure I got as little HANDLING BONUS!!! BRAKING BONUS!!!....bonus's as possible.
The sound is pretty lame.  Cars sound...well decently accurate, at least some.  They aren't terrible, but there's nothing to write home about.  Car engines are quiet overall, there's major leveling issues across the board and I don't play with music either.  Overall, it gets the job done, but don't expect to be wow'ed.  Some cars (namely Nissan Skyline R34) have pitch attenuation issues.
Online portion is a dream come true....except for the fact that it's not.  Co-op is an awesome edition and cruising endlessly with friends is TRULY the meat of the game.  However, co-op doesn't mean anything, especially when you convince a friend to buy it so you can play together.  You already have all these tuned up cars that decimate the low level missions while your friend is feeling inadequate.  People disappear every time a cop chase is initiated, or you're alerted that cops are watching for you (or a friend).  Just left with a jittery name tag floating around.  It's annoying.  It works, it's not impressive, the concept is great, implemented rather poorly (but not so bad it's unplayable).  PVP matches are unbalanced, and for a wheel user, is not worth it honestly.  Once you max out your car's level through miscellaneous challenges, it becomes an arcadey mess, completely focused on top speed.
Graphics are pretty nice.  There's nothing super amazing or perfect.  I'm running tripple screens and, though it doesn't support all the bells and whistles of simulators, it does have an FOV slider that works well.  I can't complain overall.  Looks pretty good, plays nice with peripherals it seems.
Input device support:  I'm running a T500RS with a Basher boards FL2 adapter to run a G27 shifter on a seperate USB.  Works fine.  Took a minute to set it up.  Seems to be fine.  Like I said, I'm running tripples and it adds to the game greatly.  Though it won't quite run maxed with this setup smoothly.  980 4gb i5 3570 with 8GB RAM.
Story:  I don't care.  I never will care.  You can't make me.  I've already gone through the NFS underground and beyond stories and I just plain don't care at all.  Well told I suppose, but flashy and stupid all the same.
I recommend this game only because, as a wheel user with tripples and stuff, at the lower levels, this game is a great experience.  Endless driving exploration, co-op, driving with friends, just plain screwing around, drifting in Montana, some customization (though slightly limited in a way).  Stock, Street, Dirt, Raid and somewhat, Performance specs are fun to play with.  Beyond that wheel users won't have much fun with the floaty "super handling/braking" crap of the lighter cars.  It's fun having a 400hp Fiat 500, blasting away at RUF's and Zonda's like it's nothing.  The extraconfig.xml is absolutely necessary for good FFB overall.  It's hard to recommend otherwise, as there's obvious issues with the overall package, but still, it IS fun.
This is all outside the "review" of DLC and other things, which is complete BS overall.  I won't get into details, but DLC ruins some of the experience, unless you have money to throw away and get it all (then you won't have the game constantly pushing you to buy more things, as well as the online portion having less issues as a result).
7/10:  Great concept, good open world exploration, bad end game, 50-50 for wheel users (dependant on vehicle class and level), horrible over-the-top-trying-to-impress-you fan service.

As far as I'm aware, some people really dislike this title, comparing it to the other, "better" DkS1 or DkS3, and I do understand why they feel like that.
However, I personally see DkS2 (especially with SotfS) as my favourite piece from the series.
+The story holds up pretty well, like in every Souls. You get to learn a lot from environment and item descriptions, there's no much more to say here, really
+Graphics are IMO great in SotfS. Maybe one or two weirdly looking textures here and then, but overall I love them and actually prefer them to the grays and blacks of DkS3, no matter how good and realistic they are. There are so many colors in here, the lightning is good, too.
+The locations are very diverse, almost every single one of them stands out in some way.
+The way PvP and PvE is handled in this game is great - although PvE is slightly inferior to PvP. Covenants, invasions, co-op, netcode (welp..not everytime, but mostly) work really well in here, superior to both other titles from the franchise. I also enjoy the more "tactical" movement over Bloodborne-ish haste and removal of traditional shields that happened in DkS3, though that's more subjective
+The amount of different armor, weapons and their types, miracles, pyromacies is ridiculously big, which is really good if you like diversity in your looks or build, also because there IMHO better upgrade paths here that let you customise your arsenal a bit better
+Playerbase seems reasonably active, despite the age of the game
+DLC content is worth it's price, if you get the best edition; I'd personally avoid buying standalone DkS2 and then the Season Pass
+As usual, sound and music is top notch here
And now, for some cons
-I dislike the soul memory mechanic, regardless of me being able to affect it or not.
-Some people might be annoyed with how inconsistent is the terrain sometimes (ex. elevators leading you from ground level UP to an underground looking, hell-aesthetic place)
-Not a fan of many minion-based bosses, but not many see it as much of a hassle anyway
There are probably more negative parts people could point out/I forgot about, although If you want to hear my opinion, I'd reccomend to check out SotfS regardless, even if you're just being introduced to the series.

Almost 30 hours in and i'm sick of it which is sad because i played 300 hours of DD1/DDE so i had high expectations for DD2 to be similarly addivctive, but it isn't.
Below are the things i don't like if the devs want some player feedback:
- The towers were nerfed to oblivion (compared with DD1), they're near usless now which means this isn't so much a strategy type tower defense game as it is a hack and slash fest. Also you're limited to 4 towers per class now, in total!
- Because the towers are so weak now you're forced to playing with others along with all the crap that goes along with it (ie noobs with no idea what they're doing), i guess this is intended to save server badwidth?
- The eqipment upgrade system was nerfed and is terrible now, don't waste your time bothering to use it because the benefits are mediocre.
- Speaking of equipment/loot you're better off not even bothering picking up any loot because it's all terrible, and with 3 bags and a temp bag to search through after every level it's just not worth the hassle. In DD1 i used to look forward to collecting some nice loot and customizing it, such a shame.
- Finishing levels doesn't unlock more levels now, instead you're expected to grind and grind and grind the same few levels over and over again to unlock a new "tier" so you can continue to grind the same levels over and over again, which gets very boring very fast.
- They still use playverse and stupid shared taverns etc, no offline games or lan games. So every time you try and do anything you get "searching for session". You can create private taverns after joining the shared tavern, but it's just tiresome and not nessessary. Actually to quit the game it's easier and vastly quicker to do a ctrl0alt-del end task than  the game mechanics of: lclick eave game, wait 30 seconds for timer, wait for "Searching for session", wait for loading private tavern, click leave game, wait for loading of shared tavern, click leave game, wait for loading of title screen, click leave game (this time you actually get to leave the game).
- The difficulty is sometimes easy and sometimes idiotic, it's jsut so random, sometimes you can solo a level and others on that same level on the same difficulty with the same towers/players the AI will just spam 40 dinosaurs/magic carpets down one lane and even full groups will have absolutely no hope of stopping them. What's up with this?
- Coins/money, not sure what to do with these exactly, all the shops sell the same useless loot that drops in the levels.
It's just terrible compared with the original ones in my opinion, very dissapointing.
Below are things i did like:
- Very smooth and stable for an alpha.
- The few maps (10?) that there were all seemed good.
- Didn't crash on me once.

Well, where to start with this game. I heard from a few friends that this game was good and an experience, well it's an experience alright but not a good one. I've never been told by a game before that the game may crash a lot whilst I'm playing it, this game is a first.
The game uses the worst game engine, Unreal Engine, as well as some annoying game design which leads you getting stuck on railings and banisters which is unbelievably annoying when you're being chased by mentalists, which is about 90% of the game, obviously.
It's also got some of the worst game mechanics, not exclusive to this game, regenerating health and batteries to power your camera. I'll never understand why these ideas are/were considered good, but they've been in far too many games. Just like the Unreal Engine.
What's good about this game?
Well the camera view is pretty well done, all the info on the screen, HD, zoom level, battery life etc.
The night vision also works pretty well, if it didn't chew through batteries like a fat man through candy.
I like going into a horror game without any real knowledge of what the game is about and the game explains the premise of the game fairly well at the start so that was also one of the good points of the game, that's where the good points of the game end.
Story is pretty rubbish and most of the story is hidden on logs and folders, which means you have to hunt for them to find the story. Nothing really new, old semi-abandoned asylum. People run at you, you close the door and hide in a locker, you watch the enemy walk past you and then they open the locker next to you. Every. Single. Time.
The game has a single jump scare at the beginning of the game, about the first five minutes of the game, then the game falls flat after that, the usual boring stuff, things from 2004, burst steam pipes, a body falling out of a vent, things that Doom 3 did. TEN YEARS AGO.
Overall, I really wouldn't recommend it, I suppose if you can get it for £5 or the equivalent when it’s on sale. I just wouldn’t bother  paying any higher than that.

There are 2 reasons I can't recommend this game.
The first is the horrrible game balance issues.  Enemies do not respawn in this game which means there is limited gold/xp in the world.  This means if you do not build your character correctly it is possible to get stuck in the game as you have no ways to improve your character to take on certain fights.  Also health and mana regen extremely slowly so if you are using melee or magic you end up just standing around waiting until you are ready to take on the next fight.  An increased regen out of combat could have fixed this.  Other than these issues from a gameplay perspective the game is reasonable.  The interesting part of the game that the game sells itself on is the ability to turn into a dragon yet you only gain this abillity half way through the game.
Secondly there are technical issues running this on newer versions of windown (definintely windows 10, possibly 7 and 8).  If using win10 the game will lock up after 2 world transitions.  This makes it very painful to play as you need to contantly save before every door.  I was able to fix this by using a 3rd party program to hack the executable to use 4gm ram however this also resulted in the game not running from the launcher and had to be run directly which resulted in the game not working with steam ui or logging time.  I also discovered that during the install process the game installs an old version of PhysX regardless of whether you have a current version.  This then causes games such as Mass Effect 2 and 3 to crash on start until you uninstall the old version that Divinity 2 installs.

Let me preface this first: it was $3. Pretty much regardless of length or content, it's hard to knock a game at $3. That said, for any price, this was a disappointing experience.
I'm in the camp of enjoying so-called "walking simulators". I loved Gone Home for the story it told, and all the neat pieces to uncover. I enjoyed The Stanley Parable for it's humor and bits to uncover. Both were short, lightly-interactive experiences. Unfortunately, HIWOS doesn't capture much of the magic those had, and instead comes off as a cheap knock-off. Like the developer enjoyed those games, and set to create one of his own, but didn't really understand what made them good.
First, the story. The whole crux is that you're a young girl who lives in a trailer with her dad (and maybe mom, there's some ambiguity on that part). And several items, and bits of dialogue, hint at a less-than-desirable situation for the main character. The problem is, the game was *so* short (~40 minutes to play through at a slow pace) and the amount of content *so* little that you barely have time or methods to feel for the situation before it's all over. So you never really connect with the story at hand.
Speaking of, there's a pitiful amoung of content to interact with. Some ~20 items total you can pick up (which just lets you spin their models around), and maybe a dozen spots that trigger dialogue. Simply put, there's no content to look at, touch, hear, explore to help pull in the player.
And despite the lack of content in the game, they opted for a larger map than something like Gone Home. Instead of cramming the trailer with items to look at and build the story, they places items miles apart, with nothing but a slow saunter to move between them. Of the forty minutes in my first play-through, half of it was spent holding the W key and waiting to get somewhere notable. A snail's pace works in a small area with lots to explore. It doesn't here.
And lastly, just as you hit the *first* moment where you feel like something is happening, you're given speed and freedom. Finally. And seconds later the game is over. Also, ending the game simply quits to desktop and there's no saving. Minor points, but strange nonetheless.
The loop back around, again, it's $3. For an hour of your time. That's hard to really be upset about. But time and price be damned, it was simply not enjoyable. It feels like the exact type of "walking simulator" that lends creedence to the criticisms of actually-good games, like Gone Home or Stanley Parable.
If you're dying for such a game, and MUST spend your $3, then fine. But there's a list of similar titles that, even at a higher price, are much, much better stories and experiences than this. You're best off passing. It's simply not good.

Free-roaming is no novelty - games like Grand Theft Auto and Driver have been doing this for almost two decades, and titles like Need For Speed Underground 2, Shutokou Battle and Burnout Paradise, among others, have tried to apply such gameplay concept to racing games, with mixed results - but free-roaming through an entire country (or at least a scaled-down version thereof) is a whole new idea. And The Crew manages to offer just that - storming through highways on a fast car, looking for new events and maybe some interesting sights. The important question (which shall be answered in this review) is: does it really work?
Superficially, The Crew offers some really impressive content: a giant map for the player to explore to one's heart's content, a could-have-been-better-but-not-bad car list, plenty of tuning options (not as complete as what was offered by Need For Speed Underground some fourteen years ago, though), variable weather and time of the day; those things can easily elicit the player's attention (and, as a matter of fact, they really got my attention for a first moment) and may be really satisfying if expectations are kept somewhat low of if the player just wants some casual driving fun. Because, once the initial appeal is gone and after putting some hours delving into the game, some players may notice that The Crew offers *just* that - a game that is best played as a casual experience, even though it tries hard to take itself seriously.
Driving through the streets, avenues and highways of the USA, perhaps the most appealing part of the game, becomes boring too quickly; the game map is astonishingly huge, and yet it is underused, making speeding through a sparsely populated road just as fun as a prolonged family trip. Car handling just does not feel right; cars feel weightless, the brakes work a little too well to be realistic (even in accordance to a "simcade" game's standards), and any sharper turn, however subtle, puts your car in a powerslide. It reminds me a little bit of the Playstation's port of San Francisco Rush, with some elements borrowed from Sega's Outrun 2 (a game which is sadly missing on Steam). There are also some bugs (my car became completely unresponsive for no apparent reason once, and sometimes the game just refuses itself to launch, even though my computer exceeds the minimum requirements), though I believe Ubisoft may be ironing out the most serious offenders. The events scattered though the map are also nothing to write home about and may get old pretty quick, and the dialogues and cutscenes are kinda forgettable (the Japanese voiceovers, however, are excellent). The always-online requirement is really irritating and sometimes can ruin the experience (just try to imagine yourself riding through a laggy and unstable virtual road).
The Crew has a brighter side, however. Graphics are gorgeous, the cars are nicely modeled, speacial effects are top-notch and the landscapes and cities are believable (even though they're a bit underpopulated and somewhat lifeless and bland). Sound is also really good, with realistic-sounding engines, tires screeching and crashes. And I really encourage the players to stop by a residential area and watch the virtual denizens chat for a while; it really adds a little bit of life to the game (and I also encourage you to change the audio language to Japanese).
Does The Crew satisfy the premise of bringing a whole virtual country for virtual drivers to race around and be a bit more useful than a bunch of joyriders? Well... no. The abovementioned flaws may be off-putting for players looking for a more serious challenge and rewarding gameplay, and the lag issues and questionable car control can even anger consumers looking for an arcade-y game to kill some time which would be best spent on other activities. However, The Crew is a game which rewards patience and persistence (I mean, A LOT of patience and persistence), even if such reward isn't that great.
It is an interesting game, in the end. But it could have been more, it could have been much more. - 6,5/10

Quick Summary: Dark Souls 2 Scholar of the First Sin is an “upgraded” version of Dark Souls 2, including not only the 3 DLCs but also making very noticeable changes to some of the game’s original areas. This game is long, it’s difficult, and it’s rewarding if you can make your way through to the end. Honestly though, this is one of those games that’s more fun on replay than it is to play for the first time.
This version of the game is 64-bit (Direct X 11), but it looks the same to me and runs at the same frame rate on my 6 year old PC. The changes from regular Dark Souls 2 are not only cosmetic, the enemies and item locations are also changed significantly. Certain areas in the game are now far more difficult than they were in the regular version. For example you’ll find increased concentrations of enemies in some areas, and some bosses from the early parts of the game reappear on your path later on. Additionally, a couple of entire areas are now “blocked off” unless you spend rare resources to unlock them. You could say this makes things easier because you no longer “have to” complete those areas, but you also miss the loot you could be collecting. On the plus side, a couple of areas from the regular Dark Souls 2 are tremendously easier in SotFS (for example: Dragon Shrine).
Like the regular version of Dark Souls 2, SotFS doesn’t really give you too much story from just playing the game (except for an awesome opening cinematic). You can feel that the game is based on an amazing lore/story, but if want to dive into it you have to do some research elsewhere.  There is very little narration, and the instructions you receive from NPCs are quite vague (and may have nothing to do with your objectives). You play a person cursed to slowly become a mindless undead “hollow.” Your primary goal is to explore the fallen kingdom of Drangleic and find the King, who may have the answers you need. Spoiler alert: he doesn’t have any answers for you. Along the way you will do battle with other hollows, giant beasts, and various demonic bosses. Make your long way to the throne and challenge the true monarch of the realm, as well as Aldia, the Scholar of the First Sin.
The game is played in Third Person Perspective, viewed from behind kind of like the Batman Arkham games, Saints Row, or Darksiders series. The majority of the game’s action is hack and slash melee combat, with a very strong emphasis on dodging/blocking. I know what you’re thinking, of course you try to avoid damage, but in this game you need to become proficient at avoiding enemy hits MOST OF THE TIME. Healing is limited, and not something you can consistently rely on. This means that blocking with a shield and learning to time your dodge rolls will be the most important skills you can learn as a new player. If you’re used to other RPGs like Diablo, Torchlight, Darksiders, or Dead Rising you will need to change your gameplay mentality because practically every enemy in Dark Souls 2 from the beginning of the game to the very end can kill you in about 5 seconds. As other people have said, the game is hard but (mostly) fair. When you die it will be because you made a mistake (dodged too late, tried to fight 2 guys at once, or fell off a ledge).
The money of the game is the same as the experience points: souls. Every time you defeat an enemy you get rewarded with souls that you can spend buying items or leveling up your character stats. The cost of leveling up rises every time you “buy” a stat point, so by the end of the game most of the shop items will look cheap compared to the cost of leveling up even 1 stat point.  This need to hoard souls is challenged by the fact that every time you die in the game, you drop all the souls you are currently holding. You have a chance to fight your way back to where you died and try to retrieve the souls, but if you die again before picking them up, the souls you dropped vanish forever.  You’re going to lose a lot of souls throughout your adventure, mostly through stupid choices like trying to run past enemies to retrieve your dropped souls, then getting swarmed.
Dark Souls 2 has an unusual co-op system where players can leave glowing signs on the ground that can be seen in other players’ games if they’re in the same area and near your “soul memory” (how many souls you’ve ever gathered, including the ones you’ve lost or spent). You can use these signs to summon the sign leaver into your game as a phantom, usually to help with a boss. Or if you’re a hardcore single player kind of person, you can just ignore the signs and do everything yourself. You’ll still need to deal with invaders though. Invasions are when other players (or powerful computer controlled characters) enter your game for some player vs player combat. If you’ve played regular Dark Souls 2 you’ll notice that Scholar of the First Sin has a great deal more invaders (both human and computer controlled). And since SotFS has a larger player base, there will be more people for you to cooperate with as well. Sadly, a person with regular Dark Souls 2 cannot cooperate with someone playing SotFS.
You should play Scholar of the First Sin if:
+You liked other Dark Souls games you’ve played. Maybe you played regular Dark Souls 2 and thought “I wish the game was harder.” Or you want to play the 3 DLCs, which are included in SotFS.
+You are looking for a long game to play. If this is the first time you’re playing Dark Souls 2, you can expect to spend at least 70 hours trying to finish the campaign (if you attempt the DLCs). If you’ve played before, it will still take 50+ hours. The DLCs: Crown of the Sunken King, Crown of the Old Iron King, and Crown of the Ivory King are quite long and extremely difficult, adding convoluted areas, more enemy types, and some unique loot for you to scavenge.
+You are looking for a serious challenge. Every enemy encounter could mean a quick death for you, and the giant bosses will smack you around like they’re the hero and you’re goomba #2.
You should NOT play Scholar of the First sin if:
-You are just looking for a casual game. Dark Souls is brutal both in difficulty and in the time investment. When I played the original Dark Souls 2, I quit playing after a few hours and came back years later determined to see it through.  I played through a second time immediately after, knowing what parts I could run past and what parts I should take slowly.
-You’re looking for a game where you can grind for experience to make your play easier. For example when you’re playing Diablo or Torchlight and you’re having a tough time, you can level up a little and try again with a higher level. In Dark Souls 2 it’s almost always a better idea to just get through to the next area. The solution to your problems is not coming back with more life, it’s learning to avoid getting hit. Your character’ power increases very slowly throughout the game. Every level-up makes an almost unnoticeable improvement to your character.
Overall, if you’re looking for a game that you’ll feel proud of beating, Scholar of the First Sin is quite a thrill ride. Just remember that your goal is not to become “strong” enough to trade hits with your enemies, it’s to become “good” enough at avoiding damage that you can kill or get past them. The game also offers New Game + options (restart the game at higher difficulty with all your gear) for people who really want to punish themselves.

So this is a short game. A VERY short game, but It is worth the money. It is calming, and relaxing. I play games to get away from the stresses of the real world for a little while. But then there are times when I don't want to play games because there are stresses in Games I don't want to deal with, be it boss fights or grinding frustrations or just simply that I don't feel like getting shot at or dying. This is the game to get away from the Real world and Video games. There is absolutely no negative consequences to this game. You can't fall off the world or die in any way. You fall down, you get back up. The puzzles are easy, and the game is very simple. There is no instructions on how to play or what keys you need, becuase you don't need them. Its intuitive. One thing worth noting is the difficulty of the campaigns. The AI are smart and aggresive. It features a hot-seat gametype which can be tedious if you don't like waiting for your slow friend, though the AI in Custom Game will be a worthy, oppenent in an actual player's stead. Let me get a couple things out of the way. First, I don't consider this to be a "bad" game in spite of the glaring red mark, but I can't really see myself recommending it to anyone either. Second there are some pretty terrible graphics issues right out of the gate, and if you do decide to pick it up I strongly encourage you to check out the pcgaming wiki page for it, as well as updating all relevant software. I admit that I haven't finished the game at this point, but I've also lost any interest in continuing.
The combat in Divinity 2 is pretty comparable to something like World of Warcraft, you get a skillbar and a number of passive(dull minor % buffs) and active skills. The skills you can learn are limited by only your character level, which is pretty cool as it allows you to be open and creative with how you build your character, avoid the various crap skills, etc. When actually putting them into practice though, I found that it was the usual tedious rinse repeat of skill rotations, and for the most part enemies were easily avoided, especially early on. After a few hours in the game you'll run into quite a large number of enemies whose attacks cannot be avoided though: spell casters with instant hit point blasts, archers whose normal attacks can usually be avoided but whose special skills curve through the air magically tracking you. In fact a couple of the more annoying boss battles I experienced were against archers who had an undodgable stun (something like four seconds!), that they followed up with an explosive shot and various other attacks. The first of these encounters I had to cheese by exploiting line of sight, the second one I eventually realized could be blinded, and I wound up reloading until I got a successful blind before being stunned and gibbed. Ugh, and enemy healers, just annoying. Or maybe I'm just a bit jealous because when I got out of tougher fights in the earlier portions of the game I had to prance about looking for something else to do while waiting for my Hitpoints and Mana to ever so slowly crawl back up. Thankfully they seem to recover when you're in dialogs and inventory screens.
The autosave function is a joke. In my playthrough I could count on it triggering maybe once every 3 hours. It's a bit painful to discover that after coming from more modern titles, but then the quicksave instinct quickly returns...and allows for any imaginable amount of save scumming you are comfortable with. Spend XP to mindread someone then reload? Sure, why not? I actually made an effort not to do this, but it still feels like a design oversight.
Ah, but you do get to turn into a dragon...after several hours carving through the first few areas of the game. It is great at first...buuuut it got old pretty quick for me. Dragon gameplay is completely segregated from human gameplay, which admittedly is kinda necessary to keep the human side relevant without putting in something like a "dragon gauge" or whatever. Still, it's kinda silly to not even be able to see enemies on the ground while you're in dragon mode. In one instance I was flying around inside a giant cavern disabling barriers to get at a necromancer, when I dropped the last one I was expecting to be able deliver a big ol' dragon ♥♥♥♥♥smack, but no one was there. I transform to human and land and the necromancer is there ready to take me on. Great. Transform back into dragon, he runs off and disappears into the aether. Very disappointing. At first playing as the dragon felt empowering and kind of awesome, but then it quickly felt very easy and also inconsequential, because nothing I did as a dragon was going to make my human life much better.
The writing kinda reminds me of various bioware games as far as the overall plot goes, but without much of the binary  meter driven morality. Most of the dialog options didn't seem to matter all that much though, and seemed to amount to a binary I am or am not being an ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ here. NPCs are eh, believable if not charming, fully voiced except for the main character which is impressive. Their animations seem pretty spastic at times for my taste, but it's pretty good still. No NPC party members outside of some short quest related instances, at least for the duration of my playthrough. I feel like that would've made a large difference in my impression of the game too, so more's the pity.
The game holds up fairly well visually and has some amusing if simple puzzles, and clever tricks here and there. There is definitely some respectable take away if you can stand the lackluster combat and mechanics, being trapped in a room after quicksaving, etc.

I'm going to be honest up-front: I only had the willpower to play the first half of Tyler. Going by the Steam achievement stats, less than a fifth of players who start Tyler even get that far. Besides, the game's issues are in its core design, so I can't imagine it takes a turn in the back half that could redeem it.
Tyler's central puzzle design might be familiar to you from popular mobile games like Flow Free. You've got a grid with color-coded pairs of nodes, and your goal is to connect each pair of nodes, ensuring that each square in the grid contains a node or part of a line.
So far so good. That might be a little thin, so Tyler dumps a bunch of extra
on top, extraneous mechanics that don't directly interact with the core puzzle design. The problem is that none of the stuff makes the puzzles more interesting or is worthwhile in its own right, it only makes the game irritating to play.
The first stuff: when you create a path between nodes, those cells rise from the ground. A completed level forms a staircase to a key that takes you to the next level. This is because of...
The second stuff: every few seconds, bombs will drop onto the level. If it explodes before you run over and whack it, it will destroy any adjacent paths you've made and potentially disrupting your staircase climb to the end of the level. This is nonsense. This is nothing but busy work, constantly interrupting your path-making to run across the stage and whack bombs. It's not a puzzle element, it's not engaging arcade gameplay, it's not even difficult, it's just an annoying interruption. But before you even start making paths, you need to deal with...
The third stuff: at the start of each level, obstacles are scattered over the grid. Before you can make paths through those squares, you need to remove them with weapons. This could have been an interesting puzzle element, perhaps with a resource management component: find the path that allows you to collect all the ammo necessary to remove all the obstacles. But you don't have ammo, and the weapon you need is always available. All you do is walk up to each obstacle in turn, select the correct weapon for that type of obstacle (machine gun for rocks, flamethrower for ice, etc) and hold down the fire button for a couple seconds. Again, it's pointless busy work.
There's a bit more stuff, like levels where some cells are inaccessible until you pull a lever, and gadgets that can help with the various inconveniences but run on a cooldown, but that's the bulk of the game. Playing Tyler is like playing a simple game on your smartphone while the most persistent mosquito on the planet lands somewhere on your body every few seconds.

First thing I have to say before I write this review is : NO, it's not that annoying as everybody says about DLC's. It's not true, it never bothered me while playing the game.

That what best describe my feeling about Banished. It's an excellent game, but it falls short of it's own potential and just leaves you wondering "why?". It came so close to be the perfect replacement for Dwarf Fortress. It should've been the chosen one.
Basically, what you get is a pretty well done and beautiful "medieval" city builder. You'll find yourself looking at your growing hamlet with pride, I guarantee. It's just beautiful. Mechanically wise, there's a reasonable amount of options available to build a self-sustained colony with your personal touch; plenty of planning too. You can manage your resources and labor efficiently with well designed interfaces. Banished isn't forgiving, even on medium difficulties. Your first settlements probably won't last long, but it's part of the fun.
However, it could be ten times what it is now. It's so damn close to striking a balance between the overly complex and totally ugly Dwarf Fortress and the more shallow but beautiful city builders, I feel almost angry thinking about it. Firstly, it's near perfectly polished, meaning the small issues will be a rock in your boot. For example, why can't stockpiles be dedicated to certain products to maximize production ? Why can't I manage citizens do's/don't's ? Why can't barns or stockpile be divided in absolute values ?
Secondly, higher tiers are lacking. The first ten hours more ore less sum up a the game. It only gets bigger from there. I would've loved a or second tier building (castles, manors, workshop's) growing classes with different needs or second tier resources (gems, precious metals, art and crafts) leading to new levels of productions. Why isn't this in there ?
As it stands, the game feel like an extremely well made but unfinished product. While I recommend it, it infuriating how close it was to being legendary.

I've played numeros ARPG's over the years... I started with Diablo 2, then played Diablo 3, Path of Exile, Torchlight II, and other games that are similar but somewhat different (magicks 1/2). I think Victor Vran is an amazing ARPG. The combat is extremely fluid and rich, reminding me of diablo 3. Where i felt Torchlight II was somewhat lackluster in combat and i got the feeling that i was just dps-kite and wait for mana-dps-kite and wait for mana, etc. I feel that Victor Vran completely eliminates that feeling.
Combat: First of all, there is no mana bar in this game, at least traditionally. There is a yellow meter called the overdrive meter, which can be charged in various ways depending on your characters outfit (read: class), which can be changed throughout the game. The changing of the outfit throughout the game was nice because it made it so you didn't need to commit to anything and that your playstyle can adapt as you get gear better suited to one outfit or another. Anyway, the overdrive meter, as its called, is used to power your demon abilities. Like i said ealier, it can be charged in various ways depending on the outfite, but it is most generally charged by doing damage. This means that in dry periods with few enemies, you likely won't be using abilities, but when you got mobbed by bosses or ads, then the bar will fill up fast and you can start slamming those demon powers. This helps to eliminate one of my torchlight complains about mana.
The other wonderful thing about the combat is just how generally fluid it is. The game is perfectly optimized for a controller, as it isn't cluttered with 9 abilites on an action bar (which i know a lot of people may like as it necessarily provides options and niche abilities). There is also a built in dodge/roll key, as dodging is vital to staying alive. The weapons in this game, which of course define how your character's combat plays out, are nice as the skills tied to each weapon will generally build around itself for a neat playstyle. The tome (free dlc) for instance, produces gems with basic attacks that, when picked up, reset the cooldown to your other abilities. The scythe collects souls of enemies when you auto-attack, and the skills (a daze and whirl) became lengthened depending on how many souls you have when you used the skill. Combining all of these elements to the game creates a very mobile, action packed combat system that really shines.
Customization: In this game, there is not a lot of customization. In fact, there is nothing in this game that can't be undone at a whim, as all of the customizaion is simply what gear you have. That's right, there are no skill trees or speccable stats anywhere. I would normally be upset at this as i really like to build my own characters around a playstyle i want and make something somewhat unique. But, this is not a problem at all. The gear varies pretty typically in the game, but it is obvious that the game was not meant to be one where you make a full mage or rapier specialist. In this game, you play as Victor Vran, who can do everything, which makes it rather nice. As i mentioned earlier, you can switch playstles on a whim if you just pick up a new weapon you really like. If you have a crit build, for instance, and find a really nice hammer, then you can just flip over to a new outfit, throw in some new abilities, and you're suddely a viable hammer user. no strings attached.
With the gear in this game, there are a couple categories, with almost all of them being completely straightforward. The only one that isn't, is the destiny cards. When you level up you have a certain amount of points that can be allocated to your destiny cards. The destiny cards have a class type, such as "Strength" or "The Moon", which offer a special effect "higher crit chance" and "frost explostion on crit" respectively. They also have a point system to them, so the higher point value a card, the more powerful the effect is. There are a lot of different cards that range from more health, to life on kill, to crit chance, buff duration, damage at the cost of life etc. These effectively act as that traditional skill tree, offering all the passive buffs you could want. But, just like the rest of the stuff i've said, they can all be switched out on a whim and a whole new set of cards could be swapped in.
Plot: The plot is relatively conservative, at least at first. Without going into spoilers, you play as Victor Vran, a hunter in the darken times with gargoyles, demons, vampires, skeletons and the likes. You got a message from an old friend, Adrian, calling you out to the city of Zagoravia, which is teeming with demon influence and is a deathtrap to hunters, like yourself. When you arrive you find a few survivors still holding on in a tower keep, which include your merchants and the queen. It is your mission to find out your friend and slay some baddies along the way.
Hexes: Before i finish, i just wanted to mention one thing in this game called a hex. There are five hexes which act as modifiers on the game and can generally be toggled on and off depending on what mode you are playing. (in hard mode the hexes can't be turned off). The modifiers make the game more difficult and will do things such as give enemies regen, or just randomly damage your character, but playing with them on also increases your experience and gold, i think. I just thought this was worth mentioning, since it gives seasoned ARPG veterans an interesting challenge to throw in the mix of the usual affairs.

Very fun game, Victor Vran was a fun, fast action paced arpg.  You have a variety of different weapons to use at will, equiping any two at a time and have the ability to swap between them in combat.  You also have two potion slots, and two (spell?) slots.  Each weapon will have a basic attack and two special attacks.  Then as you build overdrive you can use your spells, which according to how you build your character they can assist you in many different ways.  The next thing you have is destiny cards.  These basically sum up your attributes in a way.  While one might give you 100 crit damage, the other one might give you 5% crit chance.  The slots for destiny cards has to be unlocked and there is a point system on how you can equip them (the higher level destiny cards cost more points.)
So after that, the loot.  You get lots of weapons, destiny cards, and spells but i believe the only three pieces of armor I had gotten were from quests.  There are a lot of similar creatures throughout the whole game.  Skeletons, spiders, essences, vampires, and maybe a couple more.  There were no blood in the game, so it made a better choice to play with my younger son.  Most of your defense will be from dodge-rolling out of the way of danger.
Your weapons damage and stats can be increased by transformation.  Combination of three spells can upgrade the weapons stats, then certain runes will increase the damage.  The story did not take too long to beat and this is another one of those games where you can keep putting the difficulty up, leveling, completing challenges  and dont forget playing coop with others online.
Victor Vran was a fun game for me and I would recommend it if you like hack&slash dungeon crawler type games.

What can we say about this game? For starters I'm glad I'm the only one who enjoys it, and I do in fact enjoy it very much, It has a good blend of difficulty and accomplishment, even though there are no actual objectives in the game. It's a lot like Kingdom for keflings minus the giants.
The pros:
Challenging but, once you have had some experience, generally fair.
Not exactly breath taking, but the visuals are pleasant to look at.
Easy to learn (hard to master)
Can be played for 10 minutes, or 4 hours and still enjoyable
The cons:
Managing health and happiness seems to make little difference and is generally only difficult to fill in the last half of a star/heart
Fires are absurd. You can lose your entire village even though a well is sitting right next to the very first that catches fire.
Could have had more depth involved in the production of goods.
Harvesting queue goes in order of first selected rather than what is closest. So a large patch of trees 10 miles away will be harvested first, rather than a single stone where you want to build a house if you've slecected the trees first. Thankfully you can canel actions.
I find it a little odd how egalitarian the game is considering its set in medieval time. This may sound like just a quirk, but when you consider not only can the women can do dangerous jobs like hunting and quarry work which have a fair chance of accidentaly killing them, coupled with the fact they can die during child birth and are the only ones who can give birth, you start to appreciate why our ancestors generally didn't put them in dangerous jobs. At any rate, females are just as likely to die as males (perhaps slightly more so given that they can die during child birth) and are the only ones who can continue the lineage, so you are left wishing you could micro manage somewhat who did what jobs.
Aside from this I would just like to see more of the game. DLC's and expansions. I have not looked into how much mods are available for this game, however.

This is a AAA game masquerading as a B-Rate film in video game form, and it is
better than I expected.
A lot of users cover the mechanics in their reviews, which are actually pretty ♥♥♥♥ing deep, so I'm going to tell you quickly about the theme and style:
Victor Vran is the video game every B-Movie junkie wishes they knew about.  At first, you will probably think that the cheesy voice acting and awkward plot are just a good dev making a bad mistake.  I did, and I was wrong.  Since  Haemimont Games are responsible for the Tropico franchise, I should have known better.  They obviously set out to make a B-Game, and they ♥♥♥♥ing hit it out of the park.  The more you settle in to this one, the more it'll worm it's way in to your favorites.
The setting is a bit Victorian Gothic, and Vran looks and plays like Diablo combined with Devil May Cry.  The voice acting is a touch wooden, but not over-the-top.  Just enough to fit the tongue-in-cheek vibe of the narrative, and it progressively improves as you start to realize the intent behind this game.  Speaking of narration, the narrator himself is just about my favorite part of the game.  He keeps up running jokes, an interesting dialogue, and (of course) drops some references to just about every leg of gaming/nerd culture that can be comfortably fit in to the game's narrative.  The plot does dip in a place or two, but nothing worth noting.
I can not recommend this game enough to anyone who enjoys ARPGs, Classic Horror, B-Movies or just a well-tuned game that doesn't take itself too seriously.  Now, as far as those game mechanics I mentioned earlier, this is the fastest rundown I can give you:
Several different weapon and ability types, all of which function differently, allowing you to really fine-tune your playstyle.  The game looks great and runs great, and the movement and mechanics are mostly pretty sound.  You might miss a jump here and there, or be bothered by the lack of inversion for camera movement, but it ain't gonna kill you.  Good enemy variety, great music, online co-op (local announced but not implemented), PvP, a Survival Mode, Hardcore Mode, and the constantly changing Cauldron of Chaos that provides a steady stream of new challenges and killer loot.  Transmutation, for those that are familiar with the item mechanic, is pretty solid.  There are also Bounties and Treasure Hunts (shareable between players, ffs!), and there are
, although inventory management can become a pain.
I'm forgetting♥♥♥♥♥♥ and I know it.  I don't care.  Buy the damned game and find out what I missed, because it's ♥♥♥♥ing worth it.

This is the best Dark souls game. The PvP is superb and the story is enjoyable although long and drawn out. However, the game allows you to replay your favorite parts selectively as if you were in NG+ so you don't have to play through the whole game again to get special loot.  The weapons in this game are great in number and many of them are viable in PvP, whereas in other Dark souls games only a few weapons are good. The weapons in this game are very fun to use and have a large diverse moveset.  'Grinding' in this game is fair and you probably won't even feel the need to grind for items. I did though, because I wanted to upgrade practically everything.  The bosses in this game are the best in the souls series. This is especially true for the DLC content, which even on their own would be one of the greatest gaming experiences of all time.  This game has a large cast of enemies and personalities.  The story is quite decent and at the end you will be wondering who the true villain was.  PvP in this game is most active in the Brotherhood of Blood covenant arena, although there is another arena that is considerably less active (with different arena maps) and there is also the option of invading other players. I played this game mostly in 2016 and I doubt there is really anyone left to invade at this point. However, the arenas are active, but you will probably be facing the same opponents over and over again.  The opponents in the arena are good but don't post much of a challenge to me, probably since I found one of the best play styles in the game that they have a hard time countering (dark infused roaring halberd running spin attack, with offhand sanctum crossbow). I win about 80% of the time in the arena. Sometimes the opponent is simply better at dodging and stun locking you.
I recommend this game for both the single player and PvP aspects. Even if PvP were to die out, the game would still be 100% worth it for the single player alone, which even features NPC friendlies that you can summon for boss fights and even some areas in general.

In a word: The Best WW2 simulation game out there... With that said, this game is one of the best strategy games available. It might not have the appeal of some of the other AAA titles like Starcraft but it offers insane amounts of replayability.
In this game you take control of any country in the world from 1936 up until 1948 (or even further using mods, more on that in e sec) and guide it through the events of WW2. You can follow a historical path or you can carve your own path through history.
Fascist USA? Check!
German victory in USSR? Check!
Italian superpower? Check!
You can do what you want. It is that simple.
That said though... It has a HUGE learning curve. Maybe the most difficult Paradox game, and that is saying something. If you are patient this game will reward you like few games can. Trial and Error is this game's moto. Can you take it on? I know I can!

Considering the price, with DLCs included, buying it during steam sales is a recommendation if you are willing to find a history-based strategy game that you can sink plenty of time in!

Well, where to start with this game. I heard from a few friends that this game was good and an experience, well it's an experience alright but not a good one. I've never been told by a game before that the game may crash a lot whilst I'm playing it, this game is a first.
The game uses the worst game engine, Unreal Engine, as well as some annoying game design which leads you getting stuck on railings and banisters which is unbelievably annoying when you're being chased by mentalists, which is about 90% of the game, obviously.
It's also got some of the worst game mechanics, not exclusive to this game, regenerating health and batteries to power your camera. I'll never understand why these ideas are/were considered good, but they've been in far too many games. Just like the Unreal Engine.
What's good about this game?
Well the camera view is pretty well done, all the info on the screen, HD, zoom level, battery life etc.
The night vision also works pretty well, if it didn't chew through batteries like a fat man through candy.
I like going into a horror game without any real knowledge of what the game is about and the game explains the premise of the game fairly well at the start so that was also one of the good points of the game, that's where the good points of the game end.
Story is pretty rubbish and most of the story is hidden on logs and folders, which means you have to hunt for them to find the story. Nothing really new, old semi-abandoned asylum. People run at you, you close the door and hide in a locker, you watch the enemy walk past you and then they open the locker next to you. Every. Single. Time.
The game has a single jump scare at the beginning of the game, about the first five minutes of the game, then the game falls flat after that, the usual boring stuff, things from 2004, burst steam pipes, a body falling out of a vent, things that Doom 3 did. TEN YEARS AGO.
Overall, I really wouldn't recommend it, I suppose if you can get it for £5 or the equivalent when it’s on sale. I just wouldn’t bother  paying any higher than that.

I discovered this game 2 years when a buddy of mine from my dorm played it. At that time, i wasn't really interested in the game as i was more into a game's application of things like design, graphics and immersion at the time. Plus, it's just fun seeing him get so frustrated that i ddn't wanna experience it myself. That all changed when he decided to use my PC one time and installed the game . The f*cker even decided to make his steam auto log in every time i turn on my computer as if purposefully luring me into playing it.
Sadly. It worked. Cuz a few hours later, i was playing the sh*t out of it on his account.. all i could think of was that this game is all about patterns and timing, and for the most part, its what makes the game enjoyable. Aside from the story and interesting mechanics that is. Sadly, 6 months later, he transferred to another school, which ment taking down his steam account from my PC. But i did remember some of the achievements and decided to pirate the game and see how far i can go to achieve em without being notified. Big Mistake. It took me atleast a year to memorize all the patterns and a couple of months to perfect it.
A couple of months later, i decided to install the game when humble bundle offered it on one of their usual listings. I thought i could get all the achievements in less than 3 hours. As a lover of Open-world, I wanted to get into this game.  The things stopping me from doing so were a veritable mountain of design and technical problems.
The game ran fine, and with my GTX 780 benchmarked at 190 fps at reasonable settings.
However, when I got into the game, there was massive amounts of screen-shake and screen tearing as a result.  I could not enable V-sync, because even though I benchmarked at upwards of 200 fps in some places, the framerate was locked to 60 with it on, and 3/4ths of the time would get cut to 30 fps.  However, that isn't the most damning thing about V-sync, as turning it on gave me a full second of lag, making all my movements, aiming, and shooting feel as if I were underwater.
The guns also have depressingly low ammo caps, and it is nigh impossible to find ammo for guns other than SMGs or the Pistol, and impossible to find that without starting a fight.  Another small design I take issue with is that when you save your game manually, and load it, it starts you at the nearest "Friendly" area.  Meaning either the starting area, or any strongholds you have helped liberate.  This means that near the start of the game, you cannot roam, as doing so will either end with you back near the start when you save and quit or die.  The game is open world, but a cruelly directed open world.
Another problem is that if you are off the ground for more than a second, your character will go into a freefall sky-diving pose, and instantly gain about 25 mph of forward speed, leaving you to smack into walls, massively overshoot even simple jumps, fall off of towers, fall off of buildings, and generally be extremely imprecise.  Compounding that problem is that when you go into the freefall pose, the screenshake returns and it jerks your mouse around, and you don't have free mouse aim while freefalling, so using your hookshot accurately is simply impossible. Without a lucky, desperate shot, you'll fall far from your mark.
And now we come to the big issue - Motion sickness.  If you have ever gotten motion sick while playing a game, or even if you get carsick, do not pick up this game. When firing weapons, the screen shakes ridiculously, to the point where it seems as if my monitor was glitching up, and I tried many different settings to try and fix this.  When driving, the screen shakes and bounces all over.  When falling, the screen whirls and shakes, and refuses to stay in a stable position.  When you use your hookshot, you are in for a second or two of insane camera shaking, and if you're trying to go long distances in a helicopter, I feel bad for you, because even at a stable altitude and only pressing forward, the screen will bob up and down at least 10 degrees every second or two.  Enabling motion blur or fiddling with any of the other settings will not improve this ludicrous camera shaking.
I don't get motion sickness or simulation sickness anywhere else. This game has given me both.  It made my head hurt when playing for more than an hour.  I wanted to get into it, instead I dove headfirst into design problems that made me sick.  I'm sorry I purchased it, stay away from it.

Victor Vran is pretty much your generic RPG. The game is fun to play and enjoyable in most aspects, but it's not anything special.  I do recommend this game for it's positive traits, but know ahead of time that there are also some considerable negative traits.
You have a third-person isometric camera view that you can rotate around your character. You kill things, they drop loot. Difficulty level can be adjusted with any combination of 5 hexes that will cause you to lose health, increase movement speed or attack of enemies, etc. Each area in the map has secrets to find and optional challenges to complete that grant loot, experience, or gold. Your character can equip two weapons, an outfit, two special abilities, two potions, and up to 5/6 cards that grant various perks. Each of these items have their own traits, and you can swap them out from the inventory menu while out in a level, so you can essentially customize your character to exactly suit your play style. You will occasionally find bounties and treasure maps that require you to visit 3 to 5 areas in the map in order to get even more bonus loot. I felt all of these elements meshed together very well to create a fairly enjoyable game. The game also runs incredibly smooth with no lag or frame rate drops to speak of.
By the way, your character also has the ability to jump, which I seldom seen in RPGs. Jumping is great! It offers a nice way to bypass a group of enemies, and it integrates very well for finding secrets.
Despite all those aspects that I enjoyed, there were far too many aspects I didn't enjoy:
Menu controls are not intuitive, especially when using a controller. I switched to keyboard and mouse every time I went into my inventory or traded with a merchant.
Leveling up requires you to access the inventory screen and choose 1 of 3 bonuses you get for leveling up. If you want to do this while in a map, your character will continue to be attacked while you are stuck navigating through 3 menu screens before the level up is complete. The game should instead just give you the stat bonus for the level and let you choose the item bonus later, but instead you have to choose your bonus before you get the stats increase.
The thing that completely ruins this game for me is the inventory management. This is hands down the number one reason you would NOT want to play this game. Early on, you have to spend an awful lot of time managing your inventory if you want to always be carrying the best gear. You pick up so many weapons early in the game that you're almost guaranteed to get something that is better than what you're currently using. Later in the game, monsters get more powerful but Rare and Legendary items don't get any stronger. This means you are unable to keep up with the growing difficulty in defeating monsters, causing you to die more often or constantly run away from a fight so you can heal. To account for this, you have the ability to Transmute weapons and items, making them stronger or improving their secondary effects. The problem here is that it takes hundreds of items to level up a pair of weapons to max stats, so if you later find a weapon you like better, you have to repeat the process. AND, you can only increase the stats of an item by using items of equal rarity or better. This means legendary weapons require legendary items in order to level up. In the 26 hours we played, I found a total of 9 legendary weapons, so it was impossible for me to level up any of them any considerable amount.
Transmutation is clearly meant to be a key element of this game, but I hated it. The game punishes you for not choosing a single weapon and sticking with it forever. I liked playing with the Hammer, Rapier, Shotgun, and Mortar, each of which has a particular situation they are well-suited for. Unfortunately, Transmutation is designed so that I must pick one of those to use at all times, unless I want to spend another 20 hours getting enough legendary items to upgrade all of them.
If you play through the game once to finish the story, it will be fun. If you try to actually level up your character in a way that suits your play style, you'll end up grinding for hours through the same level trying to find more and more items to use in Transmutation. I personally hate grinding, especially since now the only reason to get better weapons is so I can replay levels I've already completed. No thanks!

I bought this game on Christmas day based on a recommendation from one of my friends. So far, it's easy for me to understand, and I'm loving the game so far, despite that it's early access.
I can see a lot of potential with this, it's like Blockland and BeamNG.drive had a baby, and made brick rigs. I even love the fact you can throw your creations off a canyon, and watch them get obliterated into several pieces, and possibly explode.
Now keeping some of the other reviews in mind, this game is off to a good start. I'm actually glad this game allows controller support, and you can make a variety of great vehicles in game (I mean seriously, LOOK AT THE WORKSHOP!), but I think the game is lacking some things:
==========
1. Better 3D sound engine: You can hear sirens and guns from a mile away, and it can confuse people considering that it sounds like the sirens are right next to them.
2. Avatar customization: While true you can select a profession and have a different layout of the avatar, it's rather boring that you're someone surrounded by other people wearing blue pants and a red shirt that says "Hi, my name is Bob".
3. More performance and engine physics: Now let's implement Garry's Mod's ACF engines. It would be awesome to have a variety of engines and different engine sounds. Or maybe to the least, just an option to select different types of engine sounds on the current engines that we have. Give us some more options to customize the performance of our cars!
4. Better server control: No offense, but the community so far hasn't been so pleasant, and I'm pretty sure it's been the same thing to you, my reader of this review. It's hard to find a server where you can show off your creations and drive together in peace, rather than just have some @$$hole fire turrets at you constantly for no reason. True as a host you can kick them out of the server for the session of hosting, but then what if you're not the host? You don't want to leave. No. There should be an option not just to allow "God Mode", but rather to have the option to disable guns on vehicles. Because maybe you want to think outside the Private server, and not limit yourself to just showing your friends your cars. Get the "Nice People" involved.
5. More GUI Sounds: You get the Lego Digital Designer feel while you're inside the editor, it would be cool to have little clicking noises when selecting bricks, and then some sort of "plant" noise when you place a brick. C'mon, it'll be cute.
6. Finally, a tutorial on how to play the game: This could be conquered best if there actually was a "Tutorial" world instead  showing you how the game works. While it took me a few seconds to realize the interface of the game, it could be a mouthfull to other people trying to learn the controls.
==========
Overall, I think the game is great despite some of the concerns I had to address, this game has a lot of potential, and I know it's early access, but I think it's safe to recommend this game regardless.

What is Victor Vran?
I'd just like to start off by saying: This game is to the Isometric Dungeon Crawler genre, as Borderlands is to the FPS genre. It changes several things up mechanically and progression-wise, while still retaining several core mechanics of games similar to it.
This game is probably the least serious game in the genre. Victor Vran features plenty of humor, references, and more humor. In fact: Legendary Weapons are more often than not either a reference, or just something completely goofy. For example, let's take a look at the 1st legendary I got: The Nekonomicon. No, I didn't forget the R. Upon collecting 10 of the orbs that drop from enemies and random destroyables in the environment, my next attack triggers Neon Cats to rain down around me. They do PLENTY of damage, and are a hilarious sight.
What are the good and bad things about this game?
+ PLENTY of different playstyles you can go for, despite all skills being linked directly to the type of weapons your using.
+ NIce Graphics. For being labeled "Indie", I can hardly see the difference between Diablo 3 and this (in terms of quality, not style/theme)
+ Humor Galore. Everything from "The Voice" (which serves as the narrator for the most part), to the items you find/use, has a chance of turning into a moment where your death will be because of laughter.
+ NO CLASSES! While some may view this as a bad thing, you don't ever pick an actual class. You're free to swap things out whenever you want, and have fun with it.
+ Sound Design is nice (with a few exceptions, but not enough to criticize).
+ No connection issues. I haven't had any major issues with the online portion of the game, though the synchonization is a bit wonky.
+ Legendary weapons SCALE WITH YOUR LEVEL! If you find the Nekonomicon and enjoy it like I did, you can use it as long as you want without it falling off in terms of damage.
+/- No role designation.  What you are, is what you act like you are and are set up for. If you want to be a tank, just put on durability equipment and charge in in front of your allies. There are no healing setups though.
-..... Hard to think of... I guess I could criticize how one of the areas didn't seem to be properly identified as a high level area, causing TREMENDOUS frustration, but that's about it....
Overall: I'd give it 8.5/10. It is so much fun, I can't get enough of it. I don't care for games like Diablo, yet this game had me hooked for nearly 14 HOURS YESTERDAY. I whole-heartedly recommend it to fans of the genre who want a silly twist thrown in.
