First of all I have only played about 3 hours of the game, so this is more of a first impressions than a review but those first impressions did lead me to not want to play the game anymore or the New Vegas game which I have also purchased prior to playing.
Based on those first few hours of game play I am praying that most of the things I did not like about this game have been change for Fallout 4 or its going to be one of the quickest refunds of my life. To find out why that is, please read on.
My initial impression of the game when starting out in the vault was quite favourable. I liked the way they introduced me to the game and found it felt quite unique. But once I progressed to outside the vault, things for me, started to go downhill.
The pacing really slowed and I found the combat to be ridiculous. For example. I was outside in the wildness close to the vault armed with a pistol when a dog attacks me. Now in most other games if you shoot the dog in the head it dies, but not in this one, I unloaded round after round into that dog at point blank range, only for the dog to not react in the slightest and for me to end up dying. How can you unload a mass of bullets into the head of any animal and it not at least be somewhat affected if not die. So for me the combat sucked.
Next was the questing experience which I found to be very slow and tiresome. Having to go around an unfamiliar dreary environment and question loads instantly dislikeable people, being given choices of dialog none of which I wanted to pick, to get exposition and to set out what I needed to do, made the pacing feel very slow and unrewarding. I found not only did I not care about things but there was nothing in the begining that was strong enough for me to want to get invested.
Now to the UI. The pit boy looks on the surface to be a great idea, but in practice it’s a terrible menu system and the UI is very clunky and not very intuitive. I feel they used it to minimise the amount of UI elements on the screen, but to give you just one example of where this minimisation of UI fell down was in combat. Not being able to track my health whilst in combat because the only place it could be seen was on my pit boy felt ridiculous to me, especially as you could not have your pit boy on the screen at the same time as you are in combat. This coupled with the fact that all mapping and directions are also on your pit boy made navigation woeful.
Overall the game felt slow, clunky (from an animation and mechanical perspective) and unrealistic, and there was so much of an (and I hate to use this phrase but I can’t think of a better way to describe things) uncanny valley feeling about the people and the physics, I found playing fallout 3 to be a very aggravating endeavour. This coupled with the detached way you interacted with everything in the world constantly reminded me that this was just a video game rather than an interactive immersive storied experience I had read and heard everyone talk so fondly of.
TLDR. The asthetic, setting and enviroments are stunning creations from wonderful imaginations but in the end the faults I found with the game play, UI, animations, combat and questing, meant I just could not get invested enough to want to play it long term.
I hope this helps some of you who are looking to buy it, but please remember this is my personal opinion of just over 3 hours of play, your experience and feelings about the game could be very different to my own.

Victor Vran is marketed as an Indie game, but it simply doesn't feel like one. The game has the kind of generous polish you'd expect from a higher budget project.
This game shines in its combat interactions. It is very addictive and can be enjoyed for countless hours. The precision is superb and the creatures' AI can be quite challenging. The only issue with it, is that there isn't enough. Unfortunately the game itself on normal mode will feel easy to any experience gamer. Start a game on Hard and you'll encounter some of the problems with Victor Vran. The balancing of the game is basically an exercise in changing numbers. Creatures have more armor, hit for more and may be faster. You can tweak these characteristics by enabling handicaps called Hexes, but in the end the fights do not change much. Once you've mastered all creatures, then the game becomes an exercise in finding better equipment and it basically becomes a grind.
Victor Vran's equipment scheme is a basic one compared to other RPG types. Most of the equipment that is found (weapons) is useless and can either be sold or transmuted. This is my second critique of the game in that it doesn't really establish any links with the character you are building. It's basically like a Chinese buffet. You can do everything you want as long as you're grinding for it. Demon Powers and Destiny Cards as more equipment are supposed to replace a skill tree, but the level of interest isn't great due the limited options or the limited benefits they bring.
My third and final critique is that the story isn't very enticing. It's very basic and unfortunately it doesn't really immerses the player effectively. The game exposes too many challenges while the story is unraveling and it's really easy to get side tracked just trying to get better equipment to answer those challenges.
With these 3 point in mind, this game still rocks. I'm actively wishing for a sequel where these issues are answered.

An incredible take on the city building genre. Similar in a way to the old Sim City games, or possilby Cities XL, but with a few twists. Almost everything for your townspeople has to be brought by them  when they are exiled. You have limited amounts of food, clothing, and tools with which to survive. Prioritization is key in this game - do you expand quickly to have a large population, or do you ensure you can clothe and feed everyone first? Do you build a dock so you can eventually trade, but risk getting disease or be isolationist?
The gameplay is interesting in that there are no overarching goals - no moving on to the next map, no "unlocking" buildings. The question is, do you have the resources to build something? There is no tech tree - though that could be an interesting update, but I understand why the developer wished to leave that out of the initial game.
Developed by only one individual this has as much "polish" as I've seen in several other games. The graphics are not the most sophisticated, but this is not a drawback. Instead they help build the atmosphere for the game.
I'm hoping the mod kit comes out soon - I'm curious to see what sorts of tools the developer will entrust to the players, and what sorts of creations the players will be able to make out of this.

overall, my experience with Victor Vran has been positive. instead of game like Diablo, which are very large, open areas pretending to be small, enclosed ones, Victor Vran has a mix of both closed, and open areas, with varied terrain, and a range of weapons that have unique physics which accomodate or are penalized based on them. the mortar, for instance, is very good from above, but more difficult to aim from below, especially on the side.
there are an array of weapons that vary greatly. there's the rapier, a single target, close range weapon. this weapon offers high armor penetration, and quick strikes, allowing you to dodge in and out and pick off tough enemies first. then there's the hammer, a weapon whose sole job is to slowly smash the ground into crowds of enemies, to do large amounts of damage. personally, I think the hammer needs armor penetration, given the role of combat hammers vs. armor historically, but that's just my opinion. the hammer also compliments other weapons as one of its attacks finishes with a life steal buff that remains when you switch weapons. the sword is a weapon that is excels when you time your attacks and special attacks properly. the third swing of your sword makes enemies vulnerable, making the next attack against them a critical, and your main special attack has its cooldown reset on critical, allowing you to endlessly cycle your attacks. mess up on your cycle, however, and you suffer greatly, as there is a delay at the end of your third swing, like if you fail at striking effectively with a real sword. every weapon has a unique playstyle to it, and you can equip two at a time, and cycle through the two you have equipped, letting you compliment your attacks.
Victor Vran doesn't collect armor in the way that traditional RPGs do, assembling them piece by piece, discarding them as you level. the weapon system does that, and you can grind out new weapons forever. Victor doesn't concern himself on grinding out the perfect buckler to accompany his shiny chestplate. no, he's satisfied with an outfit that provides him with passive bonuses, and altering his playstyle. to compensate, he collects demon cards, which grant him further passive bonuses, some to him, some to his strikes, and others are penalties that he applies to those he strikes, or that strike him. one argument against Victor Vran is the simplicity of the equipment system, but those claims are made by those who have not gone very deep into raising the power of their outfits, or their demon cards.
there is a potion and bomb system that is very simplistic. I was, and still am underwhelmed by the effectiveness of bombs, for the same reason I am for the levellable 'potion' - the medkit. they use static numbers for damage and healing, rather than a percentage, like ever other potion does. this makes them useful early in the game, but they quickly lose usefulness, especially if you play on a higher difficulty.
lastly, there's a supplimental active ability system in demon powers. there are four main groups of demon powers. the first is the direct attacks group. these are meteor, shockwave, and boomerang. these abilities don't interrupt your regular attacks, and some have secondary effects. the second group is sustained direct damage attacks. in this group are dark mist (turn into a cloud of poison, weakening and damaging enemies), sunray (fire a continuous beam from your hands), and purging flame (control a zone of moving flames, damaging enemies in an AoE). the third group is passive effects. in this group are sanguine aura (health regen/armor), berserk aura (+damage to everyone in range, even mobs), and diamond (damage absorb/ranged reflect). the last group is utility. in this one is blink (teleport, damage a single enemy, and make him vulnerable), pull (shoot out a number of projectiles, pulling them to you, and stunning them for a period of time), and time bubble (create a zone in which enemies and enemy projectiles are slowed, but friendlies and friendly projectiles are not). I find that the powers in which you lose the ability to be active aren't powerful enough to justify using them, while enemies that use them don't have to lose the ability to be acive. in particular, enemies have the ability to place a sunray that spins outward slowly from a focal point, that you do not.
the difficulty system is achieved in the way of 'hexes' that make enemies more difficult, but also provide more experience and loot (a la Bastion, et al). there is also a hard mode, which turns on all hexes and supposedly provides some other buff to enemies, but I've been unable to locate any documentation about this to confirm it.
in Victor Vran, you can also jump, which is useful both from a time saving standpoint (as in other games, you would have to go all the way around, just to get over that stupid railing), and an exploration one (to find secret areas). you can wall vault up to twice before landing, which means you can scale some two-wall areas to reach otherwise unreachable areas, some hidden, and some not. this helps to eliminate a lot of wasted time, and also makes level design less bland. dodging is also a very important mechanic, and allows you to both travel faster (Victor Vran's version of the FPS bunnyhop), and also avoid enemy attacks. it immediately interrupts attacks, which is a welcome mechanic, one that some games lack (Fight the Dragon, I'm looking at you).
it runs reasonably well on my system, using Arch Linux, but there have been some technical issues. principally, F1 (used to file a bug report) has created an instant crash on Linux for some time, and has still not been addressed. former incarnations of the game also seemed to be a bit more optimized, and there are some random crashing and networking issues.

This is the best Dark souls game. The PvP is superb and the story is enjoyable although long and drawn out. However, the game allows you to replay your favorite parts selectively as if you were in NG+ so you don't have to play through the whole game again to get special loot.  The weapons in this game are great in number and many of them are viable in PvP, whereas in other Dark souls games only a few weapons are good. The weapons in this game are very fun to use and have a large diverse moveset.  'Grinding' in this game is fair and you probably won't even feel the need to grind for items. I did though, because I wanted to upgrade practically everything.  The bosses in this game are the best in the souls series. This is especially true for the DLC content, which even on their own would be one of the greatest gaming experiences of all time.  This game has a large cast of enemies and personalities.  The story is quite decent and at the end you will be wondering who the true villain was.  PvP in this game is most active in the Brotherhood of Blood covenant arena, although there is another arena that is considerably less active (with different arena maps) and there is also the option of invading other players. I played this game mostly in 2016 and I doubt there is really anyone left to invade at this point. However, the arenas are active, but you will probably be facing the same opponents over and over again.  The opponents in the arena are good but don't post much of a challenge to me, probably since I found one of the best play styles in the game that they have a hard time countering (dark infused roaring halberd running spin attack, with offhand sanctum crossbow). I win about 80% of the time in the arena. Sometimes the opponent is simply better at dodging and stun locking you.
I recommend this game for both the single player and PvP aspects. Even if PvP were to die out, the game would still be 100% worth it for the single player alone, which even features NPC friendlies that you can summon for boss fights and even some areas in general.

Ultimate Chicken Horse (UCH) is a Level Designer-like Platformer. When you're in a level with other people, you can add platforms and traps each round. When everyone's done placing their objects, you then play the level. Your job is to be the only person to get to the goal, and prevent the other players to also succeed. If everyone makes it to the end, nobody gets points for that round (unless someone got an object called a Coin.). If everyone dies, nobody gets points for that round.
The controls when the level you're in takes some time to get use to. To me, they were really floaty the first time I played the game, which caused some accidental fails (like accidentally falling through a small gap). While they do need to get use to, the control layout is simple and easy to learn. I played this game with my Ps3 controller (I did some thing that makes my computer think my Ps3 controller is a Xbox 360 controller.), and the controls never got confusing, but since they're floaty in this game, again, they need to get use to.
When in the Build-like Mode, you can place 1 object every round (but I think you can change the amount of objects you can place down in the rules). In Party Mode, you and the other players get 4-5 random objects to choose from every round. If you see an object you want, you need to be quick, since the other players can take that object away from you. In Freeplay Mode, you get to select 1 object of your choice every round. If you want to place down a trap? You can do that if you want! Want to delete an object someone placed? You can do that if you want!
If you're the host, you can change the rules for your game. You can increase rounds, change the Game Mode, etc. So if you want your game to be different or more interesting, you can try to do that.
At the start of the game, you only get 3 levels, 4 characters, and no outfits. In order to get more levels/characters/outfits, you need to find these boxes with a "?" on them in the levels you have. If there is a box, a ? appears on a level in the Lobby. In order to get the boxes, you just need to touch them or put a trap next to them. It's easier than it sounds.
The Soundtrack and Artstyle are really good. Can't say anything else.
There are problems with the game: Bugs and Online Issues.
-When I was playing with other people I don't know, one of them said that they couldn't select an object, even though he was pressing the left mouse button on the object he wanted. Because of this issue, he/she couldn't put any objects down, only the the two players and I.
-I put stairs on a rotating object that had honey on it. At first, the stairs rotated like I wanted to, but then the stairs stopped rotating and was at a different place the next round.
I've encountered more bugs, but those are the bugs I can think of right now.
-When playing Online, things are out of sync at times. Like for example: I jump into a saw that's rotating, and I fail. The next player jumps, and even though it looks like he/she touched the saw, he/she is still going. Or like an arrow hits a player, and he/she's still going.
-Some things do disappear from a player's view. Sometimes an object disappears on a player's screen, which might screw them over.
Overall, if you want a really fun party game, Ultimate Chicken Horse is for you! Don't want to get 4 copies of the game? No worries! You can hook up 4 controllers to your computer and play the game together, just like that. In my opinion, 15 dollars is worth it for the super fun gameplay that never gets old.
Highly Recommended!

Home is Where One Starts sets the stage for a unique gameplay experience where players could have easily recaptured the long lost essence of their childhood. Unfortunately, once the stage is set the actors simply walk off stage, the curtain falls and the lights go out.
Let me be clear, this game could have been amazing! The ambience is top notch. The visual quality, setting and music craft a solid foundation for what could have been a deeply moving emotional experience. There simply isn't enough meat on the bones on this one to satisfy the hunger generated by the first five minutes of the game.
You begin standing on the side of the road in front of a decrepit mobile home out in the country. You've missed the bus for school but because your negligent father isn't home you decide to go exploring rather than find another means of transportation. I'd venture to say 99% of the people reading this review experienced at least one memorable day like this in their youth - a day of relatively rare freedom laden with adventure and self discovery hinting at a future of independence not yet realized. Those days are some of the most vivid memories of my childhood.
So with a setup like this Home is Where One Starts could have been insanely good but, to be blunt, you can fire this game up and "complete it" in 20 minutes. That is simply unacceptable, even with the $3 price tag.
If you're looking for a first person story driven exploration game I highly recommend Gone Home instead.

While I may have enjoyed myself and I would recommend it to others, not everyone is going to like this game. If you like walking sims and enjoy playing them a few times over to get the full experience of them, Home is Where One Starts is certainly something I'd suggest. It's cheap, but for just how short the game is, it still feels a little bit heavy on your pocket.
You play as a child and explore the surrounding areas of your home, which is a trailer in a rural area. Each bit of dialogue and description is a reflection of what was likely a difficult time in your life, so it's a game in which you don't want to just blow through the dialogue.
This game is intended to be thoughtful and your imagination is supposed to also do a bit of work when you find items scattered in the area. What was this girl's life like? What did it become? Did she miss the bus on purpose that day?
The game works. Gameplay is simple exploration and I didn't encounter bugs. The game itself is very pretty, even when you are in the more gritty and shocking parts of this girl's life. A swingset surrounded by trash is a very thought-provoking image that may hit some gamers a little harder than others. The music is very soothing as well.
No jumpscares. No faking out the player. It's more like a short story you can interact with. This game also allows you to explore freely (for the most part) until you start bumping into invisible walls, so feel free to walk off into oblivion, much like a bored child who really is skipping school.
It's not awful and there's a bit of a niche market for these games. Your garden variety gamers should skip this, though.

Home is where one starts... Well, there are some things that should be said from the get go. It's a Unity game, it's a "walking simulator" and it's very very short. If these three things are things you avoid in games, HIWOS is not going to be the quintessential interactive narrative game that'll blow you away. It is, in my opinion, pretty good though. The writing is sparse but good. I like the voice actor. The game is pretty but it's Unity pretty so it's the kind of pretty you've seen a hundred times over most likely. The interactive elements are very few and far between which is a shame. If there was just more content and more of a story, this could truly be a game to remember. Instead it's just a pretty setpiece with some genuinely good writing every 5 minutes. Home is where one starts is less a book than a poem. It's a nice poem, but it's like most other poems. You read it once, think "oh that's nice", but it has no lasting impact on your worldview or emotions. It was only a dollar on sale though, so if you don't mind spending a dollar to listen to peaceful music and hearing some nice voice acting and writing over 40 minutes, then go ahead. Home is where one starts is not a bad experience at all, merely a transparent one.

I have changed my review from negative to positive. Scroll down for my original negative review. I'm changing it to positive for two reasons:
1) I eventually realized that initially I did not understand the point of the game. This is a wonderful work of minimalist/slice of life interactive storytelling, but I was expecting/looking for something different when I first played it. So, a large part of my disappointment stemmed from not getting what I expected. As it stands, the game is very successful at what it sets out to do.
2) I only realized the first point because despite not enjoying the experience at first, I found the game entering my thoughts long after I had completed it. I've dedicated more thought to this game than many others recently, and that is something I value quite a bit.
TL;DR I initially didn't like the game because I was expecting something different. I thought about it a bunch and finally understand, so I changed my recommendation.
*ORIGINAL REVIEW*
With a heavy heart, I unfortunately cannot recommend this game.
I think it's a little much to ask people to pay for this experience. I'm a fan of walking simulators in general, but only when the story/experience is interesting. The premise here had loads of promise, but unfortunately the game didn't do anything to develop the premise. It's just a premise, then over. There's no real narrative payoff (although there is a very, very small emotional one), and that seems like a pretty big thing for a walking simulator to be missing.
Invisible walls could have been disguised in some way. Instead they are immersion breaking as they suddenly and unexpectedly stop the one action the player is allowed: walking. It hurts even worse because the words "invisible walls" are literally a part of the spoken dialog, drawing unnecessary attention to itself. Aside from that, more detail could have been added throughout the world to give examinable items and locations a little more weight. This would have also helped develop the narrative.
This game has an interesting setting, but that's about it. If it had been free or much closer to free then I would feel better about the lack of content and story development. I think David Wehle has some great potential as long as he can find and deliver the right story (in its entirety). I'll be keeping an eye out for the next project.

When I first saw the game, I thought this was a Van Helsing clone (Can't argue with the familiarity). But when I finally got the game, I could see the difference. The game has the stereotypical charm of an ARPG like Torchlight, but the developers have changed a few things for the game to stand out from the others. The jump mechanism has been added in the game which surprisingly works well in this genre where all you do is click to other areas to evade attacks. Along with this change, there are a lot of changes to the control scheme of the game that tries not to decrease the life span of your mouse with incessant clicks (Though they are still pretty much there). Full voice acting is a welcome addition to the game and it's done well. Character progression has been also done differently as you don't invest in skill sets, but acquire powers from time to time as loot or purchases (Each weapon has a different powerup as well). The major gripe I have with this game is the variety. After playing for 2 hours or so, you feel like you have experienced what the game is all about. Games like Torchlight present you with abundant variety for you to remain glued to the game for hours unlike this one. However, the challenges in the game might ameliorate this deficiency if you have OCD like me. Would definitely recommend a purchase at a discount.

Coming in to this right after Wings of Vi I can say it is not that hard.
Personally I think there are too much checkpoints in some areas outside the overworld.
The hardest sections are the optional ones you have to go through to get the collectable trinkets.
Upon beating the game it told my that the most deaths per room I had was 236, I assume that is the collective total of the overworld and rooms without a name. Realistically I think the hardest section for one specific trinket would be ~600 deaths, but the game didn't emphasize it as the hardest room as it was split into like 6 rooms without a checkpoint. That's something I would have like to have seen more in the game, sometimes it felt I needed a checkpoint every ten steps.
Since it is not that hard I'd suggest getting it for the surreal experience heavily reinforced by the amazing soundtrack.
Like seriously, it took me only 1875 deaths to beat the game and get all collectibles which is less than 9% of all deaths it took me to beat WoV and get all secrets on normal mode. And a good 1000 of my deaths came from the optional areas for the trinkets and another 100 from trying to plain up brute force out of a certain area instead of actually thinking of the obvious solution.
However I see the case with getting all achievements being kind of the same like with Crypt of the NecroDancer where the game by itself is not that bad but some achievements are downright insane.
It was also quite nice to see that the first achievement I got was beat the game and not like other games which award you for beating a tutorial, the the first level and so on.
I'm not a perfectionist, but I have about a 85 percent average completion rate, but I can already say I won't 100% this game ever as "Beat the game without dying" in a game that is not a roguelike would require way too much practice for me to even come close to getting that.
TL:DR
It is not that hard if you do not try to do everything, get it for the experience, beat the game any%, enjoy the amazing soundtrack and surreal atmosphere.
Edit.
Played through all of the pre-installed player created levels and downloaded some more, you can definitely get lots of longevity out of this game if you enjoy the mechanics, much like in Super Mario Maker.

This game was a lot better than I expected.  Very similar to Diablo II; better in most ways, worse in a few others.  For an indie game, this has great graphics, decent replay value, and a good amount of content (kept me occupied for over 25 hours in my first playthrough, not including elite challenges).  Linux performance is great, too.  Read any of the positive reviews and they'll tell you all you need to know about what makes this a great game that's worth buying (it definitely is worth buying).  But I do have a few complaints:
1.  The ability to dodge is great and something I use all the time, but shields would've been a nice option too.  Very often I'll find myself in a situation where dodging damage is simply unavoidable.  Considering there are some challenges expecting you to make X amount of kills without getting injured or stay above Y% life, this gets to be pretty annoying.
2.  There seems to be a poor balance to the weapons.  The shotguns, scythes, and rapiers seem to be overpowered while the hammers, swords, and mortars are almost uselessly weak.  Considering each weapon type has it's own set of advantages, this also makes certain challenges nearly impossible to achieve.
3.  Gold is pretty much worthless.  Your inventory is unlimited, there are all sorts of items to help increase your gold count, and you can easily find everything you need that is as good or better than what you can get from the merchants.  The only thing I ever found myself spending gold on were transmutations.  The gold could've been more useful if you had a limited capacity in your inventory, and if the merchants had better things for sale.
4.  Though the level of detail in each level is great, having at least some of the maps randomize like they do in other games would've been nice for replay value.
5.  I'm not sure why, but this game seems to be seriously lacking bass in my surround system.  It doesn't seem to take advantage of the rear speakers either.  Not a big deal, just a little weird that only 3 of my 6 channels were used.
You already know if you're going to enjoy this, so why are you reading reviews when you could be Nepping?

The concept of editing the level as you play it is very original and surely brings a unique game feel. You can try to make the level as hard as possible to mess with your opponents, but it will be equally hard for you! This game is all about gauging risks, and finding balance between how hard you want the level to be for you and the others. Surely, skilled platformers players are advantaged, but you can be surprised by how things turn out.
There is a place to a lot of "playing style" in the way players edit the level. Some of my friends place as many lethal traps as they can; others will just mess with their opponent with sticky and gliding platforms; some will place teleporters as soon as possible.
It will also happen that there is only one path to the end and that only the best ones will make it, or that there are several ways of finishing a level and that players will choose in which path they feel the more confident.
One of the most emergent games ever!

I can't recommend HOI 3. Being a fan of the predecessor, with undreds of hours of playtime, I've never felt at home with the third installment.
I looked forward to see the concept enhanced and refined, receiving a sandbox game giving me even more options to play out all the crazy "what if" scenarios.
Instead I got a pretty clunky piece of software which ran at a considerably lower speed without making any real use of the 3D graphics engine, apart from introducing tons of micro DLCs for unit types.
But what annoyed me most, is the fact that the game is way less transparent than the predecessor, offering even less freedom of choice. It mediates the player: Instead of giving him more control, it forces him to follow the pace of the predestined alliances if he wishes to actually take part in the game. While this can be circumvened with lots of ingame time, th fact that you are resigned to watch the computer play persists.
Moving your armies, executing certain troop movements like a grand encirclment is not what you are supposed to do. You just watch time tick away, while the computer is moving the troops.
HOI 3 was a huge disappointment for me. I really tried to get in touch with it, but even after several playthrough as minor and major powers I didn't feel involved the way I did with HOI2.
Funny enough I discovered "Arsenal of Democracy", a modification to enhance and refine HOI2, months later. And it was exactly what I hoped HOI3 would offer me. All it lacks is the larger amount of provinces which are provided by HOI3.
Playing Arsenal of Democracy, I don't see a reason to return to HOI3.
So, no recommendation. Sorry, Paradox. Hope you'll do better with HOI4.

At first a traditional RPG, it soon shows its true colours as a charming adventure full of wacky characters (Bellegar, the Rhyming Mage, is great) and weird quests, but also with many dramatic moments and cruel situations. Personally, I liked that swinging mood a lot, as it offers a contrast with other more straight-forward RPGs. The story in intself is quite long, so it should take you more than 50 hours to see the end.
Technically, the graphics are ok (it has aged pretty well) and both music and voice acting are very good. The controls and animations feel a bit disjointed, and that can be a problem in some combat situations and specially in the platform jumping related puzzles, but in general they work well. Also, combat can be a bit unbalanced on ocassions, having you advancing trhough hordes of minions without a problem and then being one-shot by a boss (luckyly, this only happened to me in very few instances, and I was finally able to overcome that pesky enemy). The dragon form didn't add much to me, just another layer of exploration to the huge maps.
All in all, a good experience for its presentation, story, quests and characters, with some minor problems with controls and combat.  It goes on sale from time to time, so for my is a win-win.

To list some of it's problems; It has grossly exaggerated animations, the audio is really imbalanced, for example, the player character's voice is very loud, and certain effects such as fireball sounds are very loud, yet npc dialogue is very quiet, and the music alternates in different tracks between too loud and too quiet, combat is really awkward, it reminds me of mmos, yet not as balanced, it acutally has platforming sections despite the controls and especially the player's ridiculous jump being, again, clumsy, it constantly jumps to cutscenes, for which it sheaths the player's weapons and then jumps immediatly to combat, forcing you to draw your weapons again while being attacked, when it didn't make any sense to sheath them in the first place, the enemy AI is braindead, the story and characters feel generic and predictable, moments of significance are handled carelessly with little to no regard for attempting to impress the player or make transitions feel significant, and I feel like it demands too much attention from the player when the game isn't enjoyable or rewarding in the first place.
Some positives are that the game is visually pleasant, and most of the voice acting is well done.
But ultimately I don't understand why this game has so many positive reviews, I just can't recommend that anyone buy it, there are so many other more worthy games to spend your time and money on.

.Story.
In the 2016 elections, anyone can run. Play as a giant form of presidential candidates Hilary Clinton, Barack Obama, Bernie Sanders, Ted Cruz, or Donald Trump and try to win the popular vote by running around the states.
.Gameplay.
You run—literally—using the mouse. In fact, the entire game can be played via your mouse, though there are a few hotkeys that correspond with the number keys.
The race is on. (See what I did there?) In order to conquer districts, you’ll need to get there before your enemy and sway your constituents with honeyed words that you may or may not mean. You know, like an election. The squeaky voices that utter these honeyed words are aggravating, but if you listen closely, you’ll hear phrases that you might actually expect the flesh and blood candidate to say in real life. That was a nice touch.
So long as the coloured ring around your candidate’s feet are touching your constituents, who are much, much smaller than you for whatever reason, you’ll convert them into loyal campaign supporters. Sort of.
A claimed district will change colours to match your candidate.
Constituents’ loyalty is easily swayed by the other candidates, so you’ll need to touch claimed areas frequently in order to lock them and stop them from being claimed by another candidate.
Locking only lasts for a few seconds and so expect to run back and forth frequently—especially if you expect to win over that state at the end. The game will tell you when an opponent is attacking one of your districts, which is helpful, but it needing to drop what you’re trying to claim in favor of saving what you already own quickly becomes tedious.
Revisiting areas will also allow you to pick up the cold hard cash they’ve produced. This cash is a key factor in your campaign because…
That’s right, folks. If you circle the mouse around your candidate, you can encourage your constituents closer to you by showering them with campaign funds. This makes it easier to convert larger groups of people at once, but take care you don’t go broke.
A timer will tick down, indicating when the next city over will wake up. Once a city is awake, you can run to it, which is quite slow, and then start conquering districts anew.
You’ll keep doing this until the timer on the final city runs out. Then, you’ll be taken to the stats screen where you’ll be shown how well you did. After, you’ll be allowed to choose another state… And you start from the beginning of this section.
You do this again and again until you or one of the A.I. becomes president. I’ll be completely honest: I couldn’t find it in me to play until presidency.
.Longevity.
The game has three difficulties, five candidates to play as, and you get to choose your own campaign trail (sort of).
It also has special ability cards, each of which fall under one of three categories: attack, defense, and support. These allow you to do a range of things like double your range of influence, trap other candidates to prevent them from running around and touching your stuff, and flip a claimed territory to neutral so that you can claim it for yourself without any fuss.
*Unlocking cards is a matter of fulfilling arbitrary tasks given to you. If you're going for them and trying to win the popular vote at the same time, you're in for a rough ride.
Regardless, there’s not really a good amount of differentiation in gameplay.
.Pros.
.Cons.
.Bottom Line.
If you’re hardcore into politics and have a high tolerance for repetition, this may be worth a shot. If not, well… You’re better off just watching a YouTube video and having a laugh. You’ll still get about the same amount of content and it would be free as opposed to spending the 9.99.

text:
Before you call me a heartless ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ who should be impaled and burned at a stake for disliking a game about such a touchy subject, let me explain.
I don't entirely hate this game, the concept isn't bad but the game is a really poor execution of what it intended to be.
Home is Where One Starts is a narrative first person 'game' which focuses on a broken home where a small girl lives with her drunk dad, now there's a strong subject in this already. So it's got the attention of people, now. Where the game fails isn't in the main story, which. Is still very underwhelming. But it fails in that some things you'll need to explore to learn about, and with the slow paced walking and boring looking visuals and lack of music to keep you occupied until you find these things. That's what makes me feel like this isn't worth my money
It says that this game is in the same style of other games like Gone Home or Dear Esther, I've never played Gone home, but i have played Dear Esther. And the thing with Dear Esther was that the narration in the game was focused on the main path, if you strayed off the path there wasn't anything to gain but for you to maybe admire some fine scenery or purely curriosity. And what Dear Esther had as an advantage for you to actually explore was it's interesting enviorment, atmosphere (and for an idea game) really good looks and that is what actually motivated you to explore further, even if there's little if even any gain for doing so.
This game faults in the thing that it's more open world, it's not liniar. You're free to walk around in an open plain but yet limited by invisible walls in this game, in Dear Esther the island you were on was very open, but it only allowed you to walk where you actually could, there wasn't any invisible walls or anything, at least not that i came across. They always made sure that if there was some place you couldn't go to, it was because it was either too steep hill, a fence blocking the path or just a vast ocean. This game is limited even if it offer exploration, with its invisible walls everwhere and frankly the visuals aren't that nice or too appealing to give you that desire to stop and admire the look, neither does it to explore as the are is very booring. I feel that you would have been best off in this if they focused more on telling the story a bit more, rather than letting you walk around on a small plain and find a few things here and there that you honestly might not care about. Like if you walk up to a graveyard the narrator (which is the girl) will more or less just say how she one time got spooked going there. I mean, sorry. But what is there for good in me knowing that? In Dear Esther they spoke more unclear, and with metaphores meaning you'd have to think, and puzzle the story the narrator explains toghether, so you can't just walk completely braindead, but in this game you can.
I feel this game failed to suck me in with any atmosphere and the fact that it cost almost half of what Dear Esther does (when not on sale), a game that has more land to explore, greater atmospher, better narration and more interesting vissuals just makes me unable to call this a worthy purchase. If you feel it's worth a try, i'd say go for it. There isn't anything in this game that'll occupy you for 2 hours, so you can refund the game after you've played it.
If this story was written by the dev who went through this as a child, then i'm sorry for what you've gone through. But i simply dislike the way the story is told. Not the story itself.

Welp, since I have nothing to do today, might as well speak my mind on The Crew, which is something I have been intending to do for a while.
This would also be my first serious and semi-long review, so enjoy.

I remember how hyped I was for it when I saw the first E3 announcement back in 2013. I thought "Wow, this game looks perfect for me. Nice cars, huge map that is the entire U.S.A, seamless multiplayer, etc." Long story short, by the time the game released in 2014, I had forgotten completely about it due to my addiction at the time called Team Fortress 2.
Well, in early 2016, I bought The Crew, since I had nothing else to play and didn't want an Xbox One just to play Forza Horizon. I thought it could be a decent alternative, which, surprisingly, was a pretty okay alternative at the time. I actually had fun in The Crew, doing story missions and meeting new people to do them with was a nice experience. Building cars and leveling them up was also a much better experience than I thought it would be.
The thing with The Crew is that it's not necessarily a bad game with a bad concept. Infact it had a TON of potential. A racing MMO is a cool concept, and The Crew was a good attempt at it (keyword: "was"). I genuinely enjoyed playing through the story. But the thing is, once you beat it you realize there's nothing left, well, except for one thing. PvP. You try PvP races with your, uh... what's the performance measure called again? I don't know. Forgot. Let's just call it "level" for convenience's sake. You try PvP races with your level 900 Perf spec RUF, and realize that you are getting completely crushed by cars that are level 1299 (I think the new cap is 1399 though). You wonder what to do, and decide to look up some guides on the community hub. You find the car levelling guide, which tells you that you must farm late game skills (which are in the western side of the map) and eventually level your car to a competitive 1299 (or 1399). This ARPG is full of innovative game systems. Basic powers come from the 8 weapon types, not classes (there are no classes). Additional powers come from 2 slotted consumables (of 12) and 2 slotted Demon Powers (of 10?). Additionally passive abilities come from destiny cards, 5 slots of lots and lots. The remaining slot is a costume slot, which can be core to your build.
Some nice features such as seemingly unlimited inventory space and straightforward upgrade paths (no RNG in the gear upgrade system) make this a single character game with maximum tweaking and rebuilding potential.
Combat is good fun and can be spectacular, though in large zones frame rate problems are genuinely serious and do detract from the experience.
One great system is hexes which allow you to tweak the challenge level very precisely beyond the basic difficulty modes as presented. This allows you to manage the difficulty of each encounter if you wish. Load all 5 hexes for maximum difficulty or just 1 if you want just a bit more challenge. In game challenge modes prompt you to try different hexes on individual maps.

If this game were a Saturday-morning cartoon from my childhood, it would be "Geralt of Rivia meets Van Helsing and goes to Torchlight."
In "Victor Vran," the dark-n-edgy world of serious, "gothic" horror meets just the kind of "click/ move/ dodge/ explore/ find stuff" experience that you would expect from a Diablo inspired dungeon crawler. The developers got their core gameplay right: The weapons are well balanced, yet easily distinguishable from one another (especially with their supporting special-abilities). Significant challenge comes from not being able to spam your healing items. Opponents are varied throughout the critical-path to the endgame, and manage to usually be more than just damage sponges.
...and there are a couple of good, solid plot-twists, too.
As to downsides:
Like some other games that feature it, "synthesis" of loot isn't all that much fun. It takes a lot to make the weapons more interesting than they already are, and the loot-combo outcomes don't usually get you much. In the end, I just shrugged my shoulders a the mechanic. In the same vein, loot drops pretty slowly, and it's tough to get anything that is really nifty, or a basic-but-noticeable improvement over what you're already carrying.
The above plays significantly into the game actually getting very "samey" after you're more than about 50% along. This is not to say that the main game path doesn't keep revealing new enemies and environments to you - quite the opposite, in fact. The issue is that all the ancillary places you can visit end up feeling like filler. After a short while, there really isn't a reason to go looking around in all the areas that are available. The rewards for doing so are abstract, and a little stingy. You might complete some challenges, level up, and get some extra money, but it doesn't do much to give you an extra edge - and even with a variety of monsters and environments, at some point the "tweak these variables and repeat" thing gets pretty obvious.
So...stick to the main game, and enjoy it. I personally can't see spending tens upon tens of hours with "Victor Vran," but going through the core experience was definitely worth the price of admission.

Having put nearly 100 hours in to this game, gotten the true ending and seen most of what it has to offer, I can say this is my favorite of the Rebirth series and can very much reccomend to fans of anime, moe, and JRPGs.
Gameplay is more or less the same as in Rebirth 1 and 2. The combat system isn't incredibly deep, but it works and is fun enough (though I still feel the Break chain of attacks is relatively useless). HDD attacks feel a bit more balanced and not nearly as broken as in Rebirth 1.
Story wise, though the Neptunia games have never had strong stories, but this one feels the best to me. It follows Nep as she is transported to another dimension, the world of the 1980's game industry, which is a novel idea and leads to fun geeky jokes about the era. The characters have always been what drives the Neptunia games, and this one brings back nearly every previous character in some form, which I adore.
I found the game relatively easy for most of the main story, but that post game content, dungeons, and Colliusum battles require strategy and will kick your♥♥♥♥♥if you aren't prepared, which I really like. It's an appreciated difficulty bump for more hardcore players.
If I had complaints, the biggest one is the continued recycling of dungeons and enviroments. There are only a handful of dungeon layouts, and "new" dungeons are simply old ones with a new enemy coat. This was a problem in Rebirth 1 and 2 and it's a bit irritating it coninues here. The required amount of level grinding is also very grating.
But overall, Rebirth 3 is my favorite of the Rebirth games and I don't regret putting in the time. Had a lot of fun! Must play for fans of Nep Nep.

You have to have good network to play this game.
I thought the concept of 'private games' meaning I could play a local version of it, but I was mistaken. Even for the private games it would need to connect to the central server and maintain a continuous connection.
Maybe I would think highly of the game if it was playable for me. To be honest, I think the graphics and gameplay are totally fine.
I live in a place where the ping to this game's servers are high, and this game will randomly hang, teleport your character around and do all sorts of mysterious stuff.
This game is (currently) very unforgiving for the players with high ping, and the server-client model does not handle high latency well. I have played other games with high ping, but it does not affect overall experience because the client knows how to smoothen the 'time gaps' caused by high latency well -- this game doesn't. Having your character 'blink' around because of sync issues between client and server is very annoying.
I think if a game needs a constant network to play, it should set up more servers across regions to improve the experience.

Outlast mixes horror and exploration well, and manages to shock right to the end of the game,  through the use of near instant death scenarios coupled to the hope you might live through running and hiding mechanics.
The first person body implementation is the best I can recall and dramatically increases the tension in the game as the immersion is near complete - this is a major selling point to me as I find first person simulators with floating hands painfully disengaging.
The non player AI is wonderful. There is minimal yet sufficient telegraphing, and they dont cheat (cant see in the dark, engage in reasonable search routines, etc).
There are loads of documents/etc to be collected which add to the story, but thankfully there arent any achievements so I didnt worry too much about potentially missing anything as I ran for my life.
All production values, the graphics, sound, music, voice acting, animations etc are top notch, along with excellent level design, lighting, etc etc. Zero bugs/glitches.
Im struggling to think of anything that I can criticise, apart from the ending which I am mixed about. I think the only thing that didnt quite personally gel with me is that the character never took a weapon and went on the hunt - I would have with all but two antagonists. But then again, this was a game where you were playing a well defined character, and he wasnt a fighter, so fair enough.
EDIT: AH! I do have one criticism: there were no FOV option or other advanced graphics options. I play 2-3 feet from a 40" screen (immersion!). I like 100deg, whatever we had here felt like 90, so it wasnt terrible, but it didnt suit my preferences. Also, there should be options to turn off things like film grain, motion blur etc (I dont have these in real life, why would I want it in a game?!). But nothing was actually bad enough here to cause me to quit and google how to change these things in a config file, so while in principle its suboptimal, in practice it wasnt a concern. To Red Barrel: More options are always better as it allows customisations to our heterogenous preferences!
The last game that I enjoyed this much in this vein was Call of Cthulhu Dark Corners of the Earth (DCE) (sadly it crashes on steam, so I cant replay it). I think I prefer DCE because it had similar mechanics, but it also had locational damage which affected your mobility, and period weapons which were nicely modelled. On the flip side, DCE had some slower moments in the early game which went on perhaps too long, whereas the pacing between exploration, terror and fear in Outlast felt just right. I would love for Red Barrel to recreate DCE, or a game like that (ie - more Outlast please, but with some weapons thrown in to mix it up!).
I plan on buying an Occulus Rift when it is available, but I am not sure I want to play Outlast with it. There were more than a few moments when I found my heart racing, and I determinedly mentally calmed myself ("after all its just a game"). I dont know if I could take Outlast with a higher level of immersion. I'm not even sure I want to find out.

OVERALL RATING: 4/5
My opinion of this game has slightly changed over time, but nonetheless this game is still fun as heck to play with a group of friends!
I'll just go over everything in this game individually.
Versus Mode: 5/5
This is the main gamemode of Skyhook, and it's the best part of the game. You play using grappling hooks, which can be used to move around and attack. You can also melee to knock hooks away and to attack as well. The physics in this game are fantastic, and the gameplay is fast. The items that randomly pop in don't feel overpowered but they don't feel useless either.
Quest Mode: 3/5
People definitely seem to have mixed opinions on this mode, and I can see why. It's not especially fun, and sometimes easy difficulty levels can be so much more difficult when all the enemies shoot you at the same time. That being said quest mode is a good way to challenge yourself if you feel like you've mastered the game, and beating certain levels well enough unlocks new character skins.
Characters: 4.5/5
At the time of writing this review there are 5 playable characters. The only difference between characters is how they dodge, which is good, because huge character ability diversity could cause one character to be picked more than others for their usefulness. The characters themselves feel unique, and each one has a very creative design. Originally the developer planned at launch to have 3 unlockable characters, but at the time of this review it's only one, which is my only problem with this game's characters.
Overall, this game is fun to play with friends, and is definitely worth getting considering it's low price.

A friend got me this game as a Steam gift, so I figured I'd try it out! Here're my thoughts on Divinity II:
Pros
- The dialogue is actually pretty humorous, and it doesn't come off as if it's trying too hard. The guards at the beginning are funny. :P
- There's only a moderate level of customization options, BUT you can change your name, appearance, and even your gender and class at any time.
- The ability to mindread in exchange for experience adds a cool layer of depth you don't normally see to character interaction.
- Pretty good about not being entirely linear. You find yourself wandering around a lot, doing what you want to do, until you run into enemies that are too high for your level. That's really the main metric that makes you stop from venturing into certain areas.
- I'M A FRIGGEN DRAGON GUYS DUUUDE
Neutral
- There's a pretty even number of memorable and unmemorable characters you run into.
Cons
- The game isn't incredibly engaging. It feels like it's missing something, but I can't put my finger on what.
- The music is very sub-par and almost unfitting. I find myself pretty much always listening to external music through Spotify or something while playing.
- Melee is wayyy harder than being a ranger or mage. That's not too rare in RPGs, but it's pretty much by leagues and leagues here.
- The lack of romances makes me sad, just because I love those. Also, everyone reacts to you the exact same, no matter your race or gender.
- A lot of the guards' faces look exactly the same.
- You frequently get trapped in areas where the level around you is way too high and you have little way of knowing until you're already engaged in a fight. Some say the game is just "hard," but there's a pretty clear difference between needless reloads and a game being truly, properly challenging.
So there you have it. Divinity II is fun in its own way, but I can't play for longer than an hour or two at a time, for whatever reason. The game isn't engaging for long periods, I suppose.

"Divinity II" is a rather... interesting game. It is an RPG in the same vein as "Gothic" or "Two Worlds". But what makes this game unique? The dragon form of course! Yes, in "Divinity II" you can turn into a dragon at almost any time. Sounds fun, right? It totally is. I had a lot fun playing this game. However, the game does have some major flaws.
The character creation is very disappointing. There's a male and a female player model and a small selection of different faces and haircuts, that's about it. That character progression, however, is quite fantastic. Skill and attribute points can be freely distributed, making every kind of character possible. Want a ghost summoning ranger that wields two-handed swords? Totally possible.
One of the biggest issues with this game is its inconsistent difficulty. Some enemies are weak while others are powerful as hell, making combat often a bit frustrating. Close to the end of the "Ego Draconis" campaign a certain boss had an extremely powerful "Magic Blast" ability that killed me in one hit, leaving me no time to do anything at all, so I was forced to lower the difficulty to "casual".
Certain types of enemies are outright annoying to fight. I don't know why Larian thought it was a good idea to give enemy archers the "Stun Arrow" ability. Yes, they can stun you. And when there are more than 3 of them around, they can even stunlock you.
Some of the difficulty issues are offset by the regenerating health. When you're low on health, you can just hide somewhere and wait until you are at full health again.
Another problem is the dragon form itself. In human form you will fight different enemies than in dragon form, for some reason. Human-sized enemies will disappear once you enter the dragon form, and they will reappear again when you return to human form. I don't know why Larian did it like this, because it takes away a lot of the fun, in my opinion. Exploring Rivellon in dragon form is quite fun though. You can tell that the game's (small) world was crafted with great care. It features beautiful mountains, canyons, towers, everything. It looks fantastic.
It is pretty apparent that Larian put a lot of effort into the NPCs, as they are definitely one of the game's strengths. The voice acting and behavior of the NPCs feels quite realistic. The dialogues are a bit disappointing, though. Most of the dialogue options don't even change the outcome of the dialogue in any way. But you can read the minds of most NPCs, which will often reveal new dialogue options and quests.
I was quite surprised by the seamless transition between "Ego Draconis" and "Flames of Vengeance". Once the former's outro cinematic ends, the latter campaign's intro begins, without having to start a new game for "Flames of Vengeance". However, the expansion is quite disappointing, partly due to the fact that you're forced to play the majority of it without being able to use your dragon form.
The game's story is overwhelmingly unoriginal and I'm not a fan of the ending. It's lack of closure is rather frustrating. I hate it when developers end games like this and then don't release a sequel for several years. And with "Original Sin II" being in development right now, I doubt there will be a "Divinity III" any time soon...
Although "Divinity II" has a few flaws and even feels a bit incomplete sometimes (it is quite apparent that Larian wasn't able to release the game's full potential, likely due to time constraints), it is undeniably fun to play and I recommend it to anyone who is interested in RPGs.

Rating: 8/10
Overview: Isometric Action RPG
Similar Games: Bastion, Van Helsing, Dungeon Siege 3
The Good:
+ Art style and colour.
+ The combat is more engaging than your typical ARPG. Dodging and jumping are important if you want to stay alive.
+ Weapon skills feel good to use, every weapon type (hammer, shotgun, swords et. ) has 2 unique action skills associated with them.
+ The game features plenty of maps, each one as 5 normal and elite challenges, providing plenty of replay ability.
+ Mix and match different passive abilities to fit your play style
+ Toggle difficulty parameters i.e monsters do extra damage, monsters attack faster etc. to make the game more challenging
+ Boss battles are impressive and require some strategy to defeat them.
+ Multiplayer is still somewhat active
+ Soundtrack
The Average:
In terms of character builds, the game is not as robust as your average ARPG. There are no character classes, skill trees or gear you need to worry about. Skills are tied to the weapon you use. This is not a bad thing necessarily, as the game is more 'pick up and play' and gets you into the action quicker. If you are looking for a deep ARPG to play, this isn't the game you should be playing.
Using the same voice actor as the witcher was not the best idea. I feel like I'm playing the witcher as opposed to a new character. With a few changes, you could call this game the Witcher Action rpg.
The Bad
-This game has the exact same problem as Dungeon Siege 3; the loot is boring. Loot is an important aspect to any ARPG and this is one major aspect the game falters on.
- The story is boring and uninteresting. I found it very difficult to care about the characters or the world.
Conclusion
You saw the name, saw a few screen shots and thought this is a really bad action RPG clone. You would be wrong. This isn't a bad ARPG, it's just geared more to a 'pick up and play' style of game. I had a lot of fun with the game and if you enjoy replaying levels to complete challenges this game will provide many hours of fun.

This game isn't going to hit a magical "price/playtime" ratio but for $1.49 on sale, this game is so, so well worth it. It's relaxing and gorgeous, as well as fun to play. You could probably knock it out in about a half-hour of play, but that doesn't mean it's not worth the cash.

The 1 major selling point for this game, has to be the atmosphere.
The sound design, the level design, the level of detail, the animations, the voice acting (Geralt, people!), the special effects, it's all brilliant. It's so good, that after about an hour or 2 playtime, I need to quit the game and just sit and stare for a bit, to slow my heartrate a bit.
I guess some people might not like the fact that there isn't really a class system in this game, but on the other hand, you get dynamic class switching. All you do is open your inventory, change your load out, and you've changed your entire playstyle. It's really cool to experiment with all the different weapons - and so far, I've seen quite a few different ones.
There're a ton of dungeons, and also a random generated gauntlet type (I haven't been there yet, it unlocks at level 26 and I'm only 16), but it basically is a dungeon that increases difficulty through 5 stages.
The game has co-op as well, up to 4 Victors can play together. I dunno how this works either, but people seem to enjoy it, random grouping as well as with friends.
For 20 bucks, this game isn't expensive considering the amount of content you get. Anything cheaper, especially below 10 bucks, could be considered a steal/insta-grab.

It's biggest weakness is also its greatest strength -- the crushing difficulty, especially if you go for all the trinkets. Third installment of the neturnia game series released on steam, now it's hard not to openly compare it to the other two before it but so I won't really try, sorry. As far as game difficulty goes its in between the first and second one, the first Re:birth being the hardest and the second being the easiest.
The easiest point of this game is the shear number of characters you get though DLC (which appears be to DLC mostly if you have saves from the previous games rather then buying) outside of the DLC characters it has the smallest cast of playable characters being only the CPU's, (so take it as you want on the DLC characters being bad by making it easier or good to make up for the lack of characters).
Combat system is the same as the previous two with a few diffrences, first off collusium battles are easier now with the monsters being less OP, second off you are given the option of switching KO'd character with there back character, and third, the EX system of the game for combat has been drastly changed, rahter then a shared EX gadge that is shared by the party it is based on the individual characters SP, alsong with those changes SP regenerates a little per hit and all characters have there SP locked at 1000 (no increasing it this game). Along that some line of though I want to add this means you can't spam HDD all the time, your SP doesn't recover when you leave a dungeon, it only recovers from battle or items, but a small plusside (for the DLC characters at least) everyone has an HDD action, or rather none CPU's have Awakening, more or less a super sayain golden aura with boosted stats.
Music is still more or less the same with a few plans that can let you change the music (but only the default or a single alt.)
Another new addition (Which can be really annoying if your a completionist) is a challange system, basicly you do something a number of times and you unlock stuff (mostly small stat ups with the final level of the challanges being a large stat up, but also some plans), the ploblem here is that some of these are beyond annoying such as one challange where you have to run away from battle, the final level of the being run away from battle 3000 times (and again just one of several) and also it only applies to the active characters (meaning for the one were you have to walk around the map for so many meters you have to do with ALL the characters to competly complete it).
Story wise you'll see a lot of similarity between the anime version with some base setting from the second game (and somehow a lot of refrensing to the first). The story was good and had a lot of good build-up with a bit of acualy game history in it (you'll more or less see the game industries history be built up and refrenced a lot, specially with processors for the CPU you unlock frequently at the start of new chapters). Fans of the series most likly already know that Plutia is a main character so lots of great stuff to expect (Including a priceless scene between Iris Heart, IF, and Arfoir).
Overall tone of the game feels more like the first one with the more wacky and sillyness that you've come to love (or might come to love) from the series and managing to mix in nicely a somewhat serious tone channeling more of the same feel with the first Re:birth but with a lot more fourth wall breaking in this, to a point where even some of the villians do it.
Overall if your a fan of the neptunia series, or wanting to play a less intensive/serious RPG this is a good game to get and unlike the second Re:birth without any major game breaking DLC (except an experience booster plan but easy enough to ignore)

This game is intensely fun, and for a time I was addicted to it. Dealing with hordes of enemies is fun, being able to get a high level tower built that is then able to decimate the enemies on your lane feels amazing, managing multiple lanes and shutting down threats that may be able to break your tower defense is deeply engaging.
I had lots of fun comboing the towers and skills of my heroes together to amazing effect. From making anti air defenses attack the regular enemies in a lane via launching them into the air, electrocuting a enemy drenched in water, or introducing a frozen enemy to a high speed canonball was intensely satisfying.
And then you reach level 20.
To ease players into the game, as well as stopping new characters from getting stomped, you are gated into maps within a hero range. Aside from the first two tutorial tiers, each range is limited by 5 levels. As you ascend from 5-10, 10-15, and 15-20, new concepts are introduced such as physical / magical resistance of enemies per lane, ogre spawns during the final wave of a map, and in general new harder enemies that you need to deal with.
To complement this, you are introduced to a selection of maps for every level range that you are able to play on. The introduction tier gives you an easy 3 lane map, while harder levels can have up to 6 lanes, and more if you let sub-cores die during the map. The idea behind this is to give each map in the game a chance to leave an impression on a player, so when you get to maximum level, you would have likely played every map in the game.
The Throne Room is a map you get access to from level 20 onwards.
In general, the game has many growing pain issues. The explosive traps just don't do their weight in damage, compared to a turret that costs the same amount of points. There's plenty of others though, some spec skills per hero are useless because their effect is too weak per skill point spent. Some "towers" are useless due to just being too weak, or being redundant, largely a mixture of both at the same time. The resistance of a lane I mentioned earlier does provide notable damage reduction, resulting in a loss of efficiency per lane if you attack them with their resisted element. Unfortunately, the resistance is low enough that it's still perfectly viable to defend a lane with the "incorrect" damage type if you're specced for tower damage in the first place.
Playing through the game can be a frustrating experience at times, as any game where you have contact with another human being can be. Sometimes you'll have a good group that can do the hard maps that you've been struggling to do with other randoms. Other times you'll be playing with three huntresses that insist that explosive traps are useful and they'll spam their lanes, and your lanes with them, sucking up the Defense Units you need to build towers that can actually kill enemies. In general though, everyone seems to really enjoy playing the game and you'll have an enjoyable experience playing the game.
Unless you reach level 20 where the only map played is Throne Room, one guy asks for all the tower building mana from everyone and everyone else plays along because why play a game when you can just not play a game? The Throne Room is a map that can be effectively cheesed with minimal effort. I can't even describe what happens because there's so many ways to lock this map down. This map has reached the point where people are posting videos about how they beat it on the hardest difficulty using the bare minimum of turrets, whereas the other maps are a struggle to even complete without a good team.
This so far amazingly fun game is thoroughly ruined by the community that doesn't like to play it.

As I accomplished every achievement, and, being a big fan of this game at the same time, I think that I already have enough understanding of the game as a basis to write a review, let's weigh up the pros and cons first:
+ Funny and long storyline, 3 endings for players to choose, a walkthrough would take about 25-40 hours, depending on your choice to enjoy the story and gameplay.
+ Extremely cute characters makes players immerse rapidly into the game.
+ A wide range of varieties of weapons, items and crafts (plans) are provided.
+ Almost impossible to get stuck (because of difficulty) in the game as you can always gain reasonable amount of XP (a.k.a Experience Points) from enemies that have similar strength as you.
+ Pretty soundtracks can be found here.
+ Well-designed CGs.
- Without achievement guides, it is too easy to miss important items that are necessary for further accomplishments in the game.  This problem was even more serious in earlier Neptunia games. It is recommended to read the guide carefully before starting the game if you want to get as many achievements as possible. Not so much of a big deal as a disadvantage, but still, better to be aware of missable events ^^.
As I mentioned, I’m a sincere fan of this series, so I’ll try to cover as many general aspects as I can possibly think of:
This game, which can be called HDN re birth 3 (on PC) or Victory (on PS3) for short, is a tactical role-playing game in which players take control of 4 characters both in the front line and the rear line (meaning 8 in total). This makes this latest product different in a more catchy way, probably easier to get the gist of the gameplay compared to the 2 earlier Neptunia games; for new players of HDN, I suggest you to play this first (like me), because this one gives less penalty compared to the 2 earlier ones. When a character dies, for example, in HDN Victory, the system still allow switches between the K.Oed character and the rear character, while in others you need to revive the dead before doing so, also, you have all the characters from the earlier games to use, and so on…….. but don't worry, the story in this game is settled completely differently from the earlier ones, only the same characters remains
.
However, sometimes you will still face challenges, in this case, there are two ways:
Develop a strategy or to train characters by fighting monsters from time to time. You can slay bosses which are difficult to beat at the first encounter more easily with the 2nd solution, but in my case for example, I always try to beat the boss with strategies in spite of being difficult, which wine and dines my own tactical strategy ^^, and well, sometimes this takes time -.- .
About the characters, well, let's say that you will never have enough with them, their cuteness is really, unbeatable (even I cannot resist >^<), in my opinion, this is a special and important feature for this series, every character is different, which is why the use of strategy becomes interesting here
.
Speaking of items, weapons and crafts, we have an abundant amount of which in this game, this keeps leveling up the character’s ability as players upgrade their equipments while training. Crafts, which are called plans in this game, play an extremely important role in this game, some plans gives you extremely powerful weapons while others provide very useful items, many maps even require the corresponding plan to be unlocked, therefore, as far as I’m concerned, it is important to sometimes pause from advancing the storyline in order to get some plans done, this makes the gameplay a lot easier. There are different ways to get a plan done, some requires you to gather items from enemy drops, others needs you to gather ingredients in the field of a dungeon...... et cetera. Don't worry about getting bored, even exploring them can be fun ^^.
Soundtracks and CGs in this game are also well done. Idea Factory, together with Compile Heart, created its own style of character’s painting design which is genuinely unique, you can’t find anime artworks with similar ingenuity of manga creation elsewhere. Soundtracks are generally a good background support to the gameplay, although I can’t think of anything extraordinary, these soundtracks are special for me personally in terms of melody, hopefully you will enjoy them as well ^^.
About potential bugs, I don't think that I encountered more 5 bugs after 82 hours of gameplay, so for me, the gameplay is pretty solid. I'm sorry for players who often experiences crashes in game, I am not really helpful here...
Thank you for reading this review, I hope that this did give you a general idea on the system of the game as well as the main features. However, I have to say that even if it did, it remains only a vague introduction, there are tons and tons of things which only you can discover in this game, no descriptions can really work for HDN series. The only way to learn and have a deep understanding of it is to give it a try ^^.

Hyperdimesdion Neptunia Re;Birth3 V Generation is the sequel to the last game, Hyperdimension Neptunia Re;Birth2 Sisters Generation. However, the stories did not connect to each other.
After I played the last two games, I like this the most because of a lot of new features that added to this game. And even more content than ever. You can easily put a lot of hours to this game. Trust me. Now lets talk about advantage and disadvantages.
Advantages:
-+1 Combo: You can perform 5 combos right now and another EX Finishes.
-Easier to explore Stella's Dungeon: Instead of explore the actual dungeon in Re;Birth2, this game become "Areas". One area includes a lot of items. Easier to finish. And you can deploy her while you are in dungeon too.
-Easier to acquire plans: Plans that you will get you will find less plans because Stella will find it for you.
-Explore the actual Nation: Instead of every nation in the same map, you have the large map that includes nations and each natio have it's own map.
-More dungeons than ever: Means you can grind easier.
-Leader effect: You will get bonus stats based on what character is the leader.
-Better looking menu: Why I frogot about this. It's easier to understand.
Disadvantages:
-Some crashes and framerate drops: Still better than the second game. But in first game I got zero crashes and framerate drops. Especially wheh I fight the CPUs I got bad framerate drops. Even I have an awesome rig.
