There are two complaints I have:
1. When playing online, there were some network issues. No lag, but on one level only the host could see an elevator moving. On another level, when one player picked up a coin, it never moved for the other player's screen (and actually both players claimed the coin that round).
2. The unlockables are not universal. If I grab a box that unlocks a level, then that level is only avialable on games I am hosting. And, sometimes the person who gets the box doesn't get the unlockable! I got the squirrel character when my friend grabbed the box (and he was hosting). It's annoying to only have one person "progress" in the game at the expense of others, and especially annoying when one person puts in the work for no gain.
Overall, though, I like it and expect it a good, laugh-inducing game. So long as you aren't one of those people who throw furious tantrums when things don't go your way!

I'd consider Outlast to be way more of a thriller game with jump scares, than a horror game.
There's usually a point in these kinds of games where the scare tactics fade away, and you notice the mechanics behind them. Once that occurs, the game suddenly has a lot less tension, since instead of being super afraid of the monster pursuing you, you're now just paying attention to their looping routine around the level.
That happened within the first 20 minutes of Outlast for me. It's not necessarily a terrible thing, but it did remove a lot of tension from the game from that point on. It continued to degrade from there, as you find out that dying is often more advantageous than hiding, as it gets you to the starting point in the many "Go find three Fuses/Turn two cranks/Pull two lever" 'puzzles' the game throws at you. When caught, you get a very clear look at a 3D rendered generic looking monster, which tears away any remaining fear of them. The sound design does a pretty good job at trying to restore some of it, and the chase sequences remained pretty okay because of that alone.
The thing that made games like Amnesia really special to me, is the looming sense of dread. Outlast never really had that for me. The nightvision camera effects were cool though, and the game does have it's moments of legitimate spooks. It's just more often than not, you're left with a bad stealth game, with increasingly ineffective jump scares.
I'll still probably check out the DLC, since I liked the game well enough. I just wished that the spooks lasted longer than they did.

Nothing here is necessarily going to blow your mind, it's a very small, brief tale of a woman revisiting her old home and bathing in childhood nostalgia, both good and bad, but in such small things comes great beauty. The simple act of slowly wandering around a field under a twilight sky can be incredibly meditative in itself, listening to the rustling leaves high up in the autumn trees or watching the tall grass sway with the gentle breeze. It's very easy to become lost in the setting or to spend the meandering strolls between points of interest just imagining how the subject of the story passed the time in these same places, too. Even if there's nothing to really do, just inhabiting a setting like this feels like reward enough.

The overall area of play (and I use the word "play" here very loosely), is relatively small, and while there is narration to accompany some of your discoveries, it's very much a case here of "show, don't tell" and letting the player fill in the blanks with their own imagination. That approach can be a powerful tool and help make for a much more personal experience as we imprint our own meaning and significance upon the story, and is definitely one of this game's great strengths.

Even as low as the standard price is, it may be an issue for some people given the short length and minimal content, but still, if you're feeling contemplative and are in the mood for a pleasant walk around some fields and woodlands on a nice day in the South, then I can think of no better place to visit than here.

A tl;dr to start
--------------------
Pros: Great lines, great lore, a solidly long campaign.
Cons: Frustrating gameplay, unintuitive progression and a ridiculous waste of potential
Overall: If you took the 'game' out of this game, it would be stellar.
--------------------
Divinity has always been strong with story and the world really nets any player willing to immerse themselves. But I am time and again flung right back out when I find myself fighting the game itself instead of enemies, puzzles or the like. A myriad of problems ranging from punishingly steep character progression costs, many quests requiring an hour or more of searching for a button in a badly lit room or being forced to trudge through huge enemy level jumps.
The game is meant to be difficult, but there is a difference between punishing a wrong choice and requiring the player to save every few seconds for fear of being trapped in an area twice their level. It is a roller coaster of geart narratives, hilarious and deep characters, and heaps of dissapointment. For every heartfelt chuckle or legitimate moment of curiousity I had there was a moment or three of a frustrated sigh, loading the last save and trying once again to complete some menial task or fight. There were a few moments where the narrative progression almost made it all worth it, but sadly the game's peaks do not outweigh its trenches. Worst of all, the second bit (Flames of Vengeance) greeted the player with a choice, end sequence and resolution that, to put it quite blunty, felt like it was pulled from the nearest rancid pile of trash, slapped on for the sake of completion.
I am incredibly dissapointed to not recomend this game, as the world, characters and overall plot are some of the best I've seen in a fantasy RPG. But the fumbling in basic gameplay, design and simply the actual 'game' bits of this title ruin it as an overall experience.
I get what they were going for, but save your bandwidth. There's not much going on here at all.

cons?:

It's a super hard platformer similar to games like They Bleed Pixels or Super Meat boy. You will die a lot.
However instead of expanding your movement from the basic platformer set, the game simplifies your controls to three buttons: left, right and 'action.' Action is mapped to 'w' 's' 'up' 'down and 'space.' I have three complaints for this game, the first is that there is no button remapping. For this style of game i like to use IJKL instead of arrows keys to move due to my broken left arrow key. Luckily i can still play, but it's a feature that's always very helpful. This super simple control setup means VVVVVV is all about the small moment to moment challanges. Think of games like geometry dash where the big picture isn't as important as whats right in front of you.
While the game is technically a metroidvania( in that you have a huge open space with which you can explore a world with tons of little collectables) the levels themselves are super linear. The rooms are rarely ever larger than the screen and the jumps are super tight. This game is hard, you will die a lot. With games like this i always appreciate when the dev goes out of their way to make every room feel fair. When you move from one room to the next in metroidvania style the game almost always makes the area you immediately enter in safe. Not only this, but the game liters the area with checkpoints, often two checkpoints in the same room so you never have to do more than two hard jumps in a row.
This simplistic style of game however leads to my next problem: the only saves when you reach a teleporter (one exists at the start of every level), not when you hit a checkpoint. This means even if you hit a really hard jump and you're just so done with this part of the game, you just just quit and try a different level in metroidvania fashion. If you quit all the progress you make up to that point is completely gone, and it feels the whole spirit of metroidvania doesn't exist. There's not really mid-level teleporters or unlockable shortcuts, you have to finish every level in one shot (which probably isn't too bad for the average gamer as the game is fairly short, but i found this pressure immensely stressful and made the hard levels that i can't afford to quit less fun).
My final issue with the game is extremely minor. Let me say at this point that this game is incredibly fun and for nobody is this next point going to be a dealbreaker. If you like what you read, pick up the game. This next point is mostly for the devs of the game.
I hate how all the achievements are focused on adding some vague sense of replayability to the game. Most fo the achievements are something like "beat the game in less then 200 deaths" "beat the game in less then 100 death." There are time trial achievements, which i don't mind but these achievements seem geared towards people who excessively play your game, and i suspect none of those people need achievements to motivate them to %110 complete your game. To me, achievements are best used to encourage people to roleplay in a game, really push them towards the core engagement. Things like "collect all collectables" fit this idea for metroidvanias because the goal of metroidvanias is to explore a lot. Things like "beat the game again and git gud" aren't something the average player is and should ever be interested in. If you're trying to cater to a hardcore audience, i feel achievements probably aren't the ideal reward.

At first glance it may look like another Diablo clone, but it is clear that a lot of thought went into this game. It is a really fun game with some strategic depth to it. The narrator reminded me of Bastion, at times. You sort of build a ... bond with the treacherous git.
Unlike other games of its kind, the character path is not determined by characters' skill but through a combination of demon power talismans, destiniy cards and the suit he wears. You can make minute changes to each one to suit your needs at the moment. Leveling up only changes how many destiny points you can have on your deck so there is still a difference between a low level and a high level character but the mechanism is ingenious.
Then there is the bounty/treasure map mechanic. Everyonce in a while you will get a bounty or a treasure map which requires you to visit old haunts for new loot and monsters to fight. You can share and use other players' bounties as well (there is a forum thread for this purpose). This combined with elite challenges unlocked after finishing the game adds a lot of replay value.
If you are a Linux user, you may be glad to hear that the game works great in Linux.

Victor Vran is a really interesting case of taking your typical ARPG hack'n'slash game and mixing in some more direct control than the genre got us used to, as well as turning the class and build issue on its head. What we get is a really enjoyable exercise in mowing down hundreds of enemies without much repetitiveness kicking in.
Character progression is tied to loot much more than usually in such games - since Victor has no skills of his own, only the set of them dependant on the weapons (you can quickly swap between two) wielded, the best tools of destruction you get are going to influence your experience quite a bit until the next big drop. And we are talking real variety. With the sword in hand the game is a crit-based slash-fest, shotgun provides some more control and a slight rhythm-element, scythes add secondary resource to strengthen your attacks, tomes provide great positional control at the cost of engaging in a 'minigame' of picking up special powerups... it is quite a treat, and no two types of a weapon work the same. In the later parts, Legendary versions of the weapons start appearing - these don't just give different stats, they also directly modify some of the abilities granted by your weapon.
To back these up, Vran can also equip up to 5 Destiny Cards, that grant either passive or triggered bonuses (and can randomly have another one in the form of Wicked/Divine boon), two Demon Powers (additional activated skills, weapon-agnostic) and an Outfit, which modifies stats and/or base mechanics of the game, usually related to the charging of Overdrive, a fancy name for what is basically a rage-bar that powers Demon Powers.
And that's it. No talents, no skills, no attributes... quite a novelty, with its own set of upsides and downsides. The good is, once you find a weapon type you like more than the previous you use, switching is not a problem. With a proper set of Cards, Powers, and Outfits, any combination of weapons can be re-adjusted to. Which, in turn, kills much of the possible repetitiveness.
Thankfully, the high dependence on gear doesn't hurt as much - the crafting system in Victor Vran is built to make sure you can continue using just the weapon you like the most; leftover loot can be used to increase critical chance, damage, and power of special properties of your weapon, going even as far as adding one property of your liking (provided you can 'craft' it). By combining lesser weapons of a specific rarity and type the player has a chance to craft a higher-rarity weapon of the same type, so getting better sort of your favourite weapon isn't all that hard either.
At the same time, this means that no specialized and truly intricate builds are achievable. Which becomes even more apparent as some of game's balance issues are revealed. Victor Vran favours critical hits by the virtue of having a lot of effects that can be triggered either on a critical hit or overkill (killing an enemy with quite a bit more damage than was needed), of which critical hits are easier to achieve. If you back it up with the fact that Sword is a premiere critical-hit based weapon and Sword-centric Destiny Card is stupidly powerful for sustaining yourself... yeah, you can guess how I built my character pretty much by default. There are also slight concerns about some weapons being just too unwieldy or fun but not powerful enough (non-legendary Tomes are problematic, and Lighting Gun seems like the clunkiest thing ever to me) but it might be on the fact that I wasn't the greatest player skill-wise.
Despite the above, you can still enjoy any sort of weapon combo you decide to stick with, and if it happens to be too powerful... well, the game has you covered. With 5 activable Curses, which strengthen your enemies in specific ways while increasing the experience gain, you can quite easily make sure that the enemies can and will overpower you. Mix in the map-unique Challenges, which are sets of arbitrary tasks to perform for additional rewards (and 5 more of them for each map are achievable once you complete the game once) and there is a lot to do.
So, the gameplay is great, but what else is there? ... not much, actually.
The story is more of a throw-away, even if it doesn't present itself terribly. It is just uninspired and serves mostly as a reason for all the slaughter to occur, rather than a point of focus. Voice acting is kept on a sensible level, aside from how edgy our protagonist appears - both in lines and delivery, but the lines aren't inspired all that much overall. Side characters have some interesting bits to say sometimes, and the Voice proves to be amusing on a handful of maps, but that's about it. Just a slight spicing for the gameplay.
Art and music actually positively surprised me, especially the latter - fits the mood perfectly, even if the mood is built on the premise of your typical 'spooky' invasion of countless ghosts, skeletons, vampires, gargoyles, spiders... if not for occasional elementals, you could say that the entire range of enemies is just Halloween scares. Thankfully, the lack of interesting creations is backed up by how varied their methods of attack and ways to deal with them are.
I can safely recommend this title, great fun for a good price - at the time of writing, I had 22 hours clocked, which is enough to complete the game with around 70% base challenges done. Which puts me at roughly 35% of them now that new ones appeared.

Victor Vran is a breath of fresh air in a genre(arpg) that has toed the line for decades.  It offers three different control schemes, gamepad, mouse & keyboard, or just mouse which is the usual fare. The default is WASD + mouse which is very fluid and engaging.
You can jump and defensive roll, which is something not often seen in these types of games, both are used to good effect in evading or exploring the various maps for secret areas.
As of writing this I'm merely 3 hours in, but the game has impressed me enough for me to take a short break to sing it's praises.   Now to the details...
Outfits mostly just change how you play the game in small but important ways such as one giving you overdrive(ultimate attack)  by being damaged, one that charges when you crit, and one that slowly charges on it's own and will stay filled.
The loot reminds me of Guild Wars 2, where a base item type will grant you 2 different special attacks along with the tried and tested affixes that range from finding more items, health leech, armor penetration and attack speech.
The voice acting is fairly solid, and humorous while the graphics will not amaze you but they are quite good in their own right both the sound and visuals mesh expertly together.
The game runs and plays smooth as butter. (I'm not sure how the online is but it sports 4 player co-op with chat rooms and the like)
Really, if you like ARPGs-  GET THIS GAME NAO!

Victor Vran is a fun action RPG (diablo/torchlight/etc) with a few interesting twists.  You play as Victor Vran - no matter what style of character you intend to make. There are no skill trees or tranditional point sytems.  When you level up, you get a pre-set bonus and then one of 3 items.
The variety in the gameplay comes with the fact that attacks and specials are linked to what type of weapon you have. Each weapon type has 3 attacks.  On top of that, you have charge attack specials, which are loot-based specials that are triggerable when a meter is full (it fills up when you attack stuff).
One other point of interest is that the game is split into actual levels. Each level has challanges associated with it if you choose.
Pros:
- Play whatever style you like. The ability to use anything is nice.
- Challenges will keep you coming back (and post-game loot hunting).
- A good challenge solo without being impossible.
- Multiplayer is implemented well. Start as lobby that anyone can join.
Cons:
- Not many, honestly.  If you like these kinds of games, you will dig it.

Few people are aware of my crippling video game addiction (mostly because I spent too much time playing therefore I have no social life) so today I’m outing myself and putting this problem to good use.
Banished is the indie game brainchild of one man, Luke Hodorowicz, the founder of Shining Rock Software.  There isn’t a specific back story to the game; all you know is that you were banished (for an unknown reason) to a remote area and it is up to you to plan the city and keep your villagers alive.  It’s like a hybrid of Starcraft, SimCity, and the Civilization series.
I've spent roughly 48 hours playing this game.  The first thing I noticed is how effing difficult this game is.  I started playing on medium difficulty, fair weather, and disasters enabled.  After a quick and painful death about 20 minutes into my adventure I had to switch to easy with mild weather.  I left disasters enabled because I couldn’t 100% cheat.
Strategy is absolutely key in this game.  Villagers need to have enough food and firewood to make it through the winter.  Some clothes would be nice but my villagers quickly realized they can’t always get what they want.  Without depleting my resources too badly I was able to set up a woodcutter, fields, livestock pens, fishing dock, hunting lodge, and a house for people gathering materials (food, herbs, etc) in the woods.  Boom!  Everyone had a job and the town made it through the harsh winter with enough food and firewood.
It was about this time I realized the game also mocks you.  I was celebrating my victory over winter by looking for a place to build a marketplace and a trading post when I suddenly got alarms that villagers were dying.  First three villagers, then ten…What the ♥♥♥♥?  My boyfriend would dub this episode “The Spring of Death.”  It all started with the tornado that killed all but five villagers.  They started to rebuild their houses and stockpiles and just when it looked like they might bounce back…they ran out of food and died.
Overall, the range of play is great.  The maps are large and plentiful.  Each map (I’ve only played three but there are many more) has a water supply for fishing docks and trading posts.  Some locations are easier to play than others.  The location where all my villagers were wiped out was particularly difficult because it was surrounded by water and trees with little room for movement immediately.  Hence the total destruction of everyone living within three feet of each other.
Unlike many strategy games players have everything they need right from the start.  All players really need to be concerned with is hunting down raw materials like wood, iron, stone, and coal.  Otherwise all buildings, skills, occupations, livestock, seeds, etc. are immediately available for construction and use.  This may be off-putting for some gamers but I didn’t mind as it just made me think a bit more about strategy: Do I want a schoolhouse to teach children to be more efficient laborers or do I want the church to keep up village moral (unhappy villagers are not useful laborers)?
There is no story line which is great because I hate to play a plot based game.   Also it doesn’t appear to have a finish line either which is new to me. There is no way to “win”.  The whole purpose of the game is simply to survive and grow your town into a thriving medieval metropolis.  Occasionally things pop up where villagers might steal food and you have to decide how to handle that but there is no central plot based play.
I loved this game.  Hardcore.  Even when I knew I wasn’t going to be able to survive a particular map I still gave it my all (I got a little involved) for the sake of the villagers.  I think that’s the thrill of the game: knowing that I could lose at any moment made the little victories that much sweeter.  Well worth the frustration and the money.

Skyhook is a 4 player local multiplayer arena fighting game centering around a grappling hook mechanic and one hit kills. The game is similar to games like Towerfall and Samurai Gunn. It is very easy to pick up and learn, and has a decently high skill ceiling that involves reaction-based dodging and good usage of the grappling hook to get around.
Every player has a hookshot, which allows you to cling onto platforms and move around the arena quickly. The hookshot also works as a weapon, allowing you to kill other players, along with a melee mechanic. At any point, however, you're able to dodge, which gives you invulnerability frames, allowing you to pass through attacks. Each character has a different style of dodge, which is the defining factor making them unique.
Skyhook offers both a good multiplayer and single player experience. With a roster of 5 characters, and 4 different game modes, the multiplayer is fun and addicting. The controls are very responsive, and any mistakes you make don't feel like it's the fault of the game. Skyhook offers a good amount of content for it's current price. ($10)
Multiplayer fights are the main draw to Skyhook. As previously stated, there are 5 characters and 4 modes. There's additionally 5 different arena types, each with 2 maps each. The maps contain unique elements, turrets, moving platforms, and drive-able ships, but none of these elements are overburdening and take away from the game itself. Additionally there are items delivered randomly via chests, offering various, but not overbearing effects.
The main game mode is straightforward, be the last one alive in a fight where everyone has a set amount of lives. The other modes include 'skyball' where you have to carry and throw a ball into the enemy's goal, 'grab the loot' which requires you to hold on to a bag to increase your score, and a mode that limits the amount of hooks you can shoot, with the only way to reload being standing on a platform. These modes are fairly unique, and don't feel like just a side-thought to the main game.
There is no online multiplayer currently, only local multiplayer. The developer has expressed interest in an online mode, but this is not guaranteed.
The single-player experience has not been neglected. There is a quest mode to the game that offers several unique challenges, each with their own individual high scores and achievable medal tiers. There are no online leaderboards for the top scores, however. This mode also allows you to unlock additional skins for characters, as well as the unlockable stage and 5th character.
Additionally, this game has bot AI that allows you to play the multiplayer modes by yourself. While the AI performs well in most scenarios, it has a tendency to sometimes fall off the stage or sometimes get stuck, though these issues are not terribly bad. The AI has extreme difficulty with the lava stages, however, and will often jump itself into lava a lot.
If you are looking for an enjoyable local multiplayer game that allows you to easily pick up and play with a group of friends, I would recommend this game. If you are looking for strictly a single-player game, this may not be the best choice, but you may be interested in picking it up when it's on sale.

A good RPG game that is very much in the Larian mold, though it does have a few blemishes.
The (ground) combat is quite basic, aim at a target and mouse click for each attack (no combos, just attacks) with a hotbar for skills, potions, etc.
Combat in dragon form is... underwhelming sadly. Much the same as ground combat in terms of mechanics but with the added annoyance that normal ground enemies despawn when you take flight so you can't even make a good zombie bbq.
The actual combat difficulty swings between very easy and keyboard-breakingly hard, depending on how tanky you are and if you get stun-locked into place while every critter in the area takes a shoe to your scaley butt.
The storyline is good, but not earth-shattering and if you have never played the previous Divinity games you may be left scratching your head as to who certain characters are and why they are so significant.
The voice acting ranges from being solid and entertaining to hillari-bad, but overal its tollerable.
The graphics are pretty enough, though not jaw-dropping and the game's performance is fairly solid most of the time, with occasional weirdness like the odd "falling through the world" glitch cropping up a couple of times and a persistently occuring choppiness and slow-down that kept cropping up after the game had been running for a few hours.
So where (if at all) does this game shine? For me, Divinity II shines in the humour that persists throughout the game. There are references, easter eggs and zany antics cropping up throughout the game, but they are rarely rubbed into your face. Rather, when you spot them you can smile to yourself or facepalm at one or another.
Score-wise, I give
a 7 out of 10. An enjoyable title set in an established world which fans will enjoy, marred by a slightly temperamental game engine and a B+ narrative. If you like RPGs then its worth playing at least once.

As a little girl in a remote US town you have just missed the bus to school and decide to explore the surroundings of your house reminiscing about the experiences you had there: after a bit you'll muster the courage to go to your father's room, with whom you have a very difficult relationship, to get something that'll let you have at least a measure of freedom.
Home is Where One Starts offers a short but quite interesting story, it's just a shame the gameplay as a whole is made dull by a slow walking speed and areas that feel too empty.
-the story itself, as narrated by the protagonist, is simple but engaging enough: it also manages to have a few truly heartfelt moments
-the voice actress does a pretty good job
-while the graphics are quite simple they work well enough
-nice soundtrack
-some textures are downright ugly
-the walking speed is horribly slow and this makes exploration a boring chore
-some items are hidden in really hard to find or remote places, this paired with the slow walking speed makes trying to find them a truly dull and frustrating affair
-for a game so interested in story and memories the fact quite a lot of interactive objects have no voiceovers attached is truly a missed chance
-it's very short
Home is Where One Starts is a decent story-driven walking simulator with a good concept and is able to provide some great food for thought to those willing to overlook its shortcomings. I did enjoy the story told by the girl and the moment of pure freedom the ending provides but the walks between important places/objects were dull at best due to the terrible walking speed paired with an explorable zone that, while not overly large, is big enough to make your lethargic movements a problem. The fact some objects are also very well hidden kinda goes against the fact the player'd be able to experience the story...why do I have to wander the woods aimlessly to find an important object? It's not fun and serves no real purpose.
As mentioned before the fact many objects can be picked up and examined but provide no voiceover is also a shame...sure I can imagine a story for them but I think it'd have been much better if the girl told us why they seem meaningful enough to be picked up and how they ended up where they are.
Home is Where One Starts sadly aeppeared after games like Dear Esther and Gone Home gave us much better examples in the genre and it suffers from it. That said I still enjoyed my time with the game and that's why I'm giving a thumbs up despite its problems.
Should you buy it? It depends. If you're ok with the aimless wandering or with following a guide so that you can cut on the painfully slow exploration then go for it, the story has enough merits to warrant a playthrough. If not you can safely skip it and go for better games in the genre. Just be sure to get it for the 1$ sale price or on a bundle.

Verdun is one of those games where you go in thinking it's all skill based, and keep that mindset for the first few hours of gameplay. The pistols and rifles require a large amount of skill to wield properly, which is rightfully so. But then you stumble along an MG and go 40 and 7. 10/10, historically accurate. Especially feel immersed with squad names in this game like "No Frenchies In Our Trenchies" and "My Baguette is Long and♥♥♥♥♥♥♥quot;. Devs really outdid themselves.
But in all seriousness, the devs did a fantastic job balancing the game and making it fun to play. What most people don't seem to realize is that the classes counter each other. Machine gun kits are countered by rifle kits, rifle kits are countered by trench raiding kits, and trench raiding kits are countered by machine gun kits. It's very interesting how a team that communicates in team chat to counter the enemy almost always wins. This game is also fairly realistic. You aren't going to be a one man army in this game, rushing into trenches and murdering the entire enemy team. Most semi-automatic pistols can down you in two bullets from across No Man's Land. If you can handle spending the first few games getting creamed, then this game will quickly become a favorite due to its unique pacing, ultra-realistic theme, and rewarding gameplay.
My only complaint is that you always have 7 to 8 magazines/clips with almost every gun. I think you shouldn't have so much ammo that running out is never a problem. A large facet of World War 1 was that both sides had to scramble for equipment because they weren't used to fielding such large armies. Maybe the devs should reduce the ammo sizes to 3 reloads. Maybe they should implement a feature where you can pick up the guns of the deceased. Maybe they should make it so that the longer the game goes on, the less ammo you spawn with. hmmm....the product page fairly well describes this games story actually:
" is a short, first-person exploration game in the same vein as Dear Esther or Gone Home. It’s an experience where every object has been carefully placed to tell a poignant story—a story about childhood, hope, and the miracle of memory. You play as a little girl from a broken home somewhere in the American South. Exploring the lonely countryside reveals clues and vignettes which help the player answer the question of where home is—and how one can get there"
although maybe some of that is actually a bit more ambiguous in the game itself.
That said, it was a pleasant little journey around the little girls home, and the triggers for unlocking memories were cool (or rather, the items and places were....). It was just a very nice way to spend a half hour or so. Definitely wander around and click on any objects that are different than the normal trash lying around, and wander everywhere. There are invisible fences (that are sort of indicated by visible fence posts, lol), so you really cant wander off that far and there is generally something to find in every direction.

Napoleon: Total War is easily the most divisive of all Total War games. Some folks love it, some folks hate it. It is, to be fair, an almost carbon copy of Empire at first glance. The most noticeable difference is that Napoleon concentrates exclusively on Europe whereas Empire allows the player to conquer the globe.
Beyond first blush, Napoleon does feature some improvements over Empire that make it worth consideration. Chief of those is better coding - Napoleon is accepted by most to be a much more stable and better running game than Empire. It is also better looking. AI is supposedly markedly better, however that is debatable. There are a number of mods available that greatly improve the Napoleonic experience - but you're fine running the stock game.
If Empire and Napoleon look too similar to you - if muskets and dragoons are all the same to you, you may prefer Empire over Napoleon due to the globe. But... If, like me, you have a fascination with the Napoleonic Wars, you owe it to yourself to give Napoleon: Total War - beyond dominating Europe, there is also a series of historical battles and campaigns that are very enjoyable.

I first played MM in the 90s and had fond memories. I picked up MM6 as part of the sell here on Steam intendeing a few hours of fun over the holidays. I was disappointed.
I think the basic problem with this game is that it doesn't know what it wants to be when it grows up. It has some character development but not enough to hold one's interest. It has city development but the options are straight forward and uninteresting. Most of my time was spent fighting battles and this is the most disappointing part of the game.
The battles are highly artificial and repetitive. The battle board is always the same size with perhaps a few rocks or tree stumps thrown about. There is no ZOC so the enemy just walks around your army. Many tactics therefore make use the edges or corners, giving it the feel of a chess game . You can only deploy 7 units. The size of the units is not constrained, so I had my 1200 archers next to my 33 spearmen. I just couldn't get the feeling of fighting a real fantasy battle. Worst of all, it just felt like the same thing again and again.
BTW, if you don't have a stable full time internet connection you will not want this game. Unless you are online you are not allowed to have many in game perks. If you lose the your connection in the middle of the game it just dumps you out and you can't get back in until the connection is up again. An off line mode is offered, but once you go online again, there is no way to go back to off line.
I still think there is a market niche for a game like this if it achieves a better blend of character, city and army development. MM6 is close but just doesn't get there.

This game can be complex at first. It might take a while getting used to, but if you are a world war II buff, definitely get this.
Especially so  if you felt like Hearts of Iron IV was not even a challenge at all. Seriously, 200 hours on HOI 3 and all I got to show for it are 2 full games playing as Germany Conquering the world and some random playing of several minors here and there that lasted until 1939 when♥♥♥♥♥♥hit the fan and I just quit. Have not even touched any of the Allied or the USSR as I am daunted by the task of playing them.
Meanwhile, on HOI 4, everything is simplified and while it gave more flexibility in terms of diplomacy (Major Nations now have national focuses, allowing them to go ahistorical such as France joining the Comintern, as compared to HOI 3 where Factions were considerable more static. AI Italy, in a normal game of HOI 3 would almost certainly join the Axis all the time). While the role playing element was highly fun in HOI 4, the warring side of the game was lacking and did not show any semblence of the depth and micro that HOI 3 had. It simply did not satisfy the military nous within me.
Fighting the war in HOI 4 is like colouring in a colouring book. (Assuming you arent doing something insane like world conquest with Tannu Tuva). In the end, you still got a complete picture but it just doesnt feel as satisfying as HOI 3. Fighting in HOI3 is like drawing on a canvas. It was tedious but the picture that you get at the end is damn well more satisfying. You felt like a real commander, microing each individual unit to help you gain victory. You feel more like an accomplished artist, not some 7 year old that was instructed to go shade some circles in a colouring book.
You could just hand over your units to AI, much like HOI 4, but you won't cos the AI that controls your units here is rudimentary and should only really be used for garrisoning conquered lands and swatting rebels that pop up. The HOI 4 AI was meh, but it was functioning.
Both games are good in my biased opinion (I always dreamt about directing military operations when I was young so this series was pretty much a dream come true for the armchair strategist in me) but both have pros and cons. HOI 3 is much harder to get into and very terrifying for a newbie but it feels more rewarding. HOI 4 is good in that games dont take as long as they do in HOI 3 and it is a much gentler entry into the world of grand strategy than HOI 3 is.
TL;DR pick up HOI3 if you want a more complex game then HOI 4.

Definitely worth getting if you get the chance.

First off, let me start by saying; GET THIS GAME.
I'll explain, I've played many open world (and closed) RPG games, and I can honestly say this rank among the top 3 for me. I played this game ALL THE TIME on the Xbox 360, and I'm SO GLAD that PC had a version of it aswell.
This game, is a game you can VERY EASILY sink hundreds of thousands of hours into, and I honestly mean that.
I'll get to the pros and cons, but seriously, just buy this game.
PROS:
The dialogue is funny, crisp, and refreshing. There are SO MANY WAYS to approach any scenario in the game. A conversation which can end in bloodshed can just as well end in a new ally gained. VERY GOOD if you enjoyed some of the older Dragon Age games.
The storyline is amazing and feels so intricately designed.
The characters are unique and memorable and bound to earn your love.
The gameplay is dynamic and well polished.
Combat is intense and you have a vast array of weapons and spells to tailor to your liking.
There are SO MANY quests, and each and every one of them feel unique and crafted with love, not following standard RPG clone formula.
The music, the environment, the creatures, all of which are aesthetically pleasing on a grand scale. Every location is beautiful and unique, and you actually feel immersed.
The load times are very short, which is nice when you just want to get into the game and play.
CONS:
While I cannot necessarily fault the game for this, I still must bring it up. The content was heavily reduced and many features and areas were cut for the sake of portability to consoles.
No mod support. I feel like this is key for maximizing the life span of an RPG game (look at bethesda titles.)
Combat, while I did praise it in the Pros sections, it can be a tad bit clunky at times.
That's it. I really can't think of anything else to write here.
If you're like me, and love beautifully crafted games...buy this game.
If you're STILL hesitant, at least get it on a sale, they have them pretty frequently.

I could make a joke about this game then say "10/10" at the end, but I believe this game deserves more than that.
This game is absolutely incredible, anyone who says its anything less of a masterpiece is mentally handicapped.
First of all, the area to explore is massive, I have over 200+ hours on it (I played a lot of it while on offline mode, so the hours on my account don't show the full amount) and I still havn't gotten around to looking over all of the areas.
Second of all, the quests are amazing. Starting off with the main story, it is incredibly fun. From starting as a kid in the vault to fighting off the Enclave forces alongside a gigantic robot named Liberty Prime, it is a non-stop good time.
As for the DLC's, most are equally incredible. Broken Steel, The Pitt, and Point Lookout are all amazing to say the least. While Broken Steel adds onto the main story and raises the level cap, The Pitt and Point Lookout give you entirely new quests and areas to explore, both of which are awesome. To a lesser extent, Operation Anchorage and Mothership Zeta are both somewhat decent addons, but failed to meet my expectations. Operation Anchorage was very short, I finished it in about 2 hours without rushing it, and Mothership Zeta was incredibly repetative and dont even get me started on what it attempted to do to the Lore.
Alongside the Main Quests and DLC's, many of the side quests are also fantastic. One that really caught me off guard was a short little quest called "Oasis" in which after exploring the dull wasteland, you find yourself in a lush green paradise, where you meet a mutated man-turned-tree named Harold. The story is quite interesting, and depending on which ending you chose, can leave you quite upset.
Now lets talk about the graphics. Yes this game is a bit outdated, but I for one think it looks fairly decent, and still hold up to some games today. As for the textures, they are quite flat, but I dont think you will really be paying attention to that while your gunning your way through hordes of Super Mutants and Ghouls.
The enemies in this game are also amazing. There are plenty of enemies scattered across the Capitol Wasteland, from little pests like Radroaches and Bloatflies to the incredibly strong Deathclaws and Super Mutant Behemoths, there is little time to sit around a campfire and sing ballads about your fallen comrads before a gang of Raiders come to ruin your good time.
These Raiders wont be much trouble however if your properly equiped. This game comes with a bunch of weapons which are all fun to use, such as the Combat Shotgun, the Hunting Rifle, and everyones favourite, the Fat Man. Most of these weapons also come with one or more "Unique" variations, which usually grant higher damage or special abilities, all of which are very useful when things start to get a little rough.
Lastly, entertainment. I am not stretching this at all, and I dont think what Im about to say will change anytime soon. This game is the best game I have ever played. It is absolutely insane how good this game is. If I could play only 1 game for the rest of my life, it would be this. The story is great, the graphics are good, the area to explore is huge, the enemies are awesome, the replayability is off the charts, and if you ever start to get bored, a quick look over at the Nexus will keep you playing for hours on end. Refunct is a genuinely amazing experience.
The game itself is a simple platformer game where as you walk across platforms, the world begins to take form and gain life. As you proceed to walk across the buttons presented by the world, the world grows allowing you more room to play in.
The game introduces new mechanics as you continue to expand the world, without ever telling you how they work, but they are all easy enough to figure out from either common sense or prior gaming knowledge, and the lack of hand-holding tutorials is a nice breath of fresh air in today's gaming market.
The game itself takes less than 20 minutes to complete, but it is definitely worth the look.

Outlast is a first-person survival horror game. As an investigative journalist you explore an abandoned mental asylum. There you will find yourself soon being hunted by some sick individuals who still wander its halls.
Most of the time you will spend between heart pounding encounters exploring the hospital, trying to find clues to the mystery that landed you there in the first place. You will also spend most of that downtime dreading the next encounter because you never quite know when its going to hit you next.
Outlast is a dark game. Without your handy camcorder and its nifty night vision display, you would not be able to play this game. Survival depends almost exclusively on managing your supply of camera batteries for fear of losing your ability to see. You must keep a close eye on your camera battery at all times and remain aware that the battery will drain faster if the night vision is turned on. The night vision effect itself is portrayed beautifully and really manages to capture the essense of a found footage film.
Combat is not existent and emphasis is instead placed on trying to outsmart your attackers and hiding in moments of desperation. When you can not shake your attacker, the best option is to break line of sight and find a place to hide. As a result, the gameplay feels like a satisfying game of cat and mouse. Situations often boil down to a desparate run for survival that have you barreling over objects and looking back over your shoulder as crazed madmen pursue you.
The game looks fantastic and the sound design in Outlast is awesome. The sound is the glue that keeps the whole thing together. Everything from ambient noise to your own character's heightened breathing in moments of panic is excellent.
Outlast is the best horror experience I have had in years. It is a must have for fans of the horror genre.

Outlast is a rare treat in games. Taking a cue from your local Haunted Slaughter house, you'll be dropped into a bonified carnage simulator, not only deemed with the task of out cunning your foes, but to endure and survive your Hellacious Night at the Abandoned Asylum. You'd mistake this place for a chop shop dealing in body part with how strewn about the limbs and organs are. Yet, a FPS/'Freerunning treatment of the trending “Run fast or die faster” gameplay, a la Slender and a handful of others, is a visit too tempting to pass up. So please make yourself at home, as my head-space can be quite cramped at times. Ignore that door closing behind you, it's only so my thoughts don't run amok...
Outlast is a soon to be released PS4 title gaining a lot of locomotion with its earlier PC release. Eager to dive into the game but looking for a field impression first, I looked to the online game streaming site <Twitch.TV> for a live streamer give the game a run. And needless to say, what I saw was more than enough to earn a credit of only $20 on Steam.  I played it on a Nvidia 560 Ti, which is a lower-middle end graphics card by today's standards, but it was more than enough to play the game at full settings. I was also buddied with my Xbox 360, and gained a Mirror's Edge vibe from the game's action-movie pacing.
I didn't suffer any crashes or hiccups from play and the clarity and use of high resolution textures caught my eye more than once. Though they were mostly seen through the blur of running past the many armed assailants you'll have to hide from.
Truly though, anyone that's an avid reader of Fangoria, or fan of any studio reproduction of gore will fawn over this game. This, behind a laundry list of FPS games released this year, is by far the most bloody game I've played to date; and you never fire a gun once. Forgotten and decaying fleshy organs sit neatly on bookshelves, waiting to be discovered. New minted, squeamish heads are presented in some mock Farmer's Market fashion as they not only gross people out, but tell unwanted stories of struggles and murders as you comb bathroom stalls and used hospital gurneys for clues that bide you deeper into the madness the blood soaked walls tell.
You're playing as Miles Upshur, a freelance journalist answering a vagrant email from an ex-Murkoff employee. The writer breaks his long silence about Murkoff's extortion of the psychiatric patients of the Mount Massive Asylum and leaves you with the task of breaking this ripe story that's sure to gain more than a nod from the Associate Press, given you're still alive to tell it. And so, you take the most dusty and deserted of roads out to the joint, armed with just your camcorder and a snazzy tan winter coat. (seriously, if you look at your feet, you look like you're going to a Willie Nelson concert)
One area that Outlast doesn't have a strong foothold in is getting the player to worry about their resources. You basically don't have any. Given that the horror element is tied to you escaping from the Asylum, your mission statement is smartly handled by the pious, if mad, Father Martin.  Father Martin preaches to you to guard your life and record everything. It's a cool way to headline the objective of the game, as you have to survive the blood-hungry hoard of asylum patients by disappearing under old beds and forgotten lockers. One could only wonder the lucid horror of having to share your vacant locker with a deserted old tuna fish sandwich. You'll feud with yourself on whether the true horror lies inside the door or out.
This horror game has a bit of an edge on the rest as a means of handling failure. Death will not result in a lengthy trek back to redo a big portion your lost progress. No long spans of time between save rooms [absent in this game] and no miscellaneous items to hoard and clear inventory space for. You're taking the pilot seat in this carbon copy horror movie simulation, complete with your squeaky, rustic gates ghostly shutting behind you as you enter the compound.
Now, griping about checkpoint respawns in any game is an uphill battle, and you're more than likely to run into them on the playthrough. The respawns offer a consultation for parties in favor of  progress loss being a punishment. The heart of the issue is that you're being robbed of punishment when, after dying, you're forced without option to pick up at the start of a given scenario. This is to mirror the PS4 version of the game on it's release, more than likely, as Red Barrel plainly wants to avoid static on the two versions having differences. And once it became common knowledge that, “Yes, if you don't leg it when you see a man holding a machete, that has 1/3 of his face floating in the rank sewers you just escaped from,” the action beat of running and hiding becomes second nature. And Miles must have some years spent on the track, vaulting over overturned bedding and hoisting up into large,  person-sized vents overhead with a runner's grace. Parkour, or free-running, is a clear strength you have over your foes as they curse themselves once they've lost your trail. Frankly, I blame all that red meat.
To roundabout, the game is fun. Once you're willing to have a suspension of disbelief, the game does a great job of making the horror's real for the poor, clumsy soul you're playing as. The free-running elements are definitely a welcome new spin and help drive the narrative of not only Miles' frailness, but he's willpower to trudge forward and see his goal to the end. So long as he can see in the dark that is... You might want to make sure you always have batteries on hand, too... Not seeing more than two feet in front of you while you amble in the dark and brushing shoulders with a chair leg-wielding brute ain't the best feeling...

The story centers around a girl who lives in a trailer in the woods, alone with her possibly abusive father. She misses the bus to school and chooses to explore while her father is at work. The first-person narration describes what the girl is like and how bad her home life is, mostly describing memories, and finally, describing one big decision the girl has to make to change her life for the better.
I don't like the tag "walking simulator" because it implies that story-driven games like "Home is Where One Starts" are just walking around and looking at stuff. I mean, if you strip it down to its bones, that's exactly what it is, but... in order to enjoy games like these you have to find a way to connect yourself with the emotions that are being presented in that walking around and looking at stuff. How does the scenery in the game make you feel? How does the music make you feel? Are you worried about the protagonist and what might happen to them?
If you pick up a bloody knife in a survival horror game, it's just a weapon to you, right? But if you were to pick that up in a, cough, "walking simulator" game, you have to imagine what the protagonist would feel when finding something horrific like that in an empty house. You can't think of games like this is "games", you have to think of them as books or movies where you control what happens. You have to think of them as experiences. That's when you can start to enjoy them.

The game feels like a mash-up of Diablo/Torchlight, Bastion (narrator and player control), and Van Helsing. Victor Vran is a superb addition to ARPG games like Diablo and Torchlight, with minor differences that allow you control your character's movement using the keyboard and lets you jump and roll around. Attacking and using special attacks or spells is the same as in other games. The loot in this game is pretty limited with only a few different types of weapons and only a handful of armors to select. Leveling up is not as exciting as in other games as you merely only get health or destiny points, where destiny points allows you to equip different cards which all have different perks (this is where the majority of the character customization comes from). The game is ~20 hours long if you want to see all the areas and play the story in detail while finding all the secret chests scattered around each area. The game adds challenges for every area, which start out pretty fun but near the end of the game the challenges get ridiculous and can be frustrating. Once you beat all the regular challenges there are elite challenges that get unlocked which are even more insane. The game has a bottomless pit and an area that has a randomized dungeon to increase the longevity of the game, however the end game is shallow compared to other ARPG games. Overall, the game is a lot of fun, very well done and If you're looking for an ARPG game this is a must play.

This is a terrible game. Don't play it. Here's why:
-GAMEPLAY-
> Completely stiff and awkward movement, much worse even than demon's souls
> The combat is tedious and awkward, with hundreds of persistent and annoying oversights and bad decisions
> Terrible animations, often with intentionally poor telegraphing
> Several poor choices in regard to stat progression which feel like a labor instead of advancing
> Loose, unpredicatable hitboxes and collisions which often make absolutely no sense
> Slow, awkward bosses, which require technical technique instead of skill
This game is extremely easy, by far the easiest of all the souls/borne games, however, the miriad of issues and oversights in regards to gameplay make some areas, enemies, or bosses frustrating in a very bad way. Situations are common where taking damage is unavoidable, or where animations are so poorly made that the player may not even know what hit them. Recovery on attacks is so long that enemies have plenty of time wind up attacks of their own. They game often puts the player in unfair situations, punishing them for no mistake of their own.
-WORLD-
> Short, gamey levels that feel random and often don't make physical sense (non-euclidean)
> Lots of stupid enemy triggers and placements that are not designed to be playable so much as annoying
> Levels are split into messy, fragmented zones which don't mesh well
> Dozens of random locked doors to which one may or may not randomly acquire keys in unrelated areas
> Mostly annoying, often whiny NPCs who have absolutely no redeeming qualities (very few exceptions)
> Generic, repetitive enemy design, with very limited move-sets
Only a few areas are actually pleasant to look at, and the world is almost never fun to explore. Nothing is exciting or interesting, and instead feels clumsy and amateur. Often there are random rooms with no purpose, or things that look navigable but aren't. Several levels feel obligatory, as if a 'fire level' is a requirement of an rpg. Items, objects, and enemies are strewn about haphazardly, often with no regard to realism or lore.
-VISUALS-
> Persistent lazy texture work, a downgrade from original designs
> Many levels have good design on paper but are poorly executed
> Character artwork is positively ugly - like the otherwise normal blacksmith who's green for no reason
> Blown-out, cheap looking post-processing and effects
> Ridiculously blurry motion blur, better disabled
Dark Souls 2 is a lot sharper than its muddy ancestors, and SOTFS run well. However, the game manages to be persistently ugly, with only a handful of exceptions. Everything feels lazily made, even more lazy than this review.
-STORY-
> Random-feeling lore, with lots of things that don't make sense or fit into the world
> Generally lazy attempts at pleasing fans rather than building a good world or story
An embarrassment when compared to Dark Souls 1's fantastic and intriguing, even heartbreaking world.
-INTERFACE-
> Navigation relies too much on the d-pad for both tabs and sub-menus
> Camera movement is primitive and awkward (many issues)
> HUD is 'fancy' but is over-designed and clashes with the game's supposed aesthetic
They never got this quite right until Dark Souls 3, but even then, Dark Souls 2 is by far the worst, given it being the third in the souls/borne series.
-AUDIO-
> Inconsistent and forgettable music
> Annoying, dissatisfying combat sounds
> Clunky, heavily layered UI sounds
> Poor stereo work - sounds never quite sound like they're coming from where they are
Sounds like a 2005 game, a poorly made 2005 game.
Overall I give this game a Don't Touch Even With a Very Long Stick / 10. There are so many good games, and as far as I can tell, this is
not one of them.

Victor Vran is a welcome and healthy addition to the action RPGs that brings rhythmic combat to the clickfests we are accustomed to.
It does what it does well: the emphasis might not be on the quantity of the loot or the high customization of your character but rather on the way you time your attacks and dodge out of the way. It doesn't take itself seriously and has some pretty huge winks at other games. This lighthearted tone goes throughout the game with a voice inside Victor's head that offers some good jokes here and there.
I just wish that the developers used these mechanics to deepen the gameplay even more and make it more varied. I have to admit that after finishing the main story in coop, I just felt that I saw everything that the game had to offer. Sure, there were plenty of other challenges to tackle but I did not want to go back and slay hundreds of the generic spiders, skeletons and vampires. (And don't get me started on those essence type of enemies...)
The game could have definitely used more weapon and enemy variety because its combat system is what makes it unique among other ARPGs. After a couple of hours, you figure out what weapons and spells work for you the best and that's pretty much it. You're stuck with generic landscapes and enemies for the rest of the game and this will be a letdown for many players.
Ultimately, it earns my recommendation because in coop, it is fun with a friend. However, I wish it offered a bit more variety in its gameplay and setting to hook players in the long run. For this reason, I recommend picking it up on a sale.

I loved the first one, and it feels as though it's going in the right direction, but as it stands it is still far enough stray that they may come across Bugs Bunny after he's passed Albuquerque.
Pros:
+Improvement on Map Level Design
+Encourages players to be more proactive in playing, instead on relying on towers for the whole thing
+More enemy variety, not just more goblins, orcs, ogres, and god damn explosions.
+Items FEEL stronger. You find a strong item, you feel the power as you smack them down.
+Seperate mana pools for Abilities and Towers. This means you are more willing to use abilities which pays off more.
+"Sub-Cores" which you don't NEED to defend, but it helps since if they break more enemies spawn and they spawn really close to your main core.
+Maps are DIFFERENT. They have some kind of trick to them that really pays off. Some are just simple traps, some have special items such as "MAgic Sentries" which effectively act as a placeholder turret.
+Classes feel more balanced. Now you don't have barrage of hyper-spears while somebody like Huntress is struggling keeping traps going.
+You get rewarded win or lose, but more for wins.
Cons:
-Forced Leveling. Progression should be made through completion, not through playing a lot. If you have a level up system, it should make it that playing a lot makes it easier, but should not be mandatory. In fact, if you level up too much it doesn't matter since you get downscaled back to the level the stage is at. And if you don't level up enough you can't move on. This means you effectively MUST be in the level range to play stages. If they had the option to choose to downscale yourself, or to upscale the stage, that would be fine but you should not be forced to only have so much power.
-Weaker skill point system. The upgrades for skillpoints are terrible. In DD1, you could upgrade your towers or a certain stat. Here, you can upgrade abilities, which would be nice.... if they were so unbalanced and poorly done. Example: My Monk levels up. I can choose to upgrade where I deal 50% more damage on my next Melee attack. Alternatively, I could upgrade my Lightning Aura to just permanently deal roughly 50% more damage all the time, and when we both deal the same rough starting DPS, which will you think I will choose? If you could upgrade states or some special bonuses, it'd be fine but as it stands, you will only really be putting points into 2 things.
-Single Player = No Go. You CAN play alone. You CAN also stick your hand onto a hot stove. Unless you have some kind of magic, you won't. Everybody has a special chest at the start of each wave for tower mana, but this means in single player you are effectively getting 1/4 of the possible mana as you get in 4 player. This means less towers, and since there are more enemies, and they are more powerful overall, and more spots to cover, it is nearly impossible. This is also fed into the fact that you can't get ahead, meaning you don't have the power to even attempt a solo run of most stages. If they had something such as scaling, or allowed you to not be downscaled it would be possible, but as it stands most stages need a MINIMUM of 2 players, and these usually have to be good players.
-Lack of a real story? I am going to places getting attacked. Yay? This may change in the future, but as it stands you really don't know why you are there other than "THINGS! KILLING! DEADLY! YOU MUST STOP THEM!"  At least the first one had that you were kids that basically called hells army to you, and you are making your way through stopping them.
-No Boss Fights? I may not have made it far enough at time of writing, but as it stands I have yet to run into a single boss. And I thouroughly enjoyed those in the first one.
-Towers feel more of a support, than an actual defence. If you plan on relying on your buildings, you aren't going to make it far. This isn't a bad concept, but it means you can never turn a blind eye to anywhere enemies can come in, since they will get chipped away and that's it.

Banished is a village simulator that strongly emphasizes survival. In the early days, you’ll scrounge the wilderness to ensure your tiny band has enough food and firewood for the winter, while over time your priorities will evolve to meet the demands of large populations via agriculture, better tools and clothes, and education. Your villagers are extremely fragile, creating a strong feeling of urgency when planning your town and choosing how to direct your workers. Long periods of ideal prosperity can be suddenly broken by mass starvation or disease. You can either closely micromanage many of the game’s systems, such as resource stockpiles and worker professions, or set them to run mostly automatically with little need for player input. As you play out several towns over decades, however, the lack of meaningful variety becomes clear: every map is largely the same, random events are more repetitive annoyances than interesting game-changers, and there’s no particular advantage of choosing one crop over another. Banished challenges and engages you while learning the ropes--and is quite satisfying once you’ve built a sustainable town--but lacks lasting appeal after mastering its mechanics.

A new gimmick is introduced: Mind Reading. You can spend some of your exp to read minds and find out various useful information, like passwords, locations of items or keys, or even get the illusive stat/skill point boosts.
As well as turning into a dragon later in the game where you can pretend to be the pyro and do the W+M1 thing.
Combat is in 3rd person, and only in 3rd person. It's like a more floaty Fable, or Enclave, or something, except you can't block, and you can only dodge and jump. You got your Melee, your Ranged, and your various melee, ranged, and magic active and passive abilities.
Also speaking of 3rd person, like the previous games, theres plenty of items strewn about the world, as well as some hidden switches, but why they didn't put in any first person mode is beyond me, because your character's neck is really stiff, and you can only look down so much, and its a general pain to pick most stuff up in general, unless your looting a container, or those floaty item bags enemies sometimes drop.
Thankfully, there isn't like 9 different stats to choose from on a level up like the last game. Instead, there's just 5. Although for some reason, instead of the traditional 5 stat points per level up, you only get 4 this time around. That kind of sucks.
The game's difficulty is like a coin, on the first half, the game is hard and vaguely unforgiving, and on the other half, it's♥♥♥♥♥♥easy. Like any good RPG I suppose, the previous games did pretty much just that too, and until you get to the second half of the game, you will die many times, and when you die, the game does not respect your time, locks the controls, and shows your character twitching out and dying. So trying to go to the menu or quickloading in rage won't work until the game finally tells you the obvious: You've died, load a savegame. Although quarter way through the game you get access to the battle tower, a base instance of sorts where you can *finally* stash your items, increase your cap of certain skills from a trainer, as well as access to an alchemist, necromancer (managers your minion which you can then summon after you first enter the battle tower), and an enchanter. You can also send out 3 dudes out on an adventure to gather ingredients, ore, and gems for you. They can be equipped better for a fee to do it "faster", and reduce chance of injury. So finally, the game gives you a breather after you reach this damn tower. As with the other games, it pretty
much gets easier the further you are in the game. My strategy towards the end of the game was spin to win: Whirlwind spam, as its literally faster than my standard attacks maxed out and knocks everything within range flat on its♥♥♥♥♥or dead. Ahh, classic whirlwind spam. As well as using the not-omnislash move on enemies that must absolutely positively die, that's always fun, especially when it glitches out and plays a really corrupt version of a transformer transforming.
The game progresses a bit similarly to the second game, and is roughly split up into 3 acts, once you're past an act, you can't go back. Each act has a fairly big overworld to explore and quest in and whatnot.
Waypoints from the first game are back, except you don't need a scroll to activate them. You just approach them and use them, and you're off to an activated waypoint of your choosing. You can jump 4 inches in the air, then later 8 feet in the air, but why you can't sprint in this fairly vast world just brings my slightly impatient♥♥♥♥♥♥to a boil. Although you can get around pretty fast when you have access to your dragon form.
Divinity as usual has it's sense of humor, and it's references. I always get a good laugh every now and then from certain dialogues.
Divinity II uses the Gamebryo engine, roughly the same one that Oblivion used, so it runs slightly like garbage, although I've only had one crash in my nearly 50 hours of playing. So it's pretty stable, and it loads areas relatively fast. Let me tell you one thing though, it does not feel remotely like Oblivion, except for the somewhat dodgy framerate,
some of the lighting, and those silly 2D sprite tree leaves. Although I did get a Morrowind vibe from the game treating herbs and ore veins like loot containers, although unlike MW, this game actually has a take all items hotkey (E), so you don't have to get hand cramp PTSD flashbacks.
When physics objects like barrels roll around, they play some sort of ominous death beat on a pair of ghost bongos. I don't know either. It's kind of funny but also really disturbing.
...And like every good RPG, the merchants will rip you off blind, aka charge you 10,000 gold for that rusty old dagger thats been sitting up the merchant's bum for the past decade, and give you jack♥♥♥♥♥♥for that literal holy grail in your posession. You can mind read merchants to (usually) get them to lower their prices by like 5-10%, or some other minor amount. Doesn't seem to help with selling stuff to them though.
A lot of things feel very finite, like herbs will never regenerate, and enemies don't seem to respawn, at least not until the last third of the game. This is what the previous games seemed to do, but it was mostly fine, because the previous games weren't ultra stingy with potions in the first third of the game, and merchants actually restocked. You'll find yourself stuffing your character with food consumables to save on potions early game.
Let me remind you, like the other games' AI, enemies will relentlessly pursue you until you're at least a thousand feet away, or incredibly dead. So you have to deal with them, or somehow convince your character to get the lead out and run away for twelve hours anyway.
Although the fairly finite resources thing is remedied after you get access to the 3 runners in the battle tower, in which you can send them out, return to the field, return to the tower, and they'll be back in an instance, hopefully not injured and ready to give you the stuff you asked them to find. So you can pretty much farm most of your alchemy/enchanting materials to your hearts content if you want, or you could avoid the serious cheese and just do it every now and then if you have a crippling fear of the game getting too easy.
Speaking of cheap, the RNG containers are back. So you can once again save and load over and over until you get some good materials, or recipes, or equipment or whatever. One time I got 2 of the same exact potion recipe in the same chest. Neat.
After I beat the game, I was like "Oh boy, that was pretty decent, now time to take on a silly bonus campaign with my now overpowered character, Dragon Age style!" Then I proceeded to click New Game - Flames of Vengeance, only to find out it was the last 3rd of the game overall. *facepalm*

This game wouldn't be half as good as it is without the variety of items and skills as well as the huge amount of choice the player is given throughout the many interactions with the inhabitants of the world.
If what Fallout 3 comes with wasn't enough, the mods and the modding community for the game open up the possibilities for what one can do to an almost limitless amount.  With how long the game has been out for, there are many staple mods that improve the Fallout experience drastically for the better without changing what the game is at it's core.
This game, like an onion, has many layers, and even if it may seem like, at face value, something that is singular without variety, only when you start to peel back the metaphorical layers do you truely see this for what it really is.

I did like this "game" but I realize it may not be everyone's cup of tea. This is one of those "video games as art" pieces that may or may not give you the feels, but is certainly all about evoking a feeling or an emotion in an experimentally narrative way. There really isn't a traditional story with a start, middle, and end, nor are there lots of fully fleshed out characters. You aren't going to find drama, plot twists, or anything that feels like it's heading anywhere to some sort of conclusion. Instead this piece puts you in the frame of mind of someone else for a brief (and I mean
) period of time in a way that let's you inhabit that person's mind and perhaps share something of their perspective. If you loathe games like Going Home, or the Moon Sliver, then you should probably avoid this one, but if you are open to something different and you want to have a brief, but possibly sweet, experience, give this one a go. You've probably dropped three or four quarters in an arcade game or pinball machine before and ran out of lives/balls within 5 minutes. Why not take a chance on this game?

Refunct is a game about jumping on things. Set in a seemingly endless expanse of calm ocean, you hop around blocks and pillars protruding from the water. Landing on a block changes it from white to earth and grass hues, restoring color to the world as you scramble about looking for buttons to produce more landscape.
If that was it, there wouldn't be much reason to play Refunct. However, there's an impressive level of artistry at work beneath the simplistic surface. As you play the game introduces you to additional mobility options in a very natural way, ditching tutorials in favor of intelligently designed challenges that help you uncover new techniques yourself. Exploring these options will also lead you to collectible cubes hidden around the map, and another side of the world that is haunting in its beauty.
That gets to the heart of Refunct's appeal, because the atmosphere in the game is unexpectedly rich. The minimalist landscape is cold and stark, but grows steadily more inviting both as you fill in color and as the sun rises over the ocean. You'll see the shadows grow short and the colors become crisp, along with the soundtrack reaching an uplifting swell. Details like this make the game an engrossing joy to play, and though the end comes in about 20-30 minutes it is so charming you can't help but love it. Refunct is an absolute pleasure to play, from tight controls to gorgeous presentation, that I can recommend it to anyone without reservation.
