Ironically, like my review of Neptunia 2, which was quite delayed, I am once again going to be reviewing Neptunia 3 mostly as a sequel, though I shall also try my best to review Neptunia 3 as it's own game, also akin to my review of Neptunia 2.
Nah, still Valkyrie Profile. I doubt anything will change this fact for a long time.
Definitely. Hyperdimension Neptunia Re;Birth 3 Victory Generation is a brilliant game and well worth playing if you're even remotely tempted.
Well, not alot, really.
To my knowledge, Neptunia V was the first in the series to use the current "freeish movement" battle format that has been used in the rereleases, the Re;birth series, so while a slightly updated rerelease of V nicely rounds out the first three games of the series, it does feel a little silly.
Not that I care, I'm not buying a Ps3 just for Neptune. (I totally would, though).
That being said, the Re;birth series
also port Neptunia to the Vita and consequently, the PC.
While I stand by my statement of "not alot, really", this isn't necessarily a bad thing. The format of the game they have works, can be quick for that post-story grinding and doesn't feel like a chore when you're near the end. It's good.
Ok, alright, I'm sorry.
The story is new, obviously. It's quite good, as well. I thoroughly enjoyed it, though in my opinion the story of Neptunia 1 is better, the story of Neptunia 3 is still very good, if not a little better in some aspects. With a new story comes new characters. Some are "new", while others are actually totally new. Plutia, Lady Iris Heart, is fantastic and shall hopefully be a staple character in the future games
.
With a new story, we get a new dimension, but unlike Neptunia 2 to Neptunia 1, Neptunia 3 is set in the same universe as Neptunia 2, and is a direct sequel to it. This new dimension is effectively gaming in the late 1980's and early 90's, and it's awesome. Fun fact, this makes some of the characters in it older than my glorious self.
Challenges have been
borrowed from Fairy Fencer F, and a little character scaling has been adapted into them. While they don't really do anything important, some of the challenges grant very nice and useful things if you manage to finish them off, but this may take a while.
Neptunia 3 is also the first in the series to use in game cutscenes, albeit very few. They are enjoyable, and a nice break from Visual Novel presentation.
Nepstation! I almost forgot Nepstation. A mock TV show that is inbetween chapters and separate to the plot. 'Tis a fun little breather as well as having extra stuff to do and win.
Neptune, obviously, as does her sister and all of the other main cast. A good chunk of side characters also make an appearance but the Oracles are on holiday, or something.
Stella's Dungeon also makes a return; it's bigger and better and less invoking of your ire if you have any plans to 100% the game's achievements. Doing so will still take a great amount of time, however, and I personally cannot be arsed with that. Despite the length that Stella's dungeon lasts, it always gives you useful things and also gives you some key things, such as Plans for increasing combos.
Other than that, alot of what you will expect from Neptunia returns. The game still retains it's humour, BAMs, optional dungeons, post game content and a large amount of attire for the girls.
You know what else returns? THE SOUND SETTINGS DEFAULT TO MAX. STOP THIS.
There's... actually extremely little to say here that wasn't already said for Neptunia 2. As aforementioned, sounds still default to max, but other than one seemingly rare game breaking bug that I had, which can be fixed with a little help from Google (I don't know if the developers have fixed it officially at this point), there's nothing new or different.
To be fair, this is a good thing as the port quality of the previous two games was pretty solid and this is no different.
As with Neptunia 2 to Neptunia 1, all the dungeons and so on look nicer, there's some newer enemies here and there, while the UI and menus all look better and more streamlined.
The resource management has been rearranged a bit; the EXE drive is taking a break for this installment and the mana has been standardised to 1000 at all levels. I like this, skills no longer cost disproportionately high amounts of mana early on, and mana potions are now worthwhile past Chapter 2. Mana also regerates a little between turns, I believe.
The Mana is divided into four chunks, and special moves now use up to all four of those 250 mana chunks to cast, further providing relevance for mana potions. Sadly, nothing else has been rescaled,  combat-wise, so Formation and Coupling Skills are still fairly redundant, the tier 2 super moves are still generally the best, while the AoE supers are still blatantly the strongest. That and Neptunia
doesn't have a worthwhile final Power attack, though she does feel a little stronger.
Much like with the rest of the Neptunia series, I'd happily pay full price for Neptunia 3 and enjoy it for what some may say is too long. As it happens, I once again bought the game on release sale for £13, Yay sales.
I love this series, and as such, have since bought and played alot of the new Neptunia VII on the PS4
. That does mean that I'm unlikely to grant you with another Magnum Opus review for a while, but I'm afraid we shall all have to deal with it.
Also, it must suck to be in your older sister's shadow. Especially when your older sister is so utterly perfect and amazing and there is now twice as much perfection for you to compete with.

Emotional “a day in the life” story experience
Calm no-rush feel with no time related events
Free exploration
Easy and fun-to-acquire achievements cover all dialog triggers
Main character is a little girl with an awesome elephant backpack who likes electronics and space
Short with almost no replay value
Almost all the gameplay is centered on story dialog which only comes in English and has no subtitle option
The player isn’t given an explicit goal
It’s not always clear everywhere the player should go to trigger necessary dialog
No where does it tell you you can crouch, but you need to for a side dialog
image
The game is pretty short, but in that time the story is sweet. Almost everything is told through the dialog which is limited to only English and has no option for subtitles, making this a game you can really only get the most out of if you can hear and understand what’s being said. Some basics of the girl’s past can be gleaned without the dialog, but the player will miss her personal feelings on things and a lot of the detail. Since there is no branching or any sort of time dependent events, the game lacks any replay value unless you’re looking for achievements. The achievements are fun and completing them all means you’ve found all the interactable items, dialog triggers, and “secrets” in the game, which gives a sense of completion. Partly because of there being no time related events, combined with the scenery and dialog, the game has a very relaxing feel to it that asks the player to simple sit and experience the story. The exploration is free form and everything except the last area (which unlocks after all the required dialog is triggered) can be done in any order. Along with this free form theme, the player isn’t given an explicit goal when starting the game. After exploring a while, it’ll become clear that the goal is to trigger the story and once you’ve found it, figure out a way to open the locked tool shed. There’s no puzzle to this part, you only have to explore the proper areas to trigger the necessary dialog before you’ll be told where to get the shed key and it’ll become obtainable. Another somewhat minor annoyance in the lack-of-direction department is that the player can indeed crouch in the game, but nothing tells you this. It’s only needed to get one side dialog, but for players trying to get the related achievement the game leaves you to figure that out on your own. Overall I found the story a wonderful although short experience. Players that are a fan of non-stereotypical female protagonists will also notice that the little girl in the story is a fan of electronics and space and has a gameboy in her room.

Like most Indie Games on Steam, you've probably never heard of Skyhook. It's a local multiplayer action platformer, or a less fancy term would be party game. As of late the market has become very saturated with party games. They have become the newest trend in gaming, from Nidhogg, Towerfall, and Gang Beasts, you name it, they come in just about every flavor. Skyhook looks to make a name for itself in a big market. Now while this title is still in active development and on Early Access, the basic core mechanic of the game is in place.
Why that would be grappling hooks of course! Who doesn't love grappling hooks, they're the best item in all of Zelda games and Batman! Skyhook challenges you with murdering your best friends using grappling hooks in its multiple arenas/levels. If grappling hooks aren't enough, hop aboard the floating ship and blast them in the face with a cannon. Now I will admit that there is only a certain amount of content to be explored here in Skyhook. Despite this though, with the right group of buddies, Skyhook can have some very dynamic and interesting battles as you bounce around its levels like a monkey on crack.
Of course Skyhook features the same delicious amount of pixel goodness we have come to expect from party games. The characters are all very colorful, designed neatly and seemingly have a bit of personality. The level designs are pretty solid and allow for some pretty crazy matches as you desperately try to hook your friends to death. There are some bugs though, this is Early Access. The floating ship can be piloted into a position which makes it unusable and it just floats there like a log. Bugs are to be expected though as development continues.
Other features include items that can give you a key advantage in combat, from invisibility, to mirror imaging yourself on the other players. These items add a bit of "brawl" style flair to matches and a little break from just hooking people over and over. Multiple people can also use the same keyboard for Skyhook, including controllers which I find to be a bit more intuitive with these types of games. Thankfully Skyhook does feature full controller support, so there isn't much stress in finding one that works. Also other game modes like Team Deathmatch, Deathmatch, and Steam Tank which limits your grappling hooks.
I had fun with Skyhook, but of course the major caveat of the game is that it requires other people to play with, in order for the game to be enjoyed. With no online multiplayer and no current single player campaign, there is only so much you can play before you move along. Now while it is still early to make a call on Skyhook, I feel the game does have some interesting potential. Grapple hooking enemies isn't the newest concept but still can be innovated in some interesting ways. Adding shifting levels dynamics like on the level seen above is a good example. Perhaps a level that is scrolling sideways/up or take a note from Speedrunners and make a racing level but solely based off your grapple hooking skills. Make a level that has glowing stars to be collected behind several dangerous obstacles, first to three wins. These are just some examples of what Skyhook could become.
There are many possibilities for Skyhook, as long as the developer continues working passionately. I am happy to say that while cruising the Skyhook Steam forums, I noticed a daily development blog that had scores of minor tweaks and updates being made. This is the kinda thing you want to see out of a developer, and should put some fears to rest for those burned by Early Access games before.
Speaking to the future of Skyhook, the developers planned features include more characters, more levels/hazards, more powers ups and environmental effects, new vehicles and mounts. Not to mention a single player/co-op campaign that will have 40 levels and other unlockable goodies. It is important to underline that online multiplayer is not a planned feature currently.
So if you're in the market for a fun party game, want something that combines elements of Mario, Smash Bros, and Speedrunners, Skyhook might be just the game you're looking for in your gaming library. Just remember to make sure you have some friends who don't mind coming over instead of playing online

As someone who enjoyed Gone Home, Life is Strange, The Moon Sliver and Mind: Path to Thalamus, I thought I would enjoy this game too. Turns out I didn't.
First, it is stingy with the voice bits: I found interesting items that I thought would certainly trigger a monologue, such as the swing behind the house, which I thought would lead to a digression on the character's childhood. But nope, nothing happened when approaching that one and several other landmarks.
Second, it has one of the poorest implementations of invisible walls I've ever seen. There's for instance a big open wooden gate leading towards a house in the distance, but when you try to cross the threshhold, you simply can't advance anymore. Several other areas won't let you advance any further without even so much as fences to try and mask the invisible walls. Stinks of laziness by the dev's part.
Finally, the landmarks that do have audio bits are very far apart and don't have any indications, meaning you'll spend most of the playtime walking slowly and aimlessly, trying to guess where to go next.
The only thing this game has going for itself is the faily soothing and melancholic atmosphere, which it manages to pull off despite the outdated graphics. It's super short and, even though I got it in a sale at the Humble Store, I still feel cheated off my money, which is something I've felt with very few games ever.
If you like exploration games, Gone Home, A Story Of My Uncle, and Mind: Path to Thalamus are all much better options.

This is very much aimed at people who enjoyed games like Gone Home and Dear Esther- if you didn't like those then turn away now, there's nothing here for you. It's short (I doubt it will take anyone more than half an hour to complete) and more of a mood piece than an actual story, but it's creatively solid and quite poignant, giving the feeling of inhabiting a single, important memory.
Steam is becoming infamous for quick, lazy cash-grabs made of Unity assets; this isn't one of those. It's very clear that the game was made on a low budget, but the developer has worked smartly with their limited resources to make something with a cohesive and solid atmosphere, helped by great music and voice acting. And I absolutely loved the ending, for reasons I won't go into here- simple but powerful, like the rest of the game.
My only real complaint is that the game area is quite large and cluttered with trees and other objects; this gives you a wider area to explore but can also make it unnesecarily difficult to track down the points that trigger narration. I think a more compact world would have worked better.
Again: if you hated Gone Home, don't pick this up thinking you're going to like it. It's even more Gone Home than Gone Home was, if that makes sense. But if that game grabbed you and you're looking for a quick fix while you wait for Fullbright's follow up, definitely check this out.
I hope the developers go on and to bigger and better things, they've clearly got some real creative chops.

General characteristic:
To be honest I didn't expect much after this title,but now I gotta admit that I was wrong :) Victor Vran is really good aRPG.All the basic mechanics are made well,the game adds to the standard range of moves also dodges,making the fights more dynamic and jumping,which lets you to reach for example for secrets.
The main story was a little bit too obvious for me from one point of the game,but I liked it anyways.The plot took me about 10 hours,but a person who likes to max out the games will find here hundreds of hours of gameplay more taking in account how many challenges there are.
There's a few types of weapons that the character can wield,including scythes,swords,rapiers,shotguns,hamers etc. Every type of weapon has 3 different skills.Additionally Vran can use various special powers powered by the overdrive.
You won't find here the standard statistic points known for example from the 2nd Diablo,those are modified by the Destiny Cards found on the battlefield.
Advantages:
+A few new systems in the genre
+Good soundtrack
+Good,dynamic,engaging fighting system
+A sea of loot for the main character
+Every weapon has a different feeling
+Vast content,letting for many hours of fun
+The multiplayer mode
+Well-made locations
+The Destiny Cards let you for many builds
+References to the pop-culture
+Some funny moments with "the Voice in Vran's head"...
Disadvantages:
-...but mostly it's boring and adds nothing to the story
-Jumping in an aRPG is a nice novelty,but it could have been made better
-The locations are not randomly generated so you'll be getting back to literally the same places
-I faced a few problems with controls
-Soulless main and side characters
-Too predictable story
-Just a few,one-piece armours for the protagonist
-A demon hunter in a hat? I've seen it somewhere...
-Some boss fights are boring
-THOSE DAMN ENEMIES,GETTING BACK TO LIFE! :D
Conclusion: I don't regret buying Victor Vran.Satisfying fights and dark atmosphere make it a great experience.If you look for a new aRPG to spend some time with ,then it may be a good choice,especially if you have someone to play with, you'll surely enjoy it.

A nice relaxing FPS platformer with a feel-good ending.
Bad things first. The platforming is a bit unintuitive at first; your character will climp up the edge so sometimes you can make a jump despite it seeming like you can't make the jump. The elevator/lift mechanic actually adds to your jump height if you jump whilst it is moving. Knowledge of this is never clearly presented to the player and it is not required to complete the game (though it is required to complete the achievements).
You'll get used to the somewhat-clumsy platforming, and if you've read this, you'll know about the elevators. Putting those aside, Refunct is a brilliantly designed feel-good platformer. It teaches you almost (see above) all of its mechanics incredibly intuitively. There are no text prompts though you might need to visit the controls page to find there is no sprint, and there is a crouch. The way Refunct teaches the controls is what modern game and interaction designers strive for.
Coloring in all the platforms by being on them was unexpectedly fulfilling and the ending put a smile on my face. The soundtrack is relaxing and fits the feel of exploration and wonder that I feel Refunct is trying to evoke.
The features listed on Refunct's store page are all accurate and not just hype.
I would definitely recommend this game to anyone.

First and foremost, please bear in mind that this is a "walking simulator" style of game.  There are no puzzles, no enemies (at least not in the traditional sense, i.e. no combat), no stats or levels.  Please know this when you're buying the game so you know what you're getting.
Let me just say that I love this game.  It is VERY short, but I don't feel cheated by the cost as it's only $2.99 at full price and I feel like the atmosphere and exploration is worth a few dollars.
This game is entirely based on exploration.  It feels like you're essentially walking through a child's memory of a single day in her life where something a little unordinary happens.  You aren't force-fed the details of her life; it's up to you to look around, walk around, see the items and scenery, listen to the occasional narratives, and then build your view of her life from that.  There are many things you can see that don't have attached narration, leaving you free to form your own ideas.  If you take time to really pay attention, it crafts an intriguing (although extremely sad) look into a broken home.
The music is soothing, calm, and very pretty and fits the atmosphere.  The narrator does an excellent job, believable and not melodramatic.  She sounds like an ordinary person, which is exactly how she should sound.
Graphics are decent, not necessarily top-of-the-line but I felt they painted the scene nicely.
So if you like the exploration/walking-simulator genre of games, this is certainly worth a playthrough (or two, if you missed things).  If you feel the price is a little high for the length of the game, wait for a sale, but I felt that the full price was reasonable.

Outlast
Genre: Survival horror
Engine: Unreal Engine
Platforms: Microsoft Windows, PlayStation 4
Note: This game includes violence and hard gore.
Introduction:
Outlast is a first-person survival horror game set in an asylum. The main character "Miles Upshur"."Miles Upshur" a freelance journalist, receives a tip-off from an anonymous source about Mount Massive Asylum, a psychiatric hospital owned and operated by the Murkoff corporation."Miles Upshur" is incapable of combat, except for certain scripted sequences in which he pushes enemies away. To navigate the environment, the character is able to climb to ledges, vault over low obstacles, crawl, and slide in narrow gaps. Except for vaulting, enemies are incapable of any of these maneuvers, which gives the player a certain edge. In addition, the player can survive encounters with the inmates by hiding inside of lockers or under beds, although certain enemies may search the room and attempt to locate the player for a short time before moving on.Since much of the asylum is dark, the player must use Miles' video camera to see, thanks to its night vision function. Using night vision consumes batteries, replacements of which are scattered throughout the environment.When injured, Upshur must avoid taking any further damage for a while, which will allow him to recover.
Pros:

- Very dark atmosphere.
- Fast-draining night vision camera keeps tensions high.
- Very good sound design.
- Absence of weapons requires smart uses of hiding spots.
Cons:
- The graphic isn't the best.
The Verdict:

WARNING FOR FPS NEWBS
This game is not for the ones who hates dying over and over again. It took me many hours of playing (about 6) before I started feeling like I was getting any good at the game. The shooting mechanis take a lot of getting use to as well, hipfiring is essentually not a option in this game unless you are either really lucky, using the shotgun, or proned and using a luger (best hipfire gun when prone from my experience). Learning how to unlock the new classes in frontlines took me a while to figure out as well but once you do it easy to gain experience and get more guns quickly. Part of the learning is the map layout and finding the best sniping, advancing, and cover when attacking/defending and such. Again though, excpet to die a lot, esspecually since this game has a one shot kill for all gun (depending on range, and where you hit plus what weapon you use). All explosives will kill you instantly and there is a lot of that in this game so be prepared to die from unexpected explosives. The only thing you can really avoid are grenades if you see them fall near you or hear them hit the ground, just hope the person did not cook it and you have time to get away.
Game design and balance
I find the game is balance very well, for the most part although certain classes like the belgains and scottish squads are rarley used due to the fact the other squads just symply have nicer guns to use (iron sights wise). The front lines play out nicley and there is always at least one game running in all the different modes during all times of the day. All the maps play out very well and have their different play styles very similar to the real life comparision (from what little research I know). This though can make certain maps a lot more chaotic and will have a lot of spawn and die several seconds later from Machine gun fire that dominates the playing feild.  This can be countered however with squad captains who can fire gas, mortar, and artiller fire. There is also a smoke screen however I find it does not last enough, about 10 second. Although it fires fast, I feel it should last a lot longer.
At the end though, once you figure out the games realistic mechanis you  can rack up a lot of kills and with few deaths. I would recomand this to anyone and find the commuity in the game very enjoy able and friendly. However if you ever join a game where one squad has all the players in it with the same name and all level 100... find a new match, I think they might be hackers and typically dominate the whole map and like to try and push everyones buttons. Out of the houndred of hour I have played this has only happened twice so its a very rare occurance.
This game is a very fun game to play and I look forward to the upcoming stand alone expantion Tanningburg. See you on the front lines!

When most people write a review, there's a strong "This game is amazing!" or "This game is the biggest pile of crap ever sold on Steam!" but in this case, I just don't recommend it because I didn't like it. There's nothing awful about it. The graphics are nice enough, the music has a nice sound, and it has what looks like some decent controller support. The game is voice acted, and the voice acting is pretty nice, and the loot seems okay, though not as deep as most ARPG fanatics would likely desire. The game's jumping controls while in a hedge maze were rather laughable while using a mouse only, but it isn't a huge complaint. In short, the game's alright. It might even be "good." I just don't feel compelled to stick with it. If you're absolutely dying for more ARPGs in the Diablo vein, you could play this if you've ran out of the best alternatives I've found, such as The Incredible Adventures of Van Helsing series and the Torchlight series, and other fan favorites. So it's not a bad game from what I've seen; just not something that thrilled me, and unless you have a controller, it'll feel a bit wonky at times.

Its time for me to write my very first Review, and its going to be about The Crew.
This, was a fun game with a lot of potential, but Team Ubi and Ivory Tower Turned it into... well, into what it is now,
I've spent some hours on it, there are ppl with more hours than me but anyway,
people might think that somebody with a lot of time spent on a game would obviously recommend it
but thing is, i saw it going down slowly... and the potential got wasted.
First lets state the important and obvious details about this game:
Not sure if i should list this as pros and cons, so i'll just list the good and bad about each feature:
-Specs: This is of the main features of this game, i even dare to say its the core to the crew's gameplay, when i just played it, it was cool as you see when you pick your first vehicle, you can have every spec on that vehicle, That being, Street, Dirt, Perf, Raid and Circuit(drag, drift and Monster truck if you have WR Expansion but i'll get to that later), but as you progress in the game you start noticing that its only incomplete, while this is indeed a cool feature, its quite lacking, most of the vehicles in the game only come in Perf spec, wich is annoying, yeah, we get it, not anybody would turn a Lamborghini Aventador into a raid vehicle, but thats the fun part of a video game, do things you can't do in real life, So, as for the specs, i find it quite lacking, specially because some of my favorite vehicles only come in one spec...
-Customization: When this game came out, there wasn't a lot of racing games with this option, So this was a nice adition to someone's library who is looking for a nice racing game with this feature, while its not perfect, its decent, but as i said, its not perfect, why? first, choosing the color, you have to choose from an already existing color list, if your favorite color is not there, you are screwed, the parts you can choose from, some are nice, but i wish they were better, you can't choose  your wheels color, customization parts are only for Street, Dirt, and Performance specs, Raid and Circuit, you can only change paint, decals and wheels, there are some elements on the customization menu that are actually empty and only makes you wonder why the heck are they there?? like the Fender one, That being said, Customization is there, it sorta do its part, but i just wish it was way better, like letting you blend your own paint, put the materials you wish on whatever part you wish, etc.
-Graphics and optimization: The graphics are not top notch but for me, they were enough to say it looks good, specially after the visual overhaul they did, not much else to say. As for the optimization, it sucks, there are graphic glitches that are still there from the very beggining of the game,like the stuttering, doesn't matter how amazing or beefy its your computer, it will ALWAYS stutter and have fps drops randomly.
-Gameplay: a lot of people find it bad, it feels stiff, clunky or whatever, as for me, its good, the controls are not that bad, the races andevents are good(but quite lacking...) the physics are quite odd but not odd enough to ruin the game, the best part of the gameplay? you have a really big world to play, the bad part of it? the devs were lazy enough to cover all that ground with all kind of events and racing tracks, instead, they added a game mode where players can create their own races, wich its not that bad, but not that good either, a poor excuse to cut work and let players do the devs work.
So, overall, the gameplay its just Decent.
-PvP: while i have'nt spend a lot of time on pvp, i can say that its only for those with very good conection, or else you will just get glitchy af races with oddly moving trafic, pvp its indeed one of the main features of the gameplay, and at first it was amazing, but with time less and less players were available to play with, it still have a good playerbase but still  feels a bit dead sometimes, cant really say much about pvp so i'll just leave it on Neutral

Divinity 2 is a top down 3rd person role playing game.  It is a typical swords, bows and magic type of fantasy world.  The one addition to your normal RPG is the ability turn into a dragon at specific points in the game.  It is hard for me to state why I enjoyed the game so much.  It is just a great and interesting top-down RPG, something that is hard to find these days.
The good:
1. The normal RPG type stuff is done excellently.  The quests, equipment, skills, etc.
The bad:
2. Your character always sheaths his weapons during dialogue.  Thus after talking to enemies you have to redraw your weapons wasting valuable time.  You may die before you even drew your weapon.
3. Movement during combat is not always fluent.  If you are hit (e.g. by an arrow) while jumping the character is instantly moved to the ground and staggered wasting time and momentum.  Even worse, when swinging your weapon there is no correlation between clicking your mouse and actual swings.  Sometimes attacks are fast and sometimes slow and I have no idea why.
4. My personal preference is for RPGs where you deploy a team of units with different skills.  Here you only have yourself and summoned creatures.
The ugly:
4. Being a dragon is totally disappointing.  When normal you can only attack ground units.  When you are a dragon cannot attack ground units only certain towers and flying units.  Surely you want to be a dragon to flame those annoying units that swarmed you on ground.

If you're expecting Dark Souls type combat you will be sorely disappointed. When reading about locking on to enemies and roll dodging in the manual it sounded reminiscent of Dark Souls, but I had to remind myself.
There are a lot of interesting abilities that are limited by both mana consumption and cooldowns. There's also not a strict class system which I really like in RPGs. There's not a huge amount of character customization in terms of appearance - much closer to Morrowind than Skyrim in that regard.
There are some annoyances such as not having quest markers for NPCs. There was one who gave me a quest, but then moved to a different location because he was involved in a side quest. i have avoided writing a review for this game for the longest time because i don't really know where to begin. For me, this is the best game of all time. Bar none. Maybe it is because i love open world sandbox games. Maybe it is all the science fiction movies and books i have consumed over the years. Or the freedom to do and be whatever i want. But whatever the reason, it has given me 1300 hours of pleasure on the PS3, at the measily cost of $160. With Fallout 4 on the way, i want to give this game a proper goodbye with a review.
1=inferior

genre: 3 out of 3
Fallout 3 is one of the best open world sandbox games in existence. After you have played the opening vault once, you can go where you want, do what you want, be what you want. Do you want to go find your dad, or blow up a town? Do you want to help a highrise of snooty aristocrats, or slaughter them in their sleep? Or do you just want to scavenge the wastes and become a trader. Does the plight of humanity tug on your soul? Well, be the scientist that saves the world instead of the one that destroys it. It is totally up to you. North, south, east, or west, you decide. And i love that freedom. There are markers that tell you where to go for your quest, but you can ignore these if you wish. You can play for hundreds of hours without finishing the main quest. I have done just that many times.
customization: 3
you can create your own character with their own unique look, their own unique strengths, their own unique skills. And when you level up, you can choose what kind of special abilities (perks) they shall have. You can go the science route and pick a character that is good at computers, medicine, and robots with cybourg inplants. Or you can create a character that is a night stalker who gets energy from bloodpacks and eating the bodies of their dead enemies while killing their enemies in their sleep. Or are you a survivalist who has high resistance to radiation and bullets? Play as you want. Personally, i play as a night-stalking female survivalist ninja who weeds out the weak and useless so as to make humanity stronger. How will you play? If you don't like these options or any of the others in vanilla Fallout 3, why not find a mod? There are thousands of them on the internet.
story/relevance: 2 and 1/2
one of its weaker points. The story of the father who wants to bring pure water back to the Wasteland is a bit of a cliche. Many of the missions are a bit standard. I don't play these type of games to be a part of a story, but to make up my own story in a unique game world.
What the game does excell at is telling story through the environment, whether through computer logs or the ruins you travel through. There are hundreds of examples, but i will just give a few: the cages with tiny skeletons in them, the half-skeleton lying next to an automatic rifle and radaway, the skeleton sitting in a tub with a toaster. The Fallout 3 world is haunted with the stories of those who died before you came into existence.
as for relevance, you do get to choose whom to save and destroy. In fact, you can kill just about everyone you come across. And isn't this relevance of a sort?
gameworld: 3
this seems like a real place, with its own groups of people, its own history, its own rules. It truly seems like a real place one could visit, with monuments and wacky religions and characters along the way. I spent hours just wandering around the ruins of Washington checking out all the places i have never visited in real life. It is a place i wouldn't want to visit, but love living in. This is one of the biggest reasons i love this game. So many places with so much detail.
innovation: 2
when i first played the game, it seemed much more innovative to me than it does now. The perks came from fallout, the world from science fiction, the karma from Knights of the Old republic. Even VATS came from the earlier Fallouts. As a late-blooming gamer, it took me a while to find these sources. Still, the way the game combined them all together...that was a bit innovative. I especially loved their take on VATS. I still get thrilled watching my queen of the Wasteland knock the head off of a raider at 500 yards.
mechanics: 3
i played on PS3, and the game played like any other sandbox game i had played on the PS3. Nothing stands out here, other than the beautiful VATS system. Do love the fact you can save anywhere at any time. Even in mid fight. As i write more reviews, it will become obvious that i am very picky about the mechanics of saving. The karma system was a bit wacky, with ones character being able to erase the massacre of a whole town with the giving of enough money. I guess it is a Catholic society. And why does stealing make you as evil as killing would? Otherwise, the mechanics of the game kind of faded into the background. And that is good.
replayability: 3
this is always a big concern for me. As a father of 4, i can't spend $60 on a 4 hour game, even if that game were to cause me to see Jesus or Mohammad or any other holy man. Fallout has replayability in abundance. There are many quests that have binary choices. And even if this were not the case, i can think of 6 or 7 different character builds. My favorite is the night stalker/weeder. Can also play as a scientist, survivalist, thief/con man, beserker, pyromaniac. ninja...And every character type you play creates a different gaming experience. With DLC and mods, the replayability is almost endless. 1300 hours for me. And that is without the mods. Need i say more?
uniqueness: 3
even with the previous Fallouts, i think the Wasteland is a unique world. I haven't come across another world quite like it. Not even Fallout Vegas. The Vats system, the Karma, the customizability, the radiated Washington ruins....all seem to be original. Or at least handled in an original way.
graphics: 2 and 1/2
on computer, they are a bit better. On PS3, they aren't much to look at. But one doesn't play Bethesda games to be blown away by the graphics. One plays them to be blown away by the depth of detail.
final score: 25 out of 27 or 92%.

This game doesn't beat around the bush. It's a very straight forward and extremely functional CB that unlike most others, sets it's challenge around balancing your limited population and infrastructure needs on a knifes-edge. The importance of building and planning your town in such a volitile state gives the games mechanics a very weighted feel to it, especially early game.
Most of the fun is had during learning phase of the game as you diligently tweak and customize your town, keeping an ever watchful eye on the wellbeing of your people. However, all the fun comes to an abrupt halt once you find a system that works, and when everything is working flawlessly your job as governor quickly becomes obsolete.
The goal set for Banished is so simple that once your town stabilizes, there is really nothing left to do. Your people don't gain skill or evolve in any direction. Without threat of invasion or attack or some higher goal or purpose other than to eat, poop and die, it really takes away your motivation to keep playing.
Once this game get some love from the modding community it could become something special. At this stage it just feels like a very empty game. I'd say it's worth the money even though it's seriously lacking in content and replayability.

I feel that if DS2 had been released before DS1, or maybe by a different developer, it would be viewed better. This is understandable, because DS1 is a flawed masterpiece, and it's pretty damn hard to top. Unfortunately there are quite a few glaring flaws in DS2, even if you ignore its predecessor.
For starters, you can't opt out of PvP. The nice thing about DS1 is that if you were hollow (undead), you couldn't be invaded by another player, so the only way to do PvP was to either become human or join a covenant (in-game factions mostly designed with PvP in mind). In DS2, the game forces you into PvP because being hollow no longer stops invasions. The change makes no sense, especially considering DS1 had enough of a problem with PvP cheaters.
Gameplay received other stupid changes; for example, dying (going hollow) now lowers your maximum health by 5%, and continually lowers it by 5% each time you die until you have 50% of your maximum health left. The only way to reverse this is to use a human effigy, which makes you human and resets your health bar to what it
is. This is a stupid mechanic because effigies are fairly uncommon drops, and this is Dark Souls, so you WILL die a lot. The issue is that since the reduction is % based, you will ALWAYS need to burn effigies to nullify the health loss, whether you're level 2 or 200; otherwise you'll die to hits your character, statistically, should have survived. It's cheap and punishes players for the trial and error gameplay that Souls is supposed to reward you for.
Some gameplay elements are way clunkier this time around too. For one, enemies deal ridiculous amounts of stamina damage, to the point where having your guard broken is a common occurence even against non-boss enemies. This means that even classes that are supposed to be able to "tank" enemies just can't do it, because there isn't ever enough stamina to. Backstabs are also notoriously inconsistent. The animation looks better, but backstabs often fail to register and then later register from the same position, or register but enemies fall out of the animation, or (my favorite) it'll register but you'll actually get hit/backstabbed
. You really can't make this up.
Another issue is that DS2 tried WAY too hard to step out of DS1's shadow, and FromSoft decided that more bosses (41 vs 26) and far more ways for you to be insta-killed would fix this. Unfortunately, many of DS2's bosses are garbage/poorly designed (Prowling Magus, Covetous Demon, Demon of Song, Dragonriders, Royal Rat bosses, the Gank squad in the cave of the dead, I could go on), and several others were obviously copy/pasted: The Old Dragonslayer is identical to Ornstein from DS1 but with dark magic instead of lightning, The Smelter Demon is copy/pasted into the Old Iron King DLC, and Aava, the King's Pet is copy/pasted into two different boss fights twice in the same expansion.
Many bosses this time around also have unblockable grab attacks, several of which insta-kill you. DS1 had unblockable grabs too, but they almost never insta-killed, and they were extremely telegraphed. This time around, even non-boss enemies have grabs that can always insta-kill you no matter what your health is (Mimics, Trolls/Ogres), and several bosses have similar insta-kill attacks/combos that are barely telegraphed at all. Apparently the protagonist can block a dragon's fireball, but not a salamander tongue.
No, really, I didn't make that up. That's a thing in this game.

New Game+ is also more annoying this time around, as FromSoftware seems to have decided that turning every single fight into a 3v1 or 5v1 = more difficulty, when in reality it's just lazy and leads to more reloads because you couldn't avoid a stun-lock.
There are also unnecessary gameplay simplifications in DS2, from limiting weapon reinforcement (DS1 has about seven upgrade paths, DS2 has one and infusions) to forcing weapons/armor to be extremely fragile. Seriously, what kind of paper-mache sword breaks after 20 swings?
Since no one would ask for clunkier mechanics and overly-simplistic design, I'm assuming FromSoft made these changes because they were afraid DS2 would be too easy. Instead, they just made a game that feels a lot more cheap than difficult, even if you don't compare it to its predecessor.
Storywise, DS2 is objectively subpar to the original; in particular I (and many others) was dumbfounded by who the last boss was, because the game doesn't  convey its story and history enough for you to understand its overarching significance. I think 8-10 of DS1's bosses had an emotional investment from the player in their lore. In DS2, I think a similar thing happened on 2, maybe 3 bosses, and keep in mind, DS2 has 41 of them. DS1 had 26.
There are a
positive changes from DS1 that should be noted, such as an exponentially better inventory system, brighter HUD, shimmying up/down ladders, and the fact that DS2 just has
better graphics/texturing. Hell, the biggest issue with DS1 was that the steam version basically
DSFix to play, and DS2 doesn't have this issue. But ultimately, these are too few and far between to placate the negatives.
Overall, DS2 is still a good game; just not a good Souls game. Drangleic is beautiful, and its history is good to learn if you can ever actually decipher its crappy storytelling. But overall, DS2's stupid gameplay changes, forced multiplayer, poorly executed story, and garbage bosses hamper it far more than is acceptable. I do recommend DS2 because I still enjoyed it in spite of its flaws. But I enjoyed DS1 far more (my DS1 hours are kinda deceiving, I've got about 150 additonal hours on DS1 offline). If you're looking for an entry point into the Souls franchise, pick up DS1 instead. It's superior in nearly every way.
FromSoftware can do better than this, and they know it. I
hope they learned their lesson in DS3.
TL;DR:
7.0/10, It's a good game, but not a good Souls game. Expect a lot of unblockable insta-kills, and expect to be ganked on if you play online, which you can't opt out of. If you're new to Souls, play Dark Souls 1 first. It's better in
every way.

You don't necessarily have to run into a showstopper bug very often, but even then, the level design throughout all the campaigns is pretty horrendous. You're often forced to just skip turns in order to build strong enough an army to defeat a final opponent, who is, btw, just passively waiting in his own castle.
The story isn't written badly, but the overall experience is worse than Heroes V and not anywhere near its predecessors.
Lastly, the game isn't very well optimized. It doesn't look bad, but for what you get, it actually demands way more than it should off of your PC. The framerate can very often drop pretty low even on today's high-end machine.
To sum up, do not buy this game unless you're a huge fan of the series who doesn't want to miss on the developments in the story.

Home Is Where One Starts is a short game. It's not for everyone, but for those that like "walking simulators" (BTW ♥♥♥♥ that name) will most likely enjoy this beautiful little piece of narrative driven story telling.
You play as a unnamed (Six?) year old girl as you walk around the area of your home. This game is basically a woman retelling a special morning of her childhood.
The visuals are very nice, not the best I've ever seen in unity, but it definitely sets the mood along with the sounds which are quite nice.
The music which mostly consists of The Tumbled Sea's song called "//", a very nice piece of ambient/post-rock(?) music, however the quality of the song is somewhat downgraded in-game which has been a small annoyance but nevertheless works well and fits the environment.
Even though the game's length is usually 15-30 minutes, you can still search for achievements which I did (I have them all now).
Therefore, I suggest this game, it's price, it's length and atmosphere. It's too good to not recommend.

Victor Vran is a hack and slash RPG made by Haemimont Games (Tropico series, Omerta) that sadly came too late to face its subgenre rival, The Incredible Adventures of Van Helsing trilogy by Neocore Games. But let's not turn Victor into damnation, that would be a pity.
Whilst many hack and slash RPGs typicaly use mouse for both movement and attacking, Victor Vran has mouse controls only for attacks. All your moves are done by classic WASD key set, with added rolling and
. Finally an isometric ARPG where you don't have to just stick in flat tunnels, you can even "bounce-jump" between walls! It's worth mentioning that even though I'm talking about keyboard and mouse controls, the game is also optimalised for controllers (
).
Many RPGs usually ask for many pieces of equipment for your character, like gloves, wrist armors, chest armors, etc., but Victor Vran does that conversely. You have only one slot for complete armor; developers took weapons and spells with higher priority. And that's reasonable, as every weapon type provides you a new skillset to use, so every weapon plays differently. You can choose from swords, guns, hammers, mortar guns and more.
Spell system reminds me of Diablo I, as you find new spells throughout your adventures, or just buy them at the town's vendor. Disappointing fact is that there isn't a big spell variety, there's just a protective bubble, few auras and few offensive and utility spells. That also applies for enemies, since the skills they use are the ones you can get and use too. Well, even the enemies doesn't provide much variety, but I still find that reasonable with developers' budget.
I've recently bought Diablo III, so I can put one important thing to comparison that made me really excited about Victor Vran - in D3, if a friend won't rush through the content for the first time with you, you have to play through really easy game for many hours, even on the highest difficulty possible (for your first character). Victor Vran allows enemies being easy on you only at the beginning - after a while you'll get hexes, which provide a difficulty system similar to Bastion, i.e. you pick which elements of the game get harder, to get higher experience gain as a reward.
What's the main selling point of Victor Vran, is ubiquitous secret passages with chests and challenges. Each location has a few secret places and a set of five distinct challenges that aims to break player's single playstyle - the game openly want you to try all possible weapons and strategies, with tasks like "kill X anti-melee enemies with hammer", "beat the boss without using potions", "kill all enemies without using spells", or "kill hundred skeletons in 120 seconds". If you consider yourself being completionist, those will offer you a lot of entertainment for many hours.
The story of the game is nothing more than average ARPG filler, I don't even feel like I should talk about it with passion; only truly important thing about the story (besides nice static cutscenes) is the narrator. If you like narrators that want to mock you and make you laugh, you'll love the narrator there. Though every character besides the narrator is deadly serious in the game, the developers tried to be funny too much at some places, so expect the "arrow in the knee" joke or meeting GebaN.
If you don't like playing alone, you can play it with up to 3 friends at time on co-op, or you can visit PvP duelling arena. If you hate paying for DLCs, you can send a happy mail to developers, as they made all game DLCs free (Tome of Souls weapon, Cauldron of Chaos Map, Highlander outfit) - don't forget to install them if you are buying the game!
I got surprised by the game's optimalisation, as it's running well even on low-end computers, and it has many graphic options and UI scaling. But nothing's perfect, once you get into zones with hundreds of enemies at one place (which is even in the first hours of the game, I hope you don't have arachnophobia), the game starts to lag badly.
Victor Vran is a good hack and slash RPG without complex features that offers entertainment for many hours, especially to completionists who expect huge amount of bonus tasks and challenges. Low variety of armor equipment and spells are compensated with good weapon variety and different skillset for each weapon type.

Yeah, it's goofy and good.
To elaborate: Victor Vran pretends it's an APRG in the vein of Diablo. In reality, it's more of an action game with a bunch of RPG elements. There's a lot of buffs and debuffs and damages and armors but most of it can be ignored during the slaughter. The key gameplay mechanics are dodging - something you'll be doing a lot of in the action game way, by rolling from projectiles, jumping over shockwaves and whatnot - and mastering weapons.
There's under twenty weapon types, but each handles differently (by having three attacks associated with it) and each has different mechanics associated with it - so with a shotgun you'll be timing shots and executing enemies, with a scythe you'll harvest souls of and use them to empower your moves and with a rapier you'll be counting your hits to get the maximum out of its combo-empowering abilities.
You can switch between two weapons on the fly and you aren't locked out of any by stat requirements - simply because there aren't any stats. You get passive boosts by equipping a set of cards with values associated with them and figuring out the most effective hand of cards you can use with your limited capacity is actually quite fun.
The emphasis on action gameplay is also further reflected in level design - the maps aren't randomly generated and there is a set of challenges on each one to complete for extra loot and experience; those range from "accidently fulfilled" to "good luck figuring out a build that can do this" in difficulty - and if that isn't enough, another set of (really rather ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ly) challenges for each map opens up on beating the final boss.
Graphics are nice enough, could use less spiders but that's a pretty common issue with RPG devs running out of ideas. I think this game actually suffered a bit in the story/presentation department by coming out at around the same time as Incredible Adventures of Van Helsing, with which it apparently shares a lot of style - hell, even logo/title screen with a steampunky hatted hunter looking in your general direction. I wouldn't call Victor Vran derivative, though; for one, his hat gets mercilessly mocked throughout the game.
Which brings me to the story and writing and what's actually tying all that murder together. The story is minimal - there's this cursed city and you're there to figure out what happened and destroy the ancient evils, blah blah skeletons vampires ghosts demons. The game is thankfully aware of how shallow this is and pokes fun at it quite a lot. Victor Vran doesn't take itself seriously - at all. Your constant companion is a snarky voice in your head that isn't ever afraid to deliver a low blow to your confidence - from the abovementioned hat mockery through pondering the meaning of mass murder for loot and experience to videogame references. The jokes are mostly rather memetic in substance and a lot of them fall flat but they're usually delivered fast enough to make at least some of them stick - my favorite is probably the Stanley Parable dungeon.
I don't think this game will ever become a beloved classic, but it's definitely a step above the typical point-and-kill ARPG in gameplay and gets a lot of points in my book for its admitted and embraced silliness. Definitely worth getting on a sale.

Re;Birth3 V Generation is basically a direct improvement over the previous entries in the series, and in many ways is even superior to the most recent mainline release, Victory 2. The quality-of-life improvements in R;B3 from previous entries are substantial, and the game itself, for those who haven't played Victory, is superb.
The Neptunia franchise, for those unfamiliar, features fairly standard JRPG gameplay, but the main attraction are the visual-novel-esque story and character interaction segments. In contrast to mk2/R;B2, Victory/RB;3 features a story that is far more about the characters than an overarching plot (though one is present). Most of the time you spend playing the game will probably be spent watching the very colorful cast interact with each other. The initial party (and main characters in this entry) of Neptune, Plutia, and Noire is an excellent combination of personalities that really sells the more slice-of-life atmosphere present in R;B3 compared to its predecessors. I think it really should be mentioned that Kana Hanazawa, who provides the voice for Plutia, is near her best in this game, demonstrating an absolutely masterful range and stellar performance.
Having played and enjoyed all of the main games in the franchise, I personally find Re;Birth 3 to be the most entertaining and fun entry in the series, narrowly beating out even V2. If you have played any of the other games in the series, I strongly encourage you to purchase this game, and if you have not yet played a Neptunia game but are interested in the series I think RB;3 is the best place to start.

Overall: Pitfall Planet is a good game. I'd estimate a 4.5 hrs play time for a first run.
Art: Good, lays out the puzzles nicely.
Music: Great, really sets the mood and is memorable.
Controls: Spot on, walking feels free and lining up throws is easy.
Pitfall Planet is game where you solve puzzles in order to collect gold. Most of the puzzles are about how to get from point A to point B. Effectively exploring the level and collecting the gold along the way. Sometimes there's boss battles, which are nice to highlights of the game. The difficultly curve feels natural, starting off easy and progresses to hard. The first half of game takes about an hour to finish, but the difficult puzzles of the second half, took about 3 to 4 hours (In my first play through).
The game is beautiful, the screen shots don't do it justice, I'm a fan of the clean and smooth surfaces. Each level has details in the right spots. There's a cute side story that give a window into the planet before the game's events. The sound track sets the mood appropriately. The songs are mostly chill beats I could hum along with and they put the pressure on for the action levels.
I've played through the game solo. If you use the single controller option you can play both characters at once. To get the most out the game you should play with a friend. Being able to see the look of rage on a friends face when you throw them into lava, or onto a monster is priceless.
Occasionally my brain misjudges how far apart platforms are from one another. And it can be hard to tell if there's an invisible wall to save you from falling off a part of the map or not. In general, it's pretty good about having safety nets where you'd need them.

WARNING:If you haven't played the game yet, this review contains a big amount of spoilers! If you don't want that, don't read until you've played the game yourself!
VVVVVV. An 8-bit style 2-D platformer that defys logic in many ways. This game is a MUST BUY if you are a fan of old school games. In this game, you take control of Viridian, the captain of a dimension hopping ship with a crew of six. One day, they run into some sort of interference and have to teleport away. Unfortunately, the interference causes everyone to be sent to random locations in an abandoned, mysterious, and barren section of the multiverse. As Captain Viridian, you must find your missing friends, who lie beyond some challenging obstacles created by the inhabitants who once lived there.
Just like every other platformer ever released, you can move left and right across the numerous areas this game has. This game has an open world, about 20x20 in area. Instead of scrolling, you move across the grid by getting to the edges of an area in, for the most part, either direction, though some areas will wrap in at least two directions. This is very similar to how I Wanna Be The Guy handled its game world. However, by changing one single mechanic, this game goes from a standard platformer to a very unique experience. You see, Viridian can't jump in a normal way. Instead, he can switch gravity at his will to get past an obstacle. This allows for some very clever puzzles and challenges with platforms that can move and disappear, moving enemies, or even lines that auto-flip you in mid-air.
The overworld of Dimension VVVVVV is split into six very distinct areas: Your ship is the hub that you return to after each level, and is the smallest part of the map at 3x2; The outside is the largest area of the game, comprising of the dimension's colorful yet empty landscape; The Space Station, where you first take control of Viridian after the opening cutscene, is the largest defined level in the game, so big that you visit the place twice during your playthrough; The Laboratory is located beneath the ship and is where you are introduced to the gravity lines; The Tower is located east of the ship and is the only scrolling level accessible through normal means; and The Warp Zone is accessed from the northeast corner of the map after you go through a maze, and this introduces Warp Tokens that teleport you, as well as the wrapping rooms. There are teleporters all over the map that allow for easy access to areas you've already visited. Aside from that, there's also The Polar Dimension that you warp to after rescuing the third, fourth, and fifth crew members and is not located on the main map.
There are, as mentioned, five crewmates to rescue:
-Doctor Violet(Space Station 1)-She gives you the ship's coordinates at the start of the game so you can teleport there at the end of the first stage.
-Doctor Victoria(Laboratory)-She loves to study new things and is very worried about her crewmates.
-Professor Vitellary(Space Station 2)-He's the smartest of the crew and can pretty much understand everything that happens.
-Officer Vermilion(Tower)-He is very brave and will venture out into the world around him to help you find the other crewmates if you rescue him.
-Chief Verdigris(Warp Zone)-He is very committed to repairing the ship so you can escape.
Hidden among the world are twenty shiny trinkets to collect. Collecting them unlocks the ability to play songs on the ship's jukebox, and find all twenty of them will reward you with something special. They are spread out all over the map:
-The Space Station contains six trinkets
-The Laboratory contains four trinkets
-If you talk to Victoria twice after rescuing her from the Lab, she gives you a trinket
-The Tower contains two trinkets
-The maze leading to The Warp Zone has a trinket, and The Warp Zone also contains a trinket
-The outside, excluding the WZ entrance puzzle, contains four trinkets
-You are awarded a trinket for beating the game
The game is very colorful and charming. The graphics are very well drawn, and the color makes it look even better. Many of the spaces in the grid are named, and many of the names are very amusing and have pop-culture references in them. The story is simple and easy to follow, and the dialogue between the characters can be very entertaining.
Don't let the game's color fool you! This game is very much a throwback to classic gaming in not just the graphics, but also the difficulty. This game is HARD, and I mean, VERY HARD. Many of the areas require plenty of skill to pass. A few select trinkets will REALLY test your patience if you are new to the game. In particular is the infamous Veni Vidi Vici trinket in SS2 that forces you to flip into a spike filled chute, hit a disappearing platform, and fall back down on to the trinket. That said, the difficulty is very fair and follows a smooth curve if done in a specific way. It makes you want to complete each part to see what new challenges lie ahead, and all it requires is a bunch of skill and patience.
When all is said and done, VVVVVV is just an incredible game, possibly the best indie game ever made. Everything about it is just so well done. There are optional modes unlocked after certain requirements are met. You can do time trials on the levels, activate a mode that flips everything upside down, or, if you are a true man among men, try to beat the infamous No-Death mode. And there's also a level editor and some pre-installed player levels for you to try out, and you can download more if you find some. Overall, this game gets a well deserved 10/10 from me. It really does hit all the right notes, and is well worth the five bucks I spent to play it.

After the massive and unwieldy campaigns of Empire it was very relieving to play Napoleon. It condences and streamlines the best of the previous Total War, and the close focus on Napoleon works for the games benefit. There are three main campaigns: Italy, Egypt and Europe. Italy and Egypt can be played through in a weekend, rely much on scripts and are likely aimed at new players. Europe is the keystone, and takes many days to finish.
Graphics are improved, as are the sounds, and the interface is very clear. The single-player is completed with Campaigns of the Coalition, where the other powers get to try world domination, and scenarios retelling Napoleons famous battles. These battles may be the most rewarding in Vanilla. AI has great difficulties with making balanced armies and then leading them in battles, but the scenarios are built more like interesting puzzles. The multiplayer battles have a cutthroat reputation and there will be challenge there. Campaigns can be played in multiplayer too but that is not practical.
Darthmod is absolutely vital, as with all Total War games. The Greek Darth Vader will always get my vote for greatest modder alive. It is a permanent blemish for Creative Assembly that they refused to hire him. Perhaps it was envy, perhaps not, we do not know but should enjoy the fruits of his skill, intellect and passion for completing Total War. Napoleon: Total War is fit for series veterans as well as newcomers and comes highly recommended.

This review comes from an entirely subjetive point of view, this is just my opinion of the game and im heavily biased towards the first and the third game and im only going to focus on the PvE. Also, im sorry if I come up to be pretentious in some points, im just a fat weeb that has nothing better to do than to write♥♥♥♥♥♥on the internet.
If you are a PvE and lore centred person, I can't recommend this game.
From the start, the games tells you that it follows the "Dark Souls is all about the difficulty" philosophy since it has an achievement that is literally called "Welcome to Dark Souls" that consists of you dying. There is a stone where you can see how many people has died from the beginning of the game, and it has the "reducing your hp bar mechanic" from Demon's Souls which makes dying incredibly punishing in a game that is based on learning with each death.
But learning won't really help since it seems like the enemies are randomly placed and in big numbers. It's almost like the game rewards a more reactive way of playing but if you don't level up your Hp, some bosses can kill you with one combo and with your Hp getting lower every time you die, the next time you try to go against the boss it can be much harder. That would make you think that shields are the best way of playing because you can just block. But blocking and attacking when you are against 4 mobs at the same time is much harder than just swinging your two handed greatsword and killing everyone. It's like a weird mix between the slow and premedited combat of Dark Souls 1 and the fast combat of Dark Souls 3/Bloodborne. Also, the fact that the roll's invencibility frames work by STATS, makes taking the reactive way of playing much more punishing if you don't level up you ATT and ADP.
The game doesn't care that much about detail and the levels are really bland and boring, there are tons of reused textures, which is understandable since it saves time and money but they reused textures so much that it makes the levels look incredibly similar and destroys the inmersion. Each level seems to have been developed without thinking on the cohesion and there are things that make no sense at all (like a wharf that should be underwater or a castle surrounded with lava at the top of a windmill).
Majula feels like it's the only level FromSoftware really invested time in because of how beautiful it is but the other levels lack personality, I feel like im playing the same level over and over again but with different colours. I haven't played all the dlc's yet, but so far I can say that Brume Tower is just a more vertical and yellow Iron Keep. It feels like im playing an artificial world, there is nothing organic to it. I can't believe that this world was inhabited because there isn't any place that looks like a house at all (in Dark Souls 1 you had little houses with chairs and desks for example). Everything is created with a "gamey" perspective, not with a Lore perspective.
The bosses are also boring. The game starts great tho. At the start, you have the last giant in a place called the forest of fallen giants. It makes you think: Why where the giants killed at this place? What are the giants? Why do they become trees? It makes you get interested. But, as the game progresses, bosses become regular enemies. You have bosses literally copy pasted, you even have Ornstein from the first game, what sense does it make? At this point the game doesn't even try to be interesting. It becomes a routine: Get from A to B, kill the boss, repeat, finish the game. You even have the optional boss that is just cheap and its there for the memes (yes, im looking at you, ancient dragon). They try to connect the game with Dark Souls 1 but it's just to give you the illusion that there is deep lore. And it's such a shame because it has some original and cool stuff but it's really superficial.
Everything is just uninspired and boring. That's how I would define this game, uninspired and boring. You have the Artorias boss (fume knight), you have Ornstein, you have the Gwyn boss (Vendrick), you have the abyss boss (Nashandra), you have the gargoyle multi boss, you have the fast moving animal boss (royal rat authority), you have the boss that stays still spamming♥♥♥♥♥♥(Freja)... There are tons of reused concepts. And it's not bad to reuse concepts, hell, DS 1 reuses concepts from Demon's Souls but it has a much more interesting aura to it. It's the same with Bloodborne and DS 3, every game reuses concepts but in DS 2 it feels like the only reason they included those concepts it's to reminds us of the past glories. You have the poison level, the forest level, the lava level, the level with the godly feel (im comparing dragon shrine and Anor Londo), the abyss level etc...The reason that Vendrick is basically Gwyn, is to say: HEY, THAT GUY SEEMS LIKE GWYN, REMEMBER GWYN? HE WAS COOL. It's a game created to make money, it's not the personification of the soul of the developers. It's not a game made willingly. They even added 3 dlc's when they said that they wouldn't and they focused much more on the PvP experience than in the PvE. Yes, the weapons are much more balanced and you can create tons of builds but is it worth to focus on this instead on to focus on everything else?

And for what it's worth, I used the hardest difficulty-level to avoid the risk of things becoming too easy. But it ended-up becoming a back-and-fourth between:
a) slogging through stuff that takes  *forever* to kill, devoid of any sense of challenge or tension. And
b) finding some high-level item which then makes everything too easy for a while.
Maybe I should've played it on Normal mode and selectively-enabled Hexes, but I doubt that would've fundamentally changed anything for me.
So yeah, good game, but it's not for me.

That's too hard to type all the time. I'm just going to call the game Nep-Nep 3 from now on.
OK. Nep-Nep 3 is, at its core, a pretty much by-the-numbers JRPG. Fight monsters, level up, fight more monsters, level up, etc.  There's a crafting system wherein you take items gained from battle to make new items, as well as to unlock items to be sold in shops. The battle mechanics are a bit unique, and combine strategic placement of your characters along with combo attacks that add some variety to what would otherwise be pretty stale gameplay.
This game gets most of its fan following from 2 main points. The first is a positively ludicrous amount of fan service. The cast is made up exclusively of cute girls wearing elaborate and often skimpy outfits.  The second is the game's sense of humor. Its main character, Neptune, is extremely self-aware and very genre-savvy. She KNOWS she's in a video game and so do most of the other characters. They make comments about it constantly and they're always breaking the 4th wall, and Neptune will frequently talk directly to the player.
So if you're looking at Nep-Nep 3, you've probably already played the previous games in the series. If you haven't, here's a quick rundown of the setting. The world of Gamindustri is split up into 4 nations--Planeptune, Lastation, Lowee and Leanbox. Each nation is ruled by a goddess, often referred to as a CPU. These goddesses take the beliefs of their people and translate them into formidable combat prowess. They gain this belief, called "shares" by supporting and helping their people. They used to fight each other constantly for domination of Gamindustri. Now they all find themselves as more friendly rivals than bitter enemies (thanks to Neptune's actions in a previous game). If you think all this stuff sounds familiar, that's not by accident. The whole game is an allegory for the entire game industry (Gamindustri, get it?) The nations of Planeptune, Lastation, Lowee and Leanbox are meant to represent the hardware manufacturers Sega, Sony, Nintendo and Microsoft (in that order).  The entire world is littered with references to video games--some subtle, others REALLY blatant) and the whole thing has a vibe of "we changed the names just enough to avoid getting sued".  It's part of the humor though.
If you have not played the first two games, I wouldn't worry about it too much. There's stuff that happens there that will be referenced in this game, but they'll generally explain what they're talking about when that happens.  Also, the games are all pretty similar to each other. The big downside is they recycle a lot of assets from game to game, from enemy types to character models to even entire dungeon maps. To a degree this makes some sense as all the games take place in the same spot, and in a pretty close time frame--so the world really doesn't change much. That said, the appearance of the game is decidedly last-gen.  The character animations are stiff and the models are of a middling quality. (Then again, all 3 of these games are console ports, so that may have something to do with it)
So how can I sum all this up?  Well, if you played Nep-Nep 1 and 2 and enjoyed them, this is more of the same, so you'll like it.  If you didn't care for either of those two games, don't bother.  If you're on the fence but like a funny JRPG that doesn't take itself too seriously, I suggest giving it a go.

First, let me say that ever since I discovered the Divinity series I've loved it.  Larian clearly puts a lot of thought and effort into their games, and it is most welcome.
For this game specifically, if you're a dragon lover like me, just buy it.  Do it, you won't regret it.  It is an incredible amount of fun to fly free and burn everything that dares approach in the skies, but it retains challenge enough that if you get careless, flying demons and corrupted dragons can easily bring your flight to an abrupt halt.
In human form, there is an enormous amount of skills and spells that are ideal in differing circumstances.    The variety of enemies is significant.  Many of them fall into categories that make them similar to others, but they're certainly not identical.  Attack patterns are often similar, but even so, don't count on never getting hit, especially with numerous attacks with limited homing capacities or that hit instantly on being released.  As such, there is still a great deal of value to changing strategies against different opponents.  The bosses, however, are where the real challenge shows up.  Even if you've had no trouble up to the boss in question, be prepared to use everything at your disposal, from potions to underhanded tricks such as abusing the terrain, to win.  When you have to fight tooth and claw to get there, though, it just makes victory all the sweeter.
The story is quite interesting, though I highly recommend reading up on what happened before the game begins first.  The Divinity Wiki has a story article that gives the background to Ego Draconis, which is the first and main part of the game.
The graphics certainly aren't amazing by modern standards, but honestly they're not that bad.  They may not be pure cinematic beauty like something like The Witcher 3, but they're hardly an eyesore either.  The music and voice acting are quite impressive as well.
Also, unlike so many mass-marketed open-world RPGs, Divinity II offers actual reasons to explore, in the form of unique equipment, hidden treasure troves and interesting quests.  Poking around in odd corners is likely to turn up something special that was hand-placed there, rather than just another chest of randomly generated equipment that is worse than what you could buy or make.  And even if it does turn out to be random loot, it's likely at least as good as most merchants carry.
Unlike Skyrim, with its unlimited supply of boring fetch quests, Divinity II has quests both in towns and in odd corners of the world that have some story and challenge to solving them.  You also won't see a huge floating arrow saying "quest target is right here!", instead you will have to use the information given to you by the quest giver and your journal to locate the target.  Don't worry, it won't be that hard to find if you pay attention, and it makes the game significantly more interesting and immersive.
I could go on and on, but I'll cut it here with one final comment:  Easily one of the most addicting games I've come across in a very long time.  The others that prevent me from putting this alone at the very top?  Same developer.  That says a lot, I think.

In case you somehow haven't heard of this game by 2017, it's great. The game is very simple, with the only mechanics on your character being moving left and right, as well as reversing gravity. Rather than tacking on endless amounts of abilities, which can be fun, this game instead introduces a level-specfic gimmick, gets your comfortable with it, and demands perfection. This game can be tough, REALLY tough. But even when it's tough it so ingenius that you want to pull on. There are frequent checkpoints too in case you screw up often, as well as collectables for those who want to go the extra mile. Once you get bored of the regular campaign, there's also time trial mode for the specific levels, a flip mode where everything is upside down (which messes with you on a psychological level more than anything), and a level editor. From what I've seen so far the community isn't huge for this game anymore, but levels built into the browser can be fun, and making your own can be great as well. Overall I very much reccomend this game, so long as your aren't feint of heart.
