Home is Where One Starts...
First-person Exploration
David Wehle
David Wehle
is a first-person exploration game similar to
and
, developed by David Wehle.
If you played "Gone Home", you'll know what you are getting into. The game is about a girl who explores the surroundings of her house after having missed the bus. The area that you explore is filled with secrets and details revealing your character's story, without being too much "in-your-face".
Made in the Unity engine, the game looks beautiful: everything, from the shadows to the lightning, feels photorealistic. This is easily one of the best looking games developed with the engine.
Just like all the other games like this, you walk around and look at some stuff. There are no puzzles and there is little to no interactivity with the environment. If you play this game, you must know that you will spend most of your time walking around and listening the narrator talk about her experiences and her life.
There is really no challenge at all, but that is not the point of the game, so I won't take this into account.
Elise Wehle voices the narrator, and she makes a fantastic job, making you feel the sadness of her character. The music that accompanies you is also really good, but after hearing it for five times during a playthrough, it kinda got on my nerves.
The game took me 15 minutes to complete the first time, but there are enough secrets and achievements that will make you come back to fully explore the environment.
David Wehle created a relaxing and interesting experience, albeit short. Fans of this type of games will have a blast with it, while those who don't like them won't find anything fresh to make you feel any different toward this genre.

It saddens me that a lot of people will scoff at the title’s length, even with a super low $2.99 price point. But I cannot stress this enough – if you are someone who is willing and bale to immerse themselves into a touching plot, or someone who just likes to be moved on a level that many games simply don’t offer, then Home is Where One Starts… is a very important piece of gaming art that you simple cannot pass up. Sure it’s brief, and sure there might not be any ‘traditional’ gamey mechanics… but that does not rob it of being one of the most touching and well thought-out experiences available to date.

Home is Where One Starts is a like a bleaker take on Gone Home's formula as you play as young girl in a poor home in Virginia. While I don't think it ends up being as great as Gone Home it’s still quite good.  The dev has said that he was inspired by Gone Home and Dear Esther and I can compliment the game in that it’s much more like Gone Home and it’s down to earth humanity and getting the player involved through exploration instead of Dear Esther which was too busy verbally masturbating all over itself to form any kind of meaningful story, character, theme, emotional resonance, or player engagement. The atmosphere in HiWONS is really damn good, the writing is grounded and nicely done and the voice acting really gels with and adds to it as well. There's also enough things to find to make the game interesting, there are still things I need to find that I missed in my first playthrough. Considering that this game was pretty much made by one dude that only did it as a hobby it definitely puts some games to shame, it sure as hell puts Dear Esther to shame.
Overall if you loved Gone Home and other exploration based narrative games you will enjoy this. It's not long but I felt what was here was quality stuff. Hopefully the dev doesn't just stop here and makes more because this a nice start.

Banished is a great casual city builder/management game that's a little outside the "box" in terms of game play. Your cities success isn't weighed on how much currency you have or how big your population is per se. It's really about surviving and how well you manage your resources and people. There are no pre-set goals, but for me - that's fun. I like that I get to make it "my" game by deciding what goals/ambitions I want to impose based on how I'm feeling and what I want to accomplish. The map is fully open for you to explore. All buildings are available to you right from the start - provided you have the resources to build them. There is no "fog of war", no research trees, no advisers and/or whining citizens to attend to. I believe the game is supposed to be a medieval city builder, but I like to think of it as more of a pioneer/homesteading kind of game. In fact, I'll probably try and take it down that road (time period wise) when the mod tool releases.
Sure, Banished could use a little cleaning up around the edges...a little more spit & polish to make it really shine. Maybe a few additions here and there, but over all; I think the developer did a great job! I really like the game and would recommend it to others!

Outlast
Genre: Survival horror
Engine: Unreal Engine
Platforms: Microsoft Windows, PlayStation 4
Note: This game includes violence and hard gore.
Introduction:
Outlast is a first-person survival horror game set in an asylum. The main character "Miles Upshur"."Miles Upshur" a freelance journalist, receives a tip-off from an anonymous source about Mount Massive Asylum, a psychiatric hospital owned and operated by the Murkoff corporation."Miles Upshur" is incapable of combat, except for certain scripted sequences in which he pushes enemies away. To navigate the environment, the character is able to climb to ledges, vault over low obstacles, crawl, and slide in narrow gaps. Except for vaulting, enemies are incapable of any of these maneuvers, which gives the player a certain edge. In addition, the player can survive encounters with the inmates by hiding inside of lockers or under beds, although certain enemies may search the room and attempt to locate the player for a short time before moving on.Since much of the asylum is dark, the player must use Miles' video camera to see, thanks to its night vision function. Using night vision consumes batteries, replacements of which are scattered throughout the environment.When injured, Upshur must avoid taking any further damage for a while, which will allow him to recover.
Pros:
- One of the best survival horror games with a good story.
- Fascinating story told through documents and notes.
- Scary moments will make you scream.
- Very dark atmosphere.
- Fast-draining night vision camera keeps tensions high.
- Very good sound design.
- Absence of weapons requires smart uses of hiding spots.
Cons:
- The graphic isn't the best.
The Verdict:

Refunct is a fun 3D first-person platformer. The game's only activities are traversal and figuring out how to get from point A to point B. Its movement mechanics are reminiscent of Mirror's Edge, though there is no character model (and thus no animation accompanying any of the movements). The game design, as well as the art style is quite minimalistic (whether that's a positive or a negative is subjective but I thought it was quite alright). Moving around feels good and is fun, as is finding your way around the environment. The game's only weakness is its short length. I managed to complete the main objective in under one hour. There are collectibles but I suspect even completionists would not get more than two hours out of the game. All in all, though, it's a very solid, very entertaining 3D platformer game and I recommend it to anyone who's a fan of that (terribly underrepresented) genre.

Highly recommend to anyone looking for a challenge and a wonderful, critical-thinking story. The story requires a bit of intuition and scouring when progressing through the vast world. Leaving out area/boss names to prevent spoiling, but how I weigh the overall game can be described as follows:
Pros:
- Some innovative boss fights among the 40+ boss fights the chosen undead can encounter.
- Beautiful landscape/atmosphere the game places you in.
- Despite original state where the game was supposed to look a certain way, the graphics in textures and character models were still greatly improved.
- Being able to play in groups whilst praising the sun made certain boss fights very enjoyable.
- Improved weapon physics (looking at you dual-wielding) made the game much more fun for lollygagging once the story is complete.
Cons:
- Some boss fights as easy as grunt enemies.
- Placement of enemies and level design are to be expected as enemies feel like they are just placed about.
- Little surprises around the corner leaves some areas to be pretty forgettable, while some areas are just tediously getting through enemies and are not engaging whatsoever.
- Soul memory.
- Investing into player stats such as adaptability just to move at a decent pace in almost every action required by the game.

Given the amount of freshness and raw pure fun Victor Vran brings into the stale ARPG genre, I cannot recommend the game enough and I'm really looking forward to any potential expansions the developers care to bring.
I do, however, have several points I'd like to state about what I think would further improve the game. Don't take me wrong, the game is fantastic and it is both worth it's price and it is totally worth checking out for the reason previously stated, and that's whether you're a diehard fan of hack'n'slash genre or just a casual looking for a fun combat system, yet there are a few aspects I subjectively think could use improving:
1. No trade option nor a 'trade house' - Since Legendary weapons are very hard to reliably drop and most of the times they're totally random, you can walk through the game ending up with either a good amount of Legendaries or next to none whatsoever, and that's without counting that you may both have almost every single type dropped or just a few copies of the same weapon all over again, which is a bit frustrating if you're not a fan of ceaseless grinding, especially for players new to the game. Since Legendaries are among the most fun weapons in the game, not to mention many of their special abilities actually change the playstyle of a given weapon type, a simple Trade option would keep the new players interested in the game instead of being bored to death because of endless gray/green/gold drops all over again, while more experienced players would have the option of sharing or trading the numerous copies of the same Legendaries (that they wouldn't make use of anyway) with their friends.
2. Bounty/Hunt drops are far too few - Yes, I get the idea that they're kept low to encourage the community to work together and share their codes, but given that it's hard to find players online nowadays turns this approach obsolete. Since the endgame consists of challenges (which, once completed, aren't there anymore), bottomless pit runs (which, given the low amount of drops, are in my opinion just a test ground for trying out new playstyles against waves of enemies) and the dreaded cauldron of chaos (kudos for the implementation, more of that please!), the better or simply more reliable drop rate of Bounties and Treasure Hunts tied to some specific activity would keep more players interested in the game and give them something to do each day.
3. Endgame content comes down to Cauldron of Chaos mostly - The implementation of CoC was a perfect move from the developers, as it is essentially a damn hard challenge for players that changes every day, keeping them interested in the game and providing them with some meaningful tests to try their builds and skill. My point here is therefore not against the CoC itself, which is awesome, but because that it's the only meaningful endgame level that has some daily significance and appropriate rewards. The simple idea is that the game could really use more instances like this so that playerbase keeps growing.
4. Victor Vran II? - The point is more of a personal comment from me, so don't take it as an objective argument. As I said, the game brings lots of freshness to the stale hack'n'slash genre and I love the changes to the formula that the devs have implemented. My only wish is that they further expand upon this solid idea basis and try releasing a proper old-school expansion or perhaps another installment for Victor Vran, giving players more of everything - a bigger world, more ever-changing endgame instances, more unique weapon types, more card types, more outfits, more powers, perhaps even a customization of one's own hunter instead of playing as Victor Vran himself. The brilliant basis is already there in VV, so I really hope the devs take it further and give players striving for freshness in the ARPGs more of new stuff to sink their teeth in.

Banished is a great casual city builder/management game that's a little outside the "box" in terms of game play. Your cities success isn't weighed on how much currency you have or how big your population is per se. It's really about surviving and how well you manage your resources and people. There are no pre-set goals, but for me - that's fun. I like that I get to make it "my" game by deciding what goals/ambitions I want to impose based on how I'm feeling and what I want to accomplish. The map is fully open for you to explore. All buildings are available to you right from the start - provided you have the resources to build them. There is no "fog of war", no research trees, no advisers and/or whining citizens to attend to. I believe the game is supposed to be a medieval city builder, but I like to think of it as more of a pioneer/homesteading kind of game. In fact, I'll probably try and take it down that road (time period wise) when the mod tool releases.
Sure, Banished could use a little cleaning up around the edges...a little more spit & polish to make it really shine. Maybe a few additions here and there, but over all; I think the developer did a great job! I really like the game and would recommend it to others!

Napoleon: Total War is easily the most divisive of all Total War games. Some folks love it, some folks hate it. It is, to be fair, an almost carbon copy of Empire at first glance. The most noticeable difference is that Napoleon concentrates exclusively on Europe whereas Empire allows the player to conquer the globe.
Beyond first blush, Napoleon does feature some improvements over Empire that make it worth consideration. Chief of those is better coding - Napoleon is accepted by most to be a much more stable and better running game than Empire. It is also better looking. AI is supposedly markedly better, however that is debatable. There are a number of mods available that greatly improve the Napoleonic experience - but you're fine running the stock game.
If Empire and Napoleon look too similar to you - if muskets and dragoons are all the same to you, you may prefer Empire over Napoleon due to the globe. But... If, like me, you have a fascination with the Napoleonic Wars, you owe it to yourself to give Napoleon: Total War - beyond dominating Europe, there is also a series of historical battles and campaigns that are very enjoyable.

Verdun is more about keeping your head down and taking a pot shot at the enemy off in the distance..or is that just a rock?
Meanwhile,  you're squinting down your rifle sights,  that commrade standing right next to you in the trench, well he actually turns out to be fricken enemy and headshots you as you hipfire like a baked potato . He takes you and your squad down as you ponder "Wha da duck just happened?" Is all of my squad potatos to or were they looking at the rock?
You die lots in this game. However, kills  seem more satisfying when you have been face down chomping trench mud time after time.
The maps are pretty varied surprisingly,  although all encompass some type of trench. This makes for trying out different tactics and approaches, generally keeping things interesting.
Graphics are solid enough, while sound is ok i suppose, pretty ordinary though in my opinion.
Even still, Verdun does a great job of recreating a suitable WW1 atmosphere and brings its own type of intensity in gameplay.
While it wont be everyones "go to" shooter, i think it has it's place in the genre by just being different.
Verdun is a game I find myself drifting back to every so often.  Especially when I feel the need of a break from Arma III and the manic bulletfest of BF4. I always find myself wondering why I dont play Verdun more...

Well this is something I try not to do often. Usually when I review a game I like to have at least 5+ hours or if it has an end I'd prefer to have made it passed the games story, but I just can't play this anymore. So with my meager 3 hours I'm just goint to put my thoughts down. Also a warning that'll hopefully let you know to take my review with a grain of salt.
I'm not a huge fan of most of these rpg games in general, in a broader sense I'm not a fan of games that make you do everything alone. So this game had a strike against it for me right off the bat, because no matter how important they make your quests/missions/whatever sound you're always 100% alone (aside from your temporary summons).
Also, I know this is common in games with questing but I'm just saying. If you're trying to make someone feel a part of an epic story, the least epic feeling thing you can do is make them spend loads of time saving pigs from slaughter, or helping some farmers wife leave her husband. They feel more like chores than quests.
Pros:
Even though it's an older game it's graphics aren't terrible so it's not eye destroying if you're used to todays quality.
The story sounded like it could be pretty interesting from what little I got of it.
Cons:
Animations are♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ Jumps are awkward, attacks are clumsy, and people animate when they talk to you like they're having a siezure.
Combat is boring, this was a big one for me. You have to fight your way passed everything and even if you have quite a few skills I couldn't see it being more fun.
Difficulty is all over. I was killing things easily that were 1-2 levels under me, taking them on a few at a time, but as soon as I fight 2 things on level even though they were ranged and I dodged most of their attacks I was getting melted. When they did hit me it was dealing loads of damage and I don't know how I could've prevented it. I was done with the quests I could do before the area so leveling was out of the question, and the gear I could've bought was hardly any better than what I had on.
Voice acting is mediocre at best, there's some decent dialog but it's mostly bland and the voices were giving me a headache.
The undead I could summon were butchered in seconds, the skills I unlocked were apparently the worst I could get (I'm good at choosing like that) since they hardly made a difference and auto attacking was basically all I did.
All in all I'd recommend looking for something else, I really wish I'd have played one less hour so I could request a refund for this. I'll never touch it again.

A difficult game, at least it is for me. Mostly you have to do trial and error, and some puzzles require you to figure out.
Controls are straight-simple, moving left and right. No jumping, instead, it is gravity flipping to maneuver.
Although the control is not complicated. the very designed rooms are hard, which players need to decide what and how to move V's step very carefully and precisely. Less half a second, V falls onto spikes; more half a second, V fails to step right on a moving platform. Sometimes, a perfect one-run to avoid multiple traps is needed.
It can be so frustrating to fail constantly, seeing the death toll keeps rising up makes you want to shut the game off and smash your keyboard. For example, when I first started, about half the town was dying of starvation, so I looked to see how much food each house had. It's a good game, but what makes it good is also the problem. After a while it just started to get repetitive for me, ad I lost interest in my settlement because it just felt like I was repeatedly doing the same stuff for the sake of it. You can impose limitations on yourself to unlock the Achievements, which adds a bit of a different challenge.
It's enjoyable building your first few settlements, for sure. If you enjoy city builders or resource management, you'll enjoy the game. There's a change from a lot of similar games in that military strength is non-existent, and there's a much bigger forcus on keeping each of your citizens alive and not incinerated, frozen, and starved. In the early years, you'll get attached to these people, and you might struggle to survive. Or you might prosper, only to have a fire or a hurricane rip out the heart of your settlement and leave you in deep trouble. It's engrossing until you get a few hundred people, and that's when the repetition starts to show and I lost my enthusiasm.
It's got decent graphics and the engine is stable. It's not expensive, and there should be decent mod support to help with its longevity and to iron out the few wrinkles. It's a great achievement from a single developer, and definitely contains enough to warrant getting it.

I loved Sunless Seas. I spent far too much time with the game that I should have spent on actual college work. The atmosphere was beautiful, the story lines were engaging, and the prose was at the same time familiar and compelling in a way that few video games are. Playing Sunless Skies has made me remember everything I hate about Sunless Seas and why I flat out abandonned the game until I found a way to credit so much money to my player by fidgetting with the save file that I could literally have bought out the entirely of London, the Khanate, the Kingdom to the south, and still probably had enough money left over to purchase and pimp out a fleet of luxury liners to take me to meet Salt and host a gigantic barbecue party on the eastern shores with supermodel waitresses and enough boxed sunlight to make me forget where I was going with this story of mine. That said, it took about 30 hours of Sunless Seas to get me to the point where I was scouring the web for ways to cheat. Sunless Skies took about 30 minutes to get me there.
Now the game will tell you that cheating will ruin the experience, but the unfortunate fact is that like Sunless Seas, Sunless Skies shines in the experience and not the gameplay. It's incredibly compelling to land at a port to find that something has changed, to follow a story line with peril and danger to see the journey of a character through to the bitter end. It is not fun to have my eyes flicker constantly over to the fuel and supplies timer and to be forced to optimize my cargo bay to the very maximum just to keep myself afloat. Instead of following a story line, I've instead been forced to keep hopping from island to island to collect port reports and hauling cargo to barely make any progress in the bank. The problem with both games is that you need the money to do anything fun in the game, but the journey to getting the money you need is so irrirating and grindy that it barely seems worth the effort.
Both supplies and fuel are both too expensive, and the cost to cover the running of your ship makes it so that it is close to impossible to carry the necessary items to continue anymore than 1 plotline at the time despite the fact that your need to visit every port to maximize the revenue of each trip makes it so that you will have to keep visiting ports with story lines that you simply lack the necessary items to continue. It's a problem with the Seas version as well, it is just very difficult to follow a story line because the gameplay demands your attention so you just get distracted and keep getting ran off course and away from what you were doing before and just forget what you were meant to be doing. The game claims to not be about trading, and yet trading is the only thing you can resort to to get anywhere in the story. An irritating, boring, and fustrating trade system that doesn't reward ingenuity or courage (in the context of the game) nearly as much as it rewards route memorization and grinding. When I could see a 100 line bot being just as good as the game as I am, something has gone wrong in the game development process. It's not about continuing the story, it's like building up resources to have fun and, quite frankly, that is what having a job is for.
The game appears to want to be a game that focussed on exploration and intrigue, and yet it quickly devolves into a game where you grind youself into the ground. Making trips is far from sustainable and there is no profittable trade route and no story hook to keep you going back to a port even if there was. I understand the ambition of the developpers to make you feel alone, isolated, and tiny in a gigantic universe but the game fails at that. It's trival to avoid fights and they're so rare and unprofitable that it rarely feels worth the effort. The game is still bad at conveying what it wants you to do. Something simple like 'gray out port reports that have yet to be collected in the journal tab' goes unimplemented by the developpers. After the first rush of interest in finding a new location, the game quickly fades as it fades into a game of guessing what a text prompt will do. Just like Sunless Seas, it is nearly impossible to tell whether or not an interaction with a character would yield profit or whether it will be a drain on the already preciously meager resources at your disposal. Like I said in the opening sentence, space is large, empty, and boring. I don't understand why everyone's getting so afraid of the world, I just can't sympathize with the game's characters. With the sea, there is at least a level of unknowable danger from the surrounding waters. In Sunless Skies, you float in a void where you can see enemies approach from (probably literally) kilometers away. The fear rises as the spacecraft just sits there in response to no clear event, as if it's less tracking the fear of the characters and more tracking my annoyance with yet another gating mechanic between me and the story. There are other small issues as well. So many areas of space are identical, there is no appriciable difference between the ruins of the battle of whatever and the battle of whatsitcalled, whether aesthetic or story. There's also an issue with scenery. Aestival was a glimmering tropical gem with golden beaches, the Iron Republic is a blood red industrial hellscape, London is a sombre but pretty city with a corner hosting an alien organism, Frostfound is an irridescent fortress of white crystals, Adam's way is a gray and yellow fortress that bled the carmine of the living river, and the Kingeater's castle is a eerie green tomb of stone and statues. Just about everything in Sunless Skies looks the same. With the exception of Titania and the mountain, the entire world is basically a unifrom combination of the green of vegetation and gray of stone, or generic Victorian era architecture without any of the sharp aesthetic sense that would have distinguised, say, London from the Grand Geode. The cargo bay is even more restricting than Sunless Seas and, and this will sound incredibly petty, the fact that pretty much every port cues the same theme music is irritatingly grating and the hiss of the turning jet exhausts is so taxing that I feel a reflexive desire to rake my nails across my arms every time I hear it.
Some things have improved from Sunless Seas. The fact that you can buy supplies and fuel makes it so that you aren't as frequently irritated by the game's survival mechanic. The consumption of fuel and supplies is also appriciably slower, giving more leeway for extended engagement with what few enemies you could run across which makes the game far more skill based. That is not saying much however, combat is some of the weakest part of both titles to the point where I could think of a long list of free to play flash games, some of which is from a decade ago, that has a significantly better combat system than Sunless Skies. 1 out of 4 zones is presently avaliable. Even assuming that each island has a similar amount of plot as Sunless Seas and all 4 zones were completed in the future, I can't honestly recommend this game for over 20 euroes. With the glaring economic issues that the devs probably won't fix, I could not even honestly say I could recommend this game for 10. Now I am keeping this game, but that comes with the prerequisite that I am rather odd. There will be more content in the future, but the problems with this game is fundemental down to the very ways that the mechanics and storylines functions. I could not see myself recommending this title to anyone withot massive overhauls to the story. The game retains much of the mechanics of Sunless Sea which renders the game unenjoyable all the while taking place in a much less interesting locale. Even if I thought someone might me interested in Sunles Skies, I see no reason to recommend this over its predecessor.

This is an early access game, so pretty much everything, that I'm going to talk about, is a subject to change. You may also notice that my playtime isn't very high right now. I'm simply waiting for more content to be added, I don't want to burn myself out before the game is even finished. But I have put enough hours into it's predecessor to have a good idea of what this game is all about.

Have you ever wondered, what would happen if space travel was invented in Victorian era? This game will give you answer to that. You roam around in your space-train (no joke), find ports, trade goods, fight monsters, go slowly insane and of course make game-changing choices.

Right now you can explore only one region of the High Wilderness, it's called the Reach. It only has a few ports, but each of them offer unique quests and sell different commodity, like you'd expect. One of the ports is actually under construction and you can affect the way it's built (I haven't really gotten to this because I haven't amassed enough money).
The main mechanics from Sunless Sea are all back with some changes to them. For instance port reports work quite differently. The old mechanic would yield a sum of money, fuel and supplies for each individual report. In this game the rewards now depend on the number of reports you have. For instance one report is only rewarded with money, two will get you fuel on top of that and so on. Just like In Sunless Sea you can send out scouts to locate nearby point of interest, but now it costs you a bit of supplies, so you have to ration them carefully. Sanity meter (terror) is of course back, this time around letting it fill up has a permanent effect.
Early on exploring is quite limited, because you don't have enough supplies to really go very far without running out (a helpful tip- unless you're planning a long expedition, spend your money on fuel only, supplies can be replenished by killing monsters). So, this means you have to establish trading routes and stick to them until you gather enough resources to explore further out. Fuel and supplies cost a bit more now, but they also seem to last longer. The combat system has been reworked quite a bit, which is good, because that was the weakest point of Sunless Sea. Right now you start with two weapons instead of one, you no longer have to wait for "finding a firing solution" (wait for a bar to fill up), so you don't miss. Now you can shoot at will without having to worry about that, but you can overheat if you fire too quickly.
There is a RPG element to the game, by fighting monsters and discovering things you get experience. Levelling up will award you points, which you can spend on what this game calls facets. Each of those reveals a bit about your character and increase your stats a bit.
The writing once again is excellent, each port has it's own theme, the characters are interesting and overall mood of the game, while not as dark as Sunless Sea, it certainly has a creepy atmosphere. Lot of tension going on (especially if you read the newspapers). In conclusion, so far the game is relatively polished, more stuff is on the way- as for the closest update goes, there is a planned overhaul of a trading system.
If you want to get this game just to play it, I'd suggest you wait for it to have a bit more content. Unless of course you want to personally help this game to grow and you don't worry about bugs.

Refunct is one of those gems that, while short, leaves you smiling and relaxed. In a nutshell, it's a parkour game with evolving playing field, where you run around turning drab concrete into grass, reaching red buttons to raise more sections, and collecting cubes tucked away out of sight.
The movement is smooth, and without any hints at how to solve some of the puzzles, the environment is colored and open enough that it just makes sense. The music is peaceful, and the game forgiving. If you miss a jump between high pillars, land on the ground or the water... neither will punish you with damage. I clocked up 47 minutes, as I thought I had made a mistake and was stuck, so I restarted, but on my second run when I reached the same location, I figured out the obvious solution.
For $1.50 in the sale I am happy with the experience. I wish there were more levels, or perhaps an endless mode, which would keep me coming back frequently. Without that, there isn't much to entice you to replay.

I got this game when I was jonesing for some point and clicks, and had to do a lot of searching since the 'Hidden Object' genre came into existence between my childhood and when I got a computer that could run steam. It's one of the decent point and clicks, for sure.
While it is a Horror story, it's not very scary. A bit spooky, but it won't give you a fright, nor will it make you feel squeemish or disgusted like The Thing would. While reading up on Native AMerican spookies on this game, you would be surprised how much evil stuff they have in their mythology, it's definently worth a look too.
Anyway, the graphics are... Okay. Dated might be a better word, but not too bad. Though the female love interest of the main character suddenly wanting to do the deed was kind of weird and felt like it only happened because that's what horror movies do and wasn't what she herself would have done.
The puzzles themselves are pretty great, the parser puzzles aside. If I can't solve a puzzle, but the solution makes sense, I don't mind feelign like an idiot. That's on me. But if it's something like... taping cat hair to your face by placing tape over a cat door then it's the game. There is no moon logic puzzles here. The hardest is the parser puzzles, which are mostly just making out what old symbols mean and is a bit vague. There's a hilarious one where you bake a cake to try and impress a girl. Whiel that might sound annoying, the place you are in is only os big, so it's not hard to find everything. The outcoem depends on how well you follow the instructions. Hint: Try cooking ti with gasoline : )

After about 65 hours into Dungeon Defenders II I am happy to report that they have been enjoyable. While the overall feel of DDII remains similar to that of its predecessor, there are some things that are notably different. To start with, if you want to use each of the heroes you will have to grind them up to the higest level (currently 25 although this is bound to increase as new content becomes available) individually as the maps are now broken up into level restrictive increments such as 1-3, 3-5, 5-10 etc. You are however able to use your higher level characters in lower level maps although they will be scaled down accordingly to the highest level for the current map. This can be time consuming but presumably it is to discourage solo play and encourage teamwork and synergy between community members.
The maps feel a bit busier graphically and it was harder for me to wrap my head around tower placement than it was for the first game. In DD1, you were often able to place towers in such a way that you could guard multiple lanes with clever and well thought out placement. With DD2 placement feels more dictated and formulaic which takes a bit of fun away from the planning process.
Currently at the time of this review (Dec. 2013) only one "Stage" is available. There is not yet a "boss" fight which was disappointing but the game is still in a pre-alpha state. There are synergies now between damage types and trap combinations which are interesting and give the players something to strive for in terms of teamwork.
Item progression seems well planned, however the items have very little variation. There are generally two stats associated to one item, the first is determined by the item name (i.e.: "Rapid Fire Gloves" are guaranteed to have Defense Speed on them) and the second appears to be random. As a result of only 2 stats for each item, you are almost forced into choosing a specialization of 2 to be effective and are only looking for items with those 2 stats on them for the majority of the game.  This often leads to finishing a map, browsing through items very quickly, keeping the ones that match your criteria and selling the rest. While this seems like a good formula, I found myself quickly bored as there are only a couple combinations of items that are worthwhile at the moment (Defense Power/Defense Speed for builders, and Hero Damage/Ability Power for DPS). This meant that 90% of the items I found I sold and 10% I kept. With 20-30 items per map it felt like a lot of time selling useless items.
The inventory system is currently somewhat challenging to navigate. Dragging items onto other bags works infrequently and forces you to manually open bags and move items between open slots. It was difficult to organize them and I wanted a more user friendly experience. It would also be lovely to be able to check your inventory with 'i' like in the first game instead of being forced to visit a defender's forge.
Working with other people was sometimes more challenging than it should have been. I think this game could benefit from a built in chat system to make the process easier.
I'm looking forward to the costumes to become available in game via micro transactions so that I can lend some uniqueness to my character as currently, when there are four monks running around in game it feels very much like a clone of the person next to me which takes away from the immersion considerably.
Overall, the game was really fun up to the maximum level but there is little reason to stay and grind at the moment. I look forward to exploring additional content as it becomes available. I would reccommend purchasing the game in it's current stage to anyone who is willing to be patient as content becomes available since as of right now it is somewhat limited in scope.

This is a time where pixelart would have made a huge difference and made the entire experience a lot more enjoyable. Because the overall plot (while fairly short) is pretty good. The "supernatrual things happening on a remote research station" is not the most unique of ideas, but it works. The writing is prettt good but the plot moves to fast, having the plot take place over a few more days and have some more character development would have med the end ressult better.
The puzzles are for the most part the usual point and click. There is not that much moon logic, but there are still some pretty obtuse puzzles with contrived solutions. The entire station is very small, about 10-12 rooms including the outside areas, so if you get stuck, there aren't that many areas you have to search, but some puzzles drove me nuts because the game wanted a VERY specific way of doing things. The other puzzles are when you are doing some deductions in your investigation and use a text parser to write words. I'm not entirely sold on that they are a good idea. But there are only a few of them. Overall Alpha Polaris is heavily flawed, but is barely a recommendation due to that the stoy had me interested the entire way and I'm a sucker for the setting. At least pick it up at the next sale.

While the game itself "as is" is not so bad, the following are the points which are just plainly put, true facts which heavily outweight the positive points of the game:
- Gamebreaking bugs present
- No continuing support from Ubisoft
- Broken 3rd party DRM that you have to forcefully shut down with task manager (after you closed it with regular means via UI).
- Tactical field in sqares and not hexagons (simply put - from software engineering perspective squares are "easier" to implement).
- No communication with community in forums.
- Game must be 24/7 connected to internet (Conflux). Not a problem, except in cases where the "Conflux" is down whole weekends.
- Scenario has a "canon" story progression which must be played in specific order to really enjoy the campaign; there are many people who simply played a single faction from start to end and just spoiled the whole story. The campaign must be played with each faction in parallel...these details were not present anywhere ingame...details were provided in forums not by Ubisoft, but by the fanbase which analysed the story progression across all factions mission by mission.
- Might & Magic system which is totally ridiculous and not connected with original titles (Gain new spells by putting your level up point in a spell...there are no random spells to be found, or spells researched in towns).
- The supposed morale (Tears and Blood) system which should have led to many many different kinds of endings, yields only just a minor difference in the final missions (you end up with one or another hero accompanying you). Therefore this system is there just to sprinkle confetti around in E3 presentations and etc.

A true staple in the precision-platformer genre, VVVVVV (good luck finding a convenient pronunciation) shakes up the classic formula by replacing jumping with at-will gravity inversion, literally turning a player's gaming preconceptions on their head and providing a unique challenge that's easy to learn, not-too-hard to master.  Four levels, each with their own gimmick, are scattered throughout a fully-open overworld that's just big enough to get comfortably lost in.  Checkpoints are abundant and the casual player should not dismay, as the trickiest challenges are optional.  At the same time the hardcores and the speedrunners will feel right at home, as the game is short, controls are tight, respawning is fast, hitboxes match the sprites, and going trophy-hunting cranks the difficulty up to 11.  Special mention should go to the soundtrack, a masterpiece of techno-chiptune sound.  VVVVVV is one of those classic indie games that belongs on the shelf with Cave Story, and should be experienced at least once in a gamer's life.

Victor Vran is an aRPG similar to Diablo, Grim Dawn, Path of Exile etc. It's what I'd consider a one and done experience unlike say Diablo III which you could easily pump endless hours into, and I'd just like to say that's not nesseserily a bad thing in Victor Vran’s case.
The gameplay is quite different to other games in the genre, mostly due to the fact you can jump, roll and even wall jump which allows for exploration and unique ways to traverse dungeons. The skill system is similar to Guild Wars 2 where you're given 3 unique abilities based on the weapon you're using, and you can switch between 2 different weapons freely giving you access to 6 weapon abilities total. On top of this you're also given 2 demon powers which are strong abilities that charge during combat. Finally you're given 2 consumable slots which can be used for potions, bombs, medi kits and buffs.
Character customisation comes in the way of cards, you're given a certain amount of card slots and card points, similar to the Call of Duty loadout system. These cards allow you to build how you'd like by adding passives to your character, you can opt for a couple of high point cards or many low point cards depending on your needs. It's not the most deep system but it does the job.
Where the game really excels is presentation, it looks, runs and sounds great. I was very impressed with just how polished the game actually is. I enjoyed the art style and the overall visuals were beautiful with some fantastic little cut scenes thrown in throughout the story. Speaking of the story, it was interesting and fully voiced, and voiced well. You may recognise the voice actor for Victor Vran as he also voiced Geralt in Witcher III. The game also performs really well, I spent the entire 15 hour playthrough at 60fps locked on ultra settings, I will say one thing though, the in-game VSync is not recommended as it uses double buffering, so any tiny dip in frame rate causes the FPS to half down to 30fps. You can fix this 100% by disabling VSync in-game and forcing it on in your GPU control panel, I personally used adaptive VSync with triple buffering and my experience was rock solid.
I have to say I was pleasantly surprised with the game on the whole, it's definitely worth it even at full price, and especially so at £5 in the sale. I thoroughly recommend it to anyone who is a fan of the genre.

Warning:  Not for the epileptic, the colorblind, those with slow reaction time, or those who suffer from stress.
Welcome to
, formerly known as
and more commonly by other players simply as
.  This is your typical Stroop test, which is a game/exercise where you confuse yourself by trying to correctly sort based on whether the word matches the color or if it doesn't while challenging your reaction time to alter your judgment.  What seems simple is a hell of a chore when pressured...and you will feel dumb for making careless mistakes...one mistake and it's all over.  Take too long and it's over.
You will argue with your brain a lot on
.  Your brain may forget a color or you may implusively twitch-click the wrong answer.  To further complicate matters, this game will also throw in challenges like jumbling the letters of the word, having the connection go out, reverse your controls, flip the word upside down, or even change the background color too.  Also be forewarned, that cyan is NOT blue....and blue is NOT cyan...because you WILL forget.  That's a promise.
This game offers various challenges including a colorblind mode (where you have to play under the conditions of a colorblind individual (Meaning that you play AS a handicapped person rather than the game providing a handicap if you actually are colorblind).  It also offers the option to play the game in another language, which is good for a little education and challenge.
Though this game isn't bad, I personally cannot recommend it because I didn't find it fun.  I personally found the stress a bit unbearable at times and had to put it down several times before opting for a long grind to get the achievements I wanted.  If you accept the challenge of this free game, then have at it.  But if you suffer from epilepsy, are colorblind, have a bad reaction time, or have trouble coping with stress like I do, then this casual experience is not for you.   Be warned that if you do accept the challenge, this game will make you feel dumb and your self-esteem may be lower.
4/10  A good game...but I momentarily forgot what color red was...was it cyan?

Doing EA wrong: Refuses to open or handle bug reports unless you email them - not even an automated system on their website
. It's not 2002, asking EA customers to directly email without a set form is 101 "don't do" stuff. For an EA title, not responsive or open to actual testing.
Recent patch took less than 10 minutes to find a serious hard CTD bug, repeatable from an integer overflow mistake. Which given it was in a new feature seems a little odd that no-one spotted it or tested it.
Moderator response was... questionable, at best.
Edit: Moderator deleted bug report threads and other productive posts in some bizarre attempt to prove a point.
Currently the game is a mess:
The UI is not good - very ugly and badly designed. Multiple clicks to get to screens, button placement unergonomically done, multiple tabs to find information, money only displayed in shops, # items in hold cannot be easily seen when purchasing items, tabs only close when 'X' is clicked (remain ghosted in the background otherwise).
There seems to be a distinct muddle in terms of how mechanics / systems are going to work with competing design goals. e.g. Inventory space is now at a premium, but some has been split off into another tab ("possessions") but now there's a bank with infinite slots, but the extremely small selection of items (fuel, supplies, ammo) are reused in multiple stories and in amounts that far outstrip even the largest cargo space. Largest cargo space: 29 (in a train that will take ~10+ hours to raise enough money for); stories can use >40 of these items depending on player choices (and, of course, such resources are shared with the main game exploration - fuel / supplies).
Combat is clumsy and retro even by the standards set by classics such as "Asteroids". Each train has identical # weapon slots and identical firing arcs (direct forward) and no targeting. You can excuse the AI as not complete at this point (it is very very basic), but smooth it is not. Dynamic, fast paced, responsive? No. Not at all.
Terror is wildly unbalanced: you will fill 25% of a bar just getting to an outer port via direct travel. It is now split into hard-coded tiers which are punishing. If you have 99% of a filled bar and dock @ the main port, Winchester, you instantly get 0%. If you hit 1% into the next tier, bad luck, your character is semi-permanently stuck with it. Perma-death is attached to this hard-coded tier system, further punishing exploration.
The stories themselves lack flow and have some parts that scream "I hate fun" all over them. Given the early build expectations were low, but there doesn't seem to be any over-arching threaded narrative structure between ports, which was a low point of Sunless Sea.
The Trains themselves have less changes between them than Sunless Sea ships and are noticably similar in handling / features (tested all of them, notably the 'fast' courier and the Moloch class heavy ship - which @ 9.5k will only take you, oh, roughly 10 hours+ to grind for). Whilst this could change, given the new goal of having more dynamic combat this seems a major problem. All trains currently go exactly the same speed and there is no engine slot nor engines available for purchase: given that other items (guns, armor, utilities etc) have been in the last two builds, it seems apparent that Trains will not be getting engines or variable speeds. i.e. Do not buy the 'fast' courier trains, you will be disappointed.
Two content patches in not much has changed from the initial release, barring some basic train skins. I have completed all content in the early build.
~
As a final piece of advice: do not even attempt to play early builds without hacking in infinite money. The economy does not exist at this point in time and seems designed to limit the player from noticing the flaws lurking at the edge of the content.

This is a review based on an early access game - and therefore an incomplete game.
And it shows.  The world still feels empty and there are some annoying graphical glitches where things suddenly pop into existence.  I spent a lot of time flying through empty space - and in some region of the map there is nothing but grey-green fog so it's a rather dull space to fly through.  (When you get out of the fog, things can be beautiful though.)
Controls are annoyingly floaty - this may be realistic as you are piloting locomotive floating through thin air or vacuum, but I find it annoyingly difficult just to move around.  This is particularly a problem in combat as there is no auto-lock so being able to precisely point the front of your locomotive at your target is absolutely essential to surviving battle and irritatingly difficult to do.
On the plus, the visual design of the game is exquisite.  You will fly into areas that are simply stunningly evocative and atmospheric world Fallen London and Sunless Seas. I like the look of the interface and the artwork of cities and characters is a major step up from the more cartoony illustrations of Sunless Seas.  There's a lot of game mechanics changes from Sunless Seas that I think are improvements.  I haven't gone too far into the stories - which is the real strength of Fail Better Games and why you will be wanting to play this game - but the foundations of an interesting world appear to be there.
Don't buy this yet.  It's not complete.  Not really a game so much as a demo.  I only bothered with this early access game because I contributed to the Kickstarter that funded it and was curious to see how things were developing.  You're just better off replaying Sunless Seas and getting a complete experience.  However, definitely put this on your wish list and keep an eye on it.  If the developers make good on the potentials already apparent in this game, Sunless Skies will be a great one.
And if someone from Failbetter Games reads this, give who ever did the art for the Grave of the Silent Saint a bonus and tell your team that THAT is what they should be aiming for.  Jaw-dropping.  You know art design has worked when a player just stops playing to stare.

I've reviewed the original version of Dark Souls II, and much of what I said in that review still applies here -- the game is nearly on par for what is expected of any sequel to Dark Souls I, but falls just shy of the original's greatness due to some faulty mechanics that were implemented to solve the online meta problems. Nonetheless, this version of the game changes the maps to account for the darkness/torch game mechanic, and I consider this change as being positive since it seems to reflect the original intention of the developers when first creating that system.
Furthermore, the addition of the Three King DLC packs and the slight graphical improvements/enemy placement changes make this the ultimate version of Dark Souls II you can play. I will admit, when I heard that this version of the game was coming out, I was somewhat livid that I'd bothered to spend my money on the original and the season pass for its DLC, but if I remember correctly I was eventually given this version of the game for free since I'd already paid for the original. That's some customer commitment!
There's no reason to bother buying the first version anymore -- if you're going to play this game (and you damn well should), then buy this version of it.

Victor Vran is something that could be considered a classic if it was tailored for both the devoted audience and casual players. It's a game I almost couldn't stand because of its deviations from what I expect to enjoy from an ARPG.
Over four months ago I had first played Victor Vran for six hours before coming to the conclusion that the game wasn't for me or for casual ARPG players. Now, after 18 hours, I'm going to recommend this game—if you're willing to look beneath the surface.
I had a negative impression for numerous reasons.
I was worn-out after 50 hours of Van Helsing: Final Cut. VV's streamlined gameplay didn't convince me there was any longevity/depth. The enemy variety was/is too limited and it became tiresome quickly. Worse of all,  I had thought the game had respawned enemies every time I left a general area for a mini-dungeon. (Not the HUB.)
Only by happenstance of me testing out the Steam Controller did I learn that almost all these issues could be fixed by looking further into the game. (Which is a problem for first-impressions or people not willing to experiment with the game.)
I also learned my black mark—of respawning enemies and of erasing progress—was outright false. Something anyone who read this review, played the game and didn't agree with my thoughts should've pointed that out, not argued about the rating.
That misunderstanding is why I re-reviewed this game. Because even if I don't like a game I want to always be correct about my complaints.
There was a misunderstanding when I said progression feels stagnant. It's not that there is no depth or no way to improve yourself—the problem is that your character himself does not show gradual changes as you play, so everything feels the same.
It's better to say progression is abrupt, and entirely dependent on the player's involvement. Leveling up unlocks new things to experiment with (Destiny Card pts, card slots, a second weapon, item or demon power slot, etc.) They also unlock other additions like the transmutation system, another outfit, PvP, endless arena and Hexes (difficulty modifiers).
These are all options, options which you may or may not care about as you play. You're enjoyment of the game is based on how much interest you want to put into tweaking these options to create your own character, from the weapons/skills to your playstyle.
In order to appreciate the benefits of a "no-class" ARPG, you have to have some interest by experimenting with all these options. If that doesn't sound appealing than having a class-system laid out for you, then VV is not for you.
There are no "active" skill improvements other than finding a new demon power or a new type of weapon. But there are only eight weapons (and about the same number of demon powers): Swords, Hammers, Scythes, Rapiers, Shotguns, Lightning Guns, Mortar Guns, Tomes. Each weapon has
active skills (one standard attack, two specials), and you can have two weapon equipped and two demon powers at most. (10 total skills.)
The make-or-break deal is whether or not you like the weapon presets. On the one hand, each weapon is tailored for one playstyle and you can master it as you play. But if you don't like it, then that limits your options even further.
This could be fixed if the game offered new presets of skills. Instead, you have to find what weapon is for you—and if you combine weapon's abilities together (like the shotgun's speed boost with the hammer) you can get some interesting weapon synergy.
(I still think the combat would flow much better if the devs took a page from Bloodborne used changing out weapons as another attack skill based on your weapon choices.)
The best part about this system is you can beat the game, entirely, without ranged weapons or one specific weapon type. Something that I had originally thought was mandatory, and yet I finished the game, solo, on Normal with two or three Hexes added.
(Hexes, I have also found, made me ignore the Transmutation system entirely. I still got plenty of legendaries and good loot from random drops.)
The real source of improvement comes from building your character around the buffs of your Destiny Cards, your weapons/inventory and focusing on what weapons work best.
If you took a look at this list, you'd be forgiven thinking these things are unnecessary to pay attention to as you play:
The reality is that is your source of builds in VV, and if you want to play the game properly you'll have to figure out what works with your playstyle (and weapons). The game's spike in difficulties at some points will force you to focus on this system.
Some cards provide the basic whatever-percent value boost while others give flashier effects by taking damage or dealing out critical hits. Some will give you weapon modifiers. Some of which will help you stay alive by siphoning off health with each hit or kill.
There are also random effects (divine or wicked) that make lower-tiered buffs worth more than higher valued stuff. (A Divine Rogue 1 with armor penetration is much better than a Rogue 3 for some instances.) And because you have a limited number of Destiny Points, you have to take the time to figure out what selection is for you.
Combine the Destiny Points with each outfits'/armors' adrenaline system to use Demon Powers, and you can find as much depth in this game as you would in most other ARPGs. The store-page was not lying when it said you need as much as skill as you need a proper build.
The question is, "Will you want to invest any interest in that system?"
Again, you have to invest a lot in this non-casual-friendly system to play properly and to also understand its appeal. That is something that should be addressed as other similar games provide a simpler system, though they may be more or less complex than Victor Vran.
This isn't a cry for a game to become dumb-downed. I want more people to play this game, and I would bet that many who didn't enjoy it (based on my old review's ratings, 398 out of 503 upvotes) would come to love it if the system was developed more. (Either by more weapons, more preset options, more card variety tied to these changes, more enemy variety, etc.)
If you're not sure if the game is for you, then  I would urge you to try it for yourself on a sale, and if it is something you'd enjoy convince your friends to join up with you for cooperative play.

NTW is perhaps one of the best total war games Creative Assembly has made. Percieved by many to be an expansion of sorts of Empire Total War, I find it to be in fact a better game than ETW. Many of the campaigns feature only a small number of factions so enemy turns only take a minute or two. And with research/technology being minimalized or nonexistant at times, the focus is purely on the army movement and real time battles. This game does a great job of showing off who Napoleon really was. He was a great general who conquered so many nations in the name of France. NTW lets you command in his shoes and experience what he felt in multiple areas of the world.

The game idea had potential but they tried to implement too many already broken features. If they kept it features simpler it would have been a better game instead it's a broken mess.
Some suggestions:
-Remove the crappy minigames and mining
-Simplify resource gathering just to fuel and parts but don't make it annoying...
-Completely remove the ship population mechanics(I don't remember Dylan Hunt or any of the Star Trek captains babysitting their crew)
-Remove the crappy combat 'frequencies' and implement/unlock evasive maneuvers, random events during combat, retreats, head on collisions etc etc...
-Focus more on the actual exploration of the game... Seriously you're in a big universe with infinite possibilities and you're stuck gathering 5 or 7 types of ♥♥♥♥♥♥ resources instead of actually telling you stories
-Release the source code or make it moddable so that the actual players can make/share stories to populate this bland universe with content
Negatives
-very brief tutorial, so most of the time you're just guessing what to do
-lots of bugs
-no connection to your crew at all except stats (sent them to their deaths and my only reaction was 'whoops')
-small text on most of the UI
-exploration almost impossible due to constant resource mining and babysitting your population
-combat rather dull switching between weapon/defense 'frequencies'
-when pausing to plan my moves during combat, cannot queue the actions crew members should follow
-time passes super fast... I understand sublight engines are slow but hell, either make the illusion that I'm not traversing a solar system in real time or give us a hyperdrive engine similar to FTL
-choices of random events are too black and white and the success chances of each are the same... Seriously? Infiltrating an enemy base has the same chance of success as blasting it from space?
-no way to activate a distress signal when stuck in space (seriously?...)
-the population is completely useless. In scifis they were repairing the ship or developing new technologies but here they are just resource consumers.
-no possibility to recruit members from the population? Really? So you start off with 5-6 crew members but if they die, you're stuck commanding the whole ship yourself and with 10000 useless people on board.
Positives
+space game
+bridge command experience
+pretty visually

This game is definitely worth a go-around for fans of point-and-click games.  It is, as other reviewers have mentioned, very short--would easily take under two hours to complete if you didn't bother exploring and went to a walkthrough every time you got stuck on a puzzle.
The puzzles were the most enjoyable part of the game for me (the atmosphere being a close second).  They were varied and many...and by many I mean virtually every action you have to complete in the game feels like puzzle-solving.  Some were more frustrating than others, but there were usually enough subtle hints to follow.  I spent a good amount of time wandering around cluelessly at first, but it's not too tough to figure out how the game "thinks."  From there, things fall into place more readily.  And if you get completely lost, clicking on your character reminds you of your current task.  Always a nice touch.
Bare bones of the story were very interesting, history and mythology and all that.  Really wish there had been time to delve deeper into it.  Actual execution, not my favorite.  Characters were a bit one-dimensional, bordering on tired stereotypes.  The only horror element for the first 2/3 of the game is a few spooky noises.  And the love story really watered the whole thing down for me.  Very glad I gave it a shot and I may return to it, but probably best picked up on the cheap due to its length.

This game is a great one. I've played all three Re;Birhths(Which are remakes of the original Neptunia, Neptunia MK2, as well as Neptunia Victory). Although, I kind of regret playing Re;Brith 2. Stay away from that if you can.
Story wise, this game does not follow after Neptunia Re;birth 1, but it does chronologically take place after the events within Neptunia Re;Birth 2. Re;birth 3 begins with the 4 goddesses, Neptune(Nepu Nepu), Noire, Blanc, and Vert playing a game. As they decide to team on Nepu Nepu to have a greater chance of winning, the game "breaks". Nepgear, Neptune's sister, takes this moment to test out her new "N-gear"(I think that's what it was called), and she tests it upon Neptune so Nepu Nepu can dive into the game and see what is causing the game to be so bugged out. Eventually, after being ratted out for being so lazy dispite being the Goddess of a Nation, Nepu Nepu is forced to go do work for once. How could someone be so mean to my Nepu Nepu!? Anyways, Neptune ends up running into someone and she is then sent to a different dimension where she thinks all is the same, but it's not.
Character wise, I love every single one of them. With the exception of Uni. Uni is a bland, over the top Tsundere.(Noire is a better Tsundere) Neptune is the goddess of Planeptu- I bit my toungue -_- She usually likes to break the 4th wall constantly and she's pretty lazy compared to the hard working tsundere, Noire. Now Noire is the goddess of Lastation and is your typical tsundere. She has a hard time being true about her feelings and Neptune is usually the one to put her in that spot. She's probably my 3rd or 4th favorite character. Vert is the goddess of Leanbox. Vert generally acts like a princess. She has that look, AND that chest to fit the type too. Blanc is the goddess of Lowee. She is the quiet, "I'm going to beat the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of you if you make fun of my chest" kind of girl. She's generally like that through out the game.(Though it's pretty funny when Vert constantly teases her about it)
I've only talked about the four main goddesses because I don't want to go into the 20+ playable characters avalible for your pleasure.(Broccoli, Tekken, Mages, and Marvelous AQL are my favorites).
Now the battle system is an updated version of the combat system used in the orginal "Hyperdimension Neptunia Victory" and is combination of Breath of Fire V's and Persona's battle system. You go into dungeons and monsters or enemies are placed in certain parts of the dungeon. Now if you strike the enemy before they attack you, you are granted the first turn. This is called a "symbol attack". If the enemy attacks you first, they get the first turn. When you attack an enemy, you have addition attacks to perform. Those being rush, power, and guard attacks. Not only that, but you can swap partners, change forms(non goddesses can only "awaken"), use items, as well as skills. When you are facing an enemy, they have two bars. One for health, one for their "guard". Take out their guard points using "guard" attacks and you are granted the ability to inflict a larger ammount of damage on the enemy. They can regenerate this bar each turn though. Now like Re;Birth 2's combat system, and unlike Re;Birth 1's, you can use 4 party members. The bonus in this game's new battle system, is the ability to use 5 combos, as opposed to 4 in the previous games. Don't let this fool you. Each characters 5th combo slot have to be unlocked via the "remake system" and only certain characters can have a 5th combo slot for the earlier mentioned forms of attack.
I really like the battle system because you have to choose which attacks to use against which enemies and when you use them. An example is trying to use your high costing skills on an enemy who's guard points have not been lowered. This is a stupid idea as you will not do as much damage as if the enemy didn't have any guard. Overall, newcomers will find this battle system difficult for the first 10 minutes of game play. After that, you'll be breezing through it like Nepu Nepu does with her puddings.
Re;Birth 3 features the same map/area mechanics as the previous games. Every area/dungeon is placed on a map. You select the area and are teleported to the corresponding dungeon. A menu opens up if you click on one of the major locations such as Planeptu, I bit my toungue again -_-, Lastation, Leanbox, and Lowee. The menu that opens up allows you to access the shop, museum, Nepstation, as well as the guild. The shop is where you would buy usable, or equipable items. The museum is where you view past cutscenes, unlockable images, as well as soundtracks that are unlocked with the game's progression. The Nepstation is only avalible in Planep- I'm not biting my toungue again... The Nepstation is a bit unique. Each time you visit the Nepstation, you view an event. Now the even is where you either take a "one million Nep quiz", get certain items at discount prices, or to see some extra bit of dialogue. The guild is where you can take up quests, and complete them to earn small rewards. Some quests will have to be completed to progess the game. Every quest has a certain symbol or lettering next to them. This determines whether or not you can repeat them, or if they are story related.
One major aspect of this game, is the "remake system". Through out the game find "plans". Plans are used to alter dungeons, add certain bonus's to your characters, and to add items to the shop. To put these plans in effect, you need to get yourself some of Nepu Nepu's pudding. You actually need to get yourself some "memory". Memory increases are found at certain points in the game. One more major thing to put plans into effect, is materials you find from enemies. Most basic plans will only require low tier monster drops where as more advanced plans require drops from even certain bosses. Don't expect to be able to craft every single plan because you'll never be able to with the limited ammount of memory. You also won't be able to because you're only on your first play through of the game. Which is what I'm about to go into right now.
When you complete a single player game, you're done, that's it. When playing Re;Birth 3, you are able to play "new game plus". Nothing new really happens in new game plus, but you are given more memory with the story quests and events that you come accros in the previous run through of the game. New game plus doens't offer you any new material except for the "good ending" and the "true ending". These can both be done without going into new game plus but you would have to create whole different saves. The reason you would want to do this in new game plus is your character data and items carry over. Got a level 100 Nepu Nepu and a swimsuit but you want to redo the game to get the true ending? Don't worry, new game plus has your back with it's ability to carry over data.
The achievements in this game aren't too difficult to get, but they require some grinding to do. You'll find yourself getting half of them by just playing the game, but there are some where they require you to do major grinding like the "lovable achievements". There's not much to talk about the achievements so I'll just end it here.
In the end, was this game worth the $30(31 with DLC)? To me, yes. There's quite a lot to do and it can keep even hard core grinders busy for several hours. I would aim for this game on sale though since it's just SO GOOD for just $12. I totally didn't buy it on sale... Anyways, this game offeres lovable characters, great 4th wall breaking events, as well as relaxing gameplay that the $15 CS:GO would never do.
10/10 would recommend with Nepu Nepu and her puddings again!

Fallout 3 was a great game when it was new, and thanks to the power of mods, this game is just as good today (2015). Mods have updated the visuals, effects, and content of the game to feel like it's brand new.
Everywhere you go, there is a town or person that needs to be saved, and you are that person who can save everyone... or not. While this game doesn't offer as much freedom of choice that New Vegas offers, Fallout 3 gives you many opportunities to feel like a hero in various ways.
Newer games tend to throw side-quests at you so you can get detoured for hours doing a lot of them. Fallout 3's story progresses in a very linear fashion, and while there are many sidequests that you can partake in, you often have to go out of your way to find and solve these quests. You can very realistically go from the beginning to end of this game without doing one sidequest. It's not a bad thing, but it does make this game less immersive than more recent games of this type.
If you've never played Fallout 3 before, this is definitely one worth playing as it set the bar for other amazing games in the genre.

TL;DR, it's an overall pretty good platforming game, and worth checking out.
So, overall, I like VVVVVV. It was an enjoyable experience with an awesome soundtrack and a simple, yet creative mechanic that a lot is done with. But it's not a perfect game. It does have some problems. The smaller ones are very small, to be fair, such as the overall length of the game. It is a short game. I beat it in a little over an hour. Granted, the length is up in the air, depending on your overall skill at the game itself, but it's still a short game. So, if you are looking for a longer game, this might not be for you. Another problem with this game, is the "escort" missions. The distance that those following you follow at isn't ever defined, and that can often lead to frustating moments in the more difficult sections of the escort missions.
Now, the biggest problem I had with the game is the controls. Your character slides a fair bit, which wouldn't be the biggest issue in most games, but in this game, when you have to be very precise in your movements, you can often slide off the sides of platforms if you land a little too close to the edge. Early on, this is very unnoticable, as it's a little easier overall, but later in the game, it often leads to a large number of seemingly unfair deaths.

Simply put this is a arche-typical Fantasy-setting RPG - Single Player only.
Some things people may be wary of are:
1. The Hint system (mind read) is used by expending Level up XP to use. While this is what the description says, it's not so much expending as extending, and what I mean by that is you never really *lose* the experience you already have, you just go into what's called "Experience Debt" which has to be repaid before you can continue to gain normal experience.
2. The Tutorial Assumes you are already firmiliar with at a minimal RPGs, and probably assumes too much about your experience with action-games. What I mean by this is: The Tutorial doesn't go over more "basic" RPG Elements such as "Equipment" or "Gear" let alone "leveling" but it does give you basic controls. What I mean by it assumes too much about your experience with Action Games is...for the tutorial to cover controls is fine, but more of the advanced moves (ie rolling/jumping/dodging) are not well explained until AFTER you need them. Long Story short - the tutorials are very basic, and could use some polishing towards total newbies.
3. Although the game is a bit dated (circa 2008 - 2009) the actual game-play/graphics details and other "Preformance Effecting" Details are quite up-to-par with modern standards. This game was obviously ahead of it's time even though it's time was a while back.
***WARNING: The Next Few Sections MAY contain some spoilers. Reader Descretion is advised***
4. I have -not- encountered any spiders - yet. I have to make mention of this because this is something I personally like, but realize not everyone wants. To Progress roughly 20~ Hours into the main-line quest stream and not see a single spider (albeit some webs) enemy is a good thing to me, because I am among those who are afraid of spiders (however - I am most certainly NOT afraid of Scorpions so I'm not "Archnophobic" by a typical detail). Mostly the Enemies I *have* encountered are undead/humanoid/demihuman types. Ie 2 Legs 2 Arms and Some Form of head and torso. The ghosts have no legs just two draping sheets tho.
5. The Dragon Form - about the dragon form, although it cross-interfaces with the human form it feels more like the enemies are split into Dragon-Class (flying/structure mostly) and Human-class Enemies, and there is little combination of the two. Although you can fight some dragon-class enemies with a bow, the structures and such will not fire at a human. Moreover - the Ability/Skill system is only slightly different between human and dragon abilities, the major difference being you have (afaik) no "Natural" Skill Points in Dragon Abilities (you have to read some kinda book to get points etc). Also Although the Human form regenerates overtime at a variable rate - dragon form only heals when actively healed (ie with a spell/ability) which means you'll be using alot more of your dragon time using abilities rather than breathing fire.
*** END -Possible- Spoilers ***
Overall the game is good enough that I'd continue to play it for quite some time, however the aforementioned flaws are some of the things I wish had been explained to me before I found out on my own (which took some time)
The Story in particular is excellently told, and personally I find myself continuing to play the game mostly because the story is so mysterious and intriguing. Good Example, One quest (which I have yet to complete) has you facing against a "Veggie" Witch, which to say nothing of the comedic standpoints is very unique among the thoughts of curses when someone evaluates a game such as this. Well-thought out the story is, but at times is just plain comedic to be sure. The Main Plot is no laughing matter though, but I'll leave that for you to discover. Advice: Get Used to Dying even on the easiest settings if you don't pay attention to what your doing. On the other hand, on the easiest settings there comes a point at which you become nigh invinicible late game.
I spend 12 hours straight for 2 days playing this and was forced to take a break - now tell me what is a good indicator of a good game if that isn't.
