I've always been a fan of the Heroes of Might and Magic franchise. I am not, however, for Heroes VI. The game has improved graphics, UI, and voice acting over its predecessor Heroes V, but several mechanical changes in resources and faction combinations restrict from enjoying the newest game of the franchise.
Resources are reduced down to just: wood, ore, crystal, and gold. Mercuary, gems and sulfur are excluded that were once present in the older games of the series. Reduction of resources makes building less of a hassle, though too simplistic. Factions having their own affinity to a resource gave them a unique quality. It helped drive strategy for the hero and faction you were playing for, you strived to control them over the others as they were important to you. Just having crystal doesn't lend to exploration or additional map control that was a key factor of the gameplay of the Heroes of Might and Magic games.
But that's not the biggest gripe to have over this game. What erks me is the shared creature population pool in the campaign missions that don't allow you to build a large enough army to beat the tutorial level within a short amount of time (I was literally at month 5 still waiting on creature populations to build up to attack the last fort before I simply decided to quit). This literally makes the campaign harder and longer than necessary to mask the underlying flaws.
While Heroes V had some crippling bugs that hampered its launch in 2006, they eventually were patched and resolved, even modded. Ubisoft no longer supports Heroes VI and the last patch was 2.1.1 from October 2012. There are still game breaking bugs for quests not working corectly in the campaign that require a reload from a previous save file or a complete restart of the campaigns themselves.
The custom maps and scenarios were the only escape from the mired campaign. The game ships with a decent number of non-campaign maps and an editor to create your own. Map quality and scenarios increase as more expansions are acquired. Boy, the editor brings back some memories of building your masterpiece(s) extra-large or huge maps that took weeks to complete and then finally playing them. However, the custom maps, scenarios and map editor can't redeem this game.
With the reduction of resources and low creature populations, the game also limits to five different factions - Necromancer, Dungeon, Haven, Inferno, and Sanctuary. The previous games had a more bevy and robust roster of factions to choose from. Out of nine total factions, we are left with just these five. Four factions are familiar to the Heroes series: Dungeon, Haven, Inferno and Necromancer. The other two seem like a mash up of factions that appeared earlier in ther series. Rampart from Heroes III  and Heroes IV is combined with the Wizard (a.k.a Tower) from Heroes II and III to form the oriental themed Sanctuary. On the other hand, Stronghold makes a second appearance that is a throw back to the Barbarian (Heroes I to IV) and Fortress (Heroes III and IV) factions. The experiance is similar to  seeing an old friend after a long time, but dissapointed after finding out nothing really interesting happened has happened except maybe a change in thematic style (Santuary) or haven't improved much over time (Haven).
The game has the sence that a lot of  attention was directed into the UI, art, and graphical aspects rather than gameplay. It's a nice game to look at, but not fun to play due to numerous bugs and sacrifices in mechanics. There was even an open beta in August of 2011 before the launch that Steam members could participate in. After reviewing those members experiance, it seems Ubisoft rushed the game and didn't heed players feedback.
I have to give this a "no" recommendation for the very fact that it just isn't very fun to play, at all. I'd rather load up Heroes V even with all its faults, which were ironed out through two expansions. Sometimes I crave earlier iterations such as Heroes III that is still heavily supported by fans across the internet to this day. Did you know there were tournaments held on a website for Heroes III alone? After almost 15 years, that game is still played, not like Heroes VI.

As a long time player of both Fallen London and Sunless Sea, I wanted to support the developers, and so funded Sunless Skies on kickstarter, getting an Early Access copy of my own.
The game is quite bare-bones, with only a fraction of the ports there will be available in the full release, and only a handfull to do at each port.
It being an Early Access title, the game is glitchy at times, to the point where I had an entire port dissapear from it place, and my map fail to track where I am correctly. Not very fun when stuck in space with my crew staring at me like a freshly cooked steak. That and some words are spelled incorrectly, and the grammer is just wrong in a few cases.
The in-game economy is a mess, and it's difficult to make an actual profit whilst exploring, and with quests and port reports paying sometimes less then 10 of the in-game currency, with most upgrades costing 200-300.
Your 'ship' has little inventory space, most of which filled with fuel to make sure you can move and avoid freezing to death, and supplies so you don't have to eat those that starved to death, so trading is even more difficult, not that there's much profit.
So with all these negative factors, why do I recomend this game?
Well I don't, not in its current state.
But I have faith in Failbetter (the developing company for those unaware with their work), they've deliviered on past promises and pay attention to the wants of the fanbase, always looking for any suggestions the community should have.
The game is bad now, but should it end up anything like Sunless Sea, which also started on Steam as an Early Acces title, it would be a worthy investment to purchase now, or one later when it's more fleshed out.
And should it come out with any DLC post it's full release, I could in good conscience recomend that in advance, seeing the results of 'Zubmariner' for Sunless Sea.

I hope this "review" somehow makes it to the developers. I really like the series (is this a series now?) and I wanted to voice my opinion. Hope it helps.
--- Things What Work (and deliciously so) ---
- Train Movement and Systems:
I'm a sap for games that are in space. Also one's with dark Victorian settings and Antedeluvian horrors, hence why I'm here. So despite other people's groaning I actually like how the train you pilot moves compared to the ships in SSea. For those unaware, the train works like a real space ship. You have a forward thrust for general power and directional thrusters for course correction. It feels like I'm actually trying to wrestly a beast of protyped technology and makes for a more engaging traveling experience then what was in SSea
Also the fuel on board now serves double duty as both power for the engines and what heats the ship. Space craft in real life have to keep the interior heated because A: space is a bit nippy and B: we don't generally like dead astronauts. It's bad P.R. So fuel kinda works the same way supplies did in SSea. If you run out of fuel you run a good risk of a slow death. It's just another way to die without having to really pay much attention to anything new.
- Combat:
Combat in SSea was one of two things: a boring nautical equivalent of aircraft turn-fighting to get on a ships rear (stern...? bow...?) OR it was a "OH MY GOOD GOD BACK AWAY WHILE FIRING KEEP THAT SPIDER AWAY FROM THE SHIP" until something dinks you (seriously, to hell with the Constant Companion). I'm could skip around for joy that they took that system out to the barn for a dirt nap.
Now the combat revolves around using both your forward thruster and directional thrusters in a masterful 2D dance of death around whatever is attacking you. It's both faster paced and just plain more fun since the enemies can do it too. Also your weapons don't auto lock onto a target and can produce excess heat if you fire them too much. This excess heat can damage systems. So yea, all around a much more engaging engagment. I feel like I'm going to use that word a lot.
- Character Development:
One of my favorite things about SSea and my new favorite thing about SSkies. Before in SSea you could choose a character backstory in order to kinda role-play as someone in universe. It wasn't just a insert-yourself-here affair like most other RPGs do, but it only really affected certain character stats. Kind of a let down. In a lot of RPGs it's been found that if a game will allow you to basically insert yourself in you will act as you normally would, which is usually to be a goodie-goodie. This almost makes it pointless to add any kinda of "bad-guy" option.
HOWEVER, in SSkies as you earn experience you can unlock events from your character's past. Not only does this allow you to craft a more interesting person to RPG it up as, but evidently this will affect how characters in the game treat you. I cannot write here just how great this new format is, but it feels like your the new captain in town and as you accomplish things your story will be unearthed by the people of the Reach and your name will become either famous or infamous. Its not a choice of "Be good, be in the middle, or be cartoonish levels of evil" either. These choices make sense and come about from really good morality vs. personal gain standpoint.
--- Things What Don't Work (but I think could be improved upon) ---
- Navigating the Reach (Salesmen and Bats):
Honestly, I really didn't want to buy this game until it was released. I just didn't want to spoil anything. However, someone being a♥♥♥♥♥♥on the community hub forced my hand. This person argued that the position of the starting point (London in SSea, New Winchester in SSkies) from the western most part of a grid to the center of a circle made the time it would take to travel to each port and how much fuel and supplies you would use increase by a large margin.
This person was right theoretically (as much as it pains me to say) in how they argued it with the Traveling Salesman Problem, but not practically. The circle the Reach encompasses is FAR smaller then the Unterzee and you use supplies and fuel to a very similar rate. This means you actually get more distance for your fuel. What makes it seem so large is that there is sizeable swaths of completely empty space that would have normally been filled in SSea. This means less ports, less places to stop, less opportunties to stock up. I imagine this will be resolved.
Hey look, I explained that without being a♥♥♥♥♥♥either. Points to me!
What I really have an issue with is that damnable bat though. Like in SSea you use a bat for navigation assistance. You send it out, it looks for something interesting and then reports back with a direction to go find it. Its a nice system, but now that bat requires supplies to use. Oh god, why? There's barely anything in the Reach and you expect me to keep sending the bugger out just to return "saw nothing captain" again and again? And have it use supplies?! I understand you may want a drawback to using the bat for those that would go around spamming it, but allow me to suggest an alternative.
You mention in the writing that the bat can be a bit mischiveous. The captain has to coax it with a meal of beetles until it finally spills what it knows, right? Maybe make it so that if you over work the bat it will give you misinformation. Maybe even point you towards danger. I imagine this would be making a simple system more complex, but it's an opportunity worth mentioning.
- Writing:
Stay thy pitchforks, fandom. I love the writing in Fallen London and SSea as much as anyone. It was scary enough, weird enough, ambiguous enough, yet detailed enough to get me really (and I mean REALLY) interested in the games and it's the reason I kept coming back. I wish I had the ability to write like these people do. I am happy to say it is just as humorous and unnerving in SSkies as before, but I have two issues.
First, some lore bits are explained a bit too much. Things like the war between London and the Taccies (tackies?... tactites?... oh screw it) and what the researchers at traitors wood were looking for were explained a bit too much. Other things like the... oh what's it called? The place where you can lower your terror? I'm bad with names. Yea, it's services to clients it allowed and didn't allow was explained very well. You had to dig to get there, and once you did the full extent of what you really learned remains to be unlocked in your own head-canon. There's a disparity between what is explained well and what is not that worries me. I blame the early stage the game is in.
Second, there's a lot more character to player dialogue and more overall description text now. I actually like this. It makes every character feel different rather then in SSea, where most characters seemed like shady back-handers because the writing was so ambiguous. I like that there is more description for characters and places, but my concern is whether or not this will eliminate more of the ambiguity then it should. The best horror resides in what you do not know. I hope this game keeps to that.
--- Things What Are Broken (but hey, what do I know?) ---
- Factions (and how to identify them):
In SSea, if you locked onto something in combat it told you what it was. (Oh, hi Eater of Names. Goodbye now!). That's not a thing anymore. I'd like this system because it makes some things mysterious and when you kill it you can identify it. However, you can never identify anything later on in the game that you have already killed. Likewise, this ended up in a friendly-fire incident where I shot down a ship of a faction I supported. Other then that I like the addition of factions I can support.
- Economy:
I just wish there was one... also I sold something I bought at one port for the same price at another. What in the what? It's impossible to make money in this game...

Surprisingly well made hack and slash game. The combat feels rewarding, though at times it can be repetitive, but the polish makes up for it. Works perfectly with a controller, and even inventory management works well. It's clear the developer wanted the experience to be as smooth on controller as on K+M.
It is not a co-op game at heart. Co-op was tacked on after the fact and it is evident. Quests track separately, loot tracks separately, objectives track separately. Basically, you can play with another person, but you gain nothing. It's so separate that I stopped bothering and went to single player mode.
Is it worth $20? For the work the devs put in: absolutely. There's a lot of content here and lots of areas to have fun in. I will say that this game is more for completionist, who enjoy finding all the secrets in an area, or meeting all level objectives. If you're not into that, then you'll simply run through each level, and will most likely end up bored. For completionists, there's a lot of depth and content here.
If the game is on sale, then pick it up without hesitation. It's worth it.

Dec-12-2014
Time Played: 26-Hours
Pre-Alpha Review (Patch 1.1)
From the view of an Aprentice main with mid-lvl huntress/monk
----TL;DR at the bottom----
*There are plenty of reviews giving a Pro/con list for this game in comparison to DD1, so this is my take on DD2 as is, and where it seems to be going.
Initial Thoughts -
This is not DD1. Hands down, the hardest part of this game is other people. You can't throw down your towers without reason, you have to communicate(esp. for Hard-mode), and plan out a "strategy" which at the moment is basically Lightning aura/Gyser/Ice Tower and a Boost aura(there are other combos that work of course). Sure you can add on some towers that synergise with those as well, but that is the core layout that many people are running. (Squire - cannon/Apprentice- earth are the best additions)
---Edit: They fixed a bug with lightning aura, so it's not as op now. However, the gyser/lightning is still a strong combo.
Furthermore,  I'm glad they're willing to make changes, I wouldn't want just a reskinned DD1. Because lets face it, if you want DD1, play DD1. Any re-skin they do will always pale in comparison to nostalgia. As for me, I'm loving where they seem to be going, and hope they implement new ideas that make DD2 look like, what DD1 wanted to be.
----------------------------------------------------------------------------
Towers/Classes -
With all the negative things being said, I still think having synergy between towers is a plus. Yes, it does somewhat limit gameplay at the moment, but, it creates some purpose to playing with other classes/using various towers together. it just needs some tweeks in the way it's implemented atm. Remember, Pre-alpha.
Currently, I can think of 1-2 optimal builds for a map/character(excluding legendaries that buff certain towers and may make them very valuable). that's extreemly boring in the long run, and limits the replayablility of the game.
*More towers, combos, and specable talents would open this up some, because currently the Meta for a good team-based build seems to be -
Apprentice? Max the ice towers chance to freeze, place ice towers
Monk? Max lightning aura dmg, place lightning aura's and boost aura's
Huntress? Max the dmg the next atk does to a doused target. Or, If you want to go single target dmg, Dmg+ for target dist./ AA Full charge chance. Either way, place gysers.
Squire? (haven't played squire, so no idea) Cannons are rediculous, as are balistas.
----So, why do I reccomend the game?----
It has potential, a lot of potential. Remember, this is Pre-Alpha. They're still working out the kinks, and adding in a ton more content, this game, as is, is the foundation with a skeletal structure for what's to come, and it's shaping up very nicely. At the moment, it's meh. Not amazing, but not worth a thumbs down. IMO the game looks a lot more promissing than DD1, it both looks better, and has a more intuitive UI in place. I'm loving it so far.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------
Suggestions for the game -
. More than 4 towers per character. But you can only chose 4 to bring into a map.
. Improve lvl'ing experience. The game really starts 15+ when you have all your towers, but takes a while to get to depending on solo/group play.
. Lower chances for green chests. . . 1 non-green chest in ~70-80 runs is rediculous, and it was a blue.
. Item Drop chance not dependent on # of players in the map, but on difficulty of the map. . .
. Stat re-roll option for items. (i.e. Changing M.Def -> def)
. More Weapon options.
. Clan option in-game
. Improved UI/Overlay
. Improved Matchmaking
. lvl25+/++ and all challenge modes should only be able to be played by 1 of your characters, no Hero Deck option, unless in private play.
----------------------------------------------------------------------------
TL;DR -
This is not DD1. If you're dissapointed it's not just like DD1, play DD1. . . but you'll be missing out.
TL;DR V.(Patch 1.1 Pre-Alpha)  -
Thumbs neutral, at the moment it's ok, but has a lot more potential than DD1 IMO. Hardest part of the game is learning to communicate, and strategize. They made multiplayer mean something, so don't be a 1-man army in a group of 4.
----Currently 7/10,
could easily be 9/10 - 10/10 with some minor tweaks by Launch.
If you're on the fence, waitlist it, hopefully the upcoming improvements will push you over the edge =P
If not, it'll be Free-To-Play upon full release. . . whenever that is.

There's also plenty to do as every small dungeon has a list of around five optional challenges, with an extra set that will be unlocked after the completion of the main campaign.
The graphics in Victor Vran are pretty to say the least with good textures and plenty of detail. Even my GTX 770 has a hard time keeping up in most cases and only goes up to 72, while hovering around 48 in a lot of places.
I would definitely recommend this game to anybody looking for a challenging ARPG. Those looking for a casual experience will also find plenty to do to satisfy the asking price. If it's ever on sale, buy it up quick!

+ Period-appropriate soundtrack; works very well with the game in that it fades into the background comfortably and doesn't distract form the gameplay or player's concentration

+ Building and deploying troops offers a massive pool of information, and units can be custom-designed to work as the player intends

I've been following the developer's YouTube channel for a while now. She's given really good tips on how to make games, not just in RPG Maker, but in general. So, when it finally came time for her to release a new game, I was excited to see her product!
I'm currently very early on in the game, but from what I'm seeing, I'm loving it! Granted, it's nothing too spectacular as a game in general, but for an RPG Maker MV game, I'm blown away at how unlike an RPG Maker game it is! Some elements still are very 'default', including some sound effects and menu selection names, but I'd say that about 98% of what's in the game is not something you'd find in a default RPG Maker MV game.
The visuals are beautiful. Everything from the maps to the sprites look amazing. Not perfect by any means, but amazing. The artist has such a unique character art style that really makes the game stand out.
The battles are actually pretty fun! I'm not a huge fan of random encounters, but that can easily be adjusted in the game's menu, a feature that's useful if you're more focused on story and objectives than fighting.
Again, I'm still very early in the game, but the story is very engaging and makes you want to know what's going to happen next. Akira, the protagonist, is a likeable character who has a pretty good sense of humor yet is very serious when she needs to be.
Speaking of which, the game's style and sense of humor definitely matches that of the developer herself, as shown by her YouTube videos. It's not 'laugh out loud' funny (at least not to me), but it got me to smile and give a light chuckle at times.
I don't really have any complaints/cons at the moment, and hopefully it'll stay that way.
Overall, if you're a fan of RPG Maker games, this is certainly worth a try. If you're not a fan of RPG Maker games but are a fan of fantasy elements with a sense of humor, I think it's still worth a try.

The main things in this game would be story, combat, mining/building, and perhaps exploration.  Unfortunately all of these things are flawed.  The story is almost non-existant, the plot absent other than a few sentences of introduction at the very beginning.  I feel little for the characters I choose, their abilities simplified to integers.  The combat is annoying, based on color matching and clicking a button at the right time.  The mining is a chore, with an annoying mini-game.  Building on-ship facilities merely affects civilization happiness and 'procreation speed'.  You cannot upgrade weapons or shields... you end the game just as powerful as when you started the game (which goes against the grain of any RPG I've ever played).  Exploration is not very feasible since you have to constantly mine to stay afloat, otherwise everyone starts to die of either hunger or oxygen deprivation. I'll start by saying that I don't know a damn thing about this series. I got it just because I thought it looked cool. That being said, I wasn't entirely sure what to expect other than, well, an RPG.
The atmosphere is okay. The music is great. I liked the art style, but the actual implementation of the environmental textures and models feels a bit sloppily done, like an MMO. For example, in Aleroth City, the paved areas extend well beyond the buildings and climb up the terrain; Pavers look pretty stupid when they're painted all over the hills. I'm fairly certain these areas were intended to be hidden from view, but often can be seen by just rotating the camera.
The scale of the game is quite impressive, excellent for facilitating the dragon mechanics. The transition between the human and dragon forms is pretty smooth, but considering the enemies for each of these forms will only attack, and only be able to be attacked, when the player is in the proper form, it sometimes seems a bit pointless to restrict the ability to transform.
The quests are pretty fun. There's a good mix of variety and routine. They don't really lead the player around too much, but the difficulty of the enemies in the main story quests often make it difficult to progress without sucking all of the experience possible out of the side quests.
The combat also feels a bit weird. The majority of the difficulty comes from having to face multiple opponents at once. The game provides several options to even the odds, in the form of summons, necromancy, and charm spells, but the primary purpose of these always seems to be giving the enemies more targets, rather than providing oneself with a direct offensive output. Even tank builds feel very limited in their damage output. No matter what weapons the player has, everything is DPS, and when the enemy starts cranking out overpowered healing spells, fights drag out longer. It's all a matter of whether the player can mash the attack button until the enemy dies. There is very little real strategy.
Overall, it's okay. It's not perfect, but provides a decent amount of immersive gameplay for your buck.

Ok, this has been driving me crazy for seven movies now, and I know you’re going to roll your eyes, but hear me out: Harry Potter should have carried a 1911.
Here’s why:
Think about how quickly the entire WWWIII (Wizarding-World War III) would have ended if all of the good guys had simply armed up with good ol’ American hot lead.
Basilisk? Let’s see how tough it is when you shoot it with a .470 Nitro Express. Worried about its Medusa-gaze? Wear night vision goggles. The image is light-amplified and re-transmitted to your eyes. You aren’t looking at it–you’re looking at a picture of it.
Imagine how epic the first movie would be if Harry had put a breeching charge on the bathroom wall, flash-banged the hole, and then went in wearing NVGs and a Kevlar-weave stab-vest, carrying a SPAS-12.
And have you noticed that only Europe seems to a problem with Deatheaters? Maybe it’s because Americans have spent the last 200 years shooting deer, playing GTA: Vice City, and keeping an eye out for black helicopters over their compounds. Meanwhile, Brits have been cutting their steaks with spoons. Remember: gun-control means that Voldemort wins. God made wizards and God made muggles, but Samuel Colt made them equal.
Now I know what you’re going to say: “But a wizard could just disarm someone with a gun!” Yeah, well they can also disarm someone with a wand (as they do many times throughout the books/movies). But which is faster: saying a spell or pulling a trigger?
Avada Kedavra, meet Avtomat Kalashnikova.
Imagine Harry out in the woods, wearing his invisibility cloak, carrying a .50bmg Barrett, turning Deatheaters into pink mist, scratching a lightning bolt into his rifle stock for each kill. I don’t think Madam Pomfrey has any spells that can scrape your brains off of the trees and put you back together after something like that. Voldemort’s wand may be 13.5 inches with a Phoenix-feather core, but Harry’s would be 0.50 inches with a tungsten core. Let’s see Voldy wave his at 3,000 feet per second. Better hope you have some Essence of Dittany for that sucking chest wound.
I can see it now…Voldemort roaring with evil laughter and boasting to Harry that he can’t be killed, since he is protected by seven Horcruxes, only to have Harry give a crooked grin, flick his cigarette butt away, and deliver what would easily be the best one-liner in the entire series:
“Well then I guess it’s a good thing my 1911 holds 7+1.”
And that is why Harry Potter should have carried a 1911.

Pros:
* Very customizable playstyle

Cons:

I actually took a 1 year break when I was about 4 hours away from finishing the game, just because I got so tired of the flying fortresses. I got back because I am a completionist at heart and I wanted to see how the story ended.
*The dragonform fighting could definitely had been more developed, considering how much you are supposed to use it. It held a lot of downtime
* In fact, the normal fighting style (I fought as melee) also held a lot of downtime in terms of special moves, making it boring sometimes.

It was fairly entertaining to play this games at times, but not enough that I'd wanna replay it, and now I'm pleased to leave it behind.

Solid 3rd person RPG.  A little older, and it shows, but hardly a pixelated nightmare and it's still entertaining.  Lots of side quests, accomplishments, and so forth.  Helpful maps and (mostly helpful) journal.  Initial character setup is non-binding as you can change your name, appearance, and respec your skills within the game.   Loot is varied and reminiscent of Diablo-style randomization.  You can't craft, yourself, but you can direct others to do so and so customize your armor and weapons and potion loadout.  Quicksave, which I don't normally use, is very convenient here.  The developers made some interesting choices to ensure that you are not an overwhelmingly powerful dragon that can easily obliterate your puny human foes.   In the main game I found that my dragon form missions were not all that difficult.  The expansion, however, made up for that with a much more challenging "escort mission" battle sequence.  Flying as a dragon was...  well, comfortable, but unrealistic.  Hovering and circle-strafing seems almost magical!  :)  There is some platforming required to complete the game, but it's minimal.  Very little to no issues with responsiveness of your character, getting stuck, etc.  No camera control at all, which was occasionally annoying but not really needed; they did a good job with the automatic camera.
Awfully optimized for later Windows versions. I've had countless problems that I am unable to fix. So the game is practically unplayable.

VVVVVV (and that is the only time I will type out the title) is a fun and unique 2d platformer. The main twist is that you can't jump; instead you flip gravity. The game is short but full of collectibles and difficult. To my surprise when playing it, this game is open world, with 3 or 4 dungeons scattered about where the story happens that you can complete in any order, along with collectibles strewn about randomly. The gameplay feels solid, simple yet deceptively difficult and just about everything you can do with its one gameplay mechanic is explored thoroughly in this game.
If I were to list some annoyances, I would state that some of the puzzles seem more like luck then skill to my primate brain, and that the game can be annoying with the extent of which it wants you to prove that you can complete a type of puzzle.
However, in general, these are minor niggles.
Definitely if you are looking for a unique 2d platformer then get this game.

Obviously the better version over Vanilla DS2, vastly improved enemy placement, Items and much better balance patches overall. Plus restocking of items in the merchants early on opens up a lot of paths to explore as opposed to the linear path DS2 fored you to take early on.
It's got so many better concepts and improvements, that sadly didnt get carried over into the next game. Warping between bonfires is okay, but main features of DS2 involves it's slow-paced, methodical and tactical combat that actually punishes the button-mashers. Stamina costs for any actions is so high, but at any point it doesn't feel unfair. Unlike DS or DS3, the stat investment doesn't feel like a waste at any point.
The movement, combat, and dodges feel extremely fluid and natural, and it's convincingly human-like in combat, increasing immersion and actually being relatable. DS2 does a fantastic job of storytelling as usual. It may not have grand and awe-inspiring characters like DS1 or characters that have too dark and grim pasts like DS3, but almost all of DS2 characters are memorable in their own right. Players will forever remember not only the Kingdom of Drangleic, but also the neighbouring kingdoms like the underground city of Shulva, volcanic Iron Keep and ash filled Brume Tower, and perhalps the most memorable of all, the overly-frozen Eleum Loyce. Not just that, this game has so many bautiful locations like Heide's Tower of Flame and Dragon Aerie / Shrine. The characters are not only relatable, but also quite awesome in their own right. Lucatiel, Gilligan, Pate, Craighston and so many other NPCs leave their own marks in your characters story, and so do many bosses like The Last Giant, the Persuer, Old Iron King and King Vendrick. Bosses from DLCs also have their own backstories and are quite humane, namely - Fume Knight and Sir Alonne.
Boss battles is probably where DS2 falls short compared to DS1 and DS3. Almost all the bosses of DS2 are humanoids, wielding some or the other weapon, making them almost the same. They do have a couple of variety in terms of movesets, but that doesn't change too many things. Though famous bosses like Ornstein do make their spectacular return, they are mainly optional. Surprisingly, many best boss battles are optional in this game.
As far as PvP goes, DS2 is way better than DS1 ever was and surprisingly still better than DS3. Almost any build is viable for PvP and that's a balance rarely achieved in any game that's mainly PvE. You can even take your PvE gear into the PvP fights and it can still do good. When it comes down to actual combat, stamina management becomes extremely important. Don't go rolling around 4 times in a row, let alone unleashing a barrage of attacks afterwards. You can barely manage a full combo or rolling twice on the amount of stamina you have in the early game, so stat investment according to your play style becomes a top priority and here's where you start out making your own build. Simply looking up best builds on the internet won't do any good because those players have different play-style than yours. Make your own build. As long as the enemies die and you survive, your build is completely viable.
Lore and story of DS2 is obviously as obscure as possible, given that it's a "DARK SOULS" title. As a player you must piece it together to the best of your imagination and ability. But the lore is surely expanded than Vanilla DS2 and now there are actually multiple endings possible. Plus newly introduced characters do help a lot in shaping the story and actually giving the player a purpose, something that was felt missing in the Vanilla DS2.
Overall, Dark Souls 2 - Scholar of the First Sin is a fantastic game. Don't ever pay attention to other 's judgements over the game. Play it and judge it for yourself. It may be a bad game, but remember it's compared to games like Dark Souls, Bloodborne  and Dark Souls 3 - the games regarded as masterpieces. It's still a worthy Dark Souls games and you should keep in mind if you're thinking about buying it.
The "so-called" worst Dark Souls game is still better than the best games out there.

I feel like this early access launch has been overlooked amongst all the shiny new launches like abslover and the X-com 2 DLC. This game is still obviously in the very early alpha stages, and the developer isn't exactly huge so it's obviously going to take quite some time for this title to be close to "complete" or really even "playable" however what is there is a good start and looks like it will continue in the vein of its predecessor.
Major Cons: 1)This is hardly even a game at this point, there are a few PoIs in the game now and the first sector has all/most of its ports open at least, but there is a lack of a lot of the good mini stories available still.
2) This is an alpha which means... everything that an alpha entails. I think my first time loading I ran off into space in the wrong direction and triggered a bug that made it so none of the ports would show up.... rip me. Expect show stoppers and lots of them. If you feel like being productive make bug reports.
3) The game is obviously still lacking most of its features, I don't even think you can get a better ship at this point and the crew are still mostly placeholder cards.
Pros: 1) If you liked the first game (and I obviously did) This looks like it is going to be more or less the same thing in space. It seems like they are doing a good job of capturing the atmosphere and feeling from sunless sea and transferring it satisfactorily into a space setting.
2) Given most of it is still empty, the map looks huge, it would appear that sunless skies will be taking place over quite a lot larger space than the first. With a lot more area to cover I expect there will be a much larger number of stories to encounter and PoIs to explore than the original.
3) The addition of different factions to support from an early stage in the game as well as numerous changes to ship movement and a change to the number of stats and the way you level, would all seem to indicate that falibetter is still working on improving the games engine. This may prove to be the extent of it, but I expect that either I have missed some things or there will be more to come, in any case it's a good sign that they are trying to do more than just re-skin and re-release their previous game, it would seem they are trying to make some quality improvements on the game.
I would highly recommend picking up this title with a few caveats. Just remember this is an alpha being developed by a small studio, so don't expect huge amounts of new content weekly. Be ready to wait for a year + before this game is "finished"

I'm on a reviewing spree tonight (I just got done with reviewing Long Live The...Queen), and I just had to do this one.
Where to start?
This is...the BEST game that Paradox has EVER made, and I hope they follow the same ideas that they laid out in this one for Hearts of Iron IV when it comes out this year.
This is a wargame, pure and simple, so if you want to do societal stuff and other stuff, GTFO! This is for Jingo Reactionaries only (Vic2 reference).
In this game, you play as a country in the years leading up to, during, and a little after World War II. How well that country does during the war is ENTIRELY UP TO YOU. You can let the AI screw everything up and build ten million escort carriers and stacks of infantry, or you can manage literally everything that would have any influence on the war, from the way your economy works (war economy vs. lassiez faire, consumer goods emphasis vs. heavy industry etc.) to what you actually produce, like tanks, planes and the like.
You can even send spies to other countries to sabotage and assassinate, as well as lower the other countries' national unity to make them more likely to surrender once you start occupying their important territories.
However, the best part of this game is definitely the Research and Development. Oh My God. This is Nerd Heaven.
Ever wanted to see what the Germans could have done with King Tigers in 1941? Go ahead, try it.
Ever wanted to design your own armies, down from the very guns that the regular infantrymen use to the tactics (obviously not completely, you just research the type of doctrines you want them to use) as well as the composition of your armies?
You can have anything from a massive human wave of infantry to a highly efficient combined arms force of tanks, mechanized infantry, self-propelled rocket artillery, engineers and tank destroyers (this happens to be the type of division I always build at the last part of the game).
Once you've built all you're going to build to get the war going, whether it's ships, planes or land units, it's time to get the war going. Sometimes it starts late or early, and you can choose to start it earlier rather than later (especially if you're Germany).
After the boring peace years of accepting/declining trade deal after trade deal and staring at pop ups and sliders, the war part of the game is so amazing it feels like 10 different games are going on all at once. The land combat is flawless. Perfectly realistic and rewarding to the players that put time and effort into preparation and using real life tactics like encirclement, elastic defense, defense in depth and of the course, the most famous one...BLITZKRIEG!
Seeing your small, but highly efficient army wipe out larger forces of dumbstacks of 3 infy and 3 tank is always a joy.
Seeing your airforce that doesn't rely on bombing cities and instead clears the skies for your planes to do extra damage to their land troops is always a joy.
Seeing the navy that you build yourself that has everything it could possibly need, from carriers to battleships and heavy cruisers wipe out massive fleets without even getting scratched is always a joy.
The events in the game are here and there, but all of them are both flavorful and (mostly) realistic.
You can also select who will run your government and your armies, and making sure that you're running a meritocracy is always fun.
This game even has nukes.
10/10
P.S. Did I mention nukes?

Hyperdimension Neptunia Re;Birth 3 is a colorful and fun JRPG filled with lots of cuteness,weirdness and an assortment of many cute animu girls. The odd,yet very interesting thing is that the girls are all based or represent game consoles or game engines.
Pros:
+Very fun story and dialogue between the characters
+ Cute and likeable characters
+4th wall breaking- Adds a certain charm to the game and makes things funnier
+Battling- You will be doing a lot of battles in which you will be doing the same thing over and over again,but because of the pretty animations and cool Special abilities,it doesn't get boring
+Design of characters- All of the characters have some things,like ribbons,hairpins or clothing that clues and hints on the game console or engine they are representing
+Customization- Many accesories and clothing to dress your characters into
+Do a lot of stuff- There is a lot of grinding to be done and for the most part it is well done
+Story is easy to get into- Playing the previous Hyperdimension games is not necessary to understand the story,since it pretty light-hearthed
+Light yuri and ship-teasing
Cons:
-Technical Difficulties- Had to mess a lot with the properties and install some other stuff to get the game to function properly. Sometimes the game stilll crashes for me on one of the two PC's I played this game on.
-Too much to grind- I said that the grinding was well done,but there are some things that require an insane amount of work and time spent to be achieved. Getting all of the endings is and maxing out lily ranks is super tedious.
-Dungeon and enemy recycling- This is a very big game,which uses recycled maps and enemies to a great amount. While I can tolerate the recycling of enemies,since a lot of RPG's and other games do that,I can't tolerate the recycling of the same map for 4+ times.
-Repetition of tropes- This is an anime-like game and expect to see a lot of stuff you saw a million times before (There is the topic of breast sizes,which the characters talk about quite a handful of times. It may be funny the first or second time,but after that it gets a bit ridiculous).
-Not enough yuri - Moar is required
Overall,this game is/was very fun to play and I will spend more time playing it. Hyperdimension is one of the best RPG's I played and it will be a big favorite of mine. If you're a Nepper, that's all you need to know to buy this game.
All the humor is back and all the actually fun characters are back, which makes this as good as Re;Birth 1, but bigger, longer, and with more fanservice (Tip: Buy the extra characters and extra content DLCs, they're really cheap and it's worth it, they all come with their own events per chapter, and you'll have a good laugh).
Character-wise, the Ultradimension CPUs are slightly different from their Hyperdimension counterparts, but I'm confident you'll enjoy the differences (for starters, UD Blanc actually has a personality, and the brief flashes of the love triangle with Plutia and Noire are pure gold), and Plutia is not only a most faithful embodiment of Sega's candid 8bit days (down to the consistent use of lilac and white color scheme), her CPU form is, well, an embodiment of Sega's abusive relationship with its customers on its last days; probably the best waifu-ification job of a gaming company of all the cast.
Gameplay-wise, it's fair I give you a heads-up: As you might have already noticed from Re;Birth 2 (if you had the misfortune of playing it), Neptunia has a habit of compulsive re-using: From dungeons to monsters to music tracks, every game asset from Re,Birth 1 is re-used time and time again. But then, the point of sale of Neptunia games lies with their charismatic characters and hilarious writing, so I didn't find myself bothered by the deja-vu and neither should you.
Speaking of Re;Birth 2, if you had the misfortune of playing it, you'll be glad Compile Heart took feedback to heart and castigated their prior game hilariously.
Just as with Re;Birth 2, the last chapter and true ending require you to do some stuff. Fortunately, Re;Birth 3 is way more forgiving than 2 and the conditions are harder to miss. Just read a guide here on the forums and you're golden.
My only complain: If this game aimed for the early days of the console war... where are all the old discarded consoles?? Where's SNK? Where's Nec? Where's Panasonic? Where are Phillips and Bandai? Where's Mattel? That was one HUGE wasted opportunity. WARNING: COMMENT ON THE GAME's LAST CHAPTER
10/10, would Nep again (and probably will, New Game+ is an option). Can't wait for Hyperdevotion Noire and Action Unleashed to get to Steam.

I'm a long time fan of the Heroes series and figured I'd give VI a try. The game itself is a decent successor. I was skeptical of the reduction of used resources down to only crystal, and the inclusion of area control over mines and dwellings via a central fortification seemed like it would render the series unrecognizable. But I actually ended up enjoying those. Overall, it was pretty fun to play. When it actually allowed me to play.
The things that made me give up on the game and deinstall it out of frustration were the "Always Online" DRM and the user unfriendly UI when it came to setting up games. The always online requirement resulted in frequent disconnections, which meant being kicked out of the game I was playing and losing any progress since the last save. Sure, you can turn the DRM off, but this comes at the cost of being unable to use certain dynasty artifacts which level up as you gather experience and unlock powerful bonuses.
Finally, when I tried to set up a game outside of the campaigns, the game required me to leave the menu to figure out what the various abilities of heroes I wanted to try were. I suppose if you like random games and surprises, that might be your thing. But it wasn't mine.
A decent game ruined by nonsensical and unnecessary DRM and a user-unfriendly UI.

I loved Sunless Sea and Submariner and will likely love Sunless Skies once it has been improved; however, until that time the game is severely lacking development.
The question of (under)development is constellated around the idea of 'early access' -- what is a reasonable expectation for an early access game? Sunless Skies is honest and open about its current, low-content release; many interactions are not available and roughly only 25% of the game world is explorable. Nonetheless, the content that is provided is compelling and the quality of the writing equals the storylets of Sunless Sea.
If the only issue were the reduced content, I would happily rate the game with a positive review.
However, the frequency and number of bugs in the game make it nearly unplayable. I have gone through five captains and four of them were lost (or made to restart) due to in-game bugs. Sometimes ports are displayed on the map but aren't visible or available for interaction in the game at all. The inventory doesn't update properly with the acqusition and use of items, and it sometimes locks the player out of the menus entirely or makes it so enemy ships cannot be scuttled for the rest of the run. The game doesn't always 'pause' while reading and progressing through pages of storylets at port, and enemies can attack and sink you while you turn the page of the narrative.
As it is now, the game resembles an alpha release, where the number and severity of bugs overwhelms any opportunity for consistent play. I look forward to playing a more polished release and am confident that Failbetter will deliver it, but at this moment I cannot recommend that anyone purchase the early access game.

Full Disclosure: I backed this game on Kickstarter.
Now to the review....As FBG have made more or less clear, don't buy this Early Access game if you're expecting a finished product that you'll be able to play and progress in from the get go. This is very much an early build, and is very much still being developed. However, what we see right now is incredibly promising and I'd recommend getting involved at this stage if you'd like to submit feedback and help this game be as fantastic as possible.
The new control mechanics for the locomotives are an intriguing and positive upgrade from what we saw with our vessels in the Unterzee. The scenery that we're currently able to see is vibrant, and the new combat and customization systems are very interesting. I'm personally a huge fan of the backstory you can build for your character as you progress.
There's issues, of course. Graphics can cut in and out, Enemy Ships frequently fail to attack you, and the world still feels rather empty, and bugs.... jesus are thee bugs. However, this is all stuff that we know will be finished up as we progress.
It's an early build, but it's a very promising build, and the full release will undoubtedly be beautiful. Maybe just a tad early for EA, but they were clear about what they were releasing right now and therefore get a Positive Review from me.

After Sunless Sea comes Sunless Skies. I have admired Sunless Sea from afar, seeing it played in videos, but I haven't played it, so I was afraid of missing out on important "story" elements due to not having made my own experiences in Sunless Sea.
This is not the case. Connections are a nice add-on and not an interior machination in this game with it's own world of wonders large enough to stand on its own.
The game is in a very early stage right now, which is questionable for the price. This is pay2betatest, definitely. The game is kind enough to let you know when you are reaching the limit of the current world with little text elements. These things include Interactions with your officers, more varied loot and uses for existing one, more trainrockets to steer and more places to visit.
The controls are a bit stiff for my tasting. The flying locomotive your character is steering behaves more like a turtle on ice skates than a rocket or a train, which takes some getting used to and makes combat tedious due to non-rotating gunnery.
Apart from that the interactions part of the game is responsive and mostly sharp, with the exception of the arrows to change purchasing and selling numbers. Most of the juicy bits are hidden in walls of text full of sidetracking and events unfolding without the need of your presence. The two factions don't put you at the center of their conflict, but welcome your assistance. This creates a compelling narrative where you sometimes end up helping one faction over another only in the third degree.
I would recommend this title for anyone knowing of the dangers of early access and interested in a story-heavy ambitious roleplaying game.

As a Kickstarter backer and fan of Failbetter's other games who eagerly wants this game to improve and succeed, I'm willing to cautiously say that this Early Access game is worth its asking price with caveats.
Most of the gameplay functions to be included in the final product are in a usable condition, and look to improve significantly as updates come. As is, trading, travelling, and fighting come together to form a complete whole (though only over one quarter of the geographic area to be in the complete game).
And, although this is a bit subjective and hard to determine definitely, the story content feels incomplete. Unfortunately, it feels as if there isn't enough of it. While I must admit that I have not completed every quest line, and that this is highly personal, I do feel that only three of the ports have enough writing and content to feel lively and interesting, in comparison to Sunless Sea's ports.
Moreover, I personally think the prose style lacks the spark that separates serviceable writing from great writing. But don't let that be too strong a criticism, because my preferences are weird, inconsistent, and arbitrary anyhow.
The questlines I have finished unfortunately had a lack of fulfilling narrative resolution or climax. They just built up and... stopped. It's not clear if they're intended to be extended as more regions and ports are added to the game.

Hearts of Iron 3 is a very good attempt at WW2 Grand Strategy. Generally, It's well put together, although at times, it can be hurt by the very things which make it so good. Sometimes, the fact that the game has so much depth and is, to be honest, slightly too big for it's own boots is a bit of an issue, although as I said before, it's still a very good game. The learning curve is occasionally brutal, and if your not careful then it can be quite hard to recover from things such as your dissent getting too high, which causes your entire economy to collapse. One main frustration that I have found is that the game does seem to struggle with transporting soldiers, in big numbers, to wherever your theaters of war are. For instance, I was playing as USA during the Pacific War. Because the game provides you with so many pop ups, and there's so much else going on aside from just what your looking at, it quite literally took me 10 minutes to get through all the popups, 90% of which were informing me that the Japanese had repeatedly "won" an air battle that I hadn't even known was taking place. However, once you've taken some time to get used to the game, figure out whatever faction and nation works for you, and work out the strategy that that country needs, then it can be, I feel, one of the most rewarding and generally excellent Grand Strategy games out there.

As much as I REALLY want to recommend the game, I just can't, even after 700 hours in game. The main reason is that about half of those were spent trying to get the game to work, or replaying parts of the game repeatedly because critical crashes wiped out my data. And no, that did not happen in previous iterations of the game, I am still having crashes that wipe my saves as of September 2015 on a fully patched game on a top of the line rig. In short, if the HOI formula is what you are looking for in a grand strategy game, skip this and go for Darkest Hour (and especially for the Kaiserreich mod) or wait until HOI 4 as it looks like they ironed out all of the major flaws this game had.
________________A Few Other Flaws_________________
As if the game's crashing issues weren't enough, there are other key design flaws in the game that make it a less than ideal WW2 Grand Strategy game.
The AI is a big problem in the game, as it makes for a very underwhelming experience. For instance, the Pacific Theater is completely worthless because Japan almost never invades more than a few islands in Indonesia and always focuses on mainland China. The Pacific War can easily be won in 6 months by beelining straight for the Home Islands. The British routinely stack thousands upon thousands of men in Newfoundland and leave the Isles undefended for a very easy Sealion. When it does fight, the AI favors a straight line in direct combat and will never make use of actual Blitzkrieg tactics such as encirclement.
Resources are almost never a factor in the game. Aside from supplies, I have never run out of anything unless I did extremely foolish things. As Germany I never felt the crunch associated with the loss of Swedish Iron that prompted the Invasion of Norway (this isn't even modeled in the game), nor the crippling fuel loss by failing to secure the oilfields of Baku.
The map is not just ridiculous looking (probably the worst projection ever made in any game) it is also difficult to use, especially if you opt for sprites instead of counters. Clicking on airbases is sometimes difficult as they are overshadowed by ground units in many provinces. The provinces are not optimized well either, and it is easy to attempt to click one province and have the game register it as the same province thus killing all of your units' progress.
Diplomacy is not very functional. While it works in theory, they do not work well. As the Axis your conquests will give you extremely bizarre and nonsensical borders that are both hideous looking and nonfunctional. For instance, as Italy I staged an amphibious invasion in Split and pushed for Belgrade while Germany took the rest. After the surrender, my border was a giant green line going straight into what was Yugoslavia surrounded by German territory. This lead to a strange supply situation where, despite the obvious land connection, my supplies were instead routed via the Adriatic and then up to my garrison in Belgarde, causing undue use of transports that were vulnerable to sub attacks.
These are just a few issues that come to mind, but are by no means all of them. Overall I do like the combat compared to other games in the series, but that can't carry the game. I wish Paradox the best as they work on number 4, I am confident they will make it the best one yet. For now though, get Darkest Hour instead of this.

It's not bad, but some of the puzzles are a little obtuse. They make sense in a fashion, but mostly only in hindsight.
Minor spoilers follow:
For example, one puzzle has you carving a blank key using some deductive reasoning off of three other keys. In the end, you end up with a key like no key I've ever seen. Maybe it makes some sense if you have some knowledge of locksmithing?
I mean, why was Tully carrying so many key blanks anyways? Wouldn't it have made more sense if the player were to find some documentation somewhere regarding the lock system first?
The worst puzzles, by far, were the language deciphering puzzles.
I spent years learning Chinese and linguistics, and that's pretty obscene as far as modern languages go. Years spent learning that language, and I still can't 100% reliably look at some new character and figure out its meaning.
That's because one of the first things you learn in linguistics is that languages are arbitrary -- they're completely made-up. Languages have some logic, but mostly only to the people that created them. If they were 100% logical, then nobody would have trouble learning them.
In this game, you're expected to deduce the meaning of some symbols based on a few clues. Even worse, it's a text input puzzle. Some of the symbols had a fairly logical progression to follow, but others took a bit of a stretch.
So what happens? It becomes a typical adventure game puzzle of the player trying to figure out what clues the developer wants you to use. In the end, it just becomes a guessing game, because... well, that makes about as much sense as real-life languages, for better or worse.
What's worse is that Rune, the main character, seems to know the right answer even if you don't. If you know the answer, Rune, give us a hand, eh? Maybe Rune should give up studying polar bears and become a linguist instead?
Unless you really enjoy guessing games, keep a walkthrough on hand.
I guess it's a kind of long-running adventure game joke to have ridiculous puzzles though, so I can't fault it too much. At least there was some attempt to use logic in the puzzles -- no rubber ducks here. For what it's worth, the language thing was a cool idea, even if I wasn't a fan of the execution.
Overall, I mostly enjoyed the game despite its flaws, and most of the other puzzles were sensible enough. The in-game graphics are just fine, as is the interface. Voices are a bit too flat and monotone to be believable, but still serviceable. The 3D cutscenes are kinda goofy, as others have mentioned, but it might be a deliberate homage to older games from the 90s.
I'm not sure if I really felt any of that "slow burn horror" though. The game's pretty short, and there were definitely some tenser moments, but perhaps it was the limitations of the game's engine, animations, and voice acting that hampered it.

Since there have been some negative reviews -- and I'm not sure why -- I thought I should write one as a corrective.  I will attempt to avoid direct spoilers in the review while hopefully still providing enough information to enable purchasers to have a fair chance to decide whether or not to purchase this game.
This story is a mix of a visual novel and an adventure game.  The puzzles are logical but difficult because there are few clues and no ways of bypassing mandatory elements.  However, precisely because the puzzles are logical, they are not impossible.  It isn't a game you can stumble through, or randomly mix elements as in some pure adventure games.  The core of the game is to tell a story, and the puzzles relate to the story, so the reward for success is to progress with the story.  This is not like a mobile HOG adventure, it is not a casual game in that sense.  It is clearly a computer game.
And, despite a mild environmentalist subtext, it is an interesting story.  I would decribe the story as traditional supernatural horror.  It doesn't try to explain away the supernatural elements;  Inuit mythology is involved and the result can feel very Lovecraftian, though this story is not Lovecraftian in the technical sense, since it involves an actual mythos rather than a created one, and the focus isn't some unbeatable cosmic horror from beyond human experience but one which is defined by a kind of human experience.  Bonus points for those who find that some aspects of the story remind them of a story-within-a-story found in Lovecraft's Call of Cthulhu.  The environmentalist subtext I mentioned isn't overdone and, in the end, it twists in a way that makes this anything but a "green fable".
There is no graphic violence, though there is some blood, and violence and death do occur.  This is one mild sex scene and some brief nudity.  There is some bad language but it isn't overdone.  The events in the story relate to an actual known mental disorder peculiar to certain ethnic groups that live in the Arctic and sub-Arctic regions of North America, and that may be more disturbing for some people than others.  Stories that tie into real horrors always have that aspect.  I would consider this a PG-13 game, however, not an R.
I recommend this game.  Particularly if you get it on sale as I did, it is reasonably priced.  It is true that it is short, but given how events proceed in the game this is not unreasonable.  I found the voice acting reasonably good and the characters were in my view believeable for the kinds of characters you find in traditional supernatural horror.  If you are a fan of traditional supernatural horror, adventure games, or more complex and interactive visual novels, you will probably enjoy this game.  If you enjoy something with more action than reflection, if you need your games to have a fast pace and not to require you to think too much, or if you are easily frustrated, this may not be the game for you.  Since the game ends as it does, there is room for a sequel, and while a sequel isn't required, I would be interested in one for this game if it comes available.  Depending on your ability with the puzzles, this game should be about 4-8 hours worth of play.  My suggestion is to take an easy pace and make frequent use of saves to avoid hanging yourself up on plot points.

Warface is an online FPS game, which also features Solo, or Co-Op missions against AI-controlled units.
~Pros:
-Really good graphics and good game physics.
-Variety of game modes, including TDM, FFA, Search and destroy, and other classic ones, including some other ideas.
-An even bigger variety of guns, armor, equipment etc, which can either be unlocked by leveling up, or with money you earn by playing the game.
-Really fun to play with friends!
-It includes ranked games (Ranks range from rank 21 to rank 1 if a remember well), where you also get rewards every time you get promoted.
-You have the option to make, or join a clan.
-You can customise your profile with titles/backgrounds and emblems, which are unlocked by completing in-game challenges, like earning a number of kills with a certain gun, winning different game modes, and many, many more. As an achievement hunter, this is one of the greatest features in my opinion, and im sure that if you are an achievement hunter too, you will love it as well.
-It also includes Steam Achievements.
~Cons:
-Community. The community is decent, there are toxic players, and friendly/funny players as well, but the toxic ones exceed the friendly ones, hence i consider it a con.
-The spawning system is a bit messed up. You guessed it right, there's A LOT of spawn-killing going on in this game.
-I would consider this game to be slightly ''pay-to-win''. There are guns and armor that are superior to most of the ones  you can buy or rent with the money you earn by playing the game. It's not that big of a deal in my opinion, they dont make a huge difference, but still, they can be rather irritating at some points.
-No voice chat.
-There is this thing that when you are dead you can spectate your teammates that are still alive, on a 3rd person camera which allows you to look around. This can be used to give away the enemy's position, and especially in game modes where you have only a sinlge life per round, it can help someone win a 1v6 round without breaking a sweat.
Finally, i would definately recommend this game. It has a lot of features for a free game and it is very well developed. Especially if you team-up with your friends, you'll love this game!

If you're looking for a great game for a low price then look no further. VVVVVV is a platforming masterpiece that is centered around one idea. What if instead of jumping, you flipped gravity so that you're constantly flying from the floor to the ceiling.  While the idea is simple the execution thorough and complex. Every single screen and level is wonderfully expands upon what you can do with this concept. Sometimes you'll be racing through a level with ease, doing nothing but taking in wonderful soundtrack and tight controls. Other times you'll find yourself pushing yourself harder and harder to get past this one screen or get this one trinket, an in game collectable. Either way the fun never stops. I would recommend this game to everyone especially those looking for a challenge.

This review is about sunless skies in its current state, and contains no hopes, dreams, imaginations or illusions. No part of this review is based on planned or proposed future content, it judges entirely on what currently exists and is playable.
I purchased this game on early access within two minutes of release. I'm a longtime fan of Failbetter games, and i intend to follow this closely. This review particularly, I intend to update regularly.
Right now, in its current state, sunless skies is lacking content, but what exists is rich and enthralling, enough that ive spent almost 70 hours on it
Three patches have passed since my last update. I requested a hotfix for bugs, and surprisingly, it was granted. Many of the previous bugs are now solved. The most significant issues still remaining are inadequate support for 1280x1024 resolution, and money not showing in shops
The new Trade system is wonderful, and rich with narrative opportunities. Each port has special bargains that involve interacting with colorful characters and buying cheap goods from them to resell. There are no more consistent traderoutes to grind, but this new opportunity system feels better.
Originally, making money was too difficult. The pendulum has now swung the other way. A bit too far actually, making money through trade is very, very easy, and it kind of overshadows quest rewards. It is enjoyable though
There are some balance issues and rough edges that remain. One of the circus quests can ask you to hunt an impossibly rare monster - so rare you may as well just give up. Thre's no consistent way to gain the items needed to reduce Condition, which can permanantly screw up your captain if you let it rise too high. And carillon requires special soul flaw qualities, with no indication of how to get them. Quite a few questlines still don't adequately value your time spent. The circus, nature reserve and traitor's wood most notably.
The removal of manual saving is a sore spot. It prevents saving and retrying many stories, and can sometimes get you stuck in unwinnable situations - forcing you to pass on the legacy. Manual saving is still possible via backing up some files, so it's a shame the developers felt the need for such draconian restriction
The overworld feels rich and detailed now, thanks to an overhaul in world generation. It is still somewhat lacking in interactivity though, and there's still quite a bit of downtime when travelling. It could really do with an autopilot that could steer for you while you browse the journal. That said, there are many beautiful things to see. All the ports are crazy huge in terms of traveleable area, with lots of pretty surroundings to explore
There's a nice variety of purchaseable trains, although right now they feel poorly balanced. They don't seem to clearly fit roles or specialties, and the power gains over the baseline feel a bit too small. Oddly, there's no engine slot anymore, and no way at all to influence your movespeed. The small number of equipment slots in general is a little concerning for future development, right now there's a clear best equipment setup and its easy enough to buy
Combat is realtime, and based highly on skill and predicting trajectories. It's kind of hard but enjoyable. Rewards from combat vary substantially and aren't too well balanced. Also some monsters - notably the scrive spinster, are far too rare. in my 70 hours of playtime i've only met two. One killed me, the other escaped. I have a circus quest to kill one and it seems impossible
Crewmembers and their associated quests are currently unimplemented
In summary, the major issues:
5:4 aspect ratio support
Shop usability/interface issues
Quest difficulty/reward balancing
Train/equipment Balance
Lack of equipment
New regions
It needs content, but there's enough for now - and in a sufficiently polished state, to recommend it. Despite the issues, sunless skies right now is worth its purchase price. It remains a little rough, and a little unbalanced in many areas, but the writing and atmosphere is brilliant, the world is beautiful, the trade system is engaging, and the combat is pretty good.

As someone that loved Sunless Sea, this definately gives me the warm and fuzzies. The art is absolutely amazing, the music just makes your ears happy and the feeling of being a successor to Sunless Sea is there. That being said, there are some blaring issues that I think you can really attribute to being an early access.
Anyone that hasn't played Sunless Sea for many hours isn't really going to understand much of anything that's going on. It very much immediantly drops you into the deep end and says "sink or swim". The controls for your train(?) feel very loose and sloppy and that leads to combat feeling very chaotic and painful. A little autopilot help getting into and out of ports couldn't hurt anything. I understand that this is in the air, not the water, so it's not going to be exactly the same.
The world, while beautiful, feels very empty. It really does feel like an empty sky with a few interesting points of interest, and I do mean a few. Interacting at ports really gives off a browser flash game kind of vibe. It just doesn't really have that satisfying feeling of progression and exploration and really seems to be more of a CYOA than an in depth story.
Speaking of exploration, the bat uses up your resources?! What? Why are we being punished for exploration? You get to choose between exploring the world and discovering new places or surviving. As a brilliant young girl in a commercial once said, "Por que no los dos?".
When in the ports, buying and selling needs work. As far as I could tell, there's no indication of the amount of money you have and no indication of how much space you have in your hull. I guess you're just expected to remember everything or pay for the costly error of accidentaly buying to much fuel.
TLDR; the world is beautiful, music is great. It feels very much like early access, sloppy and incomplete. But I imagine this will be fixed and I for one am very excited for this new adventure.

I am writing this review based off of the fact that this game in Pre-Alpha (1.1), and I am going to assume most things like the following will be fixed and ironed out in time:
-The ♥♥♥♥♥♥ progression.
-The matchmaking works, but the system itself (Dividing players and maps by level) is odd.
-Some perks are bland, and there are not enough perks.
-No corny story to half care about.
DD2 is a lot like DD1. The best way I can describe this game for DD1 players is this: if you enjoyed playing a damage dealing hero you will love DD2. The removal of directly upgrading stats upon leveling up has made every character more well rounded. So if you focus on tower stats with your gear, you will still be able to make a difference by directly attacking. If you focus on player stats instead of towers, your towers/auras will still be able to do at least something for the team. This allows you to not have to choose a playstyle (towers or personal dps), and instead mix the two, choosing which one you want to be a better than the other. This does not mean that your towers are that much weaker though. A squire with Tower-HP will have barricades twice, if not three times as strong as someone without the necessary points invested in Tower HP. But the game expects you to use this fact that all characters are more well rounded. You cannot play this game like a TD. You have to be active on the field or your towers will be overwhelmed. Take that as a con or a pro, I personally and caught between the two.
What you do get for leveling up is a perk point or two. These are like talents that you dump points into to buff the way you want to play your hero. Currently each hero has 6 perks, 3 focused on towers and 3 focused on the hero. Good system with potential, but right now is not much to freak out about.
A few quick notes to finish this off:
-The game is really pretty.
-Good map design. Overwhelming at times when you first see a new map, but they are open and easy to learn.
-It is really really nice looking.
-It isn't a MOBA.
-New enemy types demand new tower / aura setups to deal with them.
-It is difficult.
-It runs very well for a "pre-alpha". FPS drops almost never happen and loading is fast.

is an action based hack n slash ARPG. It is fairly simple; with three main active skills, three secondary skills (weapon swap), two special abilities and two potions. Everyone plays Victor Vran as a character, so in co-op mode, you're running around with your double. Outfits make you look slightly different, and choose your "class", but class provides a static bonus that can change the way you play in fairly minor ways, rather than any skillset. Instead, customization comes from each weapon having it's own abilities, and you can pick and choose which weapon you use. In fact, you will need to use specific weapons for specific scenarios and have to learn the skillsets of all of them if you want to complete any bonus objectives. There are dozens of different runes (spells), and then there is an interesting collectible card system, which is basically a small way of customizing your powerups depending on what the rest of your build is. So it is definitely a simple system - but not as shallow as it may initially appear, with the ability for two different Victor's to have quite different playstyles. Playing through with a co-op partner, we never ended up with the same build and we both liked different spells and weapons. I enjoyed being "encouraged" to change up my comfort zone to max out stars on an area, but was never forced, since you can complete the entire storyline and every map without doing the bonus objectives.
Bonus objectives add challenge and replayability to every map, some of them are very hard, some are very easy. Each map has secrets, most of which are fairly easy to find, but do require you to pay attention. You can activate different map-wide abilities to up the challenge, such as taking periodic damage, mobs hitting harder, or moving faster, and then challenges are things like finding secrets, not using special powers, not healing, not dying, defeating enemies with a certain weapon, or timed speed runs.
Combat is fluid and responsive, very action-packed with combos and colourful animations and special effects. Weapons are progressive and upgradeable, with epic items having interesting special effects - often centered around being fun and different rather than overpowered, which is nice.
The story itself is a little bit meh and predictable, but the narrator is very well voice acted. Victor himself is quite dark and a wee bit emotional and dramatic, but the narrator is tongue-in-cheek amusing. Dry wit, peppered with pop culture, puns and meme's - many of which made me groan a little. The game definitely panders to those who will get the references, and whilst at times I facepalmed a little at the jokes, most of the time it had me smiling as well, and certainly was a different take on telling a story. I love to experience something unique in storytelling,and this definitely achieved that.
Having completed the main storyline, I don't feel much incentive to go back and 100% the areas right now - but might pick it up in future to play with friends as the co-op is seamless drop in drop out, so it would be very easy to return to with another partner. It took me around 13 hours to complete the main story and every map - but I could see it taking two to three times that if I wanted to five star everything. Overall it is a fairly simple but very fun, well presented game that I thoroughly enjoyed and would be happy to recommend.
