Into the Stars is a game in which you command a city sized spacecraft from one end of a galaxy to the other, carrying the last of the human race to their new home.
The most important task in this game is to manage your resources. Depending on the modules you select for your ship, you will need Hydrogen, Carbon Dioxide and other elements to power your shuttles, life support and more.
Depending on the difficulty you choose, you could face enemy AI in combat anywhere from one or two times to practically constant battles at the higher setting.
The mechanics are well balanced and fun. The game has an old school PC game feel that is very enjoyable and addicting. The balance involved in managing the civilians on board the Ark, stopping at planets to acquire resources and maintaining vital systems is well done. The combat is similar to an old SNES RPG where everything depends on using the right ability at the right time. Every action has a cooldown timer that changes depending on your crew and equipment.
I have mentioned old school PC and SNES games when describing this game. The majority of this game involves completely 2D GUI assets. The combat is done in 3D, but in a way that absolutely feels two dimensional. You spend 90% of your time viewing these GUI assets which are reminiscent of a high quality board game. Playing Into the Stars actually felt very much like playing Pandemic the board game for me. Flying the Ark through space is the only truly 3D part of this game and this is done very well with incredible visuals. The mining mechanics, while not unenjoyable are basically a mini game that is very much like a cell phone app. You control a falling drill through what looks like the periodic table of elements and make sure it crashes into the right squares.
The comic relief in this game is somewhat painful at times. It's not easy to find the right balance of serious gritty gameplay and humor. At times, this game gets it wrong and feels like it's making a joke of the whole idea. Paradoxically, this enhances the old school PC game feeling that I mentioned previously. Which for me is why I am recommending this game. If you like Space Quest, Wing Commander, Pandemic, or just want a game that does something different, unique and fun, this is a great game.
Into The Stars did crash twice while playing. Both times required me to start a command prompt and kill any unresponsive tasks using taskkill. The task manager could not even be accessed during these crashes. If that is a deal breaker for you, do not get this game. I also experienced a bug at one point that left me stranded in space spinning in circles. I had to kill the task and restart at my latest save. Another problem is that you cannot "save and continue". You can only "save and quit". Which means you have to exit to the menu every time you want to save and load the save you just created.
The game has it's faults visually as well. On the bridge of the ship, there are three animated crew members who are all identical. You will be staring at these three crew members the entire game, knowing that they are cloned meshes that do not represent your actual crew members you have selected. You will notice the one closest to you typing on a keyboard. the animation of the hands is strange and the fingers bend and move awkwardly in unnatural directions. There is also a short clip that plays when you land your mining rig that is not the highest quality and looks like an animation from an old Space Quest game. Markers that track NPC ships will always display in the background, showing through whatever GUI is currently open such as the mining mini game or the mining rig landing sequence.
If you've been playing SciFi PC games since the 80s, Add Into the Stars to your wishlist and get it when it goes on sale. Into the Stars brings back something I didn't realize was missing until now and does so with a next gen 3D galaxy in the background. This game is a lot of fun, however, paying $20.00 may leave you dissapointed since the game is prone to crashes and has compatibility issues for some players. This is why I recommend to wait for a sale. I paid $8.99 for this game and certainly got my money's worth.

What a ride! Outlast, not for the faint of heart, a game that puts you at the edge of your seat the whole way through (and occassionally jumping off it). I think this game achieves what others cannot; together with the great visuals and music, create a believable, yet grossly disturbing atmosphere that envelops you, making you yourself the protagonist. The gameplay consists of finding your way around and fleeing from enemies. Don't expect to do any fighting. If I recall correctly, I don't think you hurt a single soul in the game... but that's what makes this IP so unique. This may be one of the few games out there where it takes away the fight from the fight-or-flight concept, making you a victim from the beginning to the very end of the game.
The AI is not bad, considering they do put up quite the scare. Since there is only a handful of enemy types, their behaviour becomes predictable. Death scenes are mediocre and not the spectacular ones you find in Dead Space. They just don't hold up to the intensity built up from your attempted escape.
Maps are pretty linear unfortunately. Scripted events lock doors and unlock others to limit where you can go. Perhaps this is a good thing, as a sandbox-freeroaming asylum is something you don't want to get lost in. (Certain objectives are already hard enough to find...)
Other than these minor shortcomings, the game does brilliantly in everything else. The graphics is good (but some frame rate drops), music sets the scene well, and the atmosphere is simply stunning! If you play this game, I recommend looking around for various rooms and passages, since they might contain batteries and notes. These notes are great as they help lay the background of the story, and the story is pretty good! The campaign is of a healthy length (took me around 6 hours?). From hindsight I think this could've been a bit longer, but towards the end of the story I was asking myself when this will all finally end!
If you are looking for a thrill ride, look no further. This game is worth every penny.

Outlast is an interesting survival-horror game with quick pacing, intense atmosphere, and scares-a-plenty.
The visual design is strong and consistent. The team did an outstanding job of mimicing the sound, look, and feel of a night-vision handicam. This is one of the main hooks of the gameplay, and serves as an interesting mechanic.
The various antagonists you meet in the game are quite interesting, with the most fascinating getting the least screen-time and the least exploration. Trager is one such character that certainly could have used some more material.
The sound design is solid, though the musical chords oftentimes run over what you're trying to hear. The music is the typical "rising violin" chords, sometimes supplemented with eery vocalization. This is used far too often, and becomes an annoyance before long.
The game is fun and tense, but begins to outstay its welcome far before the end. The game feels flat and ultimately, other than the scripted jump-scares, was not terribly scary in the slightest. Much of the lack of fear came from how unabashedly safe and formulaic this game is. The musical cues ruin any pretense of suspense, and the AI's predicatability is laughable. There are so many short-sighted design decisions that were made to up the "OMG SO SCARY BRO" momentary reactions, that the long-term creepy/immersive aspects of the game suffered.
This game is the pinnacle of Michael Bay-style horror. Quick moving, exciting, tense, but ultimately flat and shallow. Once it is over, it is over. Nothing sticks with you past the second you click close.
Good, but safe/shallow. Booga-booga scares get old far before the game ends. Could have used more atmospheric and story-based horror elements to increase immersion and player investment in the story/outcome.

This one disappointed me, and it may be purely personal so take from it what you will.
What i thought we were gonna get was something like FTL via Battlestar Galactica: You'd jump into a system collect what resources you can, deal with what events transpire and then jump out, hopefully before your pursuers jump in. Unfortunately what we get instead is really just this one huge system where you're traveling from place to place (world/asteroid) to world/asteroid) all in what seems to be sublight speeds.
I don't get the time scale of this game, it seems to take no time at all to travel anywhere and yet your resources just boil away into nothing constantly. I could accept it if i was jumping from one system to another that such a thing would come at a cost and a time scale but when you're traveling between locations in (what seems to you to be) real-time and everything just vanishes on you you get a sense of disconnect from your input the game's mechanics. Simply sitting still seems to allow days to vanish in the blink of an eye, and it makes me feel like the timescale has been ramped up just to far in an obvious attempt to make the game more difficult.
Tbh the difficulty i encountered from this game only came from the time and resource management aspect, the enounters are pretty easily handled and when the only challenge comes from a constant time pressure i very quickly found myself not enjoying the experience.
I know i haven't clocked in too much time into this game, but that is representive of how long it took for me to make an assessment of all the game had to offer (excluding any endgame qualities it may have been holding back till later) and decide that i was not enjoying myself.

The game relies heavily on the storytelling and while it does a wonderful job on it, the slow burn and difficulty of the puzzles aren’t for everyone, especially those used to a more action-oriented game. It may not be as scary as other horror games, but it has its moments of tension and manages to build up at an admirable pace. As it stands, if you’re a fan of Victorian or Lovecraftian horror, Alpha Polaris is a beautiful mix of the best of both worlds and for a first game by a small Finnish development team, this is a pretty impressive end result.

KEY NOTE: I have only played the first few levels, and I received this game from a friend for free.
Interstellar Logistics Inc is a quirky indie title made using Unity, a fairly accessible engine with capabilities ranging from hand drawn basic platformer mapping all the way to the scale of Ori and the Blind Forest. It's accessibility allows creatives of all talents to express themselves very uniquely, which is clearly shown through this title.
The concept of the game is very simple: fire the cargo from the cannon to its respective destination, a space station that will portal it to the customer. It plays much like the old flash-based physics launchers from sites like MoFunZone and Miniclip, which makes me glad they've opted to only charge 5 dollars for it. I do not (at this time) know how many levels there are, but I hope there are enough to justify that pricetag for its simplicity.
The cutscenes implemented are very cute and have their own funny takes on corporate politics with some cliche's thrown in here and there, though it almost feels ironic. It is very amateur, but I do not mean that in a bad way in the slightest. It has a special charm that can only come from a one man or very small team working on their first projects, and its naivity keeps it very special in a world filled with over saturated tastes. It's nice to see someone's work come together and actually have its release.
Gameplay, as I mentioned, is much like old physics-launchers. The controls are a little hard-pressed at first, and I did experience a bug where the level and buttons didn't actually load so I was forced to restart the first level, but it was almost immediately graspable. There are some trial and error aspects to the game, but the developer knows that and has a system designed to work around that trial-and-error method. It is a flawed system, and I would like to see a vector indicator or at least some sort of indicator for how strong a planet's gravity is, but even leaving the trial and error method works.
This game does not appear to have any sort of story, which is perfectly fine. It is centered around gameplay and having a short sit-down to play for a few minutes, have some fun, and then pop off to your own other tasks or games. Small titles like Interstellar Logistics prove that a game does not always have to be ridiculously ambitious to be fun.
The game is fairly easy, at least based off the first set of levels. The trial and error system makes it very easy to know where and how fast you should be launching cargo, so I'd love to maybe see more advanced systems in the future, like multiple launches or possible enemies trying to take cargo that you can guide with thrusters. That's a personal suggestion should the developer(s) continue work on it.
TL;DR Interstellar Logistics Inc. is a quirky indie title that will likely make you smile and have fun for at least a few minutes, and it gives an unsatiable want to play through and complete all it's levels.  There are a few bugs (as can be expected with a Unity game) but I'm sure they will be addressed, as well the addition of a quit button on the main menu would be very useful. For five dollars, it'll keep you entertained for at least a short while.

(Lengthy bit where I ♥♥♥♥♥ about Ultima)
The Divinity series is interesting. It's a series that clearly and openly takes cues from the old Ultima series; a series that has the distinction of having some of the best RPG's of all time AND some of the worst. If I were to describe the first Divinity game, Divine Divinity, in a nutshell, it would be "Ultima 8: Pagan, but good." Divinity 2 gets a similar description with regards to the disaster that was Ultima 9: Accension.
It's a large, open world third person action RPG. The game will expect you to do a lot of exploration, talk to a lot of people, face some pretty damn challenging enemies and solve some pretty interesting puzles, like playing a game of riddles with a talking treasure box. The game also does something very well that Ultima 9 failed at miserably; making you feel powerful. In Ultima 9 your character was the Titan of Ether, a god in a sense, and both the story and the game itself didn't even seem to notice. At an early point in Divinity 2 your character becomes a Dragon Knight, which is a really big deal for the setting, and the changes that it inflicts upon your character over the course of the game are pretty substantial, and most importantly, they're actually FELT. Not just within the contet of the game, but the series as a whole. The distinction between your character in Divinity 2 and the other characters you play as over the course of the series, even taking engine differences and personal customization into account, is literally night and day, and it does an excellent job of making you feel like a budding top-tier entity in the world of Rivellon.

Divinity II: Developer's Cut is a highly under appreciated game that does not receive the attention it deserves. This is basically the Collector's Edition of the Game of the Year version of the original game. Simply put, the original game was very buggy and re-released with DLC, a new game engine, and many bug fixes. This improves on that re-release.
To compare it to more well known games, it features combat similar to the Elder Scrolls series, loot and upgrades similar to Diablo series, and (less influential) dialogue chooses from the Mass Effect Series. There is also a tremendous skill tree from which you can mix and match all play styles without restriction (other than your level). Two unique features in the game are mind reading, which usually allows you to find additional loot, and turning into a dragon, which has very smooth controls but less expansive combat.
The story is kind of all over the place, but it needs to be mentioned that the ending of the main game is terrible. I will not spoil it, but the game ends without any kind of big moment. There are, however, some twists and a tone that isn'y present in many games. The included DLC is great in terms of flushing out an entire city with numerous type of unique people, personalities, and quests. However, once again the main story is not consistent with the ending again feeling pretty cheap.
Overall, Divinity II: Developer's Cut is a really good game. There are some bugs with it (I really only experienced 1 bug that didn't let me finish a side quest, but it was corrected in Developer's Mode). It may not blow you away, but it is still a very fun experience that allows a large amount of freedom. The game is a great buy on sale, but still worth the full price if not on sale.

I'm very split about how to review this game, but ultimately I would not recommend it for the time being. The story is very good, the environment is gorgeous, the world and lore feels a lot more developed than a lot of ARPGs, etc., but the game does suffer from a lot of bugs and other issues which seem to get progressively worse the longer you play. The gameplay is decent and has its own flaws and quirks. This game has a huge amount of potential but seems to become more and more unplayable. I really want to play this game more, but it's just too broken. I reached about 30 hours in before the game got to where I just can't progress any further. I've tried using previous save files, but some bugs still get triggered and it's not worth repeating hours of the game to see whether the bugs show up or not. I really want to recommend this game because of how much I enjoyed what I could play, but it's just way too buggy.
I've encountered several bugs which range from annoying to completely game breaking. The longer I play, the worse the frame rate becomes, to the point I have to save and restart the game. The only issue is, the frame rate has gotten permanently slower no matter what settings I try. When I first started the game would be about 60FPS (at the cap) but has fallen to average somewhere between 20-30FPS (sometimes falling as low as 10FPS for no real reason) even in the same areas I got 60FPS before. It doesn't seem to be an issue with my computer, but a bug in the game itself since it only really happens with this game and several other buggy games. Certain cutscenes will also crash the game randomly.
I've also had a bunch of random physics and control bugs which aren't too bad but are extremely annoying. I've managed to clip into things and come close to sequence breaking from issues with the physics. If you land on certain objects (things which you can very easily jump on), you can get stuck to the point of having to reload a save file. Sometimes the game will freak out and the controls lock up or get stuck performing the same action if you perform an action while moving or if you use a spell while attacking. If I use the dragon's flame attack and cast a spell, sometimes the dragon will get stuck attacking with flames, and be unable to move left or right, until I click several times. I've had several other issues during combat where my character gets left unable to move or attack and the camera stays locked until I cast a spell (it isn't a status effect), but I can't figure out exactly what triggers it. The dragon form targeting seems to have broken permanently in my game and will randomly jump between targets on the screen (literally all of them) even without moving (mouse or keyboard) and with stationary enemies being the only thing on screen.
Certain quests have been rendered impossible because of bugs as well. The General Raze fight is impossibly bugged on my game. The first time I played I ended up dying as I opened the menu, then I reloaded from an earlier save and the Walking Armour spawns were broken. If I reload from any previous save and work back to that point, the spawns are still broken. The number of spawn points has doubled (the healing pods spawn them), each spawn point spawns about the same number of things that the whole room did before the bug (could be more, hard to tell since they spawn inside each other), and the delay time dropped to somewhere between 10 and 15 seconds or so per round of spawns. They spawn so fast and with so many that it is quite literally impossible to kill them all. They continue spawning in the same spot past the point the game AI stops trying to control new spawns. The dragon form seems to have broken on my game after resetting my skill points since it doesn't get any increase in health or other stats when my character levels up. I do get random dragon skill points every couple levels for some reason though... Certain battles which require dragon form have glitches with enemies spawning, like the Zagan fight, where the other things keep spawning even when the nest towers are all dead. There are other minor bugs like certain quests where you choose who to give something to or whatever are either both completable or both incompletable depending on the savefile (played through the first 2 hours like 3 times on different files, had the first savefile be completable for both options for an early quest, normal choice the second, and incompletable the third). I've also failed to find certain NPCs which are supposed to be in certain areas, I don't know if these have been because of any kind of bug or just not hitting the right trigger.
The gameplay is overall very fluid and fun, albeit extremely unforgiving. If you level properly and fight very strategically, you can get extremely overleveled very early on. Of course, the game is unforgiving with your stat points so if you plan poorly, you can completely gimp your character until you get a lot more stat points. Combat is pretty easy to follow though it is easy to get overwhelmed depending on what kind of character you play. Certain parts of the combat system can get annoying, like enemies healing faster than you can kill them, no real blocking mechanic, and other minor glitches. The biggest drawback in the gameplay is the fact the difficulty ramps up pretty harshly with very little warning. It's usually possible to take on higher level foes if you're used to playing with Dark Souls style tactics and can lure enemies away. Certain areas are almost impossible without coming back later even if they should be the right level for you to beat. Tricking the enemy into falling off the map or knocking them off doesn't seem to net you experience though, which can ruin certain areas since enemies don't respawn.
The story, lore and environment are what really shine in this game. The story itself is a pretty stereotypical bad guy turned hero type thing, but the way it's told is what makes it actually good and not just a complete cookie cutter type scenario. Lore seems to be mainly divided into books and interactions with people. People in towns don't always have something important to say but usually have something unique. You have NPCs who feel more alive than most RPG NPCs. Towns feel like they're filled with people rather than just reskinned NPCs from the town back. NPCs also feel like they have personalities; their motivation for their actions aren't just good or evil. You also have choices to make that aren't just black and white, good or evil, but hinge on personal judgement. You can try and glean more information from other NPCs but the choices are almost never obviously good or bad, but just different which is a nice change of pace. I don't know how it ends since my game broke too badly to really hope to complete, but it was definitely building up pretty awesomely.

Amazing game, a truly different ARPG experience.
Classic story, classic Van Helsing universe, it's the gameplay that makes it shine:
instead of weapons having almost no effect on the skills of the character (like most ARPG out there), the skills available to use here will depend (almost exclusively) on the type of weapon equipped.
This means that you will swap weapon types often to fit every situation: sometimes it's better to go 1vs1 with a Rapier, sometimes you'll need a good old Hammer to crush those swarming spiders, and sometimes you prefer to stay the hell away using a Lightning Gun.
Also, in this game you can jump and evade by rolling over.
The consequence of those design choices is that it's far more action-packed than any Diablo or Diablo-like game, and that your personal skill actually matters. Yes, you can be "good" at this game, and it will make the difference.
I should mention that I never tried the normal mode, started in hard mode and loved it.

This review is for the final game. I've completed the first Act and have aquired the "hex" system for increasing difficulty (explained below).
As a long time fan of the action RPG (ARPG) I'm always on the lookout for new entries in the genre that Diablo made famous. With some glaring exceptions, the ARPG over the last few years has not disappointed with games like Torchlight 2, The Incredible Adventures of Van Helsing, and Diablo III (post auction house). I'm happy to report that Victor Vran is another excellent example of ARPG done right.
Graphics: Let's start off with the least important (and least impressive) thing in this game. ARPGs rely on visual indicators to tell you what kind of attacks you are being subjected to and they can't clutter the screen with tons of words and icons like a MMO or traditional RPG. Victor Vran's art style is clean and fits the dark tone of the game, it's not visually amazing even with everything cranked to the max, but the information the game and its user interface delivers to the player is streamlined and I never had trouble figuring out what I was looking at or what exactly an attack was.
Sound: Fittingly spooky music, good voice acting (the main character sounds remarkably like Geralt of Rivia), and some really "meta" lines from the narrator (which you will either love or despise, believe me). The weapon attacks sound great from the boom of the shotgun to the weighty thumps of the hammer.
Gameplay: Ok, let's get down to what really counts here. What makes this game worth playing amongst its peers? The action it puts back in ARPG. Victor can run and jump, roll deftly, and leap down from ledges to explore lower areas. The gameplay feels great and the controller interface is nice and smooth without taking away from mouse-driven staples like clicking away frantically at monsters. The skills are weapon based, but the game really encourages you to switch weapons often and doesn't use a skill tree so you're always going to be very efficient with every skill in the game (more or less depending on your other gear synergy, of course). Fans of the genre may lament the lack of a sprawling skill tree with tons of customization options, but this game places skill above build and you will need to actually learn how each skill interacts to clear all the "kill monsters with x weapon" challenges.
Victor can also equip potions and bombs (on cooldowns, no spamming) as well as two magic spells called Demonic Powers. These powers range from beneficial auras to meteors that fall from the sky. The destiny cards you find or get at level-up grant your passives and can be swapped on the fly to mess with your build. There are also outfits that change how your demon power is restored (amongst other bonuses) so there is plenty to tinker with even without the skill tree.
The most interesting thing for me about the gameplay was the challenge system. Each map has a few challenges to complete that really direct your gameplay. The effect of these challenges cannot be understated because their presence keeps the game from feeling repetitive. On one map you may be trying not to take a single hit and on the next you may need to use a weapon that you haven't mastered yet. Past level 12 you pick up "hexes" which are similar to Bastion's gods or Transistor's limiters in that they reward you with greater prizes for suffering buffs to your foes and debuffs to you. The rewards are so amazing that I was tempted to leave them on, and they even have a leveling mechanic of their own to intice completionists.
Victor Vran is a lot of fun. I don't know how long the game will remain fresh without different classes and skill trees, but for the money to time ratio, it's a definite "buy".

Banishing is a relaxing yet challenging settlement building game, with a realistic approach. The game can get boring at times however weirdly it can also get addictive at the same time. It is like watching paint dry but getting addicted to the fumes.
Instead of creating a large settlements like most city building games it is an effort just to build one building whether it is a house or a town hall. Every building requires a lot of resources and when built consumes a lot of resources. During the winter resources get used up more and the game becomes a survival strategy game. This makes managing your resources tricky. It is a realistic approach to building a settlement which makes this game very challenging.
As well as managing the resources you also need to keep an eye on the state of your population. Health, happiness and age are very important in this game. I believe the most popular mistake people make in this game is having an aged population after building a nice little town for them. Very soon they begin to die and you are left with just a few children who are unable to operate your buildings and survive. There is a lot to think about in this game.
The graphics are sharp and detailed, which is important in a game like this, as you will be staring at the same thing for quite some time waiting for your building to build or just staring at the screen waiting for resources to build up for your next objective.
The sound effect are good however the clanging of tools do get annoying after long play and long play is the only option in this game to accomplish anything.
Controls and interface work well and makes the game easy to navigate to the right bit of information you require. As well as the overview windows of your settlement each building has it own window which can be optionally displayed. A mouse is required for most of the controls with minimal keyboard control.
Overall it is a good down to earth realistic approach to building your own settlement. However to achieve anything in this game expect to be playing for hours. There is an option to speed things up which is very useful however that can lead to mistake specially for new players.

Bought this game recently when I tried a demo version at Pax East and loved the concept of the FTL/colony ship manager/space cruiser simulator with rock/paper/sissor combat style and bought a key from them right away. Glad I did before looking at the steam reviews or I wouldn't have bought it and I think it's overall been a positive experience. Think it's on sale now for $12.  I've only gotten a couple hours in, died twice due to resource loss and I think it's a good game with nice graphics and music and love the scope of things they are shoot for with the random events, rewards and feel of managing a bunch of people in a tin can fleeing crazy aliens but there are multiple issues I've have so far.  I'm going to keep playing for a while trying to figure them all out. I'm trying to remain positive but have a couple issues to note I hope will be fixed in future patches.  I like the game enough to review it and recommend with the caveat of stuff like the following to be considered.
1. Waypoints are general direction, not specific. This game lives Adam's phrase "Space is big. You just won't believe how vastly, hugely, mind- bogglingly big it is." When dealing with a 3 dimensional flight, I need to be able to target places more easily so I'm not flying around wasting resources correcting my course.  Also you are only allowed 1 waypoint marker. I'm not a fan of that but the inaccruate part bugs me more.
2. Planetary interactions are difficult to note.  You collect resources and trigger events by getting close to planets then it glows and tells you to interact with it and then you stop and orbit it. Apparently there are some large asteroids in game because some of them don't allow interaction. also if you are too close to the planet and a nearby event, pressing F will warp you back to the planet and you still lose your resources.  It would be useful if all planets you can see in the sector glow, get tagged and named, since many of them look the same from far away and getting turned around and heading back to where you've previously been is annoying.
2. Unclear instructions even with manual regarding upgrading ship. I'm trying to figure out how to improve my ship's capabilities like STORAGE. I need it badly but don't know what I have to earn or what I can do now with inventory.
3. 3rd person camera. Little glitchy, trying to look around using middle mouse button and other buttons doesn't always work and it randomly seems to reset to forward position.
4. Markers(?) there are, so far what I've found, blue and green 2 arrowed markers. Blue is a still event(derlict ship) and green is an alien vessel. but they are small and hard to notice in game. the map doesn't acknowledge them so you need to constantly switch between 1st and 3rd to look for them.  The awesome blue/green space gas wisps while looking nice also makes it hard to know if there is something there.
5. Aliens. I've only been able to interact with 1 so far. But the problem was I had to speed up very quickly and run a intercept course to interact with a ship going in an unknow direction. Now this probably realistic to life but how close I had to be felt aggressive and wasteful.  A communication signal you can send at a certain point to talk would be very useful or a path marker to intercept.
6. Planetary event that are triggered with the people you assign seem to have a random success percentage but haven't done enough to be sure.
7. What is Nitrogen for in game? Also I ran into a engine that instead of helium ran off Biomatter which helped starve my civilians :)
That's what I have for now. I'd give it a B- with a chance for a higher grade with more improvements and tweaks but those things logically take time for developer. I think they have most of the core concepts there and with more critical reviews by people who play it it will be a decent game.

VVVVVV is a fantastic pixel platformer--one of my favorites. The controls are simple (left-right + gravity reverse), and the level/room designs make excellent use of the control setup. Overall the difficulty is moderate; however, there are few spots that are considerably difficult (yet do-able ... if you're willing to spend an angry 15 minutes or so trying and failing in a rapid cycle).
The pixel art gives a consistent, Atari-2600-ish feel throughout (although it is a larger game with smoother controls than anything I ever played on my od Atari--this, of course, is the charm and advantage of retro pixel platformers).
Finally, I really enjoy the soundrack (if it were availabel for purchase, I'd pick it up). It can be repetitious, but it's catchy enough that I don't mind it (and you end up having the option to change the song).
VVVVVV is often on sale, but even at full price ($5), I would consider it money well spent.

Alpha polaris is truly an interesting beast.  It is a point and click "Horror" game that was very underwhelming. Here is why
First off, the controls. Obviously, a point and click game does not have the most intricate system of controls, but none the less there were some problems here. Interacting in the game could be difficult, as when you try to select an item you often will leave a room instead, forcing you to go back and try to select the item again. It can happen four or five times in a row depending on which item and room it is. On top of that, the loading screens in between rooms are ten to twenty seconds on average. This would not be a problem, except for the fact that you have to go through a black loading screen for every room.
Second, the story. I will not go into the actual story too much as I want to avoid spoilers. My main problem is how unsatisfying the resolution was. After suffering through multiple days of loading screens, I was hoping for a lot more than what I got. It's sad, because the buildup was done well, however it seemed to rush the ending for whatever reason. What makes this more sad is that it has a very good story and story idea, but because of the games format it seemed to be held back. The game progresses through in game days, each days end marking a new progression in the story.
And the gameplay, oh the gamplay. It was very good at times, but then you get things that are pointless or difficult, and sometimes both. Like baking dessert. In a horror game. Again, this would not be bad, but the item selection and loading screens make it feel like a chore more than a fun bit of filler. Some of the interactions are hard to figure out and some items hard to find/obtain. I do give it credit for not having the main character pick up things he does not need and just carry them around. This is mostly due to the self contained environment.
My biggest problem though is that it just was not scary. Most of the scares were done in cutscenes, but they are easily (and sometimes accidently) skipped. The ones that were in game didn't have a great effect. And this is because I really wasn't able to connect with any of the characters. I don't even remember most of their names. And because this is not first person horror, I don't even really care about what happens to me. Because this is point and click, you can't even die, at least not as far as I can tell.
Overall, the game was not horrible, but it needs work. Reduced loading screens and an increased ease of item interaction would make it much more enjoyable. Flesh out the story and you might have a great game. If you are looking for an interesting, albiet it frustrating, point and click, I would say check it out. If you want some scares, I don't think this is the game for you. I hope the game gets worked on and improved in the future, but for now, that's all I can say.

I bought this game after thoroughly enjoying Divinity: Original Sin. Do I love this game just as much as Original Sin? Definitely--and I love the developers for maintaining my faith in RPGs.
Some plus points:
+ Questing. Minimal hand holding, quests that were actually fun and required you to be aware of what the characters tell you. There is some freedom of choice on how you want to complete them as well.
+ Exploration. The game rewards you for taking your time to explore the world. There are many secrets hidden around, whether on paper or in a locked cellar--to which the key you'd have to find using hints the game subtly gives you.
+ Wonderfully written dialogues and like able NPCs. I'm someone who enjoys games with characters that can make me feel for them. This game has no companions, but the NPCs are so quirky with their own individual personalities, it more than compensates.
+ Music and voice acting. If you played Original Sin before this game as I did, you might hear some familiar tracks. I didn't mind, they're well done and really help keep you immersed. Voice acting was a joy to listen to.
+ Combat difficulty. Many modern RPGs I've played at normal difficulty are much too easy. I feel that Divinity 2 has done a good job at balancing. I had to make use of obstacles to avoid missile attacks, dodge and heal and not simply button mash mindlessly.
Some negatives:
- Camera angle during combat when using certain skills bugs out a little.
- Not much character customization
- Crafting and Enchanting are done through NPCs, oversimplified in my opinion. I loved the manual crafting system available in Original Sin. (Of course, Original Sin is newer.)
Summary: Recommended for fans of story driven RPGs. Great for players who appreciate immersion and do not like too much hand-holding when it comes to questing and progression. Also great for those who love to explore and find secrets! Lastly, if you do decide to buy and play it, make sure you play the second part (Flames of Vengeance) that comes included in the Director's Cut as well!
Happy Gaming :) I sure had a good time.

Wow! I gave this game the cold shoulder due to the silly title and late Playstation 2-level graphics. Picked it up on sale and can say unequivocably: Huge mistake to not jump on this immediately. This is one of the best, most daring ARPGs ever made, full of original ideas and excellent game design.
The first thing I liked: This is a much more skill-based ARPG than a clickfest. It expects you to work on your facing, dodging, and using terrain and abilities appropriately. The monsters have wind-ups and tells on all their attacks and so positioning and paying attention is important. You will have abundant potions but they are on a LONG cooldown so you can't chug your way through fights. Don't get me wrong - this is not Dark Souls but compared to ARPGs where you basically walk through your skill cooldowns and watch everything die it's a big step up.
Second thing I liked: not a bunch of fake choices. When you have a decision to make, it's a real decision between very different choices. Very rarely are you making weenie choices about +3% extra damage stuff. Your passive skills are collectible Tarot-like cards that drop in the world or are rewarded on level up and they all have very different effects. You slot them up and have a quota that you can't exceed.  You also have a sort of mana bar called Overdrive that fills up in different ways based on the kind of clothes you wear (it makes sense in the game, kinda) and once it is full you can use it to unleash a powerful kind of attack or magical effect (meteors from the sky, a time distortion bubble that slows enemies) - and the different kinds of effects are also cards that drop in the environment.  You also have one alchemy slot that you can fill with either a very offensive or very defensive bonus. There's also a gambling system that makes every item, including the trash drops, potentially valuable.  It's interesting and very, very solid.
Third, no bad skill trees that force me to guess-commit to builds based on a couple levels worth of scaling and some ambiguously-worded tooltips. Your "builds" are based on your weapon choice - the weapons are little skill trees that you carry around. Each weapon has a basic attack + 2 skills on cooldowns, and you get to carry two of them that you can switch between freely. Pick up a new kind of weapon? You can equip it and try it out to check out its skills, and see how it works fo your character. You might want to do Sword + Shotgun for decent single target + crowd control at both ranged and melee. Or you can go completely nuts and do Hammer + Lighting Gun, basically a heavy hitter that carpet-bombs areas and zaps bosses from across the screen when the going gets tough. Or whatever. It's a great system and is IMMENSLY satisying. You get to try all the options, make your own combos and play with a character that you enjoy and made an informed decision about constructing after weighing all the options through actual play.
Fourth, very good scaling difficulty system. The base game is fairly easy but starting around level 9 you can equip Hexes. These are cursed items and you can equip as many as you want, and they make the game harder in specific ways. Monsters start doing more damage, attacking more, and just generally being big PITAs. If you start getting your face wrecked or struggle with a particular boss (respawning resets the boss fights) then turn off a couple of the dang Hexes. Just know in your heart you cheesed it. ;)
Fifth, a challenge system. When you enter a new area you get a list of challenges. There are some pretty basic ones, like "Find all 3 secrets". Ok, sure. But some are really good, like forcing you to rush killing 40 monsters in 60 seconds (basically you're going to wade into a huge melee and start wrecking the place) and real tough ones like killing everything in the level without getting hit, or using the "wrong" tactics to fight certain monsters (fighting big stone golems that hit really hard in melee is tough!) If you manage to beat these challenges you get rewards of items, XP, and gold, and also little gold stars on the game's map. I had a blast with these, they added a nice wrinkle to the game and a reason to come back and replay some of the levels.
Now it's not a perfect game.  As I stated earlier the graphics are not great although they are 100% acceptable and communicate game information clearly (there's also a couple of nice moments). The story is kinda weak and I stopped gving a hoot after a couple hours. For some inexplicable reason they used the voice actor of Geralt of Rivia from the Witcher games for Victor so I feel like I'm playing the adventures of Geralt Van Helsing. And lastly there's no way to get a DPS comparison count on the weapons, so when you've locked in your build and started comparing and tweaking drops it gets a little tedious to have to eyeball 8 swords to figure out which one is the best.
But overall this is a great ARPG and absolutely worth every penny of the full price. I hope you'll give it a chance. I'm glad I did.

Decent little platformer - think Volgarr the Viking but with some roguelite elements (ie different weapons/armors/oils started with and dropped from enemies). Honestly, this game is quite a lot better than I was expecting it to be. There's a surprising amount of creativity on display here, and I was pleasantly surprised by how varied and interesting the different areas are.
With that being said, I'm not going to continue playing. I managed to make it to like the fifth area or so and had an alright time, but I don't really feel like going any further with it. The way the permadeath is handled is a big turn off for me.
I think permadeath is a pretty hard concept to get right, and in this case they haven't quite managed it. If you look at some of the best roguelite games (stuff like The Binding of Isaac or Crypt of the Necrodancer) you'll notice that the permadeath is accompanied with some kind of clear progression system that advances between playthroughs. You'll die a lot, yeah, but at least you die while having made some kind of progress - a new item, character, enemy, etc that you have a chance to use in a future playthrough that helps things feel a bit more varied.
Angvik, on the other hand, feels like a slog to me. Don't get me wrong, the levels are fun, but I really am sick of replaying the first couple of areas at this point - it doesn't feel rewarding to me when I get sent back to the very beginning to replay the same areas I've already played a bunch of times and can clear with relative ease to then die on one of the later sections because I get barely any chance to practice those parts.
In short I think if you're really into platformers (which I am not, mind you) you will probably have some fun with this - it's a really cheap game, pretty challenging, with a surprising amount of creative variance thrown in. If you're alright with the permadeath aspect you will probably find this enjoyable. On the other hand if you're a platforming scrub like me you may want to just give it a pass.
Tentatively "recommending" this because I think if you enjoy the idea of a permadeath platformer you'll probably enjoy this - it's just not my thing.

A solid RPG. I played the entire game -- 67 hours (the Director's Cut includes both the original and the expansion pack, Flames of Vengeance.) I liked the streamlined skill tree -- it made it easy to try new skills. Plus, you don't have to pick a class. I used explosive arrows from the Ranger tree, and a couple skills from the Meele tree (whilrwind, thousand strikes) -- when I wasn't tossing fireballs.
The early game is pretty basic, but after awhile, you get to become a dragon, and that made the game uniquely fun (the dragon never felt as powerful as my human form, however, which seems really counter-intuitive. You also can't wipe out humans on the ground with your flame breath -- that would no doubt be too easy.)
My biggest issue was the vague quest system. There are no markers for the subsequent steps in quests, and what exactly you need to do is not spelled out. A lot of the quests left me scratching my head, wondering where the game wanted me to go next. I have limited play time, and while I like to explore, I don't really enjoy retracing the same steps over and over as I run around the countryside or in town, trying to remember where Bernard or Benedict or Brutus was when I picked up his quest days earlier.  Keeping track of 20+ quests and each one's next steps required more devotion to detail than I was willing to spend. If you find that to be the case, you might do what I did, and print out quest guides from Game Banshee or the various Divinity wikis (or have them in a browser and Alt+TAB, of course). I'm a completist, and didn't want to miss any side quests. BTW, I played Divinity: Original Sin before this one, and that game's questing system was perfect!
My only other complaint was it takes far too long to get your home base -- so managing your inventory is a real pain, unless you spend skill points to be able to lug more stuff, or sell off stuff you're not even sure you need yet.
Other than that , I had a good time and would recommend the game to anyone who likes fantasy RPGs.

This review contains SPOILERS.
Please bear in mind, the following is my opinion alone. You may disagree with my opinion.
This review is for Part One, Ego Draconis.
Divinity II: Developer's Cut is a brilliant game, possibly (with the exception of Skyrim) the best.
Firstly, you have all the classic RPG elements - goblins, evil necromancers, legends and prophecies and stuff, and of course female armour which seems to protect you more the less of it there is. That makes perfect sense, right...?
There's a plot twist early on in the game in which you become a Dragon Knight - a Dragon Slayer blessed with increased power who can turn into a dragon by using the Dragon Stone.
A fecking DRAGON. That fact alone makes the game amazing.
You select a class at the beginning, but you can eventually sort of make your own as the game progresses - you're not entirely stuck into one class like Mage or Necromancer or Warrior or Archer, you can morph them into something new. I call mine a Battle Mage - A Mage/Necromancer who has some Warrior skills.
Of course, as with every game, there are cons. The level design for Sentinel Island is simply appalling - it takes twenty million years to get anywhere and once you get there you have to engage in a short conversation and then travel for another twenty million years to go and have another short conversation and then you travel for another twenty million years to get to the bloody totem to choose the person you want for a specific role.
You have to do that four times.
The switching between Dragon and Human could also be a bit smoother, and so could the movement when you are a Dragon.
There's also the problem with the female armour.
RATINGS
Graphics - 6/10
Gameplay - 8/10
Story Originality - 3/10
The Actual Story - 6/10
Value for Money - 5/10 - Should be more like £10.99 not £12.99
Replayability - 5/10 - You can re-play the game with different classes but eventually it will get boring
Length - 6/10 - I haven't yet finished my current game and I have spent about 6 hours on it
Extra Special Feature - You can become a dragon. Need I say more?
My Final Rating:
8.5/10

Allow me to go on a rave about this game and how its incredibly simple concept is more enjoyable than it should be. This is a mind game where you're given a colored word and given a few seconds decide whether the word is or isn't describing its own color. It's simple as can be and seems like it'd get boring after the first few times, but the game throws more and more mechanics as you go on. There's a progression system in place where you're travelling through every country in the world and after a correct answer you go to another country; answer a certain number of colors correctly you'll move onto the next level, another continent. Visually the game imitates a CRT as you're travelling the world through your television and alongside this is a chill soundtrack that changes for every continent spicing up the game along the way.
Along the way you'll be earning points for every few correct answers and be able to purchase skips, 2x the points, or a second chance. You can also rack up a combo if you answer quickly, the combo system gives you both points and a way to see how well you're doing. As you move on from continent to continent the game will start throwing new mechanics at you such as reversing your input or removing it completely! There are also visual effects that may happen such as flipping the screen or fuzzing it out. These change ups keep the game from becoming too repetitive or easy since you'll have to stop and think about what's going on.
Overall it's a nervewracking adventure around the world that will make you constantly question your decisions and sanity as you forget basic colors because of the risk of losing it all (unless you bought another life). It's a fantastic experience that's great for playing solo or making fun of your friends. It has achievements and is also free! It's easy to understand and well worth taking a glance at.
TL;DR: It's brutal and will make you question if you really learned anything in kindergarten.

What a ride! Outlast, not for the faint of heart, a game that puts you at the edge of your seat the whole way through (and occassionally jumping off it). I think this game achieves what others cannot; together with the great visuals and music, create a believable, yet grossly disturbing atmosphere that envelops you, making you yourself the protagonist. The gameplay consists of finding your way around and fleeing from enemies. Don't expect to do any fighting. If I recall correctly, I don't think you hurt a single soul in the game... but that's what makes this IP so unique. This may be one of the few games out there where it takes away the fight from the fight-or-flight concept, making you a victim from the beginning to the very end of the game.
The AI is not bad, considering they do put up quite the scare. Since there is only a handful of enemy types, their behaviour becomes predictable. Death scenes are mediocre and not the spectacular ones you find in Dead Space. They just don't hold up to the intensity built up from your attempted escape.
Maps are pretty linear unfortunately. Scripted events lock doors and unlock others to limit where you can go. Perhaps this is a good thing, as a sandbox-freeroaming asylum is something you don't want to get lost in. (Certain objectives are already hard enough to find...)
Other than these minor shortcomings, the game does brilliantly in everything else. The graphics is good (but some frame rate drops), music sets the scene well, and the atmosphere is simply stunning! If you play this game, I recommend looking around for various rooms and passages, since they might contain batteries and notes. These notes are great as they help lay the background of the story, and the story is pretty good! The campaign is of a healthy length (took me around 6 hours?). From hindsight I think this could've been a bit longer, but towards the end of the story I was asking myself when this will all finally end!
If you are looking for a thrill ride, look no further. This game is worth every penny.

Outlast is an interesting survival-horror game with quick pacing, intense atmosphere, and scares-a-plenty.
The visual design is strong and consistent. The team did an outstanding job of mimicing the sound, look, and feel of a night-vision handicam. This is one of the main hooks of the gameplay, and serves as an interesting mechanic.
The various antagonists you meet in the game are quite interesting, with the most fascinating getting the least screen-time and the least exploration. Trager is one such character that certainly could have used some more material.
The sound design is solid, though the musical chords oftentimes run over what you're trying to hear. The music is the typical "rising violin" chords, sometimes supplemented with eery vocalization. This is used far too often, and becomes an annoyance before long.
The game is fun and tense, but begins to outstay its welcome far before the end. The game feels flat and ultimately, other than the scripted jump-scares, was not terribly scary in the slightest. Much of the lack of fear came from how unabashedly safe and formulaic this game is. The musical cues ruin any pretense of suspense, and the AI's predicatability is laughable. There are so many short-sighted design decisions that were made to up the "OMG SO SCARY BRO" momentary reactions, that the long-term creepy/immersive aspects of the game suffered.
This game is the pinnacle of Michael Bay-style horror. Quick moving, exciting, tense, but ultimately flat and shallow. Once it is over, it is over. Nothing sticks with you past the second you click close.
Good, but safe/shallow. Booga-booga scares get old far before the game ends. Could have used more atmospheric and story-based horror elements to increase immersion and player investment in the story/outcome.

Click here to read my full review at Mouse N Joypad;
While it lacks the finesse needed in the genre, Alpha Polaris nails several key areas. They took one of nature’s most beautiful anomalies and added a dark presence to it. You’ll truly feel the isolation of living out in the tundra. Unfortunately, the developers seem like they tackled a larger project than they could handle, and the game focuses itself in all of the wrong areas. Characters are boring, most of the action takes place during the day and paranoia is exchanged for rationalism. All of the details feel smooth and polished, but gets lost in its poorly paced and executed storyline. Hardcore fans of PnC adventure games will find things to love, but everyone else will have problems with Alpha Polaris’ missed opportunities.
The game is an impressive undertaking for a small team, but the developers at Turmoil Games have sadly missed the mark. The game has an amazing premise; you’re a biologist named Rune Knudsen, who’s residing in a research center for an oil company in the icy hills of Greenland. You are not Nova, the woman who’s slapped on all of the promotional material. She’s a microbiologist who works for the company and was born into an indigenous tribe native to the icy wilderness. Rune is there to study polar bears and was given a room in the facility to paint the impression that the company cares about the environment. After capturing a sick polar bear, the lead researcher Al returns from an expedition with news. Not only did he find oil in a giant crevasse, but has also found an old cave with piles of bones and ancient symbols on what appears to be the hide of something (or one).
This kicks off the ‘Horror’ aspect of the title. From that night on, the characters all experience waking dreams, where they envision themselves doing awful things to one another, and a looming presence that beckons them. The Northern Lights roll in, causing electrical interference and blocking radio transmissions, leaving our scientists with no outside communication. The next morning, the polar bear escapes, leaving a trail of blood as it runs off into the white unknown.
And this, sadly- is where the game begins to fail. None of the characters show any sign of fear. The facility seems the same, and everyone just goes on about their day, despite everyone having a minor freak out the night before. I know I’ve already made one comparison, but I think bringing up John Carpenter’s The Thing is justified here. In that movie, the unease stemmed from the creature that was terrorizing everyone; but it wasn’t the central fear. It was the people around the situation. The paranoia, mistrust and savagery of the characters were the main grab of that movie. In this game, everyone just continues- brushing everything off. No one accuses anyone of releasing the polar bear, or even acts irrationally. You have to wait until night for anyone to start acting irrational again, which makes the day segments as scary as a sponge cake.
All of the occult stuff is pretty terrifying, and the Lovecraftian nature of this beast looming over the station is an amazing setup. Your characters are isolated, vulnerable in a hostile and unforgiving environment; and yet you spend half of your time in the safe daylight, making deserts. But when it does hit, it hits pretty hard, and I never thought I would think of the Aurora Borealis as being scary, but this game succeeds in making it terrifying. Sadly, everything your character does is reactionary, and you never really feel like you’re making decisions, but rather watching a movie unfold until you can get back to the ‘pleasant side’ of the game.
There’s a romance angle with Nova, who is a far more interesting character than the unfortunately named Rune. She’s the one you spend an eighth of the game preparing a tasty snack for. She has a much more interesting backstory, and I felt would’ve been a much better protagonist than the dull Norwegian bear stalker. I guess they wanted to focus on the ‘environmental themes’, but sadly these messages are as subtle as Birdemic. Too much dialogue is spent on this shoehorned in message when the story is really about an occult. Maybe I didn’t make the connection, but these two ideas don’t blend very well, and I would’ve loved to see a more focused approach to the scary elements of the game.
With it’s pacing problems, the game also feels like it holds your hand, walking you to the next puzzle every time. When the game does hit its conclusion, Alpha Polaris starts to flow. Characters turn on one another as they question their own sanity and actions. This kind of stuff should’ve came in sooner, but better late than never. Once again, sadly, the game’s twist is pretty predictable, and the ending falls very flat. The game leaves you little to maul over or contemplate and didn’t stay with me at all. No amount of darkness and isolation will make this as scary as some of gaming’s greats.
The puzzles are as divided as the crevasse in the game. Some of them are so simple; you’ll do them in your sleep. Some are so difficult; I had to look them up in a walkthrough. Maybe I’m just dumb, but there’s a key puzzle that I doubt I would’ve ever gotten, and even having the answer after an hour’s worth of head scratches, I’m still confused on how it made sense. Sometimes the game will give you a vague idea of what to do next, only to find that a small map has been added to a back wall somewhere between scenes, expecting you to notice. The puzzles that do work are amazing, though; I enjoyed one where you have to use tracking equipment by moving around and triangulating coordinates.
One of the best parts of this game is the audio design. When it comes to horror games, this is a must. Music is free, open source catalogue music, but it’s used perfectly. When the darkness hits, the game’s tone shifts into one of the most terrifying I’ve experienced in a while. Slow and methodical, the subtle use is refreshing in an era of using heavy-handed soundtracks to convey a fright. The voice actors are also top notch and sound like they were directed very well for an indie title. The dialogue could’ve been cringe-worthy, but the actors deliver every line with precise execution.
Cutscenes are well paced, and might be some of the scariest parts of the game. Both because of clever camera movement and direction, but also because they look like they came right out of The Adventure Company’s catalog. To say they look best suited for the early 90’s would be kind. They’re very stiff and lack any polish. The developers seem like they know this however, so they cleverly hid these shortcomings by placing the slower moving moments in darkness, while using fast-paced editing in more lit conditions. Despite the very dated graphics, they do a great job with the tools they had.
At the end of the day, Alpha Polaris does many things right but falls on its face too many times for me to fully recommend. If you’re a fan of games like Syberia or Broken Sword, you’ll probably get some enjoyment out of this one. I mean, in all honesty, adventure games seem like a guilty pleasure for many fans, so what’s one more? If you’re not a fan of the genre, this game won’t change your mind. It’s marred by too many structural problems, and while it hits moments of amazing atmosphere, the rest of the game feels like a slog. I do commend the team for tackling an ambitious and unique experience, and I hope they continue honing their craft because, for a first game, this was a good entry.

I would like to write about this game since I looked the Divinity series with big contempt and this was a shame. The reason was that they always called Divinity an Action, Diablo-Clone RPG and I am a more traditional RPG fun. No matter whatever are the superficial similarities between them, Divinity is very different than Diablo. It is more like an old school RPG, with action gameplay.
The Rivellon lore is quite generic, but the stories and the quests are interesting and unique. A better comparison of the game would be the Gothic series. This means no hand-holders in the quests, Few quest marks, and solving quests through reading books and thinking. There is also a lot of exploration and a lot of hidden things in the game. But let's be more Concrete
Story: At first sight it looks like an effort to cash in the fantasy fans love for dragons. This was also another reason for my initial contempt. Even if this is truth, the Rivellon world is full of shady characters and violence which exists beneath the surface of a fairy-tale-like fantasy. Even if the creatures living in Rivellon are quite generic, nevertheless their actions aren't. The plot can get boring sometimes, but it get's really good after the Hero goes to Aleroth, which is full of interesting quests and a lot of funny characters. For this reason STORY 7/10.
Gameplay: The game has aged a bit and it is obvious. There are some game bugs but they are not gamebreaking, Using the Dragon can also get cumbersome sometime. Riddles can get annoyingly difficult sometimes. but usually in the side quests. There are interesting and immersive battles and a nice addition of a baldur's gate like pause system. Companions AI is cute, but not fantastic. For this reason GAMEPLAY 8/10 (or 9 if you are lenient because of the age of the game)
MUSIC: 10/10(whoever is involved with the Divinity series knows why
VALUE FOR MONEY(I bought this extremely cheap because I liked the Divinity Original Sin in an Anthology offer): 20/10
GRAPHICS: OLD BUT CUTE 8/10
IS IT FUN? HELL YES. OVERALL: 8/10. An well above the average RPG with it's own personality and being able, despite the flaws to keep friends of the genre entertained for about 100 hours.

Hearts of Iron III is a grand strategy game of Paradox Interactive which lets you play ANY nation during the time of World War II. You have to manage your economy and production, politics, diplomacy, espionage, trade and most importantly your armies. Unlike most other Paradox Interactive games the focus of Hearts of Iron obviously lies on building, structuring and leading your armies through the world, either as Axis, Allies, Comintern or as a factionless nation. Play as Germany and conquer Europe, play as the USSR and spread communism, play as Austria and resist Germany, play as Poland and side with Stalin...

What sounds rather known to strategy gamers is actually one of the most in depth and unforgiving game mechanics I've seen, which is responsible for the game's appeal but also for its frustration to new players or people who don't want to spend hours failing to learn the game. You will literally spend hours learning which units are suited for which tasks, terrain and conditions. You will have to learn how to command army theatres, army groups, armies, corps, divisions, fleets and your air force to conduct a succesfull invasion. And the best thing: The tutorials don't explain anything I just mentioned.
However, once you've managed everything this game becomes incredibly fun and satisfying. Conducting a successful invasion with a million men involved, encircling entire armies with your tank divisions and seeing your nation's name reaching from Lissabon to Vladivostok really makes you feel like you just mastered the game.
Definetly recommended to everyone who loves an in depth and difficult grand strategy game or who is simply interested in WWII.

In these, you control large, complex portions of a nation state's resources to wage war, conquer, thrive and, well, win. Hearts of Iron 3 is set in the specific timeframe of the Second World War: You'll be able to choose where and how you start, in any year ranging from 1936 to well into the end of the war. Once you choose your country, its time to dive into the game: Politics, diplomacy, industrial production, army, naval and air force management, intelligence, espionage, economy and everything else you can fathom will be under your control. Atmospheric psychological horror point-and-click adventure with beautiful enviroments, good voice acting, fitting music, likeable characters and for the most part great and imaginative puzzle design. Even have old school text parser type puzzles in it.
Classic point-and-click adventure fans should feel right at home here. Saddly you only have 1280x800 resolution but even still game looks fine. Faces on 3D character models may sometimes look like wax figures but huge hand-drawn portraits in dialogue window are very beautiful indeed. Enviroments are especially beautiful and night sequences with northern lights are breathtaking and eerie.
Perhaps notepad could have used little bit more. I really love natural looking notes, books and magazine cutouts in my adventure games, it just makes it feel so much more lifelike enviroment and luckily what they have feels very authentic, giving great backstory and making it feel like real place where real people might live. I guess it's bit nitpicky thing to say but notes in Syberia series were huge reason why I fell in love with it back in the day as well.
One of my all time favourite point-and-click adventures and really hoping to see new game by Turmoil Games someday.

You know how simulators that you play are basically "click, plant, get food, you're good?" Well, this simulator is nothing like that. There are no monsters. There are no enemies. It is just you against mother nature.
The most scared that I have been while running a simulater happened during this game. I was having a great time. I had 100 citizens, a huge amount of food (over 5000), and I was ready for the upcoming winter. Except, the first time that it snowed was in early Autumn. It killed all of my crops and I didn't have enough firewood to warm the houses. My population dropped to 40 over the course of two years. My town still hasn't recovered.
All in all, the game is great. I haven't come across any bugs or anything that really kills the gameplay. It is pretty slow in the beginning, resources are hard to come by and the winters are unforgiving. But, play for a while, learn how everything works, and soon enough you have a bustling city.
The only thing that could be improved on is the number of structures that we can build. It took me 7 hours to build everything, and I played on 1x speed for 5 of those hours.

OVERVIEW
Refunct is a calm, peaceful first-person platformer about restoring a bland world into a grass wonderland. It was developed and published by Dominique Grieshofer. This world has a dynamic day-night cycle, vibrant colors and a casual experience. With many different platforming structures such as lifts, springs, pipes and wall jumps, the game is easy to learn and fun to play.
PROS
+ Immersive
+ Stunning Visuals
+ Casual
+ Easy To Pickup
+ Achievements
+ Controller Support
+ Steam Trading Cards
+ Cheap
+ Beautiful Soundtrack
CONS
- Short (Estimated Time: 40 minutes to 1 hour)
- No User Created Levels
- Not Much To Do After You Finish
CONCLUSION
With a calming atmosphere and stunning visuals, the whole concept is just soothing. Most people would assume that a game that you could finish in less than an hour is a lack luster game is completely wrong, it is an immersive world with a wonderful soundtrack and an easy to learn game. With no tutorial slowing the game down, you get pushed in head first into this world. That may sound scary to some, but you are eased into the different platforming abilities that it's easy to pick up on.

If you enjoy playing with legos and building things to blow up/destroy this game is worth a look:
The good:
-Graphics are quite good.
-Building is relatively easy and your imagination is pretty much your only limitation.
-User interface is fairly intuitive.
-Newly added mirror feature makes creating creating vehicles much easier.
-Physics system is quite cool.
The Okay:
-Fine tuning vehicles can be a bit rough at times (especially off-roaders).
-Trains are rather quirky but fun to build in spite of it.
- Variety of bricks (though the developers are adding more quite often).
Things I wish they would improve:
-Variety of maps (currently it's rather limited).
-The size of the maps (some can be quite small).
-Physics related to suspension/wheels (quite often my offroaders lose their wheels and/or axles).
-More variety in wheels/axle components.
-More variety in power plants.
-Train connections and wheel to rail physics (often you will lose your wheels on the rails because the train wheels behave like vehicle wheels).
Overall I enjoy this game in given that it is early access there are some limitations which is to be expected early on. The developer seems quite active and often adds new features and content which is nice for an EA game.  If you enjoy building things out of blocks and/or want to hit back up your childhood (in a sense) and build with "legos" to destroy things I would suggest this game.  It has a Multi-Player aspect which might strike your fancy but I've not tested it to really delve into that aspect.
I simply enjoy the sandbox environment, perhaps in time the dev will add an AI element to the game but right now it is very much sandbox about building and destroying things on your own or with your friends.  If you're looking for a "living" environment this game probably won't do it for you.  If you (and your friends) enjoy building whatever comes to mind and destroying it or racing one another's creations I would consider this game.

Refunct is a very refreshing and fluid experience. For such a short game, it was satisfying to play and was definitely worth the 1.50$ spent. It feels like thought and effort went into making it, and that immediately sets it apart the bad apples that comes through Greenlight.
--------------------------------------------------------------
Refunct is a 3D parcour platformer at the same time it has a relaxing, peaceful atmosphere.
Refunct immediately puts you into the game when you start it up.  But that's okay because the game doesn't need to annoy you with any tutorial, the mechanics are easy to learn on your own.
Your objective is to bring this cubey little world back to life, by activating beacons placed around the area. As a result more parts of the world rise out of the water. At the end a little surprise awaits.
--------------------------------------------------------------
Several elements allow you to navigate the area;  elevators and springboards launch you into the air. Slides transport you to unreachable platforms, some need be wall jumped.
There are a few collectibles that challenge you to think about how to reach them, but none of them are frustrating.
Even though the game is short I had an enjoyable playthrough, the mechanics are easy to understand. The game has beautiful minimalist visuals and sountrack lend themselves well to the game and encourage you to explore the neat enviroment. It really is a neat little harmony.

First off this game is in alpha. This means that the game still has issues and isn't feature complete.
TL;DR The game has a few issues but is still quite good.
I have enjoyed this game so far it has many features I enjoy more than Dungeon Defenders 1.
The gathering mana system has greatly improved. Instead of going around to all the chests on the map you just have to interact with one. The other thing about the mana system that is a huge improvement is that you don't lose mana when you pick up a large chunk for example, if you only have space for 5 mana left and you picked up 10 in DD1 you would lose 5 mana in DD2 you gain 5 mana and 5 mana drops on your player. The only issue I have is with dropping mana, you can only drop 10 at a time and there is no drop all mana button.
The sub-core system is fantastic in my opinion. You can easily just build up around your main cores and deal with extra mobs released from destroyed sub-cores or you can spread your defenses out more, take that risk and the payout is a fair bit more exp.
The skill / tower build system now gives you four options instead of five. This is both a pro and a con to me. The fewer skills and fewer towers you have, the more balanced the game will be. This is because it will be that much simpler to balance, but on the other hand that extra skill or extra tower would be nice. The placement system for some of the monk's auras are slightly aggravating. If you build the monk's auras first you can then place traps or towers quite close to then, however if you build traps or towers first then you can't place the auora in the same spot as if you did the order the other way around. On a side note all the towers look quite nice.
Mob pathing seems to be fairly good. I have had a few issues where mobs get stuck behind the spawner wall and have had to use skills to kill them. I get the occasional mob stuck on a wall but as the game development progresses I am finding this to be less and less of an issue. Also flying kobolds are♥♥♥♥♥holes.
The maps are pretty exciting. They look quite nice and every map has it's environmental traps. The environmental traps can also be activated from a player shooting at it which is nice for when you can't get over there in time but there have been a few times when a stray shot has activated it. The maps are also where the game shows being in alpha a little bit. There are still a few ways to get outside of some of the maps, but as of the latest patch (November 21 2014) many of those have been fixed.
Solo play versus group play is a huge difference. The ideal way to play this game is with a party of four. This is due to the item drop system giving higher chances to parties with more people in it.
The game still lacks a trade system that makes me sad, but it looks like it's coming. There are references to it in the config files for the game.
I know there is content missing and I am looking forward to seeing how the game development progresses.
