What's going on here?  I have a personal conflict.  I want to encourage this developer, and be positive due to what this game could be with such ridiculous ease, and I don't want to be a sucker who gives someone too much credit while they take advantage of people.
This game gives me the impression that one of six things happened.
1. A few established people tried to help a friend get started, and he didn't follow through.
2. Someone wants to test minimum development that makes a game (possibly interesting).
3. Someone wants to test the minimum fulfillment that isn't Kickstarter fraud.
4. A new, small team got started, fell out, and quit (would be sad).
5. Someone decided to milk Kickstarter and Steam for easy money without doing any work.
6. A solo dev had something really bad stop their work. (would be sad)
This game has potential that could be so easily realized that I know programmers who could finish it in an afternoon, and I could in a weekend, tops.  The interface simply isn't finished.  It has a mutually contradictory design philosophy (a short board game design that isn't short and is more RPG than board game).  It has had the same crashing and freezing bugs for six months as of this review, apparently (according to a dev post) arising from dependencies on Internet Explorer (weird and alarming).  Saving and loading are not implemented, and it deletes its own saves (player is punished for the design self-contradiction).  Its most interesting feature (away missions with stories) may be completely faked with decisions that do nothing.
It's like a game was just almost made.  Just almost.  It's like someone worked hard enough at a sham that they almost accidentally made something anyway.  Or it's like something really neat was in the works, and then something went terribly wrong.
There may be an explanation.   If at least the interface is finished, the crashes and freezes are fixed, and saving and loading is squared away, then I could write a review that forgives the potentially faked gameplay and incomplete copy of FTL's mechanics.
It's just so close to being a complete little game while falling short with such simple things that I don't know how to react to it.  Did something bad happen to the developer?  Should I feel sympathy?  Should I be encouraging a new indie dev with the guts to get started before learning to program, so maybe they'll finish their work?  Should I feel ripped off?

Okay so, the first thing I want to address is the difficulty of the game. I've noticed a few reviewers talking about the difficulty of the game when it comes to playing solo. I myself enjoyed Dungeon Defenders 1 alone and rarely went online (partly due to the amount of hackers, but that's besides the point), so obviously I would be spending a vast majority of my time on this game offline or with a select group of friends, meaning if the game is much too hard for one person, I wouldn't be playing this game much at all, nor would I like it to be quite frank. However, as you can see, I've given this early access game a thumbs up. Why? Because it's not as hard in single player as others may believe. The entire game actually feels much easier overall compared to the original dungeon defenders.
The mechanic that stands out as to why it's easier, is that
While it's true you still need to be close to the towers to begin the process of repairing or upgrading them, you still move freely, and can carry on fighting enemies or go elsewhere on the map while it's repairing. A little bar on the side of your crosshair shows you the progress of the repair/upgrade so you're still conscious of your tower in the meantime. You can only upgrade or repair one tower at a time, like in the original dungeon defenders, but the fact you can no guard the tower yourself while it's repairing for example, ends up helping you in the longrun. Personally, this is a very welcome change to the core game as it feels like I'm now doing more than just running around the map repairing my towers; It's more of an incentive to fight yourself.
Just to let any readers know, I've tried out all four of the heroes
and had little trouble beating the first few maps with each of them
grinding for experience to level up nor switching between heroes mid-game. I'll admit, the huntress is a little hard to play solo as she uses traps, but as they're so small and use little mana, you can place many of them around before filling out the max tower limit. The Monk is clearly made to play as part of a team seeing as it has health and tower boosts, but he can still very well stand his own ground alongside his defenses. Oddly enough, the Squire and the Apprentice felt very similar, as their first two towers are ranged projectile defenses and barricades. When playing as either of them, by the time I got to the final wave, I could (and did, to prove it to myself) sit back and watch as my towers did all the work. In my opinion, that doesn't make playing as them "easy", it just means I created a defense that was effective on the map.
Moving on, let me just say this game looks so much better than Dungeon Defenders 1. If you've seen the trailers or screenshots, as many of you have, you probably already know that. Besides the overall look and the new animations, it's just the little things I love most in games like this. On the first map, there's a tree with a squirrel on it, and sometimes it'll run down and jump on the fence posts and take a look around before running back up the tree. Things like that make the levels feel more unique and less hollow. Levelling up towers make them look drastically different, such as Squire's level 2 cannon getting taller and aining studs, or Apprentice's level 2 fireball shooter gaining eyes. This means you can know what level your tower is from a distance, just by looking at it, which is great for the fast-play action of this game.
Bottom line, this game takes everything from Dungeon Defenders 1 and improves on it. Gameplay feels smoother/more inviting, the whole game looks better, the enemies are fiercer and even the Tavern is vastly improved (don't get me started on the item upgrader, I love what they've done with it). However... content-wise, there's not a lot of replayability right now besides finding weapons, changing the difficulty of the available maps and switching up characters, and that is literally the only reason why any self-respecting tower-defense fan should not have this game already, in it's current state.
If you're new to the Dungeon defenders franchise, then you should definitely go play the original game and wait for this game to become free-to-play. If you've played the original game, are a fan of the series, and want to help support the developers and watch this sequel go through it's development process, then you should get this game for sure, whether you want to play alone or with others.
If I didn't know any better, I would never have believed this game would be free-to-play, as the quality here is much too good compared to most current games in the field.

Another horror game where you can only run and hide, Outlast doesn't do a whole lot that's new but it stands tall as a strong, polished game that's genuinely scary. Essentially Amnesia-style gameplay in a new setting, it's good-looking, well-designed and doesn't fall prey to many of the pitfalls that remove the horror from supposedly scary games - it knows when to use silence and emptiness to full effect and doesn't ramp up the action as the game progresses, barring the weak ending.
Jump scares come often and can get predictable, and aren't the main strength of the game. It's the organic horror that comes from being stalked or looking for a hiding spot in a panic that really makes it memorable. The sheer gore and disturbing elements, including sexual overtones to the antagonists, are uniquely unnerving though they might alienate some players. Good horror doesn't need to be gruesome, after all.
Fairly short and with a very weak final act much less compelling than the rest of the game, it's not for everyone, but is fine fuel for those who love the unmatched rush of feeling genuinely afraid.

The update is good, really good. It adds variety to your builds, the stages are more fun than ever before and there is at last a sense of progression and an end goal of sorts.
Unfortunately we have this community here that simply thinks that every update released for this game destroyed it (yeah, by this logic the game was destroyed over 5 times).
One of the main complaints is that the game is just too hard now... Is it..? Is it REALLY? I would understand if it was too hard because the mobs glitch or the damage/hp values are too high (I've heard that the berserker orcs just pass through your defenses in Chaos IV, and yes, that needs to be fixed ASAP but it's not the reason why the game is getting so many negative reviews). What I've seen for 6 hours is people placing their weak, redone poison towers that need to be strenghtened by shards expecting that they'll mop the floor with Chaos I+. What they don't understand is that the entirety of endgame is redone and you're supposed to work your way up again.
I tried something like that, got rekt, went back to tavern, checked out all the reworked towers, thought of a strategy and there, while in solo my defense towers barely went below 80% most of the time.
My main complaint is still there though. I went to Chaos II, and you see all those weak scrubs, leeching expecting to be carried by you because your towers are 5x better than theirs. I don't want to build everything for you, If I wanted the whole map I'd play solo. And then when you build they just sit and afk? What the hell is this? And then they dare call this a "team game" and call you a♥♥♥♥♥because you didn't build for them? This is the main reason why we had such losers in endgame that followed the Poison Tower meta and didn't know anything else.
For the first time we're able to play both Hero DPS AND Tower DPS, there is no excuse for you to ask me to build for you, if your gear sucks that means Chaos 2-5 isn't the place for you and you need to grind some more.

Honestly this game should still be in EA, it doesn't feel like a finished game to me, it's just soooo boring. FTL keeps you entranced I can't say the same for this game.
Population alerts:
The population alerts or whatever they call them are just a joke. You literally get one every few minutes then just click a crew member to do it, when I was looking into buying the game that really captured my interest thinking they might flesh it out but nope. You click on the crew member and after like 30 seconds it's over and it just keeps happening again and again and again, it's boring.
Away missions:
The away missions are.... uninteresting, it doesn't really matter which one of the three you pick they're all pretty uninteresting and just go down to a roll of a dice and you can't even influence or take part in any of the decisions like per say in FTL where you could fight off a boarding party that might've happened due to a text choice you made. You just click a mission pick the people with the best stats and send them off roll the dice, repeat over and over and over.
Combat:
Combat is probably the most user involving feature of this game, you match frequencies (colors) to shields/weapons and all that jazz.
City Management:
City management is just... weird, like it was just slapped on to complete a list. My understanding of it you make buildings with resources to get stat buffs to your populations like adding a police station or whatever they call it to increase security in your civilian populations. It's completely bare bones, pretty much like everything in this game.
Conclusion:
I hardly ever write somewhat detailed reviews besides occasional thumbs up and short wording so my friends will know I like it. Into the Stars was an exception, it just disappointed me so much that I had to give my two cents. The whole captain simulation gave me a nerdgasm because I love Star Trek and I love FTL so I bought into the EA after watching a little bit of play throughs on the youtube and thought they'd add some more features... they didn't, not to my standards anyway.
What they added to my knowledge:
- Difficulty modes (good job on that one)
-City Management
- Minor tweaks like allowing you to send away teams down more than once
tl;dr

Ok the proper review. Is this game scary? No. Why? because the game itself while being excellent has a major flaw that completely ruins the element of immersion in the dark and desperate struggle you are meant to have been thrown into.
Outlast uses an excellent setting, clever lighting, sound and other visual effects such as the camera nightvision to create an appropriate atmosphere. You are alone, you are vulnerable and you can not fight these tortured freaks so you have limited options, run, hide or more often both.
But wait, this sounds excellent! And yes it should be!
Sadly, here come the problems, the game is first really generic, the fear element depends totally on the person playing it since it uses jump scares way too much. These are often in very predictable places so you can tell something is going to happen if you press that button or open that door, and others were more annoying than scary. The story is linear and sadly quite boring, it didnt have the depth to pull me in to really care about what was going on. Now avoiding enemies using stealth by hiding in or under things, running away to hide again when spotted, should have been fantastic, but the enemy AI is appalling, the fact I am able to run around ignoring the enemies instead of hiding and sneaking around them is a let down. they also seem to teleport closer to you when activating objectives forcing you to run or hide, only to have them give up, walk away and sometimes disappear entirely from the location, making no sense and leaving you free to walk about unperturbed.
As of writing this I am working on game completion but have abandoned stealth in favour of my new game style called "Crazy kamikaze survival mode" where I just run through hostiles to trigger objectives or pass them by with minimal use of hiding in lockers. If this was MGS i would be in a cardboard box right now :)
This game is visually excellent but sadly let down by linear gameplay, predictability and with terrible, terrible enemy AI that spoils the potential this game had to be a real horror experience. If you want to try it out look for gameplay vids on youtube first or buy the game when its on sale.

Divinity II Ego Draconis and Divinity II Flames of Vengeance comprise Divinity II: Developer's Cut.  The former the original and the latter the expansion.   Depending on how you play the length of the entire production can easily extend past 100 hours.
To start, customization was a disappointment.  Selection is limited to a male and female model with appropriate sound samples from which to pick.  Want to sound like a noble or a soldier then Larian has made that happen.  What Larian did not make happen was allow me to choose an avatar in my chosen image.  The hair and beard and color of both can be chosen but only female or male and human at that.  The game has goblins, why can't the player be a goblin?
Once my disappointment over the customization screen had dissipated it was time to immerse my self in the world of Riverlon.  Much like Risen, the player starts as a complete non descript.  In terms of the game's systems,  the player character might as well have been just expelled from the womb.   Barely any attributes or acquired skills make up your profile and depending on your skill level as a gamer and how you allocate your initial allocation of attribute and skill points, the game can be rather unforgiving.  Some would think challenging forcing a strategic approach, others may be put off.  I thought the former and welcomed the challenge eagerly building my character for the tasks ahead.  Im that context the game starts the player much like Risen or Gothic.
As you progress in Divinity II you become more powerful and the game eventually will become easier.  Late in the base game there was a distinct lack of difficulty balancing by Larian.  While the game continued to be entertaining the lack of eventual difficultly was a serious issue.  While the game has multiple difficulty settings encompassing casual through nightmare, this wasn't enough.  An additional difficulty setting was needed or the skills needed to be toned down though the game does make you feel very powerful from a role playing perspective.
My opinion on difficulty may be more a product of playing as a pure Mage.  I cannot speak for Fighter, Ranger or playing a mixed class.  Also note that for a good portion of the base game the game was extremely challenging even on normal.  Divinity II is not on rails and you are free to explore areas outside of your capabilities.
The player is free to allocate skills to any category.  Categories are broken down by Priest, Mage, Fighter, Ranger and general category to remain unnamed.  Want to be a Battle Mage, a Ranger Priest, no problem.  The elasticity of the skill system allows for such combinations with the only limitation being that the skills are level locked.
Potions, Crafting, Botany and Gemstones all play significant roles.  Potions can be purchased though there is an alchemy system based on plants.  Potions are not limited to health and mana and include attribute based potions as well.  Potions interestingly have many level classifications with the strength of the potion increasing with the level.  Crafting is gem based and like alchemy, the ability to craft is available to every player character.
Divinity II is a 2009 production and looks like it was made in 2009 though in some places the game visually shines but over all the game still looks good.  Voice acting is top notch and professional.  I was disappointed to see the re-use of npc models, a pet peeve of mine, though Larian did an adequate job covering up this sin and the issue didn't appear to be as egregious as Gothic 3.
Combat was simply fun and skills utilized by the player are accessed via the standard 1 through 0 keys or can be reassigned to any key.  All game functions can be re-mapped including quick save.  Combat is as simple as swinging your weapon and using skills.  Blocking is non-existent and points can be put into the passive skills like evade.  The player can also roll out of harms way.
The Developer's Cut allows the player to start the base game and expansion as originally released or in what amounts to a debug mode.  Both versions are save game compatible.   In the debug version, the console is accessed via F11 and you are free to do as you wish.  Want to give yourself an apple ?  You can do that.  Mostly I stayed out of the debug version though I will come clean so to speak and admit to pumping 5 points into encumbrance to satisfy my pack rat tendencies and because I'm no fan of dealing with limited inventories in action rpgs.  It bears to mention that the starting inventory limit can be managed without putting any points into encumbrance.
Divinity II and expansion are worthy for multiple reasons.  Divinity II comprises originality, professional voice acting, great game-play, questing and a great soundtrack (accessible via install).  A top notch action RPG.

The dark of the night was lit up by the bombs dropped by the He-111s and Fw-190s. RAF Hurricanes tried to respond but were met by the escorting Bf-109s. The bombers pounded the remnants of the British army dug in around London and throughout Kent, the motley handful of survivors from a disastrous attempt to turn around the war through a raid on Germany itself via Kiel. Few survived that as the British army was quickly cut off, surrounded and annihilated.
However tonight the bombs weren't the only thing falling from the sky.  Other shapes came down, softly, dangling beneath canopies. Paratroopers of the XXIV Fallschirmjäger Korps commanded by Generalleutnant Student dropped throughout Dover, immediately assaulting the harbour and RAF Hawkinge. Less than half an hour later, with the battle for these key locations ongoing, explosions rocked the coastal defences as three Admiral Hipper class Heavy Cruisers opened fire whilst landing craft flooded into Dover, disgorging thousands of marines in support of the paratrooper drop. The Home Fleet could do nothing to disrupt the landings, with the Channel being completely dominated by the German main fleet consisting of the battleships Bismarck, Tirpitz, Schlesien and Scharnhorst  in support of the gargantuan super-battleship Götz von Berlichingen with an escorting screen of destroyers.
But all of this was a distraction from the real attack. A couple of hours after the initial assault, with all of the British attention on Dover, almost a hundred and fifty miles further west a second wave of paratroopers dropped onto Bournemouth. The British Army had nothing in the area to respond with other than handfuls of local garrison troops and Home Guard units which were quickly overwhelmed by the elite German troops and the harbour taken. With the door now kicked in transport ships steamed into the harbour, disembarking the XVII and XXII Panzerkorps which quickly spread in all directions. The biggest push being, of course, for London and from there to Dover.
On the outskirts of London a brief armour battle broke out with the remanants of the once-proud British armoured divisions fighting tenaciously but hopelessly to prevent the assault from breaking through into the capital itself. Eventually, however, the inevitable happened and as paratroopers stormed the gates of Buckingham Palace the British Army retreated from London. The forces fighting in Dover, now cut off entirely and surrounded, fought ferociously to break through with some limited successes. But for many, completely out of fuel and ammunition, all they could do was surrender. Britain was not yet conquered, but with two supply routes from France forced open and more German divisions arriving every hour the end result was no longer in question, it was just a matter of time.
I sip my coffee in a Parisian cafe as I study the reports from across the Channel. Five long months since the first attack but now the British Isles are almost completely pacified. I sign off on the orders to begin transferring the Panzerarmees under my command back to France and from there to the eastern front, as well as to Student's recommendation to let his two Fallschirmjäger Korps cross the border into Ireland to finish off the last potential threat in the theatre. I lean back in my chair and sigh with fatigue, staring at nothing.
A cough brings me back to my senses. An aide holds out a piece of paper, snapping a salute, a staff car idling behind him. Raising a brow I take the paper and read it. Stalin has finally made his move with an attack near Königsberg. Worse, a large force of the Red Army has also assaulted Finland and the Finns are close to breaking point. My attention is needed in the east, personally.
I stand, carefully settle my cap into place and drop some money on the table and make for the staff car whilst asking the aide to find out the progress on the Panzer VIII Maus super heavy tank project I ordered for development. I think I'm going to need some very big guns for this one...

A very overlooked game, due to problems and a messy release (thanks to the publisher). It also couldn´t hide its obviously intention for a console release, which lead to clunky controls and the typical "port" feeling on the pc (despite the game being released on pc first). However, Larian is a great Dev-studio and seems very dedicated to iron out its mistakes and thanks to the Directors Cut we get a very good open-ish RPG experience.
*Graphics and Sound*
They still look very pretty and while it can´t keep up with time, the art style and overall love for detail creates an environment that holds up, combine this with the fantastic soundtrack and immersion is given in this game. Sometimes bad textures stick out and not much variation in animation, however the game is several years old and its nothing to really sniff at. The soundtrack is really fantastic, i would go so far as saying that it is one of Larians biggest strength in all of their games. Keep the sound up and you won´t be disappointed. The atmosphere created is spot on!
*Technical side*
I have not seen one bug, whatsover. I also had zero crashes on Win7 64x. Obviously thats just my experience and others my vary.
*Gameplay*
I´m pretty sure controler wouldn´t be in issue, this of course can be helped with free 3th pary software, however i choose keyboard+mouse and it worked fine. The combat is action-hotkey oriented, however movement makes a difference (like jumping and then smashing down on enemies). Most of the enemy fire can also be dodged. Still, it does become a bit repetitive after some time, this might be because i choose a melee character to play, but it certainly has also to do with the very odd power curve in the game. While at the beginning one could sometimes struggle in fights and go thru some health potions, you later become a monster and just hack thru enemies. The game also rewards exploration and riddle solving giving you (in my opinion) sometimes overpowerd items as a reward, this making you to powerful early on.
Neverless, combat is sufficiently and the dragon form mixes it up enough. Riddles and hidden treasure were a big surprise, sometimes very hard to catch/see and some required actual thinking. Thats rare.
Respecing is always possible when the player gets his strongehold. There is also crafting in the game, which except from enchanting, i never needed though.
An important thing i need to mention that others pointed out wrongly. Yes it is openworld-ish, but more in the theme of Baldurs Gate (actualy less): you get your main story and you can explore the current zone(s). But not progress further until you finished your main quest in these. So its not like Skyrim and the world is also not that big.
Also it is true that you can´t import your save from the first one...but i think there is an autosave generated because the directors cut treats the game as a whole with the expansion AND you have your gear/money and everything still when you enter the x-pac section of the game.
*Story*
Story is important in a RPG and Divinity 2 does deliver but also lacks depth. The story isn´t bad and there are some twists and turns, especially at the end. Any RPG player however won´t find a lot of surprises, its pretty generic. However, the big strength in Larian games are the side quests, filled with hints, riddles, very funny dialouge and options. They are the main drive force of the game, and to me, are the interesting part. There are also enough of them to keep you playing.
*Overall opinion*
For 20.- its definitely worth the purchase, even better with a deal. Its a good RPG that rewards exploration and thinking, with a not so great combat system but lots of humor and interesting quests in it.
Overall i think the ambition behind it was just bigger than the budget (this reminded me a LOT of Kingdoms of Amalur). Still, i expected much less and was really surprised.

This is a review from someone that played DS2 after having played the first and third in the trilogy.
I had a great time with this game. I don't think it's as satisfying as the other two, but I also think it doesn't deserve a lot of the hate that it gets. I will definitely say that certain parts feel more difficult than they deserve and I can understand someone having an emotional response as a result.
The main differences in gameplay from the other two games are the health regenerating items and the fact that enemies stop respawning after they've been killed twelve or so times. I think these things make the game tolerable considering that the difficulty is considerably higher. All three games have unfair sections, especially the first one, but this second game has some particularly frustrating parts. You can say Git Gud or whatever, but I beat the last two games with very little help and my experience with this one was different.
One thing that pops into this game that isn't common in the other games is an impaling move that certain bosses and regular enemies have. The hit boxes for these are the size of the boss and it makes for some really frustrating gameplay. I could accept it if the hitboxes were that wide and the move did little damage, but it would often be the case that I would be visibly out of the move's range and still lose three quarters of my health. The ogres spattered about the game have a similar hold move that have impossible hitboxes. I also have an issue with NPCs invading when hollow. It creates an annoying challenge when I just wanted to grab an item and use a Homeward Bone or just rest at a bonfire. Thankfully, the extra healing items can mitigate this.
There are other things people complain about, like certain bosses just throwing enemies at you, like the Rat Authority, but I think the mechanics of dealing with groups is pretty good when the hitboxes are fair. There is also the fact that illusory doors have to be touched with the action button instead of hit or rolled through; something that makes likely well wishers to accidentally block doors with their messages. There is no way to open an illusory door when a message is right on it, no way to dismiss it or to just open it regardless. Thankfully they fixed this in the next game.
The last complaint I want to address is about the level design. I like a lot of the levels, but the sense of interconnectivity isn't there. Shortcuts are not quite as important and there is a lot of extra running around that I think could have been made efficient. I spent over sixty hours in this game and I think a lot of that was retreading old areas that didn't have shortcuts.
The optional DLC areas the Frigid Outskirts and Iron Passage were pretty frustrating to defeat without help and were definitely deserving of an extra bonfire. The Cave of the Dead is much shorter than those two, but the bosses were something I could not defeat without people to help aggro one or two of the three enemies. I understand wanting to have an area where co-op could be necessary, but there should be a way to do it alone.
Some positives:
The combat is still good for the most part. Exploration was pretty fun and stressful, as it should be. The first third of the game was really nice, with the interconnectivity staying pretty apparent. Though it disappears a bit later, it was cool to spend a long time in what felt like a small world, only to see more of it appear. This is probably my favorite part about the Souls series; spending twenty hours thinking you've explored the majority of the game then opening a door or pathway into a whole other realm filled with new dungeons.
I do like how there are multiple ways to get through certain areas just in case you hit a difficulty wall. For instance there are multiple ways to get to The Lost Bastille and The Gutter. You can open the door to Winter Shrine either by beating the four big bosses of the early game or earning one million souls. These sorts of things are clever and kept me curious. I also like that certain areas needed to be revisited without a lot of annoyance. For instance, revisiting the Forest of Fallen Giants reminded me that I had certain keys and left a few doors unopened. While the challenge was no longer there, since my character had leveled up quite a bit, it was nice to find new parts of locations I thought I had already explored.
I like how carrying a torch around the Undead Crypt can reveal the shadows of hidden hollows, and how lighting the statue/crypt can give you new enemies to fight in what is admittedly a small area. I like how going into all the memories gives you souls which weaken Vendrick enough that beating him is not a challenge, if you somehow have the urge to defeat an old decrepit hollow who suffered for his people, you heartless ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥.
The story is solid. This game gets a lot of flack for being less oblique about the plot, but I accept it. It fits very well into the middle of the trilogy. I was able to pick up a lot of the plot details without having to spend a lot of time reading item descriptions.
There is plenty of environmental storytelling, for example: the Dragon Shrine is filled with enemies who only attack you if you avoid their champions. The average sized soldiers thump their chests in a sign of respect and will let you pass as long as you defeat the largest one in the area. In Dragon Aerie, you can leave many of the dragons alone, but if you're sloppily running through and smashing the eggs, you'll get murdered as you try to cross a bridge. The game has many responsive moments like this, and it really builds immersion.
DS2 also fixes some thing that I had problems with in DS1. I didn't fall off of a slanted surface that should have held me like I did so often in DS1. Overall the geometry is less of a problem and movement is pretty smooth. There aren't any required and uncomfortable platforming parts, which is great. Fast travel is a very welcome feature from the beginning of the game. Vendors also have an expanding product list as you give them souls and this makes farming for upgrade items much easier and less frustrating. Finding and quickly upgrading weapons is a godsend when a person is trying to find the right moveset and damage per srike combination that is so important to play comfortably.
In closing, while this game has a lot of flaws it still carries the addictive qualities the Souls games are well known for. Worth playing, especially if you're craving more Souls experience. This may be my least favorite, but that still puts it miles above other games. Have fun!

These are some of the good ones that were introduced in 2, but were removed in 3 for Weapon Arts? Which were quite sad to be honest.
Dark Souls 2 doesn't rely a lot on nostalgia from the previous title, and moves further with the series, and not making a lot of references to previous titles unlike 3... Not that I don't have anything against 3, but feels like it was made just for "Fan-service" and was just made just because they could...
Either way, Dark Souls 2: Scholar of the First Sin, is probably the best (for me at least, in addition with being the minority to think so, too...).

Banished is a good concept, and I got some enjoyment out of it, but it's a one-trick-poney, and the trick doesn't go that far. It's a city builder with very little in the way of progression. Only a couple buildings can be upgraded (from wood to stone). The AI is occasionally frustrating. The game is rock hard at the beginning, but if you can survive long enough to get your population under control.... that's it. You expand at a snail's pace, till you're out of room. There's no tech tree, no missions, no customization (beyond where you decide to place the limited number of building types in the game), no unit variety, and no depth. Walk the tightrope between gathering food and building houses.... and you've beaten the game. There's nothing to reach toward beyond survival, and survival is only difficult at the beginning.
It's a city-builder, where the city-building isn't the fun part. I reccomend you wait, and see if there's a content patch or something. There just isn't enough here, to justify a game that's twice the price of Terraria.

Outlast begins with you trying to uncover a mystery in a psychiatric hospital you play as Miles upshur a freelance journalist although not much is told about him and you have barely any knowledge about him through the entire game, Obviously because this is a horror game you don't walk into an asylum filled with puppies and a man asking you if you would like to buy some ice cream no you get dead bodies and crazy people trying to kill you hooray!!!!
Graphics: 8/10 The game is fairly impressive in the graphics department not the most colourful of games but given it is a horror game this is fairly expected most textures are done fairly well and i never thought Outlast was a particurlarly ugly game at any point, The camera is done very well although sometimes when the light is on there are some issues with the brightness but overall fairly impressive, The game does unfortunately suffer from fps drops at various points but the game was fairly smooth most of the time
Sound 7/10 The game's sound effects and music are very atmospheric and done well although one sound that really got on my nerves was the guy breathing like an asthmatic who had just run 50 miles as this got in the way at some crucial points in the game and distracted me from trying to hear where the enemy was
Gameplay Positives: The addition of the camera and it's night vision adds a good element of horror to the game as enemies look particurlarly more menacing in the night vision mode you have to use the night vision light in very dark places at certain points and with the camera zoomed in it makes things more tense, you also have a battery bar that drains when you use the light this makes the player worry about whether to use the light at certain points or not
The ability to hide in various places when trying to evade enemies such as hiding under beds or hiding in a locker is a good idea i have not played many horror games except for resident evil outbreak and amnesia  where you could do something like this but be careful if trying to hide when the enemy is right next to you as you will just be yanked out of your hiding spot
Finding notes and documents scattered throughout to explain some of the story and give you a better understanding also listening to the ramblings of patients is interesting and gives you more of a feel for the game
Gameplay Negatives: Too many batteries the game is littered with batteries everywhere i never once ran out of batteries and had plenty spare this ruins the tension of losing all your batteries and having no light because batteries are so easy to find
This game is repetitive encounter an enemy and hide until you can find a way past, this is scary at the start but after doing the same thing for 10 times you quickly catch on the fear factor disappears rather quickly and the enemy just becomes an annoying obstacle
Boring quests throughout the game where they repeat the same process find and turn on/off valve or find a key surely the developers could have come up with some more interesting ideas than this why not add some puzzles to the game which would challenge the player more and offer something a bit different than the same thing over and over again
The game is way too easy there are no puzzles in the game and once you figure out the enemies pattern it becomes a breeze
Overall Outlast is a game worth playing at least once it looks fairly good offers some good scares and there aren't many horror games out there like this if you can ignore the generic bland story and often repetitive level design than you'll probably have a decent time playing this

This game is overall decent, and seeing as it is free you should definitly try it out, even if you will be leaving in frustration after a few days. Here is my review to help you fully comprehend what you're getting into:
OK, so gameplay-wise this game is decent, most of the starting guns are equal, and the playerbase can be relativily friendly at times... HOWEVER...
-This is one of the slowest games on Steam, the ingame money you earn compared to what you have to spend in repairs is lopsided; and forget actually buying/repairing good weapons and gear (you earn 150-250 dolars per gamemode even with a good score and it costs this and usually more to repair items). Also, guns are unlocked at random in ever increasing XP costs (you earn anywhere from 200-300 per good match) and the decent guns and upgrades are ONLY availible from this (unlock values increasing from 1000 all the way up to 100000+); and many players do not see them because the XP cost to unlock them becomes too high. And heres a note to that one Developer responder: Yes you can rent weapons, but for a unreasonable price that cannot be sustained for any period of time.
-You can get bonus XP and Money from winning a match or Co-Op session once a day, but this is again, only once a day. This is the only time when you actually get the amount of money and XP that is needed to progress, so it has very low replayability value.
-CO-OP is very fun, but again the lack of proper reward amounts and shaky servers make them more of a detriment to your weapon and gear status then it's worth
-There are plenty of people who pay money to get items, and this is definitly a P2W game. Players with money can afford what would otherwise take F2P weeks. These weapons are INSANELY better then yours, and you wll have to get used to campers with 1-shot weapons on almost every server you join. You can also pay money to increase the amount of $ and XP from a match, and these people will get 4-5x what you earn, meaning they unlock everything faster, get things faster, and generally learn how to make your life miserable faster then you can keep up with.
-Matchmaking is crap: you wait 3-5 minutes to be put in an unfairly matched game(withthe aforementioned P2Wers) With no guarantee that the players will stay. In terms of Co-op, this can turn an already hard mission into impossibility as you face off alone against hordes of enemy AI
-The AI in Co-Op does not scale well. After a point the AI doesn't change movement patterns, but just increases damage to a point where a single bullet will down you, and yet they still charge stupidly towards the team, making an odd combination of difficulty that is intensly frustrating. This isnt helped by the fact that the AI also has one of the most accurate firing patterns I have ever seen in a game, it is very rare to see them miss a single shot.
-DEVs do not seem to listen to the community despite the inumerable complaints and suggestions, preferring to put up obvious paywalls rather then keep the meat of their playerbase.
Note: I see that a Dev has taken to responding to reviews and spouting complete and utter falsehoods about gameplay and progression. Dont think we havent noticed your last ditch attempts to save the game.
-DEVs are also inconsiderate, and completly deleted ALL user accounts earlier this year and took a very long time to explain and fix the issue. There is no guarantee they wont do it again. (take this into account before you get too deep)
-DEVs have paid several YouTubers to play this game, and is it just me, or did they all look bored... And was that fake enthusiasm as they sat through the hedious lobby wait times? XD
Ultimately this game is fun, but if you plan to play with the intent to win/succeed you are in for a LOOOOOONG journey of  pain.
EDIT: Did some research, and apparently it costs more ACTUAL MONEY to repair a sniper over time in this game then it does to buy a REAL gun maintenance kit. Wow. I didn't expect this game to be this dissapointing. When you look at the screenshots and videos on the store page, the game looks like a high quality indie game, but actually it is a very very poor quality game. The only high quality thing is when you fly around in space, but even that gets old really fast.
The menus are a complete joke. Is it that hard to make good looking menus? They look extremely amateurish. And that is a big problem, because a huge of part of this game is doing things in menus. That's right. This game is almost a text adventure. But the presentation of that text is extremely boring and dull. A game which does this much much better is FTL. The presentation in that game is so much better even though that is a 2D game and there is also a lot of text based things.
The events you encounter on planets are extremel dull and boring, you don't even need to read the text really. The background pictures for the events are terrible. But the thing is also from a gameplay perspective they are all boring as hell, because there are no interesting rewards.
Getting new modules doesn't really feel like a reward, because you never get to see those modules anyway. The modules are also just texts in menus and better modules don't really have better effects. In FTL on the other you can see your entire ship. When you get a new system you can see how it is installed in a room and you can tell a crew member to man that system. Also when you upgrade the modules it gets new or better abilites. And FTL has tons of modules, it is impossible to have every module in the game in one ship. There are lots of decisions involved what module to choose and what module to upgrade. Into the stars has NOTHING of that.
The ship management is a complete joke. Well there isn't any ship management, you have city management, which is extremely weird. The proportions of the ship feel really weird. Apparently you have 10.000 people in that tiny space back in the ship, which IS tiny, if you compare it to how big the cockpit is.
The city management feels completely unneccessary and feels like they just added it to hide the fact that this game lacks any depths, so they just throw more stuff in it. But the city management itself is also extremely dull and annoying.
The game has lots of small annoying things, like how you always have to wait for that stupid animation when you switch to cockpit view, or how you sometimes have to press the button for free camera multiple times.
The mining mini game is another thing which just feels completely unneccessary.
The combat is the biggest joke of this game however. This is probably the most dull combat system I have ever seen in my life. Their poor attempt to give the combat depth with those weird frequency things is laughable. You just look at your enemy, choose a different color than his shield. That's it. You look at the enemy attack's color, choose the same color for your shields, that's it. Doesn't help that the animations are TERRIBLE, the evade animation made me laugh loudly in my room. And while the design of the player ship is really cool, the enemy ships look really bad and uncreative.
Man there is much about this game I don't like I probably even forgot half of it, and that is a big shame, because from the screenshots and videos this seemed like a really cool game, like a 3D FTL, but FTL is a billion times better. Don't compare this to FTL, just don't. All this game achieved is make me want to play FTL again.
The worst thing is I can't get a refund because I bought this from a third party website, even though this is probably the game that deserves to be refunded the most from all the games I refunded so far.

comparable to Amnesia. If you're looking for a game in that area you'll have to go somewhere else.
Where Amnesia focuses on the terror of the unknown in a slow way, Outlast chooses to approach it differently.
You start out driving up to the mental asylum where you'll be spending the remainder of the game, immediately after that you are thrown into a modified version of hell. Literally speaking.

The game sets out to do one thing, scare you. Your heart will be racing while 'Outlast' delivers an extremely thrilling experience.
The 'first person horror' seems to be trendy at the moment but 'Outlast' is definitely a strong leader of this recent genre.
If you're considering this game, but just not too sure what to expect, please read on...
The story begins with our hero, Miles, a freelance journalist who gets a tip off to investigate an asylum that for many years had closed down but has recently opened up as a charity organisation. Curious to discover whats inside, Miles discovers the place has been over run by various inmates who are victims of scientific experimentation. Stuck inside he must find a way out and along the way he will collect documents to reveal more history, writes notes about what what he witnesses and has a small video camera to record everything inside.
Fear generates well in games where players cannot defend themselves against threats. 'Outlast' mastered the ability to make players feel emotions of anxiety and panic complimented with intense pursuit moments.  Miles cannot attack the dangerous mad men inside the building. They are much stronger and bigger or armed with deadly weapons. This takes away the players ability to defend themselves and will force players to focus on swift decision making, evasion and hiding in various furniture in rooms or even in the pitch darkness. However, Miles' camera features a night vision light which can be used to navigate in the darkness but drains batteries and players will hope to find them scattered throughout the adventure.
The environment is breath takingly stunning and effective in producing an isolated atmosphere. The grain filter provides a realistic look of an old vintage mansion and adds a misty view to where ever you roam. Nightvision is slightly blurred staying true to the realism of a real camera and details provided on body parts are truly gut wrenching. Shine on viscera gives it a fleshy look, well shaped blood stains look remarkably accurate and inmates faces look like actual mutations and burns. Assisting the visuals is a fantastic soundtrack. There isn't too much music in the game, but if you play this game with headphones (I played with a 7.1 surround sound headphones), you will admire the creaking floorboards, footsteps from down the hall, and rain patters on the roof. If you're hiding, music adapts to your surroundings and creates ambience to your current scenario.  You'll hear scratchy violins and deep brass play to intensify the dramatic moment of fear nearby and if you don't feel like screaming, don't worry, Miles was provided with a voice actor who does an amazing job of trying everything he can to breathe quietly while hiding, gasp for air while running and panic while fleeing.
The game is only four hours long, but could be much shorter on a second play through. Many players will be tested on their patience to move from place to place while a threat is randomly patrolling and  bravery will be needed when encountering a few various characters who no doubt will have you cornered if you make that wrong step down the hallway or picked an unlucky hiding spot.
'Outlast' pushes 'first person horror' to a new depth with its graphic atmosphere, chilling enviroment and incredible detail. It's not a game for the casual player as you'll need to be very good at FPS navigation if you expect to do well in this game.  You won't play this game comfortably regardless of how many lights you leave on and the lingering fear of the unknown never leaves you. You will always walk cautiously and quietly hoping to avoid making the slightest sounds but the game is truly unforgettable and suited for dare devils. Try it with headphones, in the dark and home alone but even if you don't do that, it doesn't matter anyway...
You will still be frightened.

VVVVVV takes a simple mechanic (flipping gravity) and explores it to its fullest potential. Between the wonderful music, creative levels, and charming retro art style (more in homage to the C64 than the NES) your first playthrough will be a joy from beginning to end. And if you put down the game there, the experience would be worthwhile.
But the game's real challenge comes from trying to beat the game with the fewest number of deaths. On a casual run, deaths have no real impact, aside from taking you back to your last checkpoint, of which there are plenty. But once you know the layout of the game, the focus changes from exploration to mastery. Personally, I am not one to care about time trials or speedrunning, or any arbitrary reason to replay the same game over and over again, but VVVVVV is a rare exception to that; the gameplay and level design is just so tight, that each playthrough feels as fresh as the last. And the game length is just perfect for the occasional replay to try and improve your death count.
I think this game has something to offer all fans of retro platformers, whether that's exploring the simple world and finding its secrets, trying to collect all of the optional (and often frustratingly hard) trinkets, or replaying the game to improve upon your best score.

TL;DR: Buy it!
Victor Vran is a Baldur's Gate-esque game which can be played via controller or alternatively (Diablo-style) by keyboard.
The game itself is fast paced and throws big hordes of monsters at you.
You can fine-tune your difficulty by activating hexes (penalties) which weaken yourself or strengthen your foes in exchange for better rewards.
The game itself features several different weapon types, each weapon type is tied to a set of 3 skills. Weapons can be swapped mid fight meaning you will have 6 skills to use. Skills can be swapped at any given point of time by changing your primary or secondary weapon in your inventory.
Legendary weapons will eventually upgrade your skills and add bonus effects (E.g. a Rapier will make your dash leave a burning trail).
The story is solid, nothing revolutionary but not bad either. A witty (Van Helsing-style) narrator adds a humorous touch to it.
The game is fun on your own - but even more with friends!
If you don't have any - feel free to ask other players in chat to join you ;)
Treasure Hunter/Bounty quests can be freely shared with other players online!
The only downside is the lack of a multiplayer trading system.
Conclusion:
Victor Vran is an extremely fun Action RPG which will keep you occupied for quite a few hours. it's fun on your own an even more fun with friends!
